11982-eighty-years-and-more-reminiscence:
Elizabeth Cady Stanton's Eighty Years and More, covering 1815 to 1897, opens with an epigraph that woman's place in society marks the level of civilization. Stanton dedicates the volume to Susan B. Anthony, her steadfast friend for half a century, and the contents run from childhood and school days through a long public life.

The reminiscences trace Stanton from a girlhood in a judge's household to the women's rights movement she helped lead, with friendships, campaigns, and family life woven together. Written late in life, the book is both autobiography and argument: a record of what one woman saw change, and what, in her view, still needed changing.
12288-the-witchcraft-delusion-in-colonia:
This study of the witchcraft delusion in colonial Connecticut, 1647 to 1697, draws on court records and grand jury presentments from the Connecticut Historical Society. A presentment from Fairfield charges the widow Mary Staple, Mary Harvey, and Hannah Harvey with suspicion of witchcraft, abominable in the sight of God and man.

The book traces trials, testimony, and acquittals, with depositions like Goodwife Seager account of prayer against Satan and gossip about who was no witch. It shows how fear, neighbor quarrels, and legal forms combined in a small colony. The study is documentary rather than sensational, letting records speak. It remains a key source for New England witchcraft beyond Salem, where fewer died but suspicion ran deep.
22806-the-bronze-hand-1897:
The Bronze Hand is a mystery story dated 1897, built around a woman's voice that arrests its listener with sudden, extraordinary emotion. The catalog record names no author. Tales of the 1890s loved an object with a secret, and a bronze hand promises one: a relic, a clue, or a token from a buried past.

Any words from those lips, the narrator says, would have drawn my attention. But this utterance carried such marked emotion that curiosity woke in me at once, and interest with it. Curiosity is the detective story's true engine, and this one starts it early. The story proceeds in the era's manner: respectable people, a strange inheritance or summons, and the past reaching, literally, into the present.
25622-beatrice-d-este-duchess-of-milan-1:
Julia Cartwright, Mrs. Henry Ady, writes this study of Beatrice d'Este, Duchess of Milan from 1475 to 1497, as a study of the Renaissance, published by Dent in London and Dutton in New York. The first edition came in November 1899, with a sixth in May 1910. Bianca Sforza, painted by Ambrogio de Predis, fronts the book.

Chapters follow the Este house at Ferrara, Lodovico Sforza called Il Moro, wars of Venice and Ferrara, and Isabella d'Este. Beatrice, Duchess of Bari, wins popularity at court in 1491, and Cartwright sets her brief life among artists, courts, and Italian power politics.
25769-more-cargoes-1897:
W. W. Jacobs writes More Cargoes, published by Frederick A. Stokes in 1897, a set of sea tales told in the voice of Thames watermen and sailors. Contents list Smoked Skipper, A Safety Match, A Rash Experiment, The Cabin Passenger, Choice Spirits, and A Disciplinarian.

Brother Hutchins, The Disbursement Sheet, Rule of Three, Pickled Herring, Two of a Trade, An Intervention, and The Grey Parrot follow. Money changers, the lost ship, and smoked skipper close the run. Smoked Skipper opens at Wapping Old Stairs, where a rough man with a new sea chest trots off with a small lad of fourteen in tow.
25874-birds-illustrated-by-color-photogr:
This April 1897 number of Birds Illustrated by Color Photography offers short bird lives told in the birds' own voices, with color plates to match. A woodpecker explains how its sharp bill pecks holes to store acorns, cracks nuts in tree crevices for breakfast, and guards its hoard from thieves while keeping friends by a mild temper. Its nest, dug as hall and living room inside a tree, gets a plain, fond account.

Letters up front praise the new magazine, with the New York schools chief and the head of the National Teachers' Association both signing on as pleased readers. Rail ads for the Monon Route fill the back pages, touting parlor cars and fast trains to the Nashville Centennial and the health resorts. The number aims at homes and schools keen to know birds by sight and habit.
25983-birds-illustrated-by-color-photogr:
The May 1897 number of Birds Illustrated by Color Photography continues the magazine's bird lives in plain words with color plates. Letters up front repeat the praise of the New York schools chief and the teachers' president for the first numbers, calling the magazine beautiful and interesting. Rail ads for the Monon Route fill the back pages, promising parlor cars by day and palace sleeping cars by night.

Bird notes describe nests with care. One nest, built in a stump cavity three feet high, took the stump's irregular shape and was packed with leaves, grass bits, stems, moss, and decayed wood, lined with hair. Another nest sat in a mill brace hole, where watchers saw birds carry in materials unafraid. The number teaches young readers to know birds by home and habit.
30081-the-arena-volume-18-no-92-july-189:
Volume 18 of The Arena, July to December 1897, edited by John Clark Ridpath and published in Boston, gathers a half year of reform debate. Henry Clews and Ridpath open on the citadel of the money power and the true inwardness of Wall Street. A symposium on honest money hears William Jennings Bryan, Wharton Barker, and others. Credit and prices, the American and French constitutions, and Japan's new civil code follow.

Later pages add John Ruskin as a type of twentieth-century manhood, the single tax in operation, natural and social selection, psychic forces, and an industrial fable, with poems closing the run. The volume shows a progressive monthly at full stretch, arguing money, morals, and science in one place. Readers of Gilded Age reform will find its hopes and quarrels intact.
30103-birds-illustrated-by-color-photogr:
Birds Illustrated by Color Photography, volume one, number three, is dated March 1897. The issue opens with a letter from the State of New York's Department of Public Instruction, dated Albany, December 26, 1896. It thanks the publisher for the first publication of Birds and asks to be entered as a regular subscriber. The superintendent calls it one of the most beautiful and interesting publications yet attempted in this direction, and wishes the handsome little magazine abundant prosperity.

 The bird writing itself speaks in the bluebird's own voice: when it sings, buds and flowers whisper that springtime is coming. The bluebird nests in a box the farmer puts up near his barn, or in a hole in an old tree. It raises four or five little ones before going south again when winter breathes.
30523-birds-illustrated-by-color-photogr:
Birds, a monthly serial illustrated by color photography, volume two, copyrighted in Chicago in 1897, aims to promote knowledge of bird life. Its introduction describes a series in accurate colored portraiture and popular, juvenile biographical text, covering a considerable portion of common North American birds.

Many more interesting specimens from other countries also appear, in a form the editors claim superior to rival bird publications and far cheaper. Monthly parts won a warm public reception for volume one, for which the editors give grateful thanks. The serial suits families, schools, and young bird lovers who learn best from pictures and plain text.
30666-birds-illustrated-by-color-photogr:
Birds Illustrated by Color Photography, volume one, number six, for June 1897, closes the first half year of the serial, with volume one, January to June, now ready as a book. The bound volume runs two hundred twenty-four pages, with sixty full-page illustrations made by the new process of color photography.

Suited to old and young, in a neat, durable binding, it sells through newsdealers and booksellers and by subscription. Cloth costs one dollar twenty-five, half morocco one seventy-five, and morocco two twenty-five, with mail orders to Nature Study Publishing in Chicago. Three annual subscriptions earn a cloth binding, four a half morocco, and five a full morocco.
33646-the-arena-volume-18-no-93-august-1:
The Arena for August 1897, volume eighteen, number ninety-three, opens with David Starr Jordan, president of Leland Stanford Junior University, on evolution. He asks what it is and what it is not. Jordan, addressing the Starr King Fraternity of Oakland, observes that the word evolution is used by many in many senses, and often in no sense at all. Some dread it as the downfall of religion and social stability, while others hail it as if progress were secured by uttering the name.

Further articles in the issue include John Clark Ridpath on the segregation and permanent isolation of criminals, Norman Robinson, Emily Dickey Beery, Stinson Jarvis, Miles Menander Dawson, and Coates Kinney. The Arena was a leading progressive monthly, and this number shows its range: science, reform, economics, and literature in one lively volume.
40531-a-century-in-the-comptroller-s-off:
A Century in the Comptroller's Office is a record of that office in the State of New York from 1797 to 1897. It was written by James A. Roberts, the Comptroller of the day. The book came out at Albany in 1897 from James B. Lyon, printer, with a picture of State Hall. A note states that old and varied spellings have been kept as printed, as far as could be done.

The book opens with a date. On 17 February 1897 fell the one hundredth year of the setting up of the office of Comptroller of the State of New York. The man who then held the office trusts, he says, that no charge of vain pride will be laid on him for what follows. He has gathered and set down, in honor of that hundredth birthday, the chief facts that bear on the office and its past.
arxiv-2412-05097:
Haowu Duan, Alex Kovner, and Michael Lublinsky extend a quantum framework for how particle distributions inside fast hadrons change with energy. In their first paper, the team borrowed the Born-Oppenheimer idea to describe a speeding hadron's wave function. Here they use it to track two distribution types: one spread over sideways momentum, one integrated.

Each distribution obeys an evolution equation with a straight term and a curved one. For the sideways-spread type, the straight term reproduces a classic equation, with a physical link between its two resolution scales. For the integrated type, it recovers the standard splitting equation at moderate momentum shares. At tiny shares, extra gluon splittings bend that equation. The curved terms share one origin: stimulated emission, where gluons prefer already busy states. That effect mimics shadowing in the net correction.
arxiv-2412-05697:
Orizon Ferreira, Boris Mordukhovich, Wilkreffy Santos, and João Souza wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-four on a math method for hard optimization problems. The problems involve functions written as the difference of two curved functions. A known method gains speed by taking a boosted step, but it can fail when the functions have kinks and no smooth slope.

The authors propose a version that allows careful inexactness in two places. The inner subproblem is solved only roughly, within a set error limit, and the step size search need not improve the value at every step. They prove the method is well defined and that its limit points are true critical points. Tests show it beating two rival methods in practice.
arxiv-2412-05997:
Vittorio D'Esposito and co-authors take first steps toward a doubly quantum mechanics. Their paper appeared in 2024. In ordinary quantum theory, space and measuring devices are classical backdrops. Quantum gravity hints that geometry itself may be quantum. The authors build a version of quantum mechanics where the shapes of systems, devices, and reference frames are quantum states too.

They work out spin measurements by replacing the rotation group with its quantum version. In the new setup, probability itself becomes an operator, with non-classical traits. For near-classical geometry states, measuring still works, but a built-in blur appears. Observers swapping quantum bits to align their frames can never align perfectly, even with endless bits. The blur is a concrete, testable difference from the standard theory.
arxiv-2412-07697:
Young stars sometimes flare violently as they gulp gas from their disks, and Siwak and a large team of co-authors report a fresh case, Gaia20bdk, in the Sharpless 2-301 star-forming region. The outburst began in twenty eighteen. Old survey data pinned down the quiet star: about two point seven times the Sun's mass, at three point three kiloparsecs, still wrapped in its birth material.

New light and spectrum records show the classic marks of an FUor, the best-known class of such eruptions. Disk modeling puts the flare's glow at one to two hundred times the Sun's output, fed by a heavy inflow of gas. The team calls for continued watching to track the flicker and learn what drives it.
arxiv-2412-08997:
William Erickson and Nicholas Jones classify a family of number sets in a 2024 mathematics paper. Two sets are called homometric if the gaps between their pairs of points match exactly, when points sit on a ring of positions. The authors solve the case where each set has five points, for rings of any size.

Their classification lists six families of matching pairs and one family of matching triples, up to shifting or flipping the ring. They also give a formula that counts all such pairs and triples. The result settles a problem left open for smaller set sizes decades ago. It also gives a clear test for a signal recovery problem in crystallography.
arxiv-2412-09197:
Isaac García and Jaume Giné characterize when a planar system's equilibrium is a center, using the complex curves that wind through the singularity. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Telling centers, where orbits loop closed, from foci, where they spiral, is a classic hard problem. The systems here depend analytically on parameters.

An invariant analytic curve always passes through the monodromic singularity in question. The authors tie centerhood to one specific integral of that curve's cofactor. Degenerate centers are covered by the same test. Several consequences and applications follow from the characterization. A single integral test replaces case-by-case hunting. The partition of parameter space into centers and foci becomes computable in principle. The result serves the qualitative theory of differential equations.
arxiv-2412-09697:
Sangjin Lee and Kwonsang Lee build new tests for how a treatment's effect on paired, cut-off results shifts over time. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four.

Past tests for such data can spot a broad effect across a whole follow-up span. They say little on when an effect starts or how it grows or fades. The new tests give each person a score tied to life at a set time, built from stand-in views of full data. They can probe both set times and the long run. The team adds checks for hidden bias in studies where chance was not used to assign the treatment, and shows the method on a Korean aging study.
arxiv-2412-10597:
Blaine Hoak, Ryan Sheatsley, and Patrick McDaniel measure texture bias on real data in two thousand twenty four. Image classifiers lean on texture more than shape. That bias is among the strongest known in vision models. Past measures failed to capture real world robustness effects.

Their Texture Association Value scores reliance on specific textures. Accuracy and robustness both swing with texture alignment. Natural adversarial examples turn out to be texture cases. Over ninety percent carry textures mismatched to their true label. Models then err with high confidence on those images.
arxiv-2412-11197:
Seema Satin wrote, in two thousand twenty-four, on stochastic gravity, in which space and time can shake with quantum waves. The view aims to tell how the first big clumps of mass took shape in the young cosmos. Its core is a pair of kernels, one for noise and one for loss. Both are built from the quantum stress of scalar fields.

Her step is to treat those fields like a fluid: the hydrodynamic approximation of the loss kernel. She also moves the view toward the decoherence limit, where quantum acts fade into plain acts. A like step was made not long ago for the noise kernel. Hers does the same for loss in a fluid at near light speed. The work could let the view probe clump growth near when the inflaton field faded in that way.
arxiv-2412-12497:
Xin Yi and co-authors propose, in a 2024 paper, a cheap fix for large language models whose safety training has been undone by harmful fine-tuning. A few bad training examples sent by a user can break a model's alignment. Past fixes need heavy computing and fresh gradient training, which many providers cannot afford for each case.

Their method, called NLSR, needs no new training at all. It builds a safety reference model, finds the neurons most tied to safe behavior, and copies those neurons into the damaged model where they differ most. Tests showed large safety gains across tasks while task accuracy stayed high. Only a small part of the model changes.
arxiv-2412-12997:
Umer Butt, Stalin Varanasi, and Günter Neumann build the first large search benchmark for Urdu in a 2024 paper. Urdu is spoken by millions but lacks the datasets that power modern search research. The team machine translated a major English retrieval collection into Urdu and used it to set baseline results.

Systems were first tested with no Urdu training, then fine tuned with a multilingual method adapted to the new data. The tuned model's scores rose clearly over the zero shot baseline on both ranking and recall measures. The authors stress the social stakes: search access in low resource languages is an inclusion issue. Their approach should transfer to other South Asian languages.
arxiv-2412-13397:
Rajesh Gopakumar, Rishabh Kaushik, Shota Komatsu, and two colleagues rewrite the Feynman diagrams of a supersymmetric gauge theory as a sum over strings, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. The theory is N=4 super Yang-Mills, and the correlators studied preserve half of its supersymmetry.

Each individual diagram maps onto a Riemann surface with specific moduli, the mathematical shape of a closed string's worldsheet. Strikingly, the diagrams land on discrete lattice points of the string's moduli space rather than on chopped-up worldsheets. The construction works to all orders in the expansion in inverse colors. Concretely it runs through a two-matrix integral with a dual string description. The picture gives a microscopic view of open-closed string duality in this corner of the AdS/CFT correspondence. It also predicts that one closed string theory can admit several open string descriptions.
arxiv-2412-14597:
Salma Rahmouni and co-authors revisit the near-infrared fingerprints of kilonovae in two thousand twenty-four, the glowing debris of merged neutron stars. The famous two thousand seventeen event proved such mergers forge heavy elements, but naming the elements behind each spectral dip is hard, especially in infrared light.

The team systematically searched measured atomic energy levels for all heavy elements with strong infrared lines. Most candidates were lanthanides and actinides, whose complex atoms pack many low levels. Earlier work credited two elements for features near twelve to fifteen thousand angstroms. The new search adds gadolinium as the next strongest suspect, thanks to its half-filled shell and low-lying levels. Its lines also appear in a peculiar star's spectrum. Simulations confirm gadolinium reshapes the twelve-thousand-angstrom feature.
arxiv-2412-15097:
Chloe Gaudu reports, for the CORSIKA 8 Collaboration, on the status of the successor to the world's standard air shower simulation code. For over two decades, CORSIKA 7 has been the top Monte Carlo code to model extensive air showers from cosmic rays. Its single-block Fortran design and hand-tuned code have made upkeep hard. They have also made it hard to adapt to new compute paths and to extend to complex models.

CORSIKA 8 is a full rewrite in a modern, modular C++ frame. It has reached a physics-complete state. It supports top high-energy hadronic interaction models and electromagnetic cascades. It also supports many interaction media, including cross-media showers, and better radio emission calculations. The report gives an overview of current functions and shows validation results. It also treats future plans for growth.
arxiv-2412-15297:
Poyatos and three co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-four on faint flares from small red stars, caught by the CHEOPS space telescope. Flares are bursts of light from a star's magnetic field. Past missions found bright ones with ease but missed the faint end. Faint flares can shape the air of planets near such stars, so the gap matters.

The team built a wavelet based cleaner to lift faint flares from noise. They tuned it by planting fake flares and checking which came back. Close to three hundred flares were found across a group of red dwarfs. The cleaner raised finds by about a third. Size counts fit a bell shaped curve more well than a power law.
arxiv-2412-15897:
Alexander von Bank and colleagues present an improved decoder for error-correcting codes that runs on brain-like spiking networks. Their paper, from twenty twenty-four, concerns low-density parity-check codes, widely used to fix errors in transmitted data. An earlier decoder from the same research line used a single spiking network to handle part of the decoding math. That shortcut worked poorly when each variable node in the code connects to only a few others, because the rough estimate lost too much detail.

The new design runs several spiking networks side by side for the same step, giving finer resolution and a wider range of message values. On a large test code, the improved decoder matched the performance of a standard widely used decoder. The result keeps alive the hope of decoding with much lower energy use, since spiking hardware works only when events occur.
arxiv-2412-16097:
Matteo Nerini and Bruno Clerckx studied smarter signal-bouncing panels for wireless networks in a 2024 paper. Such panels, placed on walls, reflect radio waves toward users to fill coverage gaps. A newer family rewires the panel elements in groups, giving more control than a plain panel, but at higher circuit cost.

Most earlier work assumed waves with a single polarization, while real systems use two. Nerini and Clerckx derive the growth laws and the best trade-off curve for the dual case. Panels grouped in pairs gave large gains over plain panels in both scattered and direct channels, while keeping circuits modest. The results guide builders choosing how much complexity a panel deserves.
arxiv-2412-17097:
Eduard Emelyanov studied how time evolution extends to completed spaces in a 2024 working analysis paper. The setting is Archimedean vector lattices, spaces that combine algebra with an order form, and one-setting semigroups, which describe steady evolution like heat flow. Such spaces are often completed by adding limit points. The question is whether an evolution defined on the first space extends to the completion, uniquely and well.

For positive semigroups, Emelyanov establishes that an extension to the ru-completion always exists and is unique. An extension theorem for a continuity class on spaces with a regularity property follows. Letting later results drop the assumption that the space was complete to begin with.
arxiv-2412-17497:
Sergi Masot-Llima and Artur Garcia-Saez test how the wiring shape of a tensor network affects its training, in a 2024 paper. Tensor networks, born in quantum physics, now serve machine learning as flexible data structures. Their geometry can be regular or mixed, and the best shape for learning was unclear.

The pair train networks of varied shapes to encode a random quantum state, using gradient methods on a modern supercomputer. Densely wired structures reached lower error, succeeded more often, and trained faster than sparse ones. They also share tricks to cut memory use in sparse layouts and measure what those tricks cost. Graphics processors sped the work greatly. The guidance helps designers pick shapes before burning compute.
arxiv-2412-18097:
Nan Yang and co-authors present LangYa, an AI system for forecasting the world ocean, in a research paper from 2024. Standard ocean forecast systems solve physics equations on grids, which costs much compute and lets errors build up. AI models run faster, but a single model that spans times and couples air with sea remained a gap.

LangYa trains on 27 years of global ocean reanalysis data. A time embedding lets one model issue forecasts from one to seven days ahead. A coupled module mimics air-sea exchange, and a self-attention module steadies training. A custom loss sharpens forecasts of the thermocline, the layer where temperature drops fast. The team reports more reliable forecasts than rival numeric and AI systems.
arxiv-2412-18197:
Hiroyuki Chihara computes a key quantity for an imaging transform in a 2024 math study. The d-plane transform averages a function over all flat slices of a given dimension, a model for tomographic scanning. Reconstructing the function uses a filtered backprojection formula, whose core is the normal operator built by composing the transform with its adjoint.

Chihara computes that operator's symbol directly. The symbol factors into the symbol of a fractional power of the Laplacian times a constant from an invariant integral over the extra dimensions. The factorization gives a fresh route to the reconstruction formula, confirming the classic result from a new angle.
arxiv-2412-18397:
Ning Sun, Pengfei Zhang, and Lei Feng design an experiment-friendly way to spot a new kind of symmetry breaking. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. In mixed quantum states, a strong symmetry can soften into a weak one. That shift marks a distinct phase of matter. The usual detector needs multi-replica correlation functions. Those are hard to measure directly in the lab.

Their scheme uses randomized measurements instead. Random Pauli measurements are taken on the state as prepared. A second round follows after charged operators act on it. With many samples, the key correlator comes out exactly. With few samples, phase boundaries can still be estimated. The protocol fits tools experimenters already have. Exotic mixed-state phases move closer to direct observation.
arxiv-2412-18897:
Sangita Dutta and co-authors wrote a 2024 physics paper on synchronization shifts that jump twice, in networks where links bind three or more nodes at once. The base play is a known one: nodes with their own rhythms pull to one rhythm as ties grow. With pair ties, the shift to synchrony is smooth or sharp. Three-way ties can make it sharp.

The team asks what blend gives a two-step explosion: a jump up, then a jump more, on the way in or out. Two ingredients are the key. The three-way ties must be in play. And a share of the joint synchronization grade of the whole group must feed back on those ties. A known mathematics trick supports the simulation findings. For a wide class of such networks, the blend gives the twin explosion.
arxiv-2501-00697:
Michael Bennie and six co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on counter speech in Mandarin Chinese. Counter speech replies to hate speech with calm, firm words. Tools for it in Chinese are near nil, though the language is used world wide. The team built the first such data set for mainland China, named PANDA.

They used a language model as judge, plus search tricks and round based picks, to draft replies. Human checks then vet the drafts for quality and fit. Their study maps which groups get maligned and which speech marks flag hate in this tongue. They also show gaps in open Chinese hate data. The limits of a model as judge in Chinese stand out as a key find.
arxiv-2501-02797:
Tadikonda Shiva Sai, Hemanth Kolla, and Konduri Aditya test a reduced model for reacting flows in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Chemical systems in flames involve many linked quantities, so modelers compress them into a few components. A method based on co-kurtosis captures stiff chemistry better than the standard approach in early checks.

The team now tests the compressed model in full simulations of ignition in a uniform reactor. They evolve the system with a standard solver and with a neural solver that folds time stepping into training. The neural solver cut error growth across steps and gave more accurate profiles. The authors say the manifold could serve large parallel flow solvers.
arxiv-2501-03197:
Cyrus Mehta, Ajoy Mukhopadhyay, and Martin Posch extend a graphical method for juggling many hypotheses into adaptive two-stage trial designs. The graph method draws a trial's testing priorities as arrows: when one hypothesis falls, its error budget flows to the next. Adaptive designs complicate the picture, since treatments may be dropped, sample sizes re-estimated, and even the hierarchy revised after stage one. Family-wise error must survive all that freedom.

Two preservation strategies compete: combining p-values across stages, and conditioning the stage-two error rate on stage one. The paper lays out each method's statistical machinery. A large simulation experiment then compares their operating characteristics head to head. Multi-arm, multi-endpoint trials, common in modern drug development, are the beneficiaries. Adaptivity without error control is just optimism; this work prices it honestly.
arxiv-2501-05197:
Drago Plečko and a team of co-authors build a causal frame for health equity in twenty twenty-five. Big data now lets researchers trace why health outcomes differ between groups. Their framework analyzes disparities with causal inference rather than plain statistics. They apply it to intensive care outcomes by race and ethnicity.

Cases come from Australia, comparing Indigenous and non-Indigenous patients, and from the United States. There, African-American and White patients are compared. The authors show common statistical measures of inequity are not enough. Instead, a disparity should be attributed to the mechanisms that generate it. Among their findings, minority patients tended to be younger at admission with worse chronic health. Readers get a method for moving from gap-watching to cause-finding.
arxiv-2501-05297:
Kuzucan and co-authors ask how a planet's air shifts the habitable zone and whether microbes could grow at its hot edge. The habitable zone marks where liquid water can persist on a surface. Air makeup moves those edges, and water alone does not promise life. The team used a 3D climate model for planets near the inner edge. They refined that edge for hydrogen-rich and carbon dioxide air for the first time.

In parallel, lab tests grew E. coli under the modeled conditions. Growth and survival were tracked across the settings. Pairing climate math with live microbes grounds habitability claims. The study tests more than where water stays liquid.
arxiv-2501-05697:
Fusheng Deng, Gang Huang, and Xiangsen Qin estimate the Green kernel for a twisted geometric operator on domains with boundary. Their 2025 paper studies the Dolbeault Laplacian acting on forms that take values in a bundle, over a region inside a Kähler manifold. Such kernels are the building blocks for solving the associated equations.

The authors prove global bounds that hold uniformly up to the boundary, including versions with one or two boundary factors. They also bound the kernel's derivatives in both natural directions. From these bounds flow Sobolev-style inequalities that keep boundary terms visible. In the lowest dimension the first-order bound pays a logarithmic price. In top degree they gain quantitative solvability without assuming the domain bulges the usual way.
arxiv-2501-06097:
Chinnarasu leads a team of eight on this paper from two thousand twenty-five. It runs a classic nuclear model, the Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick model, on a neutral atom quantum computer with a variational solver.

Ground state energies are found for spin systems of up to fifteen spins. Two encodings are tried. In one, each spin takes its own qubit. In the other, a Gray code packs the spins into far fewer qubits, a count that grows with the log of the spin count. The lean code, plus a noise stretch trick that cleans the read, lands much closer to the exact energies. The work shows a small quantum machine can host a real physics model with care.
arxiv-2501-06897:
Chen and co-authors present ActiveGAMER, a system that maps a space by choosing where to look next, in this 2025 paper. It builds scenes with 3D Gaussian splatting, a fast rendering method using soft blobs. Older neural field methods were too slow for active exploration.

A rendering-based module scores which new viewpoint would teach the system most. The planner mixes broad exploration with fine detail passes and picks keyframes at two scales. The robot then moves on its own, filling gaps as it goes. On the Replica and MP3D benchmarks the system beat earlier approaches in both shape accuracy and visual fidelity. Complete, faithful maps help robots plan and people inspect spaces remotely.
arxiv-2501-08497:
Myles Joshua Toledo Tan and Panayiotis Benos answer a call to put accuracy first in AI diagnosis by urging a wider lens, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Accuracy matters, they grant, but fairness, privacy, and layered identity can be flattened into mere scores. Their rebuttal asks for work across social science, ethics, and public health.

Clear explanations must sit at the core of design so users can trust and check the tools. Layered traits, like race plus sex plus income, can stack harms that single marks miss. The authors propose a frame that holds accuracy beside fairness, privacy, and inclusion. Readers get a plea for diagnosis tools that serve mixed publics well.
arxiv-2501-09497:
Yun Chen, Yuqi Wang, Jingjun You, Yingqi Liu, Su Yi, and Yuangang Deng propose making molecules inside a light cavity so atoms and molecules radiate together, in a 2025 paper. Ultracold atoms in optical cavities are a prized testbed for many-body physics. Their scheme uses the cavity to help bind atom pairs into molecules, which creates long-range three-way interactions among cavity light, atoms, and molecules.

Past a threshold pump strength, the molecules settle into a self-organized square lattice. That marks a joint atom-molecule superradiance, with a broken symmetry. Unlike earlier atomic versions, the light output grows with the cube of the atom count, a bosonic boost. Strong entanglement between light and matter flags the transition. The authors say the setup opens fresh ground in quantum superchemistry.
arxiv-2501-09797:
Karan Tiwana, Edoardo Lauria, and Antoine Tilloy set out a new way to compute mean values in field theories that have a line flaw. Their paper appeared in twenty twenty-five. The theories live in one space plus one time dimension and describe bulk matter with mass. A line flaw breaks the clean case and makes direct sums hard.

The trick is to run time across the flaw, not along it. Sums with the flaw then turn into mean values in the clean case, which a smooth matrix state can handle well. The team tests the plan on a known theory with a field flaw. It works in weak, strong, and border cases alike.
arxiv-2501-10297:
Simone Daniotti, Matte Hartog, and Frank Neffke measure how coherent the economies of United States cities are, in work from 2025. A city's coherence is the typical distance between the skills its activities need. Diverse economies support growth but force cities to build many unrelated skills, which is costly.

The team tracked the urban system from 1850 to today. They used census records covering over six hundred million people for the early period, plus patent and job data for recent decades. Despite huge shifts in where activity sits, average coherence barely changed over 170 years. Coherence also falls with city size at the same rate in every era and dataset. The authors read this as a universal constraint on how cities diversify, set by size itself.
arxiv-2501-11097:
Huichao Zhang, Pengyu Wang, Manyi Li, Zuojun Li, and Yaguang Wu encode floorplans as latent codes over adaptive unit regions, in a representation meant to serve many tasks at once. Their paper from twenty twenty-five contrasts the offer with raster images, which over-segment, and room graphs, which throw away geometry. A geometry-aware density map is clustered into boundary-hugging unit regions. A trained network then reads density and semantic maps into compact codes per region.

Interior planning, floorplan metric learning, and generation all run on the same encoding. Experiments beat state-of-the-art rivals in accuracy and visual quality across those tasks. Ablations show the slicing choices matter. Architecture tools gain one representation where three formats used to compete.
arxiv-2501-11197:
Udekwe and co-authors present Q-RESTORE, a framework for rebuilding road networks after disasters with fairness built in. Fast recovery matters most in underserved areas, where isolation deepens harm. Classic methods prize raw function and speed of planning over equity. Low-income areas often lose out under those rules. The new frame pairs quantum computing with equity goals. A hybrid quantum solver picks which road links to restore within budget.

The solver weighs the needs of low-, middle-, and high-income communities side by side. Priority goes to keeping all groups connected to vital services. Compute speed is treated as a means, not the end. The authors frame fair recovery as a design constraint, not an afterthought.
arxiv-2501-15597:
Alexander Kaganovich studies how the Higgs field could have driven the early universe's fast expansion inside a two-measure theory of gravity. The paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. In this theory, the Higgs is the only field rolling through the young cosmos. A built-in constraint ties a key ratio to the field's value.

That tie turns fixed settings into ones that shift as the field moves. The resulting push can match what sky data say about the expansion era, with a mild link to gravity. It needs a very small self-coupling during that era. After expansion ends, the falling field flips the sign of its mass term and breaks the symmetry. The same drift then lifts the coupling to its known lab value. The model even covers strange starts where the cosmos begins in a phantom-like state.
arxiv-2501-16797:
Suprabha Mukhopadhyay, Yuto Bekki, Xiaojue Zhu, and Laurent Gizon test shortcuts used to model slow waves on the Sun, in a 2025 paper. These global inertial modes have only recently been observed, and they may reveal the Sun's inner spin. Modelers often simplify the gas equations to save computing time.

Using one code framework, the team computes the modes three ways: with full compressible physics and with two approximations. One shortcut, the anelastic form, matches the full result closely under both even and solar-like spin. The Boussinesq form, which drops density layering, gives clearly different modes, above all for patterns with strong radial motion. The verdict tells solar modelers which shortcut is safe and which distorts the very modes they chase.
arxiv-2501-17297:
Mustafa Saeed, Diya Batool, Muhammad Muzammil, and Nomaan X probe the thermal character of gravity with spin models in a 2025 theoretical physics study. Euclidean approaches to gravity treat spacetime with imaginary time, a setting where temperature-like behavior might be built in. The authors place Ising-like models on several classic backgrounds and watch for phase transitions in the spins.

Flat space with acceleration horizons, black holes, and cosmological spaces each appear, including cases with no horizon or zero temperature for contrast. Sorting which background property, curvature, horizon, or temperature, drives the transition clarifies what hot means for gravity itself.
arxiv-2501-17697: Tom Banks writes a short review essay for younger physicists in a 2025 paper, the third in a series reviving old arguments. His topic is a habit of thought in string theory: treating the theory's settings as if they were the settled values of fields. Banks argues that this picture misleads. He walks through arguments first made at the start of the century, in plain terms, so a new generation can judge them. The essay is a caution about importing field-theory instincts into quantum gravity.
arxiv-2501-18997:
Gyuseok Lee and four co-authors bring diffusion models, the engines behind image generators, into recommender systems that suggest items to users. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Diffusion recommenders clean noisy taste signals to guess what a user wants. Adding noise, though, can wash out the personal detail that matters most.

Their model, CDiff4Rec, builds fake users from item features to enrich the signal. It then borrows taste cues from both real and fake neighbors who behave alike. That mix rebuilds fine-grained preferences more faithfully. Tests on three public data sets beat rival systems. The gains come from joining item content with shared taste signals. The work suits shops and media apps that must keep suggestions personal. It also shows generative tools can serve ranking, not just media.
arxiv-2502-00597:
Jose Rocher-Gonzalez and co-authors work on combining two congestion tools for the fat-tree networks that link supercomputers. Their 2025 paper starts from the fat-tree shape, which offers many equal routes between any two nodes. Multi-path routing can spread traffic across those routes and lower congestion.

A second tool separates flows into queues, yet the authors' earlier work showed spreading can backfire by scattering congested flows across queues. Their proposal adds restrictions on how alternative routes are chosen, so spreading and queue separation reinforce rather than fight each other. The target is a network that handles the bursty traffic of computing centers without hot spots. The work is a design step toward pairing the two schemes in real machines.
arxiv-2502-02297:
Blot, Shadrin, and Singh give a new proof of Faber's formula for socle intersection numbers, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The numbers live in the tautological ring of the moduli space of curves. Their proof draws on Gromov-Witten theory of the elliptic curve. Recent work by Oberdieck and Pixton supplies the key relation.

A refinement of that argument yields a beautiful new tautological relation. Straightforward computation with double ramification cycles completes the proof. Those cycles enter recursion relations for KdV hierarchy Hamiltonians. The note is short but connects several deep theories. Curve counting and integrable systems meet in one formula.
arxiv-2502-05797:
David Pearl, James Intriligator, and Xuanjiang Liu survey wearable technology in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Wearables have moved from gadgets to daily companions in health, work, and well-being. The authors trace that history and map what comes next.

Artificial intelligence, connected sensors, and augmented reality now drive personal, adaptive devices. Good wearables, they argue, need user-centered design, ethics, and teamwork across fields. Modular builds and greener materials answer sustainability concerns. Risks such as data privacy and algorithmic bias still shadow the field. The paper offers a roadmap for wearables that enrich lives while growing in ethical and sustainable ways. Integration with daily life is the field's defining trend.
arxiv-2502-05997:
Liu, Puckett, Wu, Hariri, Zhang, and Zhang report in twenty twenty-five light-guiding chips built on full-size factory wafers with extremely low signal loss. Such chips route light for communications, sensors, and quantum tools, but making them at wafer scale without cracks is hard. The team combined tuned wafers with a new etching mask method to carve the guides.

The finished guides kept light so well that quality scores beat prior marks, with both lab-grade and factory-style patterning. Ringing the guides produced frequency combs, trains of evenly spaced colours, proving the planned light-bending trait. The authors say the route fits standard foundry lines, opening mass production of high-grade photonic chips.
arxiv-2502-07597:
Leyun Gao, Alim Ruzi, Qite Li, Chen Zhou, and Qiang Li ask whether the spooky linked behavior of quantum particles can be tested with free-flying electron-positron pairs. Entanglement is well proven for confined electrons, but pairs traveling freely, especially at high energy, are hard to test because their spins are hard to measure.

The team studies pairs created in a fixed-target experiment, which gives a controlled source where linked events appear in known parts of the phase space. Knowing the state in advance, they show how each particle's spin pattern can be read from a second scattering off separate targets. Comparing those patterns would reveal the polarization links and allow a Bell test on the pairs.
arxiv-2502-07997:
Carson Valdez and co-authors build light circuits that can cancel a signal with extreme precision in a 2025 paper. Such nulling, where two light waves erase each other, matters for sensing tasks such as imaging faint objects near bright ones. Making it work on a chip is hard because tiny build errors upset the balance.

Their design joins pairs of interferometers, devices that split and recombine light, into a mesh with built-in redundancy. A step-by-step tuning method then corrects for build flaws and stray reflections. On a silicon chip platform, the mesh reached cancellation levels above eighty decibels. The result points to compact photonic tools for astronomy and other jobs needing very high contrast.
arxiv-2502-08897:
Yukun He, Jiaoyang Huang, and Horng-Tzer Yau study Gaussian waves and edge eigenvectors of random regular graphs in two thousand twenty-five. Past work showed near eigenvectors of such graphs tend to Gaussian waves. The spread of those waves could sit anywhere in a set range. Their proof pins the edge case down in full.

For edge eigenvectors the variance must equal one, they show. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors also part ways in the limit. Their frame links Green's function behavior to eigenvector limits. That link may serve other problems in random matrix work. The proof is an alternate route to a known claim.
arxiv-2502-09097:
Tianyi Huang and four co-authors build a fake news detector in twenty twenty-five. Their model is a transformer improved in two ways at once. A bidirectional gated recurrent unit is woven into the architecture. Bayesian optimization then tunes the combined model. The authors say this pairing is applied to fake news classification for the first time.

News text is first turned into numbers with TF-IDF features. Two experiment sets compare the designs. The recurrent-enhanced transformer alone reached very high test accuracy. Adding the Bayesian component nudged test accuracy slightly higher still. Training accuracy was perfect in both cases. Readers should note those near-ceiling scores when judging the claim. The work shows a hybrid stack squeezing the last fractions of accuracy from a benchmark.
arxiv-2502-10297:
Julien Siems and five co-authors present a new linear recurrent network design in a 2025 paper. Linear recurrent models rival transformers for sequence tasks while running faster, but their state transition matrices force a trade off between speed and power. Simple diagonal matrices are fast yet limited in what they can track.

Their design, called DeltaProduct, takes several small update steps per token instead of one. That yields richer transition matrices built from a product of reflection like transforms, with a knob to balance power against cost. Theory shows state tracking improves as steps increase, within finite precision limits. In tests, the model beat its predecessor on state tracking and language modeling, and handled longer sequences better.
arxiv-2502-10897:
Liu and colleagues found tangled filaments inside a fast hydrogen cloud in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Warm neutral gas was thought to churn too gently for filament networks. Using China's giant FAST telescope, the team mapped a cloud racing toward us at hundreds of kilometers per second. The twenty-one centimeter hydrogen line revealed its inner structure.

For the first time, such a cloud resolved into slim, velocity-coherent filaments. Curves, hubs, and webs layered through the data cube. The density pattern bore the skewed signature of shock compression. Simulations of supersonic magnetic turbulence reproduced the look. The authors propose that shocks alone can weave filaments in thin warm gas. That offers a route to structure in the young interstellar medium.
arxiv-2502-10997:
Ruihan Wu and Yu-Xiang Wang tighten the loss bound for private online choice learning, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. An open problem asked for the best case-wise rate when picks must stay differentially private. Prior bounds left a gap that grew with time rounds.

The new upper bound drops the time term and keeps only log terms in action count and privacy. A weaker fixed-loss setting is then solved exactly, with matching upper and lower bounds. That solved case guides where the main gap still sits. Readers in private learning get a sharper rate and a clean subproblem with a full answer.
arxiv-2502-12197:
Norman Mu, Jonathan Lu, Michael Lavery, and David Wagner probe how well language models stick to their system prompts. Their paper from twenty twenty-five notes that system prompts set context, format, persona, and safety rules. Models often drop a guardrail or botch a clash between system and user demands. Robust holding to the prompt is thus a core safety trait.

The team built fresh test and training sets from real prompts in the GPT Store and HuggingChat. Realistic fine-tuning data lifted scores by a wide margin. Inference-time tricks, such as classifier-free guidance, helped too. New reasoning models from OpenAI and DeepSeek gained, but unevenly. The authors close that current tools fall short of sure robustness. More work is needed before system prompts can be trusted as hard rules.
arxiv-2502-13997:
Ye Wang and five colleagues present SigStyle, a style transfer framework focused on an artist's signature style. Signature style means the recognizable traits of an image: geometric patterns, color palettes, and brush strokes. Earlier methods transfer style without explicitly capturing what makes a style distinctive.

SigStyle extracts that signature using the semantic priors inside a personalized text-to-image diffusion model. A hypernetwork fine-tunes the model efficiently from a single style image, and learned style tokens then reconstruct content images in that style. A time-aware attention swap preserves content during early denoising. Beyond standard transfer, the framework supports local transfer, texture transfer, style fusion, and style-guided generation, outperforming existing methods in evaluations.
arxiv-2502-14897:
Hamid Moradi-Kamali and colleagues labeled crypto tweets by what the market did next in a 2025 study. Sentiment tools usually ask human readers whether a post sounds upbeat or downbeat, then assume price follows feelings. The authors argue that words move markets in ways readers cannot reliably guess, so past market reactions make a better teacher than opinion labels.

A finance-tuned language model trained on market-derived labels beat classic sentiment benchmarks on short-term trend calls by a clear margin. Adding market and timing context through prompt tuning pushed accuracy higher still on a curated set of major Bitcoin news events. Traders get a signal grounded in outcomes, not impressions.
arxiv-2502-15197:
Zhaoxuan Wu and a team of co-authors present a method to speed up large language models, in two thousand twenty-five. Their method is called TETRIS, and it works when many requests are served at once. A fast draft step proposes words, and a larger model then checks them in parallel.

Older methods pick draft words for one request, or for a whole group at once. TETRIS picks the most promising draft words for each request in the batch. That choice means fewer words are rejected and less computing power is wasted. Tests and theory both showed higher acceptance rates than the older ways, which matters for providers with limited capacity.
arxiv-2502-17397:
Yoeri Poels and four co-authors, with two large fusion teams, present a study from twenty twenty-five on sorting plasma states in a tokamak. High energy yield needs strong confinement, which comes in distinct modes. Auto labels for these modes aid big studies and live control. Modes blur near shifts, and sensors can fail or drop out.

The team blends many data driven models, mixed by both model type and sensor group. One model type tracks change over time; the other uses boosted trees on fixed traits. A fully labeled set of just over three hundred runs will be shared in public. Scores show the blend sorts the three modes well. It also copes with lost signals and gives trust scores with its calls.
arxiv-2502-18597:
Rikako Yamamoto, Luke Alexander Turnbull, and Marcus Schmidt lead a large team on this paper from two thousand twenty-five. It gives bulk evidence for altermagnetism in MnTe, a leading hope for this new kind of magnetism.

Most past checks used thin films or surfaces, so the bulk case stayed open. The team cut a thin slice from a single crystal and shot X-rays through it, mapping magnetic domains at the nanoscale. The signal matched the marks that altermagnetic order should give, in both shape and size. Since the slice is thick, the order must run through the bulk, not just the skin. The method now stands as a tool for screening other hopes.
arxiv-2502-20097:
Rickard Karlsson, Bram van den Akker, Felipe Moraes, Hugo Proença, and Jesse Krijthe study Qini curves when treated units interfere with each other, in a two thousand twenty-five statistics paper. Qini curves weigh a treatment policy's incremental gain against its implementation cost.

Standard estimation assumes one person's treatment never affects another's outcome. In marketing and public policy that assumption fails, and ignoring interference biases the curves. The authors formalize clustered network interference, where interfering units form independent clusters, and propose three estimation strategies suited to different conditions. A marketplace simulator mimicking an e-commerce setting lets them compare the strategies and their bias-variance trade-offs in practice.
arxiv-2502-20297:
Virgile Guémard and Gilles Zémor build new families of quantum error-correcting codes. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Quantum Tanner codes pair two classical codes on graphs drawn from surfaces. Lifting a code to a covering space makes longer codes from short ones. The authors study lifts of odd index. They adapt tools from cellular homology to track the symmetries involved.

For any odd lift, the new code keeps at least the old dimension. Its distance is capped by the index times the old distance. When the dimension stays equal, the distance is at least the old one. These bounds also cover an earlier lifting method by Guémard. Several explicit families close the paper. Moderate lengths make the codes plausible for real hardware tests.
arxiv-2502-20797:
Rob den Teuling and five colleagues derive formulas for spin waves in the van der Waals magnet CrSBr, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. They treat both monolayers and antiferromagnetically coupled bilayers. An in-plane external magnetic field is applied throughout. The analysis spans antiferromagnetic, ferromagnetic, and canted phases of the material.

Closed-form expressions give the spin wave frequencies and precession amplitudes in each phase. Frequencies prove tunable by the applied field in all phases. The authors dissect what controls the magnetization dynamics. Intra- and interlayer exchange interactions both matter. So do triaxial anisotropy and intralayer dynamic dipolar fields. The results give experimentalists a map for interpreting spin wave measurements in this layered magnet.
arxiv-2503-00697:
Yiyang Lin and co-authors build a system that converts quick frozen-section tissue images into the richer style of standard processed slides. Their 2025 paper serves pathologists during surgery, who judge tumors from frozen sections. Those fast images suffer contamination and blurry nuclei, while the high-quality preparation takes far too long for the operating room.

Their framework transfers stain style while repairing detail. One module borrows tissue information across image resolutions to offset contamination losses. Another works in a wavelet form to guide fine detail, sharpening nuclear structure. On their data set, the method beat all competing approaches. Cleaner intraoperative images could steady the benign-versus-malignant calls that decide how much tissue a surgeon removes.
arxiv-2503-00897:
Fine-tuning image generators with reinforcement learning can steer them toward goals that resist direct scoring, yet the standard method, PPO, is touchy and costly. Shashank Gupta and co-authors study the trade-off between two classic approaches. REINFORCE is simpler and lighter but noisy and wasteful with samples, while PPO is steadier but heavy and sensitive to its settings.

Their answer is a hybrid called leave-one-out PPO, or LOOP. From REINFORCE it borrows drawing several images per prompt and correcting scores against a baseline built by leaving one sample out. From PPO it takes clipping and importance sampling, which keep updates stable and reuse data well. Across several black-box goals, LOOP improved the generators while using samples better than either parent method. The authors present it as a practical balance between efficiency and final image quality.
arxiv-2503-01397:
Farhana Javed and Josep Mangues-Bafalluy measure how fast smart contracts settle on a live Ethereum test network, in a 2025 paper. Their application hosts agreements between telecom providers sharing 6G resources, in two phases: preliminary deals and enforcement. Four contracts split the phases. Gas fees, block size, and traffic volume were all varied and timed.

Most transactions finalized within thirty seconds, with medians from eleven to twenty-four seconds. Crowded blocks swamped fee effects when the contract logic was heavy. When logic was light, fees decided the pace. Statistical tests confirmed both patterns strongly. The authors advise matching fee strategy to contract complexity when designing such marketplaces.
arxiv-2503-01497:
Ramkrishna Acharya presents a method for drawing in the air with a finger in this 2025 paper. A camera watches the hand, and strokes appear on screen. Such input could serve sign language, sketching, and hands free writing. The method uses classic image processing rather than deep learning.

First, the system learns the background from early frames. It then subtracts that background from live frames to find the moving hand. A hand detector cuts false shapes before that step. The fingertip is taken as the top of the hand outline, and a dot is drawn there. Drawn text can be read by an optical character tool. Tests reached a delay of only 100 milliseconds, fast enough for natural use.
arxiv-2503-02697:
Guohui Guan, Jiaqi Hu, and Zongxia Liang study saving and investing when people value liquid wealth in this 2025 paper. Their agent holds a bond, a liquid risky asset, and an illiquid risky asset. Selling the illiquid asset costs a share of its value. The agent also gains utility from holding liquid wealth itself, not just from spending.

The team maps the decision space into buying, holding, and selling zones for the illiquid asset. All three zones are shown to be nonempty. The best policy is derived in theory and computed in numbers. Valuing liquidity makes the agent hold more liquid wealth and spend less. It can even lead to a short position in the illiquid asset. Risk aversion shapes whether liquidity raises or lowers spending.
arxiv-2503-03897:
Maria Parilli, Sergi Martinez, and Carlos Mastalli give a new way to hold end-point rules in a class of control methods for robots. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

The base method plans a path by steps of slope, and is used in live control and fast solvers. Past ways to add end rules were rough or slow. The new way is exact and settles at a fast, squared rate. It copes with rank gaps in both end and step rules. It works for both ways of stating a robot's motion. The team shows it on a broad set of robot tasks, with code shared in a known solver.
arxiv-2503-05197:
Yu Feng and eight co-authors design StreamGrid, a framework that lets point cloud chips work in a steady stream instead of fetching data again and again. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Point clouds feed robots, cars, and scanners, but shuttling them off-chip stalls the pipeline and burns power. Classic buffers that fix this for images do not fit point clouds' odd access patterns.

Two tricks unlock streaming here. One forces the work to split along set lines, and the other ends each chunk at a fixed, known point. With those in place, data flows through once with no off-chip trips. The framework also sizes the on-chip buffers on its own. Tests cut buffer size and energy sharply for small accuracy cost. Against top accelerators it ran far faster and leaner.
arxiv-2503-05597:
Giorgia Proto presents, for the ATLAS muon community, how new particle detectors are built and certified in Munich. Her report, from twenty twenty-five, covers resistive plate chambers for the collider's phase-two upgrade. Each unit stacks three thin gas gaps in one frame. Fresh low-threshold electronics read them out.

Production began in twenty twenty-four for the high-luminosity era. Triplets are assembled at the Max Planck Institute. A cosmic ray stand then runs certification tests. Its design targets robust, efficient quality control. Performance measures decide whether each detector ships to the ATLAS cavern. Assembly steps and test protocols are laid out in full.
arxiv-2503-07397:
Kha Vo and Chin-Teng Lin present an algorithm from two thousand twenty-five for teaching large teams of agents to cooperate or compete. Multi-agent reinforcement learning struggles as teams grow, since agents affect each other constantly. Many methods lean on shared rewards or a fixed agent order, which large real systems cannot promise.

Their method, called Q-MARL, borrows a graph technique from quantum chemistry that predicts molecular traits from atom positions. Each agent sits at the center of its own neighborhood graph, and those graphs serve as training samples. A message-passing network handles interaction inside each graph, while a depth setting keeps training light. Actions blend votes from all graphs holding the agent. Tests show the method handling thousands of agents.
arxiv-2503-07997:
Shimmy Rukundo, David Wang, Front Wongnonthawitthaya, Youssouf Sidibé, Minsik Kim, Emily Su, and Jiale Zhang wrote this survey in two thousand twenty-five. It reviews the sensing tools used in shops that run with no cashier, where buyers pick goods and leave while the system tracks what they took.

The survey sorts prior work by task: tracking stock, watching the store space, tracking people, and stopping theft. It weighs the strengths and limits of cameras, RFID tags, weight sensors, vibration sensors, and LiDAR, and how they are joined. It also notes hard problems such as blocked views, scale, and speed of data handling. The authors close with paths toward systems that cost less and guard privacy better.
arxiv-2503-09797:
Benjamin Towle, Xin Chen, and Ke Zhou offered a new way in 2025 to make a splitting model admit its doubt. In medical images, edges are truly ambiguous and annotators disagree, so a single mask hides clinically meaningful doubt. Multiple choice learning trains several forecast heads to propose other masks, but the count is frozen at design time. And its winner-takes-all training lets one head dominate while the rest drift into irrelevance.

SeqSAM generates masks one after another in an autoregressive sequence, in the spirit of a recurrent network, wrapped around the Segment Anything Model. A bipartite matching loss keeps every generated mask clinically related rather than redundant, and because generation is sequential. The system can produce as many hypotheses as a clinician wants to inspect. The authors report notable quality improvements, giving reviewers a spread of defensible segmentations instead of one overconfident outline.
arxiv-2503-12597:
Zhuoqi Liu and co-authors wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five about a giant glowing cloud of gas around a distant quasar called 3C 57. Gas moving between galaxies and their surroundings shapes how galaxies grow. When a quasar lights that gas, it can be seen as a large nebula.

Using the MUSE instrument, the team found the cloud is long and fairly symmetric, with gas moving toward and away in a matched pattern. Two stories could explain it: gas in slow rotation, or gas blown out in two cones. The gas is far more stirred up than gas in nearby calm galaxies. Neither story fully fits, so the authors leave the case open for more work.
arxiv-2503-12697:
Mohamed Chabab, Samir Iraoui, and Hicham Sriba wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It reads the heat phases of a charged black hole in anti-de Sitter space, under massive gravity, from the light the hole sheds.

The team first maps the hole's shadow and its emission rate. Their new recipe keys on the peak frequency of the emission spectrum. That peak, paired with the shadow's size, tracks the hole's thermodynamic state with care. The link holds for both photon modes and heavy bosonic ones. In effect the brightest tone of the hole's glow serves as a probe of its phase change points. The work ties what a far viewer sees to deep facts about the hole.
arxiv-2503-12797:
Xinyu Ma, Ziyang Ding, Zhicong Luo, and seven colleagues tackle knowledge-intensive visual grounding in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The task asks a model to locate an object named by a fine-grained, domain-specific term rather than a generic description. Multimodal large language models know many entities and ground generic phrases well, yet often fail to use that knowledge for specialized concepts. The authors call this the knowledge-grounding gap.

Their remedy first builds knowledge-guided reasoning data that pushes models to activate relevant entity knowledge while grounding. Then KARL, a reinforcement learning framework, adjusts reward signals according to how well the model has mastered each entity. The team also releases KVG-Bench, spanning ten domains with over a thousand curated test cases. Experiments showed consistent gains over baselines and stronger generalization to unseen categories.
arxiv-2503-13797: Jeth Arunseangroj and co-authors wrote a 2025 mathematics note on Adinkras, graphs used to picture pieces of theories with supersymmetry, a deep symmetry. The search is for complete pieces that sit inside theories formulated off shell, and the team works with sixteen-color systems. The topology of an Adinkra matches a known mathematical form, a quotient of a cube. The note revisits that match, with an eye on a named open problem: how to complete the off-shell form of a known theory of light and charge, the Maxwell theory.
arxiv-2503-13997:
Svetlana Karpova, Federico Sanchez, and Dana Douqa propose using neutrino events to map the beam that made them in a 2025 particle physics study. Long-baseline experiments shoot a neutrino beam across great distances and measure how the particles change flavor. Precision depends on knowing the beam's shape and origin, normally taken from simulations.

Events recorded off the beam axis in the near detector carry clues about where neutrinos were produced. Observables tied to the azimuthal angle of the neutrino direction can pin down the average production point from real data. The method cross-checks simulations and can reveal alignment problems in the beam line.
arxiv-2503-14397: Timothé Alezraa and co-authors ask how the early cosmos gained more matter than antimatter, in work from 2025. They work inside grand unified models set in five dimensions, folded on a bounded shape. In such models, a process called leptogenesis can seed the excess of matter seen today. The authors search the allowed settings of the models for cases where that seeding works well. They find such cases do exist, and the extra dimension sits at a scale far above the tera-electron-volt range.
arxiv-2503-14897:
Vaibhav Rathore and co-authors tackle a harder form of image grouping in a 2025 paper. The task is to sort images into known and new classes in a new setting, when only labeled images from a different setting are available for training. Shifts between settings often break existing methods, and peeking at the target setting during training is not always possible.

Their system trains in short episodes that mix real and synthetic settings, so it learns features that do not depend on one setting. A weighting scheme then adjusts the base model based on how each fine-tuned version scores. Tests on three data sets beat adapted rival methods. The approach suits cases where the target images cannot be seen until the model is used.
arxiv-2503-15597:
Yoshinobu Fudamoto and a large team of co-authors wrote this astronomy paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on a crowd of galaxies found deep in the reionization era. The James Webb telescope caught them at a redshift of about 8.47, roughly five hundred fifty million years after the Big Bang.

Nine galaxies share that distance, confirmed by a bright oxygen line, with a tenth likely member. The clump is six to eight times denser than the average field at that age, the richest confirmed gathering known so early. One member hosts a small active black hole, a so-called little red dot. The odds of stumbling on such a structure in so small a surveyed patch are under five percent in current simulations. The authors say dense cradles may have sped up early galaxy growth.
arxiv-2503-15897:
Junho Kim, Gwangtak Bae, Eun Sun Lee, and Young Min Kim teach machines to find analogies between three-dimensional scenes, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Understanding scene context helps machines adapt prior knowledge to new or noisy environments. Learning every possible layout from data is intractable. The authors instead target relational commonalities between spaces.

They define scene analogies as smooth maps between scene regions that align spatial relationships. Their neural contextual scene maps extract descriptor fields summarizing semantic and geometric context. Fields are aligned holistically, coarse to fine, to estimate the map. Working at region level reduces reliance on individual feature points, adding robustness to noise and shape variation. Experiments show analogies found across diverse indoor scenes. Trajectories and object placements transfer between scenes, suggesting uses in robotics and augmented reality.
arxiv-2503-15997:
Paul Schulz, Thorsten Hempel, and Ayoub Al-Hamadi automate the making of 3D data sets in two thousand twenty-five. Finding objects in 3D is key for robots, augmented reality, and image search. Training needs large, well tagged sets, but they are slow and dear to make. Few public sets exist, with a narrow range of classes.

Their pipeline uses radiance fields to build high quality 3D models of any object. Those models feed a tool that makes fake training data. The pipeline is fast, simple, and largely self run. Pose nets trained on its data scored well in standard scenes. The work eases a key block in 3D vision.
arxiv-2503-18297:
Yishen Liu and co-authors built a model that writes medical reports from scan images. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with a task that needs expert skill. Big general models often miss the fine points of such reports. Medical images also look much alike, so models blur key traits and fit noise. The team aimed to sharpen how the model tells like images apart.

Their network pairs a vision part with a text part through a shared focus trick. A weight step boosts faint but key image tags. A three stage text part then polishes each line with the image parts in view. Tests on three public sets showed strong scores. Readers get a model built for the quirks of medical text.
arxiv-2503-18697:
Julia Le Bihan and Bartosz Kołodziejek study random perpetuities, sums that feed on themselves, in a 2025 paper. A perpetuity obeys an equation where the value equals a random multiple of itself plus a random add-on. The light-tailed case, where huge values stay rare, is their focus. They introduce a local measure of dependence and a matching transform to describe how the far right tail decays.

They then follow the running version, where each step multiplies and adds afresh. A clean scaling sequence exists so the running value, divided by it, settles between fixed bounds. Its limit is pinned down explicitly. The work sharpens the math behind insurance-style recursions and random growth.
arxiv-2503-19897:
Lifu Wang, Daqing Liu, Xinchen Liu, and Xiaodong He ask whether image-making models need very large text encoders. Their 2025 paper notes that encoders grew from small models to the huge T5-XXL. Large encoders read prompts well, but they also carry much skill with non-visual text that image models never use.

The team trained smaller T5 models by teaching them from the large one, using image data picked for quality and meaning. Their T5-base model made images about as good as those from T5-XXL, while being far smaller. That cut in size lowers the graphics hardware needed to run top models. The result makes high-grade image making open to more users and smaller labs.
arxiv-2503-21697:
Lorenzo Clemente asks when a formal series can be called commutative, and whether a machine can decide it. His paper is from two thousand twenty-five; the pack row gives no title or year, so the text head is the source. A series maps strings over an alphabet to rational values; it is commutative when the value ignores the order of symbols.

He shows the call is decidable for all classes that form an effective prevariety, a wide frame that holds the classic rational series. Three newer machine kinds, polynomial, shuffle, and infiltration automata, each form such a class, so their calls are decidable too, a new result. Uses reach past series, to solvability in sequences and power series for fenced kinds of equations.
arxiv-2504-00597:
Jirui Qi, Raquel Fernández, and Arianna Bisazza tested in twenty twenty-five how consistently language models use foreign-language context in retrieval-augmented question answering. In multilingual retrieval, the passages fetched may be written in a different language than the user's question. Whether models truly use such passages, rather than being helped or hurt by language quirks, was unclear.

Across four models, three data sets, and forty-eight languages, a clear split emerged. Models are surprisingly good at extracting the needed facts from a passage in another language. They are much weaker at answering in the expected language. Distracting extra passages hurt quality whatever their language, though distractors in the question's own language pulled slightly harder. The study separates retrieval quality from context use, guiding multilingual system design.
arxiv-2504-00697:
Robots working near people are often out of sight, so their noise may be the only clue to where they are. Marlene Wessels, Jorge de Heuvel, Leon Müller, Anna Luisa Maier, Maren Bennewitz, and Johannes Kraus tested how well people can place three robots by sound alone, inside virtual reality. Hearers listened to a moving robot for three seconds, then pointed to where they thought it stopped.

Robot type changed both how close and how steady the guesses were. A wheeled service robot was hardest to place, above all without an added alert sound. Yet people rated that same sound as the most pleasant and trustworthy of the three. Skill and liking pulled in opposite directions, a tension the team flags for robot design.
arxiv-2504-00997:
The authors introduce a new bracket that tracks how measurable quantities evolve in mechanical systems that both dissipate energy and roll under constraints, in a 2025 paper. Contact geometry handles the dissipation side, describing systems like engines losing heat. Nonholonomic constraints handle the rolling side, forbidding sideways slip. Combining the two is delicate.

Working in both the Lagrangian and Hamiltonian pictures, the paper defines the contact Eden bracket. Feeding any observable into the bracket returns its rate of change, the way the classic Poisson bracket does for frictionless systems. The authors also identify a special family of observables whose motion stays unconstrained, a clean sub-behavior inside messy dynamics. The result is a tool for theorists modeling real machines, which always leak energy and rarely move freely.
arxiv-2504-03997:
Seyedeh Baharan Khatami and co-workers rebuilt offline ranking review on causal grounds in a 2025 paper. Search and pick teams judge new rankers on logged clicks before risking live tests, but logs are biased: popular, top-placed. Conforming items get clicked for reasons unrelated to quality, and the missing clicks are not missing at random. Their setup reweights the logged data to mimic random exposure, converting the bias form into a missing-at-random problem that standard metrics can handle honestly.

Black-box tuning tunes the reweighting, guided by neural estimates of information-theoretic quantities. The causal formulation is system-agnostic, applying to any ranker whose outputs can be rescored. Tests validate fairer, more generalizable offline checks.
arxiv-2504-04897:
Tiziana Calamoneri, Federico Corò, and Giacomo Paesani study a guarding game played on networks, in a 2025 paper. Guards stand on some nodes of a graph. Each round, an attacker picks a link, and the defender slides guards along links so that every link still has a guard at one end. The question is how few guards can hold the network forever.

The team studies this eternal vertex cover problem on series-parallel graphs, a family built from simple series and parallel joins. For a smaller subfamily called melon graphs, they prove the best guard count can be computed in time that grows in a straight line with graph size. They also conjecture that the wider series-parallel family is hard in the formal sense, which would make their subfamily result a sharp border between easy and hard cases.
arxiv-2504-05097:
Liu Xiao, Li Zhiyuan, and Lin Yueyu boost a fast recurrent language model at run time without retraining its weights, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The model is RWKV-7, which keeps a running state rather than a growing cache of past tokens. Their method, called state tuning, grows and tunes only that state while the model runs.
