A small watcher model first learns how the state moves. A kernel trick then enlarges the state, and a decorrelated update rule tunes the larger state for the task. A small tuned model beat larger models on the target task in their tests. Readers get a cheap way to gain skill where compute is tight.
arxiv-2504-05797:
Phuc, Dang, Li, and Hung ask whether a faint nuclear resonance can sit on top of an already excited state. The pygmy dipole resonance is a small bump below the main giant resonance in neutron-rich nuclei. It probes the nuclear surface, where two kinds of vibration mix. Their test case is a neutron-rich germanium nucleus.

The team applies a phonon damping model, with and without pairing between nucleons. An exact pairing treatment predicts two gamma-ray lines with pygmy character at mild heat. Those energies match a recent experiment closely. Bookkeeping by energy levels traces the effect mainly to the first excited state of the nucleus. Surface mixing of isospin appears alongside. The hot resonance, they argue, grows from the giant mode coupling to loose particle and hole pairs.
arxiv-2504-05997: Andrii Kurkin, Kevin Shen, Susanne Pielawa, Hao Wang, and Vedran Dunjko prove universality for IQP circuits with hidden units in two thousand twenty-five. These quantum circuits form a generative model that trains on classic machines. Loss can rest on expectation values alone, which keeps training cheap. The plain model cannot make all distributions, a proven limit. Hidden units, traced out at the end, were guessed to lift that bar. Two proofs here confirm the guess. One is asymptotic, the other needs a sane count of extra qubits.
arxiv-2504-06697:
Stefan Albert Horstmann and co-authors study why software developers fail to build privacy rules into their code, in work from 2025. Privacy law in Europe sets duties such as user consent, purpose limits, and data minimisation. The team ran a five-hour programming study with thirty professional developers.

Each developer solved three privacy-sensitive tasks, in one of three setups: no help, privacy prompts, or a privacy expert on call. Nearly all solutions broke the rules, with most tasks failed by most developers. Prompts and expert support helped only slightly. Developers reported deep trouble with basic duties, yet few asked the expert or searched online for help. Low confidence did not lead to help-seeking. The authors argue better tooling and training are needed.
arxiv-2504-08897:
Jiaqi Lin and Abhronil Sengupta test how spiking neural networks trained by local rules withstand adversarial attacks in a 2025 study. Spiking networks, which communicate in brief pulses, can be fooled by inputs changed almost invisibly, like ordinary networks. Most attack studies assume training by backpropagation through time, a method with little biological realism.

Local learning rules relax those global requirements and look more brain-like, but their security was little studied. The authors examine adversarial robustness across four local training approaches. Knowing whether local learning hardens or weakens a network matters for neuromorphic hardware placed in open environments.
arxiv-2504-09497:
Aishwarya Sarath and Markus Böttcher modeled the light expected from a slowing jet blob in the X-ray binary MAXI J1348-630. During its 2019 and 2020 outburst, the system threw off a blob of plasma that later decelerated as it left an empty cavity and struck the gas between stars. An early reading of that slowdown implied more energy than the outburst could supply, but a smoother density change brought the estimate down to a realistic level.

The pair borrowed a blast-wave model from gamma-ray burst research and added energy losses and radiation drag for the fast electrons inside the blob. Their simulated radio and X-ray light curves closely match the observed ones, and the main emission peaks in X-rays.
arxiv-2504-10597:
A large working group of physicists, led by Chiara Arina, Benjamin Fuks, and Luca Panizzi, surveys dark matter models in a twenty twenty-five whitepaper. The models are of the t-channel kind, where dark matter talks to normal matter through a go-between particle. The report comes from the LHC Dark Matter Working Group at CERN.

The team ranges from the simplest setups, with one dark matter type and one go-between, to richer ones closer to full theories. For each class they weigh what colliders, the cosmos, and sky surveys can say. They also cover both fast-decaying and long-lived particles, and many ways dark matter could be made in the early universe.
arxiv-2504-11497:
Chang Liu, Emmanuel A. Olowe, and Danial Chitnis use a large language model as an agent to size parts in analog circuits, in work from twenty twenty-five. Sizing transistors by hand takes much skill and many rounds of trial. Machine learning helps, but still needs many runs and lacks design know how.

The agent links the model to circuit simulators and data tools through careful prompts. It tuned several basic circuits to meet target scores. Among the models tried, one stood out and was then used on a larger amplifier with nine score targets. In the best test group, the agent met the goals in up to sixty parts in a hundred runs. The work shows a path to faster circuit design.
arxiv-2504-13097:
Chayan Patra and Rahul Maitra sped up a workhorse quantum lab science method in 2025. The change-based eigensolver searches for a molecule's lowest energy by tuning a quantum circuit, but noise, flat regions. Local traps in its energy landscape stall the search and waste costly hardware time. Their formalism splits the circuit's settings into a small main set and a larger auxiliary set. Based on a guessed pecking order in how fast settings matter during tuning.

Only the small set is optimized straight, under an adiabatic shortcut. The rest are rebuilt afterward without further change-based search, then folded into the energy through fixes that plunge the estimate toward better minima. Resource use and accuracy both improve in their account.
arxiv-2504-14897:
Hu and three co-authors squeeze plasma sim data with a physics-first pack tool in this twenty twenty-five paper. Such sims can fill drives by the vast unit if each mote is kept in full. The speed spread of motes holds the tale of heat and beams in the gas.

Inside, bell-curve mixes stand in for the full speed spread of the mote cloud. A bin step first cuts the math load, then chip gear fits the mix live. The pack keeps the mean speed, heat, and beam birth facts that plain packs lose. Its squeeze rate ran to ten-thousand-fold in the tests the team ran. Run time sat on par with stock pack tools, or beat them in spots.
arxiv-2504-14997:
Yongwoo Choi, Hyeon-Dong Son, and Ho-Meoyng Choi compute the gravitational form factors of the pion in a light-front quark model. Their 2025 paper asks how the lightest hadron distributes momentum and pressure inside itself. Form factors encode those maps, and one of them, the D-term, probes the pion's inner mechanics.

The team apply one construction consistently to both the matrix elements and their Lorentz structures. That care removes extraction ambiguities that plague similar models. Tuned to match the pion's known decay constant and charge shape, the model yields a D-term near the value chiral theory predicts. Its mechanical radius comes out largest among the pion's radii, and its two-dimensional pressure and shear maps satisfy the required stability checks.
arxiv-2504-16097:
Buzelin and co-authors design LGA-ECG, a model that reads heart tracings with both local and global attention. Heart disease is the top cause of death worldwide, so sharp ECG tools matter. Transformers catch rhythm patterns well but often miss fine waveform shapes.

Their fix blends convolutional bias with global self-attention in one model. Queries come from averaging embeddings across overlapping convolution windows, which spotlights local shape. Keys and values span the whole sequence, keeping rhythm context in view. Tests on the CODE-15 dataset beat prior top models. Ablation runs confirmed each part of the design earns its place.
arxiv-2504-19197:
Sandipan Dhar, Nanda Dulal Jana, and Swagatam Das review adversarial methods for changing a voice's identity in a 2025 survey. Voice conversion keeps the words but swaps the speaker's vocal character, enabling film dubbing, singing conversion, and aids for people whose speech is impaired. Generative adversarial networks, two models trained in opposition, became a leading engine for the swap because they produce natural sounding output.

The review sorts techniques, open challenges, and recent progress. Conversion quality still hinges on disentangling content from identity, the problem every method in the survey attacks from a different side.
arxiv-2504-20097:
Junran Guo and a large team of co-authors showed drone spotting with no camera, at city range. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with a hard task: small drones far off, key for safety and watch work. Camera ways need sharp, costly shots and eat power. Their way reads one photon pixel range echoes and calls the craft by data, with no image made. Past runs of that way reach just a few hundred meters.

Their new build stretches that reach in a true field test in a city. Readers in sensing get proof that photon lean gear can name a drone across town, at low kit cost.
arxiv-2504-20197:
Aryeh Brill offers a geometric way to think about what deep neural networks learn, in a 2025 paper. A network turns raw data into internal patterns of activity, and splitting those patterns into features a human can name would make the systems safer and easier to trust. Brill treats the learned features as a coordinate grid laid over the shape of the data itself.

To study that grid, the paper models a typical data distribution as a random lattice, a mesh with random links. It borrows tools from percolation theory, the study of flow through such meshes. Features then sort into three kinds: those naming the broad context, those naming parts, and those naming the surface. The model lines up with recent findings from work that probes networks directly. Brill closes by pointing to questions the lattice picture raises for future research on how networks build their inner maps.
arxiv-2504-20897:
Ekta Chaubey and Vasily Sotnikov extend a tidy recipe for particle physics integrals to the elliptic case. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Feynman integrals, which encode particle interactions, become far neater when written in a canonical form, and special integrand bases can force that form.

In the simpler genus-zero world, bases built from logarithmic forms with whole-number leading behavior do the job. Elliptic curves push the problem to genus one. The authors argue that one careful choice of algebraic forms, avoiding derivatives, is the key step. The resulting integrals obey a new special form of differential equation. Order by order, their solutions stay pure functions. The authors conjecture the recipe works in general.
arxiv-2505-00097:
Nishita Jadoo, Terrence Pierre Jacques, and Zachariah Etienne present superB, a tool that lets a black hole simulation code grow from one machine to a whole cluster. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Gravitational wave science needs ever sharper simulations of colliding black holes. The team's base framework writes fast code from Python, but it ran on a single node.

The new extension auto-generates a task-based, cluster-ready version of the same physics modules. It splits the grids and manages the talk between parts. On one node its results match the old code bit for bit. A head-on black hole collision run reproduces the expected ringdown tones. On sixty-four nodes it ran about forty-five times faster than the single-node code. The upgrade readies the framework for long inspirals and rapid event follow-ups.
arxiv-2505-01597:
Simone Servadio published an aerospace engineering paper in 2025 on particle flow filters. Such filters track uncertain systems, like spacecraft, by moving sample points. The points flow toward the most likely states instead of being reweighted. A drift term pushes them, and a diffusion term keeps them spread out.

Servadio derives new forms for both terms using high-order polynomial expansions. Older methods based on straight-line approximations become simple cases of the new one. Differential algebra carries the math directly on the polynomial forms. Two new filters result, differing in where the expansion is centered. Numerical tests showed clear gains over standard flows. The gains were largest against the exact flow comparison.
arxiv-2505-03497:
Stijn Cambie and Michiel Provoost study edge-colouring games set by Erdős and by Bensmail and Mc Inerney. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five; the pack row gives no title or year, so the text head is the source. Two players take turns to colour edges of a full graph in their own hue. Each aims to grow a graph trait in their own sub-graph, such as the largest clique or the top degree.

In the fair form, they give a first step toward a known guess, a new guess for the degree game, and spreads of both games to wider graph kinds. In the biased form, where turns colour unlike counts of edges, the degree and vertex games are settled, and one clique case is proved.
arxiv-2505-06197:
Tronconi and Venturi ask whether the Higgs field alone, dressed by quantum corrections, could have inflated the early universe and seeded primordial black holes, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Higgs inflation needs no new inflaton particle, which makes it economical, but producing black holes requires a burst of large curvature ripples.

Their model starts from the tree-level action of gravity plus the Standard Model Higgs. A series of higher-dimension operators, standing in for quantum corrections, modifies the dynamics. Inside a minimal effective field theory framework, they present two viable versions. In both, the ripple spectrum matches cosmic microwave background observations on large scales. On small scales it grows enough to collapse into primordial black holes of asteroid-like mass. Such black holes could, in principle, make up all of the dark matter. The paper ties the universe's largest mystery to its best-known particle.
arxiv-2505-07097:
Shaul Zemel shows how to normalize higher Specht polynomials in a matched way so a stable version of them can be defined, in algebra tied to symmetry groups. These polynomials give bases for key representation spaces. The work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The author also splits a non transitive action by other scholars into its orbits. A basis of higher Specht polynomials from further work is shown to respect that split. For a set size, the orbits match subsets of the positive integers below that size. The representation for a set is then linked to two for the next size up, one the set itself and one with the top number added, a lift of the branching rule.
arxiv-2505-07597:
Junfan Yi, Ke-ke Shang, and Michael Small propose a new way to locate moving objects in three dimensions in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Older methods need costly gear or fixed reference objects to measure angles. Their approach needs neither, and it leans on math plus artificial intelligence.

The model uses the time pattern of a moving object to infer its relative angles, then solves for its position with a standard matrix method. In tests, three cameras tracked a drone. An improved vision model read the drone's flat positions, and the math model turned them into three-dimensional coordinates with low error. The authors say the method suits targets that do not cooperate.
arxiv-2505-08597:
Laura Torchia and Massimo Capone present a 2025 theory study of a two-band superconductor that can flip into an insulator. Their model pairs an attractive pull between electrons with a repulsive exchange term tied to spin alignment. A strong sound-wave coupling in real materials can flip the base pull negative while the exchange stays put. The team solve the model at zero temperature and half filling.

Even with no exchange, two bands give the flip as the pull grows, unlike the one-band case. Exchange makes the pull act stronger and hastens the flip. The flip arrives as the particle weight fades to zero, much like the famed Mott flip. Attractive systems thus host a correlated flip of their own. The work guides hunts in real two-band materials.
arxiv-2505-08897:
Felipe Augusto Tasca, Paulinho Demeneghi, Víctor Marín, and Willian Goulart Gomes Velasco prove a P-theorem for inverse semigroupoids in two thousand twenty-five. Their tool is ordered partial actions and their globalizations. Every such action of an inverse semigroupoid admits a globalization, they show. That bridge links ordered actions of groupoids to McAlister style triples.

The multi-object version of those triples is the new form here. From it the P-theorem falls out in full. Each E-unitary inverse semigroupoid is a semidirect product from such an action. The action lives on a multi-object semilattice in their build.
arxiv-2505-09497:
Sourav Pal and Abhik Basu study traffic-like shocks in single-file motion with a bottleneck in two thousand twenty-five. Particles that move one way in a narrow channel model many real flows, from cell cargo to city traffic. A shock, or domain wall, is a sharp line where density jumps.

Their model is a simple grid automaton in a closed loop with a fixed particle count and one slow spot. At high entry and exit rates with many particles, the shock shape stops depending on those rates, a new kind of universality, though edge layers still vary. At low rates the shape does depend on the rates. Extra tuning can also free the shock to wander.
arxiv-2505-12697:
Li, Chen, Shao, Lian, and Liu wrote in twenty twenty-five about a code embedding model trained on massive synthetic data. Embedding models turn code into numbers that capture meaning for search. Retrieval tools in software work depend on such models. Good training data for code are scarce, which limits past models. The team built a huge synthetic data set under rules stressing diversity, reliability, and usability. Their model, CodeR, trains on that data with a staged learning plan.

The plan transfers knowledge across mixed data sources step by step. Tests covered sixteen varied code retrieval tasks. CodeR beat existing baselines by clear margins on those tasks. It also generalized well to domains outside its training set. The authors release code and the trained model openly. They aim to support further work on code search.
arxiv-2505-12897:
Piotr Borycki and co-authors present EPIC, a way to explain image classifiers with prototypes, in this 2025 paper. Explanation tools split into two camps. Post hoc tools work on any trained model but give coarse heat maps. Built in prototype methods explain clearly but need special training from scratch.

EPIC bridges the two camps. It runs on pretrained models with no architecture change. Yet its explanations show representative image patches, like prototype methods do. Users see concrete examples behind a prediction instead of vague hot regions. The method aims at general use across models and datasets. That breadth was the weakness of earlier prototype systems. Faithful, readable explanations support trust in deployed vision systems.
arxiv-2505-13397:
Benoit Dherin and five co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on use of classic equation solvers as the engine of deep learning. Gradient descent, the workhorse of the field, is the plainest solver of the gradient flow equation: the Euler step. Far sharper solvers exist, the Runge-Kutta family chief among them. They have seen little use in deep learning so far.

The team tests high order Runge-Kutta solvers as training engines. They map where the solvers strain and craft fixes. Key tricks of modern optimizers are folded in: preconditioning, pace that adapts, and momentum. The aim is a solver that tracks the flow more true and more stable than Euler steps.
arxiv-2505-14997:
Jeong Rae Kim and co-authors published this materials physics paper in 2025. It reports the growth of thin films of niobium monoxide, NbO, a superconductor with an unusual crystal structure: a rock-salt lattice with a quarter of its sites empty in an ordered pattern. Making such films is tricky because the compound holds an uncommon oxidation state and needs growth temperatures above a thousand degrees.

Using molecular beam epitaxy, the team compared substrates and found sapphire worked best for clean, single-phase films. The films superconducted at temperatures up to 1.37 kelvin, on par with bulk crystals of the same material. The authors say the work removes key bottlenecks in growing high-temperature films of reluctant compounds. It also adds a vacancy-ordered material to the thin-film superconductor toolbox.
arxiv-2505-16597:
Chuhongxu Chen and nine co-authors warned in twenty twenty-five about a trusty electrode. The silver-silver chloride type can contaminate the nanofluidic work it serves. These are prized for how stable they are in micro- and nanoscale fluidics. Yet in chloride-rich solutions the coat on one dissolves. It forms silver complexes that drift into the trial.

The team showed silver particles plating onto graphene by electrodeposition. The source was that dissolved silver and nothing else. That gives a plainer account of a recent claim of an ionic flow-induced current in graphene. The current in fact comes from silver plating. It does not come from the claimed ionic Coulomb drag effect. The team urges care with these in delicate systems. The slow loss of the coat is easy to miss. It can change how a result is read.
arxiv-2505-16797:
Hanyue Lou, Jinxiu Liang, and colleagues turn ordinary video into training data for event cameras in a 2025 computer vision study. Event cameras report pixel changes with microsecond timing and huge dynamic range, but learning algorithms for them starve. Real event data are scarce, and existing simulators produce files too bulky to move or store. Their video-to-voxel pipeline simulates event streams efficiently enough to scale.

Compact simulated data let event vision models train at the scale their accuracy demands. Better event models serve fast robotics and low-power sensing, where ordinary cameras blur or saturate.
arxiv-2505-16897:
Ashmita Das, Anjana Krishnan, Soham Sen, and Sunandan Gangopadhyay study a 2025 radiation effect that arises when an atom falls past a horizon-like edge while sitting in a high-grade cavity. The effect is called horizon brightened acceleration radiation. It gives a way to probe how motion and gravity-like settings change the light an atom emits or absorbs.

Most past work linked the atom to the size of the field wave itself, but that choice leads to blow-ups in a key limit for light fields in low dimensions. The authors instead link the atom to the field's momentum, for both a point-like atom and one with real size. They find how the chance of a jump between energy levels changes under this choice. The new link also removes the old blow-up in a natural way.
arxiv-2505-17897:
Zi-Ao Ma and seven colleagues wrote a 2025 paper on judging AI-made images in a way people can follow. Text-to-image models now draw well, and someone must grade their output at scale. Human grading is slow, and using pricey closed models adds heavy cost.

Open models trained on critique sets are one fix, but good critique data is scarce. Their system, T2I-Eval-R1, uses reinforcement learning to teach an open model to reason about image quality. The grader explains its scores, not just spits out a number. Clear reasons help users trust or challenge each grade. The team aims for cheap grading that stays open to inspection.
arxiv-2505-18297:
Andersson, Gnoatto, and García Trillos solved a hard equation family with deep learning in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Backward stochastic Volterra equations model problems where today's value depends on the whole past path. Classical solvers nest time steps inside time steps, which explodes in cost. Their network learns both solution fields in a single training stage.

For the simpler decoupled case they prove an error bound with the expected time-step rate. Experiments matched that rate closely. Accuracy held steady from a few variables up to five hundred, while graphics hardware kept run times nearly flat. The same solver handled fully coupled systems too. The authors aim it at stochastic control and finance problems.
arxiv-2505-19397:
Jiawen Zhang and co-authors test whether time series foundation models can stand up to adversarial attacks, in work from twenty twenty-five. The models forecast well with no task training and now enter high stakes systems. Their weakness under attack had barely been probed.

The team built a test frame tuned to time series limits, with scale free scores for white box and black box attacks. Across six models, small tweaks reliably bent forecasts into trend flips or false drifts. Longer context windows raised the risk, and flaws near the forecast horizon stood out. Attacks moved poorly between models, which hints at model specific flaws. Simple attack aware fine tuning gave large robustness gains at low cost.
arxiv-2505-19597:
Zheng Wang and five co-authors build a light speech-cleaning system for two-channel sound in loud noise, by a join of classic and learned parts. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Learned multi-channel cleaners do well, but they are too heavy for scant gear, most of all when noise drowns the speech. The classic part gives a rough split of speech and noise. A trimmed learned net then refines the speech. The team tests ways to use both the raw sound and the rough split to the full. The system cleans speech well with few terms and low cost. It suits small tools that must run live.
arxiv-2505-19797:
Yiqun Zhang and his fourteen co-authors, publishing in 2025, ask whether teams of small open language models can beat the giant closed ones. Their recipe, called the Avengers, sorts each incoming question by topic. It looks up which small models have done best on that kind of question, and lets the top ones answer several times and vote. The system pools ten open models of modest size and needs no retraining.

Across 15 test sets covering math, coding, logic, general knowledge, and emotion tasks, the combined system beat GPT-4o and its newer siblings on average. The margin was largest in math, about 18 points over GPT-4.1, and about 7 points in coding. The team also reports the method holds up on new kinds of questions and does not depend much on which sorting or voting parts are swapped in.
arxiv-2505-19897:
Sun and a large team introduced ScienceBoard in twenty twenty-five, a testbed for AI agents doing real scientific work on computers. Language model agents can now operate software through screens and interfaces, much like a human user. Such agents could speed routine research tasks, but judging them needs realistic tests.

ScienceBoard offers two parts. One is a multi-domain environment with real professional software for fields such as biochemistry, astronomy, and geoinformatics. The other is a benchmark of one hundred sixty-nine human-made, carefully checked tasks drawn from real workflows. Leading agents, including ones based on GPT-4o and Claude, solved only about fifteen percent of tasks overall. The authors analyze the failures and draw design lessons for building more capable research agents.
arxiv-2506-00097:
Mostafizur Rahaman Laskar and Richa Goel present a quantum method for forecasting data that changes over time. Their paper came out in two thousand twenty-five. Time series forecasts matter in fields from weather study to molecular motion. Standard tools can be heavy and slow to train. The authors aim for a leaner model that runs on real quantum hardware.

Their Quantum Time Series model writes scaled data into single-qubit rotations. Fixed patterns of entanglement then carry the time structure of the data. Training cost grows only with the log of the data size. They test the model on IBM quantum hardware. The results are set against classic methods to show where the quantum route holds up.
arxiv-2506-00197:
Shen and three co-authors probe how pet chat tools leak their fed files in this twenty twenty-five paper. Fed files lift tool replies, yet their facts may slip to sharp asks. Past work showed ask tricks lone; true leak roads may run wide.

Inside, six score ten thousand tools' files and flows fed the hunt. Five leak roads fell out, from tag lists to run-box acts. One run tool flaw let sharp asks pull whole files down near full. Near three in ten leaked files bore rights marks in the pool. The team sets fix steps for tool hosts and file feeds.
arxiv-2506-01597:
Yixian Zhang and co-authors bring a faster style of training to reinforcement learning policies written as flexible kernel functions, in a 2025 paper. Such policies can take many shapes, but training them has been stuck with slow first-order methods. Second-order methods, modeled on Newton's approach, converge faster yet seem to demand inverting an endless matrix in this setting.

The team sidesteps the inversion by training against a reshaped goal with a cubic penalty term. A classic theorem then shrinks the endless problem into a finite one sized by the amount of trial data. They prove the method settles at a local best point with fast final convergence. Tests on a toy investing task and standard benchmarks beat first-order kernel methods and other second-order rivals in speed and reward.
arxiv-2506-03397:
Nourozi builds fresh codes from plane curves and a learn-aided read plan. The curves rest on split forms, a set class of bends. One case uses the F3 field with a set curve form. It gives a code of length 27, width 13, and span 4. That code yields a quantum code with the same three marks. The read plan runs in two steps to fix code flaws.

Step one runs a greed search on the flaw signs first. Step two trains a Deep Q net to fix the rest. Noise tests use a mixed flip frame for the code runs. The learn step cuts fail rates by a vast span next to greed. The work thus widens both code clans drawn from such curves.
arxiv-2506-03997:
Alviano, Giordano, and Theseider Dupré set out a frame in twenty twenty-five for if-then thought in answer set programs. Such programs solve hard tasks by rules that list what must hold. Their frame adds soft rules that say what holds in the most plain or most liked cases.

The frame pairs a soft fact base with a plain program and lets users ask what follows from the pair. Its sense rests on a ranked view of worlds, with a known soft logic as a plain case. If-then claims are coded back into the same program kind. They also give a cap on how hard the task can get.
arxiv-2506-04197:
Roy Araiza, Marius Junge, and Peixue Wu build a noncommutative optimal transport framework for quantum channels, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Their channels act on von Neumann algebras. The central object is a Lipschitz cost measure. It prices the minimal cost of moving between quantum states through a given channel.

A companion Lipschitz contraction coefficient measures how much a channel shrinks Wasserstein-type distances. The authors establish basic properties of both quantities. These include continuity, dual formulations, and behavior under composition and tensor products. Applications recover known quantities such as expected group word length and Carnot-Carathéodory distance. When the contraction coefficient falls strictly below one, entropy contraction follows. Mixing time estimates then become available for certain non-symmetric channels.
arxiv-2506-05697:
Valeria Ramirez and Christian Valqui compute the Groebner basis of a system of polynomial equations connected to the Jacobian conjecture. Their paper came out in 2025. The conjecture, a famous open problem, asks whether a polynomial map whose derivative has constant determinant must have a polynomial inverse.

A Groebner basis is a special generating set that makes a polynomial system tractable, much as row reduction tames linear systems. By computing it, the authors gain full control over the system in question. They then describe the solution set completely, listing exactly which points satisfy all the equations at once. Complete descriptions like this are rare for systems tied to open conjectures. The work gives other researchers a firm foothold for testing related cases.
arxiv-2506-06897:
Mahault Albarracin and Dalton Sakthivadivel offer a theory paper from twenty twenty-five on what it means for a living or artificial system to be resilient. They work within the free energy principle, a framework that treats staying alive as keeping a workable model of oneself and the world. Earlier work used that framework to model resilience from the outside. The authors argue instead that resilience sits at the center of the framework itself, because keeping an identity requires constant adjustment.

On their view, a system holds together by reshaping its self-model as conditions change, and that reshaping takes energy. They sketch a general framework for thinking this way and give simple models to show it in action. The paper will interest readers who study adaptive systems, self-organization, and theories of life.
arxiv-2506-07197:
Jia-Jie Han and six co-authors compute rare particle decays in this two thousand twenty-five physics paper. The decays involve the Lambda b baryon, which can split into a proton plus a light meson. Of interest is CP violation, a subtle gap between how matter and antimatter behave. The team studies a list of such decays, with pions, kaons, and related mesons in the final state.

They use an approach based on perturbative quantum chromodynamics. Their sums include effects up to second order in the strong coupling. They add finer details of how quarks are shared inside the hadrons. The resulting rates and asymmetries form a clear pattern. For the best-known channels, the predicted violation is as small as current data suggest. Other channels may show larger effects worth hunting at colliders.
arxiv-2506-08297:
Nhat Thanh Tran, Fanghui Xue, and colleagues redesign the attention mechanism at the heart of transformers in a 2025 study. Full attention costs grow quadratically with input size, while the cheaper linear variant cannot focus sharply. The authors define attention generally enough to contain both versions, then prove a dispersion result: spread too thin, attention loses the signal as inputs lengthen.

Their design localizes tokens and averages within neighborhoods, borrowing the efficiency pattern of state-space sequence models. The goal is attention that scales to long image token streams without going blurry, a standing need in computer vision backbones.
arxiv-2506-09297:
Caio da Silva and three co-authors put Newton's method, adapted to curved spaces, through a thorough numerical trial. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Optimization on manifolds arises when answers must obey shapes, such as sets of perpendicular frames.

The team compared the curved-space method with the classic flat version patched with extra constraints. The test problem came from quantum chemistry: finding the lowest energy state of molecules. Across one hundred twenty-five molecules, the curved methods converged more often, needed fewer steps, and cared less about the starting guess. The authors also study a numerical catch when the cost lives on a quotient space. A fix that ignores the smallest curvature values proved stable.
arxiv-2506-12097:
Suriyakumar, Sekhari, and Wilson set out UCD, a run-time way to un-teach chat tools. Un-teach aims to strip set facts from a tool but keep its skill. Facts in view may be soft or banned for the tool's use. Their way steers outs by twin small tools at run time. One small tool trained sans the strip set, one with it in. The gap twixt those two guides the big tool's outs.

That steer lifts the trade twixt strip force and kept skill. Two test sets, TOFU and MUSE, grade the way in runs. Gains show in strip grade and kept scores next to past ways. The team reads twin steer as a cheap, apt path here. It suits vast tools where re-train costs run too high.
arxiv-2506-13997:
Ananya Shah builds, in a 2025 paper, a topological test for gerrymandering that reads voting maps the way a geometer reads terrain. District lines are drawn by politicians, but precincts, the smallest voting units, are too small to rig one by one. So if district-level voting patterns warp away from precinct-level ones, manipulation is a prime suspect. Persistent homology, which tracks how patterns persist across scales, supplies the measuring tape.

Across North Carolina House elections from 2012 to 2024, precinct patterns stayed stable while district patterns lurched in redistricting years, a signal that classic compactness scores missed. Extended to newer maps, the method flags the Texas plan struck down as a racial gerrymander, and reads California's and Louisiana's contested maps as well. The author also turns the tool on racial vote margins directly, a first for this framework.
arxiv-2506-14297:
Victor Alves, Carla Bezerra, Ivan Machado, and three colleagues grade the quality of tests written by language models in this two thousand twenty-five study. Writing test scripts by hand is slow, costly, and error-prone, so automated generation is attractive. The team had three models, GPT-4o, Amazon Q, and Llama 3.3, generate Python test suites under two prompting styles: from text descriptions and from existing code. They catalogued errors and test smells in the output.

Most generated suites contained at least one error or smell. Assertion errors dominated, at about sixty-four percent of all errors, and lack of cohesion among test cases was the commonest smell. Detailed textual prompts produced fewer errors but more smells. GPT-4o made the fewest errors in both settings, while Amazon Q made the most. The authors also link specific errors, like assertion and indentation faults, to cohesion smells.
arxiv-2506-14697:
Aishan Liu and a team of colleagues wrote a 2025 paper on AgentSafe, a benchmark for the safety of embodied AI agents. Embodied agents are robots and virtual agents that see, plan, and act in human environments, often guided by vision-language models. When such an agent follows a hazardous instruction, the harm can be physical.

Older safety tests cover few kinds of hazard and check only the final outcome. This benchmark follows the whole chain of perception, planning, and execution, so failures can be located precisely. It systematically feeds agents dangerous instructions and scores how they respond. A fuller test helps developers find unsafe behavior before these agents are deployed around people.
arxiv-2506-15497:
Changzeng Fu surveyed machines that sense and respond to human emotion in a 2025 book on affective computing. The book opens with the history of human-computer interaction, then builds the science base from psychology and brain research on how feelings arise and show. From there it covers the main channels machines can read: faces, voices, brain signals, and body signals.

Chapters explain emotion theories, recognition from single and mixed channels, and ways for machines to express feeling back, including social robots. Uses in schooling, health, entertainment, and personal help get their own treatment. Open problems include merging messy data streams, guarding privacy, and handling the ethics of machines that act like companions.
arxiv-2506-15697:
Yi Liu and five co-authors built DeepRTL2 in twenty twenty-five, a language model family serving the register-transfer level where chips are designed. Language models had already helped write and explain RTL code. But the embedding-based chores of design work had been neglected. Those chores include searching code by description, checking behavioral equivalence, and predicting performance.

DeepRTL2 unifies generation and embedding tasks in one versatile model family. The authors present it as the first comprehensive model of its kind for electronic design automation. Across their evaluations it reached state-of-the-art results on every task tested, both the writing side and the retrieval-and-judgment side. A single model spanning the workflow could speed up how engineers draft, find, verify, and tune hardware descriptions.
arxiv-2506-17297:
Mishra and colleagues introduced in twenty twenty-five a free Python library called SafeRL-Lite. Reinforcement learning trains agents by trial and reward, but agents can learn unsafe acts. Many toolkits lack firm safety limits or plain reasons for choices. SafeRL-Lite wraps standard training worlds and deep Q-learning agents. It adds hard limits during training and tools that explain choices after the fact.

Explanations use SHAP values and saliency maps, which highlight what drove a choice. The library also tracks how often limits were broken. Tests on a constrained pole-balancing task show both the policy logic and its safety record. The code is light, open, and can be installed with pip. It aims to make safe learning easier to build and audit.
arxiv-2506-19797:
Mubaraq Yakubu, Navodini Wijethilake, Jonathan Shapey, Andrew King, and Alexander Hammers wrote this review in two thousand twenty-five, with one surname spelled in a variant way in its text. It takes stock of auto methods that cut the pituitary gland and its tumors out of MRI scans.

The team sifted dozens of studies of auto and semi-auto methods. Deep learning rules the field, with U-Net kin the most used. Scores swing wide, above all for the small gland, where auto cuts can fail hard. Tumor cuts fare better, and semi-auto cuts are steadier. Many papers skip key facts such as field strength and tumor size. Bigger, more mixed data sets are the clear need.
arxiv-2506-20097:
Wang Bill Zhu and four co-authors presented PSALM-V in twenty twenty-five, a system that learns the rules of actions in visual worlds by trial and error. Symbolic planners need each action's preconditions and effects written in the PDDL language; hand-writing them is the bottleneck. Language models can draft them, but earlier attempts assumed text worlds, full observability, or explicit error messages.

PSALM-V instead interacts with the environment: it proposes plans and candidate semantics, executes, and explains failures by refining a tree of beliefs about each action's rules. It even infers the problem file itself. On the ALFRED household benchmark it raised plan success from thirty-seven to seventy-four percent under partial observability. It also induced correct rules for two games and a real robot block-stacking task.
arxiv-2506-21397:
Datta and Samanta study how a supercooled phase change reshapes gravitational wave signals in twenty twenty-five. Some extensions of the Standard Model predict the early universe supercooled before changing phase. Such transitions themselves generate strong gravitational waves. The authors ask what they do to waves from other sources.

Their test source is a network of metastable cosmic strings. A supercooled phase triggers a burst of thermal inflation between the sources. That inflation suppresses the high frequency part of the string spectrum. Regions of string parameter space once ruled out by LIGO reopen. The combined signal still matches pulsar timing array hints at low frequencies. Future detectors could see the distinctive two part spectrum.
arxiv-2506-21497:
Jiashuo Wang and seven co-authors teach chat models to hold a user's interest in social talk, by learning from how the talk later unfolds. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Past work taught models to plan acts or draw on facts, but the link from such steps to true engagement is weak. The team uses the user's next move, tied to the aim of the talk, as a direct reward sign. They build a fake user to trade lines with the target model. A search method then roams through paths the talk could take. The aim is a chat partner that learns what keeps people in the talk.
arxiv-2506-21897:
Twisha Chattopadhyay and seven co-authors show how a 3D printer's secrets can leak through video in this two thousand twenty-five security paper. Factories often watch printers with cameras, since print areas can be unsafe for people. The team shows that such footage gives away the design being printed. Their system tracks the printer nozzle as it moves. It turns that path back into the machine instructions, called G-code.

The system also recovers settings such as feed rate and extrusion rate. A checker then proves the stolen instructions match the original print. The attack threatens makers in fields from health care to defense. The paper warns that camera feeds of production lines need guarding like any other trade secret.
arxiv-2506-22197:
Darius Eros and Sebastian Gieger prove a Cartan-Hadamard claim for space-times with no need for smooth form. The work came out in 2025. The old claim says a space with no more than flat bend has one path of least time span for each pair of points.

Their form is built by hand from parts, not smooth curves. It works in the young frame of Lorentz-style length spaces. There, bend is set by side-by-side checks, not slope math. It takes an old find for plain gap spaces to this new home. It broadens the smooth claim of Beem and Ehrlich. The core is a new sense of near-in bend fit for such spaces. With world-wide time form and a link term in place, time-like paths of least span exist for linked points, and each is the sole one.
arxiv-2507-00697:
Huadong Gao, Yuhui Huang, and Wen Xie analyze a numerical method for a classic equation in a 2025 mathematics study. Poisson's equation links a function to its sources, but rough boundary data break standard methods. Textbook approaches need boundary values with more smoothness than many real problems provide.

The authors work with very weak solutions, which make sense of the rough case. They apply a mixed finite element method named for Raviart and Thomas directly, without first smoothing the data. Their proof shows the numerical solution converges to the very weak solution. They also establish how fast that convergence happens as the mesh is refined.
arxiv-2507-01197:
Dhamdhawach Horsuwan tunes a common industrial controller by its spectrum in a 2025 paper. The controller is the proportional-integral type, a two-knob workhorse, and the plant is the awkward kind that integrates its input and answers late, called IPDT. The goal is one tuning that makes both following a setpoint and shrugging off disturbances decay at the same clean exponential rate.

His method minimizes the spectral abscissa, the slowest decay rate among the closed loop's poles. A semi-discrete model captures the integrator and the delay while letting the dominant poles be pulled out cheaply. Those poles are mapped back to continuous time and polished against the exact delay equation. The result is a single gain set with no hand-set trade-off weights. Simulations show faster settling and better safety margins than the classic tuning rules.
arxiv-2507-02897:
Nathaniel Chen and co-authors built an AI controller for a fusion reactor that regulators could actually inspect. Fusion control systems increasingly use black-box AI, which safety rules struggle to accept. The team instead used a deliberately simple, linear, and interpretable design. It watches camera images of the DIII-D tokamak's divertor, the exhaust region where hot plasma must be cooled before it strikes the wall.

The controller doses deuterium gas to hold the exhaust plasma in a detached state, hovering off the wall without collapsing the reaction. In tests it tracked the target within about two percent, through both detachment and reattachment. Because every step of the method is transparent, the authors argue it offers a template for compliant AI control in future reactors.
arxiv-2507-03197:
Jiarui Li and five co-authors open a black box in immunology in twenty twenty-five. T cells spot antigens that MHC molecules present through their receptors. Knowing how that binding works is key to grasping immunity and to building new cures. Transformer models such as TULIP predict the binding well but give no account of how they reach a call.

Older ways to explain a model cannot cope with the encoder-decoder transformers used here. The team puts forth QCAI, which puts a number on cross-attention interaction. Cross-attention is where receptor and peptide meet inside the model and weigh each other. By gauging its strength pair by pair, the method shows which contacts push the model toward its call. The gain is a read on the workings: which links the model leans on, not just its final call.
arxiv-2507-03497:
Pieter Kleer and Daan Noordenbos study when to stop and take an offer, knowing only how the best offer is distributed. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. A sequence of correlated offers arrives one by one. The full correlation pattern is usually unknown in practice. The authors assume just the law of the maximum value. They then guard against the worst correlation that fits it.

A simple threshold rule proves nearly optimal in that worst case. The threshold is the monopoly price of the maximum's distribution. The result needs the expected maximum to grow slower than the count of offers. A second result rounds out the picture. Decision theory gains a middle path between ignorance and full knowledge.
arxiv-2507-04797:
Zuo Ye, Yubo Sun, and Gennian Ge build codes that can fix bursts of lost symbols, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Such losses can hit stored data in a tight cluster or in one small spot. A good code adds as little extra data as it can while still fixing the loss.

Their code first picks sequences whose step-by-step changes stay close to balanced. Two added checks then help pin down where the loss sits. The new codes use less extra data than the best prior ones, and the method is simpler. The authors also give a fast way to encode any input.
arxiv-2507-07297:
Chengfei Wu and five co-authors built a bench to test if vision models truly ground their thought in images. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with large vision-language models. Such models ace visual questions, but they may ride on surface cues and set bias, not on real sight. Their bench, MagiC, grades more than the end reply: it grades the step path and how that path lines up with image proof.

The set holds thousands of machine made questions and a core of hand built ones with marks, reasons, and boxes. Fifteen models were graded on it. Readers who build vision AI get a way to split true grounded thought from lucky pattern play.
arxiv-2507-08597:
Md Tanvirul Alam, Aritran Piplai, and Nidhi Rastogi present a malware detection method in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Machine learning classifiers degrade over time as malware evolves, a problem called concept drift. Keeping them current needs fresh labeled data, which is expensive to annotate. Active learning helps somewhat, but semi-supervised use of unlabeled data remains underexplored for malware.

Their algorithm, ADAPT, uses pseudo-labeling: the model confidently labels new samples itself and retrains on them. The method is model-agnostic, working with neural networks and tree-based classifiers alike. Experiments spanned five diverse datasets covering Android, Windows, and PDF malware. ADAPT consistently outperformed plain baselines and competitive benchmarks. The authors argue pseudo-labeling is a practical, cheaper route to keeping malware detectors effective as threats drift.
arxiv-2507-09697:
Xi Yang, Haitao Chen, Lucas Kreiss, and five co-authors present a microscope that photographs areas at detail in this two thousand twenty-five optics paper. Large-area microscopy at submicron resolution tends to trade off field of view, resolution, and speed, and centimeter-scale samples are but rarely flat, forcing mechanical scanning to stay in focus. Their instrument, PANORAMA, takes a single shot in place of that. It re-images the sample through a telecentric photolithography lens and a large-aperture tube lens onto an array of micro-cameras.

Each camera in the array runs its focus live, so curved or uneven samples stay sharp across the whole field. The upshot is gigapixel imaging over sixteen by nineteen millimeters at under one micron resolution, with no scanning. The team stresses throughput and adaptability for biomedical and materials imaging, where large, imperfect samples are the norm, not the exception.
arxiv-2507-10597:
Grégoire Pierra and Simone Mastrogiovanni wrote a 2025 chapter that introduces the use of gravitational waves to study how the universe expands. Gravitational waves are ripples from events such as merging black holes. Their signals carry a direct measure of distance, so they can act as standard sirens, much like standard candles in older astronomy.

The chapter explains two main approaches, called bright sirens and dark sirens, and what data each one needs. It covers the math used to draw cosmic measures from wave events, and how the choice of which events get detected can skew results. Worked examples show each method in action. New readers get a clear path into a fast-growing field.
arxiv-2507-10997:
Michael Hatzon, Eugene Ivanov, Aaron Quiskamp, and Michael Tobar report, in a 2025 paper, a readout trick. It lets the faintest thermal hum of a resonator stand out from the noise of the instrument itself. Measuring thermal fluctuations in microwave and mechanical resonators pushes amplifiers to their limits, because the amplifier's own noise floods the signal. Their system splits the signal into two channels and cross-correlates them.

Under the right conditions, the amplifier's intrinsic noise, shared by both channels, cancels in the cross-spectrum while the resonator's true thermal peak survives. On a room-temperature sapphire cavity at nine gigahertz, the thermal peak's contrast improved by more than sixteen decibels over a single channel. The authors note that telling broad from narrow fluctuations is exactly what dark matter searches with cold resonators need. The method is offered as a general sharpening tool for precision measurement.
arxiv-2507-13097:
Adithyavairavan Murali and nine co-authors present GraspGen, a system that generates six-degree-of-freedom grasps for robot grippers. Their paper came out in 2025. Six degrees of freedom means the grasp is specified by position and orientation in space, which is what a real robot arm needs.

The system uses a diffusion model, which builds a grasp step by step from noise, paired with a scoring network that filters the samples. A new training recipe teaches the scorer using the generator's own outputs. To scale up, the team released a simulated dataset of more than fifty million grasps across many objects and grippers. GraspGen beat earlier methods in simulation, led a standard grasping benchmark, and worked on a real robot with noisy camera input.
arxiv-2507-13297:
Amy Roberts and eleven co-authors described in twenty twenty-five how a dark matter data set was opened up for wide use. Dark matter makes up most of the matter in the universe, yet no one knows what it is. Tests that hunt for it produce data locked in custom formats and one-off software, which blocks fresh analysis.

Working with the National Science Data Fabric, the team converted a calibration data set from Cryogenic Dark Matter Search detectors into an open, layered format. They built a web dashboard for viewing signals and released a Python command tool for large jobs and machine learning. The goal is to lower the bar for new collaborators and make results easier to check and reuse across fields.
arxiv-2507-13597:
Toi Tachibana, Kouichi Hagino, Kenichi Yoshida, and Qiang Zhao compute properties of spin-polarized nuclear matter in a 2025 arXiv paper. They use the relativistic Hartree-Fock method with a point-coupling model. The model simplifies the exchange terms into the same form as the direct terms.

They define a spin slope parameter for spin-symmetry energy, mirroring the known slope for isospin energy. When neutrons and protons polarize in the same direction, the two slopes move against each other. When they polarize in opposite directions, the spin slope barely depends on the other slope. The authors show both patterns follow naturally from their model.
arxiv-2507-14797:
Beier Zhu and co-authors speed up, in a 2025 paper, the sampling of diffusion models, the image generators that build pictures by slow steps of denoising. Each step follows a differential equation, and cheap solvers make errors that blur quality when few steps are allowed. The authors' solver spends each step more wisely.

Their method, an ensemble parallel direction solver, gathers several slope readings at each step and blends them, which cuts the error of a plain step. Since the readings are independent, they run side by side, so the wait stays low. A small set of tuned weights, learned by distillation, keeps training cost tiny, and the solver can also plug into existing samplers. Across four image benchmarks it beat rival fast solvers by a clear margin at the same latency.
arxiv-2507-15697:
Vaibhav Tiwari, writing alone, tests whether the mass distribution of merging black hole pairs has a real gap. The 2025 paper uses the chirp mass, a combination of the two masses that gravitational wave detectors measure best. The inferred distribution shows peaks, with a sparse stretch between two of them.

Comparing models with and without a suppressed rate in that stretch, the data strongly favor suppression, at very high confidence by one test. A second, more cautious test still supports a feature at good confidence. A similar gap in single-object masses had drawn doubt. The author traces the difference to a correlation between the heavier and lighter partners, which clusters chirp masses at set values. Formation theories for black hole pairs gain a sharper target.
arxiv-2507-15897:
Yoo, Kim, and Hong made discrete generators take fewer steps in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Discrete flow models produce high-quality text-like or image data, but they decode step by step. That slowness traces to a factorization shortcut the models need for large data. The authors measure the shortcut's error with a quantity called conditional total correlation.

Their method, ReDi, repeatedly re-pairs starting noise with target data to shrink that error. Each round provably lowers the error measure, so the process converges. Fewer decoding steps then suffice for good output. The repaired pairings also trained strong one-step image generators. The authors pitch the idea as a principled route to fast discrete synthesis.
arxiv-2507-16897:
Markus Amano, Minoru Eto, Muneto Nitta, and Shin Sasaki study a lattice of twists in dense quark matter under a strong magnetic field. Their paper from twenty twenty-five uses holographic QCD, which maps the strong force to a gravity dual. The pattern in play is the chiral soliton lattice, a ranked stack of twists. Set edge terms on the gauge field and quark mass let it form.

The team shows this lattice is the ground state when a magnetic field and baryon density are present. In the dual view, the twists act as spread-out branes. Each twist matches a vortex type in the five-dimensional bulk. Two sources of baryon count merge into one bulk charge. The pion decay constant shifts with field strength. For massless pions they give a closed form that fits lattice results well at strong fields.
arxiv-2507-17797:
Shubham Toshniwal and co-authors present GenSelect, a way to pick the best answer from many model outputs, in this 2025 paper. Language models can sample many candidate solutions in parallel. Scoring each one alone wastes the model strength at comparing options. Pairwise comparison, in contrast, grows costly as the pool grows.

GenSelect has the model reason at length over the whole pool and choose the best one. That uses comparison strength while scaling well with pool size. Tests focused on math reasoning. Strong reasoning models did well at the task with simple prompts. They beat existing scoring methods. The approach offers a practical route to better test time scaling for hard problems.
arxiv-2507-18697:
Shraddha Mohnani and a large team model the afterglow of a gamma-ray burst in a 2025 arXiv paper. The burst, GRB 230812B, was among the brightest seen by the Fermi monitor. Its afterglow spans many wavelengths and carries clues about relativistic shocks.

The team studies the spectrum and timing from X-rays to very-high-energy gamma rays. Two emission parts overlap in this range, and telling them apart needs data near the turnover. A single 72 GeV photon was among the key finds. The modeling tests what the data imply for spotting such bursts with Cherenkov telescopes. Microphysics of the shock and the burst's surroundings are the wider stakes.
arxiv-2507-19197:
Youngmin Seo and eight co-authors built WACA-UNet in twenty twenty-five to predict voltage droop, called IR drop, across chip layouts. IR drop threatens chip reliability, but full simulation is slow. Recasting the prediction as pixel-wise regression on physical layout maps is faster, yet prior models treated all input channels — metal, via, current maps — as equals, though their importance varies.

Their Weakness-Aware Channel Attention recursively boosts weak feature channels and reins in dominant ones, in two gating stages, inside an attention U-Net. On the public ICCAD-2023 benchmark it cut mean absolute error by about sixty-one percent versus the contest winner and raised F1 score by about seventy-one percent. The lesson: channel imbalance is a real signal in physical design data.
arxiv-2507-19497:
Alex Leitch and Celia Chen argue that AI art research asks the wrong questions about style, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Detection, authenticity, and automation dominate the field, they say. Yet human style grows from creative struggle, as artists wrestle with influences and technical limits to find a way of seeing.

Modern generators flatten those choices into copyable patterns and drop their origins. The authors propose tools that record where a style came from and how it changed inside generated images. That shift would steer the field toward lineage and choice, not just polished output. Historical cases back the argument.
arxiv-2507-19697:
Alrubyli and five colleagues predict which places people visit in pairs, using business type codes in twenty twenty-five. Knowing that a coffee shop visit leads to a gym visit helps city and retail planning. Past models leaned on distance alone, which misses why unlike businesses draw unlike crowds. Their network learns a code for each industry type as it trains.

The data held near ninety-five million paired visits across most United States states. Their model more than doubled the fit of the best past methods. Rank quality of the top guesses rose by about a third. Splitting the huge task by state made it run at scale. Business meaning, they show, is a strong signal.
arxiv-2507-19997:
Lallement and colleagues describe in twenty twenty-five upgrades to TAPAS, an online service that predicts how Earth's atmosphere dims starlight for any site, date, and direction. Astronomers must subtract this telluric veil from their spectra, and modern air models plus molecule databases make sharp predictions possible. The service blends global weather profiles with extra climate data and runs a line-by-line radiation code at resolutions that keep every absorption line's shape.

Upgrades stretch coverage into the near-ultraviolet and deeper into the infrared, refresh the molecule data, and add nitrogen dioxide to the species list. Users can also force the water column to match their observatory's own reading. Checks against telescope spectra of a hot star showed close agreement, and the models even calibrate instrument blur.
arxiv-2507-20097:
Mahboob Ul Haq models charge noise in superconducting qubits with a new stochastic process in a 2025 physics study. Charge noise is a main source of decoherence, the loss of quantum behavior that limits these devices. Standard noise models often assume steady statistics, while real noise drifts and remembers its past.

A memory multi-fractional Brownian motion framework lets noise statistics change over time while keeping long-range memory. The author reports that the model reproduces key experimental features of decoherence. Matching real noise more closely can sharpen predictions for qubit lifetimes. That in turn guides shielding, materials, and control choices for quantum hardware.
arxiv-2507-20297: Shenghao Hua studies the size of special values tied to one fixed elliptic curve, in a 2025 paper whose abstract is brief. For each imaginary quadratic field where the curve has rank one, a derivative of its L-function can be formed. Hua proves a one-sided central limit theorem for the logarithms of these derivatives as the field varies, mirroring a known result for a related family. He also shows that many of these derivatives are not small, so the values do not all huddle near zero.
arxiv-2508-00497:
Jinghui Zhang and five co-authors present SocialAlign, a system that forecasts public response to events at two scales at once. Their paper from twenty twenty-five notes past tools made two misses. They gave generic replies with no personal flavor, and they tracked single sentiments while missing the crowd's spread. Crisis teams and policy makers need both views.

At the micro level, a tuned language model crafts personal comments with matching sentiment. Expert modules split the work by topic and user profile. At the macro level, the system models group sentiment spread and aligns it with real trends. A new data set, SentiWeibo, gathers true exchanges from the Weibo platform. Tests on it and a second benchmark beat strong baselines. Gains showed in accuracy, clarity, and spread to new cases.
arxiv-2508-01797: Meshach Ndlovu and Jean Baptiste Gatsinzi settle the rational homotopy type of a bundle space in a 2025 math note. The space is built from the tangent bundle of complex projective space by projectivizing each fiber, a standard move in geometry. Rational homotopy type captures a space's shape as seen by rational algebraic tools, ignoring torsion detail. Their result names the type exactly: it matches a quotient of a unitary group by a product of three smaller unitary groups.
arxiv-2508-04397:
Oorna Mitra, Mallika Roy, and Enric Ventura solved a twist matching puzzle in a class of solvable groups, in a mathematics paper published in 2025. The groups, BS(n,1), mix a loop with a stretching rule. The puzzle asks: given two members and a self-map, can a third member twist one onto the other by the set rule? Earlier work left this class open.

Their method settles it with a step-by-step test that always ends. They also prove a related fact: the self-map group of these groups can tell whether two words name members that some self-map can swap. Both facts aid the wider craft of group tests. The paper speaks to those who build such tests.
arxiv-2508-05697:
Lammers, Holik, and Fernandez study how quantum software must handle scarce hardware. Today's quantum machines sit in the NISQ era, with few qubits and high error rates. Their coherence times are also short, so long tasks fail. The authors argue that resource care shapes both design and use of quantum code. They review how current NISQ work treats physical and logical resources.

The paper ties those limits to software engineering practice. It backs the field of quantum resource estimation, which gauges cost before code runs. Good estimates help teams pick hardware and plan for scale. The goal is quantum software that stays reliable as machines grow.
arxiv-2508-06797:
Alexander Hammerl and four co-authors design evacuation control for large cities in a 2025 paper. Their framework plans releases of cars into a road network when demand is uncertain. A bathtub-style model tracks how trips complete over time across the whole network. Control takes the form of staged departure orders or ramp metering at entry points.

They prove that under a common condition on trip distances, the best release pattern falls steadily over time. With an entry cap it becomes a single switch from full release to throttling. A flood case study on a low, dense island in Copenhagen tested the policy on thousands of random demand cases. Controlled release cut expected queue buildup clearly.
arxiv-2508-08897:
John Parker and Manvendra Somvanshi study closed billiard paths inside polygons drawn on a hyperbolic surface, where space curves away like a saddle, in a 2025 paper. A billiard path bounces off the sides at equal angles and returns to its start. For any set of such loops, the authors define the average loop length and ask which polygon shape makes it smallest.

They take two families of shapes. The first is even-sided polygons with all right angles, whose loops come in cyclic families. The second is a four-sided Lambert shape with one sharp corner, whose loops come in mirrored families. In the first family, the regular polygon, the most even shape, wins. In the second, the winner is the shape with a mirror symmetry along its long axis. The proofs draw on the theory of surface deformations.
arxiv-2508-08997:
Sizhe Yuen and co-authors present a framework that gives each agent in a multi-agent language model system its own structured memory. Such teams promise strong collaborative problem solving, but fixed context windows erode memory consistency, role adherence, and procedure following. Their method keeps role-aligned memories that grow out of each agent's own outputs. The memory stays focused on task-relevant content and keeps each specialist's viewpoint.

A generic memory template applies to new problems without hand-crafted prompts. Benchmarks on three datasets, covering planning, fact checking, and a household task world, show performance at or above leading rivals, with the highest consistency. On a complex data pipeline design task, the approach scores better on five quality measures, from scalability to documentation. The authors argue intrinsic memory is a practical fix for a core weakness of agent teams.
arxiv-2508-11397:
Marko Orozović and co-authors show, in twenty twenty-five, that adding holes can raise the magnetic ordering temperature of an atom-thin magnet. Two-dimensional magnets offer atomic-scale control of magnetism. The team studied monolayer chromium triiodide, a prototype layered ferromagnet, with a multi-scale theory: density functional calculations, spin models, and orbital analysis. Charge doping, done by gating or charge transfer, tunes the exchange forces between spins and the spin-orbit effects that set direction. Hole doping proved remarkably efficient at strengthening both.

In the undoped sheet, symmetric exchange governs ordering. When hole-doped, directional terms grow to rival it. At high hole levels, the Curie temperature, where magnetism fades, can pass two hundred kelvin. The work shows how anisotropy engineering can stabilize warm magnetic order.
arxiv-2508-11497:
Feiyue Zhao and Zhichao Zhang add graph reasoning to image recognition in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Standard vision networks read images on a fixed grid, which limits how they capture links between distant parts. Their framework builds graphs at two levels inside the network.

One level models links within small windows of the image, and the other links summary nodes across windows for a global view. A further module balances low and high frequency signals, keeping edges and texture while avoiding over-smoothing. The module is light and can plug into standard networks. Tests on classification, detection, and segmentation data sets showed broad gains.
arxiv-2508-12197:
Maria Vasilyeva and three co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on flow in wet, elastic ground with mixed traits. The coupled set of sums for this flow is not linear, which makes it slow to solve. They use a grid method in space and a two grid solver for the coupled sums. The solver pairs a sharp coarse grid with smooth passes on fine patches.

Building that solver each step would cost too much. So they split the sums into a fixed linear part, solved in a hidden way, and a rest part handled in the open. The split keeps the scheme stable, which they prove. Tests on a two dimensional case show the solver is robust and the time steps stay true.
arxiv-2508-12497:
Rupak Chatterjee used modular operator theory in twenty twenty-five to study how entanglement can be harvested from a quantum field. He also studied how it bends under change. In harvesting, two detectors start apart. Each one couples to the field. They come out entangled. They draw on the links that are in the field itself.

Chatterjee works in the Tomita-Takesaki framework. He builds the modular conjugation operator for detector qubits of Unruh-DeWitt type. The harvested entanglement then equals a simple expectation value. That value uses the same operator. He extends the work to open, noisy qubit dynamics. He defines a curvature of entanglement as a second derivative. It gauges how sensitive the result is. At special self-dual points, this curvature matches quantum Fisher information. The results tie two settings together through one algebraic structure.
arxiv-2508-13597:
Tang and a team including Wang and Rong found in twenty twenty-five the first firm sign that galaxy groups spin as a whole. Spin of such groups may tell how they formed and grew. They use two large lists of groups built from a sky survey, with thousands of groups in each.

They split each group by a trial line and read the speed gap of its parts. True groups show a gap far from the shuffled fake groups. Stacked pics show red and blue sides split by the spin line in a clean way. Spin speed grows with group mass and with range from the core.
arxiv-2508-14197:
Tinghan Yang, Md Ashiqur Rahman, and Raymond Yeh detect image symmetries with CLIPSym, asking a vision-language model to lend its semantic eyes to a geometric task. Their paper from twenty twenty-five notes that symmetry detection has resisted decades of hand-crafted cues. CLIP's pretraining on captioned images may hide symmetry hints in language itself. A rotation-equivariant decoder, part transformer and part group convolution, reads the CLIP features.

A prompting scheme groups frequent object-based prompts so the language encoder's cues land where they help. Three standard datasets fall to the new state of the art. Ablations credit each ingredient: the pretraining, the equivariant decoder, and the prompt grouping. Geometry tasks gain a semantic ally.
arxiv-2508-14697: Jacob Thompson and Elizabeth Winstanley study quantum effects on a curved space-time in twenty twenty-five. The setting is three-dimensional anti-de Sitter space, a standard model space in gravity research. They look at static solitons, stable lumps with a regular center, that solve a linearized quantum-corrected form of Einstein's equations. The correction comes from a quantum scalar field in a thermal state. They compute the soliton mass two ways, by quantum field theory and by relativistic kinetic theory, and compare the answers.
arxiv-2508-15597:
Ahmed Mimouni and Ludovic Patey published this logic paper in 2025. It studies Ramsey-like theorems, statements saying that however the pairs of natural numbers are colored in two colors, some infinite set of numbers has pairs that avoid a given pattern. Such theorems sit inside a larger program that ranks math statements by the computing power they hide. The authors ask whether any of these statements are computably trivial.

Their answer is no. They build a single computable two-coloring such that any infinite set avoiding any pattern can be used to compute a function that no simple diagonal method can produce. They also sort the theorems by whether they preserve various forms of immunity, a notion of sets that resist computable intrusion. The sorting depends on the shape of the pattern being avoided. The work feeds into the reverse mathematics of Ramsey theory.
arxiv-2508-16797:
William DiCarlo and Lorenzo Sadun explore, in a 2025 paper, the typical shape of random networks under two constraints at once: how many links they contain and how many triangles. In one puzzling region, theory expected the typical network to split into two blocks, but simulations hinted at three. The authors map that region of link and triangle densities numerically to find where the three-block, or tripodal, pattern actually holds.

They show the tripodal region ends at a sharp boundary, where the typical graph jumps suddenly to the two-block form rather than shading into it. They also find at least one more sudden jump inside the tripodal region itself, where the numbers describing typical graphs change abruptly. The work clarifies a corner of random graph theory where smooth expectations failed, and shows phase changes hiding where none were predicted.
arxiv-2509-00197:
Ruojing Jiang and Franco Vargas Pallete study minimal surface entropy on hyperbolic three-manifolds in 2025 and how Ricci flow helps bound it. Minimal surface entropy counts how fast the number of minimal surfaces grows with area, in an exponential sense. Minimal surfaces are surfaces that locally minimize area, like soap films.

For metrics close to hyperbolic in shape, with sectional curvature at most minus one, entropy reaches its minimum only for the hyperbolic metric itself. Conversely, among metrics with scalar curvature bounded below and non-positive curvature on the cusps, entropy is maximized at the hyperbolic metric, given infinitesimal rigidity. Ricci flow convergence rates drive the second result. The work ties a counting invariant tightly to the most symmetric shape.
arxiv-2509-00397:
Murayyiam Parvez, Annus Zulfiqar, Roman Beltiukov, Shir Landau Feibish, Walter Willinger, Arpit Gupta, and Muhammad Shahbaz present SpliDT in 2025, a system for running decision trees inside programmable network switches. In-network machine learning enables real-time traffic analysis and security checks at line rate. Decision trees suit data planes, since they map to match-action tables, but prior builds must compute all input features upfront.

That upfront rule forces a small, fixed feature set per flow, which caps accuracy and scale. SpliDT partitions inference over sliding windows of packets, assigning distinct, variable feature sets to parts of the tree. Stateful inference thus grows richer without breaking hardware limits. The design targets scalable monitoring inside the network itself.
arxiv-2509-00597: Thibault Damour, writing alone, remembers Yvonne Choquet-Bruhat. He describes the impact of some of her key results on gravitational physics. Her work helped put Einstein's theory of gravity on firm math ground. Damour also traces how his own contact with her changed over the years. The piece is both a personal tribute and a guide. It shows why her work on the equations of general relativity still matters. Readers in physics and math both have reason to care.
arxiv-2509-00697:
Chandradew Sharma, writing alone, analyzes thirty-four years of Nifty 50 index data, from 1990 to 2024, to map how Indian equity returns behave across horizons from days to decades.
