Gillessen and a large team of astronomers report a third gas cloud near the Milky Way's central black hole in this 2025 arXiv paper. The black hole, Sagittarius A*, is fed extremely weakly, so the few Earth-mass gas clumps nearby form a valuable reservoir. The cloud G2 swung past the black hole in 2014 and lost energy to its accretion flow, while the similar cloud G1 had passed thirteen years earlier. Some models claimed such clouds hide a central star.

New infrared data now reveal a third clump following almost the same orbit, eighteen years after G2. Finding three stars on such matching orbits by chance is effectively excluded, the authors argue. They instead identify one connected gas streamer, G1-2-3, shed by the massive binary star IRS16SW. Small differences between the three orbits track that binary's own motion, and updated simulations support the wind origin.
arxiv-2510-01097:
Dong and four co-authors give the first universally composable security analysis of the Tendermint protocol in this 2025 arXiv paper. Tendermint powers many consortium blockchains with high throughput and fast finality. Earlier proofs treated it in isolation, though deployments run it alongside protocols concurrently. Nobody had formally checked termination when Byzantine adversaries adaptively delay messages. The universal composability framework is built for such composed settings.

The team constructed an ideal UC model capturing Tendermint's phase-based rounds, dynamic timeouts, proposal locking, and leader rotation. They proved the protocol realizes that ideal model against an adversary who selectively delays traffic. The guarantee: safety and termination latency hold while fewer than a third of nodes are Byzantine, provided delays stay within the protocol threshold. Worst-case termination latency scales quadratically in the number of faults. By the UC composition theorem, the properties survive composition with blockchain components.
arxiv-2510-01197:
Suleymanli and co-authors test whether today's language models can turn official statistics into correct charts for lay users. National data portals hold trustworthy numbers, yet scattered tables make them practically inaccessible. A helpful model must find the right table, reshape it, and draw a sensible chart unaided.

Eight models faced twenty-five tasks built on Dutch public statistics. A three-part scoring frame graded retrieval, code quality, and visual design separately. Base models wrote decent code but stumbled on data manipulation and chart design. An agentic setup with self-correction pushed the best model above nine out of ten. Retrieval failures poison everything downstream, since wrong data charts beautifully. Iterative self-correction, not raw size, separated the best performer. Official statistics deserve interfaces that respect their authority. Twenty-five tasks kept the evaluation broad rather than deep. Citizens gain charts without learning query languages.
arxiv-2510-01297:
Feng and co-authors build a simulated city where language-model citizens, firms, a central bank, and a government run a miniature economy. Classical models flatten human differences for tractability, while older agent simulations follow rigid hand-written rules. Their framework, SimCity, lets agents reason in plain language instead.

Four agent types trade in frictional labor, goods, and financial markets. A vision model even places new firms on a growing city map. Against a checklist of famous macroeconomic regularities, the simulation reproduced patterns like the Phillips curve naturally. Plausible responses to outside shocks added to the realism. Engel's law and Okun's law join the checklist of reproduced patterns. Natural-language reasoning makes every decision inspectable after the fact. Geographic expansion and macro dynamics share one environment here. Heterogeneous goods keep the marketplace from collapsing into one price. Interpretability is the selling point.
arxiv-2510-01397:
Tripathi, Dunkel, and Skinner build the simplest honest model of cells patterning themselves by talking to neighbors. Development demands ordered structures from local chatter, but collective decisions have resisted clean theory. Their tractable model quantifies how information actually flows between cells during patterning.

A speed-accuracy trade-off governs the collective outcome, as with single decision makers. Globally optimal patterns do not always maximize information transfer between cells. Individual cells can look suboptimal while the collective thrives. Information shared between cells even rises and falls non-monotonically in time, a pattern echoed in fruit fly data. Local communication is the only channel the model's cells possess. Stochastic chemical kinetics supplies the borrowed mathematics. Lateral inhibition in fly skin gave the experimental mirror. Conditioning on final fates reveals hidden exchanges between equals. Collective computation is not scaled-up individual computation at all.
arxiv-2510-01497:
Durst, Rittenhouse, Sadeghpour, and Eiles build a framework for impurity atoms whose interactions with a surrounding quantum bath refuse to be simple. Standard polaron theory assumes the bath tugs spherically and additively, which real impurities violate. A giant Rydberg atom inside a Bose-Einstein condensate makes the failure concrete.

Internal-state degeneracy makes the interaction depend on configuration, not just distance. Stronger coupling mixes partial waves and creates distinct polaron and molaron resonances. Radially and angularly excited bound states become reachable in the spectrum. The framework generalizes beyond this example to impurity problems everywhere. Additive pseudopotentials are the conventional shortcut being retired. Mean-field energy at high density stays curiously state-independent. Boson species and density tune where the resonances appear. The Fröhlich paradigm is the named boundary of older theory. Excited bound states enrich the experimental signatures actually available.
arxiv-2510-01797:
Gyurik and seven co-authors map out a meeting point between quantum computing and reservoir computing in this 2025 perspective paper. Reservoir computing trains only a simple readout, while a fixed complex system does the hard signal processing. Quantum systems offer huge state spaces and correlations with no classical match. The authors argue they could serve as powerful, practical reservoirs.

Their focus is neutral atom quantum processors, which are available on real hardware today. They describe a workflow that moves memory into a classical part of the system. That hybrid design dodges the damage that repeated quantum measurements would cause. Quantum feature maps earn a central role, because they lift data into the vast quantum space. The authors also survey applications and the main obstacles ahead. They present quantum reservoir computing as a natural candidate for near-term quantum advantage in learning tasks.
arxiv-2510-01897:
Caro, Petruševski, Škrekovski, and Tuza compute a new graph parameter for grids and chessboard boards in this 2025 combinatorics paper. An odd independent set is a set of vertices with no edges among them, where every outside vertex sees either none of them or an odd number of them as neighbors. The largest such set size is the graph's odd independence number. It partners a recently introduced coloring parameter, the strong odd chromatic number.

This second paper in the series tackles grid-like and chessboard-like graphs. The authors pin down the parameter for many board families and piece-move graphs. For the knight's graph on a large board, they bound the value between two close fractions of the board's area. Their bounds differ by only a small margin in the leading coefficient. The paper also records cases where the number is one or infinite.
arxiv-2510-02197:
Nsengiyumva, Niyitegeka, and Umuhoza identify pigs by the vein patterns in their ears in this 2025 agriculture paper. Ear tags tear out and microchips cost too much for small-scale farmers, and both target pure breeds. Ear vein patterns offer a noninvasive biometric that works on cross-breeds. The team collected eight hundred ear images from twenty mixed-breed pigs using a phone and simple backlighting.

A multistage vision pipeline enhanced vein visibility and extracted features. Those features form a biometric signature for each animal. Among the classifiers tested, support vector machines performed best. They identified pigs with precision above ninety-eight percent across the mixed-breed herd. The full process averaged just over eight seconds per identification. That speed makes pen-side use realistic for small farms. Fragile physical tags give way to the animal's own anatomy.
arxiv-2510-02297:
Zhang, Lu, and Deng propose Interactive Training, a framework for steering neural networks while they learn. Their 2025 paper questions the usual fixed recipe. Standard training sets all settings before the run starts. When training wobbles, experts must stop and restart. Interactive Training inserts a control server into the loop. A person or an AI agent can watch live progress. They can adjust optimizer settings mid-run. They can also swap training data or restore checkpoints on the fly.

Three case studies test the idea in practice. Interactive runs showed better stability than static runs. They also depended less on lucky starting settings. Users could reshape training as their needs changed. The framework is open source. The authors picture agents that monitor logs alone. Such agents would catch faults early and fix them without waiting.
arxiv-2510-02497:
DiBrita and co-authors explain quantum learning models by scoring each input feature. Their 2025 paper presents a framework called HattriQ. Quantum models hide their reasoning inside fragile state evolution. Classical explanation tools break on quantum circuits. Measuring a state collapses the very thing being studied. HattriQ computes input gradients directly on quantum hardware. A Hadamard test construction makes those gradients measurable. The scores follow the popular amplitude embedding of inputs. Faithfulness of the attributions comes with proofs, they report.

Tests covered Bars and Stripes plus two image datasets. MNIST and FashionMNIST supplied familiar classification tasks. The method produced sensible feature rankings on hardware style circuits. Parallel ancilla tricks keep the scheme scalable. Interpretability is a trust requirement for quantum tools. First of its kind claims mark the novelty here. Parameter and layer attributions are planned next.
arxiv-2510-02597:
Gupta and co-authors transcribe guitar audio into tablature that keeps expressive technique marks. Their 2025 music technology paper presents a tool called TART. Piano transcription is far ahead of guitar transcription today. Guitar adds two headaches that piano lacks. Slides, bends, and percussive hits carry musical meaning. The same note can also sit on several string and fret spots. TART chains four stages to solve both problems. A pitch stage converts audio to MIDI notes first. A classifier then labels the expressive techniques used. A transformer assigns each note its string and fret. A recurrent stage writes the final tablature.

The authors call it the first system of its kind. Training drew on guitar adapted datasets beyond tiny samples. Early results look promising, though work continues. Bigger and more varied training data are planned. Guitarists could gain automatic notation that respects style.
arxiv-2510-02697:
Sharma and co-authors find spectroscopic evidence of a Kondo resonance inside layered ferromagnets. Their 2025 condensed matter paper studies a cobalt based layered family. Two dimensional magnets promise advances in spintronics. Their electrons live double lives, part localized and part roaming. That duality produces exotic ground states in correlated materials. The team tracked the electron bands across temperatures. High resolution photoemission spectroscopy supplied the spectra. Theory combined density functional methods with mean field tools. A peak grew above the Fermi level at low temperature.

The peak emerged below one hundred kelvin. Its growth with cobalt content matched the theory. Spin splitting survived above the magnetic transition. That persistence signals non-Stoner magnetism in the material. Core levels barely moved across the transition. Disorder left a dip that deepened as samples cooled. Kondo physics inside a ferromagnet is a rare pairing. Quantum critical behavior may sit nearby in this family.
arxiv-2510-02897:
Rozhkov and co-authors report record-cool electron beams from a photocathode material. The spread of sideways energy in the beam is called mean transverse energy. Lower spread means a brighter, sharper beam. The team studied a multialkali compound built from sodium, potassium, and antimony. A cesium-rich surface gave it negative electron affinity. That state lets electrons escape with ease.

Their measurements beat a standard rival material by a wide margin. The sideways spread was about half that of gallium arsenide cathodes. The cause is a refraction effect at the surface. Electrons inside carry a small effective mass, then jump to free mass in vacuum. That jump bends their paths into a narrow cone. About half the electrons rode that cone with tiny spread. Warming the cathode flipped its affinity sign. The total spread then dropped below the thermal level.
arxiv-2510-03097:
Agarwal, Melnikov, and Pedron sharpen a subtraction scheme for collider predictions. Proton collisions that yield a photon plus a jet test quantum chromodynamics. Theorists compute such rates with slicing methods. Slicing discards events below a cut in a shape variable. The discard is safe only if the leftover error is tiny. Those leftovers are called power corrections in the cut. This paper computes them at next-to-leading order.

The channel studied is quark-antiquark annihilation into photon plus jet. A realistic jet algorithm defines the jet in the work. The method came from color-singlet production studies by the same school. Momentum reshuffles and Lorentz boosts do the heavy lifting. This is the first such result with a jet in the final state. No photon isolation step was needed for a physical answer. Tighter errors help LHC tests of the Standard Model.
arxiv-2510-03197:
Thomas and Wahlström estimate how hard a lift feels from wearable sensor data. Lifters rate exertion on the RPE scale to guide training. The team recorded single-arm dumbbell curls with two sensor types. Inertial units tracked motion while EMG electrodes tracked muscle activity. Sixty-nine sets and over a thousand repetitions formed the dataset. Statistical features fed a lineup of learning models for comparison.

A random forest classifier won the comparison clearly. Exact exertion calls landed only about two times in five. Calls within one point of the truth were far more common. Nearly nine in ten estimates fell inside that band. Eccentric phase timing was the single strongest predictor found. EMG data helped, but only by a small margin. Placement sensitivity and signal quality may have capped its value. Bigger, more varied datasets top the authors' wish list.
arxiv-2510-03397:
Morales-Alvarado presents a 2025 arXiv paper on using large language models to discover equations in high energy physics. Physicists often need formulas for collider observables that no one can derive from principles. The study applies the LLM-SR method, which asks a language model to propose candidate equations as programs. Tests begin with lepton angle patterns whose true law is known. The method then tackles unknown forms for boson production at the Large Hadron Collider.

In the control test, the method recovered the known analytic law. Its accuracy matched rival methods inside the training region. On the unknown boson coefficients, it produced compact formulas with accuracy on par with existing tools. Its guesses also held up better when pushed beyond the training region. Built in physics knowledge steered the search toward forms with behavior. The work suggests language models can serve as partners in formula hunting for particle physics.
arxiv-2510-03597:
Alemohammad, Wang, and Baraniuk present a 2025 arXiv paper with a counterintuitive fix for image generators trained on their output. Fine tuning a model on its synthetic images normally degrades it, a failure called model collapse. Their method, Neon, first fine tunes on self generated data. Then it reverses direction, extrapolating the weights away from the degraded model. The theory shows why this works: samplers favor likely regions, so synthetic and real data gradients point against each other.

Reversing the update steers the model back toward the data distribution. The correction needs as few as a thousand synthetic samples and under one percent compute. It worked across diffusion, flow matching, autoregressive, and moment matching models on three data sets. On ImageNet, it pushed one model to an image quality score using a third of one percent more training. In a field starved for real data, degradation itself becomes a usable signal.
arxiv-2510-03697:
Marsh and Serafino present a 2025 arXiv paper adding expiry times to blockchain signatures so that block producers cannot sit on transactions to extract value. In fee auctions, a signed transaction never expires, so producers can delay it until including it pays them through maximal extractable value tricks. Their scheme modifies Schnorr signatures by hashing a deadline block height into the signing challenge. After that height, the signature stops validating. The chain itself serves as the clock.

The authors prove the scheme keeps Schnorr's security and efficiency under assumptions. Applied to Ethereum's EIP-1559 fee market, an analysis shows time bound signatures restore the predicted equilibrium of negligible tips. Delay stops working because waiting forfeits the transaction. The change is opt in and leaves wallet keys untouched, since Schnorr already runs beside the signature scheme. Smart contract timeouts and escrow deadlines could reuse the same primitive. Deployable defenses against extraction are rare.
arxiv-2510-04197:
Strässle, Hosseini, and Karlin present this 2025 arXiv paper on kinetic simulations of gas flows with variable thermal and viscous transport. The Prandtl number controls the ratio between momentum and heat diffusion, while the specific heat ratio varies across gases and temperatures. Many discrete Boltzmann models recover the correct fluid equations only for restricted values of these parameters. The authors develop a double-distribution quasi-equilibrium method that remains consistent across the full parameter range.

Carefully constructed equilibrium and quasi-equilibrium states recover the Navier-Stokes-Fourier equations, including moments and rates, in the hydrodynamic limit. Tests verify strict conservation, Galilean invariance, stability, and correct dispersion over wide Mach and temperature ranges. The result is a scalable kinetic framework for moderate supersonic flows and discontinuities in fluids whose transport properties differ sharply from the simplest model gases.
arxiv-2510-04397:
Van Nguyen and five coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on finding security flaws in software. Most tools that hunt for code flaws work in one programming language only. Real projects often mix several languages, so single language tools miss a lot. The team built MulVuln, a system that learns from code in many languages at once. It picks up both the patterns that languages share and the habits that make each language distinct.

Tests used a real world data set with thousands of known flaws and fixes across seven languages. MulVuln beat thirteen strong rival methods on the main accuracy score. Its gains over the rivals ranged from small to more than twenty percent. A shared knowledge core gave the system broad reach across languages. A small pool of extra settings let it adapt to the quirks of each language.
arxiv-2510-04697:
Laura Estivalez and Adriano Moura wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on counting how modules combine in an affine algebra. Tensor products split into modules, and the counts of each piece are called outer multiplicities. The setting is an affine Kac Moody algebra of type A, with fundamental modules multiplied. The authors express those counts as the number of sets of multipartitions. Their route runs through filtrations that stabilize in a limit.

A formula by Misra and Wilson counted the numbers with sets of tableaux. Comparing the two counts yields a bijection between the tableaux and unions of the multipartition sets. Building that bridge required a description of certain orbits of the affine Weyl group at level two. The result extends a rank one theorem to all ranks. Counting identities like this turn algebra into combinatorics that can be checked by hand. They expose structure inside infinite dimensional symmetry algebras.
arxiv-2510-04997:
Jiongchi Yu and five co-authors ask whether AI can speed up the study of software bugs in this 2025 arXiv paper. Empirical fault studies mine real bugs to learn how software fails. The work is slow because experts must collect, filter, and label each fault by hand. A single study can take weeks of scarce expert time.

The authors split the process into three phases, from setting goals to final analysis. They then let large language models run the pipeline on 3,829 real software faults. The automated run took about two hours on average, not weeks. Broad fault identification worked well, but fine-grained classification reached only 50 percent accuracy in their tests. The paper maps what full automation still needs.
arxiv-2510-05097:
Robin Courant and four co-authors teach AI to choreograph actors and cameras together in this 2025 arXiv paper. Filmmaking couples a performer's movement with the camera's path. Generating the two separately breaks the framing that makes a shot work. The team casts the pair as one text-conditioned generation task.

Their trick is an auxiliary signal: the on-screen framing from projecting body joints through the camera. A joint autoencoder learns a shared latent space for motion, camera, and framing. Sampling then steers both outputs toward a coherent framing. They also release PulpMotion, a captioned dataset of human motion paired with camera trajectories. Across two architecture families, the method improved coherence and text alignment, setting a new state of the art.
arxiv-2510-05197:
Joshua Kazdan and six co-authors improve forecasts of what AI models can do given many attempts in this 2025 arXiv paper. Sampling a model repeatedly turns rare successes into near-certainties. That scaling affects hard math and coding, and also jailbreak risks. Providers and regulators need pass-at-k predictions from small sampling budgets.

The authors find that standard fitting methods for these scaling laws have statistical flaws. Their fix estimates success rates with a robust beta-binomial framework. A dynamic sampling strategy spends more budget on harder problems instead of spreading it evenly. Together the changes predict rare capabilities and risks far more accurately. The approach costs only a fraction of the compute that brute-force sampling would need.
arxiv-2510-05397:
Nicolas Lanchier, Max Mercer, and Hyunsik Yun study competing populations where some offspring are born sterile in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their multitype contact process lives on a lattice, with births, deaths, and crowded neighbors. A fertile parent of a given type produces fertile offspring only with some probability. The rest arrive sterile and can never reproduce.

Mean-field theory predicts the type with the largest birth-times-fertility product wins. Space overturns that rule when the fertility probability runs small. With one type, extinction is guaranteed once fertility drops below a dimension-dependent threshold. A fully fertile type with an ordinary birth rate outcompetes a rival with a huge birth rate but low fertility. The product therefore stops measuring competitiveness, exposing strong local interaction effects.
arxiv-2510-05897:
Julià-Farré and colleagues simulate the two-dimensional Fermi-Hubbard model on neutral atoms. The Fermi-Hubbard model is a benchmark challenge of strongly correlated matter. Encoding fermions directly into qubits suffers nonlocal mapping costs. Their 2025 hybrid algorithm reformulates the model instead of encoding it.

The reformulation couples fermions to auxiliary spins, then decouples them self-consistently. A classical computer solves the resulting free-fermion problem cheaply. The Rydberg quantum processor simulates the interacting spin problem in analog mode. On thirty-six sites, the method finds the expected metal-to-Mott-insulator transition. Equilibrium runs need an automated self-consistent loop feeding the classical solver. Out-of-equilibrium dynamics of the isotropic model are also accessible. The quasiparticle weight stays finite in the dynamics studied. Programmable optical tweezers give the platform its flexible geometry. Strongly correlated matter is the broader target of the hybrid approach.
arxiv-2510-06097:
Chailloux and Hermouet of Inria Paris map how two quantum lattice problems relate in a 2025 cryptography paper. One problem hands over a quantum state encoding noisy linear equations, the quantum Learning With Errors problem. The other, ISIS, asks for a short vector hitting a target modulo q. Both underpin post-quantum cryptography.

Earlier work attacked ISIS through the state problem in special cases, but the general relationship stayed unclear. They give the first fully generic reduction from ISIS to the state problem, tolerating solver errors. For the reverse direction, they introduce an inhomogeneous variant problem and prove it reduces to the state problem. Under recoverability conditions, an ISIS algorithm converts into a state-problem algorithm. One case recovers known results for small power-of-two moduli. The paper clarifies both the strong link and the remaining barrier to full equivalence.
arxiv-2510-06197:
Blum, Liu, Xu, and Zhuang develop relative stability theory for families of Fano varieties in a 2025 algebraic geometry paper. K-moduli spaces parametrize K-stable Fano varieties, and proving them proper is key to their construction. Properness means degenerating families always admit good limits inside the space.

They define the relative stability threshold of a family over a discrete valuation ring. They show a single divisorial valuation computes this threshold. When the special fiber is K-unstable but the generic fiber is K-semistable, that valuation guides a replacement. The new special fiber has a strictly larger stability threshold. Iterating the replacement raises stability until a proper limit appears. The iteration yields a new, more direct proof that the K-moduli space is proper. The argument uses only birational geometry, avoiding heavier analytic machinery.
arxiv-2510-06297:
Chen and Sanders model consciousness as entropy reduction in a short 2025 theory paper. Their CER model has a logical basis, so it can be simulated simply. It draws on global workspace theory, integrated information theory, and an older psychological feature map idea.

In CER, conscious and subconscious contents are scenarios: vectors of patterns across channels. A feature map is not consciousness itself, only an input into possible subconscious scenarios. One scenario is selected as conscious experience, and that selection is the entropy reduction. The result is an internal simulation of the outside world. Solving problems inside such a simulation is far cheaper than experimenting in reality, a major evolutionary advantage. CER also connects to Hopfield networks in artificial intelligence. The model offers a compact, simulable alternative to purely verbal theories.
arxiv-2510-06397:
Baheri shows hyperbolic embeddings give backdoor attacks a geometric hiding place in a 2025 machine learning paper. Foundation models increasingly embed data in curved spaces like hyperbolic geometry. Near the boundary, the geometry becomes strongly asymmetric.

Baheri formalizes the exploit. Small input changes near the boundary look subtle to standard detectors. Yet they produce disproportionately large representation shifts. A simple geometry-adaptive trigger was tested across tasks and architectures. Attack success rose toward the boundary while conventional detectors weakened, matching theory. Defenses face an awkward trade-off. Pulling points inward along the radius suppresses such triggers. Doing so sacrifices useful sensitivity in exactly that direction. The paper maps both a vulnerability and the price of fixing it. The vulnerability belongs specifically to curved representation spaces, not to models generally. Deployers of non-Euclidean models now know where their backdoor exposure concentrates.
arxiv-2510-06497:
Hazrat and Mesyan extend Lawson's generalization of Stone duality to graded structures in a 2025 algebra paper. Classical Stone duality pairs each Boolean algebra with a space of its ultrafilters. Algebra and topology become two views of one object. Lawson proved a dual equivalence between Boolean inverse meet-semigroups and Hausdorff ample topological groupoids.

Gradings add degree labels, tracking bookkeeping modern algebra increasingly needs. The authors generalize the duality to graded versions of both categories. Their version allows larger morphism classes than the original theorem. More maps survive, so more constructions transfer between sides. Various illustrations show the graded correspondence concretely. Graded structures arise wherever algebras carry natural degrees, as in many ring constructions. For researchers using groupoid models of graded algebras, the theorem supplies a dictionary. Questions move to whichever side, algebraic or topological, makes them easier.
arxiv-2510-06897:
Elvar Atlason, a single author, constructs a bendable polyhedron with the fewest corners possible. The 2025 paper works in geometry, on flexible polyhedra that flex without stretching their faces. Most polyhedra are rigid, and embedded ones were long thought to be rigid too. Connelly disproved that belief in 1977, and the hunt for the simplest example began.

Steffen's nine-vertex polyhedron held the record for decades. In 2024, an eight-vertex embedded example reached the proven lower bound. Atlason gives a general method for making new flexible surfaces from old ones. The trick is cutting along a symmetric four-sided patch, then rotating or reflecting the pieces. Applying it yields a different flexible dodecahedron on eight vertices. The new example moves through a wider range than the earlier minimal one. The exposition is also simpler, the author argues. The method doubles as a fresh proof that the 2024 example really flexes.
arxiv-2510-07197:
Singh, Kapa, Joshi, and Kolathaya present COMPAct, a framework that designs robot actuators and drafts their parts automatically. Their 2025 paper targets planetary gearboxes, the compact gear sets inside many robot joints. Good actuator design balances mass, width, and efficiency for a chosen motor. Hand design is slow, and each new motor restarts the work. COMPAct searches four gearbox families for the best settings at each gear ratio.

The framework then generates the matching computer-aided design files on its own. Those files go straight to a 3D printer without manual redrawing. The team built and tested two actuators from the pipeline. One single-stage design reached solid mechanical efficiency with low backlash and firm transmission. Maps of the best designs show which gearbox family wins at each ratio range. Faster actuator design shortens the path from robot concept to working hardware.
arxiv-2510-07397:
Braseth, Klungland, and Raklev compute a neglected correction to the predicted rate for producing sleptons at colliders. Their 2025 paper concerns the hypothetical superpartners of electrons and their kin. Near the production threshold, large logarithms spoil plain perturbation theory and must be resummed. State-of-the-art work resummed only the leading power in the threshold variable. This team adds the next-to-leading power terms at leading logarithmic accuracy. The paper doubles as a short tutorial on threshold resummation at both powers, including the practical numerics.

The new terms are not small. They can rival the next tier of leading-power corrections. Ignoring them makes published error bars too optimistic, especially for heavy sleptons. Results extend to a possible future circular collider running at very high energy. To the authors' knowledge, this is the first next-to-leading-power treatment of any supersymmetric production process.
arxiv-2510-07597:
Resch and Venkitesh survey list recoverable codes, error-correcting codes that work from soft hints instead of hard symbols. Their 2025 article explains the task: at each position the decoder receives a small list of candidate symbols, and the code must guarantee that few codewords agree with many of the lists. List recovery generalizes both unique decoding and list decoding, the twin pillars of coding theory.

The codes began as components inside list decoding of concatenated constructions but have since spread across theoretical computer science. Applications and connections now reach problems far from their origin. A highlight is the recent settlement, by two different methods, that random Reed-Solomon codes achieve the generalized Singleton bound for list decoding.
arxiv-2510-08397:
Jinhua Hong and co-authors reveal fine structure in how excitons move in boron nitride sheets, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Excitons, bound pairs of electrons and holes, govern how two-dimensional materials absorb light. Insulating materials like hexagonal boron nitride need ultraviolet light for such studies, so their exciton maps were missing. Measuring how exciton energy shifts with momentum is also hard at fine resolution.

The team used electron energy loss spectroscopy with high momentum resolution on free-standing sheets. They studied single-layer and few-layer hexagonal boron nitride samples. The first bright exciton band split into two features, visible only at small momentum. Standard Bethe-Salpeter calculations had not predicted this split, they note. They also extracted the deep ultraviolet optical conductivity at zero momentum from the spectra. The fine structure matches earlier photoluminescence observations, they report.
arxiv-2510-08797:
Saxena and colleagues at Meta and Duke University release ready-made datasets for a hard problem at the heart of future cryptography, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The problem, called learning with errors, underpins encryption schemes designed to resist quantum computers. Recent work shows that AI attacks on it can rival or beat classic attacks under some settings. Yet making training data for those attacks is slow, costly, and demands rare expertise.

The team's answer is TAPAS, a set of datasets covering several versions of the problem that AI researchers can use off the shelf. The paper documents how the data was created, so others can judge its quality and extend it. It also reports baseline results for current attack methods on the new data. Those baselines give later work a fixed yardstick, and the authors close with directions they see for stronger attacks.
arxiv-2510-09097:
Yano and colleagues group words by the situations they evoke, using the newest style of language model, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Semantic frames are template situations, like a purchase with its buyer, seller, and goods. Words as different as buy, sell, and price can all evoke the same frame. Induction means discovering those groupings automatically.

Earlier successes relied on masked language models, which read text with blanks. The authors instead exploit causal models, the kind that generate text left to right, through a prompting method called FrameEOL. It coaxes the model to output a single frame name as a label, and that behavior shapes an embedding for the word. Few-shot examples and metric learning sharpen the embeddings before clustering. On English and Japanese datasets, the method beat prior approaches, and five Japanese examples rivaled a fully fine-tuned rival.
arxiv-2510-09297:
Hou and Zeng build the first language model specialized in writing the judgment section of Chinese criminal court documents, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The court view states the court's reasoning and conclusion, and drafting it from raw case facts is hard because cases vary so widely. The team assembled CCVG, a dataset of over one hundred ten thousand Chinese cases, each pairing case facts with the actual court view. On that foundation they trained a deliberately small, lightweight model named ShiZhi.

ShiZhi scored seventy on the ROUGE-1 overlap measure and about sixty-eight on BLEU-1 for generated views. It also predicted charges with about eighty-six percent accuracy and a macro F1 near ninety-three percent. The authors read this as proof that even a small model writes reasonable court views that stay legally coherent, provided it trains on high-quality domain data. Model and dataset are publicly released.
arxiv-2510-09597:
Gabriel Andres Piovano, the sole author, solves for spinning particles orbiting a rotating black hole in a 2025 arXiv paper. The setting is Kerr spacetime, the geometry around a spinning black hole, and the particle is a small body whose own spin precesses as it moves. Such systems model extreme mass-ratio inspirals, key targets for future gravitational wave detectors.

Piovano works to first order in the spin for motion near the equatorial plane. Without spin, the particle follows geodesics, while the spin-curvature force bends the path and precesses the orbital plane. Solutions for eccentric orbits come out in terms of elliptic integrals and functions, and they match earlier numerical trajectories exactly. For the first time, homoclinic orbits, which loop out and return along the same path, are solved in closed form, including spin corrections to the separatrix. A new fixed-eccentricity gauge keeps the corrections finite at that boundary.
arxiv-2510-09697:
Renee Jerome, the sole author, merges two classic models of social influence in a 2025 arXiv paper. The Voter Model describes how opinions spread through a connected population under outside propaganda. The Blotto Game, from game theory, models two rivals splitting a budget across battlegrounds to win an information war, whether over politics or advertising.

Jerome combines them into a Voter-Blotto Game. Voters sit on a graph and sway each other as in the Voter Model, while two competing parties spend across that graph as in Blotto. The project examines which components of the graph most affect how much the competing players value it. The aim is practical as well as theoretical: understanding which nodes matter most should reveal the most effective spending strategy for campaigns fighting over a networked electorate.
arxiv-2510-09897:
Kweon and co-authors present PairSem in this 2025 arXiv paper on scientific document retrieval. Finding the right papers matters for discovery across every field, yet standard dense retrieval often misses fine-grained concepts in scientific text. Such methods embed a whole document as one vector, which blurs detail.

PairSem uses a large language model to guide pairwise semantic matching, comparing texts in pairs at a finer level than whole-document vectors allow. The model helps judge which concepts two passages share and where they differ. The aim is retrieval that respects the precise terms and claims scientists search for. The authors frame the method as a fix for the weak domain understanding of plain embedding search.
arxiv-2510-10297:
Milton studies the stiffness of two-dimensional polycrystals in this 2025 arXiv paper in materials theory. A polycrystal is a patchwork of tiny crystals set at varied angles. Its overall elastic response is summed up in an effective tensor, which depends on the elastic tensor of a single grain.

Milton writes that dependence as a continued fraction, an expansion that can converge fast and respect known bounds. Exact links between grain structure and bulk response are rare in the theory of composites. A continued fraction form is useful because its truncations stay safe approximations. The result helps predict the stiffness of a material from the stiffness of its grains, a basic need in materials design.
arxiv-2510-10597:
David Rodríguez-Martínez and C J Pérez del Pulgar make the case for single photon cameras in planetary rover navigation, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Vision based navigation with ordinary CCD or CMOS cameras struggles when harsh lighting meets motion, which limits how far planetary robots can roam. The authors propose cameras built on Single-Photon Avalanche Diodes, which can detect individual photons and work in near darkness.

They present the first comprehensive evaluation of single photon imaging as a passive sensing option for exploration missions. The study explains how SPAD cameras work and details their performance traits. It weighs their advantages and limits against the perception challenges of upcoming Moon missions, with emphasis on high latitude lunar regions where low sun angles create extreme shadows. The team also benchmarks the cameras under representative lighting. Their goal is to extend range for rovers where conventional cameras fail.
arxiv-2510-10797:
Aleksandra Melnikova and Petr Matula present full 3D segmentation annotations for time lapse movies of migrating cancer cells, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Good public annotations of volumetric image data are scarce because labeling many objects through a 3D movie is slow and hard. Three human annotators labeled two sequences of MDA231 human breast carcinoma cells from the Cell Tracking Challenge. This paper describes the dataset and the checks behind it in full.

The authors show the annotations agree with the tracking markers the challenge organizers had published. Accuracy measured against the challenge's 2D gold truth falls within the margins of disagreement between the human annotators themselves. Compared with the automatically generated silver truth, the new 3D annotations better represent the complexity of the images. The authors offer the data for testing and training cell segmentation methods, and for analyzing the 3D shapes of highly dynamic objects such as migrating cells.
arxiv-2510-10997:
Jose M Betancourt studies how social networks form when people meet by chance and link up selectively, in this 2025 arXiv paper. In his dynamic formation games, agents meet stochastically and create links based on how much they value the resulting network. Betancourt shows these games can be rewritten through the values agents assign to small network sub structures, the local patterns inside a network. This lens yields a clean characterization: a game is a potential game exactly when every participant in a structure values that structure equally.

When valuations are restricted to a finite set of repeated sub structures, called motifs, the model shows phase transitions. A small change in the value of one motif can trigger a discontinuous jump in overall network density. The result connects microscopic tastes for local patterns to macroscopic network shape.
arxiv-2510-11097:
Wireless networks still send information as electromagnetic waves, but that approach is nearing hard physical limits. Shumaila Javaid and Nasir Saeed, writing on arXiv in 2025, argue that future systems beyond 6G should carry information by changing physical, biological, or cognitive states instead. Their vision paper calls this state-based approach the post-electromagnetic era and maps out what it could look like.

The authors set out ten basic paradigms, meaning families of carriers and interaction methods, that could move information without radio waves. Options include spin-based and vibration-based channels and quantum media. They also sketch a research roadmap toward networks that organize themselves and use little energy. Electromagnetic channels still keep a role, but they would sit inside a wider fabric where devices choose the best carrier for each task and setting. No experiments are reported; the contribution is the framework itself.
arxiv-2510-11197:
Gravitational-wave observatories publish not just their signal catalog but also the Bayesian posterior samples behind each measurement, and many later studies reuse those samples. Gregory Ashton wrote this 2025 arXiv guide to using them correctly. Reusing the samples often requires rebuilding the original likelihood and prior, then resampling under changed assumptions, a step many studies rely on only implicitly.

Ashton first explains how to reconstruct and modify the posterior density for analyses done with the Bilby inference library. He then compares resampling techniques for producing new sample sets, and discusses Pareto smoothing as a way to improve their efficiency. Worked examples show how to apply resampling to real observed gravitational-wave signals. The guide is aimed at researchers who want to build further analyses on the open data products released by the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA collaborations.
arxiv-2510-11397:
LHS 1140 c is a warm super-Earth orbiting a red dwarf, and earlier Webb telescope observations hinted it might be a bare rock with no atmosphere. Alexandra Rochon and co-authors reanalyze those observations in this 2025 arXiv exoplanet paper. They use three secondary eclipses, when the planet passes behind its star, recorded by the MIRI instrument at fifteen microns.

Their reduction method exploits spatial derivatives of the point-spread function, the pattern of starlight on the detector, and agrees with aperture photometry within one sigma. They measure an eclipse depth of 271 parts per million, giving a brightness temperature near 595 kelvin, consistent with a bare rock surface. The eclipse arrived about four minutes earlier than a circular orbit predicts. Stellar abundances imply a core mass fraction around 0.34, higher than the mass-and-radius estimate, suggesting the interior may hold bulk volatile material.
arxiv-2510-11797:
Nisarga Paul proves a hard limit on what neural quantum states can express. These states use a neural network to stand in for a quantum wavefunction, dodging the huge size of full quantum descriptions. Many believed such networks escape the entanglement limits binding simpler methods like matrix product states. Paul's 2025 arXiv paper shows a broad class of them cannot, at least not fully.

For feed-forward networks acting on n spins with k nonlinear steps, the entanglement entropy of any region is at most a constant times k times the logarithm of n. The bound rules out volume-law entanglement, where entanglement grows with the region's size, whenever k stays fixed. Paul also shows analytically and numerically that the logarithmic growth is genuinely reachable, so the bound is tight. The result works across many designs, mapping where neural states shine and where they cannot go.
arxiv-2510-11897:
Sara Rosenthal and four co-authors study the humans who build test data for AI assistants. Retrieval-augmented generation grounds chatbot answers in source passages, and judging that faithfulness needs carefully annotated example conversations. Their 2025 arXiv paper compares two workforces: an internal annotator group and an external one. Each group worked under a different feedback loop while creating multi-turn test conversations.

The long-running study analyzes both the chats produced and survey answers about each group's experience. The tighter feedback loop yielded higher-quality conversations. It also produced fewer of them, and with less diversity. The looser loop traded some polish for volume and variety. Neither population wins outright; each has distinct advantages. The authors close with practical guidance on using two annotator groups side by side on complex tasks. The central lesson: feedback design, not just worker choice, shapes the dataset a test finally rests on.
arxiv-2510-11997:
Ryan Shea and three colleagues build a better simulated customer for testing service agents. Judging a multi-turn support agent normally takes scarce human testers. Simulated users can substitute, but generic simulators behave unlike any real clientele. Their 2025 arXiv paper proposes SAGE, a user simulator grounded in a business's own knowledge from two directions.

From the top down, SAGE absorbs business logic like ideal customer profiles, grounding its personas in the company's actual target market. From the bottom up, it draws on product catalogs, frequently asked questions, and knowledge bases, so its questions carry realistic information needs. In empirical evaluation, the approach produced interactions that were both more realistic and more diverse than generic simulation. Sharper realism paid off in bug hunting: SAGE surfaced up to thirty-three percent more agent errors. The authors pitch it as an engine for improving agents before real users meet them.
arxiv-2510-12097:
Joshua Roberson and eight colleagues use galaxy clusters as natural telescopes to hunt the first bright galaxies. Deep fields teem with such galaxies, almost all too faint for spectroscopy. Cluster lensing can magnify a few into reach. Their 2025 arXiv paper analyzes Hubble and ground-based photometry of five candidate lensed galaxies behind cluster cores.

All five share red colors and a spectral drop-off suggesting a Lyman break, which sets a minimum distance. Modeling with the Prospector software splits the sample. Two are genuinely early, near redshift seven. Three are red, dusty impostors from redshift two. Brightness plus color constraints, the team shows, can separate the populations with limited data. The confirmed pair significantly swells the tiny census of very bright galaxies at redshift six and beyond.
arxiv-2510-12297:
Guermond and Nadathur extend a loosening of the rules for defining terms in the logic behind the Abella proof assistant, in a 2025 arXiv logic paper. Abella reads predicates through fixed point definitions, taken inductively or co inductively. Its original condition, which orders definitions to keep them coherent, is too strict for uses such as logical relations arguments about whether programs are equivalent.

Tiu had shown that a weaker condition called ground stratification can replace the strict one, but only for a version of the logic without inductive definitions. The authors prove the loosening extends to inductive definitions as well. The extension is delicate. Ground stratification for arbitrary fixed point definitions works, but weakening it the wrong way for inductive definitions leads to inconsistency. Their version matches how these relations are used in practice. The result is a step toward a more flexible way to define predicates in the full logic.
arxiv-2510-12897:
Johnson, Lauinger, Shin, and Pacaud release a software library for power grid optimization in this 2025 arXiv paper. The underlying problem, alternating current optimal power flow, picks generator settings that satisfy nonlinear physics constraints at lowest cost, and it grows very hard on large networks. Graphics processors could speed up new solvers, but modeling tools designed for them were missing.

Their library, ExaModelsPower.jl, written in the Julia language, lets users state large nonlinear power flow models at a high level and automatically produces the callback functions GPU solvers require. It supports multi-period problems and security constraints. Benchmarks on open test cases showed GPU solvers running up to about one hundred times faster than CPU alternatives on problems with more than twenty thousand variables. Smaller cases and tighter tolerances, though, favored the CPU.
arxiv-2510-12997:
Gao and Han benchmark language models on extremal problems in this 2025 arXiv paper. Extremal problems ask for maximum or minimum values under constraints, and that optimization reasoning underlies planning, control, resource allocation, and even prompt search. Standard mathematics benchmarks may not measure this skill directly, so the authors built one that does.

Their dataset, ExtremBench, adapts inequality exercises from Chinese Mathematical Olympiad training into ninety-three standardized extrema-finding problems. They evaluated leading open model families, including Qwen3, GPT-OSS, and DeepSeek variants. Performance on extremal problems did not track performance on popular benchmarks such as AIME25 and MATH-500. Some models strong at general mathematics were weak at extremal solving. Others showed the reverse pattern. The authors argue that current evaluation practices leave a real gap in measuring mathematical reasoning.
arxiv-2510-13097:
Li and Zhang analyze how shear flow disperses a passive substance in an infinite cylinder in this 2025 arXiv paper. A passive scalar, such as a dye concentration, is carried by a parallel shear flow while slowly diffusing. Two decay mechanisms compete: enhanced dissipation, where shear accelerates mixing, and Taylor dispersion, the slower spreading along the flow.

Their setting has an unbounded cross-section and very small viscosity, in arbitrary spatial dimension. Because the cylinder is infinite, the streamwise wave number ranges over all real values, including near zero. They show enhanced dissipation occurs only for high frequencies above the viscosity scale, while low frequencies exhibit only Taylor dispersion decay. Earlier work covered bounded cross-sections, where low frequencies never arise. For the unbounded case they find an extra non-degeneracy condition at infinity is required.
arxiv-2510-13397:
Wang and co-authors tackle biased treatment estimates when patients drop out of clinical studies early. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies survival data, where dropout often depends on how long a patient would live. Such informative dropout skews estimates of who benefits from a treatment. Up to half of patients may leave some studies early. The focus is heterogeneous effects, where benefit varies across patients.

Instead of assuming dropout is harmless, the team derives bounds on treatment effects for patient subgroups. This partial identification approach reports a range rather than one fragile point estimate. They also build a meta-learner that estimates these bounds with common machine learning models. The estimator carries strong guarantees, including double robustness and near-oracle efficiency. Tests and a cancer drug trial show the method finds subgroups that truly benefit. In that trial, genome-defined subgroups showed benefit despite the overall negative result.
arxiv-2510-13497:
Wang and co-authors build DistilCLIP-EEG, a multimodal model that detects epileptic seizures from brain signals and text. Their 2025 arXiv paper addresses a gap: most detection methods use EEG signals alone. Text descriptions of seizures carry extra information that single-signal models ignore. The team adapts the CLIP framework, which aligns different data types in one space.

Their model pairs a Conformer-based EEG encoder with a learnable version of BERT for text. Prompt learning inside both encoders sharpens the shared representation. A knowledge distillation step then trains a compact student from the full teacher model. On three datasets, both teacher and student passed ninety-seven percent accuracy, with F1 scores above ninety-four percent reported across the board in the same tests. The student keeps about fifty-eight percent of the teacher's size, easing deployment in tight settings.
arxiv-2510-13597:
Aguzzi and co-authors model how nuclear fuel rods deform under heat, stress, and irradiation together. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds a multiphysics framework rooted in crystal-scale mechanics. The test case is a fuel assembly with Zircaloy-2 cladding tubes and spacer grids. Conditions mimic a pressurized water reactor in normal operation.

The framework couples a crystal-plasticity model with the Code_Aster finite element solver. It captures thermal expansion and thermal creep alongside irradiation effects. Deformation proves strongly directional, driven by crystal texture and prismatic slip under radial load. Thermal creep relaxes stress early and adds strain beyond the irradiation-only case. Over the long term, irradiation mechanisms govern how the gap between rod and grid evolves. The authors aim the tool at predicting spacer-cladding contact and seeding simpler reduced models.
arxiv-2510-13697:
Sapronov and Glukhov test how pretraining choices shape a code model's skill at completing whole projects. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies OpenCoder, a modest 1.5-billion-parameter code model. Repository-level pretraining teaches models to use context across many files of one codebase. Rivals use hundreds of billions of tokens for that stage, a heavy price.

The authors stretch the model's context window fourfold, from about four thousand to sixteen thousand tokens. They train on one billion extra tokens of curated repository data, far less than competitors use. Even so, the model matches rivals on the Long Code Arena benchmark. Different repository-processing tricks all performed about equally well in their trials. Most of the gain came from adapting to a new positional scaling setting instead. Plain file-level training at the old length also stayed surprisingly strong.
arxiv-2510-13897:
Fridman and Goldstein predict breast cancer HER2 status straight from MRI scans with a dual-attention ResNet that beats transformer rivals. Their 2025 arXiv paper targets treatment selection, where HER2 status steers therapy choices. Biopsy is invasive, so a reliable imaging shortcut would streamline diagnosis. Feeding high-bit-depth scans into standard networks first demands careful intensity normalization.

Their model fuses three contrast phases, before and after dye injection, as colour channels. Triple attention heads watch the temporal sequence for transferable patterns. The team benchmarked normalization strategies systematically on a multicentre cohort of over a thousand patients. The ResNet reached an accuracy of 0.75 with an AUC of 0.74 on held-out trial data under matched protocols, outpacing both vision transformer variants tested, the authors report. A common bias-field correction slightly hurt deep learning performance, surprisingly. External validation at another institution held up without any fine-tuning.
arxiv-2510-13997:
Huifang Lyu and co-authors present a faster way to do simulation-based inference, a statistical approach where scientists learn about nature by comparing real data with computer simulations, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Sequential versions steer simulations toward the most informative parameter regions, but they work in rounds, alternating simulation and network training, which wastes time and computing power.

Their method, dynamic SBI, drops the rounds. An adaptive data set is steadily reshaped to resemble the target observation. Simulation and training run in parallel. Trained networks filter out simulations that clash with the data and propose better replacements. The authors report large gains in simulation and training efficiency while keeping inference quality. They validate the framework on two hard astrophysics problems, mapping the stochastic gravitational-wave background and analyzing strong gravitational lensing systems, where massive objects bend light from background sources.
arxiv-2510-14397:
Kaoru Sano counts how many rational numbers can reach zero by repeatedly applying a polynomial map, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The maps are unicritical polynomials, which raise the input to a power and add a constant. Their rational preimages of the origin form trees whose size reflects arithmetic constraints. Earlier work settled finiteness in the quadratic case, with conditional bounds.

Building on that work, Sano proves a result for the quadratic map with any nonzero rational constant other than negative one. There are no rational fourth preimages of the origin, points that land on zero after four backward steps in the rational tree. For higher powers, there are no rational second preimages outside trivial cases. The proof combines analysis of preimage curves, the elliptic Chabauty method, and Diophantine reduction. As a result, the number of rational preimages of the origin is determined for every degree.
arxiv-2510-14597:
Thallapalli, Alpana, Iyer, and Sharma examine, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a rare decay that could betray new physics at the High-Luminosity LHC. The decay produces two bottom quarks and a photon from a Z boson. The Standard Model can make this final state when a Z decays and radiates a photon. New physics could make it too, through an intermediate particle lighter than the Z, with spin zero or two.

The authors work out the signal's detector signature: two relatively soft jets tagged as bottom-quark jets, plus an isolated photon. They provide a quantitative framework for identifying the signal and discuss the practical challenges it poses. Several machine learning architectures check that the separating variables are stable and reliable. The study stresses that soft objects are easy to mishandle, so their identification and efficiency deserve special care in these searches.
arxiv-2510-14897:
Valls and co-authors introduce, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a way to certify that a forecast of a quantum system's behavior can be trusted. Near-term quantum devices are noisy, so measurements cover only short times, and data-driven extrapolation extends them. But an extrapolated curve can look right while capturing the wrong dynamics, and nothing guaranteed otherwise.

The authors bring in atomic norm minimization, a compressed sensing tool, as a certification layer that can audit a model produced by any forecasting algorithm. The guarantee holds when the system's motion is governed by a few well-separated frequencies. They validated the framework on spin chains of eight to twenty qubits against exact calculations. Certified forecasts had average error under a tenth of the observable's range in ninety-eight percent of cases. Even with realistic measurement shot noise, success rates slipped only slightly, showing the certificates survive practical conditions.
arxiv-2510-15297:
Luca Belli and seven colleagues, including clinicians and the team at a mental health AI company, propose a way to safety-test chatbots that talk with people in distress. Their 2025 concept paper introduces VERA-MH, an automated evaluation aimed first at suicide risk, where a chatbot's words can do real harm. Clinicians and academic experts wrote the scoring rubric, grounded in accepted practice for managing suicide risk.

The testing itself is automated with two helper agents. A user agent role-plays patients with preset risk levels and traits, holding conversations with the chatbot under review. A judge agent then scores those transcripts against the rubric, and the scores combine into one verdict. Early trials on GPT-5 and two Claude models informed the design, and clinician validation is still under way. The authors openly seek community feedback on both the technical setup and its clinical soundness before wider use.
arxiv-2510-15797:
Laszlo Gacsi, Adam Kiss, and Tamas Molnar present a brake controller in a 2025 paper. It stops a vehicle from spinning out under hard braking. The risk arises on surfaces with uneven grip. One side may be ice and the other asphalt. Such braking can swing the car sideways. Friction limits what any controller can do.

Their design uses backup control barrier functions. This safety method always keeps a known safe manoeuvre in reserve. The authors add a constructive way to build that reserve. They build both the backup set and the backup controller. The result guarantees bounded sideways motion. It still minimises stopping distance for the driver.
arxiv-2510-15897:
Kien Le Trung and Truong-Son Hy recast chip placement as a diffusion process that positions all blocks at once. Placement decides performance, power, and whether wires can be routed at all. Analytical and sequential learning methods often break hard constraints, need costly retraining per circuit, or squeeze blocks so tightly that routing chokes downstream.

Their framework, DiffPlace, denoises block positions under conditioning, with a neural backbone that passes vector messages to capture geometric links. Policies transfer to unseen netlists without heavy retraining. A decoupled guidance scheme handles the many goals: global aims enter through energy-based conditioning, while local physical limits are enforced by injecting manifold gradients during sampling. The pair aim for balanced layouts that put routability first while keeping wirelength competitive, and report strong placement quality with better generalisation than learning baselines.
arxiv-2510-15997:
Martin Ryzy and six co-authors measure the wall thickness of fusion fuel capsules with laser-driven ultrasound in the frequency domain. In inertial confinement fusion, hollow millimetre spheres hold the fuel, and implosion efficiency demands near-perfect capsule geometry. Their method excites zero-group-velocity guided wave resonances, whose frequencies encode the local wall thickness.

A contactless laser ultrasound microscope reads those resonances without touching the capsule. Along the equator of a high-density carbon capsule about two millimetres wide, the measured thickness agrees excellently with infrared interferometry reference values, the team reports. The shell's many resonances are also studied through plate dispersion calculations and finite element wave simulations. The method scales to many target materials, including metals and metal-doped targets, which broadens quality control for fusion experiments.
arxiv-2510-16097:
Eleni Straitouri and three co-authors ask how AI help can make people better at step-by-step choices, not just one-off picks. Their support tool works in a simple way. A trained AI first trims the list of moves a person may take. The person then picks from that short list. The design keeps the human in charge of the final call.

They tested the tool in a wildfire control game with sixteen hundred players. Players with AI help beat solo players by about thirty percent. They even edged out the AI playing alone by more than two percent. The team also built a learning method that tunes how much the AI trims over time. The study suggests that limiting choices, done well, can beat both full human and full machine control.
arxiv-2510-16197:
Daniel Messenger and three co-authors find hidden simplicity in a violent mixing process called the Richtmyer-Meshkov instability. It strikes when a shock wave crosses the border between two fluids of unlike density, making them churn and mix. In fusion capsules this mixing cools the fuel and saps the yield, so designers need fast ways to predict it.

Their reduced model learns a small set of hidden variables that capture the mixing, using only late-time partial views of the flow. A trained autoencoder bends the data into a space where those variables move in near-straight, linear ways. The model then forecasts the mixing quickly across many material settings and starting shapes. Beyond speed, the low hidden count hints the process is simpler at heart than its wild look suggests. That hint may steer new theory as well as faster capsule design.
arxiv-2510-16497:
Pacome Simon Mbonimpa, Diane Tuyizere, Azizuddin Ahmed Biyabani, and Ozan K. Tonguz build speech tools in their 2025 paper. The tools turn speech to text and text to speech for Kinyarwanda and Swahili. Both tongues are spoken by many in East Africa, yet lack strong tech tools. Their design splits the work between a local device and the cloud.

Two ready-made models, Whisper and SpeechT5, do the speech work. The split cuts wait time and memory use on weak devices. Peak memory stayed at 149 MB in their tests. A short text took under a minute to process on a slow chip. Survey data from Kenya backs the design for real use.
arxiv-2510-16797:
Vera Pavlova and Mohammed Makhlouf, a two-author team, adapt general text embedding models to specialized fields with a framework called MOSAIC. Embeddings turn text into numbers so machines can judge similarity. Models trained on general text often miss the vocabulary and sense of a narrow domain, yet retraining from scratch is costly.

MOSAIC trains with two goals at once: masked language modeling, which teaches domain wording, and contrastive learning, which keeps meanings apart. The stages are balanced and applied in sequence. Tests on rich and sparse domains show clear gains in ranking quality over strong general baselines, with improvements up to about thirteen percent on a standard top-ten measure. Ablations confirm each stage earns its place.
arxiv-2510-17097:
Hodek M. Garcia and Marcelo Salgado test a changed form of gravity in this 2025 paper. In this form, a curve term in the gravity laws is swapped for a wider function. The change must still pass strict checks near the Sun. It must also hold up inside dense stars built from dead suns.

The authors solve the full laws with no short cuts for round, still objects. Near the Sun, the model can hide its change much like a screen. For dead stars, they use a split law for matter at set density bands. Their results match the heaviest such star known so far. The work links weak-field and strong-field checks in one frame.
arxiv-2510-17397:
Inside a solar type star, a thin layer called the tachocline sits between the still core and the churning outer envelope, where rotation changes sharply. Camille Moisset, Stéphane Mathis, and Louis Amard examine how that layer behaves as the star ages. Young stars spin in one pattern, older stars slow down, and the outer rotation pattern shifts from column like flow to a Sun like form and beyond.

Most star models study the tachocline only under the Sun like pattern, which misses that long change. Moisset and her co-authors show that an older formalism, used in a thin layer version, can treat all the rotation regimes in one coherent way. They use it to map rotation, circulation, and mixing inside the layer for each regime.
arxiv-2510-17697:
Anjie Liu, with Jianhong Wang and three co-authors, proposes steering multi agent learning through one agent in a 2025 arXiv paper. In cooperative multi agent reinforcement learning, many agents learn to act together. Guiding the whole system toward a desired outcome is hard at large scale. Asking a human to direct every agent is impractical. Most add on mechanisms rest on trial and error evidence instead of theory.

The authors use influence diagrams, which are graphs of how agents affect each other, as their analysis tool. They define a targeted intervention paradigm that acts on a single chosen agent. A causal method called Pre-Strategy Intervention carries out the plan. It maximizes a combined outcome covering the main task plus one added goal. Experiments confirmed the approach works.
arxiv-2510-18097:
Mingjia Yan and four co-authors recast the motion of slender rods in thick fluids as a geometric field theory. Cosserat rods model things that stretch, shear, twist, and bend, from bacterial tails to soft robot arms. In slow, viscous settings inertia fades and friction rules, which suits the frame-based math used here.

Written with moving frames, the equations take values in the group of rigid motions. The form stays the same under shifts of space and guides material modeling by symmetry rules. Soft matter and robotics readers get a cleaner language for rod motion that respects geometry from the start.
arxiv-2510-18497:
Amirhossein Akbar Tabatabai works with Vitor Greati and Revantha Ramanayake. They start a broad study of a curbed style of recursion. The style is called predicative recursion. It limits how a function may call itself. On numbers and strings, it captures known classes exactly. Those classes are linear-space and polynomial-time functions. The authors extend the scheme to constructive ordinals. Ordinals give a scale for how long well-founded structures can run.

They define matching classes of recursive functions. The classes sit below a level of the Veblen hierarchy. Their main result sorts those classes in full. It applies when the set holds at least one infinite ordinal. The sorting uses the Grzegorczyk hierarchy. That is a classic ladder of growth rates. The result extends the old number and string findings. It gives proof theory a sharper map of what predicative methods can compute.
arxiv-2510-18597:
Vincent Delecroix works with Oscar Fontaine and Francis Lazarus. They compute a special shrinking of a graph on a surface. For any closed curve, one can ask a plain question. What is the fewest crossings with the graph that its family allows? A graph is a kernel when no smaller graph matches those counts. The match must hold in a strong sense. Every graph holds such a kernel inside it.

The authors give an algorithm that finds the kernel. Its run time grows with the count of edges. It rests on a tight bound for small lens-shaped regions. It uses helper routines of wider interest too. One routine measures the area a curve encloses. With the kernel ready, later questions get much faster answers. Any new curve can be scored against it quickly. That beats the past best method by a wide margin.
arxiv-2510-18997:
Fabio Apruzzi and Luca Martucci uncover a large new family of non-invertible symmetries in four-dimensional models first studied by Gaillard and Zumino. Those models pair abelian gauge fields with neutral scalars, and their equations were long thought to keep only a small integral subgroup of symmetries once quantum effects enter.

The authors show a much larger rational subgroup survives, though through topological defects that cannot be inverted. They construct the defects explicitly, including cases drawn from extended supergravity. The finding revises standard lore about which symmetries quantum physics allows in these theories.
arxiv-2510-19397:
Javier Álvarez-Vizoso and David Barral give a universality criterion. It covers layered decompositions of unitary operations. The layers alternate. Programmable diagonal layers come first, then fixed mixing layers. Such factorizations matter in quantum information and quantum control. They matter in linear optics too. Hardware can only realize certain simple operations.

The authors model the structure with a one-dimensional quantum field theory. Anomaly ideas from that model state when a set of mixers suffices. The proof is grounded in physics. It tells designers which mixers they truly need. The target is coverage of every special unitary operation.
arxiv-2510-19497:
Trung-Dung Vu, Benoit Gaudou, and Kamaldeep Singh Oberoi describe a software setup for simulating how real people choose between ways of getting around a city. Their system places language-model-driven agents inside a detailed transport simulation. The test case is Toulouse, France, a city with buses, metro, and other linked travel options.

The framework joins the GAMA simulation platform with real transit timetable data and the OpenTripPlanner routing engine. Over a simulated month, the agents made choices that fit their situations and gradually formed habits. The authors argue the approach suits personalized mobility advice, while noting limits around scaling to larger regions, live data, and agent memory.
arxiv-2510-19797:
Roey Magen and Gal Vardi prove that a simplified transformer, trained by gradient descent, can act as a nearly optimal metalearner for linear classification. Metalearning means learning from many related tasks so a new one needs only a handful of examples. Their tasks are Gaussian mixture classification problems whose mean vectors live in a shared low-dimensional subspace.

After training on enough tasks, the transformer generalizes to a fresh task using a number of in-context examples that depends on the subspace dimension, not the full data dimension. That nearly matches an optimal learner told the subspace outright, and it crushes any learner restricted to the in-context examples alone. The required training effort is likewise independent of the ambient dimension.
arxiv-2510-19897:
Jackson Hassell and four co-authors teach language model agents to learn classification tasks from labeled examples without changing any model weights. Instead of fine-tuning, their framework has the model write critiques of its own past attempts. Specific critiques are stored in an episodic memory, then distilled into reusable, task-level guidance kept in a semantic memory.

Using both memories together improved accuracy by about eight percentage points over a zero-shot baseline and beat a retrieval baseline that used labels alone. Gains varied widely by model and domain, so the authors introduce a suggestibility metric measuring how receptive a model is to outside reasoning. Pre-computed critiques also cut the model's inference-time thinking substantially, making the approach cheaper as well as more accurate.
arxiv-2510-19997:
Abraham Itzhak Weinberg proposes FAIGMOE, a guide for midsize and large firms taking up generative AI. Midsize firms face scarce funds and thin AI skill. Big firms wrestle with sheer scale and with getting many teams to pull together. Classic adoption theories, he argues, are too broad for what generative AI demands, leaving a gap this guide fills.

Four phases structure the path: taking stock, planning use cases, putting the tools in place, and running and refining them. Each phase scales its advice, on readiness, fit with strategy, risk, tech design, and staff change, to the firm's size. Concerns tied to generative AI itself, like prompt craft and hallucination control, are built in. As a perspective piece, the guide awaits tests in real firms, which the author flags as future work.
arxiv-2510-20097:
Aidan Blaser, Luc Lenain, and Nick Pizzo show that the drift caused by ocean surface waves is stronger where waves focus and steepen than simple estimates suggest. Surface gravity waves carry a mean Lagrangian drift that moves mass and aids mixing in the upper ocean. The usual practice adds up the drift from each wave part separately, as if the parts never interacted.

Lab measurements and fully nonlinear simulations of steep focusing wave packets show that practice underpredicts average transport in focusing regions by up to thirty percent. The authors derive an exact way to constrain local drift and a higher-order formula for narrow-banded fields. Local steepness, not the sum of separate parts, sets the size of the boost.
arxiv-2510-20397:
Nahual Sobrino probes heat-to-charge flow in a pair of joined quantum dots that block charge by the Coulomb force. He grows an exact-form base built by a motion law route, now for dots with lopsided links. Short closed forms come out for steady flows and for slope traits: charge slope, Seebeck rate, and heat slope.

Sobrino picks the work points that top yield and power, and ties them to near-balance ZT forms. Heat flow that bends one way is checked for both open and closed loop states, with a form for the open case. Peaks from the dot-dot force are read from poles of the Green map. They yield zones of high yield, odd heat slope signs, and real heat bending.
arxiv-2510-20897:
