Melanoma is the most lethal skin cancer, and early detection is critical for patient outcomes. Deep learning progress is blocked by scarce annotated data and severe class imbalance. They compare DCGAN, StyleGAN2, and two StyleGAN3 variants on ISIC 2018 and ISIC 2020 data. StyleGAN2 gave the best balance of scores and perceptual quality in their tests. Adding its synthetic images to training raised melanoma detection AUC on a held-out real test set.
arxiv-2603-13597: Reza Farahani and co-authors introduce DQ-Ladder, a deep reinforcement learning method for adaptive video streaming bitrate ladders. Fixed ladders overlook variation in content and decoding complexity, hurting encoding and quality trade-offs. In DQ-Ladder, a Deep Q-Network agent takes in predicted decoding time, quality scores, and bitrate levels for each segment. A weighted reward balances decoding time, video quality, and resolution smoothness. Machine learning models predict the needed metrics, avoiding exhaustive encoding runs. On 750 video sequences it cut BD-rate and decoding time.
arxiv-2603-13997: Gligorijevic and co-authors build a shared embedding for search queries and user location to improve ad targeting. Many mobile queries hinge on place, in words or by hint, as with searches for shops nearby. Their neural framework places query intent and location in one low-dimensional space. The joint code captures how intent and place shape each other. Tests show better ad ranking and query-ad relevance than methods that ignore location or bolt it on.
arxiv-2603-14197: Nguyen-Le and Matni study stochastic policy gradient methods for domain randomized control design, using the linear-quadratic regulator as the test case. Domain randomization trains on varied fake systems to shrink the sim-to-real gap. They show that fresh system samples at each gradient step lead to global optima under the right step settings. The resampled approach also gives controllers with lower final spread than fixed-sample training. Since sampling is cheap, they argue it should be the default.
arxiv-2603-14397: Ramesh and co-authors build eNavi, a person-following robot policy that learns from event cameras for dark indoor spaces. Event cameras keep high dynamic range and microsecond timing where normal cameras fail. The team records a real TurtleBot 2 dataset with raw events, RGB frames, and expert actions across several maps, in bright and dim light. Their policy fuses dual MobileNet encoders for the two streams with a transformer, trained by cloning expert moves. Tests across twelve training variants compare RGB, event, and fused inputs.
arxiv-2603-14597: Song and Xin gate agent memory with a dopamine-style signal in D-MEM. Long-term memory stores grow fast, and rewrites can cost quadratically. Their design splits fast intake from slow restructuring. A light Critic Router scores each input for surprise and utility. Calm, low-error inputs land in a fast buffer at unit cost. Shocks like contradictions fire a dopamine signal and trigger deep updates. On a noisy long-dialogue test, token use falls over 80%, they report.
arxiv-2603-14697: Limbu and co-authors plan multi-robot graph traversal with support coordination under moving adversaries. Teammates can aid each other across risky edges, cutting mission cost. Risk turns time-varying as adversaries move. Each adversary follows a first-order Markov stay-move process on edges. Occupancy spreads over a planning horizon give time-indexed risk forecasts. Those forecasts steer support picks and joint path plans. Forecast-led support beats the tested baselines on expected team cost, they report.
arxiv-2603-14897: Yu and co-authors predict transcriptomics from cancer pathology images with bidirectional transfer in BiTro. Bulk data and slide images are plentiful but lack spatial maps. Spatial transcriptomics gives maps at high cost and thin depth. Each side alone limits image-to-gene mapping accuracy. BiTro models slides at the cell level to catch cell looks and layout. Multiple instance learning links cell features to gene readouts. LoRA adapters move the model between bulk and spatial data. Both directions gain from the shared structure, they report.
arxiv-2603-14997: Flynt presents OrgForge, a multi-agent framework that builds synthetic corporate document sets with checkable ground truth. A deterministic Python engine tracks events, while language models write only the surface prose. Simulated staff changes, incidents, and customer events create fifteen linked artifact types tied to one event log. The system also models support escalation, deal risk, and invoices. In tests over ten incidents, fidelity to ground truth rose by 0.46 over chained language-model baselines.
arxiv-2603-15097: Singh and co-authors present AeroGrab, an end-to-end system for drone grasping in cluttered scenes. Given a scene and a spoken-style language instruction, the drone finds the target object first. It then explores actively to get clearer views. A grasp network proposes six-degree-of-freedom grasp candidates for each view. A collision-aware check scores every candidate, and the best grasp is flown and executed. Tests in cluttered real-world scenes showed robust, reliable grasping.
arxiv-2603-15297: O'Connor and co-authors introduce Dragonchess, a three-dimensional chess variant by Gary Gygax, as a testbed for AI transfer learning. They release an open-source Python engine for the game. Heuristic scoring functions were adapted straight from Stockfish, the top chess engine, then evolved with CMA-ES. Direct transfer failed, since the multi-layer board and movement rules differ too much from chess. Evolutionary optimization improved play a lot, shown in a 50-round Swiss-style tournament. The work shows evolution can adapt expert heuristics to complex new games.
arxiv-2603-15697: Nishida studies how light polarization bends gravitational lensing paths. The optical Magnus effect shifts a light ray sideways based on its polarization. It enters as a first-order correction in wavelength. He starts from Maxwell's equations in curved spacetime. The wave packet motion shows a helicity-dependent extra velocity. He then tests lensing near a Schwarzschild mass and in an expanding universe. A neat result follows: no Einstein ring forms from a point source. Simple lens models get analytic image solutions.
arxiv-2603-15797: Wu and co-authors ground image-language models in fluid physics to cut false claims. Language models reason well in words but stumble on PDE-governed flows. Fine-tuning per domain costs much and blocks transfer. Their OMNIFLOW design keeps the base model frozen. A semantic-symbolic step turns flow tensors into topology words. A physics-guided chain injects rules like mass conservation. Reflexive checks then verify each reasoning pass. Tests span micro turbulence, Navier-Stokes, and global weather. Zero-shot and few-shot scores beat deep baselines.
arxiv-2603-16197: Reddy and Karmakar audit six frontier language models for benchmark contamination. Public test sets are mirrored online, so models may train on their own exam. The team runs three checks on MMLU questions. One check found a 13.8% contamination rate across 513 questions. Reworded questions cut accuracy by 7 points on average. Guessing probes flagged memorization signals in 72.5% of cases. All three checks rank STEM fields as most contaminated.
arxiv-2603-16297: Equi, Khan, and Mäkinen speed up pattern matching in degenerate strings. A degenerate string holds a set of characters at each position. The generalized form holds sets of short strings instead. The best classical method runs in time O(mn+N). No lower bound is known for the task. Their quantum algorithm runs in about the square root of that scale. The team presents it through a parallel computing lens.
arxiv-2603-16397: The Fanar Team presents Fanar 2.0, Qatar's second Arabic-first AI platform. Every part was built and run at QCRI in Qatar. The work ran on 256 H100 GPUs, with Arabic scarce on the web. The core model, Fanar-27B, was pre-trained on 120 billion curated tokens. It improves on Arabic knowledge, dialects, and English skill. New parts add safety filtering, speech, vision, and poetry tools. A multi-layer orchestrator routes tasks among them.
arxiv-2603-16497: Khanal and co-authors fill a frequency gap in time series training data. Foundation models for time series mostly learn from slow data. Their msData set records a live 5G network every millisecond. It adds wireless traffic as a fresh domain for these models. Forecast tasks span horizons from 1 to 96 milliseconds. Benchmarks cover classic, transformer, and foundation models. Most foundation setups did poorly, even after fine-tuning. High-frequency data, the authors argue, must join pre-training.
arxiv-2603-16697: Grivet and Travé-Massuyès settle which method should update a matrix inverse in streaming outlier detection. The Christoffel function scores outliers, but online learning keeps inverting changed matrices. Three updates compete: direct inversion, iterative Sherman-Morrison, and the Woodbury identity. The pair derive each method's cost, then test them in Python. A simple rule emerges from the results. Rank-one updates favor Sherman-Morrison. Small updates favor Woodbury. Otherwise direct inversion wins.
arxiv-2603-16797: Belardi and co-authors stabilize guided diffusion sampling with a simple trick from optimization. Guided sampling must approximate likelihood scores that are hard to compute, and the errors add noise to each step. The team applies adaptive moment estimation, as in the Adam optimizer, to smooth these noisy scores. They report state-of-the-art results on image restoration and class-conditional generation. The method also beats costlier rivals. Tests on synthetic and real data show that cutting gradient noise improves alignment.
arxiv-2603-17097: Gacsi and co-authors present a safety control framework for constraints that mix system state and control input. Safety work often handles state limits and input limits apart, but some limits, like power, depend on both. Their method generalizes backup control barrier functions. A projection along the backup controller turns mixed constraints into state constraints. One backup pair can then hold many decoupled limits at once. They demonstrate the method on an inverted pendulum, where angle, torque, and power limits held together.
arxiv-2603-17197: Ralston, Yang, and Hu study how actions leak private information in stochastic games. Each player knows its own coupling parameter and holds a prior over the opponent's. Starting from the full information case, they characterize the Nash equilibrium through coupled Riccati equations. They then define baseline controls by averaging under each player's prior. On that baseline, they pose an alignment faking problem: one player trades fidelity to its baseline policy against learning the opponent's parameter. Results show faking can raise information gain, at a cost in detectability.
arxiv-2603-17297: Chen and co-authors locate near field targets that lack a line of sight, using a hybrid intelligent surface whose own position is unknown. Older surface aided methods assume the surface position is known, which limits real use. Their framework runs in two stages. First, the surface localizes itself, using Fresnel approximations and atomic norm methods. Then it fixes the target positions. They also optimize the surface phases to boost signal power and accuracy, and derive error bounds as benchmarks.
arxiv-2603-17997: Ho proves Ehrenborg's conjecture on spanning trees in bipartite graphs. For a connected bipartite graph with parts of size m and n, the tree count stays at or below a bound built from vertex degrees. Equality holds if and only if the graph is a Ferrers graph. The whole proof is formalized in Lean 4.
arxiv-2603-18197: Kim and Kim design access-controlled website interaction for agentic AI doing delegated critical tasks. Current sites lack fine-grained control when agents act for a user. Their design covers both the website itself and changes to an open-source authorization service. Grants are tailored to agentic AI and to the critical tasks being delegated. Tests show the access-controlled site works in practice for AI agents.
arxiv-2603-18397: Nie and Gao present FlowMS, a flow matching framework for de novo structure elucidation from mass spectra. Guessing molecular structure from spectra faces huge chemical space and ambiguous fragments. FlowMS is the first discrete flow matching method for this spectrum-conditioned task. It refines molecular graphs in probability space under formula constraints, guided by a pretrained formula encoder. On NPLIB1 it leads on five of six metrics, with 9.15% top-1 accuracy.
arxiv-2603-18497: Simeon rebuilds sparse brain circuit links from partial records with a covariance method and a Granger step. Each session records a new subset of neurons, so no one session sees the full circuit. Pairwise covariance values stack across sessions to fill in the full link matrix. A projected gradient step then applies biological rules through Granger causality. Tests show a trade-off: input boosts how well links can be found but warps the circuit's own dynamics.
arxiv-2603-18797: Prabhakar and co-authors present VesselTok, which tokenizes vessel-like 3D graphs for biomedical work. Blood vessels, airways, and nerve networks form spatial graphs that are hard to model at full resolution. VesselTok encodes tubes from centerline points plus a pseudo radius. A learned latent code captures the implicit shape of each tubular segment. Tests cover lung airways, lung vessels, and brain vessels with complex branching. The codes generalize to unseen anatomies. They also support generation of plausible new graphs and help downstream tasks like link prediction.
arxiv-2603-18997: Blasius and co-authors ask whether disk graphs in hyperbolic space have a grid-like product form. Such graphs join disks of one radius that overlap in the curved plane. They show that with a fixed clique cap, no such product form exists. This sets them apart from flat-plane disk graphs, which do have that form. For very small radii, the product form does hold. The split turns on whether the radius grows with graph size. Their proof uses a family with slow radius growth and no grid structure.
arxiv-2603-19297: Baser and co-authors predict where an edit to a language model will ripple to facts it was not meant to touch. Their CLaRE score reads activations from one middle layer in a single forward pass. It gauges how tangled two facts are inside the model. On a corpus of 11,427 facts, the scores track real ripple effects well. Gains over baselines average 62.2 percent in rank correlation. The method runs 2.74 times faster and uses far less memory and storage.
arxiv-2603-19597: Li and co-authors build a stabilizer formalism for entanglement-assisted quantum error-correcting codes with noisy ebits. The formalism uses special subgroups of products of two Pauli groups. It covers the two known coding schemes for imperfect ebits as special cases. Two equivalent forms follow, one in symplectic geometry and one in additive codes. The team uses the theory to construct new codes of this type. They also analyse how the new codes perform.
arxiv-2603-19897: Ye and co-authors link domain knowledge with fitness landscapes to explain when software tuning works. Tuning a system's settings is key to performance, but why tuners succeed or fail is unclear. Their Domland method joins spatial facts from landscape study with domain-driven checks. They test it on nine systems and 93 workloads. Landscapes prove specific to each system, with no single domain factor shaping them all. Core options that drive main functions make landscapes more rugged and tuning harder.
arxiv-2603-19997: Bila and co-authors test whether language models adjust to unreliable partners in a building task. Their Build What I Mean benchmark adapts a psycholinguistic setup for two speakers. One speaker cooperates in spirit, while the other is only literally reliable. Instructions are underspecified, so models must infer meaning or ask for clarification at a small cost. Models did spot unreliability when asked to rate their confidence. Yet they failed to act on that awareness in the task. They either asked too many blind questions or guessed when unsure.
arxiv-2603-20097: Benesh proposes a tweak to draft lotteries that leaves less room for teams to tank on purpose. Many anti tanking plans reward losses early and wins late in the season. That fixed switch point can itself be gamed. His Ex Post Gold Plan ranks teams by wins gained after their elimination date. That date is only known after the fact, so teams cannot time their losing. The metric, called REWIND, keeps the push to win alive longer. In most seasons every team gains by trying to win.
arxiv-2603-20497: Donoso and co-authors prove new partition regularity results for quadratic equations. The work is set in rings of integers of imaginary quadratic fields. They study equations whose solutions split into linear forms. This split lets them show that any finite coloring yields a solution set in one color. Side results add to the tools for such fields. One describes aperiodic completely multiplicative functions in full. Others give a Turán-Kubilius type bound and a new concentration estimate for multiplicative functions.
arxiv-2603-20597: Biliotti and co-authors study how science rewards new work by women and men. They scan 261,452 solo authored papers by U.S. scholars. Women more often join distant fields through novel reference mixes. Men more often remix concepts inside one field. Women's cross field work proved more disruptive and more ahead of its time. Yet it landed in lower prestige journals with less citation credit. Gaps closed only at extreme novelty levels.
arxiv-2603-20697: Yang and co-authors test making street level views of disaster zones from satellite images. Ground views show structural damage that orbit views miss. Yet street data is hard to get right after a disaster strikes. They try two methods: one guided by a vision language model, one a damage aware mixture of experts. A three tier scoring scheme checks pixels, semantics, and perceived fit. On 300 disaster scenes, diffusion tools looked real but invented details. Plain ControlNet kept the best semantic accuracy, at 0.71.
arxiv-2603-20797: Tiltmann reports tests of wafer scale sensor prototypes for the ALICE ITS3 upgrade at CERN. The new tracker will bend six large chips into three cylinders. Only carbon foam holds them, leaving bare silicon in most of the view. Two prototype chips, MOSS and MOST, test stitched CMOS sensors for this role. MOSS yield came to about 76 percent per region. Without two known fault modes, yield reached near 98 percent. MOSS ran past 99 percent efficiency after strong radiation doses.
arxiv-2603-20997: Basu asks when content-based routing can work in hybrid sequence models. Routing picks which tokens deserve costly attention, but he argues it needs pairwise token comparison, and that need cannot be escaped. Across more than twenty experiments and fifteen routing methods, every system with high routing precision uses pairwise comparison. Methods that skip it, such as recurrent models, memory banks, and bandits, fail badly. Two ingredients are required: per-token representations with bidirectional context, plus pairwise comparison. One design reaches near perfect routing at linear cost.
arxiv-2603-21197: Shvets builds a geometric framework for anonymous shuffle experiments in privacy. The core is an anchored affine likelihood-ratio law on the regular simplex. Each finite-output channel matches a unique anchored law. Among channels with a set local privacy level, binary randomized response is the extreme case for convex divergences after shuffling. Under a pairwise budget, he proves exact frontier results. Augmented randomized response is minimax optimal at low budgets.
arxiv-2603-21697: Tan and co-authors show that comic-style visual stories can jailbreak multimodal language models. A harmful goal is split across a simple three-panel comic, and the model is asked to role-play and finish it. Their ComicJailbreak benchmark holds 1,167 attacks across ten harm categories and five task setups. Across fifteen leading models, comic attacks matched strong rule-based jailbreaks and beat plain-text and random-image baselines. Ensemble success passed 90 percent on several commercial models. Existing defenses blocked the comics but also refused many benign prompts, they find.
arxiv-2603-21897: Sullivan and Gilbert compare planet systems in binary stars with those around single stars, using Kepler data. The sample covers 162 planets in 118 binary systems and 880 planets in 544 single systems. Both groups show the peas-in-a-pod pattern: planets in one system tend to match in size and sit evenly in log period. Differences are modest but real. Binary systems show more uneven period spacing and more single-planet cases. The authors read this as the companion star shaping the birth disk, with slow dynamics adding gentle changes later.
arxiv-2603-21997: Lenske and co-authors propose lepton double charge exchange reactions on nuclei as a probe of lepton number violation. Such violation would signal physics beyond the Standard Model. Their reactions fire electron beams in the multi-GeV range and look for positron output. A second-order formalism covers the dynamics, with a left-right symmetric model for the exotic terms. A phenomenological model predicts sizable cross sections at these energies. The rates grow fast with beam energy and target mass. Such experiments look feasible with existing equipment, they argue.
arxiv-2603-22397: Bhusal and co-authors study why bubbles slow as they expand in an early-universe phase change. Simulations had shown slow walls and weaker gravitational waves. The team tests two heating routes with steady single-bubble setups. A bubble that runs into its own hot shockwave does slow. But the slowdown hits the fastest walls hardest, so it cannot explain the wave loss. A second route tracks shrinking droplets of false vacuum late in the change. Their speeds match simulations well and link to the lost waves.
arxiv-2603-22697: Linn and co-authors realize a photonic version of the Hofstadter system. They use a one-dimensional stack of crystal layers, with a synthetic dimension coded in its geometry. By changing layer thickness, they observe the Hofstadter butterfly and chiral edge states. Stronger quasiperiodic modulation then localizes select bands in one dimension. The edge states persist and still wind across the gap. Analysis shows edge transport then runs through Landau-Zener jumps between localized states. The work links weak-drive Thouless pumping to a strong-drive pump regime.
arxiv-2603-22897: Wu and co-authors study virtual absorption modes in Schwarzschild-de Sitter spacetime. The setting uses semi-open boundary conditions. These modes match total transmission modes where reflection vanishes. As reflectivity drops, the imaginary parts of the mode spectra fall steadily. Each overtone has a critical reflectivity where that part hits zero. Driving the system at a mode frequency triggers a virtual absorption process. The modes thus mark the spectral signature of such absorption, with links to exotic compact objects.
arxiv-2603-23697: Mehidi extends the logarithmic purity theorem to a wider class of torsors. The new scope covers torsors from the Kummer log flat topology under flat, reductive group schemes. She then reads the theorem through root stacks, tying it to properness tests for tame stacks. Last, she builds a logarithmic Nori fundamental group for log regular schemes. That group classifies the torsors in play. She compares it with the classical Nori group and the tame fundamental group.
arxiv-2603-24097: Ji and co-authors present LaDy, a network that segments skeleton action sequences with physics built in. Past methods read joint motion well but ignore the forces behind it. That makes similar actions hard to separate and blurs their boundaries. LaDy computes generalized coordinates from joint positions and estimates Lagrangian terms under physical constraints. An energy consistency loss enforces the work-energy theorem. Learned forces then modulate spatial and temporal features. On hard test sets, LaDy reaches state-of-the-art scores, they report.
arxiv-2603-24497: Covi and co-authors study an inverse problem for the viscoacoustic wave equation, a model of wave motion in media with memory. The medium is described by a varying sound speed and a memory kernel that depends on space and time. Sources sit outside the region of interest, and the data are exterior measurements. The team builds solutions concentrated near fixed geodesics and proves a propagation of singularities result. Under geometric conditions, the data then fix the sound speed and all time derivatives of the kernel at zero.
arxiv-2603-24597: Alpay and Sarioglu study why it is hard to detect and fix overspecification in adaptive data-structure choice. A workload has a signature, such as ordering or sparsity. Systems may pick designs that match the whole signature when the evidence supports only part of it. They show this bias spreads through benchmark scores and preference fitting. Detection is undecidable on unbounded domains, via the halting problem, but decidable by full checks on finite ones. Under a conservative repair rule, any computable repair method has an overspecified fixed point.
arxiv-2603-24697: Zinnkann and co-authors test the relation between a young cluster's most massive star and the cluster's total mass. They model clusters with the galIMF code, where stellar masses are optimally sampled from a varying initial mass function. Cluster masses span a wide range and ages run from one to four million years. Stellar evolution tracks and H-alpha luminosities are included,. Optimal sampling matches the observed extragalactic clusters, while purely random sampling does not, supporting a self-regulated picture of cluster formation.
arxiv-2603-24797: Post and co-authors add aspect classification to meaning representations. Aspect encodes how events unfold in time, as states, activities, or completed events. Graph frameworks such as Uniform Meaning Representations need it, yet aspect is sparsely annotated. The team builds a dataset of English sentences with UMR aspect labels over AMR graphs that lacked the feature. Their scheme follows the UMR aspect lattice, with a multi-step pipeline for quality. Baseline experiments with three modelling approaches set the first benchmarks.
arxiv-2603-25297: Jiang and co-authors compute how silver atoms and hydrogen join into AgH in cold space, shedding light as they bond. This radiative route had never been studied for silver hydride. They map energy curves for five low states with high-grade quantum chemistry. Full quantum scattering then gives cross sections by spin and vibration state. Sharp resonances from near-bound states stand out, led by one channel at low energies. Rate curves fall as temperature climbs. The data feed models of metal hydride birth in interstellar clouds.
arxiv-2603-25397: Simha and co-authors judge when to send patients out of intensive care, using causal tools. Discharge timing trades a shorter stay against a better outcome, and the two aims cannot merge into one score. Records also stop once care stops, which tangles naive checks. Their frame extends a g-formula package to score stopping rules from past data, with coverage checks built in. An open pipeline runs it on the MIMIC-IV database. The results hint that some rules could beat current care.
arxiv-2603-25697: Roy presents the Kitchen Loop, a framework for self-evolving software. The loop rests on four parts. A spec surface lists what the product claims to support. An AI agent then acts as a heavy synthetic user, testing that surface at high speed. Unbeatable Tests check ground truth in ways the code author cannot fake. Drift Control watches quality and pauses the loop when it slips. Roy reports trials on two live systems over 285 or more rounds, with over a thousand merged pull requests and no regressions found.
arxiv-2603-25897: Wu and co-authors study a subtle risk for LISA, the planned space gravitational-wave detector. They model a first-order phase transition inside a Kerr extreme mass-ratio inspiral. The transition reshapes the energy flux over a narrow window. The waveform mismatch stays tiny, at about three thousandths. Yet the phase drift grows to some five thousand radians. The signal thus stays detectable but turns biased for precise inference. The authors urge that future LISA waveform models include such transition sectors directly.
arxiv-2603-26397: Kisfaludi-Bak and Marx give approximation schemes for Subset TSP and Steiner Tree on geometric intersection graphs. The graphs come from unit disks or same-sized fat polygons in the plane that overlap. Their first step finds a small induced subgraph that keeps the optimum within a factor close to one. Subset TSP then solves fast on that core, with size tied to the optimum itself. For Steiner Tree, an improved scheme reaches the same near-optimal quality in far less time.
arxiv-2603-26497: Ressi and co-authors test how well modern tools spot reentrancy flaws in Ethereum smart contracts. Many detectors and datasets still reflect old attack patterns and obsolete Solidity versions. The team builds two hand-checked benchmarks: 432 real contracts drawn from past sets, and 143 small crafted cases that isolate single patterns. They score 12 formal tools, 10 learning models, and 9 large language models. Top language models reach 0.96 F1 on real contracts, beating most tools, yet crafted cases expose weak spots in nearly every detector.
arxiv-2603-26897: Jafari-Zadeh and co-authors create current-carrying states in a spin-1 chain by tilting its energy landscape. The Babujian-Takhtajan chain gains a term from its third conserved charge, an energy current. That term leaves the eigenstates unchanged but reorders their energies. Bethe ansatz and DMRG calculations locate a phase transition at a precise tilt value. Below it, the ground state carries no current. Above it, a gapless chiral sector carries both current and scalar chirality. Cold atoms and qutrit simulators could test the effect.
arxiv-2603-27197: Tschirschwitz and Rodehorst propose KALOS, a meta-algorithm for scoring agreement between coders on vision tasks. Detection benchmarks stall when label noise hides real model gains. Standard agreement stats cannot match objects across coders. KALOS resolves spatial correspondence first, on a localization-first principle. The problem then becomes a standard reliability matrix. Its settings tune to each dataset's own agreement pattern. It extends from bounding boxes to volumetric segmentation and pose. It also reports collaboration clusters and localization sensitivity.
arxiv-2603-27297: Guo and co-authors present NNQA, a method that compiles neural networks into quantum arithmetic circuits. Hybrid quantum learning often loses accuracy to generic variational ansatzes and data shuttling. NNQA instead turns a trained classical network into native unitary blocks. The authors prove the quantum polynomial error then comes only from measurement shot noise. Tests ran on IBM and IonQ quantum processors without variational fine-tuning. Polynomials up to degree 35 scored over 99.5 percent accuracy. IonQ runs scaled to 36 qubits and depth 70 with tiny error.
arxiv-2603-27697: Some and Namboodiri cut labeling costs for video segmentation. Pixel-fine labels are slow and pricey to produce. Raw video frames cost almost nothing. Coarse labels sit between the two extremes. Their pipeline uses SAM and SAM 2 foundation models. Those models turn coarse notes into full masks. Unlabeled frames also feed the process. Annotation needs drop by about a third. Performance stays near the fully labeled level. Frame variety matters more than frame count.
arxiv-2603-27797: Anand and co-authors route each image to the right 3D reconstruction model. Robot tasks need mesh detail at varied levels. Fine grips demand rich surfaces; path checks do not. SCOUT splits scores into two learned parts. One part ranks viewpoint-based models per input. The other gauges overall image difficulty. View-invariant tools can join without retraining. Cost caps apply flexibly at run time. Tests use the Google Scanned Objects set.
arxiv-2603-28397: Pandit, MacKintosh, and Sharma sharpen the numbers for how fiber networks stiffen under strain. Loosely connected networks flop until stretching pulls them rigid, a phase transition with its own critical exponents. With bigger simulations and theory-guided analysis, the team refines those exponents. They also track how the critical strain and exponents shift when the network is sheared during one-way stretching that changes its volume. The results firm up a debated corner of soft matter physics.
arxiv-2603-28597: Karimi argues that explainable AI is, at its core, a causal problem. Many explanation methods now exist, but metrics conflict and sanity checks often fail. Karimi disputes the common claim that no ground truth exists for a correct explanation. The ground truth, he argues, is the causal model that governs the system in question. Questions about data, models, or decisions can be reframed as causal inquiries. He proves that causal models are both necessary and sufficient for such explanations. Without that grounding, he warns, explainable AI stays unmoored.
arxiv-2603-29097: Shin and Park present SR-CorrNet, a model that separates overlapping speech. Most models split speakers only at the final stage. That late split creates a bottleneck in noise and echo. Their encoder separates speech coarsely at the start. A shared decoder then rebuilds speaker features step by step. Correlations from the sound signal guide deep filters that recover each voice. A dynamic module adjusts the number of output streams. Tests on three datasets show steady gains.
arxiv-2603-29297: Singh and co-authors build a guided diffusion model for fair deals between AI agents. Each agent must get at least its outside option. The joint gain should also be as large as possible, as in the Nash bargaining solution. Their model reads the talks as a directed graph. Graph attention weighs the traits of each agent. A loss then punishes deals that break the outside-option rule. It also punishes gaps from the Nash product. On synthetic data, Nash efficiency came within 0.55 points of an oracle score.
arxiv-2603-29497: Loiseau and co-authors distill privacy judgment from a large language model into small encoders. Rating text for privacy risk matters for privacy-preserving language tools. Big models judge privacy well but cost too much at scale. They also cannot easily process sensitive data. The team trains light classifiers on privacy-labeled texts from ten domains. The teacher is Mistral Large 3, a very large model. The students have as few as 150 million parameters. They keep strong agreement with human labels at far lower cost.
arxiv-2603-29797: Krenkel and co-authors probe odd resistance behavior in the metal BaNi2P4. They add disorder with low-temperature electron irradiation and track how resistivity changes. A structural switch near 375 K dominates the response. Above it, resistivity grows in a standard linear way. Below it, the trend turns anomalous, with domains and hysteresis marking a first-order change. Hall data show the electron structure barely shifts. The team blames local barium rattling inside its cage.
arxiv-2603-29897: Yang and co-authors present UniRank, a reranker for mixed text and image candidate lists. Text rerankers sit closer to text items, which biases cross-modal ranking. Many vision-language rerankers turn all items into images, at heavy cost. UniRank scores hybrid lists directly, with no modality conversion. A tuning stage calibrates its cross-modal relevance scores. A hard-negative preference stage then adapts it per domain. On literature and patent search, Recall@1 rises by 8.9 and 7.3 percent.
arxiv-2603-29997: Khojasteh and co-authors present YARN, a frame for analogical reasoning over stories. Matching story structures is hard when entities are not pre-extracted. Their system uses language models to split stories into units and abstract them. Four abstraction levels capture unit meaning and story role. A mapping step then aligns elements across the two stories. Tests show abstractions lift performance over end-to-end baselines. Error reviews flag implicit causality as a remaining weakness.
arxiv-2604-00097: Banerjee recasts halo bias, usually handled as coefficients in a perturbative expansion, as a field in its own right. Every point of a Gaussian density field carries a well-defined, scale-independent Lagrangian bias. Halo bias then comes from geometrically selecting patches of this pre-existing field rather than from collapse itself, and the same construction extends to any linear operator on the density field. The picture reproduces the measured mass dependence of bias and explains both its Gaussian spread at fixed mass and assembly bias.
arxiv-2604-00197: Chen and nine colleagues run radiation-magnetohydrodynamics simulations tracking first protostars over about 50 thousand years, coupling radiation, turbulence, and magnetic fields. Without hydrogen shielding, Lyman-Werner feedback can suppress and end accretion, but large columns near the star weaken it sharply. In polar directions, atomic hydrogen fully shields Lyman-Werner radiation where molecular self-shielding falls short, cooling nearby gas and raising accretion and mass. The ionized region stays confined near 100 astronomical units beyond a 75-unit sink radius, as dense gas sustains recombination and blocks breakout.
arxiv-2604-00797: Tajima, Nakano, and Iida show that a Bose polaron, an impurity quasiparticle inside a Bose-Einstein condensate, gains topological traits from Weyl nodes born through p-wave Feshbach resonance. The nodes appear even without spin or spin-orbit coupling, and charged impurities bring a chiral anomaly as well. Cold-atom tests could check the prediction by watching Hall transport of the impurity cloud.
arxiv-2604-00897: Delefosse, Charantonis, and Béréziat present a modular design that splits weather forecasting from spatial resolution, applying learned generative sharpening after coarse forecasts. Trained with flow matching on reanalysis data only, the model keeps large-scale structure and variance when sharpened forecasts are made coarse again. It also adds small-scale detail that fits physics. It reaches competitive probabilistic scores at 0.25-degree resolution against an operational ensemble, at modest extra training cost.
arxiv-2604-00997: Lee and team introduce Variational Reward Factorization, an uncertainty-aware method for personalizing language models by splitting rewards into shared bases plus user-specific weights. Instead of fixing user weights from scarce data alone, it represents each user's tastes as a variational distribution in a shared space. It matches weights to probabilistic bases by Wasserstein distance, and downweights shaky estimates using a variance-attenuated loss. Across three benchmarks it beats all baselines for seen and unseen users, few-shot cases, and varied uncertainty.
arxiv-2604-01197:
Fangjun Hu and seven co-authors study learning mixed quantum states in 2026. Learning quantum states from measurement data is a central problem. It sits at the heart of quantum information and computational complexity.

They study learning to generate mixed states on a finite-dimensional lattice. Recent work on mixed state phases of matter motivates their focus. They concentrate on arbitrary states in the trivial phase specifically. Shallow channel circuits prepare the states they learn to reproduce. The question is how much data and computation generation requires. Their results speak to both physics and learning theory audiences. Readers get a careful case where quantum learning is tractable.
arxiv-2604-01597: Shu and colleagues propose Influence-Guided PPO, a post-training method using data attribution. Standard Proximal Policy Optimization trains on the entire rollout buffer, assuming all episodes help. Episodes contain noisy or unfaithful reasoning, which can hurt model results and slow training. By scoring each episode's influence via gradient math, Influence-Guided PPO identifies and drops episodes anti-aligned with a gradient. Tests show Influence-Guided PPO beats supervised fine-tuning and PPO baselines. Filtering acts as an early stop, reducing unfaithful chain-of-thought reasoning.
arxiv-2604-02297: Chong and team study thermal states in a harmonic trap at low temperature. They track Schatten norms of commutators between one body actions of the states and position and momentum. Upper bounds for the magnetic Fock Darwin case also follow. The estimates reveal several regimes set jointly by Planck constant, heat and magnetic field strength.
arxiv-2604-02697: Shao and four colleagues offer LieTrunc-QNN, a framework that explains quantum neural net training through Lie algebra structure. Tunable circuits form Lie subalgebras, and their reachable states trace a manifold. As effective dimension grows, gradients fade through concentration of measure. Restricting to structured ones shrinks the manifold and keeps gradients healthy. What the net can express then turns on generator structure, not on parameter count. The work gives proofs for both main claims.
arxiv-2604-02797: Xu, Li and Yue propose a non-compact, positivity-preserving scheme for linear non-divergence form elliptic equations. Based on the Feynman-Kac formula, the answer is an expected value over a diffusion process. A wide-stencil design with chosen transition probabilities ensures consistency and positivity. It handles anisotropic flow with mixed derivatives where classical schemes fail. Dirichlet, Neumann, and periodic boundaries reach O(h), O(h to the half power), and O(h). The method is built for hard cases where old schemes break.
arxiv-2604-03097: Zavalani builds a triangular solver for elliptic equations on curved surfaces, based on the Poincaré-Steklov method. Using Dubiner polynomial bases on triangle meshes, the method merges local solution operators in stages and reuses them for repeated solves. Tests show spectral accuracy with high-order convergence on static and time-varying problems, and reuse suits implicit time stepping.
arxiv-2604-03197: Anagnostopoulos and colleagues train a fast surrogate model that predicts blood flow for individual patients without running a full arterial simulation. Built from a virtual patient group drawn from a large clinical dataset, the model estimates arterial pressure and cardiac output instantly and screens out unrealistic inputs. Applied to real clinical data, it recovers central aortic pressure and cardiac output for screening.
arxiv-2604-03397: Stewart-Height, Jahagirdar, and Matni present a 2026 method for spotting single-limb faults in four-legged robots working remotely. Their offline learning method reads proprioceptive sensor data to detect damage, so the controller can switch to an appropriate three-legged gait. The aim is survival: a robot that cannot adjust its walk to a damaged limb cannot finish hazardous assignments.
arxiv-2604-03997: Fernando Paredes García set out ledger-state stigmergy, the hands-off teamwork of blockchain agents through shared ledger state. Sell-off keepers and trading bots act by watching funds, storage, and event logs, not by direct talks, echoing Grassé's 1959 account of creatures working through traces. The paper maps that trick onto spread-out ledgers with a step frame and three base patterns: State-Flag, Event-Signal, and Threshold-Trigger. A task-board example sets ledger teamwork against off-chain talks and central control.
arxiv-2604-04097: Sandro Roch generalized unique sink orientation results from products of two simplices to products of many simplex factors. For a product of two simplices, Felsner, Gärtner, and Tschirschnitz characterized linear-function-induced orientations as grid patterns matching two-colored line arrangements. Roch extended some of those results to r-dimensional grids and (r+1)-signotopes, widening the theory of such patterns on simplex products.
arxiv-2604-04197: E. Güngör and team studied how heat changes the Y(4500) vector hidden-charm molecule within thermal QCD sum rules, assuming a Ds anti-Ds1 molecular shape. Near the deconfinement point, the state's mass falls by 29 percent, its decay constant drops by 94 percent, while its decay width grows by 35 percent. These shifts signal the state breaking apart. The authors read this as the Y(4500) melting into quark-gluon plasma near 155 MeV, with thermal spectral parameters as signatures for heavy-ion runs at RHIC and LHC.
arxiv-2604-04697: Dessi shows that two accounts of gauge-invariant ideals for product systems over the nonnegative integer lattice in d dimensions agree. One route runs through Nica-covariant representations, plus gauge-invariant uniqueness theorems, while the other works from the definitions of the objects that parametrise the ideals. The match lets him simplify his parametrisation result with Kakariadis for the case. It describes the gauge-invariant ideal structure of quotients of the Toeplitz-Nica-Pimsner algebra. He closes with uses for C-star systems and row finite higher rank graphs.
arxiv-2604-04897: Dlamini uses fast radio bursts to probe non-Gaussianity left by inflation, a signal strongest on the largest scales where systematic errors also bite hardest. A central snag is the tangle between the electron bias of intergalactic gas and the primordial signal, which can wreck precision when the bias is left free. The cross-power between burst dispersion measures and Shapiro timing delays along many sightlines breaks that tangle internally. Dispersion traces biased electron density, while timing delays probe gravity alone, separating the two effects.
arxiv-2604-05297: Tao and six colleagues explain why a popular multi-agent learning method, value factorization, so often stalls at mediocre teamwork. Existing theory studied only the ideal case, missing the suboptimal resting points where learning actually settles. Their new stable-point concept maps where factorization can land, showing non-optimal resting points drive the poor results. Their Multi-Round Value Factorization framework then makes inferior actions unstable round by round, pushing each iteration toward a better resting point.
arxiv-2604-05397: Zhang and five colleagues argue that trust in a language model's stated confidence must be judged across whole conversations, not single replies, since user persuasion can quietly erode it turn by turn. They offer a turn-by-turn error measure, a training method called MTCal that cuts it, and a decoding strategy, ConfChat, that uses steady confidence to firm up answers. Tests show steadier scores and answers that hold up in multi-turn chats.
arxiv-2604-05497: Kim, Kang, and Choi fix two flaws in diffusion multimodal language models that reason step by step. Such models often settle on a final answer too early and lean too little on images at first. Their position-and-step penalty delays early answers, while visual reasoning guidance amplifies image signals. Tests show accuracy up by 7.5 percent with over three times the speed of reasoning with four times more diffusion steps.
arxiv-2604-05797: Yang and seven colleagues weave sensing, computing, and semantic messaging for digital-twin car networks in the near field. Roadside units serve cars with meaning-based links while millimeter-wave radar maps surroundings, with particle filtering for precise tracking. Joint tuning lifts transmission rates by 20 percent while holding sensing accuracy of current integrated schemes.
arxiv-2604-06097: Goyal and colleagues' 2026 paper presents the first systematic study of query rewriting effects on dense retriever biases in RAG. Dense retrievers show systematic biases. The team tests five methods across six retrievers. Simple LLM-based rewriting cuts bias most, by 54 percent, yet fails when biases combine adversarially. Simple rewriting cuts bias by raising score variance, while pseudo-document generation cuts it through decorrelation from bias cues. No technique fixes every bias, and effects differ across retrievers. A taxonomy splits query-document interaction biases from document encoding biases.
arxiv-2604-06297: Meerza, Wang, and Liu propose FedSpy-LLM, a scalable attack rebuilding training data from federated LLM gradients. Federated learning with parameter-efficient fine-tuning aims to protect private data, yet prior work still extracts it from shared gradients. FedSpy-LLM instead rebuilds data with larger batches and longer sequences across diverse architectures, even under PEFT. Its core is gradient decomposition exploiting rank deficiency. That enables efficient token extraction at scale. Accurate token ordering comes from iteratively matching each token's partial-sequence gradient to the full-sequence gradient.
arxiv-2604-06497: Sapkota and San tackle chaos control with hyperFastRL. Spatiotemporal fluid chaos resists adjoint control, since each regime needs its own law. It maps forcing values to policy weights, splitting tuning from steadying. A pessimistic value estimate over many environments tames chaotic reward variance. Three hypernetwork forms — residual MLPs, Fourier, and Kolmogorov-Arnold — keep Kuramoto-Sivashinsky steady under varying forcing. Kolmogorov-Arnold tracks best on unseen parametrizations, while Fourier does worse beyond training with wider spread. Batch runs trade some peak reward for a 37 percent cut in training time.
arxiv-2604-07197: Dai and six colleagues use a machine-learned Hamiltonian, a model that predicts energies and forces from quantum rules, to study oxygen vacancies in glassy silica. Standard quantum calculations grow too costly for large defect cells, and simpler learned potentials drift in bigger cells, but this approach scales linearly and cancels errors between perfect and defective cells. Trained on small cells, it predicts defect formation energies within 50 milli-electron volts of full quantum results.
arxiv-2604-07597: Rojas and Momennia study static and rotating black holes in Scalar-Tensor-Vector Gravity, or alt gravity. They derive closed-form relations giving the mass, MOG coupling, and distance of a Schwarzschild-MOG black hole from disk readings. Redshift rapidity encodes how frequency shift evolves with the emitter's proper time. For rotating Kerr-MOG geometry, they determine rotation jointly with mass, coupling, and distance on the midline. Because the coupling appears, the formulas test departures from standard general relativity, and standard results return when it vanishes.
arxiv-2604-07697: Qian and Wang study a nonlinear stochastic fractional heat equation driven by rough noise. The equation pairs a fractional Laplacian, with order strictly between one and two, against Gaussian noise, white over time, acting like Brownian motion in space. Earlier work settled well-posedness and Hölder continuity for the order-two case. This paper extends the investigation to the fractional range, adapting weighted-space techniques to the rougher setting. It establishes when solutions exist, stay unique, and vary continuously.
arxiv-2604-08197: Azarbahram and López present discrete diffusion for codebook beam choice making. Millimeter-wave comms offers high data rates via large bandwidths and sharp aimed beams, but blockage and mobility weakness hurt reliable aiming. Limited-probing beam management poses a basic problem: few beams can be tested at once, and the serving choice is limited to the probed set. With movement and noisy feedback, this becomes a stepwise, partly visible choice problem where results hinge on the offered beam picks. The paper tackles this with history-tuned discrete denoising diffusion.
arxiv-2604-08597: Wenxiao Zhang and seven colleagues build STIndex, a system that turns unstructured content into a multidimensional spatiotemporal warehouse using space and time as universal anchors. Users define analysis dimensions with set hierarchies, while language models extract and ground entities and events with document memory, geocoding correction, and quality checks. On a public health benchmark it lifts spatiotemporal extraction F1 by 4.37 percent with GPT-4o-mini, with gains on Qwen3-8B as well.
arxiv-2604-08797: Wu and Piper introduce multilingual story moral generation as a culturally grounded test of language models. Using human written story morals from 14 language culture pairs, they compare model outputs with human readings through similarity, preference surveys, and value categories. Frontier models like GPT-4o and Gemini match human morals closely and win preference votes. Yet they show far less cross language variation and cluster on a narrow set of shared values, missing the diversity of human narrative understanding.
arxiv-2604-09097: Figueiredo, Mendonça, and Terças propose all-optical switching from two states: a photon superfluid and a supersolid in a microcavity. The key is a tunable wide-range coupling from a fast electron gas in the cavity. A drift current shifts the Fermi disk, giving the kernel a below-zero region and sparking rotons. Since the field adds across wells, stacking layers with drift angles builds spatial order and multi-level versions. It runs at sub-femto-joule energy and beats most current switches on contrast and retune.
arxiv-2604-09197: Fati and colleagues test whether scans taken before treatment can forecast how a high-grade serous ovarian cancer will respond to chemotherapy given before surgery. Their system reads lesion-rich CT slices with a vision transformer and blends those views with clinical facts to predict the chemotherapy response score. On an internal set of 41 patients it reached 95 percent accuracy, while on an external set of 70 patients accuracy fell to 67 percent. The authors present the tool as early decision support for care teams, not as a proven clinical test.
arxiv-2604-09297: Gong and colleagues treat software agent skill bundles as multi-objective search objects, not static hand-crafted assets. A skill can raise success while sharply raising token cost or adding misleading guidance. Their SkillMOO framework evolves bundles through language-model edits and Pareto selection on pass rate and cost. Across 16 SkillsBench tasks, it tops pass rate rank on 11 of 12 non-zero-pass tasks, cutting costs by up to about 32 percent.
arxiv-2604-09397: Baxter and colleagues give a TeV-based measure of the local extragalactic background light. High-energy gamma rays attenuated by pair production with background photons powerfully probe that background. Using 268 spectra from 45 sources seen with Cherenkov telescopes, seven background templates need at most 10 percent rescaling to fit measured attenuation. The galaxy-count-anchored model matches closest, and TeV depths combined with Fermi-LAT GeV data reconstruct the local background in agreement with integrated galaxy light.
arxiv-2604-09497: Gisserot-Boukhlef and four colleagues challenge lexical scoring of language-model answers, showing across 36 models and 15 tasks that rigid format checks track human judgment poorly. Their replacement, BERT-as-a-Judge, is a compact encoder trained on synthetic question-candidate-reference triples that grades meaning rather than wording. It beats the lexical baseline throughout and rivals far larger model judges at a fraction of the cost, offering a practical path to reliable large-scale evaluation.
arxiv-2604-09697: Medeiros questions test-time augmentation as a default score booster. He tests it across three MedMNIST v2 benchmarks and four models. Pooling predictions over tweaked copies degrades scores versus single passes, with drops up to 31.6 points for ResNet-18 on pathology. All models degrade, growing with more views. One case breaks it: ResNet-18 on dermatology gains under 2 percent. The cause is input shift between tweaked and training inputs, worsened by batch-norm mismatch. Brightness-only tweaks beat geometric transforms, and adding the original eases but does not erase the drop.
arxiv-2604-09797: Shaw and Terhal show how morphing circuits tune syndrome readout circuits and codes for links, two-qubit gate choice, and real qubit count. Quantum error fixing codes are usually defined without stating how syndrome readout circuits run on basic gates and reads. The team covers morphing circuits for Abelian two-block group algebra codes, handling edges for flat codes, single-shot traits, and steady tests. Swapping syndrome readout circuits, run with swapping time-flipped rounds, form a two-round morphing circuit whose fault-safe traits are far easier to examine.
arxiv-2604-09897: Ortiz Capeles and six co-authors study Herbig-Haro object HH 270 with JWST, Subaru, and ALMA. JWST infrared images reveal a previously unseen collimated protostellar jet near the source, plus bipolar cavities carved by the outflow, with new knots along the jet. Subaru optical images link the H-alpha outflow to the infrared jet, while ALMA carbon monoxide data trace entrained molecular gas and dense material around HH270VLA1. Together, the views show shock-excited jet emission interacting with the molecular outflow across optical, infrared, and radio wavelengths.
arxiv-2604-09997: Duong, Möller, and Hosters build a quantum version of the lattice Boltzmann method for fluid flow. The hard step is collisions, which are nonlinear and one-way. Older quantum versions repeat costly tomography and setup at each time step. Their denoising-style collision step avoids that cost by projecting onto a flat set of equilibrium states near a chosen state. The full chain covers coding, collision, streaming, edge rules, and measuring, and tests on flow problems match large-scale behavior well.
arxiv-2604-10297: Yuan, Mei, and Zhang define product-level mixed image retrieval, where users reason about products from multiple viewpoints. They build FashionMV, the first many-view dataset for the task, with 127,000 products, 472,000 images, and over 220,000 triplets. ProCIR uses two-stage chat, caption match, and thought guidance, plus extra fine-tuning. Tests find match matters most, chat needed for match, and fine-tuning and thought partly spare. Their best 0.8-billion model beats all rivals.
arxiv-2604-10397: Luo and seven colleagues join video action spotting with guessing what happens next. Old tools bolt a forecast step onto ready made person object pairs, splitting sense from foresight. Their HOI-DA frame treats future acts as small shifts from present pair states. A cleaned benchmark, DETAnt-HOI, fixes timing slips in labels so longer range tests stay fair. Trials show steady gains in both spotting and foresight, with wider gaps at longer ranges.
arxiv-2604-10597: Ma, Wu, and Yan present COREY, a runtime scheduler for Mamba selective-scan models that sets chunk size from activation entropy, hoping to cut latency without changing outputs. At kernel level the calibrated rule matches a one-time static oracle and runs 4.41 times faster than an unoptimized baseline on a consumer graphics card, yet routed end-to-end tests disappoint: the best static chunk still wins, and even a guarded fallback adds overhead. COREY thus stands as a quality-preserving prototype rather than a throughput win.
arxiv-2604-10697: Binkowski, Adamczewski, and Kajdanowicz propose SinkProbe, a hallucination spotter for language models built on attention sinks, tokens that soak up far more attention than most. Such sinks mark a shift from broad, input-based attention to narrow, prior-led processing. Though sink scores come only from attention maps, the checker leans most on sinks whose value vectors carry large norms. The authors also show earlier methods quietly depend on attention sinks, deriving their link to sink scores. The method leads the field across popular datasets and models.
arxiv-2604-10797: Tian and six colleagues present WBCBench 2026, an ISBI challenge stress-testing white blood cell classification under three difficulties. Severe class imbalance spans 13 fine-grained cell classes. Training, validation, and test sets are strictly separated by patient. Synthetic scanner-induced domain shift adds noise, blur, and lighting changes. All images come from one site with standard staining and expert labels. The benchmark runs in two phases: pristine training data, then degraded images. A standard submission schema and open-source evaluator rank entries by macro-averaged F1 score.
arxiv-2604-11397: Frankus and six colleagues film dislocations piling up near an obstacle deep inside a millimeter pure aluminum sample under stretching. These line defects multiply, move, and pin on lattice flaws including each other. That pinning drives the strengthening of metals during plastic deformation. Until now, watching this process live inside bulk metal was not feasible. Their 3D movies show cross-slip letting dislocations escape the pile-up, producing pronounced stop-start behavior. The data support a new generation of dislocation dynamics and micro-mechanics modeling.
arxiv-2604-11797: Li and four colleagues introduce SyncFix, a method that repairs three-dimensional reconstructions by keeping multiple views consistent while a diffusion model refines them. It treats refinement as joint latent bridge matching, syncing distorted and clean views through the denoising process. Training uses image pairs alone, yet inference handles any number of views, with quality rising as views are added, and it beats current baselines even without clean reference images.
arxiv-2604-11897: Walleghem and Cepollaro compute the response of an Unruh-DeWitt detector near a BTZ black hole held in a superposition of spots in two-plus-one spacetime. After a quantum reference frame shift, the setup reads as a detector in a spread of spots within a single classical black hole spacetime. They derive the detector-field link for such spread spacetimes, ignoring backreaction. A measurement they define carries a nonclassical effect absent for a classical mixture of positions, and the mass-spread case reveals singularities in the probed spectrum.
arxiv-2604-11997: Bejas and four colleagues study Raman scattering in the superconducting phase of nickelates, where pressed and thin-film samples draw wide interest. They model three cases: two-orbital models with one and two layers, plus a bilayer model with only one active orbital. For each, they test varied pairing patterns and map their marks in the Raman response. Full multi-orbital maths with inter-orbital and intra-orbital effects are set against a summed per-band response, feeding the minimal model debate.
arxiv-2604-12197: Negrete and Ramos build a network model in which financial factors emerge from asset interactions rather than being imposed by statistics. Assets follow coupled iterated maps tied to past returns of their own and of related assets, with links growing from isolated clusters to a fully connected network through a transformed Laplacian matrix. Stable co-movement patterns then read as factors, and one regime explains asset variance well. The link between initial clustering and factor count matches a center manifold reduction.
arxiv-2604-12697: Mathieu Da Silva counts values of a binary quadratic form that are norms from an abelian field. The form is irreducible over the rationals, and the field has class number one. The paper gives the order of magnitude for the count of such values. The proof uses the fundamental lemma of sieve theory. Geometry of numbers also supports the result.
arxiv-2604-12997: Motta studies when a function tied to the fractional Laplacian, a cousin of the usual Laplacian, is forced to vanish entirely. Working with discrete sets, he finds conditions on the zero sets that guarantee uniqueness, and builds examples where it fails. The proofs pair decay estimates from discrete zero sets with analytic continuation, while the failures come from an interpolation theorem.
arxiv-2604-13297: Binh Nguyen, Nam Nguyen, and Nghiem learn models of port-Hamiltonian systems from data while keeping their energy form and stability. Their neural method drops the convexity rule common in Hamiltonian approximations. That widens the class of models it can express. It also folds knowledge of stable equilibria into training, so several isolated equilibria can stay stable at once. Two numerical tests show more accurate structure- and stability-preserving learning than a conventional baseline.
arxiv-2604-13697: Luciano, Gine, and Chemisana extend Heisenberg's uncertainty relation to relativity. The old rule needs a fix. The usual rule clashes with relativity. Middle speeds are the best place to test fixes. There, particles move well below light speed, yet relativistic shifts still matter. Their math uses kappa-deformed Kaniadakis statistics, a one-parameter twist on entropy. It yields a new uncertainty relation, and fine-structure constant data bound its key parameter.
arxiv-2604-13797: Chakraborty and three colleagues generate fonts from a few reference glyphs with DRG-Font. Capturing complex styles from few exemplars is hard, and prior methods lose local characteristics. Their contrastive strategy splits glyphs into style and content parts. A Reference Selection module dynamically picks the best style reference from a candidate pool. Style and content blocks learn style and shape priors. A Multi-Fusion Upsampling Block merges reference style with target content into the final glyph. The method beats state-of-the-art approaches on visual and test benchmarks.
arxiv-2604-13897: Lahouari and colleagues release MolCryst-MLIPs, an open database of machine-learned potentials for molecular crystals. The first release tunes MACE models for nine crystal systems, from benzamide to resorcinol, through an automated pipeline covering data, training, and validation. Mean energy error reaches 0.141 kilojoules per mole per atom. Only the tuned models map the energy landscape across crystal forms.
arxiv-2604-13997: Euraste and colleagues measure how much code language models lean on memorization rather than learning. Their perturbation method scores the gap between likely seen and unseen inputs across 8 open-source models and 19 benchmarks. StarCoder shows sensitivity up to 0.8 on some benchmarks, while QwenCoder stays lower, and suspected-leak benchmarks CVEFixes and Defects4J show low advantage. Memorization risk varies sharply by task and model.
arxiv-2604-14397: Basil and five colleagues grow WordNet-style word resources into new languages by projecting sense tags across translations. Starting from sense-tagged English text and its translation, their method maps annotated synsets onto aligned target words and assigns matching lemmas to those concepts. A bilingual dictionary sharpens the aligner and filters bad projections. Tests in several languages show the project-and-filter approach beats earlier dictionary and large-language-model baselines on precision while staying interpretable and light on resources.
arxiv-2604-14497: White and five colleagues build robust experimental designs for vibration tests that survive sensor failures under high mechanical acceleration. Standard optimal designs pick accelerometer spots and orientations in advance, but failed sensors and costly finite-element models complicate the picture. A relaxation approach enables efficient gradient-based optimization, while a binary-inducing penalty yields a binary sensor design without post-hoc rounding. Robust and classical designs look similar on the test problem, yet robust designs win on average across relevant failure scenarios.
arxiv-2604-14697: Muñoz-Lahoz proves Wickstead's conjecture in full generality. For a positive projection on a Dedekind complete Banach lattice, let alpha be the multiple of the identity given by the largest central operator below it. The conjecture says alpha can only be zero or a reciprocal whole number, previously known only in finite dimensions. As a consequence, two-dimensional Banach lattice algebras exist with no faithful representation as regular operators on such a lattice. All main results were formalized in Lean 4.
arxiv-2604-14797: Faria, Perez-Arancibia, and Tlupova extend high-order kernel regularization to the four Helmholtz Calderón operators: single-layer, double-layer, adjoint double-layer, and hypersingular. It first regularizes the hypersingular operator at high order for Helmholtz and Laplace equations in three dimensions. Singular kernels are swapped for smooth versions built from error functions plus moment-set polynomial corrections. Tying the regularization parameter to mesh size balances errors, yielding convergence rates. H-matrix acceleration covers fast-method mismatch, and scattering tests on sound-soft and sound-hard targets confirm accuracy.
arxiv-2604-14897: Han, Du, Johansson, and Rikos introduce Mix-CALADIN, a shared algorithm for consensus optimization with mixed-integer tasks, with a focus on Boolean ones. It extends CALADIN with special Boolean techniques, avoiding local mixed-integer solvers. Under a mild Lipschitz rule for objective functions, they prove convergence for convex and nonconvex mixed-integer problems alike. Tests show competitive performance against existing approaches in practice.
arxiv-2604-15397: Arminjon derives equations of motion for the mass centers of weakly gravitating bodies in a scalar theory of gravity with a preferred frame, where gravity acts as a pressure force. Using a post-Newtonian asymptotic scheme, he first derives local field equations, then integrates inside the bodies to obtain center-of-mass motion under good separation. The scalar field links the flat background metric to the curved physical metric throughout.
arxiv-2604-15497: Andrenšek describes all homomorphisms between Hecke-Kiselman monoids of finite simple oriented graphs with a set of Boolean matrices. The matrices stand in one-to-one correspondence with monoid homomorphisms from one graph's monoid to the other's. As a consequence, a Boolean matrix monoid emerges that is isomorphic to the endomorphism monoid of a Hecke-Kiselman monoid.
arxiv-2604-15797: Sersante, Georgiou, and Chisari turn the Fisher matrix method for cosmology around. Instead of estimating how an unmodelled systematic skews parameter estimates, they test whether a given systematic could explain a disagreement between two probes. They demonstrate the reversed calculation on galaxy intrinsic alignments and baryonic feedback, two effects that can shift survey results. The approach works best for small parameter offsets, yet still signals the size and direction of possible bias beyond that range.
arxiv-2604-15897: Kojo and Itatani investigate neutral and charged mesons in magnetic fields, from weak to strong regimes, using a non-relativistic quark model with a harmonic confining potential. Short-range Coulomb and color-magnetic effects enter as perturbations. Neutral and charged mesons behave differently: transverse momenta stay conserved and continuous for neutral mesons, while charged mesons show quantized sideways dynamics. Spin and orbital Zeeman effects are examined, including a cancellation that keeps high-spin charged mesons stable in strong fields.
arxiv-2604-15997: Zebendo, Cicciarella, and Rossi extend recurrent spiking neural networks that learn axonal delays at run time, adding convolutional recurrent connections. Their earlier DelRec approach showed delay learning helps, and the new convolutional version streamlines the architecture. On an audio classification task, it cuts recurrent parameter counts by around 99 percent and runs 52 times faster at inference, while keeping DelRec's accuracy. The code is public.
arxiv-2604-16097: Furbach and five colleagues tackle swarms. Swarms are peer-to-peer systems of spread-out machines that pass events to each other and progress without constant connection. Earlier swarm models could not be built up from parts, blocking design in pieces and code reuse for large applications. Their theory and techniques allow parts designed and checked on their own to be combined correctly. A software tool backs this by joining such parts automatically.
arxiv-2604-16997: Chen builds an asset-pricing model in which investors buy AI stocks as a hedge against an AI singularity that displaces their consumption. Because private AI capital cannot be traded, markets stay incomplete and AI stocks command a premium. That incompleteness distorts both valuations and the efficient path of AI development, making a case for government transfers once singularity-driven growth outweighs deadweight costs. The paper itself was generated by AI.
arxiv-2604-17297: Lan, Dai, and Li present CRISP, a system shrinking thought using a model's inner weight. Prior outside shrinkers often mismatch internal thought flow, losing key logical steps. Their analysis finds the ending token acts as an anchor, its focus pattern marking vital thought from excess. CRISP uses these focus signals to guide atomic shrinking, trimming the chain to raise density while keeping logical sense. Across backbone models and math sets, CRISP cuts token count by 50 to 60 percent without losing scores, easing thought jams.
arxiv-2604-17397: Hu and Zhang bring speculative decoding, the speed trick behind fast language models, to autoregressive video generation. A small 1.3B drafter proposes video blocks in four denoising steps, and an image-quality router accepts blocks that clear a threshold, rejecting the rest for the large target model to redo. Rejecting the first block anchors the scene, and the threshold traces a smooth quality-speed tradeoff. On over a thousand benchmark prompts, the method kept about 98 percent of target quality while running about 60 percent faster.
arxiv-2604-17797: Shi and three colleagues design WSRVOS, a weakly-trained referred video cutting method using text alone, swapping costly labels. Paired boosting uses a multi-input LLM's captions to make good and bad phrases. Two-way choice enables a match, and instance-aware sorting splits good from bad. Good-guess fusion makes pseudo-masks as guidance, and time ranking orders nearby-frame guesses. Tests on A2D Sentences, J-HMDB Sentences, Ref-YouTube-VOS, and Ref-DAVIS17 show an edge.
arxiv-2604-18097: Sarkar and Agarwal uncover a new route to switching antiferromagnets with electric current. In these materials, nearby spins point in reverse directions. They show that uneven impurity scattering creates a staggered spin polarization when combined with a band effect called anomalous spin polarizability. In a model of tetragonal CuMnAs, this new torque can rival or even outrun the usual even-scattering torque.
arxiv-2604-18397: Qiu and Zhang hunt for light from MeV-scale axion-like particles born in the Sun. Protons fusing with deuterium can emit such particles, whose two-photon decays may arrive far off the solar direction. That odd angular and spectral pattern opens new detection routes in space and at the South Pole. A critical height governs ground detection, and future sensitivities could probe photon couplings far beyond current supernova limits.
arxiv-2604-18897: Cazares presents a careful empirical study of prompt engineering for formal mathematical reasoning in the SAIR Equational Theories Stage 1 competition, deciding whether one equational law implies another. Over five weeks, more than 40 prompt variants were tested across four evaluation splits and three language models. The central finding is a single prompt ceiling: balanced hard accuracy plateaus at about 60 to 79 percent for the strongest model, despite substantial engineering effort. Three mechanisms are identified: undecidability of the TRUE case, complex rule systems hurting weaker models, and fragile prompt ordering effects.
arxiv-2604-18997: Li introduces Probable Event Constrained Optimization, a new way to optimize under uncertainty. Unlike chance models, which only cap the odds of a breach, it also demands feasibility for every event above a set threshold. Solutions then stay valid across all likely outcomes. To solve it, Li proposes a data embedded program feeding past measurements into a deterministic approximation. The approach needs no convexity or linearity, suiting nonlinear and nonconvex problems, and hinges on sizing the key data family.
arxiv-2604-19097: Jadhav and nine colleagues map hourglass magnetic fields in the G35 complex using ACT and SOFIA polarimetry. ACT 220 GHz data show hourglass fields in both subregions with distinct symmetry axes. SOFIA data confirm the hourglass shape in the north, while the south differs. Field strengths reach about 600 microgauss north and 850 south, each plus or minus a few hundred. Gravity and magnetism match in the north, while magnetism dominates in the south, likely compressed by an expanding ionized region. These are upper limits, the authors caution.
arxiv-2604-19297: Chnafa and colleagues study electron flow through gapped graphene under a laser-modulated barrier, with a scalar potential and zigzag strain applied. Using a transfer-matrix approach, they derive transmission probabilities across system parameters. Without strain, raising the gap or the potential generally lowers transmission in the central and lower sidebands. Moderate zigzag strain creates strong Fano-type oscillations that vanish at large strain, while laser amplitude boosts transmission and higher laser frequency tends to suppress it.
arxiv-2604-19697: Jin and 11 colleagues introduce StepSTEM, a graduate-level testbed of 283 problems in mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology, and engineering for judging cross-modal reasoning in multimodal models. Existing tests often let models take unimodal shortcuts when text and images repeat each other, and they score only the final answer, ignoring the reasoning path itself. StepSTEM enforces strict complementarity between text and visuals through a rigorous curation pipeline, so each input carries information the other lacks.
arxiv-2604-19797: Devarakonda and five colleagues propose a confidence-aware training framework for speech recognition in Telugu and Kannada medical settings, where annotated data is scarce and words are complex. The method blends real and synthetic speech through a hybrid confidence mechanism mixing static perceptual and acoustic similarity scores with dynamic model entropy. Unlike direct fine-tuning, it uses both fixed-weight and learnable-weight confidence aggregation to guide sample weighting during training. The framework is tested on Telugu and Kannada medical datasets, making varied data sources usable despite limited annotation.
arxiv-2604-20097: Nair and three colleagues study the Carathéodory number in cycle convexity, where a set counts as cycle convex when adding any outside vertex creates no cycle through it. They prove that deciding whether the number reaches a given threshold is NP-complete, even for bipartite graphs. Exact values and constant upper bounds follow for forests, cycles, complete and complete multipartite graphs, split graphs, and P4-sparse graphs, yielding polynomial-time algorithms there. They also characterize near-maximal extremal cases and track the number under strong, lexicographic, and Cartesian products.
