arxiv-2604-20497: Abdelrahman, Ciabattoni, and Monticone set a hard ceiling for flat on-chip inductors, the coiled parts that store magnetic energy in radio chips. They combine electromagnetic math with convex optimization to link the best quality factor to the chip area available. Quality factor measures energy efficiency, and their bound explains how ohmic and radiation losses shift with size and material conductivity. Checking published designs against the ceiling shows some near the limit and others with room to improve, while kinetic inductance offers a path toward denser, higher-quality parts.
arxiv-2604-20897: Perrier builds a thermodynamic theory of algorithmic catalysis inside the watts per intelligence view. It names reusable computing parts that cut irreversible steps for a task class while meeting bounded restoration and structural selectivity limits. He proves class-specific speed-up is capped by the mutual information the substrate shares with the class descriptor. Encoding that information costs a minimum thermodynamic price via Landauer erasure. Together these give a coupling theorem that sets a floor on how long a catalyst must run to pay off in energy terms.
arxiv-2604-20997: Garagash and Gabriel study how slip localizes in fault gouge, crushed fault rock, and its fracture energy. Their framework, with simulations, models gouge with rate-and-state friction, flash heating at high strain, and thermal pressurization of pore fluids. Shearing starts spread out, then collapses to a seismic slip surface. Fracture energy splits into a localization part scaling with gouge thickness, itself linear in fault size, plus a later part growing with slip, ignoring thickness. Flash heating switches on only at localization in fast slip, dropping strength.
arxiv-2604-21097: Gabriel Melo, Leonardo Santiago, and Peter Lu build models that mimic chaotic systems, where a tiny change at the start ruins exact long-range forecasts. Rather than chase exact paths, they match the broad patterns of the system's attractor, the shape its long-run motion traces. Their adversarial transport methods learn both the summary measures and a steady model from a single noisy data run. Tests on varied chaotic systems, including high-dimensional cases spread over space and time, show a much closer match to long-run behavior.
arxiv-2604-21197: Guilin Deng and eight colleagues reveal a privacy hole in federated large language models, where parties fine-tune together without sharing raw data. Their ProjRes attack reads hidden embeddings and studies their projection residuals against the shared gradient subspace, needing no shadow models or past updates. It nears 100 percent accuracy across four benchmarks and four models, beating prior methods by up to 75.75 percent and holding even under strong differential-privacy defenses.
arxiv-2604-21497: Shinya Yamada and 20 colleagues present the first high-resolution X-ray study of Cygnus X-1 with XRISM, observed April 7 to 10, 2024. With Resolve's energy resolution, they examine ionized iron absorption lines, measuring ionization, column densities, and line-of-sight speeds. They find an ionization parameter near 3, column densities of a few times 10 to the 21 per square centimeter, and a blueshift near 100 kilometers per second. Weak absorption before phase 0.9 gives way to strong He-like and H-like iron absorption while dipping, tracing wind motion near the hole.
arxiv-2604-21897: Soriano and six colleagues map political discourse in the Brazilian Chamber of Deputies beyond voting records. They ask how things are said, what is said, and who speaks in similar ways. Their framework combines diachronic stylometric analysis, contextual topic modelling, and semantic clustering of speeches. Applied to over 450,000 speeches from 2003 to 2025, it finds speeches growing shorter and more direct. It also finds an agenda that reorients sharply in national crises. Regional and gender identities often matter more than party affiliation in discursive alignments.
arxiv-2604-22197: Wu and Xiao sharpen estimates for joint eigenfunctions. These are special wave patterns that arise together in a quantum integrable system. Such a system has enough conserved quantities to be solved in a structured way. Earlier work improved the standard Hormander bounds at typical points by polynomial factors. The authors now prove a sharp bound at points meeting a rank k non-degeneracy condition. That result tightens how large such eigenfunctions can grow at a point.
arxiv-2604-22497: Ruozzi and nine colleagues develop a framework for real-time catheter shape rebuild, simulations and mixed reality views in endovascular navigation. They build a finite element model of the venous pathway from femoral vein to vena cava, imposing catheter motion and modelling contact to compute deformation. Tested in vitro with a sensorised catheter in a silicone replica, real-time read-outs feed the simulation. Simulated time exceeded real time by 12 percent initially and by 45 percent in the tortuous portion. Median displacement error stayed below 2.33 mm in the tortuous phase.
arxiv-2604-23297: Pupim and Scheurer explore noise magnetometry to spot altermagnetic order and tell it apart from antiferromagnetism by symmetry signs. Magnon noise spectra differ between the two orders, but the sharpest symmetry-sensitive signs sit in charge fluctuations of itinerant altermagnets. In bulk, strained, and domain-wall settings, they find noise inputs permitted by symmetry only in the altermagnet. Angular dependence of noise near domain walls also shows the orbital character, such as d-wave versus g-wave, of the magnetic order parameter.
arxiv-2604-24197: Wu and six colleagues review how frontier image models turn synthetic visuals into seeming evidence. Made photographs, documents, and steady depictions of people and places can sway decisions in news, finance, identity checks, medicine, and law. Drawing on model docs, incident notes, research, and policy sources through October 2026, they split vendor claims from real incidents, experiments, and future harms. This account links realism, text rendering, source match, editing, grounding, and cost to evidentiary weight, and argues high-stakes decisions need checked source records, trusted backup, and careful review.
arxiv-2604-24297: Schwiering and three colleagues offer all-reaching, feasible-only quantum circuits for limited choice optimization. Such circuits reach every feasible answer, including the optimum, while never giving off-limits answers. This contrasts with alternating operator ansatz schemes, sure to reach the optimum only in the limit. The authors build these circuits from a group action on the feasible set, with group representation and generating sequences. They apply the method to TSP examples, testing cases with up to nine cities against mixers.
arxiv-2604-24697: Ziheng and eleven colleagues test whether current AI agents can close the discovery-to-application gap, using Minecraft as a case study. Their SciCrafter benchmark poses parameterized redstone circuit tasks, such as lighting lamps in set patterns, where larger targets demand genuine discovery rather than memorized solutions. Frontier models under a general code-agent scaffold all plateau at about 26 percent success, with application the biggest gap. The authors break the loop into four capacities: application, consolidation, experimental discovery and knowledge-gap identification, to diagnose the failures.
arxiv-2604-24797: Li, Peng, Severini and Shafto analyze Lean 4's Mathlib library as a layered graph of 308,129 declarations and 7,563 modules. Splitting the graph into explicit edges and compiler-made or proof-driven edges, they map its structure. Three findings stand out. Human taxonomies diverge from logical groups, with about half of links across names. Developers use a median of under 2 percent of imports. Formalization shrinks semantic hierarchies, with centrality tracking language infrastructure rather than math relevance.
arxiv-2604-25097: Song and seven colleagues find the Fermi energy of diamond using PL study. In such solids, Fermi energy depends on donor and acceptor levels. For diamond that link is highly nonlinear, making direct measurement important. The authors measure relative counts of negative and neutral centers from PL spectra. They find Fermi energy from these counts plus a DFT result on formation levels of both charge states. They apply the method to several diamond samples, discussing spin coherence and charge stability.
arxiv-2604-25297: Jang and seven colleagues propose a training framework turning general models into legal specialists. It is grounded in legal needs with a focus on Korean law. Many specialist models use data sets and training methods misaligned with real needs, limiting utility where precision and reliability matter. They introduce LegalMidm, a Korean legal language model, with a method for high-quality, use-case-driven data sets and training pipelines. Their approach emphasizes work with legal professionals and careful curation for relevance and accuracy, showing effectiveness in key legal tasks.
arxiv-2604-25397: de Berg and four colleagues keep a shortcut network over changing disks by leaning on persistent data structures. That reuse of past versions lets the network stay current as disks arrive and leave, without rebuilding. Disk sizes stay inside a fixed known range, and the shortcut stretches any route by at most one plus epsilon. For fixed range and epsilon, size and space stay near linear, updates run in polylogarithmic time, and below one, epsilon also turns the network into a connectivity tool.
arxiv-2604-25797: Schmäke and Ruess present unfitted multi-level hp-refinement for finite element problems with sharp or moving features. Singularities, steep gradients, jumps, and moving sources usually force costly remeshing and constraint handling. Their method layers independently placed overlay meshes onto a fixed base mesh, superimposed across levels. Constraints on artificial overlay edges ensure global continuity, with coupling assembled over element-partition overlaps. Zones can be added, shifted, or removed without touching the base mesh. Tests keep exponential convergence for non-smooth problems at lower cost.
arxiv-2604-25897: Enwerem and three colleagues treat dexterous grasping as variational inference over hidden contact parameters and object pose. Grasping is stochastic: contact varies, sensing is noisy, and disturbances strike. Expected-quality goals ignore tail failures, and risk-sensitive methods often rely on particle beliefs that scale poorly and block gradient methods. The authors use a smooth Gaussian mixture belief plus a CVaR surrogate, enabling direct optimization of tail robustness. In simulation, robust success rises and planning time falls roughly tenfold versus particle-filter control.
arxiv-2604-26297: Jiang and five colleagues proposed NeuroPlastic, an optimizer that borrows from multi-factor synaptic plasticity, the brain's way of tuning connections by several signals at once. It scales gradient updates with interacting gradient, activity-like, and memory-like statistics, making a light layer that fits standard training pipelines. On image benchmarks it beat a gradient-only version, with clearer gains on Fashion-MNIST and with scarce data. Transfer tests stayed stable and competitive without retuning.
arxiv-2604-26497: Wang and Xiao studied whole-number points on projective varieties with two tools: the Ru-Vojta theorem and a wider version of Huang-Levin-Xiao inequalities. The tools lean on different geometric setups, transverse versus proper meetings of boundary divisors. Used on one-parameter families of unit equations, they proved that solution sets thin out, with cases split by the degrees of polynomial coefficients. The same frame stretched greatest-common-divisor estimates to exponential Diophantine equations and digit patterns in q-adic form.
arxiv-2604-27397: Zymaris extends the Mathews spinor-horosphere link to Lipschitz spinors and null multiflags in higher dimensions. Earlier work linked two-component complex spinors to marked horospheres in 3D hyperbolic space, and a later preprint took this to quaternionic spinors in 4D. His link is equivariant and lets spinors apply to horospheres in all hyperbolic spaces. It builds on Mathews spin marks, carried here to higher cases.
arxiv-2604-27497: Jazlan and three colleagues investigate server-side Google Analytics, which grows as browsers restrict tracking. In this setup, the browser sends requests to an endpoint that forwards them to the tracker, defeating endpoint blocks. They present SST-Guard, a system that detects it by matching values it must collect and share, using templates across requests, cookies, and the window object. On Tranco top-10k sites, it finds about 4 percent of domains with above 93 percent accuracy, and network classifier reaches 99.8 percent. In the wild, it finds about 4 percent on 150k sites.
arxiv-2604-27997: Govers, Šćepanović and Quercia study how AI should join team brainstorming when groups assess the impacts of an AI system. In workshops they found AI hints improved quality and perceptions for a general chatbot companion but not for a specialised kidney allocation tool. Their guidance says AI should offer hints, not answers, early on, step in only when groups stall, and help organise ideas rather than doing the inventing itself.
arxiv-2604-28197: Lee's team presents OmniRobotHome, a lived-in home testbed for human-robot interaction with dozens of synchronised cameras covering every room. A spread-out pipeline turns those streams into lasting human and object states for robot drivers at low latency, without worn gear and despite blocking. Two studies look at yielding early for safety and at wordless intent reading for help. Results show how camera reach, lag in state updates, multi-view pose, hand and gaze readings, and conduct forecasts shape task results.
arxiv-2605-00197:
Aurélien Bück-Kaeffer and 5 co-authors map the design choices behind social networks simulated entirely by language model agents. Such silicon societies are growing in number, and some now run outside controlled studies. Yet builders have little guidance on how each design choice changes the outcome, or how to check realism.

The team varies key choices, including which base model plays the agents and how the agents connect to each other. Surveys stand in for agent opinions. Some choices add up in simple ways, while others interact in tangled ways. The single biggest factor is the choice of base model. The study gives future builders a clearer sense of which decisions matter most.
arxiv-2605-00397:
Ali Al-Bustami and Jaerock Kwon release a simulation dataset for teaching robots to follow spoken directions to an object. In their task, a wheeled robot in photorealistic virtual rooms must drive to the named object and stop within a meter of it. The four settings are an office, a hospital, and two warehouses built in a leading simulator.

Each of the 1,174 recorded episodes pairs a short instruction with camera images, depth maps, and object masks, plus the expert's driving actions recorded sixty times per second. Starting distances fall into three tiers, from near to far across the room. The set covers twelve object categories, with fresh wordings and unseen categories held out for testing. Five evaluation splits probe accuracy, robustness to rephrasing, and performance on new object types.
arxiv-2605-00597:
Hyeongu Kang and Susik Yoon extract keyphrases from documents without any labeled training data, using a context-centric method they call MUDY. Pretrained language models judge global relevance well, yet they often miss phrases that matter locally, inside one subtopic of a long document. MUDY scores candidates along several granularities at once, weighing both document-wide and segment-specific importance.

One component scores each candidate by how likely the model is to generate it, weighted by its local context. A second reads the model's own attention patterns at multiple scales to gauge significance. On four real-world datasets, MUDY beat leading unsupervised baselines on top-k accuracy at various cutoffs. Follow-up analyses, quantitative and qualitative, support the design's premise: a keyphrase's importance is partly local, and extraction improves when the scoring respects the document's internal structure. Code is released for reproducibility.
arxiv-2605-00797:
Julia Chuzhoy, Sanjeev Khanna, and Junkai Song improve the deterministic algorithm for maintaining a maximal matching in a graph whose edges arrive and depart online. A maximal matching leaves no two unmatched vertices joined by an edge. Randomized methods are fast when the adversary is oblivious, but an adaptive adversary, who reacts to earlier choices, has been a major challenge.

A recent breakthrough gave the first sublinear update times against adaptive adversaries, with a deterministic bound slower than the randomized one. The new deterministic algorithm reaches an amortized update time near the square root of the number of vertices. Matching sparsifiers, sparse subgraphs that preserve key matching information, play a central tool role in the advance.
arxiv-2605-00897:
Yunhao Wang and six co-authors propose SPAT, a transmission protocol designed for meaning-based communication in future 6G networks. Such systems send task-relevant meaning rather than exact bits, but transport still relies on plain port headers that can be corrupted, causing packet loss. SPAT embeds source and target port information directly into meaning codes, reducing dependence on those headers.

Separate processing handles uplink service recognition and downlink selective decoding through target-aware gating. An adaptive-rate controller adjusts how many such channels are sent based on channel conditions and feature importance. On image datasets and in real-world measurements, SPAT beats TCP, UDP, and a meaning baseline on rebuild quality across signal levels while keeping latency low.
arxiv-2605-01197:
Ke Qiu and five co-authors present a transformer framework for generating 3D conducting gestures from music. Conducting synthesis is a hard cross-modal problem: output must follow long-range musical structure, stay synchronized at beat level, and remain plausible as a fine-grained human performance. Earlier studies were limited by sparse pose data, small data, or evaluations that did not directly measure music-gesture alignment.

The authors build a data pipeline that recovers detailed SMPL body motion from conducting videos, forming a dataset of professional gestures. Their system encodes music over time and decodes gestures autoregressively from an initial pose. A retrieval-based evaluation embeds music and motion in a shared space for alignment metrics. Experiments beat dance and conducting baselines, with ablations backing the design.
arxiv-2605-01297:
Edward Roussel and six co-authors use game theory to argue that a moratorium on machine superintelligence can be in a state's own self-interest, contrary to the prevailing race view. Their formal model of strategy and interaction between rival superpowers captures the trade-off. On one side are benefits of technological supremacy, on the other catastrophic risks of uncontrolled development.

As the perceived cost of losing control rises sufficiently relative to other parameters, imposing such a pause becomes self-interested for each state in the model. The authors further provide empirical evidence that global perception of such risk is rising. That trend, they argue, makes a stable, rational pause increasingly plausible in the current global landscape, even without assuming altruistic motives.
arxiv-2605-01597:
Yi-Cheng Lin and eight co-authors survey bias and fairness across speech technology, pulling over four hundred studies into one frame. Speech tools now gate high-stakes services, yet fairness work has been split by task and field, so patterns shared across the domain stay hidden.

The survey sets out seven fairness definitions tuned to speech and tracks the field's growth through three paradigms: robustness, representation, and governance. Metrics are sorted into six families, each tied back to the definition it serves. Bias is traced along the whole pipeline, surfacing speech-specific traps such as recording channel acting as a stand-in for demographic traits, and shaky human labels for emotion. Fixes are organized by the stage where they intervene, from data to deployment, and matched to the sources they treat. Open challenges close the map.
arxiv-2605-01697:
Gabriel T dos Santos, Roberto dos Reis, and Vinayak P Dravid model how an electron beam eats away at a metal-organic framework while it is being imaged. Beam damage caps the sharpness reachable on such tender hybrid materials, and quantitative links between dose and decay have been scarce.

Working from an in situ spectroscopy series on the iron framework MIL-101, they reduce each spectrum to window scores over bond bands and fit a physics-informed neural network per channel. A latent integrity variable decays by one shared power-law rule per channel, held in line by monotonicity, bounds, and one prior ranking two bond types. Across nine dose frames, carbon-oxygen and carbon-carbon linker channels prove most dose-sensitive, hitting half integrity at a stated dose. One low-energy window grows with dose, which they read as strength being redistributed rather than a single bond population simply vanishing.
arxiv-2605-01797:
Thomas Eiter, Katsumi Inoue, and Sota Moriyama compute the stable models of a logic program without calling a classical solver. Answer set programming reasons by rules and defaults, and its marriage to neural networks has been fruitful, yet the reasoning step still routes through standard solvers that bottleneck scale.

Their decision-propagation method alternates two moves: declare an atom false, then propagate the truths that follow. Successful runs of that alternation are shown to capture exactly the stable model meaning. A neural extension makes the decisions learnable and the propagations fuzzy, so the whole pipeline can train end to end. Experiments show the neural version learning to find stable models efficiently, with better accuracy and scalability than existing neuro-symbolic rivals on their benchmarks. The work targets hybrid systems that must reason and perceive in one breath.
arxiv-2605-01997:
Heleni Krelman, Ori Nefesh, and Liron Stern make blue and mid-infrared light inside a tiny rubidium vapour cell on a chip. Alkali vapours are strongly nonlinear, so they can mix light efficiently even at low power, but past work needed cells centimetres long. The team uses a micromachined platform and resonant four-wave mixing in continuous-wave mode.

Good overlap between light and atoms gave about twenty microwatts of blue light over a very short path, with a narrow measured linewidth. Compared with a normal glass cell, the chip achieved higher blue-light efficiency despite its shorter length. A silicon window also let them detect mid-infrared emission, at much lower collected power, from the same device.
arxiv-2605-02397:
Ivan Gnusov and colleagues measure critical dynamics in a driven quantum fluid of light. The fluid is made of exciton-polaritons in a semiconductor microcavity. Near a phase transition, spatial correlations grow and dynamics slow down. Direct tests of that link have mostly covered equilibrium systems and static traits. The team probes the disordered phase below the condensation threshold, where fluctuations dominate.

They measure the growth of the correlation length. They also measure the slowing of the relaxation time. The two obey a power law, with an exponent near two. That value signals diffusive dynamics of a non-conserved order parameter. The results extend critical dynamics from equilibrium matter to driven optical systems, bridging condensates and lasers.
arxiv-2605-02597:
Michael F. Staddon improves Fourier Neural Operators, learning models that solve partial differential equations far faster than many classic solvers. Inside such a model, Fourier layers transform wave modes with learned weights. Most physical systems do not depend on which way the coordinates point, yet those learned transforms need not respect that symmetry.

Staddon's change forces the layer transforms to respect spatial symmetry, giving an isotropic version of the operator. The constraint does two things at once. It improves model performance. It also cuts the number of parameters sharply, by up to a large factor in two dimensions and a much larger one in three. The paper is a compact design lesson: building known physical symmetry into a model can make it both smaller and better.
arxiv-2605-02797:
Dong-Hui Yang and three co-authors prove a measured form of a continuation result for a backward equation whose leading term fades at an inside point. The domain is ring-shaped. Continuation results ask whether a solution that vanishes somewhere must vanish nearby. That question feeds control and inverse problems. Fading-term equations resist the standard methods.

The proof works by approximation. Solutions of the fading-term equation are approached through solutions of nearby equations with no fading. For those, weighted Carleman estimates are proved across two separate domains. The estimates then carry the measured result back to the fading case. In this way the weak continuation property of the original equation is put on firm ground, in a form strong enough to feed later control work.
arxiv-2605-03097:
Yifan Wu proves a full support theorem for the universal compactified Jacobian, a moduli space that packages line bundles over families of curves. Support theorems control where the pieces of a pushforward sheaf can live, and full support is the strongest clean outcome.

Wu shows every direct summand in the key decomposition has full support on the base of pointed curves, and describes that decomposition through the constant sheaf on the universal curve. Two proofs are given: one blends recent support and decomposition results with equivariant methods, and a second, independent route varies stability conditions.
arxiv-2605-03197:
Kryhin and Sudhir give a complete account of quantum dynamics with memory. Standard Markovian models assume the present state depends only on the immediate past, yet many real systems remember: their current state depends on their whole history. The authors define such non-Markovian evolution under two physical demands, complete positivity and non-signalling, and characterize its structure fully. The resulting continuous-time equation extends the standard Lindblad equation with a memory integral.

That equation handles noise with any integrable power spectrum, with no further approximations, and the authors build a formalism for multi-time measurement correlations that needs no regression theorem. As a test case, they compute the emitted-light spectrum of a driven two-level system in a bath with memory: the familiar Mollow triplet gains a frequency-dependent linewidth that encodes that memory. The work opens a path to state estimation and control beyond the Markovian regime.
arxiv-2605-03297:
Van-Phat Thai, Aradhya Dhruv, Duc-Thinh Pham, and Sameer Alam add supervised contrastive learning as a light fix for accent weakness in speech recognition. Systems built on self-supervised pretraining and CTC fine-tuning score well on native speech but slip on varied accents.

An utterance-level contrastive loss shapes encoder representations during fine-tuning, with no model changes and no explicit accent labels. On the L2-ARCTIC benchmark, word error fell consistently across several pretrained encoders, with the largest relative gains on unseen accents. Representation checks showed tighter, steadier geometry under accent shifts, making the trick a portable robustness tool.
arxiv-2605-03397:
Dong Chen, Shuai Zheng, Haoyang Shao, Hongsheng Wu, Muhao Xu, Yeyu Yan, Ruifang Li, and Zhenfeng Zhu recast map search as generative retrieval of places. Vague, context-heavy queries defeat classic matching against huge place databases. Intent must be inferred from mixed personal and spatial context.

Their GenPOI framework encodes each place as a token sequence. The sequence carries both meaning and geography. A large language model then generates candidates, under proximity constraints that keep results valid and nearby. Tests used Tencent Map data with over ten million places. The generative approach beat conventional retrieval on hard general search queries.
arxiv-2605-03497:
James Rowbottom, Elizabeth L. Baker, Nick Huang, Ben Adcock, Carola-Bibiane Schönlieb, and Alexander Denker introduce GRIFDIR, a diffusion model for irregular domains. It works on meshes over complex domains. Function-space diffusion promises resolution invariance. But standard backbones favor regular grids and fail on awkward shapes.

GRIFDIR builds its score network from graph kernels. Those kernels are written as finite element functions, so the network works directly on unstructured meshes of any shape. Sampling tests, plain and conditional, covered non-convex and multiply connected domains. The method kept resolution invariance and captured distributions with high fidelity.
arxiv-2605-03897:
M. A. Anacleto, A. T. N. Silva, and L. Casarini construct a noncommutative thin-shell gravastar and study its shadow, the dark silhouette such an object casts for distant observers. A gravastar is a horizonless alternative to a black hole, first proposed by Mazur and Mottola. Such objects can still have unstable photon orbits. That makes them hard to tell apart from black holes by light alone.

The model joins a nonsingular de Sitter interior to a noncommutative Schwarzschild exterior. The join uses the cut-and-paste technique and meets the Israel junction conditions at the shell. Noncommutativity enters through a Lorentzian energy density distribution with a minimum width. The authors test stability through energy conditions and a linearized analysis. They show that photon trajectories and deflection angles shift as the noncommutative parameter grows, changing the expected shadow.
arxiv-2605-04097:
Haofei Yu, Yining Zhao, Lenore Blum, Manuel Blum, and Paul Pu Liang present CTM-AI, an early blueprint for a general artificial intelligence system. It is inspired by the Conscious Turing Machine, a formal machine model of consciousness. Today's systems remain narrow compared with human flexibility, and the authors ask whether theories of consciousness can inspire more general architectures. CTM-AI combines the machine model with modern foundation models.

The design hosts an enormous number of processors. They range from specialized experts such as vision-language models and software tools to unspecialized learners meant to develop their own expertise. Information is selected, integrated, and exchanged as each problem demands. The authors report state-of-the-art accuracy on two multimodal humor and sarcasm benchmarks. They beat multimodal and multi-agent frameworks. They also report gains of over ten points on tool-using and agentic benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-04497:
Ron Wettenstein, Rory Mitchell, and Peng Yu reformulate a popular method for explaining the predictions of tree-based models. Shapley values assign each feature a fair share of a prediction, but existing fast methods trade off running time against tree depth, numerical stability, or the ability to explain interactions between features.

Their version recasts the calculation as an integral of a related polynomial, evaluated with a fixed set of quadrature points that in practice reaches machine precision. The runtime barely depends on tree depth, and interaction values of any order come out naturally. The implementation runs on both standard and graphics processors and is integrated into a widely used library.
arxiv-2605-04797:
Michael Soprano, Andrea Cioci, and Stefano Mizzaro study how well ordinary people, working as crowd judges, can detect audiovisual deepfakes, manipulated videos where the picture, the sound, or both may be fake. Reliable human judgment matters because such fakes fuel misinformation and automated detection is not always available.

In two matched studies, they collected ten judgments on each of ninety-six videos. The videos came from two benchmark data sets. Workers judged whether a video was manipulated. They also judged which channel was faked, and when. Workers rarely accused genuine videos, yet they missed many manipulations, and agreement stayed limited. Pooling judgments stabilised the authenticity call but could not recover fakes that nearly everyone missed.
arxiv-2605-05197:
Yingshan Susan Wang and four co-authors ask whether language models inside separate grammatical sentences from ungrammatical ones, beyond merely judging which string is more likely. Models generate well-formed text and win tightly controlled comparisons, yet raw probabilities do not sharply split grammatical from ungrammatical strings overall. The authors probe their inner states with a simple linear probe instead.

Trained on natural text and made-up ungrammatical variants, the probe also worked on human-curated judgment benchmarks and beat score-based judgements. On plausibility tests, where both sentences are well-formed, the probe did worse than raw probability, as expected for a grammar-only signal. An English-trained probe also transferred well to grammar tests in other languages.
arxiv-2605-05297:
Jean-Yves Desaules and three co-authors build a systematic way to find quantum many-body scars in frustrated Rydberg atom arrays. Scars are special states that avoid thermalising while most states around them do, and they had only been observed on bipartite lattices without frustration. Whether scars survive frustration, and which starting states reveal them, was open.

Their graph-theoretic framework predicts two mechanisms. One adapts the bipartite recipe with locally entangled states to mild frustration. Another uses strong frustration to pin part of the lattice while the rest oscillates freely. Simulations confirm both, and the team finds a large family of scarred paths on the hexagonal lattice that can store information protected from thermalisation.
arxiv-2605-05597:
Heat usually flows from hot to cold, but Kenjiro Okawa, Yasutaka Amagai, Hiroyuki Fujiki, and Nobu-Hisa Kaneko demonstrate a controlled exception. Electric circuits have inductors; thermal circuits have lacked an equivalent part. Their work uses the Peltier effect, which moves heat when current crosses a junction between materials.

With thermal inertia and an alternating current, heat flows briefly from the cold side to the hot side inside one material. They derive an exact solution showing the effect is general, and demonstrate local cooling of twenty-five millikelvin in a bismuth-antimony telluride sample. The result points toward a thermoinductor for thermal circuits.
arxiv-2605-05997:
Zhangquan Chen and eleven co-authors present a framework that lets vision language models reason about moving scenes in four dimensions. Dynamic spatial reasoning from a single camera video is key for systems that must act in the physical world. Text only reasoning is verbose and imprecise for such motion, while outside geometry modules add complexity without building skill in the model itself.

4DThinker instead trains the model to form dynamic latent mental images of how scenes evolve. A pipeline builds training data from raw videos with no hand annotation, and fine tuning supervises both text tokens and these 4D latents. A reinforcement learning stage then sharpens hard tasks. Across dynamic spatial benchmarks, the framework beat strong baselines throughout.
arxiv-2605-06197:
Paul Valery Nguezet and four co-authors make deep learning for brain tumor imaging explain itself in clinical language. Black box models block clinical adoption, since doctors need reasons they can act on, not just a label. Their framework links a convolutional network's prediction to visual evidence and then to a written diagnostic narrative from a language model.

Nine network designs gain a dual output that classifies and segments at once, feeding richer features into the explanation chain. Saliency heat maps are refined into tumor masks and mapped onto a named brain atlas, turning pixels into anatomical structures. Those findings, stored in structured form, prompt three language models to write radiology style reports. Tests on 4,834 MRI images across three tumor classes compare both vision and language stages.
arxiv-2605-06497:
Cesar Damian and Oscar Loaiza-Brito revisit the Hagedorn temperature of string theory as a dynamical bottleneck rather than a static limit. Near that temperature the number of string states grows explosively. Their framework, steepest-entropy-ascent quantum thermodynamics, tracks evolution on the state space without needing a global canonical ensemble, treating temperature as state-dependent.

They derive how inverse temperature evolves and show that a reservoir feeding all states evenly would cross the Hagedorn scale freely. Slowing instead needs uneven feeding, where highly excited strings are produced slowly. Then temperature pins near the scale for a long, computable time while energy gathers in long strings.
arxiv-2605-06597:
Yiqiao Jin and nine co-authors propose UniSD, a unified framework for self-distillation in large language models. Self-distillation adapts a model using its own generated output instead of a stronger teacher, but free-form generations and task-dependent correctness make the supervision unstable. Prior work tested design choices one at a time, leaving their interactions unclear.

UniSD combines mechanisms for reliability, representation alignment, and stability, including multi-teacher agreement, an averaged teacher, token-level contrastive learning, feature matching, and divergence clipping. Across six benchmarks and six models, the study maps when self-distillation beats static imitation. A combined pipeline gives the strongest results, improving clearly over both the base model and the best baseline.
arxiv-2605-06797:
Quentin Berthet and five co-authors propose MIND, a new score for judging generative models that fixes weaknesses of the standard Fréchet Inception Distance. That standard compares means and covariances in a feature space, making it sample-hungry and vulnerable to adversarial gaming. MIND instead uses sliced Wasserstein distance, averaging many one-dimensional optimal transport distances that sorting computes quickly.

The authors report three advantages: roughly ten times better sample efficiency, about a hundred times faster computation, and stronger robustness against moment-matching attacks. Five thousand samples with MIND match the evaluation quality of fifty thousand with the older score, and even one or two thousand samples stay informative for rapid model iteration.
arxiv-2605-06997:
Anupama Sridhar and Alexander Johansen introduce Echo, a memory design for recall over very long reasoning traces. Transformer memory caches grow with every token, straining ordinary hardware. State-space models use constant memory but forget facts once the gap before a question grows too long.

Echo replaces attention layers with a spectral operator built from Koopman theory, storing history in a compact constant-size state. On a recall benchmark, a plain state-space model stayed near chance, while Echo reached perfect accuracy in every tested setup. Across five more retrieval tests, it beat both plain and hybrid models while keeping inference memory constant.
arxiv-2605-07097:
Anastasis Kratsios and four co-authors prove that a broad class of neural networks can, in principle, be learned from finite samples. Their result covers fixed feedforward networks whose layers fit inside a tame mathematical structure called an o-minimal structure. That includes common multilayer networks, convolutional networks, graph networks, and fixed-length transformers.

Learnability holds in the standard PAC setting even when parameters are unbounded, and it covers layers like attention, pooling, and normalization. The authors argue finite-sample learnability should be treated as a baseline, not a selling point. Comparing architectures should instead focus on built-in biases, symmetries, scale, and how training behaves in practice.
arxiv-2605-07297:
Mana Sakai and Masaaki Imaizumi derive generalization bounds for trained transformers that adapt to each model's own spectral shape. Earlier complexity bounds imposed fixed norm limits in advance and could grow exponentially with depth. Their post hoc bounds instead use spectral quantities of the actual trained weight matrices, layer by layer.

The spectral indices can be chosen after training, separately for each matrix type and layer, trading complexity against dimension and depth factors. Proxy comparisons suggest their complexity factors grow more slowly with depth and width than norm-based ones. The work offers a complexity-based view of how trained transformers' spectra relate to generalization.
arxiv-2605-07397:
Bastian Rieck writes an opinion piece urging topological deep learning to find genuinely higher-order datasets instead of manufacturing them. Geometry and topology have gained ground in machine learning, and message passing on complexes richer than graphs drives much of that progress. Suitable benchmarks, though, remain scarce compared with the diversity of models.

Researchers therefore often lift existing graph datasets by adding higher-order structure artificially. Rieck encourages the community to also source new datasets that natively contain such structure. Better native data, the argument goes, would prop up the foundations of the field and test higher-order models on the phenomena they were designed for.
arxiv-2605-07497:
Ramón González Rodríguez and Brais Ramos Pérez work in pure algebra, on structures that combine two interacting operations on the same object. They introduce a new category called opposite brace triples, defined inside a general braided monoidal setting. The aim is to organize several known constructions under one roof.

Under a cocommutativity assumption, they prove this new category is isomorphic to the category of Hopf braces, meaning the two viewpoints describe the same mathematics. Fixing one underlying Hopf algebra, both categories also match the category of matched pairs over that algebra. Results of this kind let theorems proved in one framework transfer cleanly to the others.
arxiv-2605-07597:
Arjun R and two co-authors study what happens when interactions between two species are nonreciprocal, so the influence of one on the other is not matched in return. Such uneven action cannot be captured by equilibrium free-energy methods. They introduce and analyze a two-species McKean-Vlasov equation derived from an underlying system of interacting stochastic particles.

With weak asymmetry spread evenly, the onset of collective order shifts but only stationary patterns appear. When the asymmetry varies in space, the picture is richer. The uniform state can lose stability through Hopf bifurcations, producing standing and travelling waves. This happens even without explicit chase behavior built into the particles. Direct particle simulations confirm these waves are real effects of the system, not artifacts of the continuum model.
arxiv-2605-07897:
Hang Wu and four co-authors manage memory for streaming video models that must answer questions about an endless feed in real time. Memory is the crunch: existing systems compress visual tokens by visual similarity, or bolt retrieval on after compression. Semantic importance then rarely guides what is kept, and the two stages fight each other.

Their framework, SAVEMem, builds a three-tier streaming memory under a fixed budget. It uses a bank of standby pseudo-questions so long-term retention follows semantic salience rather than looks alone. At query time, a recency gate sized to whether the question concerns the present or the distant past scopes the retrieval. Applied without training to a Qwen vision model, it lifted benchmark scores substantially and cut peak GPU memory nearly in half at longer inputs.
arxiv-2605-07997:
Saba Ayub, Saba Shafaq, Arslan Sikandar, and M. Jamil Aslam compute details of a rare B-meson decay. In heavy-quark limits, symmetry relations cut the number of form factors that describe how a B meson turns into a lighter meson. Those relations are only exact in the limit, so real predictions need corrections.

The authors add symmetry-breaking terms from perturbative QCD, using vertex corrections and light-cone distribution amplitudes for the decay to a K-zero-star meson plus two muons. They find the corrections shift the branching ratio and one polarization measure by only about three percent. A much larger measured shift would point to new physics.
arxiv-2605-08197:
Serafim Batzoglou introduces ReplaySCM, a benchmark that grades causal reasoning by running the answer. Most causal tests for language models score isolated answers or graph sketches. Here each of the thirteen hundred items hides a Boolean structural causal model, and the system must output a working mechanism in a restricted language.

Submissions are parsed, checked for legality and cycles, then replayed on training and held-out intervention worlds, so a mechanism earns credit for behaving correctly even if its formulas look different. The benchmark varies how much structure is revealed, from full ordering to hidden roots, and includes tasks that ask for a genuinely different model that still fits the evidence.
arxiv-2605-08297:
Daning Cheng, Zeyu Liu, Jun Sun, Fen Xia, and coauthors ask when making a residual network deeper provably helps. Scaling laws say bigger models usually test better, but a mechanism is missing. Their test case grows a trained normalized residual network by inserting one new block at an intermediate layer.

The analysis splits the question into representational gain, optimization gain, and generalization transfer. Near zero initialization, a first-order descent condition guarantees the enlarged class contains a jumpboard model with strictly smaller population risk than the original. Norm-based complexity bounds tailored to post-normalized architectures handle the transfer side, giving a qualitative test-risk mechanism for depth scaling.
arxiv-2605-08397:
Mahmoud Abo-Khamis, Eden Chmielewski, Andrei Draghici, Ahmet Kara, and coauthors speed up a classic database chore. The chore is keeping a query's answer current as rows are inserted and deleted. Results must be enumerable at constant delay after each update. Earlier fast methods were hand-built for a few favorite queries.

Their approach generalizes to arbitrary join queries. It combines delta queries, trees of materialized views, and heavy-light partitioning of the input tables. A new quantity, maintenance width, captures the update cost. It depends on where the heavy-light threshold is set. The authors show how to choose that threshold to minimize the cost. Update times match or beat the best previously reported.
arxiv-2605-08697:
Yuhao Jia and six coauthors improve knowledge tracing, the task of predicting what a student knows from past answers, by borrowing patterns from other learners. Raw answer histories hide deeper behavior patterns, so their MBP-KT framework first rewrites each history as combinations of basic meta behavioral patterns. A simple module then extracts shared collaborative signals from those pattern sequences.

General injection strategies feed the shared signal into many existing tracing models without redesign. On real world education datasets, the framework consistently boosts a wide range of downstream models. Learning analytics gains a reusable layer that captures how students behave, not just what they answered, improving predictions across model families.
arxiv-2605-08797:
Rishav Gupta, Bingkai Lin, and Xin Zheng prove tight hardness bounds for approximately decoding the most likely codeword, a core problem in coding theory. Assuming the exponential time hypothesis, their deterministic reduction shows no algorithm can approximate the parameterized decoding problem, or its nearest codeword sibling, within a fixed constant factor in the stated time. The bridge is a new combinatorial object called a cover family, built randomly then derandomized.

Earlier constant factor hardness needed a far stronger randomized assumption, and the best bound under the standard hypothesis was notably weaker. Their direct route from a gap version of linear equations is also conceptually simpler. Complexity theory gains optimal lower bounds settling how hard approximate decoding truly is.
arxiv-2605-08897:
Safa Alsaidi and seven coauthors back the hunt for a rare immune flaw with a model medics can read. The flaw is APDS, from gene shifts in one of two genes. Its signs shift a lot and match much more common ills. That slows the call for years. Line scores miss how signs play off each other. Deep models hide their grounds.

Their Shapley form swaps the line score for a game form. Signs that show up as a pair count as a pair. The clarity of the line form stays. On eight shared sets, a pair form with a shrink term wins. On a real group of more than two hundred, it splits cases from matched peers.
arxiv-2605-09197:
Gaubert and six colleagues test how human AI collectives shape opinions, using an experimental method for hybrid social networks. Participants, human or AI, were placed in five by five grid networks and asked over eight rounds to select and revise statements on a polarising topic. Three setups were compared: human only, AI only, and mixed networks with equal shares of human and AI participants.

Hybrid networks reached the lowest final polarisation, while human only networks showed higher polarisation with lower neighbour agreement. Extra experiments varied language model prompt framing to see whether instruction design might shift convergence patterns. The authors stress the findings are early and cannot yet support broad generalisations. Even so, the work shows experimental social networks can illuminate opinion dynamics in hybrid human AI societies. The method offers a controlled way to study deliberation and democratic outcomes as AI increasingly mediates public discourse.
arxiv-2605-09797:
Shahmurov claimed a proof of global smoothness for the three-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, a famously open problem about whether fluid flows stay smooth forever. The claimed argument runs in two parts. Part I treats the axisymmetric-with-swirl case in a five-dimensional lifted form, built on a lifted vorticity ratio, a regularized swirl derivative, and a squared source density.

In those variables, a derivative source and a compressive feedback form one pair-transfer mechanism, handled with energy identities, interpolation estimates, and threshold absorption. Part II gives a three-dimensional front-end stripping leakage, shell, pressure, tail, and other channels from a hypothetical singular packet. A zero final defect, the paper argues, forces the flow into a two-dimensional class, ruled out classically, or the axisymmetric-with-swirl class of Part I. This is a claimed proof, not an established verdict.
arxiv-2605-09897:
Wang, Xie and Zhang study video delivery where the receiver rebuilds pictures from compact meaning using a generative model, rather than receiving every pixel. Errors then snowball over time, useful clues are correlated across frames, and each retry costs budget, so the receiver must choose retransmissions wisely. Past work focused on representation or compression, while existing error-resilient schemes retransmit encoder-chosen frame blocks.

Their proposal makes temporally local packages the retransmission unit: packages are sent, dropped, received and committed as whole units, at the receiver's request. Under matched backbones, budgets and channel models, this package-native scheme beat block baselines on time-weighted recovery cost in moderate to harsh channels. It won mainly by stabilising recovery earlier, while final quality ended up broadly comparable and the edge faded in near-clean channels.
arxiv-2605-09997:
Wei and three colleagues built GraphInstruct, a gradual benchmark for finding skill gaps in LLM graph making. Graph data supports citation work, social networks, molecular design, and knowledge graphs, and LLMs now build graphs from prompts. Earlier benchmarks group by graph type or task domain. They average over shape detail and cannot pinpoint where in the hardness range a model breaks down.

It splits graph work into six complexity levels and five test angles, with 800 hand-written tasks, 1,582 built model answers, and a 12-model test across 45 model setups. Six findings emerged. Gap-spotting power peaks at multi-constraint combos rather than thought depth. No prompting trick wins across the board. Domain-meaning rules remain repeat-proof, pointing to lookup rather than more compute. A check-guided repeat tool with constraint-aware prompting beat the prompt cap on tested target models.
arxiv-2605-10097:
Nishikawa and Kato demonstrate H-MAPS, a proactive search assistant for scientific reading that removes the need to stop and search by hand. Reading often demands outside sources, but manual keyword search breaks flow and loads memory, while existing proactive systems read only on-screen text and miss the reader's background and intent. H-MAPS resolves that ambiguity with a three-layer hierarchical memory.

Triggered by implicit reading behaviour, the system turns hidden information needs into explicit natural-language questions, then retrieves literature entirely on the local device, protecting privacy. In a demo scenario, two researchers, one in language processing and one in human-computer interaction, read the same paper and receive profile-specific questions plus distinct tailored literature. The work appeared at the 2026 SIGIR conference in Melbourne.
arxiv-2605-10197:
Pirzada and Li study controlled inflation from long monodromic valleys in the moduli penumbra, a string-theory setting where axion monodromy offers long paths. The key question is not field range alone. A long valley can fail if heavy-sector feedback, standard distance or lost slow change breaks single-clock control. Local branch data decide whether a valley supports controlled inflation.

In the axion-saxion working theory, a branch-shifting odd term creates a plateau when a parameter mix exceeds zero. Matching single-clock control demands power p below two, or p equal to two with a large ladder ratio. Before global completion is attempted, valleys split into three kinds: no plateau, uncontrolled plateau and controlled plateau. A minimal exact family with a closed-form valley and a fixed pull gives the first solvable penumbral case that stays true, promoting the penumbra from idea to forecasting principle.
arxiv-2605-10297:
Lei Chen and three colleagues tackle rain forecasts two to six weeks ahead, a horizon where chaos makes exact prediction impossible. Their 2026 paper introduces QuantWeather, a framework for subseasonal rain prediction. Instead of giving one rainfall number, it models the full range of likely outcomes.

Most systems express doubt through ensembles, many slightly varied runs, but raw ensemble output is often poorly tuned. QuantWeather uses a dual-head design, with chance-based and single-value heads trained on separate goals and tuned jointly. It can also sample by chance from a single forward pass. In tests it showed better chance-based skill while cutting run-time computing and storage costs by a lot.
arxiv-2605-10397:
Xi Jiang and three colleagues build a visual anomaly detector that argues with itself. Visual anomaly detection matters for industry, medicine, infrastructure, and remote sensing, yet each domain defines anomalies differently, so single-domain models transfer poorly. Vision-language models offer cross-domain perception, but single-inference judgments lean on prior knowledge over fine-grained evidence. Their 2026 paper presents AnomalyClaw, a training-free agent.

AnomalyClaw turns judgment into multi-round refutation. Each round puts forward candidate anomalies and tests each against normal-sample references, using a 13-tool library for visual verification, reference parsing, and frozen expert probing. On the CrossDomainVAD-12 benchmark of 12 datasets, it improved macro-AUROC over single-step direct inference by about 6 points on GPT-5, about 8 points on Seed2-lite, and about 4 points on Qwen3-VL. An optional self-evolution extension, building an online rulebook from internal disagreement without oracle labels, added about 2 points on Qwen3-VL.
arxiv-2605-10597:
Isaac David and Arthur Gervais benchmark language model agents on binary reverse engineering. Coding benchmarks measure source software repair, and cybersecurity benchmarks measure capture-the-flag performance. But binary reverse engineering remains less specified: with only an executable in hand, can an agent work out the validation logic and build an input, serial, artifact, or key generator? Their 2026 paper introduces CrackMeBench.

CrackMeBench focuses on binary validation problems with oracles, symbol-poor binaries, local tool access, and scored submissions rather than explanations. The v0 benchmark combines eight calibration CrackMes with twelve generated tasks built from seeded C, Rust, and Go templates, run through a shell interface in a no-network Linux Docker sandbox. In a three-model evaluation, pass-at-3 on the generated split is 11 of 12 tasks for GPT-5.5, 7 of 12 for Claude Opus 4.7, and 5 of 12 for Kimi K2. The harder half separates models more sharply.
arxiv-2605-10797:
Kai Lion and four colleagues present Muown, a 2026 tweak to the Muon optimizer, a training method that rivals AdamW for preparing large language models. Muon training can let weight matrices drift upward in size, and the authors trace that drift to the size of matrix rows rather than to how aligned those rows are.

Muown treats the row-size vector as its own variable to control, while leaving Muon in charge of the remaining direction part. The authors prove it reaches the best known rates for rough, non-convex problems in both exact and noisy settings, with noise levels below Muon's in tests. Practitioners get a drop-in swap that steadies large-scale training without changing the rest of the recipe.
arxiv-2605-10997:
A. A. Arutyunov and A. V. Perelygin describe a wilder class of metrics on groups, the left-invariant improper metrics. Smith showed uniqueness up to coarse equivalence for proper left-invariant metrics, while improper metrics, whose finite balls may hold infinitely many group elements, had lacked a matching description.

Using bornological groups introduced by Tessera and Winkel, the pair maps these metrics and clears up bornological-group traits, including a test for when such a group can carry a metric. From the coarse-geometry viewpoint, classical left-invariance and its coarse cousin, bornologicity, turn out equivalent, and each coarse class of bornological metrics is fixed by a bornology. Group theorists get the missing improper half of the metric-classification picture.
arxiv-2605-11097:
A. E. Cárcamo Hernández and five colleagues propose a two-loop neutrino-mass model based on modular S4 flavor symmetry plus a discrete Z3 symmetry. After modular breaking, a leftover Z2 symmetry secures both the radiative origin of active neutrino masses and the long life of dark-matter candidates.

The model matches charged-lepton masses and neutrino oscillation data for normal ordering and predicts visible charged-lepton-flavor-violation rates. Singlet-doublet mixing gives a viable scalar dark-matter particle, while a fermionic option strongly linked to flavor violation also appears. Parameter regions matching relic density, flavor-violation limits, and direct-detection bounds give testable examples. Particle teams get a unified model tying neutrino mass, dark matter, and flavor violation together.
arxiv-2605-11397: Gyuhyun Lim studies test sets: families of sequences converging to a point that still detect every discontinuity of real-valued functions there. Under inclusion ordering, these test sets form a poset. Given natural hypotheses at the point, he proves the poset has a minimal element. He analyzes its maximal chains, showing some possess a least element while others lack one. On the sequential fan he gives a concrete case where his minimal test set is strictly smaller than the full family of convergent sequences.
arxiv-2605-11597: Chang and four others measure the interband Berry connection in the optical honeycomb lattice. Bloch band geometry shapes many crystal traits, yet direct measures stay an active research area. The team mimics electron response to light with ultracold fermionic atoms in shaken optical lattices. Excitation strength at each quasimomentum and shaking polarization maps the interband Berry connection straight. Between the ground band and excited bands 2, 3 and 4, the method reveals clear lines and Dirac strings linking K and K prime points where the connection flips direction.
arxiv-2605-11697: Nigatu and others present a motion-aware Rainbow system for joint Delta and 3-RRS robot fitting. A shape design stage tunes the 3-RRS shape to grow jam-free workspace, widening the safe search region. The arms expose a 6-degree-of-freedom subspace, with a five-dim task space skipping peg-axis spin. Fitting becomes a Markov choice process with a 12-dim state and 12 commands, trained with a shaped reward and plan. In sim it settles stably, inserts well and breaks less than vanilla DQN and an old planner.
arxiv-2605-11897: Milan Češka and four colleagues speed up optimal conditional reachability math in Markov decision processes. The standard reduction creates cyclic, hard-to-solve models. Their new method stays stable in numbers, decides thresholds in linear time on acyclic models, and matches standard reachability query speed. Built into an abstraction-refinement system, it checks millions of Markov chains at once, with speedups of multiple orders of magnitude on Bayesian network, probabilistic program, and runtime monitoring tests.
arxiv-2605-11997: Darlan Noetzold and three colleagues build a unified microservices platform for endpoint security and hate-speech risk alerting. Current tools handle data loss, productivity tracking, or hate-speech detection in isolation, delaying response. Their platform collects endpoint telemetry and applies predictive language models, routing events through RabbitMQ and serving data through Redis. Transformer models such as BERT reached 87 percent average accuracy on hate-speech risk, and the platform surfaced exfiltration and policy violations promptly.
arxiv-2605-12497: Yang and five colleagues study visual perception where the target must first be identified from outside facts before it can be found in pixels. They name the task Perception Deep Research and release WebEye, a benchmark with verifiable evidence, knowledge-heavy queries and precise box and mask labels across grounding, segmentation and question-answering views. The set holds 120 images, 473 object instances, 645 question pairs and 1,927 task samples. Their Pixel-Searcher agent searches the web to resolve hidden identities, then attaches them to boxes, masks or grounded answers.
arxiv-2605-12797: Mukherjee, Grayling and Wason study how outcome delay harms sample-size re-estimation in clinical trials. When recruitment continues while outcomes are awaited, long delays add pipeline participants who do not feed the interim analysis. That inflates the final sample size and power, raising cost. The team derives the final sample-size distribution under varied delays for continuous and binary outcomes, and assesses precision with RMSE plus two new metrics, delay impact and cost. Trials whose re-estimated size falls below the original plan suffer most, often ending overpowered.
arxiv-2605-12897: Kliniewski and four colleagues present DynoJEPP, a tool that jointly handles estimation, prediction and planning for robots in changing settings. Older joint tools let prediction and planning leak back into estimation, spoiling it and yielding unsafe plans. DynoJEPP adds a one-way link that blocks that leak, keeping estimates clean. Without it, the robot crashed in most tests; a team variant also folds in the moves of other moving objects.
arxiv-2605-12997: Xie and Luo test how neural operators that solve wave equations cope with shifts in their inputs. They compare the Fourier Neural Operator and DeepONet on a one-dimensional variable-coefficient wave equation, varying input frequency and coefficient smoothness separately. Smoothness shifts leave both models stable, with the Fourier model more accurate. Frequency shifts hurt the Fourier model sharply on unseen high frequencies, while DeepONet degrades more gently despite higher overall error.
arxiv-2605-13197: Wen and six co-authors present McCast, a memory-guided method for correcting drift in long-horizon precipitation nowcasting. Autoregressive nowcasting predicts states from past outputs, accumulating errors that drag forecasts off course. Rather than treating memory as a loose pile of states, McCast uses time-ordered memory to correct drift. A Drift-Corrective Memory Bank estimates corrections in two stages: an extractor predicts a correction, then a retrieval module refines it from historical memory. On SEVIR and MeteoNet it reaches state-of-the-art performance over long horizons.
arxiv-2605-13497: Xinye Wanyan and four colleagues propose APG4RecSim, a framework that builds user profiles for recommendation simulation. Simulated users help evaluate recommender systems in real time, yet most work lifts memory and action parts while user records are ignored. Hand-crafted records scale badly, since simulation datasets are scarce, so it builds realistic records with minimal human help. Tests on three benchmarks show it leads on discrimination, ranking and rating, lifting ranking quality by up to 7 percent and cutting rating divergence by 8 percent.
arxiv-2605-13697: Igor Nikolaevich Nikonorov, Maxim Vladimirovich Barkov and Maxim Lyutikov show the Guitar nebula is an exceptional bow-shock pulsar wind nebula. Particles escaping the nebula to form the X-ray kinetic jet must reach energies near the neutron star's maximal electric potential, marking it as an extreme accelerator. Exceptionally bright H-alpha emission requires the pulsar PSR J2225+6535 to pass through a dense low-ionisation interstellar region. The authors hypothesise the Guitar passes through a narrow dense shell of an old supernova remnant.
arxiv-2605-13897: Keshvarikhojasteh, Pluim and Veta join three kinds of patient data to guess how long a patient may live. Slides of tissue, RNA readouts and clinical notes each pass through their own encoders. A low-rank bilinear fusion step then joins the streams and models how pairs of data types combine. Risk scores from the model map to survival times through a Kaplan-Meier calibration step.
arxiv-2605-13997: Zhong, Zheng and Allen-Blanchette attack a snag in shrinking sparse mixture-of-experts layers without retraining. Three experts can pair well yet form a locked cycle when merged as a trio, so pair scores alone cannot tell which trios merge cleanly. The snag turns out to be a precise object, the harmonic kernel of the simplicial Laplacian on a 2-complex of experts, edges and faces. HodgeCover then greedily covers the harmonic-critical parts to pick merges.
arxiv-2605-14097: Parisi and four co-authors test language-model help in live group talks over charity donations. Two studies with 879 people in total put trios to work splitting a donation budget in real-time text chats with real money at stake, 7,200 dollars in all. Study one compares three frontier models as helpers, while study two compares helper strategies against no help. Help did not clearly lift group accord in either study, yet people still preferred helped chats.
arxiv-2605-14297: Alvo, Russo and Kanoria study reinforcement learning in hybrid action spaces, where discrete choices pick regimes. Standard policy gradient methods use score-function estimators with severe credit-assignment issues in high dimensions. Differentiable simulation sidesteps these issues by backpropagating. Hybrid Policy Optimization backpropagates through the simulator where smoothness permits, using a mixed estimator of pathwise and score-function gradients, keeping unbiasedness. HPO clearly beats PPO on inventory control and switched regulator problems, with gaps growing with continuous dimension. The mixed gradient's cross term becomes negligible near a discrete best response.
arxiv-2605-14897: Deproost and team introduce Critic-Driven Voronoi State Partitioning for distilling deep reinforcement learning policies into clear models. Traditional distillation minimises only behaviour distance between original and surrogate policies. The new method partitions a black-box policy into regions where a simple model class is optimised. The critic value network guides iterative introduction of new subpolicies in regions with insufficient value. Nearest-neighbour lookups assign a linear function to each point, yielding a cell diagram, with distillation claimed to approach the original using a modest set of linear maps.
arxiv-2605-15297: Pedro L. S. Lopes studies the Optimistic Quantum Fourier Transform under a surface-code fault-tolerant model for reconfigurable neutral-atom hardware. The transform's reliance on phase-gradient resources and small blocks demands mobile resources and parallel execution. His hot-zone architecture separates data storage from processing and sends magic-state factories, link qubits, and phase-gradient registers toward fixed data. Two hot zones match serial transform latency, four roughly halve runtime, and more zones approach constant time at steep cost.
arxiv-2605-15397: Kangning Cui and fourteen colleagues introduce ELDOR, a drone-based benchmark for tracking illegal gold mining in the Amazon rainforest. It covers over 2,500 hectares of annotated aerial imagery with pixel-level labels for mining activity and surrounding ecology. Four tasks test segmentation, recognition, classification, and vision-language understanding, and current methods still struggle with small, rare mining structures and fine recovery classes. An interactive explorer lets domain experts browse the data and run models.
arxiv-2605-15597: Jiale Liu and fourteen colleagues ask how to turn 3D assets into sparse panoramic RGB-D-pose data with full scene cover. Their COVER curator casts geometry from picked views into candidate panoramas. It scores added cover and docks depth clashes. Greedy picks keep standard cover-style approximation conduct. The CM-EVS set built this way holds 36,373 panoramic frames from 1,275 indoor scenes, plus outdoor panoramas in one schema. It spans all thirteen room types with a median of just 25 frames per indoor scene.
arxiv-2605-15897: Vladislav Dodon and four colleagues seek causes behind the boost and break of magnetic braking in CVs. Modeling binary change with MESA, they compute turnover span straight from donor structure rather than set rules. They add irradiation from the feeding white dwarf that heats outer layers and drives extra winds. That span spikes as the donor nears full convection, driving the break parameter and starting the period gap. Plausible rates let light-driven winds supply the needed boost, yielding tracks in line with observed traits.
arxiv-2605-16097: Zhou, Bode, and Hunt formalize cooperative transport, where teams of robots must jointly carry large items that no single agent can move. Existing path-finding frameworks lack true cooperation for such loads. They present an optimal solver with an incremental expansion strategy and a family of faster sub-optimal solvers. Tests show the expansion strategy prunes the search space sharply, while the sub-optimal solvers set a new quality-versus-speed frontier.
arxiv-2605-16197: Gutoreva, Tsim, and Papakonstantinou argue that AI safety and alignment must grow from co-regulation of the human-AI mind system as a whole, not from curbing an outside tool. AI now shapes attention, reasoning, synthesis, and choices before conscious thought, forming one linked unit with its users. Loose delegation risks deskilling, automation bias, transfer of epistemic authority, and oracle-style centralization of knowledge. The authors close with design rules for joint regulation aimed at engineers and governance bodies.
arxiv-2605-16297: Li and Ye ask which tasks inside an enterprise workflow a language-model agent can reliably handle, and under what conditions. Most frameworks judge at the activity level, though one activity can bundle work of very different difficulty. Their T-IPO model represents each task as an eight-element tuple, and their LARA rubric scores readiness across five dimensions, with compliance sensitivity weighted 1.5-fold. Tested on 127 tasks, inter-rater agreement reached kappa 0.80, and pilot deployment showed auto-completion falling from 95 percent at level one to about 40 percent at level three.
arxiv-2605-16397: Papanikolaou and four others build adaptive run-time processing for sea object detection, adding GPS track data to a YOLOv8-based model. Frames where vessels sit close together and converge fast get full-model processing, while other frames activate only part of the network. Scene difficulty is judged from inter-vessel distance and how fast that distance shrinks. The strategy maintains detection performance while cutting run time and compute cost, enabling a flexible accuracy-cost balance versus full-model inference.
arxiv-2605-16697: Wald examines ordered front-to-back any-hit traversal, a ray-tracing task that lists every hit along a ray in strict front-to-back order, even hits at the same distance. He describes several ways to solve it within the limits of the existing ray-tracing pipeline. He then evaluates those realizations against one another. The focus is guaranteeing order and completeness, not skipping hits.
arxiv-2605-16997: Zhang, Soe and Xu prove a weak solution exists for the 3D Beris-Edwards system in whole space under stable bulk conditions. The solution meets natural bounds, the distributional form of the equations, and an expanded Leray-Hopf-type energy inequality for weak-strong uniqueness. The proof avoids a direct limit in that expanded inequality, where non-corotational terms hold fourth powers. It first secures the physical free-energy inequality via hyperviscous approximation and a localised tail estimate, then derives it from a low-order chain rule for bulk energy.
arxiv-2605-17097: Belli and López classify surfaces in Sol, a three-dimensional solvable group, that hold their shape under Gauss curvature flow. They study flows tied to three symmetry directions: two shifts and one stretch. For stretch-invariant surfaces, they prove only certain flat vertical planes can be shift-flow solitons. For shift-invariant surfaces, they map the main traits of the remaining flows, both in outer shape and inner curvature.
arxiv-2605-17197: Le, Karimi and Rahnemoonfar propose OPTNet, a point transformer for segmenting post-disaster 3D scenes that learns how to order points instead of relying on fixed curves. A self-supervised sorter predicts the permutation that best preserves locality for attention, replacing costly neighbor searches and sampling. On the 3DAeroRelief dataset it beats leading baselines by a clear margin, the authors report.
arxiv-2605-17797: Chen-Rong Liu and seven colleagues propose granularity noise thermometry, a way to read temperature from light noise. The method exploits flickers in susceptibility caused by atoms being discrete, not smooth. Transmitted light shows excess noise above the shot-noise limit that grows linearly with the photon-to-atom ratio. Varying incident power yields the slope of that line, which encodes temperature directly. Closed-form results give distinct scalings for hot vapors and cold atoms, offering a noise-based route to optical thermometry with atomic ensembles.
arxiv-2605-17997: Le Su and two colleagues propose Module-Adaptive Residual Reconstruction for low-bit quantization. Residual methods add residuals to cut error from prior layers, but these can also add Hessian-approximation bias. The team shows a scaling factor on the residual term cuts this bias while keeping error correction, with module-dependent trade-offs. MARR gives each module a scaling factor to balance correction and bias, using a PID update rule with reconstruction error as feedback. Tests on language models and vision transformers show gains up to 20.2% and 4.6% respectively.
arxiv-2605-18197: Giorgia Modi's 2026 paper builds 3D scene graphs for indoor robots from RGB images alone, with no depth sensor. Perception and planning share one structured view holding object meanings, 3D geometry, relations, and multi-view evidence. On the Replica set the RGB-only pipeline matches depth-based baselines on F1 score. Active viewpoint choice on ReplicaCAD spots over double the objects of a geometric frontier baseline under the same budget. Added outside views bootstrap the graph at no extra exploration cost.
arxiv-2605-18497: Francesco Colasanto and three co-authors establish, in a 2026 paper, sharp convergence rates for empirical estimation of probability measures. They use maximum mean discrepancy with power kernels. For Ahlfors-regular measures they prove a two-sided bound decaying as N to the minus one half times one plus q over beta. The bound holds both for the worst-case N-point measure and for an optimally chosen one. The result adds quantitative rates to an earlier qualitative consistency result for energy-distance minimizers.
arxiv-2605-18597: Wenhao Huang and thirteen co-authors present Latent Action Reparameterization, a 2026 system learning a compact latent action space for language-model agents. Each latent action stands for a multi-step semantic behavior, shortening decision horizons while preserving expressiveness. Unlike hand-crafted macros, latent actions learn from agent trajectories and integrate directly into the model. Across agent benchmarks it cuts action tokens and wall-clock inference time while holding or improving success rates.
arxiv-2605-18797: Rao Fu and six colleagues stabilize the Looped Transformer, which reuses the same blocks to gain power without adding weights. Reuse lets users trade compute for quality at test time, but training grows unstable as loop counts rise. The authors trace the trouble to gradient swings and residual growth. Their Fully Looped Transformer spreads signals across all layers and reuses attention to damp swings, with no new weights. Training then stays stable at higher loop counts.
arxiv-2605-18897: Tien-Dat Pham and Xuan-The Tran reconstruct intracranial brain signals from scalp recordings for patients the model has never seen. Intracranial EEG is rich but needs surgery, and patient-specific models defeat the purpose of avoiding it. Their CAST transformer extracts multi-scale temporal features, then calibrates a channel-aware decoder from just minutes of the new patient's data.
