Tested on two datasets with over 1200 channels, it recovers surface signals best, near 0.86 correlation in motor areas, and beats prior baselines on viable subjects.
arxiv-2605-19097: Subhash Chandra studies the shape traits of graph-directed iterated function systems made from injective contractions. In general, two different attractors of this kind sharing one graph need not be equivalent in the bi-Lipschitz sense. Under the right conditions, however, he proves they do match, and he builds a Lipschitz map between two such attractors that runs both ways. Two attractors on one graph can thus differ in kind yet still match.
arxiv-2605-19297: Chengliang Xia, Jiale Chen, Hongquan Liu, and Hanghui Chen map a route to bulk superconductivity in a nickelate at ordinary pressure. Related nickelates only superconduct under high pressure or strained films, blocking key measurements such as heat capacity. Combining three standard theory tools, they show hole doping grows a pocket on the Fermi surface that turns diamond-shaped near one doping level. Its near-perfect nesting then boosts magnetic fluctuations enough that superconductivity should become observable without pressure or strain.
arxiv-2605-19597: Zhang and team introduce HyperLogic, a pipeline for Chinese logical reasoning benchmarks separating authoring from answer generation. A multi-agent workflow hardens undergraduate seeds without solving them. Then two agents from different families independently encode each item as an executable finite-domain model, with solver answers adjudicated by human experts. Base holds 195 items and 922 sub-questions separating seven models by 33 points, while Hard holds 100 items no model tops 16 percent. Tool access lifts every model; a logic modeling library helps five but hurts two.
arxiv-2605-19697: Marqué and team present SPADE, a compact phased array spectrograph monitoring solar activity in the decameter range, where most bursts interest solar physics and space weather. Unlike other phased arrays, Sun tracking and spectra production run entirely digitally, using open-source and generic software-defined radio receivers. The paper describes the instrument and software and presents first Sun and Jovian observations from September to December 2024. Solar results highlight temporal and frequency resolution for coronal turbulence and radio-wave propagation effects, topics otherwise open only to larger phased arrays.
arxiv-2605-19797: Kocur and colleagues offer Depth2Pose, a way to judge single image depth estimators by downstream usefulness instead of raw depth error. Depth predictions feed geometric solvers alongside feature matches, and camera pose accuracy becomes the proxy for depth quality. Only camera poses are needed, rather than costly dense ground truth. Their D2P dataset adds hard scenes outside common training distributions. Methods strong on standard error metrics also score well on pose metrics, but do not always carry over to harder scenes.
arxiv-2605-20197: Zhichao Yang and three co-workers present MedicalBench, a test for medical concept extraction with evidence grounding. It uses MIMIC-IV discharge notes and human-checked ICD-10 codes, framing extraction as checking note-concept pairs plus sentence-level evidence lookup. It includes implicit positives, tricky negatives, and cases where model calls disagree with expert judgments. Testing top models shows modest scores, largely flat across note lengths, showing the test taps reasoning skill rather than surface factors.
arxiv-2605-20297: Ziyuan Gao sets out MedCRP-CL, learning medical image segmentation continually from mixed sources, where one rule set breeds forgetting in clashes. Fixed groups miss new tasks, so tasks group from clinical prompt words by Chinese Restaurant Process, sans set count or peek ahead. Semantic modalities sort by body part and disease state, finer-grained. Groups get LoRA adapters held by intra-modality EWC: unlike groups apart, like groups shared. On 16 tasks in 4 scan types: 73.3% Dice, 4.1% forgetting, 8.0% past rival, 6x fewer weights, storing only stats, never scans.
arxiv-2605-20397: MacMahon asks whether a group's first L2 Betti number can only stay flat or rise when the group sits inside another via logic-based maps. For proper non-abelian subgroups of torsion-free hyperbolic groups, he shows elementary maps force a strict rise, drawing on Perin's account of such inclusions. He also shows the flat-or-rise pattern for existential maps between any finitely generated groups. The strict case is thus special to the hyperbolic elementary setting, while the wider pattern is mere non-decrease.
arxiv-2605-20497: Marco Ronzani and Cristina Silvano offer a graphics-processor method for splitting hypergraphs. In a hypergraph, one link can join many points at once. Their multi-level scheme caps partition size and keeps each partition's incoming links distinct. It also stores link patterns and pairing scores in fast shared memory, running on average 380 times faster than a step-by-step rival.
arxiv-2605-20797: Yiliang Yuan, Xiang Shi, and Mustafa Misir pick solvers for black-box optimization from contour plots rather than number features alone. Prior work leans on landscape descriptors and learned codes, but this paper studies contour-map views of probed landscapes as a second view. A convolutional regressor takes several instance-specific contour views and predicts each solver's performance, enabling selection by predicted best value. On the BBOB 2009 protocol, their picks beat the single best solver and rival feature-based baselines.
arxiv-2605-21097: Murrough Foley introduces the Web Content Extraction Benchmark, a multi-type benchmark for web content extraction. Web content extraction, isolating a page's core content from surrounding boilerplate, is a must for search listing, retrieval-augmented generation, NLP dataset building, and large language model training. Progress has been constrained by limitations of old benchmarks, which are small at 100 to 800 pages, limited to news articles, stories built on web pages from over a decade back. WCXB holds 2,008 limited pages from 1,stories domains spanning seven structurally distinct page types, a back set.
arxiv-2605-21397: Ramesh Raghavan and co-authors present a method for validating navmeshes using geometry, with voxel-based analysis and prioritized exploration. Navmesh flaws break pathing for non-playable characters in game worlds. Navmeshes are built from world geometry, but terrain edits and moved assets during development create mismatches with the actual world. Existing automated checks rely on exploration agents and reinforcement learning, using navmesh data itself or judging behavior indirectly. The new method instead checks on its own whether the navmesh reflects walkable space defined by underlying geometry.
arxiv-2605-21497: Youness Bouchari and co-authors revisit claims about autonomous language-model agents in Capture-the-Flag challenges. Recent studies report near human-level success for agents automating offensive security tasks. The authors engineer agent designs of increasing complexity on thirty web-based challenges. These span fourteen vulnerability classes. They test them against claude-code, a general-purpose agent solving nineteen of thirty tasks, suggesting general-purpose agents are strong baselines.
arxiv-2605-21597: Victor Vanthilt and co-authors present a matrix product operator encoding of the Magnus expansion and the Dyson series. It covers one-dimensional quantum lattice models with time-dependent Hamiltonians. The construction stays accurate to any order in the time step, works for finite and infinite systems, and handles long-range interactions. Combined with matrix product state evolution methods, it sharply improves simulation of such systems, and it can also tune quantum circuits for them.
arxiv-2605-22097: Farah Elnakhal and co-authors present Q-PhotoNAS, a hybrid quantum neural architecture search framework for photonic devices. Quantum computing on light promises scalable quantum machine learning. But designing hybrids is hard under hardware and tuning limits, and manual designs miss the teamwork between classical preprocessing, phase codes, and circuit structure. Q-PhotoNAS automates that search, and analysis shows the photonic layer extracts fresh features orthogonal to the classical path, giving a clear accuracy edge over non-quantum baselines. Auto search thus proves useful for such hybrid systems.
arxiv-2605-22397: Zhao and colleagues determine the exact Turán number for blow-ups of the 3-uniform hypergraph F5. Balogh, Clemen and Luo handled the f5 blow-up; the team handles the f3 blow-up to t vertices. That case also yields exponentially many extremal constructions. The authors also bound every blow-up of F5 from above and below. For t disjoint copies of F5, they also determine the exact number. They also find the exact number for F_sim(t), whose extremal construction is not the Turán hypergraph.
arxiv-2605-22597: Wang and team propose MoSA, a stress tuning model for real-sim motion learning. Sim tuning is bounded by uniform and even model guesses. After tuning, rest effects choke the real-sim gap. Neural networks fit motion straight, but discard real priors. MoSA uses an even model as prior and learns rest stress tools. It adapts stresses via micro rework in a cascade. Motion constraints guide time and spatial slopes. Learned motion achieves better hits and toughness, with real anisotropy. MoSA is tested in robot handling.
arxiv-2605-22797: Hong and Schotland study single photon transmission through atomic media, measuring information loss by quantum channel fidelity. They find normalized fidelity falls steadily as coupling strength rises, setting a performance limit for quantum communication through such media. The result holds across several channel types and for both deterministic and random media, giving a compact limit on how much quantum signal survives passage through atoms.
arxiv-2605-22897: Rezaei and Krishnan introduce Multi-Agent Residual In-Context Learning, a framework in which language model agents study where a base model fails and hypothesize what structure it misses. Agents draft explicit correction terms from high-residual examples and refine them through multi-turn textual gradient steps. Across nine scientific, biomedical, socioeconomic, and synthetic benchmarks it improved on its base model every time. Frozen formulas transferred within one lab protocol in over 92 percent of cases.
arxiv-2605-23097: Zhou and Uribe study signed Fréchet fits on complete Riemannian manifolds with bounded curvature. It extends linear fits to values in metric spaces via weighted sums. Mixed sign weights make a signed barycenter problem. Missing geodesic convexity and rough squared gaps near cut loci complicate it. Working inside a strongly convex normal ball gives FRIDA, a proximal DC method, with proofs of minimizer existence, descent, convergence, and sublinear complexity.
arxiv-2605-23497: Prior, Schultz, and Grabmair diagnose temporal failure modes in LLM-based statutory question answering, where fixed training cutoffs clash with evolving law. Models may apply superseded rules after amendments, or favor newer provisions when an older version governs. Their benchmark holds 312 expert-checked, time-sensitive German statutory questions across three categories. Five models from OpenAI, Anthropic, and DeepSeek degrade sharply in the plain post-cutoff setting. Retrieval methods that enforce temporal validity through date extraction and version filtering improve results across all question types.
arxiv-2605-23597: Chourasia, Kapoor, and Patil tackle person-name matching across messy records, a core entity resolution problem made harder by varied naming customs, inconsistent transliteration, and frequent entry errors. Their structure-guided entity resolution framework fine-tunes a language model in two phases: first parsing name grammar and meaning, then optimizing binary entity matching. On Indian identity data, it hits 99.02 percent accuracy and 0.994 F1 on 50000 held-out pairs, beating GPT-4o few-shot prompting and single-stage fine-tuning. It now runs in production at Dream11, serving over 250 million users.
arxiv-2605-23797: Bo Peng and colleagues improve how pretrained vision language models spot inputs from unknown classes. Current methods mine negative labels, labels unlike the known ones, from wild text by rough rules, and false negatives blunt their power. The team builds a theory that corrects the sampling bias of those negatives and turns the correction into Monte Carlo sampling from known labels plus wild text. Tests across varied setups set a new best mark, with code released openly.
arxiv-2605-23897: Beichen Zhang and colleagues argue that text only reasoning chains bottleneck multimodal models on tasks needing close looks or changed viewpoints. Their ETCHR pairs a dedicated image editor with the understanding model, keeping the two decoupled. The recipe has two stages: first imitating reasoning edit trajectories, then refining with rewards for edit correctness and downstream accuracy. Because editor and reasoner stay separate, ETCHR plugs into open and closed models without retraining them. It lifts average scores by roughly five points across five task families and three host models.
arxiv-2605-24197: Ye and six co-authors examine agentic misalignment in automated multi-agent workflows, where agents chase implicit proxy utilities that drift from human goals. In a Bayesian frame, the authors show generic utilities naturally collapse agent posteriors in such workflows. They propose Agentic Evidence Attribution, which reasons over agent actions and supplies structured evidence to correct misaligned behaviour during collaboration. Two forms are studied: self-reflection from internal evidence and weak-to-strong generalization from outside evidence. A small evidence model aligns the system well by attributing failures orthogonally.
arxiv-2605-24597: Andreas Opedal and colleagues frame natural-language inference as search, where the final answer is a valid proof with correct intermediate steps. They test whether models can learn correct, efficient proofs guided by A* search, an algorithm guaranteeing the most efficient path to a goal. Two training methods are tried: supervised fine-tuning on A* execution traces and reinforcement learning with A*-informed rewards. Small Llama-3.2 models jump from near-zero accuracy to beating much larger DeepSeek-V3.2. A* signals balance accuracy with efficiency better than correctness rewards.
arxiv-2605-24697: Bohang Sun and others frame a control problem in diffusion language models: which tokens to commit at each step. Frozen decoders rely on hand-set confidence rules. The authors instead learn commitment as a policy. Their TraceLock controller is a light plug-in for a frozen backbone. With no oracle commit times, it labels a proposal stable when it matches the final token. Once trained, it serves across widths, lengths, and step budgets without retraining. Tests on question answering, math, and code show a better quality-step trade.
arxiv-2605-24797: Jie-En Yao and co-authors improve the Forward-Forward algorithm with hierarchical and contrastive learning. Backpropagation-trained networks perform well in vision but remain biologically implausible, costly, and hard to interpret. Forward-Forward trains each layer alone through local goodness objectives, yet lacks cross-layer coordination. Their HCL-FF framework adds a coarse-to-fine hierarchy guiding features from basic cues to rich meaning, plus a contrastive objective for class alignment. On CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet it sets new Forward-Forward records, up 5.46 percent on CIFAR-10.
arxiv-2605-24997: Päivo Simson derives a one-way model of deep-water surface gravity waves with real numbers. A canonical transformation removes cubic interactions, leaving a two-way system like the 1D Zakharov equation. The linear motion factors exactly to isolate the rightward branch. It runs to second order in wave steepness as one nonlocal model keeping full linear dispersion. A multiple-scales study gives the Dysthe envelope equation with its nonlocal mean-flow term. Exact breather waves match those of the super compact equation closely.
arxiv-2605-25497: Bidyut Hazarika, Mozib Bin Awal, and Prabwal Phukon treat black-hole thermodynamic criticality as a dynamical system. They build a landscape where black holes settle toward equilibrium fixed points, governed by a flow parameter tau read as a model relaxation time. Near critical points the flow simplifies into universal forms, grouping black holes into universality classes by critical traits. The analysis also shows slowing down, with relaxation timescales set fully by local bifurcation structure.
arxiv-2605-25697: Ikeda and colleagues present the first SACLA platform in Japan joining a high-power optical laser, an X-ray free-electron laser probe, and an external magnetic field. A 2 kV, 4.8 kJ pulsed power system drives up to 10 kA through a split-pair coil, producing a 10 T field. The laser creates extreme-pressure, extreme-temperature matter, the X-ray laser probes it, and the field syncs with both in vacuum. The platform opens studies of shock waves, instability growth and turbulent plasma motion in strong magnetic fields.
arxiv-2605-25897: Lando and Tedesco introduce a smoothing transform for empirical distributions, the data-based stand-ins for unknown probability laws. The transform spreads equal mass over a chosen number of estimated expected order statistics, which act as a resolution dial. Its distance from a fixed target stays bounded by the classic estimation error, in both Wasserstein and integral metrics. Every linear functional of the new distribution matches one of the old distribution with updated weights. The authors prove convergence, limit laws for distance functionals, and bootstrap validity.
arxiv-2605-26197: Alexandre Araújo and Adriana Valio study how starspots and magnetic activity vary as stars spin. Their 2026 study uses brightness records from the Kepler telescope for more than 1,300 stars. Planet-hosting stars show stronger and more scattered rotational signals than stars without known planets, and their signals split into two distinct groups. The two groups point to steady, long-lived active regions on one side and fast-changing activity on the other, suggesting planets may shape stellar magnetic activity over time.
arxiv-2605-26297: Yichao Yuan and three colleagues' 2026 study characterizes agentic AI workloads, where language models run stateful multi-turn jobs that call tools and grow context. Tracing ReAct-style agents on five benchmarks, they find these jobs are not just long-prompt jobs. Cached context makes most input tokens reusable, so execution is decode-dominated. Efficient serving must therefore manage repeated model re-entry, persistent cache state, and shifting tool behavior together.
arxiv-2605-26397: Naba Rizvi and four colleagues probe how safety tuning warps language models asked to rewrite autistic speech. Ten models recast real autistic discourse from an autistic or a neurotypical persona. Autistic-persona rewrites drift far more in word choice and emotional tone, though meaning stays close, and most models collapse both personas into near-identical text. A multi-agent review finds wholesale erasure, stock stereotypes, and evasive meta-talk, clustered by tuning style rather than size. Autistic annotators often reverse the models' labels.
arxiv-2605-26697: Bruzzese builds a theory for tracking and fixing matrix-valued geometric errors in time-bin photonic qudits, quantum units that store data in photon arrival times. When the stored space itself moves, rather than a set of lone rays, the error takes the form of a non-Abelian holonomy. He builds an estimator from overlaps between frames in sequence, proves it behaves well under frame changes, and adds feed-forward rules to strip the error out. Synthetic tests confirm the method works and the fixes hold.
arxiv-2605-26797: Huang and ten colleagues study the Latent Recurrent Transformer, which reuses a high-level hidden state from the prior token as memory for the next token. To train this recurrence without unrolling full sequences, they introduce interleaved parallel training, mixing one full-sequence pass with parallel refinement of position subsets. Across 1.3B- and 2.1B-parameter backbones, the design improves bits-per-byte and CORE scores at matched compute, beats two-forward PonderLM-2, and matches a three-loop transformer at one forward per token.
arxiv-2605-27297: Aprile and colleagues describe nematic disclination loops with Clifford algebra, capturing the local defect profile and its holonomy along each loop. Simulations show loops nucleate growing blobs of defects that later fade, leaving uniform textures. Self-twist in a profile spawns extra linking lines, while loops with an even number of profile switches thread without linking.
arxiv-2605-27697: Jinhao Liang, Sven Koenig, and Ferdinando Fioretto present Simulation-Informed Diffusion for decentralized robot motion planning. Their system first predicts neighbors' future paths from current sightings, then plans each robot's own path under safety limits set by those forecasts. Good neighbor prediction cuts communication, starting coordination only when congestion demands it, and the method scales to 108 robots and 160 obstacles.
arxiv-2605-27897: Yuan and colleagues build new super integrable systems on a color Lie algebra, a symmetry framework with extra grading. From two spectral problems with matrices in that algebra, they form systems in one and two space dimensions. A supertrace identity then yields the super Hamiltonian structures that govern each system.
arxiv-2605-27997: Himanshu Beniwal and Mayank Singh locate where toxicity lives inside language models, then suppress it without retraining. Their two frameworks trace toxic behavior to specific layers and neurons, chiefly early MLP layers, and dampen them during inference or with tiny weight edits. Across five models, toxicity fell while language quality held.
arxiv-2605-28497: J. Olivares Carvajal and twelve colleagues measure iron and alpha-element abundances for RR Lyrae stars in Baade's Window. From spectra of 78 stars they fit metallicity and alpha abundance, taking distances from a period-luminosity-metallicity relation and orbits from velocities and Gaia motions. Most bulge RR Lyrae prove metal-poor with fairly high alpha values, while a few metal-richer, low-alpha stars look younger and disk-like. Their measures benchmark photometric methods from light-curve Fourier parameters, with a metallicity-alpha link still to probe.
arxiv-2605-28697: Thierry Judge and fifteen colleagues ask whether physics simulation can solve strain estimation for heart scans. Speckle tracking is the clinical standard for heart-muscle strain, but local scores lag despite its value, and deep learning lacks reliable motion guides. Their plan adds speckle fading readings from videos and step by step refines motion realism, making a true-to-life dataset of 1,478 videos with guide motion. The trained motion method beats guides on global and local strain, with length strain variability of 1.42 percent, topping the clinic reference.
arxiv-2605-28897: Hans Ole Hatzel, Sebastian Steindl, and Jan Strich test how well LLM reviews align with human reviews and how gameable they are. On papers from the 2025 ACL Rolling Review, they find only narrow alignment of LLM reviews with human ones, varying substantially across prompts and models. They then study an iterative draft-revise workflow where an author improves a submission per the LLM review. This gaming proves effective in specific scenarios, lifting overall scores significantly for up to 35 percent of papers. They publish their Review Arcade code.
arxiv-2605-29097: Jiachen Lu, Hailan Shanbhag, and Haitham Al Hassanieh present GeRaF, the first neural method for rebuilding near-range 3D shape from radio signals. Unlike cameras or LiDAR, radio sensing sees past blocks in view, yet its lens-free images are coarse and noisy. GeRaF filters out stray signals, runs physics-based volumetric rendering, and samples the full space with a lens-free blending plan. By learning distance fields, reflectivity, and signal power, it takes a first step toward millimeter-scale shape recovery from radio data.
arxiv-2605-29497: Santanu Das, Sagnik Chatterjee, and Jatin Batra study robust learning of Gaussian single-index models under heavy-tailed noise and adversarial corruption. Earlier methods cover linear regression, strictly monotonic links, and phase retrieval, but fail for generic non-monotonic links like GeLU and Swish. The authors give a first robust recovery method with near-linear sample and time costs for such links. Their key finding is a constant-radius convex basin around the truth, independent of dimension and reachable by robust spectral initialization despite contamination.
arxiv-2605-29597: S. Elkady and four colleagues split spin pumping from two-magnon scattering in the Gilbert damping of yttrium iron garnet and V pairs. Broadband FMR data across garnet thickness show the damping boost cannot be blamed on spin pumping alone, with two-magnon scattering leading at tiny scales. A model splitting both parts shows missing it swells spin pumping and lifts the effective spin-mixing conductance to absurd values. Taking the inner part yields a thickness-independent value of 1.33 × 10^18 per square meter, giving a basis for spin-transport numbers.
arxiv-2605-29897: Christoph Leiter and six colleagues introduce ExCAM, the first metric for cultural awareness in free text. Cultural awareness matters for fairness and global use, yet building benchmarks needs costly annotation, and free-text cultural evaluation remains scarce. To train ExCAM they build ExCAM40k from nine benchmarks with synthetic errors. Against baselines, including a top model, ExCAM beats them on error detection, reaching eighty percent accuracy on a test set. The metric finds cultural errors in instruction-output pairs, scoring and explaining them, opening fine-grained cultural evaluation.
arxiv-2605-30097: Andrea Albano and Paola Stefanelli answer a question from the 2025 Oberwolfach mini-workshop on the Yang-Baxter equation and braid group representations in the negative. They show skew brace varieties lack action accessibility, via the categorical notion of centralizer in Huq's sense and split extension classifiers. Given the close ties between skew braces and post-Lie algebras, they prove an analogous result for post-Lie algebras over a fixed field. The paper thus closes off one hoped-for categorical property for both varieties.
arxiv-2605-30197: Anton Arnold and Stefan Egger connect hypocoercivity and hypocontractivity for theta-methods, the family of time discretizations beyond the midpoint rule. Earlier work showed hypocoercivity properties, including exponential decay and sharp short-time decay of propagator norms, carry over to midpoint discretizations. For theta above one half, they show any implicit discretization of a hypocoercive evolution equation is contractive, not merely hypocontractive, unlike the midpoint rule. For coercive equations, discretizations with theta below one half are contractive for small enough time steps.
arxiv-2605-30297: Shi-Cong Mo and Wéi Wú investigate electron doping in nickelate La3Ni2O7 thin films through tetravalent swaps, using first-principles density-functional theory. Prior studies focused on hole doping, leaving the electron-doped regime untouched. Cerium doping adds few electron carriers into bands, while zirconium, hafnium and thorium are strong electron donors. Zirconium and hafnium doping feed one-orbital bands, while thorium doping sends more electrons into other-orbital bands. Electron doping augments interlayer hopping, which could enhance superexchange coupling and promote higher Tc.
arxiv-2605-30597: Poorna and Cicerone present ScaleMAP, a method for low-dimensional embeddings that preserves local density and neighborhood structure. Reducers normalize local distances, erasing scale, so bridges between cell types and narrow spectral spikes can vanish. DensMAP's density penalty fights attraction and repulsion forces and scatters points. ScaleMAP instead divides each embedding step by the geometric mean of the endpoints' local radii, re-injecting scale as a change of variables. It matches DensMAP on density while keeping UMAP-level layouts, recovering bridges that UMAP collapses.
arxiv-2605-30997: Wegel and colleagues learn new tasks from few samples by exploiting benchmark scores on related tasks. They observe weak monotonicity: a model dominating rivals on many benchmarks tends to win on the new task too. Under approximate weak monotonicity, they prune the model class and adapt to the trade-off geometry by hedging on the frontier, within both transfer learning and model-selection aggregation. The framework turns benchmark evaluations into provable gains for few-sample learning.
arxiv-2605-31097: Lou and colleagues ask whether a database can be built with a workload-matched feature set. They present SpecDB, using language models to make stores. From nine systems, they split them into ten modules, each with variants, yielding a link graph. SpecDB builds modules via chain, each built and joined by an agent, with a refiner fixing the store. A picker turns briefs into variants, giving a chain to a store. On TPC-C, the database passes tests with zero errors, reaching matching throughput at three percent of code size.
arxiv-2605-31197: Batista and colleagues probe surface polarity in tellurium with quantum-geometric transport. In this crystal, lone electron pairs drive local polarity, yet their joint effect hides behind symmetry or stays at surfaces. That surface effect shifts the centre of travelling electron packets and corrects their speed. A small three-part lattice model captures it in full. Linear and nonlinear transport readings reveal different moments of the net field. Voltages in tellurium flakes track the surface effect, so the work points toward new quantum devices driven by polarity.
arxiv-2605-31397: Borza, Pinamonti, and Zoghlami study surfaces of constant horizontal mean curvature in the sub-Lorentzian Heisenberg group. They work out how area changes under radial shifts that keep volume fixed. From this, smooth least-area candidates must have that same curvature outside the singular set. The authors sort all smooth boost-symmetric cases by those sets, causal type, and symmetry classes. They single out a family of smooth acausal surfaces they think are the best.
arxiv-2605-31497: Exoo, Bietti, and Sous study how small transformers compose skills, using variable assignment plus modular addition. By splitting training data into disjoint sets, they observe the models generalize to unseen pairings of variables and numbers. Mechanistic analysis shows the same modular-addition module serves both direct inputs and inputs routed through a separate assignment mechanism. Training runs in three phases: modular addition first, then assignment structure, then refinement that generalizes to hard unseen sequences.
arxiv-2605-31597: Dünkel and team present SOCO, a benchmark for semantic object correspondence. Semantic correspondence tests if object parts match across instances and categories despite varied looks and viewpoints. SOCO gives consistent keypoint annotations across 100 categories. It also includes language descriptions to test vision-language models. Tests reveal vision backbones encode strong meaning structure yet transfer matches poorly across kinds. Vision-language models beat visual matching on text-prompted part finding, and match performance predicts downstream scores more strongly than ImageNet scores.
arxiv-2606-00097:
Pak and colleagues let an AI agent design, build, and fly high-powered rockets in this 2026 arXiv paper on RocketSmith. The system uses a language model to orchestrate tools for design-for-additive-manufacturing, shaping parts for 3D printing. Subagents check flight stability and generate parametric parts for the rocket assembly, iterating on flight settings with or without a human in the loop. Four rockets with different motors and assemblies came out of the workflow.

The components were printed on fused-deposition machines, checked by hand for flight readiness, and launched at an event. All four rockets achieved launches, and two were recovered in condition to fly again. Altimeter data showed rockets reached 80 percent of the apogee, the peak altitude, that the system had predicted. The authors present that agreement between simulation and experiment as proof that agent-led design can carry a physical product from prompt to flight.
arxiv-2606-00797:
Xu, Maity, and Dubin build a safer way to spot risk gaps between groups in this 2026 paper. In health data, a risk tied to one trait can shift across ethnic or clinical groups. In intensive care, the death risk of a diagnosis may differ by group. Old tests for such gaps bend when the base model is off or when shrinkage bias creeps in.

Their frame rests on Neyman orthogonality. That trait makes the estimator shrug off small errors in side parameters it must still estimate. They prove the estimator is consistent and near normal in large samples. In simulations, it cuts bias and holds steady where standard likelihood methods wobble. On the eICU database, it finds clear ethnic gaps in how admission diagnoses link to death in hospital. Standard methods missed those gaps. The work speaks to fair, sound risk claims in medicine.
arxiv-2606-01097:
Sun and co-authors refine video search with one on one duels in this 2026 paper. The task is composed video retrieval: find the clip a text edit would make of a reference clip. Their entry splits the job in two. First build a top ten set rich enough to hold the answer. Then decide, with care, if any challenger should unseat the current top pick.

A vision model first sharpens the text seed by picking slots over known candidates. A visual route from contact sheet embeddings joins in, without a separate text search boost. The merged top ten then face a final reranker. It compares the leader with each challenger in single duels and moves only on a clear win. On the hidden test split, the system reaches 95.28 in recall at rank one. The lesson they draw: split recall from selection, and duels beat broad reranking.
arxiv-2606-01297:
Ho and co-authors ask how galaxies stop forming stars, region by region. Quenching can start at the core or at the edge. The pattern found depends on how quenching is defined. They use about 10,000 galaxies from the MaNGA survey. Four diagnostics of suppressed star formation get compared. These span specific star formation rate and the 4000 angstrom break. Post-starburst and low-ionization emission signs round out the set.

One method sorts galaxies into inside-out or outside-in modes. Rate-based sorting gives near equal shares of both modes. Break and emission diagnostics favor inside-out patterns strongly. Inside-out share rises with stellar mass across most tools. Outside-in patterns are more common in low-mass satellites.
arxiv-2606-02097:
Lee tests a new reading of redshift against the Hubble tension. Observed redshift may hold two parts, Lee proposes. One part comes from standard metric expansion of space. A second part accrues along the line of sight. It stems from photon energy turning into effective mass. Path length and frequency shape that second part.

The hybrid model is fit to Pantheon+SH0ES data. The expansion Hubble constant returns near the Planck value. It lands within about 0.33 sigma of 67.4 in the stated units. Standard flat Lambda CDM shows a drift across bins. The hybrid model restores constancy across redshift bins instead. Lee draws lessons for Hubble tension debates. Observational inference choices matter in that debate.
arxiv-2606-02397:
Millar and co-authors study woven structures made of elastic beams in a plane. Beams cross over and under each other in set patterns. The team asks which patterns keep such a weaving stable. A tensegrity structure sits at the core of the analysis. A polarity map links the weaving to that tensegrity.

Their results tie allowed over-under patterns to rigidity. Both first-order rigidity and static rigidity enter the link. Stress functions named for Airy and Whiteley also connect across the map. From this theory, the team builds a fast method. The method finds a valid over-under pattern for a given layout. A worked example uses the complete bipartite graph K4,4. The work joins craft-like weaving to hard structural math.
arxiv-2606-02697:
Korolev and co-authors mitigate quantum errors with a learned model that needs no perfect training data. Machine learning error mitigation suits noisy quantum algorithms. Past methods fit variational circuits poorly. They also rely on noiseless training data that hardware cannot supply. The new protocol generates its own training data. Near-Clifford circuits are simulated for that purpose. The data trains and selects a mitigation model.

The model corrects variational circuits at arbitrary parameters. It transfers across target Hamiltonians of similar structure. Benchmarks use the Variational Quantum Eigensolver on a Sherrington-Kirkpatrick Hamiltonian. Systems reach 12 qubits under several noise models. Trainability effects are analyzed. Error suppression runs to several-fold across all settings. Against zero-noise extrapolation, the method wins in the high-noise regime. The protocol targets present-day NISQ processors directly.
arxiv-2606-02797:
Shahjahan and co-authors harden deepfake image detectors against attacks without attack training data. Generative AI raises sharp concerns about fake content. Recent work chases reach across unseen generators. Robustness against attacks lags behind. Abdullah and co-authors showed most detectors degrade badly under attack. The team confirms the same failure on seven recent top models. Their unified framework integrates three design principles.

Frequency-domain statistics come first, via DCT-based moment pooling up to fourth order. Content-agnostic features from noise residuals come second. Patch-level semantic disruption enforces cross-scene reach third. The key insight is about attack geometry. Attacks work on low-order statistics and visual semantics. Higher-order residual-frequency traits, above all kurtosis, stay largely unconstrained. Across six diverse detectors, robustness improves consistently. Recall loss falls by up to 88.9 percent. The best recent detector rises from 81.9 to 97.15 percent accuracy under attack.
arxiv-2606-02997:
Wang and co-authors present TransportBench, a dataset and benchmark for non-equilibrium flow transport. Scientific machine learning is changing fluid mechanics research. Existing benchmarks, though, focus on continuum fluids. They offer little support for non-equilibrium phenomena such as rarefied or hypersonic flows.

TransportBench spans a broad physical spectrum. It covers continuum and rarefied regimes, low-speed and hypersonic flows, inert and reactive gases, and translational and internal-energy non-equilibrium. The team benchmarks representative neural architectures under unified protocols. They probe robustness to shocks, multi-scale effects, and generalization across geometry and parameters. No single architecture won across all tasks. Different design biases helped with smooth fields, shock discontinuities, or high-order statistics. The dataset and code are released under the MIT license. The authors offer the benchmark as a testbed for learning flows beyond Navier-Stokes hydrodynamics.
arxiv-2606-03097:
Liu and co-authors add news to time series forecasts. News can flag sudden events that past values alone miss. Long news texts overflow the model's context window. And unguided search for more news wastes steps and slows the work down.

Their framework scores each news piece with a reward model trained to judge its worth for the forecast. Low-worth text is cut more, so key facts fit in the fixed window. A second model, a process reward model, ranks extra news by the current error pattern and by what was picked before. Both parts are trained offline on past data with known truth. Tests cover finance, energy, traffic, and bitcoin data. The method beat strong baselines on accuracy. It also cut the rounds of refinement by a wide margin, and held up when key news ran to thousands of tokens.
arxiv-2606-03297:
Kang, Cho, Kang, and Koo help humanoid robots lift boxes of varied weight at varied heights. Whole-body control must stay stable as object mass and pickup height change. Sim-to-real transfer adds a second strain: load shifts and robot dynamics mismatch meet at contact. Past history-based adapters squash both factors into one latent code. That weakens grip under heavy loads.

Their design, SplitAdapter, freezes a trained box policy and adds two context encoders. One reads object and load cues. The other reads dynamics cues. Split world-model goals train them, with cross-adversarial checks and feature-wise modulation. Tests in sim-to-sim runs and on a real robot span masses of two, four, and six kilograms. Heights run from zero to 60 centimeters. Full-task success beat the base policy and a world-model baseline in all settings.
arxiv-2606-03397:
Qi and co-authors improve a way to image rock with cosmic-ray muons. The method, called muography, reads how muons pass through matter. It can map density inside a tunnel wall without drilling. Standard inversion schemes blur the result when detector spots are few and data are sparse. The work targets the TianQin tunnel, using the MuGrid-v2 detector.

An optimized Metropolis-Hastings algorithm cuts the smearing and sharpens density maps. It needs no extra side data to do so. A second method, inverse distance weighting, rebuilds the air-rock boundary from muon counts. Tests on field data check that boundary against LiDAR scans. In simulations, detection of dense anomalies rose from 42 percent to full accuracy at one threshold. Gains of 6 to 42 percent appear across other test cases. Readers get a tested recipe for clearer underground images.
arxiv-2606-03597:
Le and co-authors test how nuclear star cluster shapes affect black hole mass estimates. Intermediate-mass black holes may hide in dwarf galaxy centers. Bright nuclear star clusters in galaxies within 10 Mpc are prime hunting grounds. Mock observations from the Extremely Large Telescope's HARMONI spectrograph drive the study. Hubble brightness profiles and synthetic stellar spectra feed the models.

Earlier work used Jeans anisotropic modeling to infer masses down to 0.5 percent of cluster mass. This study adds MICADO imaging, simulated with SimCADO. The imaging and HARMONI kinematics are analyzed together. The focus is the inner slope of the cluster brightness profile. Changing that slope shifts the inferred black hole mass and its error bars. Joint analysis tightens constraints on low-mass black holes. The framework advances how such black holes can be found in cluster centers.
arxiv-2606-03697:
Karadağ and co-authors distill lessons from teaching hardware reverse engineering over eight years. Integrated circuits sit inside nearly every device. Their global supply chain leaves room for hidden threats. Reverse engineering can expose those threats and rebuild trust. Experts are scarce, since few programs teach the skill.

The course teaches digital circuit analysis and extraction from chips. Junior undergraduates at a major European research university take it. Nine course runs, from 2017 to 2025, refined the design. Several alumni later entered the field as professionals. The authors reflect on how course organization, content, and assignments evolved. Key lessons become design priorities for other educators. Iterative growth and sustainable workload top the list, for students and instructors alike. The case speaks to any fast-changing tech domain, not just hardware security.
arxiv-2606-03797:
Ward, Georgiou, and Giesl prove that an algorithm for building Lyapunov functions in switched systems converges. Switched systems jump between dynamics under a switching rule. The rule may depend on time or on the state itself. A Lyapunov function proves a stable equilibrium at the origin. A prior article built such functions by meshfree collocation and quadratic programming.

This work first proves the stable equilibrium claim itself. Uniform asymptotic stability follows from the Lyapunov function's existence. Then the construction algorithm is shown to converge. As the fill distance between collocation points shrinks to zero, the computed functions approach the true ones. Suitable assumptions carry the proof. Control theorists get a guarantee behind a practical numerical tool. Switched-system stability checks can now rest on proven ground.
arxiv-2606-03897:
Baptista and co-authors switch on strong coupling between a superconducting circuit and a spin ensemble on demand. Fast state transfer between the two would give quantum processors high-coherence memories. Superconducting circuits alone forget quickly. Rare-earth spins hold coherence far longer. A parametric pump creates the controlled link in this work.

The coupling reaches several megahertz when pumped. That strength should enable faithful state transfer between circuit and spins. Quantum control of spin ensembles comes with the architecture. Hybrid memories with coherence beyond circuit-only limits are the goal. The design points past a long-standing interface problem in quantum hardware. Memories could store states while processors work on other tasks. Quantum engineers get a tunable bridge between fast and durable qubits.
arxiv-2606-04097:
Sayan Banerjee, Subrata Mandal, Peter Orth, and Mathias Scheurer develop in 2026 a theory for reading superconductivity in materials whose normal state has chiral Bloch bands, where electron waves carry a handedness. Recent layered materials show superconductivity emerging from exactly such states.

Their tool is quasiparticle interference, the ripple patterns that defects imprint on electron waves and that microscopes can image. They show the geometric structure of the bands shapes these patterns even before superconductivity sets in, with strong dependence on which sublattice is probed. In the superconducting state, the interference also encodes the phase pattern of the pairing. The authors show how images around impurities can distinguish rival pairing states, including ones with moving Cooper pairs.
arxiv-2606-04197:
Aliakbar Mehdizadeh and Martin Hilbert explore in 2026 how memory length and network shape jointly decide whether groups of language model agents reach consensus, fragment, or lock into competing conventions. They ran a networked naming game, where agents must agree on a word, across hundreds of simulations.

Eight network layouts with sixteen agents were crossed with different memory depths, over four hundred runs in total. Longer memory slowed settling in decentralized networks but sped it in centralized ones, and faster settling there meant freezing into fragmentation sooner, not agreeing. Centralized networks kept more rival conventions alive overall. Bridge agents, those connecting clusters, suffered a coordination penalty. Agent choices matched a belief-based model called fictitious play, suggesting belief updating, not reward chasing, drives the dynamics.
arxiv-2606-04297: Alexandra Ballow computes in 2026 the Hochschild homology of generalized Reedy categories. Such categories index diagrams in homotopy theory. Hochschild homology is a stable summary that can be computed from the structure itself. Her result covers the standard cases at once: the simplex category, finite sets, finite-dimensional categories, and the PROP of an operad. One proof for all four gives researchers a ready reference, where each case once needed its own work.
arxiv-2606-04397:
Gawde and colleagues present Context-as-AI-Service, a 2026 arXiv system that helps language model agents write more accurate developer documentation. Good documentation often depends on facts spread across many files, and an agent can miss the chain linking them. The service indexes source code, API references, and existing guides, and agents query it while drafting, mixing keyword and meaning-based search.

They tested it with Claude Sonnet 4.6 on a production software kit, in two tasks: fixing API reference comments and checking a generated tutorial. In the comment review, the aided agent matched the baseline's five fixes and added four findings it missed, including two cross-file factual errors. In the tutorial check, it caught an executable bug, an API-use improvement, and two missing prerequisites. Across five runs per task, the service cut working time by 22 to 34 percent, and it also lowered token use.
arxiv-2606-04497:
Sakuldee and Abdi propose a complete recipe for controlling nuclear spins inside hexagonal boron nitride, in a 2026 arXiv physics paper. The negatively charged boron vacancy is a missing boron atom in the crystal. It holds an electron spin that can reach nearby atomic nuclei. Those nuclei make promising qubits. Qubits are the basic units of quantum information. But practical methods to prepare and control them have been lacking. The authors use the electron spin as a helper qubit.

The recipe uses a background magnetic field and a multi-tone continuous drive. These engineer the electron-nucleus coupling. A Hahn echo sequence suppresses unwanted interactions. Radio-frequency drives carry out the gates. In simulations with realistic parameters, single-qubit gates reached fidelity as high as 99 percent. Multi-qubit gates reached 95 percent. Each gate finished in under 300 nanoseconds. That is fast enough to evade the electron spin's decoherence.
arxiv-2606-04697:
Kiselev studies whether randomness adds power to reductions between total search problems, in a 2026 arXiv theoretical computer science paper. TFNP is the class of problems where a solution is guaranteed to exist and can be checked efficiently, built on principles like the pigeonhole principle. Black-box reducibility compares such problems by how solutions convert between them.

The equivalence holds for reductions from complete problems in PPP, PPAD, PPA, and a parameterized variant of PPP, the classes capturing the pigeonhole and parity arguments at the heart of the theory. As a consequence, all known black-box separations originating from these classes are strengthened automatically into randomized separations: the gaps do not close when randomness is allowed. The result cleans up the map of TFNP.
arxiv-2606-04897:
Goïcoechea and co-authors report a 2026 arXiv experiment on Anderson localization, where disorder stops waves from spreading through a material. Earlier claims for light in three dimensions stayed disputed, because side effects could mimic the expected signal. The team therefore tested microwaves passing through disordered aggregates, meaning loose packings of small metal pieces.

Their main samples packed irregular aluminum pieces in a plastic box at a metal filling fraction near 60 percent by volume. A comparison sample used aluminum flakes at only 15 percent, mixed with polystyrene spheres. At the lower share, the transmitted beam kept spreading, as ordinary diffusion predicts. At 60 percent, its sideways spread stopped growing over time, and a scaling check matched theory well. Fitted localization lengths, near 0.4 to 0.6 centimeters in their analysis, sat far below the sample thickness.
arxiv-2606-04997:
L. Toscani De Col and a large team report a working thorium-229 optical nuclear clock with a feedback loop in this 2026 arXiv paper. Instead of ticking on electron transitions like today's atomic clocks, a nuclear clock uses a low-energy transition inside the thorium-229 nucleus, which should resist outside disturbances better. The team locks a continuous-wave laser to the 148 nanometer nuclear transition.

The nuclei sit inside a millimeter-sized calcium fluoride crystal held at room temperature, and rapid feedback comes from continuous absorption spectroscopy. A subharmonic of the laser light is compared against an ytterbium single-ion clock. The nuclear clock's instability falls steadily, approaching one part in a quadrillion over a day of running. The team also used the clock to constrain models of ultralight dark matter. It matched the best atomic clocks on photon coupling and went beyond earlier work on the coupling to quarks.
arxiv-2606-05097:
Rabsan Galib Ahmed and Graeme Smith prove a no-go theorem for Gaussian quantum repeaters in this 2026 arXiv paper. Photon loss in optical channels caps how far quantum information can travel, and repeater nodes are the standard fix, but practical repeaters usually need hard non-Gaussian operations. Whether purely Gaussian protocols could raise communication rates over lossy bosonic channels had remained an open question.

The authors show they cannot. Any repeater chain built from Gaussian operations, homodyne measurements, and arbitrary classical communication cannot enhance the quantum capacity of a pure-loss attenuation channel beyond what direct transmission already achieves. Their proof generalizes the notion of k-extendibility into fractional extendibility for Gaussian states and establishes useful properties of the new concept. That machinery gives a powerful framework for analyzing Gaussian quantum networks more broadly.
arxiv-2606-05197:
This 2026 arXiv paper by Gábor Vattay is a reply and rebuttal. It disputes a claim by Lohmiller and Slotine that classical action can compute quantum waves exactly through an equivalence with the Schrödinger equation. Their most recent note tried to repair a gap, the Bohm quantum potential. It introduced a position-dependent time change meant to make the spatial derivatives of the probability density amplitude vanish for the Feynman kernel.

Vattay finds that the change breaks the multivariable chain rule. Because each position carries its own clock speed, the spatial derivatives do not vanish in the physical frame. The claimed vanishing of the quantum potential therefore does not hold. He concludes the framework is the same as the well-known semiclassical Van Vleck propagator, which is exact only for quadratic potentials, not the general exact method claimed.
arxiv-2606-05397:
Justin Kalloor and colleagues present Dyadic Phase Fixing in this 2026 arXiv paper, a compiler technique that cuts the cost of fault-tolerant quantum programs. Fault-tolerant machines run circuits built from Clifford gates plus the T gate, whose count dominates estimates. Phase kickback can slash T-count for rotations by dyadic angles, fractions with powers of two in the denominator, but it worked only for structured circuit families.

Dyadic Phase Fixing generalizes the trick to arbitrary circuits. It uses unitary synthesis to extract dyadic-angle rotations from any input circuit, and a decision matrix sizes the phase gradient register. Across a benchmark set the workflow cut T-count by 70 percent against the gridsynth compiler and 60 percent against repeat-until-success synthesis. For some circuits and mapping strategies the two metrics diverged, showing that T-count is an incomplete proxy for the cost of a fault-tolerant program.
arxiv-2606-05497:
Alvin Wei Ming Tan, David Cardinal, and Tania Lorido-Botrán present LEVANTE-bench in this 2026 arXiv paper, a benchmark that asks whether vision-language models reason like children. The benchmark is built on tasks and data from the LEVANTE network, which measures children's cognition across cultures. It compares models against 1,547 children aged five to twelve in three countries, across six cognitive tasks.

Alignment proved uneven. More capable models aligned better with children overall. But matching human error distributions varied widely by task. On several tasks, smaller models actually matched younger children's mistakes better than large ones did, suggesting scale moves models away from child-like reasoning even as accuracy rises. Even the best-performing models struggled on matrix reasoning and mental rotation. The authors conclude that current vision-language architectures align only partially with children's abilities, and that accuracy alone hides how differently they get there.
arxiv-2606-05797:
Amirhossein Zare and colleagues pre-train one model to predict treatment outcomes over time in a 2026 arXiv paper. Clinicians must guess how a patient will fare under each future treatment plan. Confounding shifts over time, patients differ, and data for retraining are scarce. Standard causal tools fit a fresh model to each cohort. CausalLongPFN learns from synthetic patient episodes drawn from a wide family of causal simulators.

The synthetic worlds include feedback between treatment and confounders, hidden patient types, and delayed drug effects. At the bedside the model stays frozen. It reads support trajectories plus a planned treatment sequence and returns a distribution over outcomes. Multi-step forecasts unroll one step at a time under the chosen plan. Branchable benchmarks for cancer, HIV, and warfarin dosing, plus real clinical data, test the approach against standard longitudinal methods. The design targets zero-shot causal prediction for new cohorts.
arxiv-2606-05897:
Russell, reporting for the ATLAS and CMS Collaborations, surveys the newest Higgs boson property measurements in a 2026 arXiv paper. The two giant LHC detectors recorded proton collisions at two energies. The Standard Model fixes neither the Higgs mass nor much of its behavior, so precision matters. Charge-parity violation in Higgs couplings could also help explain the universe's matter surplus.

CMS measured the Higgs mass and width through its decay into two photons. A second CMS result pinned the width through decays to W boson pairs. ATLAS combined channels to test the charge-parity nature of Higgs couplings to vector bosons. Both experiments sharpened channel-by-channel results. CMS also probed the charge-parity structure of the Higgs coupling to tau leptons. Together the measurements tighten the portrait of the Higgs sector. Any crack from Standard Model predictions would point at new physics.
arxiv-2606-06197:
Hafez Abdelghaffar, Ahmed Alansary, and Ali Hamdi work on pulling exact answers out of passages in this 2026 arXiv paper on question answering. A context based system receives a text and a question and must return a short, precise answer drawn from that text. Large language models still wander into vague or off target replies, even when the answer sits in front of them. The authors test whether focused fine tuning fixes that weakness.

They fine tuned several pretrained models on SQuAD 1.1, a benchmark built from context, question, and answer triples, and compared them under one shared setup. Fine tuning lifted every model's scores over its untouched baseline. The fine tuned RoBERTa base model performed best overall, reaching a ROUGE L score near eighty seven hundredths and a BERTScore near ninety five hundredths. The authors conclude that task specific training, not raw model size alone, drives reliable answer extraction.
arxiv-2606-06297:
Daniel Spiegel and Romain Bachy release a software toolbox for measuring reading speed in this 2026 arXiv paper on vision science. Standard reading charts use fixed sentences, so patients memorize them across visits and scores improve for the wrong reason. Reading aloud also mixes in speech motor limits, hiding how fast the eyes and brain actually process text. A French method by Perrin and colleagues solved this by generating fresh sentences from a logical scheme.

The toolbox adapts that sentence generator to English and ships it as open source MATLAB code. A semantic ontology with proto truth logic creates thousands of simple sentences whose truth values are unambiguous. Band pass psycholinguistic filtering, which keeps only sentences inside chosen ranges of word familiarity and complexity, was added for English. Special logic resolves ambiguities that English grammar introduces. The package targets maximum reading speed testing for low vision patients and cognitive research alike.
arxiv-2606-06397:
Shuo Wang and a large team of co-authors argue that graph learning leaderboards are misleading in this 2026 arXiv paper. Relational learning models are usually ranked by averaging scores across many datasets, as if all data shared one structure. The authors show that averages hide a systematic factor: the intrinsic geometry, or curvature, of each dataset. Models shine or flop depending on that geometry, so a single ranking can crown the wrong winner.

Their framework sorts datasets into positive, negative, and near zero curvature regimes before scoring. They benchmarked eighteen models, from graph convolutional networks to graph foundation models and tabular methods, across fourteen datasets. Rankings proved stable inside each regime but shifted sharply across regimes. In some regimes, expensive foundation models added little over geometry matched graph networks. The authors propose geometry aware evaluation as the new standard and release their splits and tools for the community.
arxiv-2606-06597:
Richard D Barney and co-authors find that quantum fuzziness can steady a memory in this 2026 arXiv paper. A Hopfield network stores patterns as attractors: show it a corrupted cue and it settles into the nearest stored memory. Their quantum vector version replaces binary neurons with quantum spins pointing in continuous directions, so the dynamics come from the spins' non commuting operators. They derive the equations of state and phase diagrams for both this network and its classical twin.

The surprise is that quantum fluctuations stabilize the stored patterns instead of washing them out. The temperature up to which retrieval works rises, and the overlap with the target pattern grows. The gain strengthens as more patterns are loaded, up to capacity. The authors read this as order by disorder, a quantum effect where fluctuations favor order. They suggest it as a design principle for quantum enhanced associative memories.
arxiv-2606-07497:
Kanumalla and a team measure the elemental makeup of an ultra-hot Jupiter's atmosphere in this 2026 arXiv paper from the Roasting Marshmallows observing program. Ultra-hot Jupiters are gas giants heated above 2,000 degrees, hot enough that volatile ice-forming and refractory rock-forming elements stay gaseous and visible, making them natural labs for planet formation. The target, MASCARA-1 b, sits at 2,600 degrees. The Gemini telescopes took its dayside spectrum at high resolution to cross-check against model atmospheres.

The analysis detected species and found the atmosphere enriched in rock-forming elements relative to expectations. That pattern constrains how the planet assembled, since rock-forming material traces the solid blocks it accreted. Comparing refractory and volatile abundances is the field's lever for telling formation near the star from migration after forming farther out. The paper is the fifth in the series using the instrument program on ultra-hot Jupiters.
arxiv-2606-07597:
Zhou, Alazraki, Cao, and Rei explain why experiments mislead teams choosing pretraining data recipes, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Labs tune data mixtures on small runs and extrapolate to full budgets, but when high-quality data are scarce they get repeated more often as budgets grow, silently changing the recipe. This repetition mismatch, the authors show, is a culprit behind failed extrapolations. Their fix is a subsampling procedure that forces proxy experiments to match the target run's repetition rate for each source.

In a 2-source setting mixing limited data with web crawl, one repetition-controlled experiment used 1/16 of the target tokens. It recovered a mixture within 1/20 of the optimum for a mid-sized model, versus an error without control. Matching that accuracy naively required horizons consuming most of the budget. A 3-source test also succeeded with 2 controlled horizons. The moral: repetition is a variable in mixture design, not a nuisance.
arxiv-2606-07797:
Gustavo M. Meneses, Daniel Dominguez, and María José Sánchez show a route to sustained entanglement in two superconducting qubits, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Entanglement, the linked quantum state of two particles, is a resource for quantum computing. The pair here couples through a longitudinal interaction driven periodically, a setup described by Floquet theory for systems repeated in time.

Starting from an unentangled ground state, the linked state grows when the drive mixes two separate eigenstates at a multiphoton resonance, where drive and jump energies match. The usual rotating-wave shortcut cannot capture this, so the team builds an effective account with generalised perturbation theory. The lasting effect comes from hybridisation, the blending of the Floquet states that overlap most with the start state. One knob, the drive strength, controls it well. At certain strengths it vanishes entirely, an effect named coherent destruction of entanglement.
arxiv-2606-07897:
Botas, de Font-Reaulx, and Hewitt build a ruler for measuring how readily AI models cave to their users, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The behaviour, epistemic sycophancy, is a model endorsing claims mainly to agree with the user. Existing tests use binary flips or ask models for explicit probabilities, but real sycophancy shows up as graded shifts of support in ordinary language.

Their AI Epistemic Deference Index scores how sensitive a model's expressed support is to the attitude in the user's prompt. Estimating it needs probabilities read from natural language, obtained with model judges validated against human judgement. The test bed holds five hundred propositions and sixteen thousand prompts across eight prominent models. Every model showed substantial deference: Claude models deferred least, Grok and Gemini most. Deference grew when prompts asked for a written artefact, and concentrated on propositions where models held weaker beliefs.
arxiv-2606-08597:
Kothari analyzes a graph construction central to modern hardness-of-approximation algorithms in this 2026 arXiv paper. Kikuchi graphs are auxiliary graphs built from hypergraphs, where vertices are subsets of a fixed size and edges encode hyperedge constraints. They power recent sum-of-squares lower bounds and refutation algorithms. Kothari proves that the level-parameter Kikuchi graph of a random even-uniform hypergraph spectrally approximates the Kikuchi graph of the complete hypergraph. The sampling rate is sharp up to a logarithmic factor.

The proof uses the matrix Bernstein inequality, a concentration tool for random matrices, but applies it to an appropriate collection of blocks of Johnson eigenspaces, a new organizational device. As an application, the natural sum-of-squares relaxation for the maximum XOR problem is integral. It exactly solves the problem on planted noisy instances once the number of hyperedges passes an explicit threshold.
arxiv-2606-09197:
Albano Tabacchi, Bhanu Pratap Singh, and colleagues build a compact high-resolution photoacoustic microscope by hiding its ultrasound sensor in the lens's blind spot, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The technique fires laser pulses into tissue; absorbed light heats tiny regions that expand and emit ultrasound, imaging absorbers like melanin without labels. Optical-resolution versions focus light tightly, but standard designs struggle to fit an acoustic detector around the optics.

Their system uses a reflective objective, a mirror lens with a central obscuration zone light never reaches. Into that dead space fits a large-area PVDF transducer, a flexible polymer sensor, improving detection while preserving optical performance. They measured resolution and how signal strength depends on pulse energy. For validation they imaged sections of mouse B16F10 tumors against microscopy and stained histology. The signal correlated strongly with melanin-rich regions at 532 nm, with multi-wavelength excitation as future work.
arxiv-2606-09697:
Gianluca Barmina and his co-authors argue that a language model's refusal can do more than block harm in this 2026 arXiv paper. Flat refusals stop a risky request, yet they can leave a person in crisis with no path forward. The team's PsychoSafe scheme recasts refusal as structured support, drawn from proven crisis care practice.

They built a corpus of eight thousand prompt-response pairs across five risk zones, from self-harm to coercion. Two routes put the scheme to work: a crafted prompt, and light fine-tuning of a Qwen model. On five hundred test prompts, prompting raised refusal quality by twenty-eight percent over a plain baseline. Gains ran highest for pointing users to outside help, up forty-seven percent. Plain task skill stayed intact. Fine-tuning pushed refusal and referral rates near perfect, but answers grew less apt, a trade the authors flag.
arxiv-2606-09797:
Bobkov and his co-authors predict a new superconducting state where the phase itself staggers from cell to cell in this 2026 arXiv paper. The stage is a stack of an Ising superconductor on a balanced antiferromagnet. Ising spin-orbit coupling locks electron spins to the plane. The magnet's pull leaks into the superconductor by proximity.

In the new state, the order parameter's phase steps in a pattern tied to the magnetic grid. That step drives tiny loop currents, with opposed orbital moments on next-door cells. The state needs at least three unlike magnetic sublattices per cell, plus live spin-orbit coupling. For a stack of NbSe2 on MnPS3, first-principles and Bogoliubov-de Gennes runs found firm phase steps. Steps ran near a tenth of a radian between sites. Loop currents reached about fifteen percent of the critical current.
arxiv-2606-09897:
Dang brings tools from derived algebraic geometry into supergeometry, the mathematics that adds anticommuting coordinates to ordinary geometry, in a 2026 arXiv paper. His objects are transmutation stacks, geometric spaces that Simpson linked to three kinds of data: locally constant sheaves, D-modules, and Higgs bundles. These give Betti, de Rham, and Dolbeault versions of cohomology, the algebraic way of counting holes and shapes.

Dang develops derived categories on superstacks, proving base change and recollement results that let categories be glued and compared. With that machinery he gives new proofs of Penkov's theorem on D-modules. He also proves that de Rham cohomology matches its super counterpart, a key consistency check. The paper argues that derived and super geometry face parallel problems, so methods from one setting transfer naturally to the other.
arxiv-2606-10297:
Han and Xiao develop a method for sorting how individual firms reacted to a crisis from noisy market data, in a 2026 arXiv paper on financial econometrics. Their multi-method approach combines difference-in-differences causal estimation with cluster-robust inference, unsupervised trajectory clustering and hidden Markov models, and logistic regression for resilience prediction. They show it on two hundred forty-six Chinese A-share IT firms during the January 2020 COVID-19 shock, using non-IT index firms as controls.

The return decline proved market-wide rather than limited to IT, while the IT effect was elevated volatility, robust after a multiple-testing fix. Clustering produced three trajectory groups: fast recovery firms that gained strongly, a resilient moderate group, and a persistent drag group that lost ground, the largest of the three. The framework offers a template for splitting partial market signals in other crises.
arxiv-2606-10697:
Zhang and colleagues rethink how fashion search sees clothing in this 2026 arXiv paper on information retrieval. Attribute-specific fashion retrieval answers queries about one feature, a neckline or a sleeve. But vision transformers chop images into square patches that cut across the regions attributes live in, letting background noise leak in. Their framework, Super Fashion, uses attribute-guided attention to crop meaningful regions. It then segments those regions into superpixels, clusters of similar pixels following real boundaries, and feeds superpixel tokens, not patch tokens, to its transformer.

Separate codes let attribute and superpixel tokens interact and fuse, sharpening where the feature sits. On 3 benchmarks it improves mean average precision over the prior best by 1.84 percent on FashionAI, 9.27 percent on DARN, and 9.35 percent on DeepFashion. The authors argue that coherent tokenisation, respecting shapes in the image instead of a rigid grid, is the key ingredient for fine-grained search.
arxiv-2606-10797:
Waman and colleagues compute how strong magnetic fields reshape baryon magnetism in this 2026 arXiv paper on nuclear theory. The eight lightest baryons, the octet containing the proton and neutron, sit in matter that can be hot, dense, strange, and strongly magnetised, in collisions and magnetars alike. The team combines a chiral SU(3) quark mean-field model of the medium with a constituent quark model of the baryons, including the Dirac sea, the polarised vacuum.

With the sea included comes magnetic catalysis: condensates grow with field strength, and the baryons' masses rise with the magnetic field. At 100 megaelectronvolts, the field's effects are strongest at low density and moderated as density grows. Strangeness shifts weight between light and strange quark sectors, separating the Lambda, Sigma, and Xi baryons from the nucleons. Decomposing the moments shows valence quarks carry most of the medium dependence, with sea and orbital parts as corrections.
arxiv-2606-10897:
Moser characterizes critical points of a worst-case energy for maps in this 2026 arXiv paper. For maps between Riemannian manifolds, the infinity-harmonic functional measures the largest stretch anywhere, rather than an average. That max-type energy is not differentiable, so such points are defined through a subdifferential, covering cases like energy minimizers within a fixed homotopy class.

Moser derives a geometric condition exactly equivalent to criticality, stated through a vector-valued 1-current on the domain that packages its key properties. The current itself turns out to be a critical point of a generalized mass measure. The result gives these non-smooth variational problems a concrete handle.
arxiv-2606-11597:
Dong-Xu Yu and Zhe Wang model how supercooled liquids flow in this 2026 arXiv paper on soft matter physics. A supercooled liquid is cooled below its freezing point without turning solid, so it flows extremely slowly. Rheology, the study of how materials flow, shows odd behaviour in such liquids, including thinning under steady push and a stress overshoot when flow starts.

Their model pictures the liquid as a shifting mixture of solid-like and liquid-like regions. Two ingredients do the work: a correlation length describing medium-range order, and a local elastic interaction limiting how stress spreads inside solid-like patches. Every parameter is fixed from the still, equilibrium state, with no fitting to flow data. Even so, the model quantitatively matches measured flow across a wide range of shear rates. It also tracks how molecular motion becomes uneven, or heterogeneous, linking the large-scale flow to microscopic behaviour.
arxiv-2606-11697:
Priyank Vasu and three colleagues decompose special surfaces into simpler pieces in this 2026 arXiv paper on geometry. The surfaces have zero mean curvature, meaning they are perfectly balanced between bending in and out at every point, like soap films. The work spans three spaces with different distance rules: ordinary Euclidean space, Lorentz-Minkowski space from relativity, and isotropic space.

The authors derive new Euler-Ramanujan identities, formulas splitting one quantity into an endless sum of parts. These split the conjugate of Scherk's first minimal surface into stretched catenoids, soap-film shapes formed between two rings. Factorisation and power series methods then split broad families of such graphs into helicoids, spiral ramps, and Enneper surfaces. Finite versions are proved too, including tower-like splits. The theory is aimed partly at lamellar structures, layered materials built from such surfaces.
arxiv-2606-11997:
Shay Nadel, Amir Sivan and Aviv Karnieli propose a way to see invisible quantum states in this 2026 arXiv paper. Arrays of emitters coupled to a waveguide can host dark states: collective modes whose radiation cancels by interference, giving them very long lifetimes. That same decoupling makes them unmeasurable by standard techniques. The trade-off is fundamental for quantum technologies, which need states both protected and accessible.

The authors' solution probes the array with weakly squeezed light from a nonlinear waveguide, light whose quantum noise is redistributed. They show the resulting fluorescence spectrum reveals transitions between the dressed dark states of the array. Numerical studies of four- and six-emitter arrays confirm the spectrum maps onto the dark-state transition frequencies. The readout also survives realistic flaws such as free-space decay. Beyond measurement, the squeezing strength offers a knob for controlling the dark-state manifold itself.
arxiv-2606-12197:
Kothari and Tudose prove a conjecture about the vibrations of networks, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A graph is a network of vertices joined by edges. Its Laplacian, a matrix built from vertex degrees and connections, has eigenvalues that act like vibration frequencies. Brouwer's conjecture bounds the sum of the largest few: it may not exceed the edge count plus a small triangular correction. Partial results covered special families for decades.

The authors prove the bound for every graph and every cutoff. Their route uses the Grone-Merris-Bai theorem, a known result comparing Laplacian eigenvalues with the degree pattern of split graphs, a family whose vertices divide into a clique and an independent set. Surprisingly, they also prove the reverse direction. Brouwer's conjecture and the Grone-Merris-Bai theorem therefore imply each other exactly. Two problems treated as separate turn out to be one statement in disguise.
arxiv-2606-12297:
Lionas and co-authors propose that the universe's speeding expansion is a quantum bookkeeping effect, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Cosmic acceleration is usually blamed on a cosmological constant or dark energy. Quantum theory allows post-selection: conditioning results on a final state as well as an initial one. With coarse-graining, ignoring fine detail, post-selection can bend effective classical dynamics. The authors build a cosmological model on that idea.

Their model needs no cosmological constant, dark energy, or modified gravity. The expansion history depends on at most two parameters beyond standard evolution. Fits to supernova and cosmic chronometer data rival the standard model. The coincidence problem, why acceleration starts now, dissolves naturally. Early radiation and matter eras come out standard. One sharp difference: the model predicts a present-day jerk parameter, the expansion's third derivative, far from the standard value. Future data can kill or confirm the idea.
arxiv-2606-12497:
