They work by releasing brakes on the immune system. The review focuses on antibodies that target PD-1 or its partner PD-L1, the two most used checkpoints in the clinic.

The authors list the drugs approved by the Food and Drug Administration. For each, they give the cancers it is cleared to treat. Companion diagnostics, the tests used to select patients, are covered in equal depth. A test result can decide whether a patient gets the drug at all. The review then turns to the hunt for better predictive markers. Picking the right patients remains the weak point of this therapy class. The paper serves as a compact status report.
europmc-pmc8010197:
Chen and co-authors review how the gut microbiota shapes human disease. The gut holds a vast microbial community that acts almost like an extra organ. When its balance breaks, the effects reach far beyond digestion. The authors focus on the pathways behind that damage. Their aim is to point to targets for prevention and care.

The review covers four disease groups in turn. It takes up brain disorders, heart and vessel disease, metabolic disease, and gut disease itself. For each, the authors explain how microbes and their products drive harm. Routes include energy uptake, bile acids, and the gut-brain axis. Short-chain fatty acids also feature. The survey ties a scattered field into one map.
europmc-pmc8016797:
Murao and co-authors review how major DAMPs escape from cells and tissues. DAMPs are the body's own molecules that, once outside cells, stir inflammation. They are tied to disorders in sepsis and cancer. Blocking them could yield new treatments. But smart blocking starts with knowing how each one gets out.

The review compares release routes across seven major DAMPs. They include HMGB1, ATP, histones, and heat shock proteins. Extracellular RNA and cell-free DNA also feature. Some DAMPs leak passively when membranes rupture in necrosis or necroptosis. Other cell deaths, from apoptosis to NETosis, contribute too. Living cells can also export DAMPs actively, through secretory lysosomes, exosomes, or open channel pores. Each DAMP favors its own mix of exits.
europmc-pmc8075897:
Li and co-authors sequence three hornwort genomes to shed light on the first land plants. Hornworts split from other land plant lines over 400 million years ago. They keep odd traits found nowhere else, from their sporophyte shape to a pyrenoid carbon trap. The team sequenced three species of the genus Anthoceros. The genomes are high quality and complete.

Family-tree analysis places hornworts as sister to liverworts plus mosses. The genomes show no whole-genome duplication in their past. Their stock of transcription factors is small and spare. Genes for flowering-plant meristems and stomata turn up in working form. Some switch on as the sporophyte builds itself. A gene for the carbon trap, LCIB, appears in hornworts alone among land plants. The authors offer the genomes as a reference for plant evolution.
europmc-pmc8260997:
Qiu and co-authors ask whether immune cells are good targets after ischaemic stroke. Stroke breaks the blood-brain barrier, a key step toward harm. That breach can bring deadly swelling and bleeding in the brain.

Blood-borne immune cells rush in and raise barrier leak. Neutrophils, monocytes, and T cells secrete inflammatory molecules. Brain-resident cells such as microglia and astrocytes add their own effects. Later, the same cell types help repair the barrier and grow vessels. Timing decides whether a cell harms or heals. The review weighs therapy aimed at each phase.
europmc-pmc8321897:
Eigenbrodt and co-authors lay out migraine diagnosis and care in ten steps. Migraine disables more than one billion people worldwide. It stays under-diagnosed and under-treated despite that reach.

A European expert panel built the ten steps by consensus. Each step rests on a review of current evidence. Two European federations endorse the statement. Early steps cover the typical features and diagnostic criteria. Look-alike conditions are sorted next. Patient communication earns a step of its own. The guide aims to make sound migraine care the default everywhere. The statement closes with management steps for daily practice.
europmc-pmc8343997:
Li, Sun, and Qin review how cancer-associated fibroblasts rewire metabolism, and how that rewires cancer. Cancer cells adapt fuel use to grow fast in poor settings. Much of that reprogramming springs from the tumour microenvironment.

Fibroblasts are the main stromal cells in that setting. Their metabolism shifts in step with the tumour's. Two-way signals pass between stromal and cancer cells. The Warburg effect and Krebs cycle changes feature in the exchange. Energy output pathways rise to feed invasion. The review maps this shared economy. Cutting its supply lines is a therapy idea.
europmc-pmc8425997:
Zhang and co-authors survey antimicrobial peptides as a fresh weapon against drug-resistant bacteria. These small peptides come from natural sources or the lab. They attack a wide range of microbes with high precision and low toxicity.

The review covers where the peptides come from and how they are built. It explains the clever ways they kill bacteria, fungi, parasites, and viruses. Their roles in the body's first-line immune defense get full treatment. Clinical uses and trials are reviewed next. The authors end with ways to tune the peptides for better drugs. Cancer uses are also in view as a future path.
europmc-pmc8500697:
COVID-19 Mental Disorders Collaborators quantify the pandemic's hit to depression and anxiety worldwide in 2020. Before 2020, mental disorders already ranked among the top causes of health burden. Depression and anxiety led that toll. The pandemic then worsened many drivers of poor mental health.

The team reviewed studies from January 2020 to January 2021 that had pre-pandemic baselines. A meta-regression linked changes in disorder rates to pandemic impact signs. Human mobility and infection rates served as those signs. Estimates cover 204 countries and territories. The authors aim to give health systems firm numbers for planning their response.
europmc-pmc8501897:
Shur and co-authors give a practical guide to radiomics in cancer care. Radiomics mines medical images for data that eyes alone cannot read. In oncology it aims to sharpen diagnosis, outlook, and treatment support. The goal is precision medicine for each patient.

The workflow runs from planning to writing up results. Tumors are outlined, images are cleaned, and features are pulled. Those features describe signal spread and pixel patterns in a region. Weak or repeated features are cut to guard the model. Teams span radiologists plus data and imaging scientists. Validation closes the loop, since it shows how the model truly performs.
europmc-pmc8529297:
Warnakulasuriya and Kerr review oral cancer screening, its past, present, and future. Oral cancer is a major public health problem that strikes more young men and women. Awareness is poor, and many patients arrive with late disease. That delay drives high death rates.

The mouth can be checked by eye, and a warning phase often shows first. Screening symptom-free people by visual exam has proved workable. A positive screen can mean cancer or a risky mouth disorder. The review covers key studies, among them one randomized trial. Screening high-risk groups pays off in cost terms. New technology may sharpen case finding soon.
europmc-pmc8688697:
Ou and co-authors track global trends in Parkinson disease across 204 countries and territories from 1990 to 2019. Data came from the Global Burden of Disease study. The team measured new cases, total cases, and years lived with disability. Rates were adjusted for age so places could be compared fairly.

All three rates rose over the thirty years. The largest patient counts sat in groups over age 65. Shares rose fast among people over age 80. The United States and Norway showed the sharpest rises in new case rates. About 30 countries bucked the trend, led by Italy and Moldova. The authors call for stronger control and care as populations age.
europmc-pmc8728197:
Meier-Kolthoff and co-authors describe updates to TYGS and LPSN, twin databases for naming and classifying microbes. Genome-based methods now drive microbial taxonomy. Name lists and sequence stores grow fast, which strains database systems. Names must follow the international code for prokaryote naming.

LPSN is an expert-curated source for those names. TYGS is a high-throughput platform that classifies genomes. The two systems are tightly linked. Updates add new access routes to shared algorithms. Database content grew by a large margin. New ways to pull the data were also built. The authors argue this tandem keeps naming fast and reliable.
europmc-pmc8772097:
Li and co-authors review liquid biopsy in lung cancer and its value for diagnosis, prediction, and treatment checks. Most lung cancer patients in China already have distant spread at first diagnosis. Tissue biopsy is invasive, and repeat samples are hard to get. Liquid biopsy offers a painless route that reflects the whole tumor.

Samples can hold tumor cells, tumor DNA, exosomes, and other markers from blood. Each type carries distinct information about the cancer. These markers can aid early detection and guide personal treatment. They also let doctors track how well a therapy works over time. The review sums up progress and clinical prospects for each marker type.
europmc-pmc8891297:
Wculek and co-authors review how tissue macrophages fuel themselves in health and disease. Macrophages guard nearly every organ. Each tissue shapes its own macrophage population. Those populations face very different fuel demands. Most knowledge of macrophage metabolism comes from lab dishes. Real tissues impose their own conditions. The review moves the focus into the body.

The authors first set out the classic in-vitro picture. They then survey macrophages at home in their tissues. Tissue repair earns its own section. Fat tissue under overnutrition follows. Atherosclerosis shows macrophages in a lipid-rich trap. Cancer closes the survey with its own metabolic challenges. Throughout, the message is context. A macrophage's fuel choices fit its niche. Disease bends those choices in tissue-specific ways.
europmc-pmc9122097:
Duan and co-authors pool studies on inflammatory cytokines in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. Cytokines are small signals that drive inflammation. Past studies disagreed on which ones track with this common liver disease. A pooled analysis can give a firmer answer.

The team found 51 studies with 36,074 patients and 47,052 controls. They tested 19 different cytokines in all. Higher levels of five markers were linked to higher risk of the disease. Those markers were C-reactive protein, interleukin-1 beta, interleukin-6, tumor necrosis factor-alpha, and ICAM-1. Three of them also tracked with worse liver harm. Many other cytokines showed no clear link. The authors say the five markers may aid early diagnosis.
europmc-pmc9130497:
Eden and co-authors report off-season RSV epidemics in Australia after COVID-19 limits eased. RSV is a major cause of lung infection, worst in the young and the old. Pandemic controls in 2020 wiped out the usual winter epidemics. Then large outbreaks hit in spring and summer, in regions far apart.

Genome sequencing showed a sharp drop in RSV diversity after COVID-19 began. Two distinct RSV-A groups had spread quietly for months before cases surged. One group then spread from New South Wales into Victoria in early 2021. The authors warn that disrupted seasons may bring larger outbreaks. They urge continued watch and sequencing for RSV and other respiratory viruses.
europmc-pmc9176297:
Baumdicker and co-authors introduce msprime 1.0, a tool for fast simulation of ancestry and mutation. Simulation is a key tool in population genetics, since many models cannot be solved on paper. Past tools each filled a niche but overlapped a lot. Msprime builds on the succinct tree sequence structure and the tskit library.

Tests show it often runs many times faster than rival tools and uses far less memory. Its many features cover a wide range of population models. The software was built openly with community input and thorough testing. That model cuts duplicated effort and lifts quality. Geneticists get a single, efficient simulator for ground-truth data to test their methods.
europmc-pmc9834297:
Gao and co-authors decode how a carbon dot nanozyme copies the superoxide dismutase enzyme. Nanozymes scavenge superoxide, the seed of most cell rust species. None had matched the speed of the natural enzyme before. Their carbon dot version crosses that bar at last.

Its activity passed 10,000 units per milligram in tests. That rate rivals what natural enzymes achieve. Chemical tweaks and theory pinned down the working parts. Hydroxyl and carboxyl groups first catch the superoxide ions. Carbonyl groups tied to the ring system pass electrons along. The dots home in on rust damaged cells by themselves. In mice with ischemic stroke, neuron cells were protected. The study spells out a structure to activity map. It gives designers rules for building better mimics. Rust stress diseases are the stated treatment target.
europmc-pmc9912297:
Singh and co-authors trace how collagen I and collagen III are controlled in tissue injury and repair. Collagen supports cartilage, tendons, skin, heart, vessels, and many organs. Collagen I gives stiff tensile strength. Collagen III forms an elastic network that stores and releases energy.

Shifts in either collagen can change disease course and outlook. Raised collagen I can stiffen heart muscle and harm its filling and pumping. The review covers control of both types across many tissues. It stresses the ratio between collagen I and collagen III. That balance shapes healing, scarring, and organ function. Readers get a broad account of why collagen balance matters after injury.
europmc-pmc9998097:
COVID-19 Forecasting Team members synthesize how well past infection protects against re-infection. Knowing that protection level helps predict future disease burden. It also informs travel rules, venue access policy, and vaccine timing. The team ran a systematic review and meta-analysis of the literature.

They gathered cohort and test-negative studies published up to September 31, 2022. In total, 65 studies from 19 countries entered the analysis. Protection was estimated by outcome, variant, and time since infection. Outcomes were re-infection, symptomatic disease, and severe disease. A Bayesian meta-regression produced the pooled estimates. Bias risk was checked with NIH quality tools. The review followed PRISMA and a registered protocol.
fenelon-maxims-saints-1697:
Fénelon defends the inner life of prayer in The Maxims of the Saints, first issued in 1697. François Fénelon was Archbishop of Cambrai. The English edition here, printed in London in 1698, gives his text on pure, selfless love of God. Around it stand the papers of the fight it caused.

The volume adds the thirty-four articles of the Archbishop of Paris and the Bishops of Meaux and Chartres, who condemned the book. It adds their declaration, and letters to the Pope from the French king and from Fénelon himself. In the sampled text, Fénelon marks the bounds of pure love with care. False contemplation, he warns, would destroy faith itself, and slide toward a kind of deism. The book is both a guide to prayer and a record of a church quarrel.
fichte-science-ethics-1897:
The Science of Ethics as Based on the Science of Knowledge is A E Kroeger's 1897 translation of Fichte's System der Sittenlehre of 1798. Johann Gottlieb Fichte meant his ethics to grow from the same root as his whole philosophy: the free, self-positing I. Where the Science of Rights ordered men together, this work orders the single soul.

Fichte derives duty from the I's drive to be wholly self-determined, answerable to its own law. Conscience, on his account, is the voice of that law, and it cannot err when honestly heard. The system gives the body, the scholar, and the citizen each their moral place. It crowns the great trilogy of Fichte's Jena years.
freeman-jerome-1897:
Jerome, A Poor Man came from Harper in 1897 with pictures by A. I. Keller. Freeman dedicated the novel to her father. Chapter one finds Jerome at twelve, basking in a secret hollow in a great rock ledge.

The hollow shields the boy from cold northwest wind while spring sun warms him. Peach trees bloom on a hill nearby, and a ploughman's shouts drift over the fields. Grown, Jerome stays poor until money comes to him and brings a heavy moral test. His long struggle to do right, in a town quick to condemn, makes a quiet and strong study of conscience.
frus-1861-d197:
Cassius Clay wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 7 June 1861. The dispatch is document 197 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Clay's first report in the file comes from his new post in Russia. He found a court that spoke warmly of the Union. His June letter began a run of good news from the north that ran through the whole war. His run of reports from Russia forms the happiest thread in the year's record. The happiest thread in the record runs north, and Clay's letters spin it.
frus-1861-d297:
Seward heard from Mr. Harvey on 25 August 1861, in a dispatch sent from abroad. Congress received it as Document 297 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. It belongs to the first summer of the Civil War, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d97:
A reply dated 14 October 1861 went from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons in Washington. The letter is document 97 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

A same day answer was swift work for the age. Seward and Lyons kept a brisk exchange through that autumn, claim by claim. This reply shows the Secretary meeting British pressure with equal speed, in the hope that quick words would keep small points small. Quick answers also denied London any ground to claim its notes went unheeded. Quick words, in that season, were a form of respect that both sides prized.
frus-1862-d197:
Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 16 December 1861, and the letter stands as Document 197 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It came from the British legation a short walk from the State Department.

Lyons wrote while his government waited for Washington's answer in the Trent affair, the dispute over Confederate envoys seized from a British mail steamer. His manner was calm where London's first reaction had been fierce. Letters from his hand in this window show a minister trying to keep a quarrel from becoming a war. Britain's first concern in Washington was the blockade and what it cost British trade.
frus-1862-d297:
William H. Seward, as Secretary of State, wrote to William L. Dayton in Paris on 21 July 1862, in a dispatch printed as Document 297 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Late July 1862 was the war's low summer for the Union: Richmond saved by Lee. A second Confederate army gathering, and calls in Europe to end the fighting by pressure. Seward's letters to Paris pushed back with facts and resolve. This dispatch shows the Secretary's method at its plainest, steady repetition of the Union's case to the court most likely to act. Edouard Thouvenel ran the French foreign ministry for most of 1862 and set Dayton's agenda there.
frus-1862-d397:
Two days after a companion instruction, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote again to Bayard Taylor in St. Petersburg, on 24 November 1862. The letter is Document 397 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed to accompany the President's annual message to Congress.

Short follow-up orders were the glue of Civil War diplomacy, since news crossed the Atlantic by ship and took weeks. Seward used them to correct, press, or calm his agents as events shifted. Paired with Taylor's own reports, this note helps a reader watch the Washington end of the Russian correspondence. In that quarter the Union enjoyed rare goodwill during the war.
frus-1862-d497:
On 26 April 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands. It is Document 497 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Seward wrote on the day New Orleans fell to Farragut's fleet, the Union's greatest prize of the spring. News of that kind was diplomatic gold, and his orders abroad made the most of it. At The Hague the victory spoke to a trading people: the Mississippi was opening, and the Confederacy was shrinking. The instruction belongs to the confident late-April round of Seward's orders. In them he told his ministers, in effect, that the rebellion had passed its peak. Europe, he said, should take note.
frus-1862-d597:
Spain's minister of state wrote this instruction on 13 December 1861 to General Serrano, the captain general and governor of Cuba. It is Document 597 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, in an appendix of Spanish papers on Mexico.

Unlike most of the volume, this letter is not American at all: it is the Spanish government's own internal order, printed in translation. Cuba was the base and the prize of Spain's American policy, and Serrano commanded both the island and its part in the Mexican expedition. The document lets a reader see the allied move on Mexico from inside Madrid's chain of command, which is why the State Department preserved it.
frus-1862-d697: A Mr. Yrisarri wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 26 August 1862. The letter is document 697 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, printed near the papers on Central America. The evidence names the writer and the date but does not state his post or his land, so this note claims no more than that.
frus-1862-d97:
A State Department letter of 11 July 1862 told Charles Francis Adams what Washington wanted done. Congress received it as Document 97 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. The letter comes from the summer of 1862, the war's second year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1863p1-d197:
From Washington on 9 May 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction toward London; the catalog title garbles the envoy's name as 'Mr. Adapts,' but the letter belongs to the run addressed to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 197 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

For readers today, these instructions reveal the thinking inside the State Department as clearly as any memoir. They show choices being made in real time, with poor information and high stakes. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d297:
An instruction dated 19 September 1863 went from Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, in London. It appears as document 297 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Confederate agents were buying ships and arms in Britain, and Washington wanted the trade stopped. Orders to London often carried protests, evidence, and legal arguments for Adams to use. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d397:
To Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this formal note on 23 February 1863. It appears as document 397 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Canada, then a British colony, shared a long border with the Union. Worries about raids, plots, and smuggling across that line sit behind part of this correspondence. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d497:
Dated 7 May 1863, document 497 is a letter from Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington to Secretary William H. Seward. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily.

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d597:
Document 597, dated 27 July 1863, records a letter from Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington to Secretary William H. Seward. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the summer of 1863. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight.

The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d97:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams on 2 March 1863 — and wrote again, and again. Twelve letters to Adams in the volume bear this one date. Adams was the American minister in London. This letter is document 97 in part one of the 1863 volume, the first of the dozen.

A dozen sheets in a day is a desk cleared at one stroke, most likely a set of set-piece notes on the file's live points. Each stands on its own in the printing, numbered in line. This one opens the batch. Read as a group, the twelve show Seward putting the whole London brief in order on a single March day.
frus-1897:
Case lists give the 1897 volume its texture. Austria-Hungary's file names its grievances one by one. Trichinae in American pork heads the list. Insane Americans in Austrian asylums follow. Three military service cases appear by name. Brazil reports an attempt on President Moraes's life. China's headings urge fostering American interests there. Riot prevention still fills its file.

Britain's thread runs quietly beneath the list. Hay writes from London on a conference project. A Washington meeting on seals draws his diplomacy. He notes the year given to the imperial idea in the colonies. Japan's minister there views the project kindly. The volume balances pork, passports, and pelts. Small cases reveal the system's daily work. Each heading is a door into a dispute.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d197:
President Roosevelt telegraphed Prime Minister Churchill on 8 November 1943, in personal message number 412, sent from Washington via the naval attaché in London. The whole message takes three short lines and deals with a single phrase in the Allied agreement about Turkey.

Roosevelt accepts Churchill's suggestion that the words commanders responsible be changed to the Combined Chiefs of Staff. He adds that he has already told Ambassador Harriman in Moscow and authorized him to attach the agreement to the protocol. The brief exchange closed the wording dispute that Churchill's telegram 493 had opened two days earlier.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d297: President Roosevelt sent Secretary of State Cordell Hull a short secret telegram from Cairo on 24 November 1943, a progress note from the conference. The Lebanon matter looks better this morning, he reports, though Prime Minister Churchill is being very firm, and Foreign Secretary Eden arrives in Cairo that night. The conferences are going well, Roosevelt adds, and the business with Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek will finish in two or three days. Chiang will then return home, and the party will start on the next leg of the trip, toward Tehran.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d397:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull sent President Roosevelt a short telegram from Washington on 30 November 1943, questioning the President's choice of Ambassador Winant for the European Advisory Commission. It follows Roosevelt's one-line answer of the day before from Tehran.

Winant would certainly be a fine choice, Hull grants. But the American representative on the commission faces a full-time job, with much detailed drafting and discussion to come. One man, he argues, cannot combine the exacting duties of ambassador to Great Britain with those of commission member and do both jobs effectively. Hull closes by asking whether Roosevelt has any further comment or suggestions in light of that objection, or whether he still wishes Winant to hold both positions.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d497:
Admiral Ernest J. King, commander in chief of the United States Fleet, joined with Admiral Andrew Cunningham, Britain's First Sea Lord, in this memorandum of December 6, 1943. The two naval chiefs signed together on the closing day of the Second Cairo Conference. The State Department printed their paper in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

When the senior sailors of both navies signed one paper, the sea war was speaking with a single voice. Naval questions, above all the shortage of landing craft, ran through every Cairo argument about land operations. A joint King-Cunningham text shows the naval partnership at its closest. Readers get the admirals' shared view at the point where strategy met the hard limits of ships.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d97: Stalin wrote to Roosevelt on November 5, 1943, three weeks before the two men were to meet at last in Tehran. The message is Document 97 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Every exchange that month carried the nearness of the summit, even when its errand was small. The record names the date and the two leaders only. The message is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1944-quebec-d197:
No official minutes exist for the noon meeting of September 15, 1944, so the editors print Morgenthau's diary as the fullest account. Roosevelt, Churchill, Eden, and the Under Secretary took up the Phase Two lend-lease agreement. The president read it carefully. He added words to the clause barring export of lend-lease goods. First came "or sold," and then "for profit."

Churchill, Morgenthau wrote, was quite emotional, at one point with tears in his eyes, and thanked Roosevelt effusively once the agreement was signed. Then Churchill asked for the Ruhr minutes, which Morgenthau and Cherwell had agreed not to produce because they made too weak a case. Put out, Churchill restated his position forcefully himself and dictated the new memorandum to a stenographer.
frus-1944-quebec-d297: Writing on 18 September 1944, Prime Minister Churchill addressed his foreign secretary, Anthony Eden, in a message kept as document 297. It appears in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on the 1944 Quebec Conference, published by the Department of State. The text shows the British prime minister briefing his own foreign secretary in the days right after the Quebec meetings ended.
frus-1944-quebec-d97:
Secretary of Agriculture Claude Wickard wrote to President Roosevelt on August 23, 1944. His letter appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume. Wickard ran the department that oversaw American food production. Food was a weapon and a relief tool in wartime.

Cabinet voices beyond war and diplomacy also reached the President. Armies and allies alike needed American food shipments. Planners expected hungry civilians across liberated Europe that winter. A letter from Wickard brought those concerns into summit preparation. For readers, it widens the Quebec story beyond generals and diplomats. Feeding people formed part of winning the peace.
frus-1945-50-intel-d197: A text titled "Memorandum for the File" bears the date 17 July 1946. It survives in print as document 197 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. No CIA yet existed: a board called the National Intelligence Authority ran the work, with the Central Intelligence Group as its staff. The form is a note to the file: no request and no order.
frus-1945-50-intel-d297:
The memorandum of 6 August 1948 names the Record by the Chief of the Special Procedures Group (Cassady) as the man it was written for. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 297 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Reform of the CIA was in the air, with the Dulles survey under way and each agency guarding its own role.

A record memo speaks to the future reader more than to any chief: it exists so the file tells the truth later. Such notes anchor the rest of the paper trail around them. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d397:
Robert Schow, the CIA's assistant director for special operations, wrote to planning chief J. Prichard Childs on 26 August 1949. The memo is document 397 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Special operations meant secret work abroad, the most guarded part of the young agency. Schow's office ran that work while Childs tried to fit it into one government wide plan. Their exchange shows the pull between secret action and central control that marked the CIA from its first years. Coordination papers like this one rarely name foes or lands, but they set the frame for all later work.
frus-1945-50-intel-d97:
Magruder wrote to McCloy again on 25 October 1945, keeping his near-monthly rhythm of reports to his patron. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

By late October the SSU's position had a shape: tolerated in the War Department, eyed by State, and priced hard by the Budget Bureau. Magruder's letters steered between those forces. Readers should attend to what a chief in his spot could and could not say. He could plead usefulness; he could not command a future. The thread's interest lies in that narrow path, walked in careful prose through the whole autumn of decision.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d197:
Alarmed, Churchill answered on 19 November 1944. This excerpt from his message number 825 to Roosevelt is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It seizes on the President's promise to bring the American divisions home once Germany falls.

Put the two facts together, Churchill argues, and the sum is grim. If the Americans sail home at speed, the French lack an equipped postwar army. They have no time to raise one and no battle experience either. Who then holds down western Germany, up to the present Russian occupied line? Britain could not take the task on without American and French help. All would rapidly fall apart, as it did last time. He closes with a hope that his fears are groundless: “I put my faith in you.”
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d297:
Operations Grenade and Veritable puzzle the combined chiefs in these minutes of 31 January 1945. The Combined Chiefs of Staff record, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, catches a live argument about Eisenhower's coming offensive in the north. The sitting opened at half past two in Floriana.

Brooke questions a line in the record: he had not understood that Veritable was free of Grenade, but rather that it depended on it. General Smith explains the ground. Bradley is advancing on the Prüm-Bonn axis, and a quick reach to Euskirchen would help Veritable as well as Grenade would. Veritable hangs on neither, he says. Eisenhower, then at Bradley's headquarters, must decide by 1 February whether to halt Bradley and shift the troops north for Grenade instead.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d397: Harry Hopkins explained a delay to the President in this note passed at the February 8, 1945 plenary. The Joint Chiefs, he wrote, had told Sumner Welles something awkward. Defending the coasts of certain South American states against Japan would be hard for the United States. That, Hopkins added, was Welles's excuse. The note concerns why some Latin American states had not declared war. An editors' footnote adds a twist: the Defense Department later found no evidence in the Joint Chiefs' files to support Hopkins's statement.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d497:
Roosevelt put the same worry to Churchill in a letter of February 10, 1945. The United States, alone among the three great powers, would have a single vote in the Assembly of the world organization. That fact might endanger Senate ratification of the Dumbarton Oaks agreement. From their talk, he understood Churchill would not object to extra American votes if needed for parity.

He wrote, he said, because Churchill understood the American political situation so well. In reply, he hoped for agreement to the suggestion, should public opinion require some proposal. The letter shows the President counting Senate votes in the middle of the Crimea.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d97:
Colonies and mandates get a briefing book paper of their own under the heading “Dependent Territories.” Prepared for the President's trip, it is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It reports that the State Department has drafted three papers and shared them with no other government yet.

One draft lays out a plan for world trusteeship. A second sets up regional boards to advise on dependent areas. A third states how such areas should be run. The topic was dropped from the Dumbarton Oaks talks, but British, Soviet, and Chinese delegates showed strong informal interest. The drafts were under review by the Secretary's staff group and by the War and Navy Departments before going to other capitals.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d197:
The American chargé in Belgrade reported a Yugoslav plea in a telegram extract dated July 7, 1945. The extract is document 197 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The full message appears later in the volume.

Foreign Minister Šubašić expressed a hope, the extract says. He hoped the Big Three meeting will make a public reference to the Tito-Šubašić agreement. He also hoped it will remind the Yugoslav government that it must be carried out. That agreement was meant to join Tito's movement with the exiled royal government and lead to free elections. Shantz adds that he and the British representative believe such action would be desirable. The fragment shows the junior partner in Belgrade's coalition government looking to the summit to hold Tito to his promises.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d297:
Melbourne's despatch from Bucharest, dated June 25, 1945, takes stock of the Rumanian armistice as Rumanians and Russians then saw it. It was the third in his series of broad reports, after pieces on the Rumanian attitude and the Russian attitude. The armistice deal, he notes, touched nearly every problem in the country.

With the war in Europe over, Rumanians asked what the armistice still required of them. Melbourne records how officials, the public, and the Soviet authorities each read its terms. Reports like this one gave Washington a ground level view of a country under Soviet control as the Potsdam talks drew near.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d397:
East Prussia's future is decided in one short recommendation in a briefing book extract dated June 30, 1945. East Prussia should be ceded to Poland, the paper advises. The exception is the Koenigsberg district, which presumably will go to the Soviet Union. The rest of the German province would pass to Polish rule.

The basic data explain the bargain. The Warsaw Polish government claimed the whole of East Prussia. The Soviet Union favored Polish acquisition of the province, or all of it except the northeastern sector. That sector, including the chief city and port of Koenigsberg, Moscow intended to annex itself. The extract shows the map of eastern Europe being redrawn.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d497:
President Truman presses Churchill for joint timing in a message dated July 2, 1945. Ambassador Harriman has informed him, Truman writes, and he concurs, that the new Polish Provisional Government of National Unity has been established in conformity with the Crimea decision. The new government has addressed parallel communications to both leaders, requesting recognition.

On the basis of the assurances the new government has given, and on Harriman's recommendations, Truman plans to accord recognition effective at 7 p.m., Eastern War Time, on July 3. Now the matter has moved this far forward, he argues, any further delay would serve no useful purpose and might even prove embarrassing to both of us.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d597:
Acting Secretary of State Joseph Grew wrote to Secretary Byrnes on July 13, 1945, enclosing a press statement. The letter is document 597 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Grew's statement, made on July 10, dealt with reports of Japanese peace feelers.

Grew gives two reasons for speaking out. First, talk in U.S. speeches and editorials about a Japanese peace offer was growing fast. He feared it would sap war morale at home. He also feared Japan would read it as proof that America would settle for a compromise peace. Second, his firm statement would clear the ground for the President. Whatever Truman later said about what unconditional surrender would and would not mean would then hit with full force in Japan.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d697:
Joseph E. Davies, head of the President's War Relief Control Board, wrote a history memo on Russia, Turkey, and the Straits. Undated and filed July 4, 1945, it is document 697 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. It briefs the conference team on the deep roots of the dispute.

Davies starts with Peter the Great, who saw in 1697 that Russia needed ice-free ports. Russia has since sought control of the Bosphorus and the Dardanelles, the doors to the Black Sea. It has also sought Constantinople, holy to the Orthodox faith. Turkish rulers have maneuvered by war and alliance to block those aims since 1640. Their clash made the Eastern Question of the nineteenth century. Davies sums up its drives in a short list. Russia and Austria thirsted for the Mediterranean. Britain guarded the India route. Christian peoples wished for freedom from Turkish rule.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d97:
Ambassador Harriman renewed his requests to Vyshinsky in a letter dated June 25, 1945. The urgent letter is document 97 in the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Eisenhower had cabled again about scouting Zehlendorf, using the Halle-Berlin highway freely, and enlarging General Parks's party at Babelsberg.

The most pressing matter, Harriman writes, is a high-frequency radio telephone terminal and teletype system in Berlin, with a relay point near Luckenwalde. Major General Stoner and his Signal Corps group, sent from Washington for the job, wait at Frankfurt. The installations take time, and late starts risk missing the conference opening. Harriman also asks that the local Soviet commander in Berlin be allowed to decide such small matters on the spot.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1097:
British drafters wrote this extract of an Economic Sub-Committee report on July 21, 1945. It treats the liability of Italy and Austria to reparations, on economic grounds only. For Italy, the finding is blunt. She already owes America and Britain about 500 million dollars for relief supplies, and the debt is still growing.

Paying that debt alone, the committee holds, would exceed Italy's power to pay abroad for many years. Neither creditor will lend her money to pay reparations, and UNRRA will not ship free goods for that end. The draft suggests other amends instead: Italy might supply, free of charge, goods UNRRA needs for Allied countries such as Greece and Yugoslavia.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1197:
On 19 July 1945 the United States Chiefs of Staff issued this memorandum, the same day as a companion paper. Two staff notes in one day show the American military team working at full pace. Each took up a different side of the summit's military questions.

The chiefs' staff had to keep the envoys supplied with the services' view while talks moved fast. Papers were drafted, cleared, and sent within hours. This one is the second of its day's pair. Together the pair shows how much paper a single day of a summit could draw from one staff.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1297:
The British Chiefs of Staff issued this memorandum on 18 July 1945. Like its American mates, it did the staff thinking that leaders later turned into choices. The British run of papers in the volume mirrors the American one, date by date.

London's chiefs wrote with their own burdens in view: a tired army, a vast navy bill, and duties from Europe to Asia. This note carries that view at the talks' start. It is preserved in an American volume because the allied staffs shared their paper. That sharing is itself a fact about how the Western war was run.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1397:
Jefferson Caffery, the American ambassador in France, wrote to Georges Bidault, the French foreign minister, on 1 August 1945. The volume prints six Caffery letters to Bidault from the turn of August 1945. The letters came as the Potsdam Conference reached its close in Germany.

France's absence from Potsdam rankled in Paris, and Bidault worked to win a place in the councils that would run Germany. Caffery's letters carried the American answers, welcome or not. This letter was written on the day the Potsdam Protocol was signed. It shows the settlement's second tier being built in parallel. A shut-out ally was being brought into the peace, on terms set here. The run of letters is the volume's fullest view of that process.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-97: Placed after document 710 without a number of its own, this brief note comes from the editors of the Potsdam volume. Editorial notes in the Foreign Relations series act as signposts in a dense archive. They link papers, explain odd gaps, and give dates the documents omit. Readers who work through the July 1945 files meet this one as a short pause for context.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d797:
Roy Melbourne, the acting American representative in Rumania, wrote to the Secretary of State on July 17, 1945. Document 797 opens Melbourne's thread in the volume. He held the Bucharest post while its chief was absent. Rumania's armistice regime made his desk a hard one. The letter joined the second Potsdam volume.

An acting head of mission writes with care. Melbourne had full duties and a borrowed title. Readers see him reporting Rumania's state as the summit opened. His facts fed the Balkan side of the talks. The document shows the alliance's eastern posts at work: small teams, large problems, and a direct line to the top.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d897:
The Acting Secretary of State cabled Assistant Secretary William Clayton at Babelsberg on July 17, 1945. The cable takes up a British note about Edwin Pauley's instructions on interim exports from Germany. A wording problem in those instructions had caused confusion in London and Washington.

The Department reads Pauley's approval duty narrowly. His consent is needed only for goods claimed as restitution, not for exports in general. General Eisenhower holds charge of supplies and allocations. The cable says Judge Rosenman backs this reading. It asks Clayton to confirm that Pauley agrees before Washington answers the British note.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d997:
George Kennan sent Washington the full text of his note to the Soviet Foreign Office in this airgram of July 27, 1945. The note, coded Safehaven, concerns control of German assets in Spain. Kennan recalls an American proposal of June 18 for a joint approach to Madrid on behalf of the powers occupying Germany.

Since Soviet officials had issued like warnings to Sweden and Turkey, Washington assumes Moscow has no objection. The note states the shared aim: to prevent German property from being hidden or drained away, and to allow return of looted goods. It says America and Britain will soon ask Madrid to let their missions take control and active management of German property in Spain.
frus-1964-68v03-d97: An editorial note in the Vietnam volume records President Johnson's mid-day press conference of July 28, 1965. United States forces in Vietnam would rise from 75,000 to 125,000, he states, with more to follow as asked. The draft call would climb from 17,000 to 35,000 a month. He pledges to meet Westmoreland's needs in full. Readiness for open talks is stated in the same breath. The Chiefs moved the same day to send the Air Mobile Division and a Marine brigade. The note marks the war's open expansion.
gao-gaoreports-b-296197:
Aerosol Monitoring and Analysis protested a Defense Department award for hygiene and safety work in GAO decision B-296197, dated June 30, 2005. The winner was Industrial Hygiene and Training. The work covered plant hygiene, safety, and green services. The firm hit how the winner's past work was scored.

GAO denied the protest. The winner got credit for past work by firms and key staff set to do this job. GAO found that credit sound. Past work by the team named in the bid can count. It need not be work by the lead firm alone. Readers can use the ruling for team-based past work claims.
gao-gaoreports-b-298197:
Tarheel Specialties protested a Homeland Security task order in GAO decision B-298197, dated July 17, 2006. The holder was USIS. The work backed a firearms and tactics training unit. Sites were in Altoona, Pennsylvania and New Brunswick, Georgia. The unit buys guns, rounds, and gear for the agency. The firm said the work lay outside the holder's schedule deal.

GAO sustained the protest. The work in the order was not in the scope of the schedule deal. An order must fit the deal it rests on. Work past that scope needs a fresh contest. Scope is a hard gate for schedule orders. The order thus fell for scope breach.
gao-gaoreports-b-298297:
Lakota Technical Solutions protested the terms of a Navy call for processor units in GAO decision B-298297, dated August 4, 2006. The goods were Signal Data Processor assemblies. A rival firm had built the data pack for the goods. The firm said that role gave the rival an unfair facts edge. It also hit a lack of vow for pack grade.

GAO denied the protest. The data pack held facts full enough for all firms to bid. An edge that comes from past state work is not unfair. Agencies need not erase such edges. Past work will yield know-how. That know-how alone is no flaw in a fresh contest.
gao-gaoreports-b-298697:
HoveCo protested an Air Force award to Porter Manufacturing Corporation. The contract covered design and build of a trailer-mounted fuel dispensing system. Award rested on a trade-off of past record and price. GAO ruled in B-298697 on November 14, 2006.

The fight turned on one confidence rating. HoveCo said its past record merited an unknown rating. The agency gave it a little confidence rating instead. GAO did not need to settle that point. The record showed the firm lost nothing from the lower mark. The award would stand on the same path either way. Harm is the core of a protest claim. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-310797:
CETENAGROUP lost its protest. GAO decided B-310797 on February 14, 2008. The Army sought a media push in Afghanistan. The push backs the Joint Improvised Explosive Device Defeat Organization. It spreads signs, ads, and shows to split bomb crews from the crowd. The award went to Lincoln Group, LLC. CETENA fought the tech scores in the race.

GAO denied the protest. How bids are scored sits in the agency's free hand. The agency must set its own needs and the best way to meet them. A loser must show the score broke that trust. No such show was made on this file.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-297:
Financial Audit, GAO-05-297 of March 9, 2005, gives the audit of a small fund with a plain task: it pays for the Senate's food halls. GAO hired Clifton Gunderson LLP to audit the Senate Restaurants Revolving Fund for fiscal years 2004 and 2003. The fund takes in meal cash and pays the costs of the halls that feed the Senate each day.

The hired firm gave the books a clean bill in full. It found the sums shown fair in all big respects, under U.S. rules. It found the checks on cash and the law firm. It found no breach of the laws it tested that was worth a report.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-897:
Lab support costs at the Energy Department are examined in GAO-05-897, a report dated September 9, 2005. About two-thirds of the department's $26.9 billion in fiscal year 2004 spending went to 28 major facilities. Five big labs got about $2.9 billion for support of their missions. GAO tracked support cost rates from fiscal years 2000 through 2004. It also hunted for savings.

GAO found overhead rates rose at two labs and fell at three. But the rates cannot be compared fairly. Contractors sort costs into unlike buckets. A shared support measure helps, yet some category definitions stay unclear. That leads to confused, inconsistent reporting. Contracts now carry more cost-cutting incentives, GAO found. A pilot lets a firm earn extra years for strong performance and savings. More savings chances remain, it said.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-97:
Electronic disability claims at Social Security are assessed in GAO-05-97, dated September 23, 2005. A new system stores claim files as images, not paper folders. It serves 144 hearing sites and 54 state disability offices. The program behind it paid about $113 billion in 2004 to over 14 million people. In March 2004, GAO urged steps to make the rollout succeed.

Since January 2004, the system has reached 53 state offices and 85 hearing sites. Full rollout was due by late 2005. But certifying offices to keep the electronic file as the official record will run to January 2007. State officials voiced worries about reliability and limits. Many said electronic work took longer and used more resources than paper. The offices also lack backup plans for emergencies, GAO found. Three of its five past recommendations drew action.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-997:
Voter registration on the ground is surveyed in GAO-05-997, a report dated September 27, 2005. Past work shows sign-up flaws can leave voters missing from rolls on election day. GAO surveyed local officials in 14 places across 7 states. The states span Arizona to Wisconsin. Each state supplied one small and one large jurisdiction. Officials spoke to sign-up hurdles, roll cleanup, and new federal voting rules.

All but 1 of the 14 officials reported some challenges with applications. Drives run by outside groups posed hurdles in 12 of the 14 places. Half cited trouble checking forms for completeness or duplicates, with staffing named as one cause. Steps included hiring more staff and contacting applicants to fix facts. All but 1 office removed names in 2004 for reasons like moves or deaths. Officials described checks meant to keep eligible names from being cut by mistake.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-397:
Combat stress can leave deep wounds, and referrals decide who gets more care. In GAO-06-397 (May 11, 2006), GAO studies post-traumatic stress disorder in service members. Many troops in Operation Enduring Freedom and Operation Iraqi Freedom faced intense, long combat. Research links such combat to a high risk of the disorder. A fiscal year 2005 defense law directed the study.

GAO described Defense care benefits and VA services for these veterans. It counted troops who may be at risk and those referred for more checks. It also tested whether the department can assure that referrals happen. GAO said the factors providers use must be identified.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-97:
Two voluntary climate programs are weighed in GAO report GAO-06-97, dated April 25, 2006. Climate Leaders, run by the Environmental Protection Agency, works with firms. Climate VISION, run by the Department of Energy with other agencies, works with trade groups. Both urge members to set goals to cut greenhouse gases.

GAO checked how far members had moved through program steps. It reviewed how agencies track progress, and what they do when members stall. It sorted the kinds of goals set. It also weighed agency claims on the share of U.S. emissions covered. Both agencies, GAO said, should do more to spur progress.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-597:
Watchdogs inside the United Nations vary in strength, and GAO-07-597, a GAO report dated June 18, 2007, measures six of them. Since 2005, the UN has tried to reform how it runs itself. Member states pour in billions each year. They want proof the money is well used. GAO picked six of the largest UN bodies for the study.

For each one, GAO checked three things. It judged whether the internal audit office meets world audit standards. It judged the evaluation office against UN norms. It then asked whether the governing boards actually receive the results of oversight work. Some offices lacked staff, funds, or a free hand to publish findings. Audit committees were missing in places. GAO urged wider use of global best practice, so boards get fast, candid word on waste and failure. The United States, as a top funder, has a direct stake in the fix.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-697:
Help for foreign nations fighting terrorists is examined in GAO-07-697, a report GAO released on May 25, 2007. Three national strategies since the September 11 attacks told U.S. law agencies to help other nations. The goal is to find, break up, and prosecute terror groups abroad. GAO checked what guidance the agencies got. It also checked how far they had put that guidance to work.

The strategies gave broad aims but few hard details. They lacked clear goals, roles, and ways to work across agencies. Only the FBI had turned the call into its own guidance. It planned more staff abroad and more joint work with foreign partners. Officials at seven agencies said they got little to no direction from top councils. GAO urged the National Counterterrorism Center to write a clear plan. It also urged State, Justice, and Homeland Security to guide and track the work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-97:
Help for states when Medicaid costs spike fills GAO-07-97, dated October 18, 2006. Recessions push more people onto Medicaid rolls. States must pay their share just as revenues fall. Federal matching rates rest on state income data. The match may lag a state's real distress. GAO built and tested three aid designs. One targets states hit hardest by job losses. One uses two years of income data instead of three. One offers a rainy day fund or loan by state choice.

No single design fits every state or downturn, GAO found. An automatic trigger would beat ad hoc relief for speed. A test model caught about 90 percent of job loss growth in 2001. Targeting must respect how downturns differ by state. Faster income data would sharpen the match. A fund or loan option gives states control of timing. The health department offered no comment on the draft.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-197:
Costly leasing of federal office space is targeted in GAO report GAO-08-197, dated January 24, 2008. GAO put federal real property on its high-risk list in January 2003. Heavy reliance on long-term leases was a prime reason. Owning often costs less when space is needed for years. Agencies still held about 398 million square feet of leased space in fiscal year 2006.

Offices take over half of that space. GAO traced why agencies keep choosing leases over ownership. Budget rules and short-term ease play large parts. The leasing agency may soon lease more than it owns. GAO argues that a clear strategy is needed to break the habit.
garland-wayside-courtships-1897:
Appleton published Wayside Courtships in New York in 1897, with rights reaching back to 1895. A verse up front muses that the meeting of true lovers' eyes seems wrought of chance. Yet the same grim law may rule there as at a grave, the poem warns.

Love stories from the country roads of the Middle West fill the book. Young farm folk find each other at husking bees, church socials, and long walks home. The romances stay sweet without turning soft or false. Garland keeps his realist's eye on the hard lives behind each tender moment, in a charming and humane gathering.
gooderige-witch-stapenhill-1597:
Alice Gooderidge of Stapenhill faced her neighbors' charges in 1597, and the full record of her case survives in print. The Most Wonderfull and True Storie sets out her examinations at length. Few Elizabethan trials left so much of the questioning itself on the page.

The claims are small and close to home: beasts sicken, children ail, and old grudges turn sour. Under hard questioning, the talk moves from harm done to pacts and spirits. Readers can watch a village quarrel grow, page by page, into a capital case. The pamphlet is a tight, clear window on a county trial.
gorky-creatures-that-once-were-men-1897:
J. K. M. Shirazi translated Creatures That Once Were Men into English in 1905, from Maxim Gorky's early stories of the 1890s. Chelkash opens the volume: a bold harbor thief takes a peasant lad on a night smuggling run. Their clash over the money shows two Russias meeting in one boat.

Twenty-six Men and a Girl sets its scene in a damp bakery, where bakers worship a shop girl from afar. Other tales fill doss-houses and roads with tramps, outcasts, and wanderers. Gorky wrote from his own years of wandering, and the tramps made him famous. His sympathy for the lowest became a signature of Russian writing. These early stories still carry raw force.
haines-cia-ufo-role-1997:
A historian inside the CIA told the agency's own UFO story in 1997. Gerald Haines, of the CIA History Staff, wrote CIA's Role in the Study of UFOs for Studies in Intelligence. His account runs from the first saucer summer of 1947 to the year 1990.

Haines tells of the Arnold wave, the secret Robertson Panel of 1953, and the long years of quiet watch. He shows how spy planes and spy craft bred many of the sightings the public laid to space ships. The piece is rare: an agency judging its own part in a myth it helped feed. It stands as the in-house word on the matter.
harsha-charita-cowell-thomas-1897:
E. B. Cowell and F. W. Thomas made the first English Harsha-Charita in 1897 for the Oriental Translation Fund. Banabhatta, court poet of the seventh century, wrote the life of his king, Harshavardhana, as historical romance. The work opens with Bana's own wandering youth before it reaches the throne it celebrates.

Ornate Sanskrit prose was Bana's glory, and the translation labors honorably to suggest it. Courts, armies, hermitages, and a kingdom on the move pass in gorgeous procession. The book stands as both royal biography and a summit of Sanskrit prose art, now open to English readers.
holderlin-hyperion-1797:
Friedrich Hölderlin published Hyperion, his only novel, in two parts in 1797 and 1799. The text here is the German original, from the second edition of 1822. No English translation of the book is in the public domain. Hyperion, a young Greek, tells his life in letters to a German friend.

He recalls his teacher Adamas, his friend Alabanda, and his love Diotima. He joins the Greek rising against Turkish rule and sees hope curdle into bloodshed. Grief turns him toward nature, poetry, and solitude in his own land. The letters read as hymns as much as narrative. German readers prize the novel as a pillar of their Romantic age.
international-weekly-miscellany-of-liter:
Numismatic archaeology heads the International Weekly Miscellany for August 26, 1850. That was volume one, number nine, at New York. A great Paris work on coins and gems, fifteen years in making, is described. It runs from regal coins of Syracuse and the Ptolemies to modern pieces.

Fiction inside gives Edward a tense parting with a woman who begs a moment alone. She gives her hand to the friend of her lost Ferdinand and slips away. The Collas machine's faithful copies earn praise in the lead article. Coins, tales, and essays share the weekly's pages in equal measure.
james-vi-daemonologie-1597:
King James the Sixth sets out the lore of witches in Daemonologie, his book of 1597. James had sat through the North Berwick trials, where witches were charged with raising storms to sink his ship. In talk form, two men weigh magic, witch craft, and ghosts. The king's voice backs the hunts and gives their proof a crown's full weight in law and faith.

He went on to rule England as its first James. His book roamed both realms at once. It shaped the hunts and e'en the stage tales of his age. Few kings wrote such a text.
james-will-to-believe-1897:
William James published The Will to Believe in 1897, a set of essays on faith and inquiry. The title essay defends our right to believe before proof is complete. Some options in religion and life, James argues, are forced, living, and momentous. In such cases, waiting for proof is itself a choice with costs.

Other essays treat morality, life's worth, and the relation of mind and brain. James writes with candor and personal warmth. The book applies pragmatism to religion without reducing faith to utility. It became a classic defense of faith as a legitimate option. Philosophers still assign the title essay.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abihail-father-: Abihail is the name of five persons, listed in turn in this entry. The first was the father of Zuriel, a Levite of the Merari line, in Numbers. The second was the wife of Abishur, in First Chronicles. The third was a son of Huri, a Gadite living in Gilead. The fourth was a wife of Rehoboam and a daughter of Eliab, David's brother. The fifth was the father of Esther. In the last two cases the Greek version reads Aminadab.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-de-balm:
Abraham de Balmes was an Italian physician and translator of the early sixteenth century. Born at Lecce in the old kingdom of Naples, he died at Venice in 1523. Near the end he served as physician to Cardinal Dominico Grimani at Padua.

His Latin versions of Hebrew works on philosophy and astronomy won him fame in the Christian world. Two were dedicated to Grimani. At Padua he gave philosophy talks to Christian hearers. He also compiled a Hebrew grammar that treated syntax as its own branch, a first. It came out as Mikneh Abram with a Latin version. Christian pupils honored him at his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adeni-solomon-b: Solomon ben Joshua Adeni was an Arabian author and Talmud scholar. He lived in the first half of the seventeenth century at Sanaa and Aden. His name comes from that town. He learned under Bezalel Ashkenazi and the cabalist Ḥayyim Vital. In 1624, or 1622 by some counts, he wrote a note on the Mishnah. Parts of it show a sharp, modern style of study. He weighs text, spelling, and points with care. Manasseh ben Israel used his calls in a Mishnah print of 1632.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ahlwardt-herman:
Hermann Ahlwardt was among the most notorious anti-Semitic agitators of his day. He was born on December 21, 1846, at Krien in Prussian Pomerania. Trained as a teacher, he became rector of a Berlin school in 1881. Money troubles followed, and Jewish friends and lawyers helped him out of them. For a time he even called himself a friend of the Jews.

He then joined the anti-Semitic movement and issued venomous pamphlets. His Judenflinten charge of 1892 claimed that a Jewish firm had sold worthless guns to the army. The charge was declared unfounded, yet his fame grew. He was elected to the Reichstag on December 5, 1892, while still on trial for libel. Four days later he drew five months in prison. In 1895 he tried to stir the same agitation in America, and failed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alcolea-1097:
Alcolea is a city in the province of Jaen, in Andalusia. Its Jewish congregation held special privileges, like many others in Spain. By its own records, a standing committee of twelve members taxed the flock. Each man was taxed by his means, a rule that bred constant quarrels. Anyone who won a tax cut from the governor was banned for a year at once.

The flock even tried to tax its own cantor, toward old debts as well as current costs. That fight ended in a lawsuit. Early in 1414 the small community accepted baptism as a body. The entry calls it one episode in the preaching march of Vincente Ferrer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alnaharwanai-jo: Jose Alnaharwanai was a Hebrew scholar of the gaonic age. He was most likely from Nehardea. He wrote a poem on the Jewish calendar. The poem runs in rhyme and in letter order. It was printed in a journal called Kerem Hemed. The entry values the poem for two things. It shows how the calendar grew over time. It also shows the shape of newer Hebrew verse.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-amico-joseph-or:
Joseph Amico, first called Amigo, was a learned rabbi. He was born in Tunis, the entry thinks. After the year 1550 he went to Italy. A hard divorce case split the rabbis of his day. Amico took the side of Moses Provencal in that fight. His rulings were couched in mild terms. He urged both sides to act with care.

A second case dealt with the law of levirate wedlock. That case came up in the year 1573. Amico held that the levirate duty comes first. Release by the rite of halizah comes after, he held. No date or place marks his rulings. Where he lived can not be fixed with sureness.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-andrada-salvado: Salvador d'Andrada was one of the earliest Jewish settlers in New York. His name first appears in 1655. He seems to have been richer than most of his fellows and active in trade. He led efforts to secure Jewish civil and political rights under Dutch rule. He claimed rights to own land, to equal tax treatment, and to trade across Dutch lands. His surname also appears among Maranos in Brazil, Mexico, and the West Indies.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-antipas-herod-a:
Herod Antipas was the youngest son of Herod the Great by his Samaritan wife Malthace at the time of his father's death. Born before 20 B.C., he died in exile about the year 39. Like most of his family, he was schooled at Rome and kept close to the imperial court.

Greek inscriptions from Kos and Delos show that he traveled widely. The entry then follows his rise: Herod first named him heir to the whole kingdom after a poisoning plot came to light, then changed the plan. Antipas became tetrarch instead. The entry traces his rule, his marriage scandal, and his dealings with John the Baptist and Jesus from the sources.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aquin-philippe-:
Philippe d'Aquin was a Hebraist born at Carpentras about 1578 who died at Paris in 1650. Early in life he left his home town for Aquino, where he converted to Christianity. There he changed his name from Mordecai to Philippe d'Aquin.

In 1610 he went to Paris, and Louis XIII made him professor of Hebrew. He appears among the accusers in the 1617 trial for the crime of Judaism against the Marquis d'Ancre and his wife, in whose household he had served. His works listed here run from Hebrew roots and rabbinic sayings in 1620 to a study of the Tabernacle and a Hebrew dictionary in 1629. The entry gives his long list of books in full.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arakin-estimati:
Arakin, or Estimations, is a treatise of the Mishnah, the Tosefta, and the Babylonian Talmud, in the order Kodashim. Its Mishnah has nine chapters and fifty paragraphs in all. Its chief task is to fix exact rules for the vows in Leviticus, chapter 27, verses 2 to 29.

Those verses set fixed rates for buying back persons or things vowed to the sanctuary. The entry explains that a vow over a person means a pledge to pay that person's rated value. Chapter one asks who may vow and whose value must be paid. Chapter two sets the most and the least a dedicator must give, scaled to his means. That topic opens side paths into the highest and lowest measures for many other duties.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arnold-1797:
Arnold, cardinal-bishop of Cologne, who died on April 3, 1151, was one of the few church leaders who shielded Jews during the Crusades. In the Second Crusade, preaching by the French monk Rodolphe stirred crowds across the Rhine provinces to attack Jews. Jews who refused baptism were tortured and killed. Arnold was persuaded, by a gift of money, to act.

He set aside the castle of Wolkenburg in Lorraine, near Konigswinter, as a refuge. Jews who fled there on September 23 and 24, 1146, could defend themselves with arms. Their left-behind property went to the bishop. When two Jews, Abraham and Samuel, were murdered on the road to the castle, a second gift moved him to have the murderer cruelly put to death. The account rests on Ephraim ben Jacob, who was himself shut up in Wolkenburg.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ascher-simon-18: Simon Ascher, born in Holland in 1789, served as hazan, reader and cantor, of London's Great Synagogue for thirty-seven years. He died at London in December 1872. Working with Mombach, the well-known composer, he helped systematize English synagogue music. English Jews kept his voice as a living tradition long afterward. The entry recalls his clear tenor and his florid recitative, full of roulades, as the sounds that defined his long tenure.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashmun-or-eshmu:
Ashmun, or Eshmun, was a Phenician god worshiped at Sidon and Carthage, and in Cyprus and Sardinia. A three-language inscription from Sardinia matches him to Aesculapius, the Greek god of healing. Near Sidon, King Eshmunazer built him a temple on a mountain and consecrated a spring and a grove to him. Strabo calls that place the Aesculapius grove.

His worship spread wide. Many personal names in the inscriptions of Cyprus carry his name. At Carthage he shared a temple with Tanith and Baal. In many names he is called Adonis, from Adon, Lord. That link leads the entry to a closing guess: Ashmun may be a local name for Tammuz, whom the Greeks called Adonis.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-attestation-of-:
Attestation is the signing of a paper by witnesses. Jewish law starts from a strict rule: a fact stands only on the word of two witnesses. In time, a written paper signed by two witnesses gained the same force as spoken testimony. But the entry draws a sharp line with modern practice. Modern witnesses vouch for a signature. Jewish witnesses vouch for the event itself.

That is why the rules are strict. Witnesses have to go through the paper word for word before signing. They must know both parties by name, or have them pointed out. The entry gives the approved wording of an attestation, built around the rite of symbolic possession. It then treats deeds of debt. A duly signed deed becomes like a public record, and the debt follows the debtor's land even into a buyer's hands.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bacharach-2297:
Bacharach is a name borne by many German Jews. It appears from the twelfth century, or at any rate the fifteenth, in many spellings. They do not form one family. The name only shows that a line came from the city of Bacharach on the Rhine, or once lived there.

The first notice of the name is doubtful. A Samuel Bacharach is cited in 1175, but the reading may mean Samuel in the city of Bacharach. A firmer case comes in the fifteenth century, with Ephraim Gumprecht Bacharach of Frankfort. From the late sixteenth century the name grows common in western Germany. The entry traces a Frankfort line through Mendel and Moses down to Naphtali Herz Gans Bacharach, who died in 1709. That Naphtali praised the responsa of Jair Ḥayyim Bacharach yet never claimed kinship, proof that same name did not mean same blood.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-balak-2397:
Balak was king of Moab when Israel came out of the wilderness toward the land east of the Jordan, as Numbers xxii.-xxiv. tells it. Alarmed by Israel's numbers and victories, he called Balaam from the Euphrates to curse them. Like most ancients, Balak trusted a curse to work real harm. He offered rich sacrifices to bind the Deity to his wish. Instead, Balaam blessed Israel and foretold its victories.

A rabbinic section fills out the man. In that telling, Balaam had foretold that Balak, son of a minor prince, would one day be king. Balak had served Sihon and succeeded him. The rabbis call him a skilled sorcerer who knew a calamity was coming for Israel but not his own part in it. They fault his lavish promises and small deeds. A critical note closes the entry, tracing the tale to the old sources J and E.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baraita-on-salv:
Baraita on Salvation is a haggadic Baraita first printed by Schönblum at Lemberg in 1877. It lists twenty-four sins that delay the Messianic salvation and put off "the end," the destined redemption. For each sin a Bible verse is quoted to show its gravity. In most cases haggadic tales from the Talmud and Lamentations Rabbah are added to the same end.

No clue fixes the work's age, the entry says. Its heavy use of the Yerushalmi and Lamentations Rabbah, and its lack of quotes from the Babylonian Talmud, point to an early Palestinian origin. It must predate the start of the eleventh century, since Alfasi's list of twenty-four hindrances to repentance matches it closely. The two are likely two versions of one Baraita. Maimonides later reduced Alfasi's list to a system. A Solomon judgment tale at the end is called a later addition.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-barzilai-giusep:
Giuseppe Barzilai was an Italian lawyer and Biblical commentator born at Gradisca, near Triest, in 1828. He studied at Casalmaggiore and took his law degree at the University of Padua. He then practiced law at Triest and won note in several hard criminal cases there.

Barzilai was also a strong Hebraist and archeologist. His works include a translation of Lamentations with notes in 1867 and a metrical version of the Song of Songs. He wrote studies on the Behemoth, the Leviathan, and Semitic ideography. He served for years as secretary of the Jewish congregation in Triest.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bebai-biblical-:
Bebai, without any added name, appears often in both Talmuds and in Palestinian Midrash as a teacher of the third century. Writers on chronology long treated all of those sayings as one man's. The entry argues that they come from two men who share a name and an age.

One Bebai taught in Palestine and sat under Johanan and Assi. The other taught in Babylonia and gave rulings of his own on oaths and daily conduct.
