The team used the Global Youth Tobacco Survey. It was run in four Peruvian cities. Students reported their smoking and related behaviours. The survey also covered exposure to smoke and advertising. Such data show where prevention should focus. School-based surveys can be repeated to track change. The results support Peru's new tobacco control efforts. They also allow comparison with other countries.
openalex-w2107915297:
Jorge Alvar, Ivan Dario Velez, Caryn Bern and colleagues produced world estimates of leishmaniasis cases. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2012. The work formed part of a World Health Organization update. National experts supplied recent case data. Published studies were reviewed alongside.

The review covered nearly a hundred countries and territories. Two main disease forms were counted separately. Skin disease cases far outnumber visceral cases. Many cases are never officially reported, they stress. True totals likely exceed reported counts several-fold. Country profiles detail treatment and control in each place. The estimates guide funding for neglected disease programmes. They remain a standard global reference.
openalex-w2132343497:
G. Aad and colleagues in the ATLAS Collaboration published this measurement in the European Physical Journal C in 2015. They pinned down the jet energy scale for the ATLAS detector, which sets how the energy of particle jets is read. They also measured how uncertain that scale is, since every jet-based result leans on it.

The team used proton collision data and balanced jets against well-measured reference objects like photons. Computer simulations gave the first calibration, and data checks corrected the rest. In the central detector, the scale uncertainty fell below one percent for mid-energy jets. It rose for softer jets and for jets far forward, reaching about six percent at the edges.
openalex-w2172927897:
Isabelle Dusfour, Pilar Zorrilla, and Amandine Guidez led this 2015 study in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases. They probed how Aedes aegypti beats the spray deltamethrin in three French overseas lands. This pest spreads several viruses. Pyrethroid sprays are the main class used against it, yet they kill it less and less well worldwide.

Groups came from French Guiana in South America, Guadeloupe in the Caribbean, and New Caledonia in the Pacific. All three lands had already met this spray failure in the field. The study set out to pin down how the pest resists in each place. Its gene activity data were posted in a public archive for reuse.
openalex-w2173352997:
Andrés Rubiano, Nancy Carney, Randall Chesnut, and Juan Puyana published this review in 2015 on global neurotrauma research. Traumatic injury to the brain or spine is among the most serious public health problems worldwide. It robs people of potential, above all in low- and middle-income countries where care is thinnest.

The authors stress that research must fit each region's own needs and obstacles. In rich countries, patients skew older and crashes dominate, while poorer regions see young pedestrians and riders hurt most. They urge cheap, fresh tools like mobile health apps, better registries, and studies designed for local realities. Copying questions from rich settings, they warn, may miss what poorer places need most.
openalex-w2563105997:
Cristian Koepfli, Wang Nguitragool, and Natalie Hofmann, with colleagues, published this 2016 methods study in Scientific Reports. It tests droplet digital PCR, a technique for counting malaria parasites in blood. Knowing parasite density exactly matters for understanding how malaria behaves and harms people. Common methods need an external standard curve, which makes results hard to compare between studies.

Droplet digital PCR counts DNA directly, with no standard curve needed. The team used it on patients and on people carrying parasites without symptoms. For Plasmodium falciparum it proved more sensitive than standard quantitative PCR, and equally sensitive for Plasmodium vivax. Repeat measurements varied far less than with the older method. The authors conclude the technique gives sensitive, accurate counts. That helps studies where absolute parasite numbers, not rough estimates, are essential.
openalex-w2582944297:
Giovanna Micarelli reviewed Marisol de la Cadena's book Earth Beings for Universitas Humanística in 2016. The review, written in Spanish, presents the 2015 Duke University Press volume. De la Cadena is an anthropologist who worked closely with the Turpo family in the Peruvian Andes. Her book follows earth beings, mountain spirits called tirakuna, and the people who relate to them.

The book tells seven stories, Micarelli explains, framed by two interludes. They cover indigenous leadership, land struggle, Andean shamanism, and collaboration with a Washington museum. Ausangate, a being that is also a mountain, runs through the conversations. The stories resist neat conclusions and keep crossing between local and global scales. Micarelli presents the book as an important statement that culture alone cannot capture Andean worlds. In them, she notes, there are more than one but fewer than many ways of being.
openalex-w4200236397:
Peter Potapov, Svetlana Turubanova, Matthew Hansen, and colleagues mapped world cropland from satellites, in Nature Food in 2021. Consistent global data on farmland are needed to track progress toward sustainable food production. The team analysed two decades of satellite records to measure where cropland grows or shrinks. Their maps cover the first twenty years of this century.

Cropland expanded faster in the second decade than the first, above all in Africa and South America. About half of the new farmland replaced natural vegetation and tree cover. Because population grew faster still, cropland per person shrank over the period. Output per hectare rose through more intense farming. The maps expose a clash between feeding people and protecting ecosystems.
openalex-w4281836397:
Praveen Dhyani, Cristina Quispe, Eshita Sharma, and colleagues review the anticancer potential of plant alkaloids, in Cancer Cell International in 2022. Cancer kills about ten million people a year worldwide. Standard treatments work, but they are costly and tumours often grow resistant over time. Plant compounds offer a cheaper, proven source of cancer drugs. Alkaloids, a family of plant chemicals, are among the most successful.

The review focuses on six alkaloids, including colchicine and the vinca drugs vincristine and vinblastine. For each it covers medical uses, how it attacks tumours, and prospects for lab-scale production. Many of these drugs stop cell division by targeting the cell's internal scaffolding. The authors aim to support affordable cancer care built on these molecules.
openalex-w7204224797:
Gabriela Patriota Casado and Marcus Mauricius Holanda published a Portuguese-language legal-historical paper in Brazil in 2026 on schooling as an instrument of citizenship. The authors trace the right to schooling in Brazil from the imperial period to the republic, following the country's successive constitutions. Their bibliographic and documentary method uses a hypothetical-deductive approach, reading books, journals, the literal text of laws, and specialized sites.

Schooling in Brazil, they argue, moved from an elitist model toward a more inclusive one, though structural problems and institutional policies still mark the system. The study also brings in the constitutional principles of public administration, an area where they find little literature joining those principles, public policy, and the schooling right. Historical understanding, they contend, is what lets Brazil face today's problems and build a fairer, more effective school system.
openalex-w7204531397:
Everaldo Antônio de Jesus and Graciela Celsa Zarate Miranda released a Portuguese-language paper in Brazil in 2026 on overcrowding in the prison system of Brazil's Federal District, read through human rights. The study reviews studies, norms, case law, global parameters, and office records. At the end of 2025, official data counted nearly seventeen thousand people in physical cells built for under eleven thousand, an occupancy near one hundred fifty-nine percent.

That imbalance does more than strain administration, they argue: it aggravates the punishment actually served and undermines health, hygiene, safety, schooling, work, legal assistance, and individualized treatment. Building more cells alone cannot fix a crisis produced by accumulated penal and procedural choices. They call for capacity regulation, controlled intake, structured alternatives, and data-driven interinstitutional control.
openalex-w7204882697:
Manuela Nedel Simonetti led a Portuguese-language review, in Brazil in 2026, on the impact of mood problems during and after pregnancy. The team selected fifteen papers released between 2006 and 2024 from three sources, focusing on depressive and anxiety symptoms and their linked psychosocial factors.

Maternal psychic suffering was highly prevalent, the review finds, mainly among socially vulnerable pregnant women, those facing food insecurity, and those in high-risk prenatal care. The main risk factors were stress, low self-esteem, reduced income, and absent family support. Non-drug interventions such as supervised physical activity and digital emotional support tools looked safe and helpful for preventing postpartum depression. The authors urge adding mood screening into prenatal care with team support, protecting mother and newborn alike.
openalex-w7204993797:
João Vitor Dal Bon Rosales and Sinésio Ferraz Bueno released a Portuguese-language paper in Brazil in 2026 on how neoliberal rationality reconfigures the ends of today's schooling. Their hypothesis is that neoliberalism's reach into schooling is not just market tools or business methods, but the very rationality by which the purposes of formation are set. The study joins Horkheimer and Adorno on instrumental reason to Dardot and Laval on neoliberal rationality.

Generalized competition and the firm as a model of subjectivity radicalize instrumental reason, they argue, producing the business-minded subject who manages and prizes his own human capital. In schooling, self-rule, student lead roles, lifelong learning, and formation are ever more subordinated to adaptation, results, job readiness, and self-management. The central problem is not missing purposes, they conclude, but ones taken for granted that equate formation with efficient adaptation.
openalex-w7211996497:
Ana Patricia Pereira Ribeiro, Lorrana de Souza Freitas, and Robson Costa Pessoa write about the nurse's role in catching sepsis early in emergency care. Sepsis is the body's runaway response to infection; it can race toward organ failure and death, and its first signs are often faint and nonspecific. In crowded emergency rooms, the authors argue, the nurse stands in the decisive position: reading the patient at triage, watching vital signs, and mobilizing the wider team fast.

Their review gathers national and international guidance on screening tools, warning signs, and first interventions. Structured clinical protocols, they conclude, must be joined with the sensitivity of nursing care itself. That pairing shortens the time until treatment begins, changes outcomes for patients, and builds care that is both safe and humane. The article makes a professional case: early sepsis recognition is nursing work at its most consequential.
openalex-w7212112697:
Adriana Martins Reis and Debora Leite Silvano set out good practice for libraries that serve autistic students. A library is a public door to knowledge. For students on the autism spectrum, that door can stick. Blocks can sit in how staff speak, how facts are laid out, and in plain bias. The pair read past studies and Brazil's laws on access to build their guide.

Good practice, they find, sorts into six strands. Welcome and clear speech come first. Then come the layout of the space and access to facts in more than one form. Staff training and a voice for the student round out the list. One strand gives each student a guide of their own. The gains, the authors note, reach past one group. A calm, clear library serves all who walk in.
openalex-w7213438997:
Emanuel Lucas Vasconcelos and co-authors compare men's and women's results in a basic inorganic chemistry course. Their 2026 document study uses records from a state university covering twenty semesters, from 2015 to 2025. In total, 411 student records were analysed, grouped by sex as inferred from first names.

Women's final averages were slightly higher than men's across several assessments. Their pass rate was also a few points higher. The authors stress that the gaps were small and described only, with no claim of a deep cause. Results must be read against the many factors behind academic performance. The name-based grouping is noted as a clear limit of the study.
openalex-w7220659897:
Karen Esteves Ezezinos led a 2026 study of land use change around the many springs of the Ribeirão Achado basin in Santana do Paraíso, Brazil. The team registered the basin's springs, nearly two hundred, and built land use maps for 2008, 2014, and 2020 to see what was happening on the ground that feeds them. Pasture and shrubs, the predominant cover, shrank somewhat over the period, while dense vegetation held almost steady.

Degraded areas and planted forestry both grew, including on land occupied by springs, where more springs sat in degraded or forestry areas in 2020 than in 2008. The advance of degradation and forestry over spring areas, the authors conclude, demands conservation and recovery actions in the permanent preservation zones that should shield these water sources. The study turns satellite categories into a local warning: the basin's water begins exactly where its cover is thinning.
openalex-w7221197697:
Aline Silva de Jesus led a seven-author study, published in 2026, on oral health in the workplace and its effect on employee well-being and productivity. Untreated mouth disease reaches beyond the mouth, the authors argue, striking at self-esteem, general health, and how well a worker can do the job.

Set in the corporate environment, their work treats the mouth as part of occupational health rather than a private concern left to each employee. Pain, infection, and lost teeth can quietly tax concentration, attendance, and performance. The study makes the case that companies and workers share an interest in prevention and timely dental care. It speaks to occupational health readers looking for whole-person arguments inside workplace wellness.
plaw-105-1-1997:
Public Law 105-1 is a joint resolution from February 3, 1997. It makes technical corrections to a giant funding act. That act is the Omnibus Consolidated Appropriations Act, 1997.

One fix rewrites the defender services line for the courts. It completes a passage on lawyers for jurors. It sets the sum at three hundred eight million dollars. The fix counts as law from the start. A second fix raises a jobless insurance figure. It goes from about twenty-three million to about one hundred seventy-three million dollars. A third fix lets school funds serve a second program.
plaw-105-10-1997: Public Law 105-10, approved April 24, 1997, designates the J. Phil Campbell, Senior, Natural Resource Conservation Center. The name applies to the Southern Piedmont Conservation Research Center located at 1420 Experimental Station Road in Watkinsville, Georgia. Any reference in a law, map, regulation, document, paper, or other record of the United States to that center is deemed a reference to it by the Campbell name.
plaw-105-100-1997:
Public Law 105-100 funds the District of Columbia for fiscal year 1998. It was signed on November 19, 1997. The act covers the year ending September 30, 1998.

Title I starts with federal funds. Eight million dollars pays for a management reform program. The money sits in escrow with the city's control board. That board is the Financial Responsibility and Management Assistance Authority. A federal payment of one hundred ninety million dollars helps run the city. It also sits in escrow. The board frees the funds to the Mayor on its own terms. The act passed as H.R. 2607.
plaw-105-101-1997:
The Veterans' Cemetery Protection Act of 1997 became Public Law 105-101 on November 19, 1997. It toughens sentences for theft and vandalism at national cemeteries. The act amends chapter 91 of title 18.

The act orders the Sentencing Commission to act. Sentences for crimes against cemetery property must rise. The rise is at least two levels. The Commission must keep the terms severe but in line with other rules. A national cemetery means the National Cemetery System. It also means cemeteries run by the Army, Navy, Air Force, and Interior chiefs. The act passed as S. 813 in the Senate.
plaw-105-102-1997: Public Law 105-102, approved November 20, 1997, codifies transportation laws without substantive change and improves the United States Code. Working through title 49 and related provisions, it corrects cross-references, substitutes one section number for another, strikes stray words from headings and chapter tables, and aligns wording between sections. One section amends the Internal Revenue Code's highway trust fund provision to fix a reference to the Intermodal Surface Transportation Efficiency Act of 1991. The act is editorial maintenance on the code rather than new policy.
plaw-105-103-1997: Public Law 105-103 dates from November 20, 1997. It waives the time limits for one Medal of Honor award. The medal is for Robert R. Ingram of Jacksonville, Florida. Ingram served as a Navy Hospital Corpsman in Vietnam. The acts of valor took place on March 28, 1966. He was then a Hospital Corpsman Third Class. His unit was Company C, First Battalion, Seventh Marines. The fight was part of Operation Indiana. The waiver lets the President grant the medal despite the deadlines in title 10.
plaw-105-104-1997:
Public Law 105-104 is a joint resolution from November 20, 1997. Congress consents to the Apalachicola-Chattahoochee-Flint River Basin Compact. Alabama, Florida, and Georgia had made the compact.

The compact states its aims at the start. It seeks good ties between the states. It seeks to end present and future fights over the river. It splits the basin's surface waters fairly. It also sets up joint water planning. The states will build shared data bases. The deal covers all waters that rise in the basin. It took effect when each state and Congress had acted.
plaw-105-105-1997:
Public Law 105-105 is a joint resolution from November 20, 1997. Congress consents to the Alabama-Coosa-Tallapoosa River Basin Compact. Alabama and Georgia had made the compact. It is the sister deal to the Apalachicola basin compact of the same day.

The aims match those of the sister compact. The states seek good ties and an end to water fights. They split the basin's surface waters fairly. They plan water use together. They also build shared data bases. The deal covers all waters that rise in the basin in either state. It took effect when both states and Congress had acted.
plaw-105-106-1997: Public Law 105-106 dates from November 20, 1997. It concerns the Plains Railroad Depot in Georgia. The depot sits at the Jimmy Carter National Historic Site. One section of the act does the work. It amends the 1987 act that set up the site. The change strikes the depot's name from a list in that act. The title of the 1997 act speaks of acquiring the depot. The text works by taking the depot off the earlier list.
plaw-105-107-1997:
The Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 1998 became Public Law 105-107 on November 20, 1997. It approves funds for the spy agencies for one year. It also funds the Community Management Account. The CIA Retirement and Disability System is funded as well.

Title I approves the money through a classified schedule. Title II funds the CIA pension system. Title III adds broad rules. One rule limits how spy work may be done. Others treat staff details and sanctions laws. Some parts state the sense of Congress. They deal with contracts and with the receipt of classified facts.
plaw-105-108-1997:
The United States Fire Administration Authorization Act for Fiscal Years 1998 and 1999 became Public Law 105-108 on November 20, 1997. It funds the federal fire agency for two years. The base law is the Federal Fire Prevention and Control Act of 1974.

The act sets the sums by year. The first year gets more than twenty-nine million dollars. The second year gets more than thirty million dollars. A later part updates the fire safety standards. Named standards now reach their successor standards as well. The statute thus stays current when the standards change. The act passed as S. 1231.
plaw-105-109-1997:
Airport land the federal government had given Cleveland decades earlier could be sold off under Public Law 105-109, approved November 20, 1997. The act permits the city of Cleveland, Ohio, to convey certain lands that the United States conveyed to the city in a deed dated January 10, 1967, for airport purposes.

The Secretary of Transportation may waive terms of that deed so the city can convey an interest in the land. In exchange, the city must receive either the fair market value of the interest or an equivalent benefit. Whatever the city receives must go to developing, improving, operating, or maintaining a public airport, or to land producing revenues used for airport development.
plaw-105-11-1997: Public Law 105-11 is a small act from April 25, 1997. It makes a technical fix to title 28 of the United States Code. The fix deals with suits against terrorist states. It changes the words of the foreign sovereign immunity rule. The old words were the claimant or victim was not. The new words are neither the claimant nor the victim was. The rule concerns members of the armed forces. The fix covers claims that arose before, on, or after the act.
plaw-105-110-1997: Public Law 105-110 is a one-date act from November 20, 1997. It makes a technical fix to the charter of the American Legion. Congress chartered that veterans group in 1919. Section 5 of the charter holds the date at issue. The act strikes December 22, 1961. It inserts February 28, 1961. No other part of the charter changes. The act passed the House and Senate in November 1997.
plaw-105-111-1997:
Veterans who believed the VA had made an obvious mistake in denying benefits gained a written right to challenge old decisions under Public Law 105-111, approved November 21, 1997. The act amends title 38 of the United States Code to allow revision of veterans benefits decisions based on clear and unmistakable error.

A new section provides that a decision by the Secretary is subject to revision on that ground, and if the error is established, the earlier decision is reversed or revised. A corrected decision has the same effect as if it had been made on the date of the original one, protecting back benefits. Review may begin on the Secretary's own motion or at the claimant's request, which may be filed at any time.
plaw-105-112-1997:
The Law Enforcement Technology Advertisement Clarification Act of 1997 became Public Law 105-112 on November 21, 1997. It carves a police exception into a ban on ads. The ban covers ads for some electronic surveillance gear.

The act amends section 2512 of title 18. An ad for such gear is lawful in one case. The ad must travel in interstate or foreign commerce. It must go only to a phone or data service provider. Or it must go to a government agency with the right to use the gear. Federal, state, and local agencies all count.
plaw-105-113-1997:
The Census of Agriculture Act of 1997 became Public Law 105-113 on November 21, 1997. It moves the farm census to the Secretary of Agriculture.

The Secretary must take the census in 1998. It then runs every fifth year. The facts cover the year just before each census. Surveys and sampling may be used. False answers given on purpose draw a fine of up to five hundred dollars. Refusing to answer draws up to one hundred dollars. No one may be fined for keeping a Social Security number private. The act passed as H.R. 2366.
plaw-105-114-1997:
The Veterans' Benefits Act of 1997 became Public Law 105-114 on November 21, 1997. It revises and extends programs for veterans. The act amends title 38 of the United States Code.

Title I rebuilds the equal employment process at the Department of Veterans Affairs. It sets who hears bias complaints. It also orders a review of that system. Title II extends other programs. It covers housing loans for Native American veterans. It covers care for homeless veterans and those with mental illness. It also widens the use of leases of VA land. The act passed as S. 714.
plaw-105-115-1997:
Drug and device approvals were sped up and reshaped by the Food and Drug Administration Modernization Act of 1997. Public Law 105-115, approved November 21, 1997, amends the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and the Public Health Service Act to improve the regulation of food, drugs, devices, and biological products.

Title I concerns drugs. Its first subtitle renews the system of fees charged to drug makers, with findings, the authority to assess and use the fees, annual reports, and a termination date. A second subtitle adds improvements, including pediatric studies of drugs and faster study and approval for fast track drugs meant for serious conditions. Later titles take up devices and other parts of the agency's work.
plaw-105-116-1997:
People convicted of capital crimes were barred from the nation's most honored burial grounds by Public Law 105-116, approved November 21, 1997. The act amends title 38 of the United States Code to prohibit interment or memorialization in certain cemeteries of persons committing federal or state capital crimes.

The new section forbids federal officials from burying such a person in the National Cemetery System or Arlington National Cemetery, or honoring their memory in a memorial area there. It covers people convicted of a federal capital crime and sentenced to death or life imprisonment, and state capital offenders as the section defines them. The bar applies only when written notice of the conviction reaches the responsible official before an application is approved.
plaw-105-117-1997:
Public Law 105-117 dates from November 21, 1997. It bars one group from relocation aid. The group is aliens not lawfully present in the United States. The base law is the Uniform Relocation Assistance and Real Property Acquisition Policies Act of 1970.

A displaced person in that group gets no payments under the act. The lead agency had one year to write rules. The rules must set fair steps for deciding who qualifies. They must bar bias by displacing agencies. They must rest on sound facts. One exception survives. Cases of exceptional and extremely unusual hardship may still win aid.
plaw-105-118-1997:
Foreign aid and export support for fiscal year 1998 were funded by the Foreign Operations, Export Financing, and Related Programs Appropriations Act, 1998. Public Law 105-118, approved November 26, 1997, covers the year ending September 30, 1998.

Title I handles export and investment assistance, starting with the Export-Import Bank of the United States. It authorizes the bank's spending within its funds and borrowing authority, and bars any spending to export nuclear equipment, fuel, or technology to a non-nuclear-weapon state that has detonated a nuclear explosive. The subsidy appropriation for the cost of direct loans, loan guarantees, insurance, and tied-aid grants is six hundred eighty-three million dollars, available until September 30, 2001.
plaw-105-119-1997:
The Departments of Commerce, Justice, and State, the Judiciary, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 1998 became Public Law 105-119 on November 26, 1997. It funds those parts of the government for one year. The year ends September 30, 1998.

Title I funds the Department of Justice. General administration gets more than seventy-six million dollars. Part of that sum funds the Facilities Program 2000. The act caps posts and funds for top offices. The legislative and public affairs offices may not grow by quiet staff transfers. A counterterrorism fund holds twenty million dollars. The Attorney General directs its use.
plaw-105-12-1997:
The Assisted Suicide Funding Restriction Act of 1997 became Public Law 105-12 on April 30, 1997. It bars federal funds from backing assisted suicide. The act states the rule in plain terms.

Congress found that such acts had long been crimes in the United States. But court shifts might make the services lawful in some places. So the funding bar needed a clear statement. The bar covers health care programs. It covers some grants under the Developmental Disabilities Act. It covers advocacy programs too. The act also clarifies how advance directives stand. Its rules reach the District of Columbia.
plaw-105-120-1997: Public Law 105-120 is a housekeeping act from November 26, 1997. It is a joint resolution of the 105th Congress. It waives a parchment rule for the rest of the first session. The rule sits in sections 106 and 107 of title 1. The waiver covers funding bills for fiscal year 1998 only. Both general and continuing bills count. Such bills may be enrolled in the form the House Oversight Committee certifies. The form need not be parchment.
plaw-105-121-1997:
The Export-Import Bank Reauthorization Act of 1997 became Public Law 105-121 on November 26, 1997. It renews the Export-Import Bank of the United States. The bank finances the sale of American goods abroad.

The act extends the bank's life to September 30, 2001. It covers tied aid credit funds. It also extends loans for nonlethal defense goods with civilian uses. Other parts clarify how credit may be denied in the national interest. Child labor joins the list of factors. A new advisory group covers sub-Saharan Africa. One part bars aid tied to Russian missile transfers to China.
plaw-105-122-1997: Public Law 105-122, approved December 1, 1997, designates the United States courthouse at 200 South Washington Street in Alexandria, Virginia, as the Martin V. B. Bostetter, Jr. United States Courthouse. The building had lost its earlier Albert V. Bryan name to a new courthouse under a 1995 act. Any reference in a law, map, regulation, document, paper, or other record of the United States to that courthouse is deemed a reference to it by the Bostetter name.
plaw-105-123-1997: Public Law 105-123, approved December 1, 1997, designates the federal building courthouse at Public Square and Superior Avenue in Cleveland, Ohio, as the Howard M. Metzenbaum United States Courthouse. Any reference in a law, map, regulation, document, paper, or other record of the United States to that federal building courthouse is deemed a reference to the Howard M. Metzenbaum United States Courthouse.
plaw-105-124-1997:
America's quarters were redesigned state by state under the 50 States Commemorative Coin Program Act. Public Law 105-124, approved December 1, 1997, provides for a ten-year circulating commemorative coin program honoring each of the fifty states.

Congress found that the program would honor the federal republic, teach young people about the states' history and geography, and modernize coinage that had not changed in twenty-five years. It also found the coins could earn the Treasury large sums, including an estimated one hundred ten million dollars from silver proof sales and billions more in indirect earnings. The act then directs the issuance of redesigned quarter dollars over ten years, commemorating each state in turn.
plaw-105-125-1997: Public Law 105-125 dates from December 1, 1997. It amends the Communications Act of 1934. The topic is the status of eligible telecommunications carriers. That status brings support from universal service funds. Some carriers answer to no state commission. For them, the Federal Communications Commission makes the call. It names the carrier and sets the service area. It may name more than one carrier for an area. Extra care is due in areas served by a rural phone company.
plaw-105-126-1997: Public Law 105-126, approved December 1, 1997, extends the authorization to use official mail in locating and recovering missing children. Under the program the act continues, official mailings carry material meant to help find missing children. The act's single section is titled as an extension of that authorization, and the measure adds other purposes in the standard closing phrase of its heading.
plaw-105-127-1997:
The Hispanic Cultural Center Act of 1997 became Public Law 105-127 on December 1, 1997. It backs a Center for Performing Arts in New Mexico. The center sits in the New Mexico Hispanic Cultural Center complex. The act covers its design, building, furnishing, and equipping.

Congress found deep Hispanic roots in the land. A Spanish shipwreck hit the Texas coast in 1528. Friar Marcos de Niza entered New Mexico in 1539. Don Juan de Onate founded a capital in 1598. By the 1990 census, about 650,000 Hispanics lived in the state. Most had roots there of ten generations or more.
plaw-105-128-1997:
The Museum and Library Services Technical and Conforming Amendments of 1997 became Public Law 105-128 on December 1, 1997. It fixes the Museum and Library Services Act. That act runs the federal institute for museums and libraries.

One change concerns hiring at the institute. The Director may hire technical and professional staff outside the standard rules. Their pay may also sit outside the standard rates. Such staff may not pass one fifth of the full-time staff. Their base pay may not top the GS-15 rate. A later part treats special libraries. The act passed as S. 1505.
plaw-105-129-1997: Public Law 105-129 dates from December 1, 1997. It makes technical corrections to the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 1998. One fix clarifies a cross-reference in title 10. The rule concerns electronic commerce in defense buying. A second fix raises one sum tenfold. The sum marks fifty years since the Korean conflict. It goes from one hundred thousand dollars to one million dollars. Each fix counts as if it stood in the first act.
plaw-105-13-1997: Public Law 105-13 is a short act from May 14, 1997. It extends the terms of some members of two commissions. The groups advise on Medicare pay. One is the Prospective Payment Assessment Commission. The other is the Physician Payment Review Commission. A member whose term would end in 1997 serves longer. The new end date is May 1, 1998. The act changes nothing else about the groups.
plaw-105-130-1997:
The Surface Transportation Extension Act of 1997 became Public Law 105-130 on December 1, 1997. It keeps highway and transit programs alive for six months. Congress was still at work on a new version of the Intermodal Surface Transportation Efficiency Act of 1991.

The Secretary of Transportation sends funds to each state. Each state gets the same share it held in fiscal year 1997. The share rests on obligation authority for the federal-aid highway program. Inside each share, set parts go to named programs. They include interstate upkeep, bridges, and air quality work. A minimum allocation is part of the math.
plaw-105-131-1997: Public Law 105-131, approved December 2, 1997, designates the United States Post Office building located at 1919 West Bennett Street in Springfield, Missouri, as the John N. Griesemer Post Office Building. Any reference in a law, map, regulation, document, paper, or other record of the United States to that post office building is deemed a reference to the John N. Griesemer Post Office Building.
plaw-105-132-1997:
The Lower Brule Sioux Tribe Infrastructure Development Trust Fund Act became Public Law 105-132 on December 2, 1997. It grants the tribe some benefits of the Pick-Sloan Missouri River Basin program.

Congress found that two dams drove the need. Fort Randall and Big Bend are key parts of Pick-Sloan. They overlie the east edge of the Lower Brule Indian Reservation. Their waters flooded the tribe's best lands. Those were the fertile, wooded bottom lands by the river. They were the tribe's most productive farm and pasture land. They were also its homeland. One past law took 7,997 acres for Fort Randall alone.
plaw-105-133-1997:
Public Law 105-133 dates from December 2, 1997. It sets a goal of 2,500 Boys and Girls Clubs of America sites by the year 2000. It amends a program part of the Economic Espionage Act of 1996. The club grant power sat in that act.

The new aim is seed money for 1,000 more clubs. Public housing projects and distressed areas come first. The total must reach at least 2,500 sites by December 31, 1999. The Bureau of Justice Assistance makes a grant each year. The grants run for fiscal years 1997 through 2001. They build and extend clubs where they are needed.
plaw-105-134-1997:
The Amtrak Reform and Accountability Act of 1997 became Public Law 105-134 on December 2, 1997. It reforms the laws on Amtrak, the national passenger railroad. It also funds the railroad. The act amends title 49 of the United States Code.

Title I holds the reforms. One part covers how Amtrak runs its trains. It treats the basic system and route tests. It covers mail, express, and auto-ferry work. It also covers trains run at the request of states. Commuter service and joint bus service appear as well. Later parts treat buying and other sides of the business.
plaw-105-135-1997:
The Small Business Reauthorization Act of 1997 became Public Law 105-135 on December 2, 1997. It renews the programs of the Small Business Administration.

Title I sets the sums for the agency's work. Title II treats financial aid. One part revises the microloan program. It adds a welfare-to-work microloan effort. A second part covers small business investment companies. It allows five-year pledges to those firms. It aims help at underserved areas. It also treats fees and program reform. Later parts cover advice services and the women's business programs. The act passed as H.R. 2261.
plaw-105-136-1997: Public Law 105-136 is a short act from December 2, 1997. It amends the Immigration and Nationality Act. The change funds refugee and entrant aid for two years. The old text named fiscal years 1995, 1996, and 1997. The act strikes those years. It inserts fiscal years 1998 and 1999. The change takes effect on October 1, 1997. The act passed as S. 1161.
plaw-105-137-1997:
The Aviation Insurance Reauthorization Act of 1997 became Public Law 105-137 on December 2, 1997. It extends the federal aviation insurance program. That program sits in chapter 443 of title 49. It covers aircraft when private cover is hard to get.

The act ties the value set on an aircraft to trade practice. The Secretary must use sound business practice from the aviation insurance field. The same test caps the insured sum. A pact signed by the President counts as a finding that the flights serve foreign policy. Policies may also allow binding arbitration of claims.
plaw-105-138-1997:
Public Law 105-138 dates from December 2, 1997. It backs a Center for Historically Black Heritage at Florida A&M University. The act covers the design, building, furnishing, and equipping of the center.

Congress found a vast store of artifacts at the school. Some 500,000 items come from the Civil War era. Others come from the early civil rights movement in the Southeast. The federal government should share the cost, Congress said. The Secretary of the Interior may grant funds to Florida. The federal share is fifty percent. The act authorizes three million eight hundred thousand dollars.
plaw-105-139-1997: Public Law 105-139 dates from December 2, 1997. It makes technical corrections to the Nicaraguan Adjustment and Central American Relief Act. That 1997 act lets many Nicaraguans and Central Americans gain lawful status. The fixes edit the rules for applicants. They also edit the rules for spouses and children. One cross-reference to the Immigration and Nationality Act is struck. One eligibility phrase is cut. The word inadmissibility replaces exclusion. More fixes tidy the old rules on suspension of deportation.
plaw-105-14-1997:
Public Law 105-14 dates from May 14, 1997. It lets the President award a gold medal for Congress. The medal honors Francis Albert Frank Sinatra. It marks his work in entertainment and his humanitarian acts.

The findings praise a career of more than five decades. Sinatra worked as a producer, director, actor, and singer. He made more than 50 albums and acted in more than 60 films. His honors include eight Grammy Awards and two Academy Awards. He also won an Emmy and the Kennedy Center Honors. The Presidential Medal of Freedom is on the list.
plaw-105-140-1997: Public Law 105-140 is a joint resolution from December 2, 1997. It sets the start of the second session of the 105th Congress. The session begins at noon on Tuesday, January 27, 1998. Congress may also come back sooner. It would meet at noon two days after members get notice. The Speaker and the Senate Majority Leader act jointly on that call. They first consult the minority leaders of both houses.
plaw-105-141-1997:
Deportable people were to be identified before they ever saw a judge under Public Law 105-141, approved December 5, 1997. The act requires the Attorney General to establish a program in local prisons to identify, prior to arraignment, criminal aliens and aliens unlawfully present in the United States.

Within six months, and subject to appropriations, the Attorney General must set up the program in local jails holding people before arraignment on criminal charges. It stations at least one Immigration and Naturalization Service employee with identification expertise at each chosen facility, funded full-time, including the busiest hours. Those employees get access to federal law enforcement records and report to the court before arraignment when the Service intends to remove someone.
plaw-105-142-1997: Public Law 105-142 dates from December 5, 1997. It clarifies the Pilot Records Improvement Act of 1996. That act tells air carriers to check a pilot's records. The checks come before hiring. The fixes shift the trigger point. The duty now bites before a pilot starts service. One special rule helps small operations. A carrier may let a pilot fly for up to ninety days. The aircraft must be small, or a helicopter, on nonscheduled trips. The records check must close within that span.
plaw-105-143-1997:
Judgment money owed to Michigan's Ottawa and Chippewa Indians was divided up under the Michigan Indian Land Claims Settlement Act. Public Law 105-143, approved December 15, 1997, provides for the division, use, and distribution of judgment funds awarded in dockets 18-E, 58, 364, and 18-R before the Indian Claims Commission.

Title I lays out how the funds are split, how tribes develop plans for using or distributing their shares, and how a judgment distribution roll of descendants is prepared. It gives separate plans for the Bay Mills Indian Community, the Sault Ste. Marie Tribe of Chippewa Indians, and the Grand Traverse Band, plus payments to newly recognized or reaffirmed tribes.
plaw-105-144-1997:
Public Law 105-144 dates from December 15, 1997. It lets the Library of Congress gain land in Virginia. The seller is the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond. No payment changes hands.

The Architect of the Capitol may take title to three parcels. They total about 41 acres in Culpeper County. The buildings on the land come with it. Once held, the site serves the Librarian of Congress. It will house a national audiovisual conservation center. A second part extends the Library's grounds law to the site. Film and sound holdings gain a new home.
plaw-105-145-1997:
A rural stretch of the Mississippi-Tennessee line was targeted for development by the Chickasaw Trail Economic Development Compact, consented to by Congress in Public Law 105-145, approved December 15, 1997. The joint resolution grants consent to the compact between Tennessee and Mississippi.

The compact's purpose is to develop an undeveloped rural area of Marshall County, Mississippi, and Fayette County, Tennessee, and to create a development authority using public and private partnerships. The authority would prepare developed sites for manufacturing plants, distribution and research facilities, and regional offices. Its members are appointed by each governor, the states' economic development chiefs, the counties, and the property owners' group, serving four-year terms without pay.
plaw-105-146-1997:
The Atlantic Striped Bass Conservation Act Amendments of 1997 became Public Law 105-146 on December 16, 1997. It renews and amends the Atlantic Striped Bass Conservation Act. The act restates the whole law.

The findings call the fish a historic prize. It matters to both commercial and sport fishing. It also matters to the Atlantic coastal states. No one government runs the fish across its full range. Stocks have swung widely over time. Causes include fishing pressure, pollution, and habitat loss. The findings warn of future depletion. Good monitoring and care are the cure the act builds on.
plaw-105-147-1997:
The No Electronic Theft (NET) Act became Public Law 105-147 on December 16, 1997. It strengthens the criminal law on copyright. Online copying of music and software is the target.

The act widens the term financial gain. Gain now means getting anything of value. Even other copyrighted works count. Willful copying is a crime in two cases. One is copying for profit. The other is copying works worth more than one thousand dollars in 180 days. Electronic copying counts the same. Proof of copying alone does not show willfulness. The time to bring a case rises from three years to five.
plaw-105-148-1997:
Public Law 105-148 dates from December 16, 1997. It aids the families of passengers on foreign airlines after a crash. The act amends title 49 of the United States Code. Two parties gain duties. One is the National Transportation Safety Board. The other is each foreign air carrier.

The act adds a new section on family needs. Each foreign carrier must hold a plan for crashes of its aircraft. The Board takes on matching duties. The change extends a known framework to overseas carriers. United States airlines already worked under such a plan rule.
plaw-105-149-1997: Public Law 105-149 dates from December 16, 1997. It amends the federal charter of Group Hospitalization and Medical Services, Inc. Congress chartered that health insurer in 1939. A new charter part lets it have one class of members. The class holds at least one and at most thirty members. The bylaws set the class's rights and voting rules. They also set meeting and quorum rules. A member that is a firm must be nonprofit. The firm may not be dissolved without the consent of Congress.
plaw-105-15-1997: Public Law 105-15 dates from May 15, 1997. It amends titles XVIII and XIX of the Social Security Act. Those are the Medicare and Medicaid titles. The act allows a waiver of one ban. The ban bars nurse aide training in some nursing homes. A program may run in a facility, though not by it, if the state so finds. The state must see no like program within a fair distance. It must assure a fit setting through oversight. It must tell the state long-term care ombudsman.
plaw-105-150-1997: Public Law 105-150 dates from December 16, 1997. It amends the customs user fee rule in a 1985 budget act. The change lets fee funds pay for customs staff in Florida. The staff check passengers who arrive by ship. After set reimbursements are made, spare funds may pay salaries. The funds cover up to fifty full-time posts. The posts run through September 30, 1998. They serve passengers on commercial vessels. The posts are due whether or not those passengers owe fees.
plaw-105-151-1997: Public Law 105-151 dates from December 16, 1997. It is a joint resolution on Washington area transit. Congress consents to new changes to the Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Regulation Compact. Maryland, Virginia, and the District of Columbia made the changes. One change guards riders on fares. The board may not raise a fare without a public hearing. A major service cut needs a hearing too. Notice must run at least fifteen days. A second change lets Metro Transit Police carry their issued weapons off duty. Local limits still apply.
plaw-105-152-1997:
The Army Reserve-National Guard Equity Reimbursement Act became Public Law 105-152 on December 17, 1997. It repays soldiers sent to Europe for the Bosnia mission. The costs at issue are out-of-pocket sums for shipping personal goods. The window runs from October 1, 1996 to May 31, 1997.

The Secretary of the Army may pay a soldier back. The shipment must be one that a weight allowance would have covered on June 1, 1997. Covered soldiers deployed under orders with no such allowance. Some were coming home from Europe. The money comes from funds on hand for the allowance itself.
plaw-105-153-1997:
The Federal Advisory Committee Act Amendments of 1997 became Public Law 105-153 on December 17, 1997. It clarifies how open-meeting rules treat the national academies. The academies are the National Academy of Sciences and the National Academy of Public Administration.

Committees set up by either academy no longer count as advisory committees. But terms apply. An agency may not use advice from a committee made under an agency deal unless the committee was free of agency control. No federal officer may run it either. Committees made after the act must also meet the new membership rules.
plaw-105-16-1997:
Public Law 105-16 dates from June 2, 1997. It lets the President award Congress's gold medal to Mother Teresa of Calcutta. The medal honors her humanitarian and charitable work.

The findings praise nearly seventy years of selfless work. She founded the Missionaries of Charity. Its members serve the poor with no material reward. The order counts well over three thousand members. They work in twenty-five countries. Her honors fill a long list. She won the first Pope John XXIII Peace Prize in 1971. She won the Jawaharal Nehru Award in 1972. She won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979. She won the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1985.
plaw-105-17-1997:
The Individuals with Disabilities Education Act Amendments of 1997 became Public Law 105-17 on June 4, 1997. It rewrites and renews special education law. The act restates parts A through D of the base act in full.

Part A opens with the short title. It then gives findings and purposes. It defines the act's terms. It keeps the Office of Special Education Programs in place. It covers the loss of state sovereign immunity. It covers buying equipment and fixing up facilities. It covers jobs for people with disabilities. The restated parts became the working text of the law schools follow.
plaw-105-18-1997:
Flood recovery at home and peacekeeping abroad shared one emergency bill, the 1997 Emergency Supplemental Appropriations Act for Recovery from Natural Disasters, and for Overseas Peacekeeping Efforts, Including Those in Bosnia. Public Law 105-18, approved June 12, 1997, covers the fiscal year ending September 30, 1997.

Title I adds emergency money for the Department of Defense, beginning with military personnel: more than three hundred million dollars extra for the Army and a smaller addition for the Navy. The amounts are designated as emergency requirements under the Balanced Budget and Emergency Deficit Control Act of 1985, so they sit outside the usual spending limits.
plaw-105-19-1997:
The Volunteer Protection Act of 1997 became Public Law 105-19 on June 18, 1997. It shields people who give their time to charities. The shield covers lawsuits based on their volunteer work. Nonprofit groups and government bodies are covered too.

Congress found that fear of suits was deterring volunteers. Nonprofits, schools, and civic programs had lost board members and helpers. Communities were left with fewer and costlier services. Federal funds support many volunteer-run programs. So Congress treated the risk as a proper federal subject. The act limits the personal liability of volunteers. It then sets the protections that follow from the findings.
plaw-105-2-1997:
Aviation taxes that had lapsed were switched back on by the Airport and Airway Trust Fund Tax Reinstatement Act of 1997. Public Law 105-2, approved February 28, 1997, amends the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 to reinstate the Airport and Airway Trust Fund excise taxes that fund the nation's airports and airways.

The act resets the fuel tax provisions: the rate on aviation fuel is set at 4.3 cents per gallon for the period after December 31, 1996 up to a week after enactment, and again after September 30, 1997. Aviation gasoline receives parallel treatment, with its 4.3 cents per gallon rate applying after September 30, 1999. The drafting untangles paragraphs added by the Small Business Job Protection Act of 1996.
plaw-105-20-1997:
The Drug-Free Communities Act of 1997 became Public Law 105-20 on June 27, 1997. It gives local coalitions a federal grant program. The coalitions fight youth drug use. The act amends the National Narcotics Leadership Act of 1988. A community must first show a long-term commitment to cutting youth substance abuse.

The act adds a Drug-Free Communities chapter to the drug control statute. Its findings state a sharp rise in youth drug use. Use more than doubled in the five years before 1996. Marijuana, inhalants, cocaine, methamphetamine, LSD, and heroin all rose. The steepest rises came among thirteen- and fourteen-year-olds. The findings warn that casual use today becomes hard-core abuse in the next generation.
plaw-105-21-1997: Public Law 105-21, approved June 27, 1997, is a joint resolution consenting to Hawaii state amendments to the Hawaiian Homes Commission Act of 1920. The Hawaii Admission Act requires federal consent for such changes. Congress consents to two state measures: Act 339 of the Session Laws of Hawaii, 1993, and Act 37 of the Session Laws of Hawaii, 1994.
plaw-105-22-1997: Approved on June 27, 1997, Public Law 105-22 deals with Hong Kong's official economic and trade missions in the United States. It allows the rules of the International Organizations Immunities Act to be extended to the Hong Kong Economic and Trade Offices on the same terms as for a public international organization. It also lets the President apply a 1994 agreement on state and local taxation of foreign employees to those offices.
plaw-105-23-1997: Public Law 105-23, approved July 3, 1997, extends a research program on electric and magnetic fields by one year. It amends section 2118 of the Energy Policy Act of 1992, changing the year 1997 to 1998 in several places for the Electric and Magnetic Fields Research and Public Information Dissemination program. It also lowers one stated funding figure, from sixty-five million dollars to forty-six million dollars. Nothing else in the program is changed.
plaw-105-24-1997:
Bank branches that cross state lines are the concern of the Riegle-Neal Amendments Act of 1997, Public Law 105-24, approved July 3, 1997. The law clarifies how host state laws apply to a branch in that state of an out-of-state bank. It amends the Federal Deposit Insurance Act and deals with interstate branching.

Under the new rule, host state laws on community reinvestment, consumer protection, fair lending, and intrastate branches apply to a state bank's branch just as they apply to a national bank's branch. Where host state law does not reach, home state law applies instead. A branch may also carry on activities allowed under its home state's laws, within the limits the section sets.
plaw-105-25-1997: More time for the board reviewing Kennedy assassination records is given by Public Law 105-25, approved July 3, 1997. It amends the President John F Kennedy Assassination Records Collection Act of 1992 to extend the Assassination Records Review Board until September 30, 1998. The old cutoff language is replaced with that single date. The law also sets the amount to carry out the act for fiscal year 1998 at one million six hundred thousand dollars.
plaw-105-26-1997:
Gift annuities for charity receive protection from antitrust suits in Public Law 105-26, approved July 3, 1997. Its name is the Charitable Donation Antitrust Immunity Act of 1997. The law covers two gift forms: charitable gift annuities and charitable remainder trusts. It builds on a relief act passed in 1995.

Under the rewritten section, the antitrust laws do not apply to such gifts. State laws like them do not apply either, apart from a stated exception. A person sued over rate setting for such a gift gains immunity from suit. The shield covers setting rates of return or other terms, and planning, issuing, or paying the gifts. It also covers the cost and risk of discovery and trial.
plaw-105-27-1997: Retired federal police dogs may go to experienced handlers under Public Law 105-27, approved July 18, 1997. The law amends the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act of 1949. A federal agency head controls a canine that has been used in law enforcement duties. If the dog is no longer needed for official purposes, the head may donate it to an individual with experience handling canines in law enforcement work. The new paragraph is added at the end of section 203 of the 1949 act.
plaw-105-28-1997: Outdated Energy Department rules are removed by the Department of Energy Standardization Act of 1997, Public Law 105-28, approved July 18, 1997. It amends parts of the Department of Energy Organization Act that are obsolete or that clash with other statutes. In section 501, two subsections are struck and the rest are relettered, with a cross-reference updated. A special rule on advisory committees is shortened, and section 17 of the Federal Energy Administration Act of 1974 is repealed outright.
plaw-105-29-1997:
A wheelchair, long left out of a president's memorial, is added by Public Law 105-29, a joint resolution approved July 24, 1997. It directs the Secretary of the Interior to design and build a permanent addition to the Franklin Delano Roosevelt Memorial in Washington, District of Columbia. The preamble notes that Roosevelt needed a wheelchair after poliomyelitis, yet led the country through hard times.

The addition must be a permanent statue, bas-relief, or similar structure showing that Roosevelt's leadership for peace, well-being, and human dignity came while he used a wheelchair. The Commission of Fine Arts must approve the design plan. The Secretary must then report findings and recommendations to Congress and the President as soon as practicable, so the memorial tells a fuller story.
plaw-105-3-1997: Congress backs a presidential finding on family planning money in Public Law 105-3, a joint resolution approved February 28, 1997. The resolution approves the finding, sent to Congress on January 31, 1997, about a funding limit in the Foreign Operations, Export Financing, and Related Programs Appropriations Act, 1997. That limit, in section 518A(a), restricted obligations. The President found the limit was having a negative impact on the proper functioning of the population planning program, and Congress agreed in one sentence.
plaw-105-30-1997: Members of a gambling study panel gain legal protection under Public Law 105-30, approved July 25, 1997. The law clarifies that the Federal Tort Claims Act covers members and personnel of the National Gambling Impact Study Commission. For the cited title 28 sections, the commission counts as a federal agency and each member or staff member counts as an employee of the Government. The clarification takes effect as of August 3, 1996, and implies nothing about other commissions.
plaw-105-31-1997: One New York health plan gets a temporary pass under Public Law 105-31, approved July 25, 1997. The law waives a Medicaid enrollment composition rule for the Better Health Plan of Amherst, New York. Effective July 1, 1997, the requirement in section 1903(m)(2)(A)(ii) of the Social Security Act, known in the heading as the 75/25 rule, is waived for Better Health Plan, Inc. operating in New York. The waiver runs for contract periods through December 31, 1998.
plaw-105-32-1997: Printing rules are waived for two big 1997 bills by Public Law 105-32, a joint resolution approved August 1, 1997. Sections 106 and 107 of title 1 are waived for the enrollment of H.R. 2014 and H.R. 2015 of the 105th Congress. That waiver covers printing the enrollment on parchment or otherwise. Each bill's enrollment instead counts in the form the Committee on House Oversight certifies as a true enrollment. Both chambers passed the resolution on July 31, 1997.
plaw-105-33-1997:
Spending and taxes are reconciled across the whole government in the Balanced Budget Act of 1997, Public Law 105-33, approved August 5, 1997. The act provides for reconciliation under the fiscal year 1998 budget resolution. Its table of titles shows eleven titles, reaching far beyond the budget itself.

The titles cover food stamps, housing, communications and spectrum allocation, and Medicare, Medicaid, and children's health. Welfare, education, and civil service retirement follow, then veterans, asset sales and user fees, budget enforcement and process, and District of Columbia revitalization. Title I opens with food stamp exemptions, including a new fifteen percent exemption defined by caseload. The breadth shows why the 1997 budget deal reshaped many programs at once.
plaw-105-34-1997:
Tax cuts are enacted for fiscal year 1998 reconciliation in the Taxpayer Relief Act of 1997, Public Law 105-34, approved August 5, 1997. A note in the sample says the act was hand enrolled under Public Law 105-32, the enrollment waiver passed days earlier. Amendments in the act are read as amendments to the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 unless a section says otherwise.

Two general rules frame the many changes that follow. No amendment counts as a change in a tax rate for purposes of section 15 of the tax code. Estimated tax penalties under sections 6654 and 6655 are waived for periods before January 1, 1998, when a payment due before January 16, 1998 was underpaid because of the act itself. Those waivers kept taxpayers from being punished for confusion the new law created.
plaw-105-35-1997:
Snooping through tax returns becomes a crime of its own in the Taxpayer Browsing Protection Act, Public Law 105-35, approved August 5, 1997. The law amends the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 to stop unauthorized inspection of tax returns or return information. It adds a new section 7213A right after section 7213 in the crimes part of the code.

The new section makes it unlawful for a federal officer or employee to willfully inspect a return or return information, except as the tax code allows. The same ban reaches people described in section 6103(n) and their staff. A second paragraph covers state and other workers who received return information under section 6103. A penalty subsection follows in the sample, turning casual browsing of a taxpayer's file into a punishable offense.
plaw-105-36-1997:
Geologic maps are treated as basic national data in the National Geologic Mapping Reauthorization Act of 1997, Public Law 105-36, approved August 5, 1997. The law reauthorizes and amends the National Geologic Mapping Act of 1992. Congress restates why mapping mattered when the first act passed.

Map production had fallen sharply over two decades, even though geologic maps are the primary database for almost all earth-science work. Federal, state, and local governments, industry, and the public use them to judge environmental damage before starting projects. Missing maps led to poor design of dams and waste disposal sites, while good maps proved vital in finding fossil fuels and minerals. A nationwide program was needed to rebuild the map database at a pace matching demand.
plaw-105-37-1997: New Mexico's permanent trust funds are shielded from inflation by Public Law 105-37, approved August 7, 1997. It amends the Act of June 20, 1910, the statehood enabling act. Language saying only income may be used is replaced with distribution rules tied to section 10 of that act. The funds, including interest, dividends, other income, and growth in market value, must be prudently invested on a total rate of return basis. Distributions follow Article 12, Section 7 of the New Mexico Constitution.
plaw-105-38-1997: A transition rule for some citizenship certificates is removed by Public Law 105-38, approved August 8, 1997. It amends the Immigration and Nationality Technical Corrections Act of 1994. Section 102 of that act, as later changed by the 1996 immigration reform law, loses its subsection (e). That subsection held the special transition rule for issuing a certificate of citizenship for certain children born outside the United States. The removal takes effect as if it had been part of the 1994 act itself.
plaw-105-39-1997: Landfill land in Oregon passes to its city under Public Law 105-39, approved August 11, 1997. The Secretary of the Interior must promptly convey Bureau of Land Management land to the City of Grants Pass, Oregon, without payment. The parcel, shown on a June 20, 1997 Merlin Landfill Map, holds about two hundred acres where the city ran a landfill under lease, plus about one hundred twenty adjoining acres. As consideration, the city must agree to indemnify the United States for all liability arising from the property.
plaw-105-4-1997: A San Antonio post office takes a congressman's name under Public Law 105-4, approved March 3, 1997. The United States Postal Service facility then under construction at 7411 Barlite Boulevard in San Antonio, Texas, must be known as the Frank M Tejeda Post Office Building. Any reference in a federal law, map, regulation, document, or other record to that facility counts as a reference to the Frank M Tejeda Post Office Building. The House passed the bill in February and the Senate followed that month.
plaw-105-40-1997: A ski hill and a wildlife refuge trade land under the Warner Canyon Ski Hill Land Exchange Act of 1997, Public Law 105-40, approved August 11, 1997. If Lake County, Oregon, conveys acceptable non-federal land, the Secretary of Agriculture must convey about two hundred ninety-five acres to the county. The acres lie in the Warner Canyon Ski Area of the Fremont National Forest. The county land is about three hundred twenty acres inside Hart Mountain Wildlife Refuge. More county land in the refuge may be added for equal value.
plaw-105-41-1997:
Stamps that fund cancer research are created by the Stamp Out Breast Cancer Act, Public Law 105-41, approved August 13, 1997. Postal patrons may voluntarily buy special first-class stamps and give the extra money to breast cancer research. The Postal Service must set a special rate for the stamps.

That rate equals the regular first-class rate plus a differential of no more than twenty-five percent, set by the Postal Service Governors under their own rules. Buying at the special rate stays voluntary, as an alternative to the regular rate. Of the research money raised, the Postal Service pays seventy percent to the National Institutes of Health. The sample cuts off as it names who receives the remainder, so that share is not stated here.
plaw-105-42-1997:
Dolphins caught in tuna nets in the eastern Pacific gain a program in the International Dolphin Conservation Program Act, Public Law 105-42, approved August 15, 1997. It amends the Marine Mammal Protection Act of 1972 to support the International Dolphin Conservation Program in the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean.

One purpose is to give effect to the Declaration of Panama, signed October 4, 1995. The signers listed are Belize, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, France, Honduras, Mexico, Panama, Spain, the United States of America, Vanuatu, and Venezuela. The declaration created the program for protecting dolphins and other species, and for conserving and managing tuna in that ocean region. A second purpose recognizes gains nations fishing tuna there had already achieved.
plaw-105-43-1997: Colleges may keep sharing aid data under the Need-Based Educational Aid Antitrust Protection Act of 1997, Public Law 105-43, approved September 17, 1997. It continues favorable antitrust treatment for need-based educational aid in the Improving America's Schools Act of 1994. Schools may exchange, through an independent third party, data on a commonly admitted student's assets, liabilities, income, expenses, and siblings in college, before awarding need-based aid. Each school may retrieve that student's data only once. The end date moves from September 30, 1997 to September 30, 2001.
plaw-105-44-1997: A California reservoir gets its older local name back under Public Law 105-44, approved September 30, 1997. The reservoir created by Trinity Dam in the Central Valley Project, called Clair Engle Lake by Public Law 88-662, is redesignated as Trinity Lake. Any reference in a federal law, regulation, document, record, or map to that reservoir counts as a reference to Trinity Lake. The earlier designation law, Public Law 88-662 from the 88th Congress, is repealed outright.
plaw-105-45-1997:
Building for the armed forces in fiscal year 1998 is funded by the Military Construction Appropriations Act, 1998, Public Law 105-45, approved September 30, 1997. The law covers military construction, family housing, and base realignment and closure work run by the Department of Defense for the year ending September 30, 1998.

Army military construction receives more than seven hundred fourteen million dollars, available until September 30, 2002. The money buys, builds, installs, and equips temporary or permanent public works and real property, and pays Army Corps of Engineers personnel. Up to about sixty-five and a half million dollars may fund study, planning, design, and engineering services and host nation support. More may be used only if the Secretary of Defense notifies the appropriations committees that added obligations are needed.
plaw-105-46-1997: Stopgap funding for a new fiscal year is set by Public Law 105-46, a joint resolution approved September 30, 1997. It makes continuing appropriations for fiscal year 1998 for departments, agencies, corporations, and other government units. Amounts needed may be spent under the authority and conditions of the fiscal year 1997 appropriations acts, for projects run in 1997 that the coming 1998 acts would fund. The sample lists the agriculture act and the commerce, justice, and state act among those carried forward.
plaw-105-47-1997: Earthquake research money is authorized for two years by Public Law 105-47, approved October 1, 1997. It amends section 12 of the Earthquake Hazards Reduction Act of 1977 for fiscal years 1998 and 1999. Stated sums are added for each year in two subsections, with an equal set-aside in both years for the Global Seismic Network. At least a stated floor amount each year must support a competitive, peer-reviewed program run by the Director, coordinated with related work of other agencies named in the text.
plaw-105-48-1997: Au pair programs become permanent under Public Law 105-48, approved October 1, 1997. The law gives permanent authority to administer au pair programs, ending a string of temporary extensions. It amends a 1995 act titled An Act to extend au pair programs, Public Law 104-72. In section 1(b) of that act, the closing phrase through fiscal year 1997 is struck. Removing those four words removes the program's expiration date. The Senate passed the bill September 25 and the House September 29.
plaw-105-49-1997: Unused farm land in California becomes a school under Public Law 105-49, approved October 6, 1997. The Secretary of Agriculture must convey about twenty-two acres at 18296 Elgin Avenue in Dos Palos to the Dos Palos Ag Boosters, for a farm school teaching students and beginning farmers. The boosters pay fair market value, set by the Secretary, with size fixed by survey. At the boosters' request, the land may go instead to the Dos Palos School District. The conveyance is final, with no future liability for the Secretary.
plaw-105-5-1997:
A trade appointment bar is waived for one named official in Public Law 105-5, a joint resolution approved March 17, 1997. It waives part of the Trade Act of 1974 on appointing the United States Trade Representative. The limit in section 141(b)(3) took effect January 1, 1996, and does not reach anyone who held the trade post on that date and kept serving.

Charlene Barshefsky became Deputy United States Trade Representative on May 28, 1993, with Senate consent, and she was serving on January 1, 1996. The limit therefore never applied to her as deputy. Congress calls it fitting to keep waiving the same paragraph for her appointment as United States Trade Representative itself. The resolution then waives the provision for that appointment notwithstanding the paragraph's text.
plaw-105-50-1997:
Surplus federal goods reach poor families more easily under Public Law 105-50, approved October 6, 1997. It amends the Federal Property and Administrative Services Act of 1949 in two directions. Personal property and real property are treated in separate sections, both aimed at States and nonprofit groups.

For personal property, states may receive surplus items for donation to providers of help to families and individuals whose yearly incomes fall below the poverty line. That phrase is added right after homeless individuals in the existing list. For real property, the Administrator may assign surplus land to the Secretary of Housing and Urban Development for disposal. States, their subdivisions, and nonprofit groups may then use it to provide housing or housing help for low-income people.
plaw-105-51-1997:
A religious leader receives Congress's gold medal in Public Law 105-51, approved October 6, 1997. The President may present the medal, for Congress, to Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew. The honor recognizes his outstanding and lasting work for religious understanding and peace.

Congress found that Bartholomew leads nearly three hundred million Orthodox Christians worldwide, including millions in America. He is known at home and abroad for seeking world peace, respect for the Earth's environment, and deeper understanding between faiths. His efforts bring people of all faiths closer, and his courageous leadership for peace in the Balkans, Eastern Europe, the Middle East, and the Eastern Mediterranean inspires others. Many governments and universities had already honored him before Congress acted.
plaw-105-52-1997: Five fallen agents are memorialized in a building name by Public Law 105-52, approved October 6, 1997. The federal building at 601 Fourth Street, Northwest, in the District of Columbia becomes the Federal Bureau of Investigation, Washington Field Office Memorial Building. The act says its purpose is to honor William H Christian Jr, Martha Dixon Martinez, Michael J Miller, Anthony Palmisano, and Edwin R Woodriffe, who were slain in the line of duty. Later references to the building must use the memorial name.
plaw-105-53-1997: Court arbitration funding becomes open-ended under Public Law 105-53, approved October 6, 1997. In the Judicial Improvements and Access to Justice Act, one phrase changes. For each of the fiscal years 1994 through 1997 becomes for each fiscal year. That authorizes money for arbitration in district courts every year. Other sections improve judicial information sharing under the Civil Justice Reform Act of 1990, making one set of requirements permanent. Temporary judgeships are extended: the first vacancy ten years out ends them, except for western Michigan and eastern Pennsylvania districts.
plaw-105-54-1997: Religious workers from abroad gain three more years under Public Law 105-54, approved October 6, 1997. The special immigrant religious worker program is extended in the cited Immigration and Nationality Act clause. The year 1997 becomes 2000 wherever it appears, effective at enactment. The act's title adds two items. One is a later deadline for paperwork changes in the employer sanctions program under the 1996 immigration law. The other is a duty for the Secretary of State to waive or reduce nonimmigrant visa fees for people coming for charitable purposes.
plaw-105-55-1997:
Congress funds its own operations for fiscal year 1998. It does so in the Legislative Branch Appropriations Act, 1998, Public Law 105-55, approved October 7, 1997. Title I is the Congressional Operations Appropriations Act, 1998. Money comes from the Treasury for the year ending September 30, 1998, starting with the Senate.

Senate expense allowances match the familiar pattern: ten thousand dollars each for the Vice President, the President pro tempore, and both leaders. Each whip gets five thousand dollars, and each conference chairman three thousand. The total is fifty-six thousand dollars. Leaders also receive fifteen thousand dollars each for representation. Compensation for Senate officers and employees totals more than seventy-seven million dollars. That total includes one million six hundred twelve thousand dollars for the Vice President's office.
plaw-105-56-1997:
Military pay and operations for fiscal year 1998 are funded by the Department of Defense Appropriations Act, 1998, Public Law 105-56, approved October 8, 1997. Title I is military personnel, for the year ending September 30, 1998. Each service receives its own personnel account in turn.

Army personnel funding is set at more than twenty billion dollars in the sample's long figure. It pays active duty soldiers, cadets, and aviation cadets their pay, allowances, clothing, food, and interest on deposits. Gratuities, permanent change of station travel, and temporary duty travel between stations are covered too. Payments owed under a 1982 benefits law, the Social Security Act, and the Department of Defense Military Retirement Fund are charged to the same account. Navy personnel funding follows next.
plaw-105-57-1997:
Wildlife refuges receive a clearer mission in the National Wildlife Refuge System Improvement Act of 1997, Public Law 105-57, approved October 9, 1997. It amends the National Wildlife Refuge System Administration Act of 1966 to improve management of the system. Amendments in the act are read as changes to that 1966 law.

Congress found the system held more than ninety-two million acres in 509 units, spread across all fifty states and United States territories. The system was created to conserve fish, wildlife, plants, and their habitats. That mission was helped by letting Americans take part in compatible wildlife recreation, including fishing and hunting, on refuge lands. Such chances also taught the value of conserving fish and wildlife, and the system played a pivotal role in that wider conservation work.
plaw-105-58-1997:
A bombing that shook the nation is memorialized by the Oklahoma City National Memorial Act of 1997, Public Law 105-58, approved October 9, 1997. The law establishes the Oklahoma City National Memorial as a unit of the National Park System and designates the Oklahoma City Memorial Trust.

Congress found that few events in a quarter century had rocked Americans' view of themselves and their institutions so hard. The April 19, 1995 bombing of the Alfred P Murrah Federal Building in downtown Oklahoma City did so with great intensity. One hundred sixty-eight people died, some of them children, and thousands of family members were left with lasting scars.
