The authors say even a tightly structured game can reveal how speakers steer around ambiguity, a first step toward understanding how this rule behaves in everyday talk.
plos-pone-0356697:
Xingyue Pu and Zhigang Zhong track whether China's cancer hospital beds are shared fairly, using fifteen years of national statistics in this 2026 study. Oncology beds grew steadily from 2008 to 2022, though growth slowed. The authors measured fairness two ways, against population and against land area, using standard inequality tools that also separate disparities within regions from those between them.

Judged by population, bed allocation was quite equal and improved over the period. Judged by geography, it was severely unequal throughout, with no improvement, meaning patients in sparse regions face long journeys regardless of headcounts. Most inequality in both views came from within regions rather than between them. The authors argue policy should now chase geographic accessibility and local balance, to ease the notorious difficulty cancer patients face getting admitted.
plos-pone-0356797:
Chaoqun He and Racidon P Bernarte surveyed six hundred Chinese livestream shoppers. Half were young digital natives, and half were older adults. The survey asked what makes them buy again from a live commerce host. Their 2026 study modeled three facets of service quality. They were the host's professionalism, the interactive experience, and after-sales support. Trust served as the middleman. Generation was the dial that turns each effect.

All three facets built trust, and trust fed intentions to return. But the generations weighted them differently. Older shoppers leaned hardest on professionalism and after-sales care. The young prized interactivity. The authors advise platforms to segment their playbook. They suggest certifying hosts for older audiences. For the young, they suggest investing in interactive features, even augmented reality try-ons.
plos-pone-0356997:
Kathleen O'Connor and coauthors published a 2026 genomics study in PLOS ONE on a quiet kind of variation in Staphylococcus aureus, a bacterium behind many skin and hospital infections. Genes can spell the same protein with different codons, and bacteria prefer some spellings, affecting how much protein gets made. The team measured codon bias across thousands of genes in a reference strain and compared it with all public complete genomes of the species, sorted by disease, institution, and site.

Bias varied gene by gene and isolate by isolate. Ribosome machinery genes showed the strongest, most consistent bias everywhere, suggesting heavy pressure to keep them highly expressed. One hospital's genomes, from Nairobi, stood out as most different. In a well-known strain, higher bias scores did tend to mean more protein in culture. Silent spelling choices, they say, are a real layer of this pathogen's diversity that evolution studies have largely skipped.
plos-pone-0357497:
M. Arunadevi and colleagues published a 2026 engineering paper in PLOS ONE on a common manufacturing defect: layers splitting apart when glass-fiber composite panels are drilled. Delamination weakens the finished part, and it depends in tangled ways on drill shape, size, speed, and feed. The team ran a full grid of drilling trials on glass-fiber laminates, photographed the damage, and trained a neural network that also had the physics of cracking built into its learning rules.

The physics-informed network predicted the damage measure very accurately on held-out trials. Feed rate mattered most, followed by laminate thickness and drill diameter, while faster spindle speeds actually reduced damage by cutting more cleanly and pushing less. Interactions mattered too, especially between feed and speed. Adding the physics constraints made predictions sturdier and better at generalizing. The authors offer the model as a planning aid for shops that drill composite parts.
plos-pone-0357597:
Shuang An, Dan-ni Gu, He-jun Huang, Jun-qiang Luo, and Rong-rong Liu wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article about tourism in Tianshui, China. It models tourist loyalty, the choice to return or recommend a place. Three forces are built into the model: how crowded the place feels, what social value visitors think the trip gives them, and how good they judge the service to be.

The method is structural equation modeling, which tests how several influences act on each other at once. Crowding can sour a trip even when service is good, and the model weighs that tension. Destination managers in Tianshui and other growing Chinese tourist cities can use the results to balance visitor numbers against experience.
plos-pone-0357797:
Veronika Frybortova and coauthors published a 2026 mouse study in PLOS ONE on whether a ketogenic diet changes how the body handles ozanimod, a drug used in multiple sclerosis. High-fat, very-low-carbohydrate diets are being explored alongside MS therapy, but diets can retune the liver enzymes clearing drugs. Female mice ate a normal or ketogenic diet for four weeks; the team then measured metabolism, gut microbes, liver enzymes, and the drug's path through the body.

The diet produced the expected ketosis, raised blood cholesterol, and reshaped gut microbial communities, while most other measures moved only modestly. Liver enzyme activity shifted both ways: one family sped up, another slowed, and a third trended down. Drug exposure in ketogenic mice ran somewhat higher, though the difference was not statistically firm. The signal is small, they say, but real enough that diet-drug interactions deserve attention as the therapy spreads.
plos-pone-0358597:
Yueyi Tan leads a team of six using machine learning to map how two kinds of shops compete for space in Shenzhen, China, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Convenience stores run light, cheap, and everywhere; supermarkets and malls are capital heavy and choosy. The team fed geospatial data and measures of how people perceive streets into a stack of interpretive models that can reveal bends and interactions, not just straight line effects.

The two formats followed distinct locational logics. Convenience stores spread widely and reacted strongly to nearby competition, to the proximity of everyday services, and to how a place feels to pedestrians. The big formats clustered where returns justify their cost. Untangling which urban features pull each format helps planners zone commercial districts deliberately, and helps chains pick sites with their eyes open about which game they are playing.
plos-pone-0358797:
Sarah Alexandra Marshall leads a team of six asking what a health program for low income Black men with chronic illness would need to succeed, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The group studied is underserved in the southern United States, and one proposal on the table uses a universal basic income to open access to care. Before any launch, the researchers interviewed thirty-one interest holders, including men from the target population, about conditions such an intervention must respect.

Five themes emerged. The men typically delay seeking care. Relationships are strained by incarceration and poverty. Prison health services and ordinary healthcare are not built to help them. Community level barriers pile up. Racism and poverty are intertwined and entrenched. The authors argue any fair intervention, income based or not, must work at individual, family, community, and institutional levels at once, or it will fail the very people it names.
plos-pone-0359197:
Kateřina Abrhámová, Alexandra Gredová, Karolína Navrátilová, Mohamed Boumaiza, and Petr Folk wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on yeast genetics. It studies the intronic RNA of RPL22 paralogs, copies of a ribosomal protein gene, and reports that this RNA acts as an allosteric switch, a molecule whose binding changes a protein's behavior.

Introns were long treated as waste cut out of genes, so finding a working switch among them changes how yeast gene control is pictured. Paralogs are near-duplicate genes, and cross-talk between them can fine-tune protein production. Molecular biologists studying gene regulation are the readers for this small RNA with an outsized job.
pmc-10656797:
Tamer Mohamed Elsherbiny reports a diagnostic trap in this two thousand twenty-three case report. A premenopausal woman had years of osteoporosis with normal blood calcium and low vitamin D. She was first diagnosed with secondary hyperparathyroidism, where the parathyroid glands overwork in response to vitamin D deficiency. That diagnosis fit the standard picture. The author treated her vitamin D deficiency with parenteral loading doses to restore normal levels.

Once vitamin D normalized, the picture flipped: persistent mild to moderate high calcium appeared, with parathyroid hormone still elevated, the signature of primary hyperparathyroidism. She also had excess calcium in her urine and calcium deposits in her kidneys. Imaging found a left upper parathyroid adenoma, and surgery restored normal calcium for years of follow-up. The lesson is that vitamin D deficiency can mask the high calcium of primary disease, delaying diagnosis; such patients deserve re-evaluation after repletion.
pmc-10656897:
Mohamed Mostafa Kotb and two co-authors free wrist nerves with a wide-awake, no-band cut that uses full-strength bleed-stop shots. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-three. Two hundred folks, most women and half with both wrists hit, had three hundred eight day-case cuts from twenty fifteen to twenty twenty-one by one hand. The shot mix held a bleed-stop dose two and a half times the first-form mix.

Mean cut time was near ten minutes. No one need more numb shots, full sleep, or a night stay. Most were back to plain day acts in near five weeks. No finger blood harms hit, and one wound ill cleared with plain care.
pmc-10674597:
Jiahui Hua leads a team that compares silk gels made four ways. Their study from twenty twenty-three deals with silk fibroin hydrogels. Silk gels draw much use in medical materials work.

Gels were made by sound, by chem links, by light, and by enzymes. Light made gels were the strongest under squeeze in tests. Chem and enzyme gels were the toughest of the set. Sound made gels were brittle due to more stiff crystals. All gels let vein cells grow in lab tests. Gels sans chem agents kept cells most alive.
pmc-10694897:
Six authors present a study from two thousand twenty-three on early warning signs of pancreatic cancer. The cancer kills many of its patients, in part because it is hard to spot early. The team looked for markers in blood that can be checked without invasive tests.

They drew on a large Korean health study, matching one hundred twenty-eight people who later got the cancer with two hundred fifty-six who did not. Blood samples taken at the start were scanned for small molecules. A learning method picked out eleven that separated the groups. Gene scans then found DNA variants tied to those molecules, adding clues about how risk builds.
pmc-10698697:
Ashley Allen and co-authors published this case report in 2023. It presents a seventy-one-year-old Black woman who came to an emergency department with a widespread itchy rash. The rash had not responded to an over-the-counter allergy drug. Three weeks earlier she had been diagnosed with gout and started three medicines for it, including allopurinol. Her history included diabetes, high blood pressure, and high cholesterol.

Examination found a flat, bumpy rash that did not blanch, covering her whole body including palms and soles, with slight peeling. Blood tests showed raised eosinophils, a type of white cell linked to drug reactions. Inflammatory markers were high, liver enzymes were raised, and her old kidney disease had worsened. The report documents the presentation and lab picture. Cases like this matter because rashes and drug reactions can look different, and be missed more easily, on brown skin.
pmc-10702097:
Sharma and a large team ask in twenty twenty-three whether the male hormone testosterone explains the link between poor sleep and frailty in older men. Past studies tied disturbed sleep to frailty, but the mechanism was unknown. Data came from a European study of men aged forty to seventy-nine across eight centres, with sleep surveys, hormone measures, and a broad frailty index.

Men with the worst sleep quality had much higher frailty than the best sleepers. Both short and long sleep also linked to higher frailty. Hormone levels did fall as sleep quality worsened. Yet adjusting for testosterone left the sleep-frailty link unchanged in strength. The authors conclude the link runs through other paths, not this hormone.
pmc-10707297:
Nan Liu and eight co-authors trace a pregnancy failure pathway that runs from placental cell recycling to the immune cells of the womb lining. Natural killer cells in the decidua must be educated into tolerance by trophoblasts, with the receptor CXCR4 marking the tolerant subset. Women with recurrent miscarriage have too few of those marked cells in early pregnancy.

Culturing the immune cells with trophoblast secretions raised their CXCR4 levels. Blocking trophoblast autophagy, the cells' internal recycling, broke that education and shifted the killer cells toward a harmful phenotype. The signal ran through an IGF2 and p53 route. Tissue from forty-two healthy pregnancies and twenty miscarriage patients grounded the experiments. The work nominates trophoblast autophagy as a guardian of pregnancy.
pmc-10709597:
Hiroki Koizumi, Yuichi Yamasaki, and Hideto Yanagihara report an unusual electrical effect in a magnetic oxide film in a 2023 paper. In the Hall effect, a current bends sideways under a magnetic influence. Known forms spread evenly across the plane, but this team found a version whose strength depends on which way the current runs within the plane.

The film is a spinel oxide grown as a thin layer. Its sideways response carried a four-fold pattern tied to current direction, added to the usual uniform part. Cooling the film in a magnetic field could even flip the pattern's sign. The authors trace the effect to an electron nematic state, where electrons favor one direction, born from a stretched magnetic order in the material.
pmc-10710297:
Ho and co-authors probe how pelvic surgery and ovarian hormones shape vaginal and bladder tissue. Surgery for prolapse often fails over time and harms quality of life. The rat model mimed surgical injury to the vagina and bladder. Four groups split by surgery and ovary removal. Tissue was checked ten weeks after the operation.

Ovary removal cut vaginal wall squeeze strength in both ovary groups. Bladder dome and base showed split squeeze patterns. Gene and protein tests tracked collagen and elastin shifts. Stains showed matching tissue changes under the microscope. The work suggests hormone loss, not surgery alone, drives much of the lasting weakness.
pmc-10710397:
Yongxiang Liao and co-authors uncover a new job for a plant enzyme best known for softening cell walls. The enzyme, a polygalacturonase named HCC1, turns out to steer the loss of chlorophyll, the green pigment whose breakdown marks leaf aging and fruit ripening. A mutant plant lacking the enzyme stayed greener but grew and yielded less.

In the mutant, enzyme activity, ethylene levels, and a wall-derived sugar acid all ran low, and its cell walls grew thicker. Adding back ethylene or the sugar acid raised ethylene and switched the gene on, and normal green loss resumed. Tests with knocked-out and restored lines confirmed the gene's role. The authors conclude that this wall enzyme feeds into the ethylene pathway, linking wall breakdown to the timing of chlorophyll loss in the plant.
pmc-10710997:
Keiko Azuma and six co-authors track long-term sight outcomes across a family of retinal diseases sharing a thickened choroid. Their retrospective study was published in twenty twenty-three. The group ranges from quiet pigment changes to fluid leaks and new vessel growth.

Charts from a Tokyo hospital covered seven hundred and forty-one eyes of six hundred and thirty-eight patients seen from twenty eight to twenty twenty-one. Vision loss was tracked at several cut-offs over time. Eyes with central serous disease or vessel growth fared significantly worse than the milder types. The team then hunted factors tied to prognosis within the serous group. The data help doctors counsel patients on likely sight paths.
pmc-10712097:
Nai-Chung Nelson Chang and a large team track gene tests and blood counts in US veterans new on thiopurine drugs. Their past-look study appeared in twenty twenty-three. Such tests can head off drug harms. More than twenty thousand veterans who first took one of three such drugs from twenty ten to twenty twenty-one were read through VA health files.

Gene test shares rose from three in ten to near half by late twenty fourteen. Past a flag harm year, tests rose a bit then flat and a touch low. Most new users still got no test at all. The team call the stance one of fix past harm, not guard.
pmc-10713397:
Ping Hu and co-authors published a 2023 study on two tiny RNA molecules that may drive prostate cancer. MicroRNAs are short regulators that tune gene activity; when they misfire, cancers can grow and spread. Using data from 485 prostate cancer patients in a public atlas, the team screened microRNAs tied to survival. Two stood out: hsa-mir-503 and hsa-mir-1247.

Databases predicted which genes the pair controls. Then came lab validation. In a prostate cancer cell line, the researchers knocked the two molecules down and watched the cells. Migration and invasion, the moves that make cancer dangerous, were measured, as was programmed cell death. The knockdowns changed those behaviors, backing the statistical link. The authors propose the pair as candidate markers for prognosis and possible drug targets. The work follows a common arc, from atlas mining to bench proof, but the validation step is what lifts it above pure computation.
pmc-10717797:
Jiamei Wang, Zizhong Shi, and Xiangdong Hu study how safe pig farms in China are from animal disease, a steady threat to livestock farming. They surveyed farms in seven provinces, built a scoring system for farm safety steps, and used a rank sum ratio method to grade each farm. They then looked for the farm and farmer traits that track with higher scores.

More spending on safety steps went with higher scores. Male farmers, more schooling, and taking part in skills training each raised scores, and farms that joined cooperatives scored higher. Scores first fell and then rose as farm size grew, and more household members working on the farm also helped. The authors say raising farmer skills and investing more people, gear, and money in safety steps can lift farm safety and prevent animal disease.
pmc-10731197:
Rui-Yao Wei and co-authors report a rare case of stomach damage from poor blood flow in a case report from two thousand twenty-three. Ischemic gastritis is uncommon, deadly, and often missed, since its signs mimic other gut diseases. A scope exam is the main way to catch it.

A woman aged sixty-eight with a brain aneurysm history arrived dizzy, with chest tightness and two days of lost consciousness. Scans showed widespread artery hardening, including the vessels feeding the gut. A scope found the whole stomach lining swollen, deep purple, and bleeding, worst at the top. Tissue study confirmed dying lining. The authors stress scope and tissue checks for the diagnosis.
pmc-10735597:
Murad Taani and Mary Hook study the clinical nurse's role in asking older hospital patients what matters to them, in work published in 2023. The question anchors an age-friendly care framework built on four elements: what matters, medication, mentation, and mobility. Toolkits exist for all disciplines, yet nurse-specific evidence was thin.

A large Midwest health system rolled the framework out across five hospitals but saw no gain in nurse-sensitive patient experience scores. The authors describe a qualitative study now under way with nurse leaders and clinical nurses who ran the programme. It probes their knowledge, views, and lived experience of the approach. The findings should ground nurse-targeted training and better ways to partner with patients and caregivers.
pmc-10736497:
Shoko Miyagawa and Young Ah Seong study manual stool removal in home care in Japan, in work from two thousand twenty-three. The procedure, done by visiting nurses, clears hard stool by hand when patients cannot pass it. Seven skilled nurses were interviewed while a training simulator was being built.

Each nurse performed the task ten to thirty times a month. Patients included people with stroke or nerve damage, and those in the last stages of cancer. The skill is not taught in schools, nurses said, but learned on the job. Families struggle to assist, which is why routine nurse visits matter.
pmc-10737097:
Vadim Gladyshev wrote a 2023 study on the molecular strategies that set how long animals live. Lifespan varies hugely between species and somewhat within them, yet the general rules of that control were unclear. The team compared gene activity across many tissues in many mammal species. They looked for signatures tied to long life, and how those signatures relate to aging itself and to treatments that extend life.

Long-lived species shared a pattern: their signature genes were ancient and essential, and the pattern oddly aligned with changes seen in aging. Life-extending treatments pushed the other way, against aging patterns, acting on younger, changeable genes tied to energy use. The team also built a gene-based clock that tracks progress through a lifespan. It can measure how treatments shift that progress. The work separates what evolution does to grant long life from what medicine might do to extend it.
pmc-10737197:
Abigail Hansen, Kaarin Anstey, and six co-authors study how older Australians view driver help systems. These systems warn drivers or help steer and brake. The study, from twenty twenty-three, asks if age and gender shape trust and use. It was run with National Seniors Australia as an online survey.

More than thirteen hundred drivers aged sixty-five and up took part, and most said they use such systems. Older drivers trusted the systems more but found them harder to use. Women used the systems less than men yet trusted them more. The authors say ease of use may matter as much as trust for older drivers.
pmc-10737297:
Chenkai Wu and Qianli Xue present a set of talks on bouncing back after frailty. Their session, from twenty twenty-three, asks if frailty must mean decline to the end. Frailty leaves older people with low reserves and high risk from stress. Turning the state itself around has proved hard, and no single drug fixes it.

Four studies in the set hunt for traits that blunt frailty's harms. One finds a healthy daily routine helps most for those in poor social settings. Others weigh social ties, habits, and health marks. Frail people differ a lot from each other, the talks stress. Care built around the person may protect the most fragile best.
pmc-10737497:
Rahul Malhotra, Jeremy Lim-Soh, Pildoo Sung, and Ha-Linh Quach report a study from two thousand twenty-three on how families in Singapore share care for older adults. Most research watches only the main caregiver, leaving the wider family picture unclear. The team asked who gives which kind of help when several relatives are involved.

Primary caregivers of two hundred seventy-seven adults aged seventy-five and older with daily limits were interviewed. Three patterns emerged. In the largest, several relatives shared all three help types: daily tasks, health and social services, and emotional support. In another, families shared care but skipped formal services. In the third, the main caregiver did everything alone. Solo caregivers reported more depressive symptoms than those in fully shared care.
pmc-10737997:
Arseniy Yashkin and five co-authors study a link between thyroid disease and Alzheimer's disease in a 2023 paper. Graves disease is the most common cause of an overactive thyroid in the United States, and it had been suspected to raise Alzheimer's risk, without agreement. The team used Medicare records for older adults from 1991 to 2017.

They matched more than fifteen thousand people with Graves disease to similar people without it. Those with the thyroid disease had about fifteen percent higher risk of a clinical Alzheimer's diagnosis. The link was stronger in men and in Black patients in their data. The authors suggest shared causes may connect the two diseases, and that thyroid care could help lower dementia burden.
pmc-10739297:
Shavonnye Rath and five co-authors tested a special form of heat care for pain in older adults, in a study from twenty twenty-three. The heat uses long light waves that mimic a dry sauna. Pain is common in later life and can lower quality of life and physical ability, so new options matter.

A small group of older adults took six half-hour sessions. Some got plain warm air, and others got warm air plus the special heat. Pain severity fell in the special heat group, and pain interference fell in the plain heat group. Overall, heat helped, but the special form was not clearly better. The authors call for more research.
pmc-10739997:
Galan-Gonzalez leads a large team improving light emitting transistors with a nanostructured channel, in work from twenty twenty-three. Hybrid light emitting field effect transistors combine switching and light emission in one device. They promise simple display pixels. But emission efficiency has held them back.

Shaping the transistor channel at the nanoscale changes how charge and light meet inside the device. The team reports improved emission efficiency from that design. Brighter, thriftier versions could make active matrix displays simpler to build. They could also make optical gear for data links simpler. In such gear, one part doing two jobs cuts build steps and cost.
pmc-10741497:
Doucet, Brisebois, McKerral, and Agorastos study heart rhythm variation after concussion, in work from twenty twenty-three. A reliable body marker could help diagnose concussion and track recovery in athletes. Heart rate variability, the small gaps between beats, is one candidate.

Nearly one hundred seventy college athletes aged sixteen to twenty-two did baseline tests. Thirty who later got concussions were retested within three days and again before return to play. Surveys covered symptoms and mental health. Baseline results showed some sex gaps in rhythm measures. The team tracked how rhythm, sex, and symptoms moved together, to judge if a simple heart test can aid care.
pmc-10742397:
Ruperto González-Pérez and colleagues argue for molecule-level allergy testing when choosing mite immunotherapy, in a twenty twenty-three paper. Immunotherapy is the only treatment that changes the course of allergy, yet under ten percent of hay fever or asthma patients get it. The team profiled young patients' antibody responses to dust mite and storage mite parts at the molecule level.

Responses proved complex in every patient group, no matter the base condition. No one reacted only to the three classic mite molecules. Patients with asthma and skin disease carried higher levels to six mite parts, but no pattern marked one disease. The authors say products must match the local molecule mix that patients truly react to.
pmc-10742797:
José Verdú-Soriano and co-authors test an olive-leaf hydrogel against a standard gel on hard-to-heal wounds. Chronic ulcers strain health systems, and proof that one dressing beats another is scarce. Their trial enrolled outpatients with pressure, vein, or diabetic foot ulcers that resisted care. Thirty-five patients got the extract gel and thirty-four the standard one.

Wound area shrank by about fifty-two percent under the new gel. The standard gel managed only about nineteen percent over the same span. Daily healing speed ran about ten times higher with the extract. The authors credit balance of acidity and oxidative stress in the wound bed. That action adds to the moisture and shield work of plain gels.
pmc-10743597:
Etindele Sosso and five co-authors sum up what is known about poor sleep and social rank in Latin America in this twenty twenty-three review. Poor sleep is a broad health risk, yet rank in pay, school, and work is often left out of sleep work. No past review had pulled the Latin American proof into one place.

Inside, twenty past studies made the final set, most of them from Brazil. Higher rank went with shorter sleep, while lower rank went with worse sleep and more day-time drowsiness. Low school years also went with more cases of not being able to fall asleep. The pooled share with sleep ills was near one in four across the studies.
pmc-10745397:
Zhang and co-authors pair two nanomaterials into an ink whose glow color shifts with heat, for anti-counterfeiting. Strong, hard-to-copy marks are a steady research focus. Their mix joins upconversion particles with perovskite quantum dots for two checking modes.

The upconversion particles grew brighter as they warmed, more so at smaller sizes. That odd gain was traced to less surface quenching of the glow. Quantum dots stuck to the particle surfaces and shared energy with them. As heat rose, the mix shifted from green to pink under infrared light. Under ultraviolet light, it faded from green to dark.
pmc-10750397:
Mingliang Wang and four co-authors build a tool to spot ADHD from brain scans in a 2023 paper. Resting brain activity changes over time, and those shifts can reveal what differs in this condition. Older methods that freeze connectivity into one snapshot miss the motion. Many learning methods also only compare neighboring moments, missing longer patterns.

Their network first builds changing connectivity maps from short segments of each scan, learned from data rather than fixed formulas. A second network then reads long-range patterns across those maps before a final diagnosis step. On a public dataset their method beat leading rivals. The authors say learned dynamic maps carry more signal than standard ones.
pmc-10751797:
Anthony Bogetti, Josephine Leung, and Lillian Chong present LPATH, a Python tool that sorts molecular simulation pathways into meaningful classes. Simulations of how a molecule changes state produce many routes of differing lengths, and comparing them by hand is tedious. LPATH borrows from linguistics: it discretizes the molecule's configurations into key states, spells each pathway as a string of visited states, and matches strings by similarity.

A two-stage machine learning step keeps the state clustering affordable in memory. Designed mainly for the WESTPA weighted-ensemble package but usable with ordinary simulations, the tool recovered physically sensible route classes and their probabilities for a classic test molecule's shape change. The authors release it as open analysis infrastructure for transition mechanism studies.
pmc-10785997:
Kyriaki Katouni and six co-authors review the syndromes in which skull sutures fuse too early alongside problems across the body. In syndromic craniosynostosis the skull deformity travels with respiratory, neurological, cardiac, skeletal, and sensory abnormalities. The best known members include Apert, Crouzon, Pfeiffer, Muenke, and Saethre-Chotzen syndromes.

Each syndrome carries its own genetic signature, with mutations in genes such as FGFR, TWIST, and EFNB1 recurring through the family. Knowing the genetics aids diagnosis and feeds current drug research. Surgery remains the main treatment for the cranial deformity, with techniques advancing syndrome by syndrome. The authors press for personalized approaches, especially for the neurological and breathing complications that surgery alone cannot settle.
pmc-10808797:
Long and ten co-authors use gene tools to test if blood traits cause wild mood swings in sick old folks in this twenty twenty-four study. Such swings, named delirium, raise death risk and length of ward stays. Care and cure picks for them are still few and weak.

Inside, gene marks for one hundred twenty-nine blood traits were set next to a huge Finn gene bank. Two fat traits raised the odds of the swings in the gene checks. A third trait, a form of a known vitamin, cut the odds by a wide share. Wide scans showed the same three traits touch the risk of many other ills too. The team flags the vitamin form as a lead for new cure work.
pmc-10850397:
Shouming Li and co-authors published this tomato study in 2023. Cold damages tomatoes at every growth stage, so breeders need genes that help plants cope. The team screened 223 tomato varieties for cold response and compared their gene activity. One gene stood out: SUS3, from the sucrose synthase family, switched on under cold stress. The researchers then raised and lowered its activity in test plants.

Plants with extra SUS3 activity held up far better in the cold. They leaked less from their cells, built up more proline and soluble sugar, and kept protective enzymes working. Plants with the gene turned down suffered more membrane damage and more harmful oxygen radicals. The authors propose SUS3 as a direct target for breeding or engineering hardier tomato crops.
pmc-10908297:
Sedera Radoniaina Rakotondrasoa and colleagues reviewed tuberculosis care outcomes in Madagascar in 2023. Records came from one hospital in the capital, Antananarivo. The cohort held over six hundred outpatients from one year. Treatment success, death, failure, and dropout were all tracked. Models adjusted for other factors when judging predictors. Most patients achieved treatment success overall. Death and dropout each claimed a small share. Failure was rare in this cohort.

Women succeeded in treatment more often than men. One lung form with negative smear tests fared far worse. That form predicted dropout and death most strongly. Disease outside the lungs also predicted death clearly. Center results still missed national and global targets. The authors urge faster diagnosis for the high-risk forms. Better patient education joins their call. Tight follow-up should target those likeliest to fare poorly. Registries made this risk picture possible, they note.
pmc-11532497:
Mahsa Khadem Sadigh and four co-authors study how solvents shift light traits of 1-indanone compounds, a group of bio molecules. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Solvent pull can change how such molecules soak and give off light, and how strong their bent-light response is. The team paired math models with light tests across solvent types.

Broad solvent pull ruled soak bands, while set bonds like hydrogen links ruled glow traits. Strong hydrogen bonds boosted the bent-light response. Low-grade bent response tracked high-grade response in the same way. The team says first-grade reads can flag high-grade worth, and these compounds may suit light tool design.
pmc-11536897:
Xuyang Meng and nine co-authors linked a blood index of insulin resistance to death in hospital for heart patients, in a study from twenty twenty-four. The index blends fat and sugar measures from a routine blood draw. The question was whether it predicts in-hospital death for people with coronary artery disease, and whether the answer depends on their sugar status.

Patients were split into thirds by the index, and classed as normal, pre-diabetic, or diabetic. The highest third carried more than double the death risk of the lowest, after full adjustment. In subgroup checks, the link held clearly for diabetic patients. The authors offer the index as a cheap predictor, above all for those with diabetes.
pmc-11538497:
Paul Stammer and co-authors test whether fragments of a vessel-lining protein could flag dangerous aortic disease. The protein, VE-cadherin, glues the cells of the vessel wall together, and enzymes can snip off pieces that float in the blood when the wall is inflamed. The team grew human aortic lining cells, triggered the snipping, and measured fragment levels in patients.

In the dish, an inflammation signal set the cutting enzymes ADAM10 and ADAM17 to work and made the cell layer leakier. In blood samples, though, fragment levels in patients with torn or swollen aortas matched those in other patient groups. Those groups had neck artery narrowing or varicose veins. So the fragments do not single out aortic disease. Levels did rise and fall with the inflammation signal and with ADAM10 itself, most tightly in chronic tears, backing the mechanism if not the marker.
pmc-11548097:
Fangjie Wei and co-authors build an online inspection system for electric car seats, in an engineering paper from 2024. As electric cars spread, seat noise has become a prime source of cabin noise. Checking seats off the line by hand slows output and splits the checks into steps.

The system, built with LabVIEW software, tests seat noise and electrical functions at the same time on the line. Boards gather noise data while a controller runs the seat motor so its current can be read. A supervisor computer charts the data, judges it, and stores results for lookup. In real use, the line cycle time improved by 34.84 percent. Each seat took under 86 seconds to check, and faulty motors were caught fast.
pmc-11574197:
Chiara Longo and four co-authors use network analysis to study thinking problems in Parkinson's disease. Some patients keep clear thinking while others develop mild cognitive impairment, and the team asked whether the links among mental skills shift as the condition sets in.

They gave a detailed test battery to 275 patients and split them into two groups: 171 with unimpaired thinking and 104 with mild impairment. Treating each test as a node in a network, they found the impaired group's network looked denser, with some links between skills weakened. The authors read this as a sign of reorganization, where the mind may work around failing links to keep functioning.
pmc-11576097:
Khairunnisa Che Ghazali and colleagues share lessons from operating on blocked bowels in patients with severe lung hypertension. Their case series from twenty twenty-four reports three patients. High lung pressure makes general anaesthesia very risky. Bowel obstruction still forces emergency decisions regardless.

One man with Eisenmenger syndrome had part of his colon removed. He died six days after the operation. A second Eisenmenger patient had a stoma-forming procedure. He died after a month of heart and lung complications. A third case completes the institutional experience reported. Anaesthetic and surgical strategies differed across the cases. The series aims to improve the next patient's odds.
pmc-11576797:
When colon cancer spreads to the liver, fat showing up inside the tumors after chemotherapy may carry news about how a patient will fare. Irmina Morawska, Katarzyna Pasicz, and Andrzej Cieszanowski looked back at scans from ninety-eight patients treated between twenty seventeen and twenty twenty-two. A special MRI method flags fat when the signal drops by at least twelve percent between two kinds of image.

No patient showed tumor fat before treatment, but twenty-nine did afterward, close to thirty percent. Those patients lived a median of thirty-two months, against forty-eight months for patients whose tumors stayed fat-free. The team concludes that fat appearing in these liver tumors after treatment is a warning sign tied to a poorer outlook.
pmc-11599397:
Zhen Shi, Yunbing Yan, and Sen Zhang personalize how car brakes feel in this two thousand twenty-four engineering paper. Electronic hydraulic brake systems in intelligent vehicles face nonlinear behavior, and drivers have different tastes in pedal response. The authors analyze the active braking principle of the brake booster, building equivalent dynamic models plus a Karnopp friction model. From brake pedal displacement and velocity signals, the system identifies driving style and selects among sporty, comfortable, and standard boost characteristics.

A variable-gain multi-loop control strategy, compensating for nonlinear friction and inertia, keeps the variable boost behavior accurate. Tuning and verification used co-simulation between AMESim and Simulink plus real vehicle tests. Steady-state control errors stayed within zero point one megapascals across braking conditions matched to driving styles. The authors present the strategy as a feasible solution for personalized braking in higher-level intelligent driving.
pmc-11599697:
Jae Wook Jung and co-authors track pressure inside the skull after emergency brain surgery in this 2024 paper. The patients had malignant middle cerebral artery infarction, a severe stroke with swelling. Removing part of the skull eases pressure and saves lives. Still, 20 to 40 percent of patients die after the surgery.

Records covered 112 patients who had the surgery and pressure monitoring. Pressure trends over 192 hours split patients into rising and falling groups. Outcomes at three months were compared, using a standard disability scale. Favorable outcome meant moderate disability or better. Death rates also differed by pressure path. The work suggests the pressure trend itself, not just single readings, can warn care teams.
pmc-11603997:
Yuhao Yang and eight co-authors examine how insulin resistance and belly fat interact in cardiovascular risk, using a nationwide Chinese cohort, in a two thousand twenty-four population-health paper. Both measures are settled risk contributors, but their combined conduct was unclear.

Over eight thousand adults were followed for nine years and split into four groups by their triglyceride-glucose index and Chinese visceral adiposity index. Oddly, the highest cardiovascular risk sat in the group with low insulin resistance but high visceral fat, ahead of the group high on both. Formal interaction analysis bore out a negative interaction for heart disease results. The authors argue visceral fat merits attention even when metabolic markers look reassuring.
pmc-11605097:
Ayelen Toro and a large team study how coronaviruses reach the blood in a 2024 paper. The COVID-19 virus is now known to affect the whole body, not just the lungs, but its routes of spread were unclear. The team paired a mouse coronavirus model with clinical data from human patients.

Under a powerful microscope, they found virus particles inside red blood cells. Computer modeling suggested the virus spike may latch onto heme, the iron carrying part of blood pigment, to enter cells. In mice, adding a heme related compound worsened disease, while a drug that interacts with heme eased it. The work points to blood proteins as a key part of how these viruses cause harm.
pmc-11606097:
Farnush Bakhshimoghaddam and thirteen colleagues published a systematic review in two thousand twenty-four on diet patterns and fatty liver disease. Fatty liver not caused by alcohol is rising worldwide. Whole diet patterns, rather than single nutrients, may show what protects the liver.

The reviewers gathered twenty-seven observational studies and sixteen trials from sixteen countries. Mediterranean and DASH-style diets appeared to prevent and improve the disease. Western patterns heavy in sweets, red meat, and fast food tracked with more disease. Low-carbohydrate diets also helped prevent and treat it in the trials reviewed. Quality checks were applied to each study. The authors back pattern-based advice as part of care.
pmc-11610697:
João Pedro Fontenelle and five colleagues published a 2024 genetics study of the eastern spruce budworm, a moth whose larvae defoliate North American boreal forests. Budworm outbreaks erupt across huge areas, changing forest ecology and hitting the timber economy. Outbreaks involve rapid growth in numbers and in the connections between populations.

The team characterized the genotypes of outbreaking populations in Quebec and neighboring regions over multiple years. Genetic data reveal whether outbreaks spread from a few source populations or ignite independently in many places. They also show how connectivity changes as an outbreak rises and falls. Such knowledge helps forecast where future outbreaks will move and how severely forests will be affected.
pmc-11613397:
Xuefei Zhang, Shan Gao, and Shuya Wei test, in a 2024 study, whether broad, whole-person nursing care improves outcomes for older patients with long-term heart failure. Such patients face weak hearts, low mood, and poor life quality at once. Records for 120 patients at one hospital were split by the nursing style they had received.

After care, both groups felt less anxious and low, but the broad-care group did better on mood scores. They also followed their drug plans more faithfully, at eighty-five percent versus seventy. Heart pumping and chamber sizes improved in both groups, more so under broad care. The authors back broad nursing as a way to lift both body and mind outcomes.
pmc-11618097:
Wang and colleagues published in twenty twenty-four a deep learning tool that cleans noisy voltage imaging of brain cells. Voltage imaging films electrical activity, but signals are weak and noisy. Older cleaning methods assume rigid patterns for signal and noise. The team's method, CellMincer, learns from the data itself with no labels. It hides sparse pixels and predicts them from short time windows nearby.

Precomputed patterns of space and time correlation guide the cleaning. A physics-based simulator created realistic fake data for tuning. That guidance tripled the signal gain in their tests. On real data checked against direct electrical recordings, CellMincer recovered signals faithfully. It beat rival methods on signal strength and consistency. Workflows using it found neurons and activity peaks more reliably.
pmc-11618497:
Nelly Banda and seven co-authors trace how lead harm passes across mouse breeds, split by sex and by which parent was dosed. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. Lead is known to hurt fertility, pregnancy, and child brain growth. Mice breathe leaded soil for weeks, then breed in four mixes of dosed and clean parents.

Conception falls with dose, worst when both parents are dosed. Testis gene reads pin the drop on oxidative stress. Pups of dosed parents fare worse in maze and balance tests, with harm that turns on which parent was dosed and on pup sex. A dosed father's harm lands hardest on daughters, with brain gene shifts to match.
pmc-11618597:
Wu and five co-authors hardened a coded radio system against fading in this paper from twenty twenty-four. Polar codes paired with OFDM, the multicarrier scheme behind modern wireless, suffer on multipath channels. Echoes make some subcarriers noisy and others clean, and errors arrive in bursts. Two fixes are proposed and simulated.

First, each subcarrier's channel quality is fed into the decoder's soft information. That tells the decoder which bits to trust less. Second, an interleaver shuffles the coded bits so bursts scatter into isolated errors. Together the two strategies beat the conventional setup by a wide margin. The authors call both essential for future polar-OFDM systems.
pmc-11619097:
Morgan Jibowu and co-authors map a common mosquito in Harris County, Texas, in work from two thousand twenty-four. The mosquito can spread West Nile virus, so health teams need to know where it clusters. The team used trap counts from two thousand twenty to two thousand twenty-two and mapped them by place.

High counts clustered in central Houston and the north-west of the county. Some of the oldest city areas stayed high across the years. Counts also rose in areas with more social hardship, which the authors link to the built setting. Maps like these can guide spraying and watch efforts.
pmc-11619497:
Philip Rosenthal, a medical researcher, reflects in a 2024 essay on a visit to refugee settlements in northern Uganda, near the war zone in South Sudan. He had traveled there to plan malaria research with Ugandan and American colleagues. What struck him was how calm and orderly daily life in the camp appeared.

Shops sold food and phone time, homes were kept neat, and fields were well tended. Families fleeing war were given care, shelter, and a chance to restart their lives. Rosenthal contrasts this quiet success with the strain seen in far richer countries. At the border post, though, new arrivals still looked anxious, carrying little and facing checks for illness.
pmc-11623797:
Michael Zouari and Zeev Shtudiner compared how Jewish and Muslim students in Israel choose their field of study. They combined surveys with a conjoint analysis, which forces trade-offs between factors such as pay, interest, and advice. The two groups weighed the choice differently. Muslim students scored higher on individualism and gave more weight to prior work experience and to teachers' influence. Jewish students put earning potential first.

The authors argue these gaps reflect culture, social setting, and economics acting together, not taste alone. They call for education policies and support systems that respond to each group's needs and aims. Inclusive mentoring and career guidance, for example, might stress different things for different students. The study adds evidence that field choice in mixed societies is socially patterned. The authors suggest future work should cover more ethnic groups and track how early choices shape later mobility.
pmc-11624697:
Maud Muosieyiri and four colleagues tested whether Mozambique's expanded checklist finds more maternal near-miss cases than the World Health Organization's original tool. A near miss means a woman nearly died from pregnancy complications but survived; counting them exposes health system failures. Mozambique's abstraction tool adds clinical criteria to the WHO version. The cross-sectional study enrolled 2,057 women at two referral hospitals in Inhambane province during twenty twenty-one and twenty twenty-two.

Both tools were applied to the same admissions, and sociodemographic effects on case identification were examined. Extra criteria only help if they catch real cases the standard tool misses, without flooding counts with false ones. Where records are paper-thin and staff scarce, the abstraction tool chosen shapes what the system can learn from its worst outcomes. This twenty twenty-four evaluation gives Mozambique evidence for keeping, trimming, or exporting its modification.
pmc-11625897:
Sofiah Hanis Ahmad Hisham and co-authors set out how anatomy education at Universiti Sains Malaysia changed in the COVID-19 pandemic, and after it. Their 2024 piece frames the crisis as a chance to build teaching that holds up more well.

Plans took in blended learning and tools made more strong by technology. They also took in practical sessions centred on students, and more strong formative assessment. Resources in digital form joined teaching in person. Those took in a virtual anatomy museum and quizzes on histology on the web. Practical classes were made anew, round joint work, teaching by peers, and skills in how to talk with others. Feedback that kept up at all times backed learning that went on. The team reports a better grasp of anatomical concepts. They also report better emotional well-being. Lessons from the pandemic now guide how they plan for breaks in teaching to come.
pmc-11629197:
Wang and ten colleagues build an injectable gel that attacks bone cancer with copper and heat in twenty twenty-four. Osteosarcoma mainly strikes the young and often ends poorly. A newly found cell death type, cuproptosis, offers a fresh angle. Their gel combines copper ions with the drug vorinostat.

Copper targets the cell's energy cycle to trigger cuproptosis. Vorinostat blocks gene silencing enzymes and generates reactive oxygen. Together they raise a key protein that amplifies the copper effect. Light based heating adds a further attack. Injected into rat tumors, the gel partly erased the cancer without spread. The authors see a path toward clinical use of cuproptosis therapy.
pmc-11630597:
Slob and colleagues published in twenty twenty-four a cost study of a kidney drug in the Netherlands. The drug empagliflozin slowed chronic kidney disease in a large recent trial. Whether it is worth its price in Dutch care was unknown. The team built a simulation that follows patients through kidney disease stages. It compared standard care alone with standard care plus the drug. Inputs came from the trial, national cost data, and published sources.

Adding the drug saved money overall in their model. Patients also gained more than a year of life on average. Quality-adjusted life years rose by a similar margin. Checks that varied the inputs kept the same conclusion. The authors call the drug a dominant option, meaning better and cheaper. The result held regardless of diabetes status.
pmc-11632097:
Madhav Chaturvedi and fifteen colleagues published a framework paper in two thousand twenty-four on testing for new infections during outbreaks. When a new germ spreads, tests must be built and checked fast. Yet disease levels and the germ itself keep changing, which makes accuracy hard to pin down.

Drawing on lessons from the COVID-19 pandemic, the authors propose one joined-up framework. It links three parts in a loop: measuring test accuracy, modelling for public health choices, and the effects of control measures. Each part feeds the others as the outbreak shifts. The authors argue this loop lets future testing platforms serve both patient care and public health better than working in separate steps.
pmc-11635997:
Mari Myhrstad and nine colleagues published a 2024 study hunting for early warning markers of type 2 diabetes in healthy people. Type 2 diabetes is spreading worldwide, driven by excess weight, inactivity, and poor diet. The gut microbiota, the community of microbes in the intestine, also influences how the body handles sugar.

Because the disease is preventable, early markers of risk are valuable. The researchers examined healthy individuals and explored how gut microbes, physical activity, and metabolic markers relate to each other. Their cross-sectional design takes a snapshot of all three at once. Patterns that stand out in healthy people could become biomarkers, simple measurable signs that flag who is drifting toward diabetes and might benefit from early lifestyle change.
pmc-11641297:
Jose Bellver and co-authors map gut and reproductive tract microbes in infertile women with obesity. Past work linked microbes to both obesity and infertility, with mixed results. The team ran a study at many clinics, taking saliva and stool in person. Fluid from the vagina and womb was taken at the clinic, and microbe genes were read.

The gut ratio once proposed as an obesity mark did not differ by weight group. Some microbe groups were more common in one group than the other. Vaginal and womb samples looked much alike, backing the idea that womb microbes rise from below. A streptococcus-heavy womb profile was more common in women with obesity. The authors say the map may help explain poor outcomes in this group.
pmc-11641997:
Tao Li and nine colleagues published a soil mechanics study in two thousand twenty-four on how grains rotate during shearing. The strength of sand and gravel matters for foundations and slopes. Grains both slide and roll when soil is sheared, and each motion eats energy differently.

The team recast irregular grains as regular shapes while keeping energy and density unchanged. They derived how rotation changes shear stress and energy use across the shearing process. Tests on jagged coral sand and smooth glass beads checked the theory. Early in shearing, most work went into rolling; later, sliding took over. Rolling energy reacted far more strongly to load than sliding energy. The findings refine strength rules for granular ground.
pmc-11642097:
Caroline Berchtold and others studied mismatched kidney transplants in two thousand twenty-four. Donor and receiver blood groups sometimes differ. Such transplants need stronger drugs to calm the immune system upfront. Long-term kidney function matches compatible transplants, though. The extra burden from side problems was never counted. Twenty years of records supplied matched pairs.

Each such case was paired with a matched one. Returns to hospital, infections, new diabetes, and tumors were set side by side. Survival and kidney function proved much the same overall. Rates of side problems showed no real gaps. Time back in hospital also matched between groups. The feared extra burden did not show up clearly. Careful centers can offer such transplants with far less worry.
pmc-11642697:
Małgorzata Mizerska-Wasiak and co-authors evaluate, in twenty twenty-four, a triple drug therapy for children with two related kidney diseases, IgA nephropathy and IgA vasculitis nephritis. Both deposit an antibody in the kidneys and cause blood and protein in urine. Sixty-eight children diagnosed by biopsy took part. Thirty-six got the triple therapy: azathioprine, prednisone, and enalapril, for one year, with a control biopsy. Thirty-two controls got enalapril alone. After a year, the triple therapy group showed a significant drop in proteinuria, cleared in nearly all, and in hematuria.

Proteinuria fell far more in the treated group than in controls, for both diseases. Biopsy scores for two damage features improved often in the treated group. The authors discuss which children need the stronger therapy.
pmc-11643697:
Jongbeom Park and colleagues engineer a yeast to eat xylose from plant biomass. Their study from twenty twenty-four rewrites Komagataella phaffii metabolism. Plant hydrolysates hold plenty of glucose and xylose sugars. This industrial yeast could not use xylose effectively before.

Three pathway genes were added with tuned promoter strengths. A strong promoter drove the middle gene of the pathway. Weaker promoters balanced the first and third genes. The engineered strain grew far better on kenaf hydrolysate. Growth beat the native strain by a clear margin. This is the first xylose pathway reported in this yeast. Biofactories could make protein and chemicals from crop waste.
pmc-11643897:
Pereira, Tavernier, dos Santos Junior, and Vernilli published this study in twenty twenty-four on mold fluxes used in steel casting. Mold fluxes are powders that melt over liquid steel. They guide heat flow and help stop cracks from forming. The standard mixes contain fluorine, which raises health and environmental concerns. The team set out to design mixes that work without it.

The authors tested how four ingredients changed thickness, melting, and crystal growth in the flux. Four trial mixes were compared in the lab. One mix with a boron compound flowed well and formed few crystals. A fully fluorine-free mix proved too thick. The results show that fluxes without fluorine can match the old mixes, though plant trials are still needed.
pmc-11644797:
Shaklein and seven co-authors model polymer burning with a mixture fraction method, in work from twenty twenty-four. Predicting how plastic burns is harder than gas burning. Heat and mass flow between the flame and the solid surface must be captured well.

The test case was flame spread over a surface of PMMA, a common clear polymer. The team built counterflow flame solutions with the flame close to the fuel surface to capture heat loss into the solid. Tabulated chemistry then rebuilt temperature and species fields across the full case. Comparing with past numeric studies checked the method. Better burn forecasts aid fire safety design for buildings and transport.
pmc-11646397:
Ramzan and co-authors make silver nanoparticles from ginger extract and test them against drug-resistant bacteria. Drug resistance is a growing threat, and plant-based methods offer one route to new tools. The team first checked what plant compounds the ginger extracts held.

They then formed the particles at room temperature and checked them with light, X-ray, and microscope tools. Tests confirmed the particles had formed as expected. The group next measured how well the particles killed resistant strains. HPLC tests found eight active plant compounds in the organic ginger extracts, which helps explain the results.
pmc-11647297:
Helen D'Couto and a large team simulate smoking's toll on people with HIV in South Africa. Their modelling study from twenty twenty-four projects lung cancer and stroke. HIV deaths fall as treatment spreads across the country. Tobacco diseases now claim a growing share of lives instead.

Eighteen lifetime cohorts varied by sex, age, and smoking status. A microsimulation followed each group through ageing and care lapses. Quitting at the start was modelled for former smokers. Cancer risk multipliers for smokers were large in the model. Results quantify how much cessation could avert future cases. HIV programmes may need tobacco treatment built in. Longevity gains from HIV care can be smoked away.
pmc-11647397:
Yordanos Sisay Asgedom and four co-authors split the wealth gap in neck-of-womb checks in sub-Saharan Africa. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Health poll files from the zone fed the work. Pooled check rates sat near one in ten women. A fair count showed a clear rich-lean in who gets checked.

Split math laid the gap most to wealth rank it self, school grade, home place, and news reach. The team urge work on school paths, news reach in homes, and the purse base, so the poor can reach checks at rates near the rich.
pmc-11650597:
Alexandra Maier and co-authors dope hybrid nanoparticles with manganese to make magnetic heating therapy stronger. Their study appeared in 2024. The particles pair a palladium core, meant someday to carry a radioactive label, with an iron oxide shell that heats in an alternating magnetic field. Such heat, placed inside tumors, can pair with radiation or imaging. Adding manganese to the shell lattice raised magnetic saturation markedly.

Heating power rose up to 1.7 times over undoped particles. At higher manganese content, the metal gathered at the shell's rim, which further boosted heating at the tested field settings. The authors say the design keeps the extra functions of the hybrid while fixing its weak point, heat output. Stronger heating means lower doses could reach the same effect in future cancer treatment.
pmc-11651697:
Petros Perros and colleagues report a 2024 survey study of people living with an underactive thyroid. Between a tenth and a sixth of such patients still feel unwell even when blood tests look right. The team asked whether a distress-prone style of personality, called type D, helps explain that gap. Type D had been linked to heavier symptoms in other illnesses but not studied here.

The online survey drew more than thirty-nine hundred replies from many countries, with over thirty-five hundred valid. More than half of the respondents fit the type D pattern. That group also reported more anxiety, low mood, and body complaints. They were less satisfied with their care and felt the illness pressed harder on daily life. The authors suggest that how a patient is wired may shape how the illness feels, and care should take note.
pmc-11653897:
Jan Novák and five co-authors present two cases of primary ciliary dyskinesia surfacing as male infertility, in a two thousand twenty-four case report with an overview of past work. The genetic disorder cripples the tiny motile cilia that clear airways and propel sperm.

Affected men usually carry normal sperm counts with zero motility, alongside lifelong respiratory troubles such as bronchiectasis, chronic sinusitis, and ear infections. About half also have mirror-flipped internal organs, the Kartagener pattern. More than fifty causative gene mutations are known, and mechanisms beyond immotility can wreck assisted reproduction. The authors urge doctors and nurses to suspect the diagnosis from this symptom pattern and to include sperm DNA fragmentation testing in the work-up.
pmc-11654197:
Jun-Sik Lim and five co-authors measure how fast African swine fever swept through South Korea's wild boar despite twenty-three hundred kilometers of fencing, and whether the fences mattered where it counted. From the national surveillance system they extracted over twenty-six hundred cases from the first detection in October twenty nineteen through September twenty twenty-two, resolving into four geographic clusters.

The wavefront averaged about half a kilometer per week, but the eastern cluster raced at nearly one kilometer weekly, a spread the authors attribute to boar density differences across habitats. Fencing significantly affected dispersal in only two of four clusters and slowed the wavefront in none. The heterogeneity itself is the finding: barrier strategies perform unevenly across terrain and host density.
pmc-11654697:
Dawit Lee, Sanghyub Lee, and Aaron Young wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-four about a powered frame that helps people walk. Such lower-limb exoskeletons must adapt as ground and pace change. A fixed controller often fails to match what the wearer needs moment by moment.

Their system uses artificial intelligence to switch the type of help as walking mode changes. It also adjusts help with slope and times each push to the step cycle, all in real time. On a treadmill, the smart help cut the energy cost of walking more than standard help did. Tests outdoors showed good control and higher user preference. The system needs no separate mode classifier and works for new users at once.
pmc-11655597:
Mira Burmeister-Rudolph studies, in twenty twenty-four, how migrant-led civil society groups mediate between low-wage labor migrants and state bodies in the Gulf states. Low-wage migrants face major rights abuses there despite labor laws and human rights pledges. India has built an official support frame for its estimated five and a half million low-wage workers in the Gulf, with emergency funds, repatriation help, and walk-in centers. In practice, many migrants cannot reach those rights.

Upper and middle-class Indian migrant groups step in as informal brokers to embassies and local state bodies. The article traces that gap to the migrants' historic marginalization and to the informal way citizen-state ties work in India. Data come from interviews and field observation of support networks.
pmc-11665897:
Lauren N Woodie and four co-authors show that when brain and liver clocks tick in sync, mice are guarded from metabolic disease. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. Most cells hold a daily clock, tuned by a master clock in the brain. When the two fall out of step, as in shift work, metabolism suffers.

They use mice whose master clock runs short, which makes them prone to weight gain on a rich diet. Liver cells with a matched short clock are then bred in. Those mice are spared the extra weight gain and liver fat, while their short daily rhythm stays. Sync inside the body, not with the world, may be the key target.
pmc-11666897:
Mohammed Mansour Quradha and co-authors tested extracts of the plant Salvia triloba in a study published in 2024. They made three kinds of extract, one with a standard solvent, one with sound waves, and one with a newer green method. They then compared what plant compounds each extract held and how each acted in lab tests.

The standard extract held the most rosmarinic acid, a key plant compound. The green extract blocked biofilm growth best against one germ, while the standard extract worked best against two others. Some extracts also slowed signals that germs use to act as a group. Results for blocking two enzymes were weak or mixed. The work helps show which method best suits each use.
pmc-11668497:
Ahun and five colleagues ask community experts in twenty twenty-four what skills young children need to thrive. Past study has stressed school skills such as reading and math. The team asked about six broader skills, from curiosity and creative thought to self control. They spoke with parents, teachers, doctors, and program leaders across the United States.

Sixty in depth talks were held by video with a mixed group of adults. All said the six skills matter and link closely to each other. Most named self control and clear thought as the core skill. The team says care and school plans should treat these skills as goals in their own right.
pmc-11668597:
Dumbrique, Hernandez, Cruz, Pagdanganan, and Naval build a model to find collapsed lung on chest X-rays in twenty twenty-four. The condition, pneumothorax, traps air near the lung and can be life threatening. X-rays are fast and cheap, but the only sign is often a thin pleural line. That makes the condition easy for human readers to miss.

Their model blends a fully convolutional network with ideas from vision transformers, without costly attention. It works on patches and uses skip links to mix fine and coarse features. On two data sets, it beat prior models on detection and outline accuracy while staying efficient. One data set was newly built from a hospital in the Philippines. A mixed loss function gave a further clear gain in tests.
pmc-11668697:
Mingyue Liu and co-authors map the research field of vagus nerve stimulation for stroke, in a bibliometric study from 2024. Stimulating this nerve has drawn interest as a way to aid stroke recovery. No map of the field's shape and trends had been made.

The team searched a major citation database for work from 2005 to mid-2024 and charted 316 papers by 1,631 authors. Output grew steadily, with the United States in the lead and the University of Texas System the busiest institution. Hot topics include how the therapy works in animal models and gains in arm and hand function after stroke. Newer work reaches to swallowing, speech, thinking, sleep, and mood after stroke.
pmc-11673697:
Li and colleagues charted thirty years of research on early childhood teachers' well-being in twenty twenty-four. Teacher well-being shapes classroom quality and retention, and interest has grown steadily. Their systematic review maps how the field itself has developed.

One hundred sixty-seven articles from a major database, spanning nineteen ninety-three to twenty twenty-three, were analyzed quantitatively. Empirical, quantitative studies dominate the literature. Qualitative and mixed-method work has risen in recent years, promising a more balanced base ahead, while other research types remain scarce. A persistent weakness is fragmented definitions of well-being and inconsistent ways of measuring it. The authors present the review as groundwork for understanding the field's trajectory and for designing more coherent future studies on the teachers of the youngest children.
pmc-11675097:
Palma Manduzio and Evangelos Terpos set out a hands-on path to name red cell alloantibodies. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. Such antibodies form after transfusion, in pregnancy, or by other meets with non-self cell marks. A screen finds them before surgery or a transfusion, and the name step is a key risk gate.

They draw a flow chart for the work, with weight on heat, reaction strength, and enzyme use. Three teaching cases walk through lone and mixed antibodies of known kinds by the gel method. A clear chart, they argue, trims slips in the daily lab flow. A read of the field frames the cases.
pmc-11675597:
Javier Linkolk López-Gonzales and co-authors forecast air quality by splitting the signal before teaching a neural net in two thousand twenty-four. Air readings over time mix slow trends, seasonal swings, and jitter. Forecasting the raw mix at once blurs those parts.

Their hybrid first runs singular spectrum analysis, a tool that peels a series into trend, cycle, and noise parts. A memory-rich recurrent network then forecasts the parts apart, and the sums give the final call. Against rival methods the split-then-learn route proved more precise. The recipe suits other wavy data where pattern and noise deserve separate handling.
pmc-11675697:
Weidong Liu and co-authors build a stronger soft gel from plant sugars in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. The sugar chains come from Dendrobium, a plant used in Chinese herbal medicine. Mixed with a common synthetic polymer and borax, they form bonds that can break and reform.

The result is a double-network gel that is tougher and more stable than the polymer gel alone. It can stretch to more than ten times its length and heal itself in under five seconds after a cut. It also killed one common germ type while sparing others. The authors say such hybrid gels could serve as scaffolds in medical uses.
pmc-11675897:
Ruliang Liu and co-authors describe a new gel for lithium metal batteries, in work published in 2024. The gel is a solid-like material that lets charged particles move through a battery. It is built with a porous frame material that has many tiny holes and open metal sites.

The team made the gel in place from a mix of salts and simple building blocks. Tests showed strong stiffness, good flow of charge, and a wide range in which the gel stayed stable. A test battery kept most of its charge after two hundred cycles. The work points to a safer path for batteries that now use liquid fills, which can leak or catch fire.
pmc-11676697:
Haowei Dong and co-authors build a DNA test to tell two look-alike sand flies apart, in a 2024 paper. One species may spread visceral leishmaniasis in parts of China, yet it is nearly identical in form to a close cousin. Sorting them by eye leaves the kind of doubt that disease control cannot afford.

The team sequenced the full mitochondrial genomes of flies from six sites in two regions. Hundreds of fixed differences separated the species, densest in a standard barcode gene. From those differences they built a real-time PCR test that names a fly quickly. Reliable sorting lets health teams map where the risky species lives and aim control where it counts.
pmc-11678697:
Samille Henriques Pereira, Felipe Paladino Alves, and Santuza Maria Ribeiro Teixeira review vaccine plans against animal trypanosomiasis, in work published in 2024. These parasite diseases, among them nagana, surra, and dourine, hit livestock hard across warm regions. They drain farm income, above all in poor areas. Human forms have seen real progress, but the animal forms stay neglected and short of funds.

The review weighs the blocks to a vaccine. The parasites shift their surface coats, which helps them dodge the immune system, and money for new work is scarce. Any vaccine must also sit inside a control program, with vector control and good veterinary practice. New options opened by work on the immune response include messenger RNA vaccines, vector-based vaccines, and parasites weakened by gene editing. The authors call for work by scientists, governments, and the farming industry.
pmc-11679097:
Letian Hao and co-authors test a cheap, portable system that measures ground forces in three dimensions. Their study appeared in 2024. Lab force plates are precise but costly and fixed in place. The new system, built by a university with a sports technology firm, aims to travel. Fifteen male college students performed walking, running, jumping, and side-cutting moves on both the new system and a reference lab device.

Peak forces matched between the two systems for every movement. The force curves agreed closely, with consistency scores above 0.98 and small errors. The authors conclude the portable kit gives lab-grade readings in the field. Coaches and clinics could measure jumping and cutting forces without a dedicated lab, widening access to biomechanics testing.
pmc-11688597:
Norberg and a large team ask family doctors in Norway how video and phone visits reshape their work in twenty twenty-four. Remote visits spread fast during recent years and are now a fixed part of care. The team held five group talks with eighteen doctors from all four health regions in twenty twenty-two. They sorted the talks into themes.

Doctors said remote care lets them tailor care paths and bend their workday. But easy access also blurs limits, as patients grow less patient with minor illness. Sorting trivial queries from grave ones grows harder, they said. Legal duty and moral care can clash for patients with low health literacy. The doctors affirm remote care is here to stay.
pmc-11689097:
Joukje Swinkels, Jens Abbing, and Marjolein Broese Van Groenou published a 2024 study on why the kind of care older adults receive relates to their well-being. Some elders are cared for mainly by a partner; others rely on family, formal services, or paid help. Health explains much of that, but the network type may also shape how people feel.

The team drew on a Dutch aging study with ten waves over thirty years and nearly five thousand older adults. They sorted care into five types, from no care to paid care. Well-being was measured by depressive symptoms. A psychological theory framed three needs: closeness, independence, and feeling competently cared for. Partner care and no care went with the best well-being; formal care networks fared worst. Loneliness and whether care felt sufficient explained part of the gap.
pmc-11689497:
Rachel VanPutten, Claudia Drossel, and Thomas Waltz report a chart review from twenty twenty-four. They look at family caregivers of older adults with brain disorders that harm memory and thought. Those caregivers took part in skills groups based on dialectical behavior therapy, a talk therapy that teaches calm and coping skills. The groups were changed to fit high-conflict care at home.

Records came from thirty-two caregivers in eight groups, each lasting eight weeks. Many caregivers had clear health problems in their charts, yet said they were healthy on a survey. Most who left did so after a sudden health crisis. The team changed lessons on focus and on asking others for help, and they argue that caregiver health needs direct checks.
pmc-11690897:
Stuart Phillips, writing in two thousand twenty-four, asks who counts as having lost muscle mass and strength with age, a state known as sarcopenia. He works with data from a large Canadian study of aging.

Phillips notes a flaw in the tests used. The scan measure taken as a gold mark in fact counts all soft tissue, not muscle alone. When the team tried the many expert rules for this state, the rules most often did not agree on who had it. Small shifts in cut points changed the results too. He urges the field to settle on one shared way to judge the state, so studies can be matched and care plans can rest on firm ground.
pmc-11691797:
Jung Yoen Son and four co-authors published a study in 2024 on the factors that lead residents of residential care facilities to transfer to a nursing home. Few studies had examined this move, and most follow-up periods were too short to capture gradual changes in health.

The researchers used a national health and aging trends survey from 2011 to 2019. The sample included 970 people with an average age in the mid-eighties, and 143 transferred to a nursing home over eight years. Strong physical performance scores at the start lowered the risk of transfer. A college degree lowered it as well. Over time, staying active, maintaining physical strength, and having few difficulties with daily activities all kept the risk low. The findings show that preserving physical function is central to remaining outside a nursing home.
pmc-11691897:
Alexa Stuifbergen, Stephanie Morgan, Katie Trainum, and Heather Becker compare quality in rural and urban assisted living homes.
