Their 2024 study draws on a statewide assessment in a large Southwestern state. Demand for assisted living is rising, and rural areas are aging faster while their elders tend to be in poorer health.

Site visits gathered data from staff and residents at more than five hundred facilities, over a quarter of them rural. Urban homes held notably more occupied beds on average. Most residents rated their health as good or better, yet a larger share of rural residents rated it fair or poor. The study maps where rural and urban homes differ in size, staffing, and resident views, a base for targeted quality work.
pmc-11692397:
Simran Panesar, Saima Rajabali, and Adrian Wagg published a scoping review in 2024 on the role of culture in shaping attitudes and beliefs about urinary incontinence in older adults. Incontinence is common and can harm health and well-being. Shame and stigma can prevent people from seeking treatment, but culture does more than add stigma.

The reviewers searched six databases with no restriction on language or publication date and kept seventeen articles. Themes included the stress of maintaining ritual cleanliness for religious activities among Muslim women. A norm of secrecy and silence around incontinence appeared for Latina women. Caste discrimination in parts of India shaped who sought pelvic health care. In faiths that emphasize a good reputation, the stigmatized condition conflicted with that value. The review finds little research beyond the theme of stigma and calls for health programs that also weigh the burden of social isolation.
pmc-11692897:
Wan-Tai Au-Yeung, Zachary Beattie, and Jeffrey Kaye report in twenty twenty-four on links between bedroom air and light and mood signs in older adults. The signs they tracked were low drive, sad mood, and worry. Their study ran for nine months in the homes of twelve people, most of them in their late years.

Each week the group filled in short mood surveys sent by email. Sensors in the bedroom logged light, noise, heat, damp, and air grade every few minutes. Low light in the bedroom went with worse sad mood scores. More heat went with worse low drive scores. The authors say small fixes to home air and light may help ease these signs.
pmc-11693397:
Roshni Singh and colleagues asked veteran family caregivers in 2024 what they feel unprepared to do, and whether dementia changes the answer. The data come from a Veterans Affairs survey in which caregivers answered an open question about tasks they wished they were better prepared for. Answers from nearly three hundred dementia caregivers and over four hundred others were sorted into ten themes.

The two groups were demographically similar, though dementia caregivers were older and more often spouses. Comparing their answers shows which unprepared feelings come with caregiving generally and which dementia adds. Tasks around behavior, safety, and decline tend to weigh differently when memory and personality are changing. For caregiver support programs, the point is targeting: training budgets help most when they teach the specific tasks each group actually dreads.
pmc-11709497:
Anca Gabriela Frasineanu and Stephanie Gupton study the brain protein TRIM9 in Alzheimer disease in this 2025 paper. TRIM9 tags other proteins for handling and shapes neuron wiring during development. In adult brain it sits in the postsynaptic density, the receiving hub of synapses. That hub changes early in Alzheimer disease.

Mapping TRIM9 partners surfaced many synapse and Alzheimer linked proteins, including Tau. Cross checking against a disease mouse model showed a striking overlap. Nearly half the changed proteins in the model synapses touch the TRIM9 network. Adolescent mice lacking TRIM9 already show altered synapse composition. The work positions one ligase at a crossroads of development and degeneration.
pmc-11712097:
Yonah Joffe and seven colleagues report a case study, published in 2025, about a failed colonoscopy in a man with mild memory and thinking problems. A colonoscopy can find colon growths early and lower cancer risk, but it only works if the bowel is cleaned out well first. Known risk factors for poor cleaning include age and low health knowledge. The authors note that thinking problems before the exam have rarely been studied as a risk factor.

The patient, called CR, was sixty-nine and had a mild neurocognitive disorder with fast forgetting. His brain scan showed white matter changes, and he had a past history of confusion after surgery. His bowel cleaning scored four on a nine-point scale, which counts as too poor, so the exam failed. He was sent back for a second try.
pmc-11713597:
Jiaqian Wu, Ye Na Han, Nicholas Cosford, and Lutz Tautz hunt for drug-like molecules that remove a brain enzyme tied to Alzheimer disease. The enzyme, called STEP, rises under the influence of amyloid and works against the strengthening of synapses, which the authors link to memory loss. Blocking or reducing it rescued thinking in mouse models, so the target is validated but hard to drug. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team screened a thousand small fluorine-bearing fragments with magnetic resonance methods to find ones that grip the enzyme, then confirmed the grips with several binding tests.

Strong, selective fragments emerged. From the best binder they built degrader molecules that tag the enzyme for disposal. The degraders cleared the enzyme from human nerve-like cells, and one crossed into the brain and worked in living animals. The authors call them first-in-class tools against early synaptic failure.
pmc-11732497:
Michael Zarrella, Kolu Wynne, Basel Saadeh, and Gregory Gersten published a case report in twenty twenty-four on superior vena cava syndrome caused by the very pacemaker leads meant to help the patient. The great vein draining the head and neck narrows around implanted leads, producing venous congestion. Their patient also had sick sinus syndrome, the reason for the device.

Treatment combined invasive and conservative therapy. Balloon angioplasty reopened the vein, and the long-term fix was a leadless pacemaker, removing the offending hardware from the vein entirely. The authors walk through the diagnostic reasoning. As implanted devices multiply, device-caused versions of this once mostly cancer-linked syndrome are rising, and the case doubles as a management template.
pmc-11733897:
Sebastiana Arroyo-Bote and Aina Antonelli-Sastre wrote this research paper, published in 2024. It surveys dentistry students at the University of Barcelona on how well they spot tooth decay in a real case, and whether senior students lean more conservative than juniors.

Cavities are the world's most common chronic disease, so detection skill matters. Students in years three, four, and five judged clinical and radiographic images from one patient. About seventy-two percent saw early decay or cavities in the photo, and every student caught them on the radiograph. On chewing surfaces, many chose gentle sealant treatment. On side surfaces, though, nearly all jumped straight to a drilled class II filling, even in early lesions. Eighty-five percent of answers leaned on minimal intervention concepts elsewhere. The authors see a training gap between diagnosis and restraint.
pmc-11770797:
Fatma Dhaffouli and co-authors measured a calming immune protein, annexin A1, in kidney biopsies from patients with lupus nephritis, the kidney inflammation caused by systemic lupus. The protein helps resolve immune responses, and its behavior in this disease was unclear. Using antibody staining, the team compared tissue from twenty-four patients against eight healthy controls.

Patient biopsies showed significantly more annexin A1 in the glomeruli, the kidney's filtering knots. Stronger staining also tracked with the proliferative classes of the disease, in which kidney cells multiply aggressively, marking more severe illness. The authors suggest the protein could help pathologists distinguish severe from milder forms of lupus nephritis, while noting the small sample.
pmc-11803197:
Andrew Brownlow, Nicholas Davison, and Phillip Morin present the genome of the minke whale. Their genome note from twenty twenty-four deals with Balaenoptera acutorostrata. The assembly comes from a single female whale.

The full sequence runs to thousands of megabases in length. Most of it sits in twenty-two chromosome like scaffolds. The X sex chromosome is among those scaffolds. The mitochondrial genome was also assembled in full. The work comes from the Sanger Tree of Life effort. Such references aid whale biology and conservation study.  The whale species is a baleen whale.
pmc-11810897:
Jiahui Chang and co-authors study how exercise changes a protein mark in mouse muscle. The mark is called lactylation, a tag added to proteins after effort. Mice ran at a moderate pace for six weeks, while a second group rested. The team read genes, proteins, the marks on them, and small molecules in the muscle. The study was published in 2024.

The team found 159 mark sites on 78 proteins that shifted with exercise. Three marked proteins sit in the cell's power plant and help make energy. Their marks fell with exercise, while the proteins themselves rose in amount. Path checks point to energy making as the route most changed. Other routes, tied to fats and acids, also shifted and need more study.
pmc-12110497:
Bornface Chinene and Leon-say Mudadi survey pregnant women's knowledge and expectations about prenatal ultrasound in Harare, Zimbabwe. Their 2023 cross-sectional study questions three hundred eighty-five women at a private maternity hospital.

Most women agreed scans are important during pregnancy, yet nearly four fifths did not know scans can detect birth abnormalities. Knowledge about Down's syndrome was more common and rose slightly with education. Women's main expectations were confirming the delivery date and learning the baby's sex. Diagnosing abnormalities was the least expected purpose. Knowledge levels were lower than in similar studies elsewhere, so the authors call for more public education about what prenatal scanning can reveal.
pmc-12375897:
Yashirdisai Sampasivam and co-authors review how agarwood, a prized fragrant resin, forms in Aquilaria trees, in work the text dates to 2024. The catalog lists 2025. The resin forms inside the wood as a defense against stress and infection, feeding perfume, religious, and medicine trades. Demand has pushed some Aquilaria species toward endangerment. Artificial induction exists, but the biology linking microbes, wood changes, and chemistry stays murky.

The review ties together wood structure shifts, the making of the resin's signature compounds, and signals from multi-layer molecular studies. Microbes living inside the tree, notably Fusarium, help trigger formation in both wild and induced settings. Stress signals and gene switches balance defense against growth. The authors argue that joining these threads is the path to agarwood production that does not fell wild forests.
pmc-12417297:
Hardy and a team including Ward describe co-design of a digital therapy for psychosis in twenty twenty-four. Digital tools may improve access to psychological therapy for people with psychosis. Tools must fit real needs, or they will not help in practice. The authors argue for inclusive co-design that starts from people's needs, not from a fixed solution.

They present a method that mixes agile exploration with clinical rules and regulation. The example is SloMo, a blended therapy for fear of harm from others. A mixed team, including people with lived experience, shaped its functions, look, and content. Cycles of widening and narrowing ideas were tested with stakeholders. The authors close with lessons on funding, rules, and keeping lived experience members involved.
pmc-12661697:
Isabel Rodriguez and five co-authors gather views from Latino families to shape a new eating-disorder program, in this twenty twenty-five study. Teens in this community face stigma, language gaps, and few care options that fit their culture. Most existing programs were built for white, English-speaking families.

The team is adapting a brief workbook program so family doctors can offer it in primary care. Focus groups with teens and caregivers fed the first design steps. Their input guides language, food examples, and family roles in the new version. The study lays groundwork for care that Latino families can truly use.
pmc-12661897:
Chen and co-authors trace a gene pathway that drives lung scarring after bacterial toxin exposure. The enzyme TET1 changes DNA marks on the KLF6 gene. That change raises KLF6 levels in lung vessel cells. High KLF6 then turns on the S1PR3 gene and its RhoA and ROCK signals. The chain pushes vessel cells toward scar-like traits and cell death.

Lowering TET1 eased those shifts in lab cells exposed to the toxin. Extra KLF6 undid the gain from lowering TET1. Lowering KLF6 shut down the RhoA and ROCK path as well. In mice, lowering TET1 reduced lung scarring from the toxin. The authors name this chain as a drug target for lung fibrosis.
pmc-12663197:
Yanju Cai and co-authors survey work flow and feelings among dialysis nurses in China, in work from 2025. Five hundred two nurses at fourteen blood cleaning centers in Fujian took part, and four hundred sixty gave valid replies. Flow at work means deep, smooth focus on the task. The feeling scale gauges how warmly nurses hold their work.

Feeling scores ran high, while flow scores sat mid-range. Flow split by age, hospital rank, years in the craft, and pay. Feeling split by more traits, from unit size to job title. The two scores rose together in a strong link. The authors say lifting feelings may deepen flow and drive.
pmc-12687297:
Jibin Kunjavara and colleagues survey nurses in Qatar on non-drug pain relief for children. Their study from twenty twenty-five covers tertiary public hospitals. Drug-free methods are a core part of good paediatric pain care. Top hospitals should model the best of those practices.

One hundred thirty-six nurses in emergency and inpatient units responded. Knowledge, attitudes, and reported practice were all measured. Demographic traits were tested against competence scores. Sampling was proportionate across the participating units. Data collection ran through autumn of twenty twenty-four. Gaps between knowing and doing can now be targeted. Training design benefits from knowing exactly where practice lags.
pmc-12691197:
Meretukov and co-authors test large language models on non-English medical records in breast cancer care. Real-world evidence often sits locked in free-text electronic records, hard to use for research. Language models could turn that text into structured data sets, yet their reliability is still doubted by many.

The study focuses on hormone receptor-positive breast cancer cases. Records written in a non-English language add a further test of model skill. The team checked how faithfully the models extracted key facts. Trustworthy extraction would open vast record archives, in many languages, to outcome research.
pmc-12693297:
Rafael Campos Vieira and co-authors build a twin network that judges how alike two molecules are from charge maps and weak-contact art, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Charge images feed a vision net, while texture marks from density maps feed a second net. The two streams merge into one shared space trained to pull kin close.

Weak-contact data helps the model spot stand-in molecules that bind the same target in unlike shapes. Three drug sets test the system, covering leukemia, Alzheimer disease, and a cross-check set. The frame is pitched for screening, reuse of old drugs, and fresh candidate hunts. Readers get a similarity judge that reads more than raw shape.
pmc-12693797:
Giulia Bacilliere and four colleagues published an ecology study in two thousand twenty-five on a cold-loving moss in Italy. The moss Pohlia cruda grows in high, cold places across the far north and mountains. The team modelled where in Italy the moss could live as the climate warms.

They combined several distribution models and tested two paths for future greenhouse gas levels, for the years two thousand fifty and two thousand ninety. Under the middle path, suitable ground shrank by roughly a quarter to nearly a half. Under the highest-emissions path, losses ran deeper still. The authors say the work is the first of its kind for mosses in Italy. It gives planners a base for protecting mountain plant life.
pmc-12699197:
Ye Tao and co-authors build, in twenty twenty-five, a chemical method to tell apart two Chinese herbal medicines that are often confused. Sinomenii caulis and Menispermi rhizoma come from the same plant family. Mix-ups risk wrong treatment. The team used liquid chromatography to build chemical fingerprints for each herb across batches. Fingerprints of the same herb matched well. One herb contained sinomenine; the other contained dauricine, two distinct marker compounds. A mass spectrometry step then produced a digital matrix of chemical components for each herb.

That matrix became the basis of a new identification method. It successfully separated the two herbs. Results on samples with varied adulteration levels followed a correlation trend, supporting the method for quality control.
pmc-12705697:
Tianli Li and co-authors find an ancient plant protein that calms a key stress enzyme family in two thousand twenty-five. The enzymes, called PP2C-As, steer how plants meet drought, salt, and germs. Known brakes on them need the hormone ABA, but other brakes were largely unknown.

The protein, FL7, grips many of the enzymes and mutes them without ABA, by a non-rival route. With the enzymes muted, plants gain salt tolerance and stronger defense. One end region of FL7 does the gripping. Kin of the protein trace back to algae kin of land plants, near a billion years deep, and the algal versions brake the enzymes too. The layer of control thus predates land plants.
pmc-12706697:
Nathalie Heidi Meyer and five colleagues published a neuroscience study in two thousand twenty-five on reliving memories. Feeling transported back into a past event depends on more than memory traces. Body-based signals at the moment of learning may set how vivid the reliving feels later.

In virtual reality, participants encoded scenes while the team varied hand-movement feedback and viewpoint between first and third person. Brain recordings captured coupling between the premotor cortex and the hippocampus. Stronger coupling tied body-congruency effects at encoding to richer reliving a week later. Weaker coupling broke that link. The authors say bodily self-awareness tunes memory through this circuit. The effect vanished under a control condition.
pmc-12709797:
Ning Wang, Xue Wang, Xue Zhou, Guoyue Yang, and Qing Ye search for shared gene signatures. The signatures link COVID-19 with progression from liver cirrhosis to liver cancer. Their bioinformatics paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Cirrhosis is a major risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma, and COVID-19 hits such patients hard.

Comparing gene expression datasets, the team found seventy-eight genes changed in both conditions, mostly tied to the cell cycle. Network analysis singled out CDK1 as the hub gene. CDK1 levels predicted both COVID-19 and the cirrhosis-cancer cohort with excellent accuracy, and liver cancer patients with high CDK1 fared worse. Regulatory networks around the signature were also mapped, offering candidate targets for therapy.
pmc-12711997:
Zhenyu Zhang and co-authors published a 2025 study of a cell modification that a flu virus meets when it strikes. The modification, ADP-ribosylation, is a tag the cell hangs on its own proteins, and on those of the virus. The tag is hung by a family of cell enzymes, and it can be removed just as fast. The team asks what role it plays in a flu infection.

On infection, the tag count leapt up fast and wide, in a wave that curbed the spread of the virus. Mass spectrometry mapped nearly four thousand tag sites on nearly a thousand host proteins, and over a hundred on the viral proteins. Work tests show tags on the copying machinery of the virus blunt its activity. The lead shield protein of the virus fights back: it damps the tag wave. One enzyme of the family, PARP1, makes most of the wave.
pmc-12714197:
Sneh Harsh and colleagues uncovered how adult fruit fly testes keep their male identity switched on. Stem cells in the testis need a factor called Chinmo to stay male; without it they convert toward the ovarian program through a female RNA-binding protein. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team shows the missing link is a pioneer factor called Zelda, which can open silent genes. In healthy cells, small RNAs keep the Zelda message locked away untranslated. When Chinmo is lost, those small RNAs fade and Zelda protein gets made.

Zelda proved both required and enough on its own to flip the cells toward the female program. It raises two target genes that feed the female pathway, and it also turns down the Chinmo gene itself, locking the switch. The same flip could be triggered in male fat tissue, hinting at a general guard mechanism.
pmc-12716597:
Oumnia Bouaddi and a large team of co-authors study how migrants reach health care in Morocco, in a paper dated twenty twenty-five. Morocco sits between Africa and Europe and hosts many migrants in transit or settled. Care is free in emergencies and clinics, yet barriers persist.

The team spoke with migrants, community leaders, aid groups, and health workers in five cities. Fear of costs and wrong beliefs about rights shaped care seeking. Most found clinic care free and easy to reach. Still, office hurdles, language gaps, and drug costs blocked some. The authors list fixes drawn from all sides.
pmc-12718597:
Morris Gordon and four colleagues compare drugs for holding Crohn's disease quiet after surgery, in a twenty twenty-five review. About half of Crohn's patients need surgery, and many relapse after it. The team pooled thirty-four trials with 3,197 patients in a network analysis. Outcomes were symptom relapse, scope-seen relapse, and quitting from side effects.

One biologic drug, adalimumab, clearly cut symptom relapse against placebo, with fair-grade proof. Two older drug families may cut relapse slightly, on weaker proof. Another biologic probably cut scope-seen relapse. Most other options rested on very weak proof. The authors grade each claim so doctors can weigh certainty, not just effect size.
pmc-12719397:
Chalachew Yenew, Yehzibalem Azmeraw, and Almaw Genet Yeshiwas pooled studies in two thousand twenty-five on vision loss among diabetic patients in Ethiopia. Diabetes is rising fast there, and eye damage is a major complication. Their review combined results from many clinics to estimate overall burden, risk factors, and regional gaps.

About three in ten diabetic patients had visual impairment overall, but regional rates differed dramatically, from very low in one region to very high in another. Such gaps suggest unequal screening and care rather than biology alone. Ethiopian health planners gain a map showing where eye screening for diabetic patients needs urgent strengthening.
pmc-12722297:
Mark Zupancic and ten co-authors track viral DNA in blood during treatment of throat cancers in a study from two thousand twenty-five. These HPV-driven cancers answer treatment better than others, but therapy is harsh and not always curative. A blood marker could personalize care.

Two hundred sixty-seven samples from eighty-three patients were tested across diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up. About ninety-four percent of diagnostic samples carried the viral DNA. Levels fell in most patients within weeks of starting radiation. Roughly thirty percent cleared it fast; nearly all cleared it within months. Clearance speed varied with tumor site, patient traits, and treatment. No fresh recurrences had appeared yet. The authors want larger, longer studies of the marker.
pmc-12728197:
Sreekanth and co-authors ran this field study in twenty twenty-five on greengram, a small bean crop. Weeds and drought often hit the crop at the same time. Over two years the team grew greengram with two common weeds, under both ample water and drought. They tracked plant water, leaf health, stress chemicals, and final yield.

One weed, barnyard grass, hurt the crop far more than the other weed. The harm grew worse under drought. Plants lost water, their membranes weakened, and stress chemicals rose sharply. The authors say weed control and water planning must be handled together, not as separate jobs. Their findings aim to help farmers protect yields as dry spells grow more common.
pmc-12729797:
Duanqi Zhu and six co-authors test, in a 2025 trial, whether a blood vessel drug can protect the brain during heart bypass surgery. Cognitive dysfunction after such surgery is common and is tied to disturbed cerebral blood flow. The team gave a low dose of the drug, nicardipine, to half of 64 elderly patients during bypass, and saline to the rest, in a randomized double-blind design.

Ultrasound scans of the carotid artery tracked flow speeds at four set times. Flow fell in both groups while the bypass ran. At its end, the peak flow speed had recovered much more in the drug group. A second speed measure trended the same way. Brain oxygen levels and cognitive test scores did not differ between groups, and no harms appeared. The authors read the drug as a guard for brain blood flow, and call for larger trials with long-term cognitive checks.
pmc-12730597:
Pál Sebok and a team of co-authors pool studies on treatments that spare fertility in women with a risky thickening of the womb lining, in a twenty twenty-five review. This condition can lead to womb cancer, and the usual cure removes the womb. Younger women may want care that keeps the chance of pregnancy. Options include hormone pills, a hormone coil, surgery through the womb, or mixed plans.

The team pooled forty-nine studies covering more than two thousand women. About eighty-five percent cleared the condition in full. The hormone coil did better than pills, and surgery plus hormones reached the highest rates in small groups. About one in five women saw the condition return. The authors weigh these odds for women choosing between safety and fertility.
pmc-12732497:
Brendon Roets, Heidi Abrahamse, and Anine Crous tested light therapy to steer stem cells toward tendon type. Their study, from twenty twenty-five, deals with tendon healing. Tendons heal poor since they hold few cells and run slow. Stem cells could help, but a firm recipe to turn them into tendon cells is still lacking. Light based treatment has been put forth as an aid, with no set dose.

The team grew fat derived stem cells in a gel that mimics three dimensions. They shone light at two tones and a mix, at two dose levels, in one dose. They then read if the cells took on tendon traits. Readers who mend tendons learn which light set best drives this change in a gel model.
pmc-12735697:
Brenda Valle-Valdez and co-authors review, in two thousand twenty-five, intake of DHA from pregnancy through childhood in poorer countries. DHA is a long-chain omega-3 fat that the brain, immune system, and body need early in life. In low- and middle-income countries, few foods supply much of it.

The review screened work from the past decade and kept a set of studies on diet, supplements, and blood measures. Across settings, intake by mothers, infants, and children fell short of need. Higher intake linked at times to better brain growth, immune health, and birth outcomes, though results varied. The authors point to thin national data as a key gap. They call for food plans shaped to each local context.
pmc-12735897:
Xingzhen Yan, Mengying Lyu, and Ziyao Niu fuse silver nanowire meshes with an oxide filler to make clear conductive films that survive damp heat and double as heaters. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Nanowire films could replace the brittle standard transparent conductor. Their weak points are resistive junctions, weak grip on surfaces, and decay in humidity.

Spin-coating the oxide into the mesh fixed all three failings at once. The best films paired very low resistance with decent see-through clarity. They showed no decay after eight months of storage. Damp heat stability and adhesion both beat the single-material films. As a transparent heater, the composite warmed evenly while staying clear. The authors pitch it for optoelectronic devices needing durable clarity. Defogging windows and wearable warmers are natural uses. The recipe uses simple coating steps.
pmc-12741097:
Yifei Shen and co-authors developed a lab method to measure an antidepressant and its breakdown products in two thousand twenty-five. Escitalopram is widely used for depression and is changed by the liver in two steps. Placenta tissue may also change it, which matters in pregnancy.

Their liquid chromatography and mass spectrometry method detects the drug and both metabolites at once. Validation showed high specificity, good stability, and accuracy and precision within set limits, with no major matrix effects. Applied to rat liver, human liver, and human placenta microsomes, the method showed all three could metabolize the drug, at differing rates. Placenta metabolism was studied this way for the first time.
pmc-12742097:
Nasrin Tayyari and colleagues piloted detailed costing for hospital-at-home in Denmark in 2025. Home hospital care shifts treatment into municipalities. Planners need exact resource use figures. Micro-costing tracks every activity and minute. The pilot tested whether logging works. Danish municipal services hosted the model.

Provider logs captured tasks and time. Detailed measurement proved feasible in practice. The dataset suits future tariff building. Time-driven costing can build on it. Findings fit this setting only though. The sample was small by design. A randomised trial will use the log. Costing methods were refined through piloting.
pmc-12742297:
Pongtarakulpanit and colleagues report a study from twenty twenty-five on warning signs in severe COVID lung disease. Some patients worsen to breathing failure even after a drug that calms the immune system. The team reviewed one hundred nine such patients across several centers. About three in ten worsened within two weeks of the drug. They weighed health data from the day the drug was given. Three simple measures stood out as warning signs.

Low blood oxygen ratio, weak kidney function, and lower blood potassium each raised risk. A score built from the three split patients by risk fairly well. Patients who worsened died at a high rate, unlike those who did not. The authors say the score may flag high-risk patients early. They call for outside checks before routine use.
pmc-12743097:
Seungmin Lee and colleagues measure four blood markers against severity in progressive supranuclear palsy. Their study from twenty twenty-five uses a Korean patient cohort. This movement disorder lacks simple blood measures of progression. Candidate markers cover nerve damage, inflammation, and tau protein.

Sixty-eight patients were compared with thirty healthy controls. One marker, neurofilament light chain, clearly differed between groups. Its level tracked clinical rating scale severity closely. It also tracked lower thinking test scores in patients. Marker interrelations appeared in patients but not controls. A three-marker combination separated groups best overall. Blood testing could ease monitoring of this rare disease.
pmc-12743397:
Bernd Stetter and co-authors published this study in 2025. It uses explainable machine learning to sort hip patients by how they walk. The team recorded 3D gait patterns from 109 people with hip osteoarthritis before joint replacement. Sixty-three were measured again after surgery, and fifty-six healthy people served as controls. Clustering split the patients into three groups with distinct walking styles. The groups also differed in age, joint damage scores, and walking speed.

Before surgery, half to most patients in each group walked in a flagged abnormal pattern. After surgery, that share fell by roughly half. Hip bending and rotation measures drove the sorting most. Gains after surgery varied by group. The authors suggest sorting patients before surgery could forecast recovery and tailor rehab to each walking style.
pmc-12744597:
Zihao Chen and seven co-authors report a study from twenty twenty-five on predicting outcomes in colon and rectal cancer. They combine two simple blood based scores. One score tracks immune activity and inflammation in the body. The other tracks nutrition and immune health.

The team studied more than two thousand patients who had surgery to remove the tumor. They set cut points for each score and made a joint score from zero to two. They then used standard survival models to test which factors linked to outcome on their own. The joint score is offered as a low cost tool to help sort patients by risk after surgery.
pmc-12748597:
Chenxin Wang and co-authors map in 2025 how bone infection unfolds over time and place, to design better repair scaffolds. Bone infection, osteomyelitis, often returns after treatment, with failure rates above 25 percent. The team built a rabbit model of staph infection in the thigh bone.

Scans and tissue measures at two, four, and six weeks showed a steady march of damage. Spongy bone broke down first, then the hard shell lost its blood supply, then the joint end caved in. The shaft and the knob of the bone suffered in different patterns. The authors argue scaffolds should be graded, with structure matched to each zone, not one uniform design.
pmc-12752897:
Ishika Sarkar and five co-authors compare two gels as add-ons to gum care for localised gum disease. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Gum disease is driven by many germs, and plain scaling and root planing may not fully curb it. Local gels placed in the pocket can help, from drug gels to plant-based ones.

Forty-six patients are split by lot after deep cleaning. One group gets a gel from orange peel extract, the other a chlorhexidine gel. At two months, both groups gain in pocket depth and attachment, with no clear gap between them. Germ counts fall in both. The plant gel looks as good as the drug gel, at lower cost.
pmc-12752997:
Shahzad Sadiq and five colleagues studied microRNA regulation in early-onset heart muscle thickening using a rat model. The hypertrophic heart rat develops primary cardiac hypertrophy without high blood pressure. The team profiled heart tissue from two-day-old pups of this strain and from normal heart rats. Microarray screening compared microRNAs and messenger RNAs between the groups. Selected candidates were checked again with a second laboratory method.

The young hypertrophic rats already showed a higher cardiac weight index and raised hypertrophy markers. Screening found 107 microRNAs expressed at different levels. Three of them, including miR-34a, were validated and linked to known hypertrophy pathways. The twenty twenty-five study points to early molecular switches that may drive inherited heart thickening before symptoms appear.
pmc-12753597:
Rentao Yu, Xinyu Lu, and Zhuangzhuang Yue mapped cell talk in bowel cancer in 2025. Tumors mix varied surface cells and immune T cells. Single-cell studies had listed many subsets of both. Where those subsets meet inside tumors stayed unclear. The team merged single-cell data with spatial gene maps. Samples came from dozens of bowel cancer patients. Tools traced cell family paths and signal exchanges. Spatial methods placed subsets back into tumor tissue.

Nine surface cell groups and eight T cell groups emerged. Each group carried its own gene pattern and damage load. One killer T cell group showed tumor-specific activation. It exchanged strong signals with surface cell groups. Three named signaling routes carried much of that traffic. Spatial maps found those T cells beside one surface group. The authors offer the atlas for precision care research. Named routes may serve as drug targets or markers.
pmc-12756797:
Zhai and six co-authors simulated gas movement in coal mine working faces in twenty twenty-five. Many Chinese mines hold dangerous gas that can build up underground. A Y-type ventilation layout with a retained side entry boosts coal recovery and eases gas at one corner, but may trap gas elsewhere.

Their two-dimensional model, built in COMSOL software, tracked gas over time in the worked-out area behind the face. They varied advance speed and the split of airflow between routes. Faster advance stirred more gas loose, raising peak levels. Nine meters per day looked best among the speeds tested. A balanced airflow split near one to one point five kept peaks lowest at both spots. Simulated values matched field data closely, supporting the model's use for ventilation planning.
pmc-12769697:
Heng Wang and co-authors present a 2025 study of a plant compound that helps the body kill bacteria hiding inside cells. Such hidden germs shrug off many drugs, and host-directed cures are still scarce. The compound, called DEHD in short, blocked the growth of several germ types in lab tests. It also made standard antibiotics work better in mice.

Lab work showed the compound binds a protein called MDM2 and switches on a chain that keeps cell stomachs acidic. That acidity, plus a clean-up process in the cell, helps drugs reach the germs. In mice with lethal infections, deaths fell from nine in ten to one in ten when the compound joined drug care. The work names a new host pathway that drug hunters can aim at.
pmc-12775697:
Xiaowei Chen and seven co-authors pool studies on whether tumor DNA floating in blood predicts outcomes in non-small cell lung cancer. Their systematic review and meta-analysis was published in twenty twenty-five.

The team searched seven sources for studies from twenty sixteen to mid twenty twenty-four that compared patients with and without detectable tumor DNA. Fifty-two studies qualified, with samples from a dozen to a few hundred patients. Pooled risks covered relapse-free survival, overall survival, and recurrence, at several treatment time points. Study quality was scored with a standard scale. Finding the DNA generally marked worse outlook. The summary helps doctors judge how much weight to give a blood test result.
pmc-12777397:
Heling Wu and co-authors reported a fungal allergy disease that mimicked lung cancer in two thousand twenty-five. Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis occurs in people allergic to Aspergillus fungi, often with asthma. It can cause airway blockage, lung shadows, and fever that come and go.

Their patient was a thirty-nine-year-old woman with asthma and a productive cough. Scans showed solid lung lesions and enlarged lymph nodes, and a tumor marker in her blood was raised, all pointing to cancer. A biopsy plus other tests instead confirmed the fungal disease by standard criteria. Steroid treatment improved both her scans and the marker level. The authors urge doctors to consider this mimic before invasive steps.
pmc-12780097:
Leonardo Hernandez and nine co-authors map how many hospitals in the Americas sit in the path of natural hazards. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Quakes, storms, floods, slides, and volcanoes all threat care sites, but no shared map spanned the whole zone. The team built a matched list of hospitals with ER care and laid it on hazard maps.

More than twenty thousand hospitals in fifty-one lands were found. Near nine in ten face at least one hazard, with floods by far the most wide. More than four in ten sit in top-risk zones, and near four in ten face two or more hazards. Hot spots span Central America, the US east shore, and the Pacific rim.
pmc-12785897:
Buev and coauthors study a gene that helps build the tail of sperm cells. Sperm must grow a long tail to swim well. Faults in the gene NSUN7 link to weak sperm and male infertility. The team asks what the gene does at each growth stage.

They used mice that lack the gene and sorted sperm at each stage. Protein checks covered young round cells, stretched cells, and mature sperm. The gene was most full in round cells, when the tail forms. Without it, key tail and sheath proteins shifted in amount. The work helps explain how tail faults arise.
pmc-12785997:
Latika Giri and co-authors test in 2025 an AI reader for chest X-rays that works without the internet. Radiologists are scarce in poorer countries, and chest films are the world's most common scan. Their network was trained on public sets, then tuned on local films from a Nepal hospital.

The system screens one patient for 14 diseases at once, using front and side views. On a held-out test set it scored well overall, catching about two thirds of disease while almost never raising false alarms. Colored boxes marked each finding, even when several diseases shared one chest. It also ran inside the hospital's image system and offline. The authors offer it as a triage aid where specialists are few.
pmc-12786497:
Xavier Laurent, Damien Dodelin, Nicolas Graveleau, and Nicolas Bouguennec tested how blocked sight changes jumps after knee ligament repair. Their study, from twenty twenty-five, deals with patients after ACL reconstruction. Many keep movement flaws in hard tasks like the one leg drop jump. At six months, they lean on sight to make up for weak body sense. That lean can bend their form.

Patients still in rehab jumped under three sight states: plain sight, low blur, and high blur, through special eyewear. Past work used two leg jumps; this one tests the one leg form that strains the knee most. Readers in sports rehab learn if sight loss unmasks flaws that plain tests miss.
pmc-12786797:
Poliana Bellei and four co-authors turn oyster shell waste into building material in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Piles of discarded shells are a disposal problem in coastal areas. Lime mortars, used on old brick buildings, may take shell as an ingredient. The team made mortars with natural hydraulic lime. In one mix, shell powder replaced part of the lime. In another, crushed shell replaced part of the sand.

They tested the mortars in molds and spread on solid bricks like those in historic walls. Heat and humidity cycles mimicked aging. The shell mixes were then compared with a plain control mortar. The authors report on strength, physical traits, and durability. The work points to greener repair materials for heritage buildings.
pmc-12789497:
Xu and coauthors ask if doctor mothers have better pregnancy outcomes in China. Obstetric doctors serve as both providers and patients in pregnancy. Their medical knowledge may shape habits and outcomes. Data on that group in China have been sparse.

The study ran at a large women hospital in Zhejiang. It held 100 doctor mothers who gave birth from 2012 to 2022. Two hundred matched non-doctor mothers gave the contrast set. Outcomes held surgery births, urgent surgery, and birth weight. Newborn scores and pregnancy harms were also logged. Results test if expertise alone improves outcomes.
pmc-12799297:
Ohta, Ryu, and Ichinose pool proof on hard-to-treat low platelets in lupus. Low platelets are a common and grave sign in lupus. Some patients stay low despite standard drug care. Three targeted drugs have been used in small studies.

The team searched for all studies of those three drugs in lupus. Each study covered adults with proven lupus and stubborn low platelets. Pooled rates showed how often platelets rose with each drug. Harms and dose facts were also weighed in the pool. Clear pooled proof can guide doctors in rare, tough cases. The review sets a base for larger trials.
pmc-12804997:
Kai Peng and six co-authors published an environmental modeling study in twenty twenty-five on forecasting plant cover in drylands from rainfall and evaporation data. In arid regions water rules vegetation, but greenness responds with a lag that simple models miss. The team built a hybrid deep learning model pairing convolutional and memory networks.

A drought index first sorted the study area into aridity types, giving the model varied training cases. The convolutional part reads spatial patterns in the water data; the recurrent part follows long time dependencies. The model distinguished how heavy rain contributes far more to anomalies in arid than semi-arid zones. Dynamic change indices tracked cover over time, supporting land management under a drying climate.
pmc-12808397:
Fatma Alshehri and a large team report a 2026 study of infections caused by the bacterium Klebsiella pneumoniae. This germ can cause lung infections and other serious illness. Some strains are far more aggressive than the common form, and the team compared the two kinds.

They screened 600 samples and found the germ in about 17 percent. The aggressive form made up just over half of the finds. It ruled in infections outside the lungs, while the common form ruled in lung cases. Lung cases were mostly adults with breathing symptoms. Cases elsewhere hit children and older adults more, often with fever.
pmc-12809897:
Mengyuan Sui, Mingxing Zhou, and Yang Yang study emotional labor among college teachers in China in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Emotional labor means managing feelings as part of the job, by faking a display, forcing a real change, or showing what one truly feels. The team links these styles to mental health.

The survey covered nine hundred twelve vocational college teachers. Faking feelings was tied to more mental health problems, while the other two styles were tied to fewer. A strong sense of professional identity carried part of these effects. Good relations with students softened the links. Effects also varied by sex, age, and income. The authors draw lessons for easing strain on faculty.
pmc-12813297:
Nakazawa and co-authors report hidden fractures at the start of dialysis in a kidney patient. The patient was a 55-year-old man with end-stage kidney disease. Fractures appeared within two months of starting dialysis. X-ray and CT scans missed the breaks entirely. MRI found fractures in heels, foot bones, and pelvis.

Blood tests showed high parathyroid hormone and low zinc. Care paired hormone drugs, active vitamin D, and zinc. Symptoms cleared over 17 months of treatment. The authors urge early MRI for odd pain at dialysis start. Low zinc, they suggest, may add to bone fragility.
pmc-12815797:
Nari Kim and co-authors hunt for breast cancer subtypes ruled by regulatory T cells, in a study published in 2025. These T cells damp the immune attack inside a tumor, and tumors rich in them resist standard immune drugs. Sorting such tumors out could guide who gets immune therapy.

The team merged four layers of molecular data, from gene activity to proteins, across tumor samples. One cluster stood out for heavy regulatory T cell presence and strong immune dampening, and the same pattern appeared in a second cohort. Computer models of tumor and immune dynamics predicted that pairing a Treg-targeted drug with checkpoint blockade would beat either alone. Tests in mice with a suppressive breast tumor bore that out.
pmc-12819597:
Saeed Alqahtani grades dental students' crown shaping with a part-by-part rubric to test grader fairness, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Forty-five fourth-year students shaped one front tooth for a metal-ceramic crown under set rules. Four trained judges scored eight traits blind, each on a small scale.

Judges agreed well to near perfectly across traits. No judge scored higher or lower than peers in the stats. Top scores went to edge form and gum care, while cut depth and taper lagged. The author calls the rubric clear, fair, and rich in feedback. Readers in skills teaching get proof that fine rubrics calm grader drift.
pmc-12821297:
Ruoshui Liu, Thomas Kowal, Caden Chow, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2025. It compares how the two best-known compounds in cannabis, THC and CBD, change gene activity across many species and body tissues.

The team gathered 105 public datasets from humans, monkeys, mice, and rats, covering both gene chip and gene sequencing studies. They tracked which genes switched up or down after exposure to each compound. CBD produced more gene changes and more affected pathways than THC. Its effects also grouped more neatly by species and by how the dose was given. Pathways tied to zinc balance, calming inflammation, and cell stress stood out for CBD. The paper gives a broad map for judging claims about each compound's effects.
pmc-12821997:
Hongzhan Liu and colleagues catalogue a family of stress genes in barley, in this genome-wide study from twenty twenty-five. The genes, called DREB, help plants answer drought and salty soil, two threats that cut barley yields. In barley itself, though, the family had not been fully mapped.

The scan found thirty-nine DREB genes spread across all the barley chromosomes, with some copied in pairs. Their control regions carry switches that answer stress, cold, and hormones, and small RNAs were predicted to tune sixteen of them. Lab tests then showed the genes switching on at varied levels in roots, stems, and leaves under stress. Comparisons with four other species showed parts of the family kept in step through evolution. The authors say the map gives breeders and engineers a parts list for building barley that holds up better in dry, salty fields.
pmc-12828997:

pmc-12831397:

pmc-12831497:

pmc-12837597:

pmc-12838497:

pmc-12844797:

pmc-12854697:

pmc-12859997:

pmc-12865997:

pmc-12913797:

pmc-12926097:

pmc-13113597:
Katarzyna Pogoda and co-authors review antibody-based upkeep therapy for advanced breast cancer in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. pmc-13117897:

pmc-13121997:

pmc-13136197:

pmc-13141097:

pmc-13141197:

pmc-13145097:

pmc-13151297:

pmc-13152697:

pmc-13156397:

pmc-13162197:
Conlon, Preston, and Zupan survey how confident Australian speech therapists feel in tools that help people speak, in a study from twenty twenty-six. pmc-13170597:

pmc-13173497:

pmc-13176897:

pmc-13184597:

pmc-13185697:

pmc-13189497:

pmc-13190097:

pmc-13194297:

pmc-13194497:

pmc-13195597:

pmc-13203997:

pmc-13207297:

pmc-13208197:

pmc-13209297:

pmc-13209497:

pmc-13211397:

pmc-13212597:

pmc-13213497:

pmc-13214597:

pmc-13215197:

pmc-13216597:

pmc-13217497:

pmc-13219597:

pmc-13219897:

pmc-13221997:

pmc-13222197:
Enver I. Bogdanov, John D. Heiss, and Aisylu T. Faizutdinova raise methodological concerns about a study reporting no structural abnormality in Chiari malformation type 0, in a 2026 commentary. Earlier work defined the condition narrowly, requiring a blocked fluid space or small back skull compartment plus a fluid-filled cord cavity. The newer study defined it by tonsil position alone.

That wider net, the commentators argue, mixed in patients whose tonsil shift had secondary causes and normal skull compartments. Tables in the disputed paper even show graded trends: back skull area and bone length shrinking step by step from controls through type 0 to type 1. Selection differences, they conclude, likely explain the null result.
pmc-13222297:
Thi N. T. Huynh and colleagues review links between cancer carer distress and patient outcomes, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Their search found 11,911 records, of which 169 studies qualified. Pooled analyses focused on how carer and patient psychological health move together, plus how carer health relates to service use for both parties.

Distressed, depressed, or anxious carers were significantly more likely to care for patients with the same problems, with pooled effects in the small-to-moderate range. Carers in poor psychological health used general practice, mental health, and hospital services more often. Their patients took more medications and presented to emergency care more frequently. Including carers in early psychosocial care could help whole families.
pmc-13222497:
Afra Selma Taygar and co-authors interview Swedish health leaders about a planned digital therapy for chronic pain, in a 2026 interview study. Eight people, including IT staff, healthcare managers, and clinicians, talked about what would help or block uptake inside the health system. Responses were sorted with a standard framework for rollout work.

Interviewees listed eighty-six supporting factors against thirty-eight barriers. A sense that the tool fit real needs supported the plan. Barriers clustered on thin training and oversight, fuzzy decision duties, and missing needs review before rollout. Overall openness ran high. The authors say fixing those day-to-day gaps early is what will make the digital treatment stick.
pmc-13222597:
Neal Shore and co-authors compare outcomes after prostate removal surgery by cancer risk group in United States practice, in a 2026 real-world study linking medical records with insurance claims. Nearly nineteen thousand men with localized prostate cancer were split into high-risk and low or intermediate-risk cohorts using staging, PSA results, and Gleason scores, then balanced statistically.

High-risk patients faced roughly three and a half times the hazard of metastasis and of disease progression at both three and five years. Their yearly healthcare costs ran several thousand dollars higher, for all causes and for prostate care specifically. Risk class at surgery, the data show, strongly forecasts both clinical course and spending afterward.
pmc-13224197:
Muhammad Yogi Prandani and co-authors report a case where a bedside sound scan sped care after brain injury surgery, in work from twenty twenty-six. The patient was a young man hurt in a road crash. First scans showed bleeding in and around the brain, swelling, and a broken skull.

Surgeons removed part of the skull and cleared the bleed, but his state did not lift the next day. A bedside Doppler scan of brain blood flow hinted at high pressure and fresh bleeding. That clue sent him to an urgent repeat scan, which confirmed new bleeding and led to a second operation. Later flow readings improved. The case shows the scan as a bridge, not a swap, for full imaging.
pmc-13226597:
Wu and colleagues present a Chinese expert consensus on the first step in lowering cholesterol. Lowering LDL cholesterol, the panel stresses, is the most effective known way to cut heart and vessel disease caused by clogged arteries. Past studies show that active early treatment lifts the share of patients who reach their LDL goal and improves outcomes.

The consensus weighs which starting strategy fits which patient, rather than leaving the first move to habit. Choices at the start matter because delay lets risk build while doses stay too low. For Chinese clinicians, the document sets a shared, evidence-based opening play for a very common and deadly risk factor.
pmc-13228097:
Haibo Zhang, Dawei Wang, Jiebin Li, and Jing Zhang test a 2026 simple blood score as a predictor of death in acute pancreatitis, using the large MIMIC-IV intensive-care database. The albumin-bilirubin score combines two routine liver-related blood values and needs no special equipment. Records of 1,953 patients were split into three bands by score, and survival at thirty days and one year was compared.

Each unit rise in the score came with a clearly higher risk of death at both horizons. Survival curves separated significantly, and the risk relationship bent upward sharply beyond a turning point in the score's range. Links ran stronger in patients who had not received certain antibiotics or early ventilation. The authors support the score for early risk sorting.
pmc-13229397:
Connor G Wright and colleagues report a 2026 twelve-month feasibility study of a smartphone app supporting HIV prevention in women in New York's South Bronx, an area of high HIV burden. Daily preventive pills, called PrEP, remain underused by cisgender and transgender women. Forty participants received the pills, home HIV test kits for themselves and partners, and an app sending daily reminders and logging doses taken.

Most enrollees had never used PrEP before, and two thirds did not believe themselves at risk, even though nine in ten reported at least one recent risk behaviour. Interviews every three months tracked sexual behaviour and how acceptable the app felt. The study's purpose was practical: can this population use and stick with app-supported prevention over a full year?
pmc-13230297:
Philipp Ernst and colleagues explore in 2026 whether living in a high-radon area shapes lung cancer type or stage in central Germany. Registry records covered eight hundred ninety-three cases from ninety-six communities in Thuringia between 2018 and 2022. Communities were split by soil radon levels and rock-based radon potential.

Overall lung cancer rates did not differ between high and low radon communities after age and sex adjustment. One common cancer type appeared somewhat more often in high radon areas in simple comparisons. Among small cell cancers, widespread disease at diagnosis was also more frequent there in simple comparisons. Both patterns faded after correcting for many tests, and smoking data were missing. The authors treat the clues as ideas for deeper study, not proof.
pmc-13230997:
Namrata Gaikwad and colleagues report in 2026 a rare case where bowel slipped through a caesarean wound and mimicked skin infection. A thirty-nine-year-old woman returned three days after her planned caesarean birth with belly pain, vomiting, and spreading redness near the scar. The wound looked clean and she had no fever, so staff first treated the picture as cellulitis.

Scans instead showed small bowel herniating through a gap beside the scar, with early blockage signs. Surgery freed and returned the bowel, which stayed healthy, so no section had to be removed. She went home four days later without problems. Only four similar cases were found in print, and later care in those cases often meant dead bowel.
pmc-13231697:
Iden Amiri and Aya Barzelay-Wollman report in 2026 a sixty-five-year-old whose pulling vitreous gel freed itself after a deep scuba dive. The gel in his left eye had partly detached and tugged on the central retina, slowly blurring his sight. Such traction clears on its own in only a small share of cases, and surgery is the usual answer when sight worsens.

After a dive to sixty meters, he noticed a sudden shower of floaters, then sharper vision. Eye scans confirmed the gel had fully released with no tear or lasting damage to the retina. Sharp pressure swings during the dive may have finished the separation. The link is only a timing clue, so pressure effects on this condition deserve formal study.
pmc-13233597:
Jonathan Jie Lee and Daniel M. Blumberger published a 2026 review on managing treatment-resistant depression, where standard antidepressants have failed. The authors describe a pattern of drug exhaustion: each successive drug step in the landmark STAR*D trial remitted fewer patients, while relapse grew more likely. Current Canadian guidelines therefore favor adding a second agent, such as aripiprazole, after one or two adequate trials rather than endless switching.

Magnetic brain stimulation gets a long look as an option that targets brain networks, not chemical messengers. Head-to-head evidence cited in the review shows repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation beating medication switching on response and remission, and matching antipsychotic add-ons without their body-wide risks. The article helps clinicians sequence these options when first-line drugs fall short.
pmc-13234397:
Esther Wortmann and colleagues reported in 2026 on how bile acids made by gut microbes shape the lining of the colon. One such acid, deoxycholic acid, rises with long-term high-fat diets and has been linked to colorectal cancer. The team colonized germ-free mice with a defined set of bacteria that included a species able to produce that acid. Human biopsy material from patients with polyps or cancer provided a comparison.

Single-cell sequencing of mouse colon cells showed more bile-acid-sensitive surface cells after exposure. Stem cells, mucus-producing cells, and rapidly dividing cells became fewer in number. A gene tied to energy control rose, while the main mucus gene fell, matching patterns seen in human growths. In separate patients, drugs that bind bile acids were linked to more cell growth in colon biopsies. The findings clarify how microbial bile acids may influence cancer risk.
pmc-13234497:
Min Liang and colleagues combined in 2026 results from trials of online health support for people caring for a relative with dementia. Family caregivers often face heavy stress and depressive symptoms while providing unpaid care. The review gathered randomized trials from eight databases and trial registries. Interventions were interactive digital programs compared with usual care or inactive controls.

Thirty-five trials with more than three thousand caregivers entered the main analysis. Digital support produced a small but statistically clear reduction in caregiver burden. Depressive symptoms also eased modestly across the trials that measured them. Results varied a great deal between studies, so real-world benefit will differ by setting. Shorter programs, human-supported programs, and mobile delivery showed larger point estimates in subgroup checks. Caregiver age may shape how much benefit a program delivers.
pmc-13234597:
Nicolas Gautron and a large team reported in 2026 on making a key cancer drug building block in engineered yeast. Etoposide is a powerful chemotherapy medicine first derived from mayapple plants. Supply stays tight because plants contain little precursor and climate pressure limits harvests. The team rebuilt part of the plant pathway inside yeast cells.

Starting from a compound called yatein, the yeast produced an advanced intermediate used to make etoposide. Repeated strain changes improved how carbon flowed through the pathway and sped production. Bioreactor material was purified and then converted chemically into etoposide itself. Sourcing resilient plants rich in the starting compound forms a parallel supply route. The hybrid plan mixes plant sourcing, yeast factories, and chemistry to secure the medicine.
pmc-13235497:
Xinyu Liu and colleagues followed in 2026 British adults with prediabetes to see how social position shapes progression to diabetes. More than thirty-four thousand UK Biobank participants with prediabetes were tracked for a median of over thirteen years. Education, employment, and income defined social groups through a statistical clustering method. A lifestyle score combined smoking, diet, sleep, body mass, and sitting time.

Nearly seven thousand participants developed diabetes during follow-up in the cohort. Diabetes risk rose stepwise from the highest to the lowest social group in the analysis. Lifestyle factors explained about one third of the extra risk tied to lower social position. Body mass stood out as the largest single contributor among the lifestyle components examined. The authors estimate substantial fractions of cases could be prevented through lifestyle and social improvements, guiding fairer intervention design.
pmc-13237797:
Buist and colleagues assess custom-made implants for rebuilding long bones with a segment missing. Gaps in the thigh or shin bone, left by tumour removal or severe injury, are hard to bridge while sparing the nearby joint. Implants designed for one patient, built from three-dimensional scans by additive manufacturing, promise an exact fit where stock parts fail.

The study reviews how such implants performed in joint-sparing reconstructions. Fit alone is not success; the implant must bear weight for years and knit to living bone at its ends. Their experience helps surgeons judge when a bespoke implant is worth its cost and planning time.
pmc-13237997:
Frederik Heumüller and team reviewed 1,628 patients who had bypass surgery within 48 hours of a heart attack at one center between 2001 and 2023. Their focus was the 77 who suffered neurological injury around surgery. Most injuries were clot-related strokes, with a smaller share from oxygen deprivation. The injured patients were compared with the rest on risk factors and outcomes.

Injury patients more often smoked, had badly weakened heart pumping beforehand, and had needed resuscitation before surgery, and their operations ran longer. Thirty-day mortality was roughly double theirs, at about 21 percent against about 11 percent. Nearly all injury patients stayed in intensive care beyond two days. Peripheral artery disease and pre-surgery resuscitation independently predicted early death among the injured.
pmc-13238797:
Yuan and colleagues report lung nodules that turned out to be rheumatoid disease, not cancer. Rheumatoid arthritis mainly attacks joints, yet the lungs are its commonest target outside them. Their patient, a man of seventy-four with a smoking history, was being treated for rheumatoid arthritis when scans found many nodules in both lungs, around their edges and linings.

In a smoker of his age, that picture screams cancer until proven otherwise. The nodules were rheumatoid ones, a rare form of the disease in the lung. Documenting the case helps chest doctors keep this possibility alive before ordering drastic treatment, and shows why a biopsy can change everything.
pmc-13238997:
Michael Nuss, Tobias Schrimpf, and Carsten Strohmann determine the crystal structure of a lithium compound and compare it with its parent ether, in a 2026 paper. Two solvent partners keep the lithium ion alone rather than clustered, giving it a squashed tetrahedral surrounding. Such organolithium reagents are workhorses for taking protons off molecules in synthesis. The structure was solved at 100 kelvin, with disorder in one solvent partner and in trapped pentane handled by standard tricks.

The parent compound, diphenyl ether, was re-measured under the same cold conditions for a clean comparison. Putting the two side by side shows what swapping a hydrogen for lithium does to the ring system. The authors present the pair as a reference for how metalation reshapes an aromatic frame.
pmc-13239097:
Megersa Regassa and colleagues reported in 2026 two young adults in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, whose obstructed stomach outlets hid an incidental finding: pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis, gas-filled cysts in the bowel wall. Both patients had long histories of early fullness, pain after meals, reflux, vomiting, and marked weight loss from chronic duodenal narrowing. Surgery bypassed the blockage with a stomach-to-intestine connection.

During the operations, surgeons spotted the gas cysts scattered on the small intestine's outer surface, with no dead bowel, perforation, or peritonitis. They left the cysts alone, and both patients recovered smoothly with symptoms gone and weight regained. The authors argue the cysts arose from chronic mucosal damage and pressure build-up behind the obstruction. Recognizing the pattern, they say, prevents needless bowel removal.
pmc-13239997:
Shu-Yu Wu and a large team investigate a hawthorn flavonoid against high uric acid in a 2026 study. Vitexin, one of seventeen flavonoids they identified in hawthorn extract, was flagged by computer screening as the compound most worth testing for hyperuricemia, the condition behind gout.

Docking simulations suggested vitexin binds two proteins in a pathway controlling urate export. In mice with raised uric acid, treatment cut blood levels by blocking two production enzymes in the liver and by restoring export pumps in kidney and gut almost to normal. Liver, kidney, and intestinal injury eased, and oxidative stress and inflammation fell. The authors propose vitexin as a multi-target natural candidate.
pmc-13240397:
Zahra Jaafari and co-authors model why type 2 diabetes rates differ between countries in a 2026 ecological study. Using Global Burden of Disease data from 1990 to 2021, they nested yearly observations inside countries and separated lifestyle factors from development and health spending indicators.

High body mass index and the passage of time were tied to rising incidence in both models they built. Physical inactivity flipped direction between models, showing how sensitive ecological results are to assumptions. Development level consistently pointed the other way, with higher development linked to lower incidence once other factors were held. Diet low in fibre showed no stable link. Prevention, the authors argue, must join personal and structural levers.
pmc-13240497:
Lianying Chang and team argue for shaping acupuncture to each patient's biology in a 2026 review. Pain varies a lot between people, and so does relief from acupuncture. The method is used for chronic muscle pain, migraine, and cancer pain, yet trials that report only average effects may hide who gains most.

Gene studies, mostly small candidate-gene work, link variants in pain and brain signalling genes such as COMT and OPRM1 with unlike responses. Blood and tissue profiling after care shows molecular shifts. The authors split such shifts from markers that can flag response in advance. Small samples and mixed protocols limit how firm the claims can be, but the base for response-split trials is set out.
pmc-13241397:
van Wissen and colleagues at Leiden priced long-term exercise therapy for severely limited axial spondyloarthritis patients. Their randomized trial tracked two hundred fourteen Dutch participants for one year. Half got personalized exercise therapy; half got usual care. Costs and quality-adjusted life years were weighed from a societal angle.

Therapy patients averaged forty-one sessions, and uptake reached ninety-three percent. Extra physiotherapy costs were largely offset by savings elsewhere in care. Quality-of-life gains were tiny and statistically uncertain, as was the cost difference. The verdict: no clear economic winner, so cost alone should not block access.
pmc-13241497:
Maetzler's team at Kiel asked where on the body motion sensors best capture activity in early Parkinson's. 25 newly diagnosed, still untreated patients wore motion sensors for two weeks. Devices sat on the ankle, wrist, and lower back at once. Diaries turned daily doings into energy units for comparison.

Wrist and lower back sensors tracked diary motion about as well across effort levels. The ankle sensor lagged clearly behind both. Tremor hurt readings across the board, with the lower back coping slightly best. Maetzler's rare drug-free group gives trial planners concrete sensor placement guidance. None had started Parkinson's drugs.
pmc-13241697:
Amo-Tachie at Ghana describes a ninety-year-old whose standard heart failure dose turned toxic. The man had taken a small daily carvedilol dose as told for six months. Twice in one week he reached emergency care with dangerous low blood sugar. The first episode triggered a seizure; the second dulled his mind.

Pill counts proved he never overdosed, and scoring rated carvedilol the likely culprit. Stopping the drug and giving glucagon by vein restored him fast. He left care on day three with better kidney function. Amo-Tachie warns that aging livers and kidneys let standard doses build up without warning.
pmc-13241997:
Ahmad Alhabashi and co-authors publish a 2026 retrospective study of teeth crowned after crown lengthening surgery in Dubai. Crown lengthening exposes more tooth so a crown can grip, rescuing teeth that might otherwise be pulled. Long-term complication data for this pathway are valuable for treatment planning.

Records covered well over a hundred restored teeth treated over a decade at a dental hospital. Survival stayed very high at both five and ten years. Among surviving teeth, gum-related complications were the most common, followed by root and restoration problems. Patients who attended the dentist regularly had fewer complications. The authors conclude the approach preserves compromised teeth reliably, supporting its place when prognosis looks uncertain.
pmc-13242197:
Laura Roelans and co-authors offer a 2026 review proposing a mechanism for the puzzling toxicity of the fungicide fludioxonil. The chemical protects stored seeds and crops, and it breaks down quickly outdoors. Reports of harm to wildlife and possible human effects have been inconsistent, with no proven explanation.

The reviewers gathered literature from over a decade and searched for shared threads. The fungicide degrades into a breakdown product classed among perfluoroalkyl substances. That product carries a chemical group able to bind permanently to glutathione, the cell main antioxidant shield. Draining that shield would raise oxidative stress, matching the scattered toxicity reports. The authors warn the mechanism matters for aquatic life near farms and for human health assessments.
pmc-13242997:
Xunwei Deng and co-authors publish a 2026 study of a blood protein called fetuin-B in stroke caused by large-artery plaque. They compared patients with this stroke type against matched healthy controls, then asked whether the protein also predicts poor recovery. Blood was drawn after stroke onset and measured with a standard assay.

Fetuin-B levels were clearly higher in patients and rose alongside cholesterol, blood sugar control markers, and inflammation markers. Higher levels independently tracked with having the stroke and with poor functional outcome. Adding the protein to a basic prediction model improved accuracy for both questions. The relationship with stroke presence curved, while the outcome link ran roughly straight. The authors propose fetuin-B as an added risk marker.
pmc-13243197:
Hassan Ahangar and co-authors describe a woman whose breathlessness led to a rare form of high blood pressure in the lungs that surgery can cure. Their case report appeared in Clinical Case Reports in 2026. The thirty-seven-year-old patient arrived with worsening breathlessness, back pain, and cough. Scans showed an enlarged right side of the heart, very high lung pressures, and wide gaps between air flow and blood flow in the lungs.

Surgeons cleared the blocked lung arteries in a major operation, and her pressures soon improved a great deal. Only later did an unnoticed early pregnancy come to light, ending in miscarriage at fourteen weeks. The strain pregnancy puts on blood flow may have unmasked her illness, the authors suggest. The case warns doctors to think of this diagnosis in women of childbearing age with unexplained breathlessness.
pmc-13243297:
Paolo Squillaci and co-authors build carbon electrodes that turn a plant-derived chemical into useful products in 2026 work. The starting chemical is furfural, a building block made from farm waste. Their electrodes use ordered porous carbon formed around a silica mold, with one version carrying gold particles.

Tests in a small flow cell compared the carbons under acid and alkaline conditions. The glycerol-based carbon worked best, converting furfural to a valued ring compound with high efficiency. The gold version instead favored a different product at higher voltage. The team links the win to surface area, pore shape, and graphitic character. Such tailored carbons could help replace fossil feedstocks in chemical production.
pmc-13245797:
Zaizen, Koga, and Tsutsumi studied skin biopsies from patients with dermatomyositis, an autoimmune disease that attacks muscle and skin, in this 2026 PLOS One paper. They stained samples from twenty-two patients and thirteen controls to map where complement proteins, antibodies, and a viral-sensor protein called MDA5 sit in the skin layers.

Patient skin carried clearly more complement C3c and two antibody types, IgM and IgA, in the upper dermis where the inflammation occurs, a pattern pointing to immune-complex injury. MDA5 appeared in the outer skin of everyone, but in patients it also showed up strongly in inflammatory cells and tiny blood vessels deeper in the skin. The map helps explain how the skin damage develops.
pmc-13247197:
Qinqing Chen, Fangfang Xi, and Min Lv test a teaching blend for medical residents in a 2026 study. Their method pairs mind mapping with virtual patient simulation during obstetrics and gynecology rotations. Clinical reasoning is the skill at stake, since residents must link book knowledge to live care.

Records covered 80 second-year residents trained from 2023 to 2024, split into two equal groups. Both groups learned the same cases from the same teachers. The mind mapping group scored no higher on theory tests. It did score higher on history taking, reasoning, and specialty skills, and reported greater satisfaction. The authors credit the maps with organizing complex cases without adding mental strain.
pmc-13247297:
Huang and co-authors measured how canal building unmasks crabs in this 2026 Ecology and Evolution study. Two fiddler crab species living side by side in estuaries rely on matching the mudflat's color to hide from predators. The team photographed crabs in engineered canal habitats and in natural mudflats nearby, scoring body-to-background color matching with a vision-based metric.

Both species matched their background significantly worse inside canals, where construction had changed the substrate's color and light properties, while brightness and pattern measures shifted less. The authors warn that this sensory disruption could raise predation on the crabs and ripple through estuary food webs. Habitat engineering, they argue, should be judged on visual ecology too, not structure alone.
pmc-13247797:
Samson, Maximo, and Nelson combined brain chemistry and brain-network imaging in people experiencing psychosis for the first time, in this 2026 Psychological Medicine study. Sixty-seven patients who had never taken antipsychotics and one hundred ten healthy controls underwent spectroscopy measuring GABA, the brain's main inhibitory messenger, in the anterior cingulate cortex. They also had resting-state scans of connectivity in four major networks.

Patients had significantly lower cingulate GABA. Connectivity differed between groups in several networks. The key result was an interaction: in healthy brains, more GABA tracked with stronger connectivity in parts of the executive control and salience networks. In patients the relationship flipped negative. The authors argue that disturbed inhibition is woven into the network dysfunction of early psychosis, not a side note, and that the mechanism deserves direct study.
pmc-13248897:
Bounyarith, Braun, and Kucyi tested a brain scanner that asks questions at the right moment, in a 2026 proof-of-concept study. People resting in a scanner have spontaneous thoughts, but random prompts catch brain activity only roughly. Their method watched two brain regions live and triggered a thought probe whenever either region flared.

Sixty volunteers took part, and after strict exclusions about forty to fifty remained per test. Probes fired by the posteromedial cortex, a daydreaming hub, indeed caught moments of low attention to the outside world. The insula hypothesis did not hold up. The authors say the method works and can sharpen studies of wandering minds.
pmc-13249197:
Walter and co-authors screened newly arrived asylum seekers for diphtheria in Heidelberg, Germany, in a 2026 study. Europe had seen a rise in diphtheria among displaced people during 2022 and 2023. Between August and October 2024 the team swabbed throats and wounds from a random sample of one thousand seventy-three arrivals and checked blood samples for immunity.
