No toxin-producing diphtheria bacteria turned up at all. Wounds told a different story: nearly half of the inflamed wounds carried MRSA, a drug-resistant staph. About thirty-eight percent of participants lacked protective diphtheria antibodies, though almost everyone accepted vaccination when offered. The authors urge early testing, wound care, and vaccination at arrival.
pmc-13249697:
Ntais and Greek colleagues measured how well brain blood vessels flex in multiple sclerosis, in a 2026 study. Ninety patients with the relapsing-remitting form and forty-five matched healthy volunteers held their breath while ultrasound tracked blood flow speed in the brain, a stand-in for carbon dioxide response. Thinking tests and a standard disability scale completed the picture.

Patients' vessels reacted notably less than controls'. Weaker reactivity tracked with greater disability and with slower mental processing speed, and both links survived adjustment for other factors. The authors propose vessel reactivity as a measurable contributor to MS disability that routine scans miss, worth tracking alongside the usual immune markers.
pmc-13249797:
Papayanis and co-authors use a blood type clue to trace where a leukemia began, in a 2026 case report. A man with primary myelofibrosis, a bone marrow scarring disease, received a stem cell transplant from his brother, whose blood type differed from his own. Afterward his blood type switched to his brother's, a sign the donor marrow had taken over blood production.

Ten months later he relapsed with acute myeloid leukemia, yet his blood type stayed his brother's. That persistence argues the leukemia grew from relatively mature donor-lineage precursor cells, not from the deepest stem cells. The authors present the case as rare evidence about which cell stage drives this feared transformation.
pmc-13249897:
Huang and colleagues found that a mitochondrial cleaning machine needs an iron-sulfur cluster to work, in a 2026 Nature Communications study. Cancer cells must clear misfolded proteins from their mitochondria. If they fail, the proteins pile up and poison the cell. The team studied CLPX, one part of the cell's mitochondrial shredder.

CLPX carries a cluster of iron and sulfur atoms. It can only join its partner protein and cut up waste when that cluster is in place. Starving cells of iron broke the shredder. So did starving them of cysteine, a building block for the clusters. The cell then switched to digesting whole mitochondria instead. The authors map this weak point as a possible target in cancer cells that lean on the system.
pmc-13249997:
Ran Wang and co-authors present a spider-web-inspired battery material in this 2026 paper. Flexible zinc-ion batteries are safer than lithium ones, but their zinc electrodes fail early as spiky deposits grow and side reactions eat away at the surface.

The team built a layered gel that fills the battery, copying a web's mix of sticky spots and open paths for ions. Zinc ions moved through it quickly and evenly. In tests, zinc electrodes lasted 4,600 hours, over six months, and full flexible cells ran more than 10,000 charge cycles. The design could suit wearable devices that need long-lived, bendable power.
pmc-13250397:
Vasef and colleagues describe a teenager whose missing periods led doctors to a hidden chromosome condition and advanced ovarian cancer. Their 2026 Clinical Case Reports paper concerns a sixteen-year-old girl with Swyer syndrome, where a person with XY chromosomes develops as female with non-working gonads. Such gonads carry a high risk of cancer.

Hormone tests showed that her ovaries were not functioning, and chromosome testing confirmed the XY pattern. Scans found several pelvic masses, and surgery confirmed dysgerminoma in both ovaries with spread to nearby lymph nodes, staged as IIIC. She was referred for chemotherapy after the surgery. The authors stress that absent periods with this hormone pattern demand chromosome testing, so that cancer is not found late.
pmc-13250497:
Abha Pokharel and Surya Kathayat wrote a 2026 scoping review on blockchain-based self-sovereign identity in health care. Self-sovereign identity lets people hold and share their own digital credentials instead of relying on one central database. The review asks where this approach has been tried in medicine and how ready it is for real clinics.

The authors screened work published through August 2025 and included thirty-seven studies in their map of the field. Most described early designs or prototypes rather than systems running in hospitals today. Common uses were checking identity, managing credentials, and sharing health records with patient consent. The systems leaned on tools such as decentralized identifiers, verifiable credentials, and smart contracts. The review finds shared problems with linking different systems, unclear rules for who governs them, and little proof from real care settings.
pmc-13250597:
Santoro, Waghmare, and Panaretos prove a striking result about telling probability distributions apart with kernel methods. Their 2026 Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences paper works with kernel covariance embeddings, which map a whole distribution into a point in a large mathematical space. The setting covers continuous distributions on very general spaces.

The authors show that two different distributions always map to Gaussian measures that sit on essentially separate supports, making them perfectly distinguishable in principle. A classical result on Gaussian measures, the Feldman-Hájek dichotomy, drives the proof. Even a tiny change to a distribution becomes maximally visible after this embedding. They call this the separation of measure phenomenon and suggest it explains why kernel methods work so well in practice.
pmc-13250697:
Neyon Loku Gamage and Koshila Ranasinghe review silent gene regulators in this 2026 article on parasitic diseases. These illnesses hit hardest in poor tropical regions, where late diagnosis and weak treatments keep death rates high.

The review covers small RNA strands that never become proteins yet steer how host and parasite interact. Some patterns of these strands in blood mark which disease is present and how severe it is. Others can be used to switch off genes a parasite needs to live, tested so far in worms, scabies mites, and other infections. The authors warn that delivery, stability, and safety hurdles keep clinical use experimental.
pmc-13251197:
Matthew Yang and colleagues mine gene lists for the roots of male infertility in this 2026 study. About one in ten men worldwide faces infertility, yet most cases never get a clear genetic answer, even as gene sequencing keeps finding single-gene causes.

The team gathered 596 candidate genes and focused on 178 with strong evidence. Group analysis showed these genes cluster in a few jobs: powering the tiny tails that move sperm, hormone making and sensing, and DNA repair. Many also switch on in organs beyond the testes, including hormone glands and the brain. The authors tie this to wider health links seen in infertile men and back whole-person care.
pmc-13253997:
Mamo Gobe and co-authors study udder infection in dairy cows in a 2026 survey near Gimbichu Town, Ethiopia. Milk from 384 cows was tested from December 2023 to May 2024 for mastitis and for Staphylococcus aureus, a key germ behind it. Drug response tests were also run on the germs found.

Mastitis prevalence was 39.06 percent, mostly the hidden subclinical form at 33.06 percent. The germ was found in 42 percent of mastitis milk. Many isolates resisted penicillin G, amoxicillin, and tetracycline, and 22.22 percent resisted drugs across two classes, prompting calls for routine drug testing and prevention.
pmc-13254097:
M Ferrandis-Vila and a large team test whether gut bacteria are host specialists in a 2026 pig study. They classified 1,198 E. coli isolates from cattle, chickens, humans, and pigs in four countries by family tree, labeling some as host-linked and others as generalists. Then 17 drug-resistant isolates were fed to weaner pigs.

Bacteria settled in the gut within 24 hours, with shedding peaking early and then falling. Only 12 of 17 isolates were found again, and four stayed long term, one each from pig, cattle, chicken, and generalist groups. The authors say pigs may show low host selectivity.
pmc-13254997: A 2026 retraction notice withdraws a 2019 paper by Møller on parallel declines in insects and insect-eating birds in Denmark over 22 years, published in Ecology and Evolution. The journal editors and publisher agreed to retract it after third parties raised concerns. They found many inconsistencies in the data, including duplications affecting large parts of the data set, and judged the results and conclusions invalid. The author did not respond to requests for comment.
pmc-13255197:
Bao-Ngoc Mach and co-authors sequence a medicinal vine's chloroplast genome in a 2026 study. Cyclea hypoglauca is a wild climber in the Menispermaceae family, used in traditional medicine for centuries in southern China and Vietnam. The team mapped its chloroplast genome, the DNA inside leaf energy organelles.

The genome runs 159,596 base pairs in the typical four-part layout. It holds 129 genes in total, with 84 that code for proteins, 37 transfer RNAs, and eight ribosomal RNAs. The authors call it the first full chloroplast genome for this species, aiding family tree work in the family.
pmc-13255297:
Markus Grebe and three co-authors review support programs for relatives of delirium patients in a 2026 paper. Delirium in hospital brings frightening behavior, from agitation to hallucinations, and families often suffer anxiety and low mood. Their systematic review searched six databases for support programs aimed at adult relatives. Only eight studies qualified, using tools from flyers and videos to phone calls and intensive-care mentoring.

Four of six studies improved relatives' knowledge of delirium clearly. Effects on relatives' mental health were not clear. Intervention reporting was mostly poor and no study checked how the program worked in practice. The authors call for better designed and better reported trials.
pmc-13255897:
Mara Parreiras and colleagues report a 2026 feeding trial replacing fishmeal and soybean meal with defatted black soldier fly larva meal in diets for weaned piglets. Soy and fish protein carry environmental costs, while fly larvae can be raised on organic waste. Forty-eight piglets received diets with zero, three, or six percent of the insect meal.

Growth, daily intake, and feed conversion did not suffer at either inclusion level across the trial. Blood values stayed within normal healthy ranges for young pigs. Digestibility of dry matter and organic matter actually improved at the six percent level, while protein and fat digestibility held steady. The authors conclude that defatted fly meal can replace part of the conventional protein in piglet diets up to the highest level tested.
pmc-13256497:
Elizabeth Chandler, Charlotte Dorer, Valerie M Pomeroy, and Nicola J Hancock evaluate remote stroke rehabilitation in a two thousand twenty-six mixed methods study. Their focus is community stroke services in the East of England. Remote rehabilitation is growing, backed by guidelines and policy, but routine practice is less studied.

Discussion groups with staff and service users came first, mapping how remote care is delivered and felt. The evaluation then drew lessons on what helps remote sessions stay part of normal care. Readers in health services get grounded detail on models in use, attitudes on both sides, and practical factors that support lasting adoption.
pmc-13256597:
Colin J. Hartman and a large team report a 2026 study engineering antibodies against canine PD-1, the immune checkpoint that transformed human cancer care. Dogs develop cancer at striking rates yet mostly receive palliative treatment. The team built mouse and chimeric mouse-dog antibodies and tested whether they block the checkpoint's handshake with its ligand.

The antibodies did block that interaction in laboratory assays, confirming the intended mechanism. A proof-of-concept treatment followed in seven pet dogs with cancer, injecting the lead antibody, named HugPetmab, directly into tumors. Treatment appeared safe and well tolerated, with no adverse events observed, and some injected tumors showed control. The authors present the work as an opening step toward real immunotherapy options for canine patients, with larger trials still ahead.
pmc-13257097:
Przemysław W. Śliwka and colleagues report a 2026 preliminary cell study on melatonin and a related gut compound. The receptor CD16 helps immune cells respond to antibodies, and its level shifts in inflammatory and thyroid-linked conditions. Pig blood immune cells were used as the test system.

Cells cultured alone showed falling CD16 over two days, and both compounds deepened that fall. Measurements covered the share of positive cells and the brightness of the receptor signal. Adding thyroid follicular cells from the same animals changed little under the tested setup. Each treatment used a single moderate dose. Immunologists should treat the result as a first signal only. The authors call for wider models before any claim about calming immune activity can stand.
pmc-13257797:
Dirk Rades and co-authors extend a radiation dose comparison for cancer pressing on the spinal cord in a 2026 study. Patients expected to live longer may gain from higher total doses, and two schedules above thirty gray were compared with propensity adjustment. Thirty-six-month outcomes were added retrospectively to an earlier twelve-month analysis.

The shorter three-week schedule and the four-week schedule showed no clear difference in survival or local control after adjustment. Local control at three years ran high in the smaller prospective group, while survival reflected the underlying cancers. No late spinal cord injury or vertebral fractures appeared in follow-up. Radiation oncologists gain a hypothesis worth a fuller trial: a week saved matters for patients with limited time. The authors label their findings as generating questions, not settling them.
pmc-13257997:
Ting Liu and co-authors follow a combined sugar and body-shape index against multiple cardiometabolic diseases in a 2026 cohort study. More than five thousand Chinese adults from a national aging study were tracked from 2011 to 2020. The index joins a triglyceride-glucose insulin resistance marker with a waist-based shape measure, using both single and repeated readings.

About eight percent developed at least two of heart disease, stroke, and diabetes during follow-up. The highest quarter of the combined index carried well over twice the risk of the lowest quarter. Repeated, cumulative readings predicted better than one-off values, especially over five years. Patterns differed by sex, with a threshold shape in women. Community screening programs gain a cheap, noninvasive risk tool built from routine measures, suited to aging populations.
pmc-13259197:
Yuhan Liu and colleagues predict blood pressure without a cuff from radar signals in a 2026 paper. Chest reflections captured by millimeter wave radar carry pulse waveform detail. Prior radar models were heavy and used only the deepest signal features.

Their lightweight network first rebuilds the pressure waveform, then merges features from several depths to estimate systolic and diastolic values. A two stage training plan supports both tasks. Accuracy concentrated well within small error bands in their tests. Continuous home monitoring could flag hypertension risk earlier than occasional clinic checks. Device makers gain a compact model suited to bedside hardware.
pmc-13259297:
Qingqing Yang and Lili Wu dress silicon carbide in tannic acid to steer heat through plastic. Tiny electronics need materials that shed heat along chosen paths without heavy filler loads. Their 2026 composite lays the treated particles onto woven cellulose acetate fibers, then locks everything in polyurethane.

The tannic layer, sticky and self-polymerizing, coats the fibers in a dense fish-scale pattern. Along the weave, heat moved about five times better than through plain polyurethane. The composite also withstood notably higher heat before breaking down. Across the weave, conduction stayed low, proving true directional control at modest filler levels.
pmc-13261297:
Yuji Nojima and co-authors report a 2026 case of a rare benign bone lesion arising from the second rib. The lesion, bizarre parosteal osteochondromatous proliferation, was first described by Nora and colleagues in 1983. It usually affects the small bones of the hands and feet. Rib cases are rare.

Their patient was a 41-year-old man whose chest X-ray at a routine checkup suggested a lung mass. CT imaging showed a lesion measuring 4.1 × 2.2 cm in the left second rib. Surgeons removed it for both diagnosis and treatment. Tissue examination confirmed the diagnosis of BPOP, also called Nora's lesion. The authors advise including it in the differential diagnosis of rib lesions that look benign. Because the lesion can recur, they recommend long-term follow-up.
pmc-13261697:
Rachael M Cox and colleagues reconstructed in 2026 the protein partnership network of the last common ancestor of all eukaryotes. That single-celled ancestor lived well over a billion years ago, and about half of modern gene families trace back to it. Their team compared genes across 156 organisms to define the ancient core set.

They then mined tens of thousands of protein experiments from 31 living species to infer which ancient proteins worked together. The rebuilt network holds both familiar machines and assemblies never described before. Quarter of the core gene families still lack any known job, which the map may help remedy. Mining the ancient partnerships surfaced new candidate genes for human bone density and for congenital birth defects. The authors argue ancestral networks can guide modern disease genetics.
pmc-13262097:
Xinyu Miao and Lizhi Zhou report the first complete mitochondrial genome, the small set of genes passed down through the mother, for the vesper bat Myotis chinensis, in a 2026 article. The bat lives in China and parts of Southeast Asia, and only parts of its mitochondrial DNA had been read before. Their specimen came from Henan Province, China.

Sequencing showed a circular genome 16,812 bases long, holding 13 protein-coding genes, 22 transfer RNA genes, and 2 ribosomal RNA genes. Its bases were 64.7 percent A and T, showing a clear bias. Comparing 40 Myotis species placed this bat closest to Myotis nattereri and Myotis bombinus. The authors offer the sequence as a reference for bat classification and evolution studies.
pmc-13262597:
Turgut Seber and colleagues measure the pituitary gland in fibromyalgia, hunting a structural clue to the syndrome's hormone quirks. Thirty women with fibromyalgia and twenty-six matched controls underwent precision brain MRI scanning. Their 2026 study traces gland volume by hand-drawn segmentation.

The fibromyalgia group's glands were significantly larger in volume than controls', by a clear margin. Gland height, by contrast, matched between groups. Empty sella, a flattening sometimes linked to pressure problems, appeared just once in each group. What a bigger pituitary means biologically is unresolved, the authors say, urging larger studies that pair imaging with hormone levels.
pmc-13263197:
Panopoulos and co-authors track long-term nintedanib use in scleroderma lung disease. Records covered 51 patients treated from 2020 to 2025. Median age was 53, and most patients were women. Median drug use ran 33 months across the cohort. Lung capacity was read before and after drug start.

Diarrhea was the top side effect in the cohort. It forced dose cuts in 31 percent of patients. It forced full stops in 14 percent. Added immune drugs brought no new safety signals. Lung function held stable over the long follow-up in most cases. Lung checks used forced vital capacity and gas transfer scores over time.
pmc-13263397:
Ahmad Hosiian and co-authors present a 2026 case report of liver-related jaundice in an 11-year-old Syrian girl. She had two weeks of severe itching, then yellowing of the skin and dark urine. Tests showed cholestasis, meaning bile flow was blocked or slowed, yet one key enzyme, GGT, stayed normal.

Extensive testing ruled out infection, autoimmune disease, metabolic causes, and blockage. A liver biopsy showed simple bile build-up with the tissue structure intact. She recovered fully on supportive care with ursodeoxycholic acid, a bile-acid medicine. The pattern best fits benign recurrent intrahepatic cholestasis, an inherited condition. The authors present it as the first documented case from Syria.
pmc-13263797:
Amanda S Cass and colleagues reviewed in 2026 systemic treatment for large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma, an uncommon and aggressive lung cancer. It makes up only about three percent of primary lung cancers and returns often after surgery. Their clinical practice review gathers what drug therapy can offer at each stage.

Surgery leads for early stages, with platinum-based chemotherapy afterward improving survival. For disease that cannot be removed or has spread, platinum paired with etoposide or irinotecan is the usual first line, though responses stay modest. Immune therapy, standard in the related small-cell cancer, has no settled role here yet. Trials are testing bispecific T-cell engagers, engineered CAR-T cells, and tumor-killing viruses. Five-year survival sits near a third of patients. The authors press for faster research into this neglected cancer.
pmc-13264097:
Yingshan Wang and colleagues measure a retrotransposon protein in non-small cell lung cancers across patient groups in a 2026 study. LINE-1 elements are mobile DNA sequences normally kept quiet, and their ORF1p protein can appear in tumors. Lung cancers vary greatly by tissue type and patient background, so the team asked where this protein shows most strongly and what it might signal.

Expression ran higher in squamous cell cancers than in adenocarcinomas, and levels rose with age, peaking in the seventies. Differences by racial group were also reported. Links with macrophages, immune cells inside tumors, added a new angle on the tumor environment. Profiling this marker may eventually support more tailored management, though clinical use remains a future step.
pmc-13264297:
Hyonjee Yoon and colleagues link breast density on mammograms to timing of natural menopause in Korean women in a 2026 nationwide study. Dense breasts reflect lifetime hormone exposure, and density normally falls around menopause. National screening and insurance records covered more than four hundred thousand premenopausal women in their forties and fifties. Breast density had been graded at a 2009 screening. The team then recorded who reported natural menopause in later screening rounds.

About seventeen percent reached menopause during follow-up. Higher density tracked with progressively lower odds of that transition, with extremely dense breasts showing the lowest likelihood. The pattern was stronger in women under fifty and in those with later first periods. Density may carry information about reproductive aging pace.
pmc-13264797:
Zuhua Song and colleagues integrate spectral CT measurements with clinical data to predict subtle spread beyond the thyroid in tiny cancers in a 2026 modeling study. Two hundred fifty-three patients with proven papillary microcarcinoma who had spectral scanning were split into training and test groups. Twelve clinical features and thirteen three-dimensional spectral measures, which characterize tissue composition beyond ordinary images, fed several machine learning models aimed at finding minimal extension outside the gland before surgery.

Minimal spread changes decisions about how much thyroid and surrounding tissue to remove, yet standard imaging detects it poorly. Quantitative spectral features may expose tissue differences invisible to the eye. Model performance in the held-out group is the key evidence. Single-center retrospective data mean outside confirmation is required before changing operative plans.
pmc-13264897:
Lara Rowell and a large team published a 2026 interview study on maternity care in the UK during the pandemic, seen through staff and policymaker eyes. Services were rebuilt at speed, and the study focused on care for marginalised groups, who often get a worse deal. The authors took a future-facing view to guide rebuilding.

They interviewed 21 health professionals and 20 policymakers across the four UK nations. Staff said rapid changes were hard to carry out while guarding both safety and quality. The shift to virtual care made it harder to spot who most needed in-person help. Self-monitoring and remote care suited some women but hurt those with complex medical or social needs. A lack of ethnic diversity in leadership meant guidance missed minority needs. The authors link prior unaddressed inequality to worse strain during the shock.
pmc-13264997:
Gerald Olwit and colleagues present a 2026 case report on a blistering skin disease of childhood managed without the standard lab tests in south-western Uganda. The disease, linear IgA dermatosis, is usually confirmed by a glowing antibody pattern in skin samples, tests the family could neither access nor afford. Care rested on clinical judgment alone.

The patient was a 12-year-old girl whose blister outbreaks began at age two and returned at seven and twelve, each worse than the last. Large tense blisters in rings, in a string-of-pearls pattern, covered her trunk and limbs but spared her mouth. Doctors diagnosed the disease from history, pattern, and ruling out close matches. Treatment with dapsone, steroids, antibiotics, and wound care brought marked improvement within a week. The authors stress that lack of tests should not delay treatment.
pmc-13265197:
Bohan Hu and Ji Liang examine blood vitamins and carotenoids in relation to breast cancer in United States survey data, in 2026. These nutrients relate to oxidative stress and inflammation. Blood-based evidence has been inconsistent. Data came from a national health survey conducted in 2017 and 2018.

The analysis kept 2,521 women, including 91 with breast cancer. Blood levels of vitamin C and several plant pigments were measured with precise laboratory methods. Statistical models adjusted for many social, lifestyle, and reproductive factors. Flexible curve analyses and machine learning explored joint patterns. Results add blood-based detail to a debated nutrition question.
pmc-13266097:
Allan Vinícius Martins-de-Barros and colleagues review DNA repair protein patterns in a jaw tumour called ameloblastoma, published in 2026. Faults in the mismatch repair system drive several human tumours. Their role in this tumour was poorly understood. Four databases were searched without date or language limits.

Five studies covering 271 tumour samples qualified. Repair protein expression was lower than in normal tooth-forming tissue. Changes were stronger in conventional tumours than in the cystic type. Altered expression may link to growth activity, recurrence risk, and a common mutation. The authors call for more work on clinical meaning.
pmc-13266397:
Mengfan Chen and the team report advanced male breast cancer in a ninety-year-old with kidney failure, in a 2026 case report. Male breast cancer is uncommon and often found late. The patient also had hypertension and urinary retention needing a bladder opening. His left breast carried a large ulcerated, bleeding tumour.

Palliative removal of the breast was performed. Tissue tests confirmed invasive ductal cancer strongly sensitive to hormones. Hormone therapy tracked, chosen over radiation and chemotherapy given his condition. Recovery was uneventful and quality of life improved. The authors stress multidisciplinary balancing of tumour control against burden, respecting patient preference.
pmc-13266797:
Maryam Bader Alzamanan leads a 2026 analysis pooling trials of a jaw joint washout plus a blood-based injection. The joint is the temporomandibular joint, which links the jaw to the skull. The added injection uses platelet-rich fibrin, a gel made from the patient's own blood that may calm inflammation and aid healing.

Nine trials with 320 patients and 374 joints were pooled. Adding the injection cut pain more than control care and widened mouth opening by about five millimeters. Forward and side jaw movements also improved, though quality of life did not clearly change. A trial-check method backed the pain result. The authors still want larger trials with longer follow-up.
pmc-13267097:
Kyohei Otani wrote a 2026 review proposing a joined-up way to think about headache and mental health. Headache disorders, including migraine, are shaped by brain biology, feelings, behavior, and social life. Yet mental health care is often kept apart from headache care in daily practice, Otani argues.

The review drew on three databases for work from 1990 to 2025. Headache was strongly linked both ways with depression, anxiety, trauma, and poor sleep. Poor control of feelings and gloomy thinking about pain predicted lasting headache and disability. Otani's framework, called Psychocephalology, sorts the evidence into five linked domains. He urges routine mental health screening and team-based care to stop attacks becoming chronic.
pmc-13267297:
Stephan Masius and colleagues publish a 2026 protocol for a trial of a navigation aid in leg artery procedures. Doctors thread catheters through narrowed arteries using X-ray imaging that needs contrast dye. The dye and radiation carry risks for patients and staff. The Vascular Navigation PAD system aims to cut the number of X-ray runs.

Two German hospitals will enroll 160 patients with peripheral artery disease, split evenly by chance. Half get the navigation aid plus standard imaging; half get standard care alone. The main measure is how much contrast dye each procedure uses. Other measures include radiation dose, imaging time, and the number of X-ray runs. The protocol paper reports the plan only; the trial's results are not yet in.
pmc-13267697:
Andrea Fromson and co-authors report in 2026 a case where a diabetes and weight drug coincided with major relief from long-standing swelling after gynecologic cancer treatment. The patient, a cervical cancer survivor, had lived with severe leg and pelvic lymphedema for almost twenty years. Standard care for such swelling relies on massage, compression garments, and pumps, which are burdensome and often fall short.

After she started a GLP-1 receptor agonist, her swelling, daily function, and quality of life improved markedly. Most earlier reports of this drug class helping lymphedema involved arms, not legs. The authors present the case as a first signal for lower body swelling and argue for dedicated studies rather than assuming the benefit is proven.
pmc-13268397:
Roger Keller Celeste and colleagues present a 2026 study of dental coverage and gum disease across Brazil. Using the national SB Brasil 2023 survey, the team studied 7,851 adults who used public dental services. They asked whether towns having specialist dental centers, and how fully primary dental care covered the population, related to periodontal disease, meaning deep gum pockets.

Overall, about 17 percent had the disease. Towns with specialist centers showed slightly more disease, not less, though the link was weak. Full primary care coverage looked protective: towns at 100 percent coverage had the lowest disease rate, about 8 percent. The two coverage types did not interact. The authors conclude broad primary dental coverage tracks with less gum disease in smaller towns, and referral barriers deserve study.
pmc-13269597:
Yuguang Ma wrote a short research highlight in 2026 on a Nature study of quantum dot LEDs, tiny light sources for screens. Pushing these displays past 10,000 pixels per inch is key for virtual and augmented reality headsets. As pixels shrink below a micrometer, their efficiency usually collapses.

The highlighted team, led by Lihua Lin and Fushan Li, traced the loss to edge leakage from distorted electric fields inside the pixel. A precise printing method patterned pixels at up to 25,400 pixels per inch. Added nanoparticles balanced the field so light spread evenly. Red devices reached 26.1 percent efficiency with strong stability. Ma presents the work as a blueprint for sharper, thriftier micro-displays.
pmc-13269897:
Lanxin Pan and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on age-based subtypes of type 1 diabetes in children. Gut microbes, body chemicals, fats, and gene activity were profiled in 108 newly diagnosed children and 56 healthy controls. Children were grouped by onset age: under 7, 7 to 12, and 13 or over.

Each group carried its own microbe and chemical signatures. The youngest group had the highest share of B cells, a type of immune cell, at a median of 11.64 percent. The oldest group was lowest, at 5.99 percent, with more metabolic pathway activity. One gut microbe may drive B-cell growth through a fatty acid, the network analysis suggested. The authors frame the groups as distinct disease subtypes.
pmc-13270797:
Claire Miesch and co-authors describe in 2026 a switchable reaction that turns simple alcohol-alkyne starting materials into either of two valuable product families. Adding an aromatic ring at the far gamma position of a ketone is notoriously hard to control, and bulky arenes made it harder still. Running the chemistry in the unusual solvent HFIP with a strong acid catalyst opened a new path through a fleeting oxygen ring intermediate.

That route delivered linear and branched gamma-arylated ketones, including hindered and electron-poor variants earlier methods missed. Adding a hydride donor flipped the pathway, and the same starting materials instead gave alpha-arylated tetrahydrofurans in high efficiency. Calculations mapped the tangled reaction network behind the switch, giving chemists one pot with two selectable outcomes.
pmc-13270897:
Carla Huanca Challgua is lead author of a 2026 qualitative study, one based on interviews, of barriers to cervical cancer secondary prevention in Cochabamba, Bolivia. Secondary prevention means screening to find early changes and treating them before cancer develops, yet screening coverage in Bolivia stays low and uneven.

The team interviewed 30 health workers, including gynaecologists, doctors, and nurses. Workers described women's information gaps, family myths passed down, gender norms, and fear of partner violence for attending screening. Using the Quechua language in visits and offering small incentives helped draw women in. At system level, unclear rules on who should be screened also blocked access.
pmc-13270997:
Jörg Vogel is lead author of a 2026 meeting report on RNAmed, a graduate training programme for future leaders in RNA-based medicine. Funded by the Free State of Bavaria, the programme is run jointly by universities and institutes in Würzburg, Regensburg, and Munich. It trains doctoral students from basic RNA biology through to rules, ethics, and social effects.

The report covers the programme's 2025 annual retreat on San Servolo, an island in the Venice lagoon. Forty doctoral researchers, senior investigators, and guests met for three days of keynote talks, student presentations, flash talks, and a career panel. Talks featured antisense methods, circular RNAs, delivery technology, and artificial intelligence for molecule design.
pmc-13271997:
Lily Deng and Mansa Krishnamurthy review in 2026 how stem cells grown from patients can model single-gene disorders of the insulin-making beta cells. Conditions such as maturity-onset diabetes of the young and congenital hyperinsulinism arise from one faulty gene each. Lab-grown beta cells from a patient's own tissue let researchers watch that fault act directly.

Studies have turned these stem cells into islet-like clusters that reveal how gene faults disturb insulin release, cell maturation, and cell growth. Excess insulin release and overgrowth seen in patients were reproduced in the lab for hyperinsulinism. The platform now supports precision study of new gene variants.
pmc-13272097:
Justin Lyon is first named author on a 2026 case article on immunoglobulin light chain amyloidosis. That is a disease where faulty antibody fragments build up in tissues. In the patient described, matching purple hand nodules on both hands and an enlarged tongue prompted a skin biopsy. The biopsy revealed the amyloid deposits. It led to a diagnosis of multiple myeloma, a blood cancer.

The authors stress that early recognition of typical and unusual skin signs of amyloidosis is essential. That way clinicians start prompt blood workup and treatment, improving outcomes and survival.
pmc-13272197:
Colin M. Shapiro is lead author of a 2026 clinical article on sexsomnia, sexual behaviour carried out during sleep without full awareness. He argues psychiatrists should know this entity. First described by the authors in a Canadian journal, sexsomnia is now recognised as a subtype of non-REM parasomnia. That is the family of arousal disorders that includes sleepwalking.

A recent self-reported survey put lifetime rates at roughly seven to ten percent. Past-three-month rates were about six percent. Both are higher than once believed. Forensic reports describe behaviours from self-touch to non-consensual contact and penetrative acts while asleep. The authors stress the condition arises from a primary sleep disorder. It does not arise from paraphilic interests. That distinction carries legal weight.
pmc-13272297:
Ellie Mitsi and coauthors present in 2026 a case of cranial electrotherapy stimulation for chronic stress and poor sleep, tracking both symptoms and brain waves. The gentle electrical method is used for anxiety and insomnia, but evidence tying felt improvement to measured brain change is thin. Their patient had not responded to medicines.

A 51-year-old woman completed sixteen weeks of stimulation after thyroid and parathyroid surgery left her with lasting stress and broken sleep. Anxiety, stress, and depressive scores returned to the normal range, and quality of life rose. Brain recordings showed stronger rear alpha rhythm and better frontal balance, while sleep improved modestly.
pmc-13272397:
Ying Liu and coauthors review in 2026 the path from gene mapping to genome editing for making crops tolerate aluminum in acid soils. Aluminum toxicity limits farming on nearly a third of the world's usable land. The review follows how discovery tools sharpened from family-based mapping to population-wide scans and finally precise editing.

Key transporter genes that pump detoxifying acids from roots anchor the story, alongside a master regulator network and the first identified aluminum sensor. The authors then cover how high-throughput plant measurement, marker-guided breeding, and gene stacking move lab findings into fields, including editing strategies that leave no foreign DNA behind.
pmc-13272997:
Lin Cheng leads a 2026 case-control study of bone shape and second knee ligament injuries after a first reconstruction. The anterior cruciate ligament, or ACL, is often torn in athletes, and grafts can tear or the other knee can be injured. The team used CT scans from 224 patients taken within a week of surgery.

Graft rupture occurred in 16 patients, or 7.1 percent, and injury to the other knee in 22, or 9.8 percent. A smaller bony ridge height in the shin linked to graft rupture. Greater twisting of the shin bone linked to injury in the other knee. The authors identify these shape traits as independent risk factors.
pmc-13273097: Author correction notice from Sekar Tamilperuvalathan and co-authors. It concerns a paper on improving a spark-based micro-machining method for borosilicate glass with nitrogen gas help. The notice states that the reference list in the original paper contained errors. It lists incorrect reference entries that need to be replaced. The paper has now been corrected in its updated form.
pmc-13273397:
Fawaz Ahmed Prem Navaz leads a 2026 case report of a catheter fragment that traveled from a donor liver to a recipient's lung artery during transplantation. A 62-year-old woman received a liver from a brain-dead donor who had a neck-area central line in place at organ removal. Scans after surgery showed a 5 centimeter object in a lung artery branch.

All the recipient's own devices were removed intact, suggesting the fragment came from the donor, likely cut during heart removal and lodged in liver outflow. Retrieval by catheter failed due to its deep position. At six months she remained well with excellent graft function, under surveillance without blood thinners.
pmc-13273497:
Ambrine Arrar and a large team fed a pesticide mix to mice prone to Parkinson-like disease in a 2026 study. Some pesticides are tied to both type 2 diabetes and Parkinson's disease, which often occur together. The team tested low dietary doses, below accepted daily limits, over fifty weeks.

Both normal mice and the transgenic Parkinson model gained weight and developed insulin resistance on the pesticide diet, partly because insulin receptors fell in liver, muscle, and fat. Only the model mice showed early movement problems, with receptor loss also in brain regions. Surprisingly, those mice handled glucose better, because their pancreatic islets grew more insulin making cells and worked harder. Gene reads pointed to an amino acid metabolism shift in islets rich in the Parkinson protein.
pmc-13273797:
Krishnamurthy and colleagues pilot a brain stimulation treatment for language loss after stroke. Their 2026 journal article tests tDCS, a weak electric current applied to the scalp. It was paired with a shortened phonomotor treatment, which rebuilds speech sounds.

The pilot enrolled only six older men with chronic aphasia. Three received active stimulation and three received sham treatment. The active group gained in producing speech sounds. Those gains held at three months. Word naming did not change in either group. The authors treat the results as early signals only. A sample this small cannot prove benefit. They call for a larger trial to test the approach.
pmc-13273997:
Zhenmiao Zhang and co-authors describe a 2026 journal article presenting MGA, short for Mosaic Genome Assembler. Genome assembly means stitching DNA reads into a full genome. A haplotype-mixed assembly blends a genome's two parental copies into one mosaic version, which serves most research needs.

Building two separate complete copies usually takes large teams, several sequencing methods, and much hand checking. MGA instead produces a near-complete mixed assembly from long, accurate HiFi reads alone, at lower cost. The authors report that it substantially outperforms existing tools built for the same kind of assembly. The paper positions MGA as a practical route for species and projects that cannot support a full two-copy effort.
pmc-13274597:
Laurenne Schiller and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on drifting fish aggregating devices washing into marine protected areas. Tuna fleets release these free-floating rafts in huge numbers to attract fish, and currents carry them far beyond fishing grounds. Once inside a reserve, they can tangle wildlife, shed plastic, and damage habitat, all unseen.

Combining drift records, beach strandings, and expert interviews, the team estimates these devices have likely interacted with fifty-three percent of the global protected-area network by area. They stranded in 174 protected areas that shelter at least 490 at-risk species. Hotspots include the central Pacific, western Indian Ocean, and Caribbean. The authors call for tighter rules and industry accountability.
pmc-13274897:
Ximing Liu, Hongyun Cao, and Jingfan Ma report a 2026 journal article on making bamboo building material stronger and more fire resistant with a mineral glue. Natural bamboo is renewable and strong for its weight but burns easily. The team bonded it with a magnesium oxysulfate gelling adhesive and baked the composite at different temperatures.

Heat treatment at four hundred degrees gave the best balance. The glue's compressive strength held around ninety megapascals after a week of curing, but collapsed to a fraction of that at six hundred degrees. Bamboo treated at four hundred degrees kept strong bending and compression values. In fire tests it resisted for ninety-eight minutes with slow charring, keeping its structure and insulating the far side well.
pmc-13275497:
Michelle W Antoine wrote a 2026 commentary weighing hype against evidence for gut microbes in epilepsy. Gut imbalance has been tied to many brain disorders, often on shaky causal ground, and Antoine notes growing pushback against overstated claims. Her piece examines a 2026 study by Jia and colleagues that she finds unusually well built.

That study found the gut bacterium Bacteroides fragilis markedly reduced in children with epilepsy. Feeding it to mice suppressed seizures in two chemical seizure models. The effect ran through a defined gut-to-brain circuit: the bacterium switched on choline-making cells in the colon, boosting signals up the vagus nerve. A randomized trial in children with hard-to-treat epilepsy further supported benefit, giving the claim rare mechanistic depth.
pmc-13275897:
Heba Ibrahim Hamed and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on early kidney damage in type 2 diabetes. Kidney disease from diabetes is a leading cause of kidney failure worldwide. The usual warning sign, protein leaking into urine, can also be raised by high blood pressure, so better markers are needed.

The team studied three hundred diabetic patients and one hundred healthy controls. They measured three blood proteins, named KNG-1, HSPG, and Robo4, along with standard tests. Levels of all three proteins ran higher in patients and tracked with early kidney changes. High blood pressure and urine protein together shifted the markers more than either alone. Adding the proteins to standard measures sharpened the team's ability to flag patients at risk.
pmc-13276597:
Wensi Hao and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on tuning brain stimulation by rhythm in Alzheimer's disease. The disease breaks both local circuits and long-range links, and the theta and gamma brain rhythms it disrupts are vital for cognition. The team tested two stimulation frequencies aimed at two network hubs.

Thirty-six patients were assigned to slow six-cycle, faster forty-cycle, or sham stimulation for four weeks. Both real treatments improved cognition versus sham, and gains lasted eight weeks. The faster rhythm also improved language. Brain measures showed the slow rhythm boosted front-to-back information flow, while the faster rhythm boosted the reverse direction. Connection changes tracked the cognitive gains closely. The authors say frequency choice shapes which networks respond, supporting rhythm-matched stimulation as a treatment direction.
pmc-13277397:
Viviane Fornasaro-Donahue leads a 2026 interview study of how Hispanic-Latino adults view obesity and weight-loss surgery. Surgery for severe obesity works well but is used less in this group, despite higher obesity rates. The team held in-depth interviews with fourteen adults in Rhode Island who qualified for the surgery.

Many voiced fear, doubt, and wrong beliefs about the operation, shaped by stigma, culture, and personal values. Most saw surgery as a last resort and worried about complications and long-term effects. Family and friends, not clinicians, were the main source of treatment information. Talks with providers were often brief or vague. Tailored bilingual education and clearer communication could build trust, the authors conclude.
pmc-13278897:
Abdalrahman Al-slaimieh and colleagues compare pulsed field ablation with drug therapy for atrial fibrillation in a 2026 study. The ablation method uses electric pulses rather than heat to quiet faulty heart tissue. Their report is among the earliest on this technique from the Middle East and North Africa region.

Sixty-two ablated patients were matched against sixty-two registry patients treated with medicines alone. Groups were balanced on age, heart size, risk scores, and prior drug use. Readmissions for rhythm relapse or heart failure were far lower after ablation at both one and six months. Freedom from readmission also favoured ablation strongly. The authors call for larger regional studies to confirm the early signal.
pmc-13279697:
Hansong Qi and colleagues published a 2026 virology study identifying a host protein that Hantaan virus exploits to copy itself. The virus causes most cases of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome across Asia, a serious rodent-borne illness. To find host partners for the viral surface glycoprotein, the team combined deep-learning virtual screening with lab pull-down tests and mass spectrometry.

The cholesterol transporter NPC1 emerged as a binding partner for the viral protein. Experiments showed NPC1 actively promotes viral replication. It does so by an unexpected route: it blunts the cell's innate antiviral immune response after infection. Suppressing that early alarm lets the virus gain ground. The authors note this immune-damping role had not been documented for NPC1 in other viral infections. They propose the protein as a candidate target for antiviral drugs against hantaviruses.
pmc-13280097:
Bianca Maria Piraccini and colleagues published a 2026 commentary on hair loss reports linked to GLP-1 drugs, the diabetes and weight-loss medicines whose use is expanding in Europe. Safety signals from the United States prompted the authors to review what is known, weigh mechanisms, and offer practical advice for clinicians. The evidence comes from analyses of side-effect databases and retrospective cohort studies, with no prospective controlled trial yet.

The association signal looks strongest for semaglutide and tirzepatide, and analyses point the same way, strengthening suspicion without proving causation. One plausible route is the rapid weight loss itself, a known trigger of telogen effluvium, a shedding phase. Dose, route of administration, and individual susceptibility may also play roles but remain unmeasured. The authors advise warning patients about the possibility and watching for shedding during treatment. They press for research to settle whether the drugs themselves are responsible.
pmc-13280297:
Zengbei Yuan and colleagues report a 2026 study of radiomics boosted brain scans in Alzheimer disease. Amyloid beta build up in the brain is a core mark of the disease, and sound assessment guides care. The team join PET and MRI scans with a tracer called 18F-AV45 that binds amyloid. Radiomics extracts many math features from images that eyes cannot rate. The aim was amyloid status checks and a continuous burden score, called Centiloid.

Ninety four subjects had the combined scans: sixty amyloid positive and thirty four negative. Tracer uptake ratios came from seven brain zones, and radiomics features came from matched MRI structure images. Three feature sets, scan, radiomics and combined, fed three model types with ten fold cross checks. A SHAP analysis, which ranks feature weight, explained the best model. Centiloid regression used the top features as well. Image math may sharpen amyloid calls.
pmc-13281897:
Li-Yuan Chen and colleagues tested a nano vaccine against bird flu in chickens in a 2026 study. Bird flu shifts fast, so a vaccine that covers many strains is prized. One small virus part barely changes across strains, making it an ideal target. But alone it stirs weak defenses. The team packed that part into tiny plastic shells with a booster that wakes a cell alarm. Germ-free lab chickens got the shots.

Vaccinated birds switched on immune genes and grew more antibody-making cells. Their antibodies stayed strong over time. In dishes, the antibodies tagged the target on cells infected with seven unlike flu strains. After a live virus challenge, vaccinated birds showed milder kidney harm. Virus loads fell in breathing and gut lymph tissues. Lab killing tests hinted the antibodies also call in killer cells. The authors see a path to broad poultry cover.
pmc-13282397:
M Y Abd-Rabbou and co-authors present a 2026 study using stacked machine learning models to detect quantum entanglement in high-spin systems. Entanglement links quantum particles so their states cannot be described separately, and measuring it in large systems is computationally hard. The team layered several learning methods, including neural networks and tree-based models, with a final combiner model on top. Training used pure quantum states and a standard mixed state family.

The stack predicted entanglement values with consistently high accuracy and little variation across repeated runs. Errors were smallest near the extremes of the entanglement scale and largest in the middle range. The team derived scaling rules for training time, memory, and the data size needed for a target accuracy. One warning emerged: raw matrix descriptions of states grow too fast, capping scalability for the largest systems.
pmc-13282897:
Niclas Geldermann and co-authors survey doctors on water-pill care for acute heart failure, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Near eight hundred doctors in Switzerland, Germany, and Austria answered case-based questions. The cases covered first dose, checks during care, and steps when the drug works too weakly.

About half gave the guide-based first dose for new patients, while most did so for patients already on the drug. Few used urine salt checks to track care, though rates varied by land and by doctor type. Rural doctors used the check less. When response was weak, most favored adding a second blocking step.
pmc-13282997:
Soukayna Jebbar and eight co-authors reported mouth ulcers from a virus in a small child on cancer therapy, in twenty twenty-six. The child, aged two years and eight months, had a blood cancer and was receiving a bridging immune drug before a stem cell transplant. Painless, ring-shaped sores formed on the tongue, looking much like common aphthous ulcers.

Swab and blood tests found cytomegalovirus DNA, while tests for other viruses and fungi came back negative. That pointed to virus-driven tongue ulcers. The sores cleared after the cancer drug was paused and antiviral and antifungal treatment began. The authors note that this virus often sheds without symptoms, so a positive swab needs care in reading. They urge teams to keep it in mind when mouth sores in such children look atypical.
pmc-13283197:
Granite left for years in deep Fennoscandian groundwater grows its own mature microbe film, Magnus Stahle and partners show in 2026. Deep rock hosts most Earth microbe mass, yet most studies sample free-floating cells. Films on rock may hold far more cells and distinct species.

Rock pieces sat in deep water for two and four years in total. Gene tests compared film cells with free cells in the water. Films selected distinct species mixes and changed over time in clear ways. Early films were shaped by added cells that later faded from the surfaces. Mature films were ruled by sulfur-using groups and tiny partner cells. Film life differs sharply from life in open water.
pmc-13283397:
Clove-derived acetyl-eugenol is auditioned for male fertility support in Ismahil Adekunle Adeniyi's 2026 evidence review. Male factors drive nearly half of infertility cases worldwide. Cell stress, inflammation, and hormone imbalance can all impair sperm production.

The compound is acetyl-eugenol, a variant of eugenol from clove and other plants. Lab and animal work shows antioxidant and anti-inflammatory actions for the compound. It may shield sperm-making cells and support testis structure in animal models. Most proof comes from cells and animals, not from human trials. Many claims are drawn from eugenol studies, not the variant itself. Human proof is the clear missing step.
pmc-13283697:
Luis Fernando Viegas de Moraes Leme and a large team measured in 2026 how strong the kneecap's inner restraints are in children's knees. Two linked ligaments stop the kneecap sliding outward, and rebuilding both may beat rebuilding one, yet their strength had never been tested in growing knees. Seven donor knees from children aged eight to sixteen were dissected so the combined ligament complex could be clamped and loaded.

After warm-up and repeated loading cycles, the complex was pulled until it tore. Average failure load was about 167 newtons, with modest stretch under load and fairly stiff behaviour. Tears always came near the thigh bone attachment. Strength matched published adult values closely. The authors say graft choice for young patients can rest on these figures.
pmc-13283797:
Maya Yusri Rousan and colleagues studied diet, daily habits, and sleep in 2026 among medical residents in Amman, Jordan. Night shifts, long hours, and irregular meals put residents at risk of poor sleep. Fifty residents aged twenty-four to thirty-four kept three-day food records, answered activity and sleep quality questionnaires, and wore a sleep tracker over the same days.

More zinc in the diet tracked with longer deep sleep. Higher energy, carbohydrate, and fibre intake tracked with more night waking. In adjusted models, eating junk food more often predicted longer total sleep and longer light sleep. Lifestyle factors showed no clear independent link with the overall sleep quality score. The authors call diet a relevant correlate of how residents sleep.
pmc-13283897:
Back pain led to a late diagnosis of a multi-organ growth disorder in a 2026 case from A Fekih and colleagues. Tuberous sclerosis complex usually shows in childhood through brain or skin signs. Finding it near age sixty is rare and can challenge clinicians.

The 59-year-old woman had scans showing many kidney growths on both sides, larger on the right. Skin review found facial growths and a nail-bed growth that fit the disorder. Heart, lung, eye, and brain checks found no further disease in her case. Surgery removed the right kidney tumor, and tissue tests confirmed its type. A growth-slowing drug began three months later for leftover lesions.
pmc-13284297:
Light-controlled tweezers assemble, split, and propel mixed micro-particles in a 2026 study by Ao Wang and colleagues. Tiny robots need reconfiguration plus self-driven motion for complex tasks. Electric fields and fluid flows on their platform cooperate to move parts.

Assembled clusters travel along light pattern edges under their own power. Shadowing from top light creates the sideways push behind that motion. Speed responds oddly to frequency, dipping then rising across the range. Lens focusing under clear particles explains part of that pattern shift. Shifting light shapes plus field tweaks rebuild clusters at multiple levels. Modular micro-robot designs gain a versatile control route.
pmc-13284497:
Tao Nie and co-authors review, in a 2026 article, new ways to treat obesity by raising heat production in fat cells. Burning energy as heat in brown and beige fat could offset the chronic energy surplus that drives obesity. The review focuses mainly on cell and animal evidence, with human data noted only where it exists.

Regulators covered include the cAMP pathway, the PRDM16 and PPAR-gamma axis, and control of mitochondria quality and fuel use. Effects in test models look promising, yet translation stays uncertain. Species gaps, differences between fat depots, and few proven human studies all limit claims. The authors urge work that tests these pathways in people before clinical use.
pmc-13284597:
Julian Dewantiningrum and colleagues reviewed in 2026 whether a mother's vitamin D level during pregnancy shapes her child's bones. Vitamin D governs calcium handling and skeleton building before birth. The systematic review gathered nineteen cohort studies with 12,835 mother-child pairs from many regions, tracking child bone content, density, turnover markers, and fracture risk by scans, ultrasound, and blood tests.

Findings were mixed and often differed by child sex. Some studies tied higher maternal levels to stronger child bone measures, mainly in boys. Others found no link once mother and newborn factors were counted. Blood marker work generally tied maternal deficiency to higher fetal bone turnover. Proof that supplements improve long-term child bone outcomes stayed inconclusive. The authors call for standard measures and more cohorts from under-studied regions such as Southeast Asia.
pmc-13284697:
Chunai Liu, Lidong Xie, and Gang Xu pooled experiments in 2026 on generative AI in higher education, asking whether it lifts both learning and social-emotional outcomes. Evidence had been scattered, so the team gathered experimental and quasi-experimental studies published between 2021 and 2024, searching databases through January 2026. Thirty-three studies with 3,394 students were combined with random-effects models.

Generative AI showed a large positive effect on intellectual outcomes and a smaller positive effect on social-emotional outcomes, and the gap between the two was not statistically clear. Publication bias appeared for the intellectual results, and those results also proved sensitive to single studies, while social-emotional findings held steadier. Study features such as tool type and duration did not explain the wide spread across studies. The authors call the tools promising but warn that study quality varies widely.
pmc-13284897:
Ali Novelo-Sanguino and co-authors analyze cat bite patterns in Yucatan, Mexico, in a 2026 record study. Little data exist on cat attacks in Mexico, so the team reviewed health service reports from 2018 to 2023. Records came from the state health ministry database of animal bites to people.

Cat attacks made up 699 of 8,845 bite reports in the period studied here. Cases rose over time and centered on the city of Merida. Most victims were women and adults, and the arm or hand was hit most often. Rabies shots after exposure in cats were low. The authors frame the findings within One Health and call for stronger prevention and tracking.
pmc-13285597:
Reading how single sugar forms change antibody grip on an immune trigger is now doable in one run, Steffen Lippold and co-authors report in a 2026 methods study. The weak grip between C1q and antibody tails drives cell killing, and sugar tags on the tail tune it, yet standard tests blur the mix. Their column method pairs a single-chain C1q trap with mass reading.

A salt swap in the wash fluid cut sticky false binding that had plagued weak-grip work. The setup echoed the known grip ranking of human antibody classes. High-mannose sugars clearly weakened grip, while added galactose helped a touch. The authors say makers can now compare antibody batches fairly, sugar by sugar.
pmc-13285697:
Complete tooth loss in China is compared with the wider Group of Twenty in a 2026 analysis led by Yilin Zhang and colleagues. The work uses Global Burden of Disease 2023 data to track edentulism, the loss of all natural teeth, from 1990 onward. It asks what drives change in the burden and where that burden may head next.

Joinpoint regression tracks trends over time, while a decomposition step splits change into population growth, aging, and shifts in rates. Forecast models then project the burden through 2038. The authors report that China's rates fell only slightly, and that aging drove most of its rising burden. Across the G20, population growth mattered most instead. The contrast supports oral care aimed at older adults, linked with wider care for aging patients.
pmc-13286797:
Qing Yan and colleagues gather trial evidence on traditional Chinese exercise for people with Parkinson's disease, focusing on thinking, sleep, and quality of life. Their 2026 review and meta-analysis covers fifteen randomized trials found in five databases up to March 2025. Gentle practices such as Tai Chi and health Qigong are widely used, yet their non-motor benefits needed a summary.

Pooled results showed clear gains in cognition and sleep quality, plus a moderate gain in quality of life. Programs lasting at least twelve weeks with at least three hours weekly looked most favorable. Tai Chi helped thinking and daily life most, while Qigong led for sleep. People ill for five years or more seemed to gain extra. The authors advise cautious reading of the subgroup patterns.
pmc-13287097:
Shimrit Daches and colleagues probe when bodily vigilance feeds fear of cancer's return in a 2026 survey study. Somatosensory amplification, the habit of reading faint body signals as alarming, seems a natural fuel for recurrence fear, yet direct tests are scarce. Questionnaires from 116 adult survivors, averaging 47 years old, measured that tendency, emotion regulation difficulties, and recurrence fear, with anxiety and time since treatment held in account.

Neither tendency alone predicted the fear on its own. The combination told the story: bodily vigilance tracked stronger recurrence fear among survivors with low or average regulation difficulty. At high regulation difficulty, the link vanished, as if the noise floor already sat at maximum. The authors suggest screening for both traits in survivorship care to spot whose body watching is most likely to spiral into fear.
pmc-13287297:
Klaus Oberauer, Philipp Musfeld, and Frederik Aust ran six simulation studies in 2026 comparing two ways to estimate a Bayes factor, a measure used to weigh one statistical model against another. One route bridges between models. The other reads a density ratio from a single fitted model.

With many simulation draws, both routes gave accurate answers across wide conditions. Bridging grew slow and shaky as models gained parameters. The density ratio stayed fast and steady at larger sizes, though careless density smoothing could bias it. The authors give practical guidance on matching method to model size and on checking density estimates before trusting the result.
pmc-13287797:
Ahmed A Tayel and co-authors made a smart fish coating in 2026 from hibiscus pigment, zinc oxide particles made by green methods, and chitosan particles. The pigment flips colour as acidity changes, turning from red in acid toward green and yellow in alkaline fluid, which signals spoilage.

Dipped Nile perch fillets kept in a fridge stayed fresh up to six days longer than untreated fish. The coating also fought two common bacteria and showed strong antioxidant action in lab tests. As storage went on, the coating shifted from red to green, giving shoppers and handlers a visible freshness cue. The authors pitch the mix as eco-friendly packaging.
pmc-13287997:
Ping Yi and co-authors engineer a hydrogel from pig dental pulp to regrow tooth pulp, in a 2026 study. Keeping inflamed pulp alive helps a tooth survive for the long term. The team removed cells from pig pulp tissue, leaving its natural matrix behind as an injectable gel. That matrix kept many pulp-specific proteins and growth signals. Lab tests checked how immune and blood vessel cells responded to the gel.

The gel switched on a growth pathway in immune cells and pushed them toward a calming state. In shared culture dishes, it helped vessel cells activate and pulp stem cells mature toward dentin-making cells. In rats, capping exposed pulp with the gel produced a solid dentin bridge with new blood vessels. The surrounding tissue showed a repair-friendly immune profile. The authors see the gel as a candidate material for vital pulp therapy in clinics.
pmc-13288697:
Okello Ncube, Methembe Yotamu Khozah, and Wilfred Njabulo Nunu lay out a 2026 research protocol on disaster planning in Bulawayo Province, Zimbabwe. Their question is whether gender and sexual minority residents appear at all in plans for climate-driven disasters, a topic barely studied in sub-Saharan Africa.

Working through a local sexual rights center, the team plans to recruit 165 participants for structured questionnaires, focus groups, and interviews with key informants, running from April to December 2026. Ethics approval is already in place, with written consent required. Results will travel through journals, conferences, policy briefs to the local government ministry, and feedback sessions with the community partner.
pmc-13288997:
Elnora Abdurakhmanova and colleagues detail plans for a 2026 review of neck size as a liver test. Fatty liver disease is common yet often missed. Neck width is quick and cheap to measure. It tracks upper-body fat and heart risk. Past studies give mixed results.

The team will search four large databases. They will keep adult studies from 2010 to 2025. Liver disease must be shown by scan or biopsy. Two reviewers will pick and grade each study. Pooled hit and miss rates are the main goal. The team will also probe why results differ. Findings could support a simple first screen.
pmc-13289397:
Saumya susan Zacharia and Raji Thomas report a 2026 record review on medical problems during rehab after severe brain injury in India. Recovery needs work on body, thinking, and social life, yet complications during inpatient rehab were poorly described in Indian settings. Many such problems can be prevented with early spotting and care, the authors note.

Records covered 100 adults admitted for rehab from August 2017 to August 2019 with severe injury scores. Men made up 81 percent, road crashes caused 81 percent of injuries, and mean age was 35 years in the group. Fully 87 percent had at least one complication during rehab overall. Behavior and thinking issues led at 35 percent, followed by abnormal bone growth in soft tissue.
pmc-13290697:
A skin disease wore two different faces on one patient, Sandesh Shah and colleagues report in a case report from 2026 on Hailey-Hailey disease. The inherited blistering condition usually raises eroded plaques in skin folds, but atypical forms can imitate other blistering disorders.

Their patient, a 38-year-old man, had recurring itchy lesions in flexural areas that worsened with heat and sweat. His neck and armpits showed the classic eroded plaques, while the groin and other folds carried bumpy, follicular lesions with heavy leftover pigmentation instead. A biopsy showed the split skin layers and 'dilapidated brick wall' pattern typical of the disease, and matching clinic with microscope settled the diagnosis. Shah and colleagues remind clinicians that this papular variant exists and that correlation between the two views is what resolves it.
pmc-13290897:
One disease, three patterns: machine learning splits chronic traumatic encephalopathy into distinct variants, Fatima Tuz-Zahra and colleagues report in a brain study from 2026. CTE, the degeneration tied to repeated head injury, shows patchy tau buildup that varies widely between people, and the team asked whether that variation hides order.

Applying a subtype-and-stage algorithm to tau density measured across 26 brain regions, in a sample of 207 CTE cases alongside 75 controls, produced three progression patterns. One was cortex-heavy and fast, matching classic descriptions. A second spared the cortex but hit the hippocampus hard and moved slower. A third, in older cases, came bundled with other pathologies and extra tau in related regions. Daily-function scores tracked tau burden only in the cortex-heavy group. The authors say the variants should sharpen diagnosis criteria and the search for in-life tests.
pmc-13290997:
Whether removing more lymph nodes helps women with endometrial cancer live longer is weighed in a 2026 meta-analysis led by Yunlong Fan. The comparison sets combined pelvic and para-aortic node removal against pelvic removal alone or no node removal, with attention to groups split by recurrence risk.

Searches through December 2025 gathered 14 studies covering 25,432 patients, only one of them a randomized trial. Raw comparisons gave mixed answers, a pattern the authors link to sicker patients more often receiving wider surgery. After statistical adjustment for such differences, wider removal was linked with better overall survival than no removal. The risk-split results are offered as help for tailoring a major surgical choice to each patient’s likely course.
pmc-13291097:
A handheld skin checker called SkinConnect is validated for measuring skin hydration in a 2026 device study led by Frédéric Flament. Built for shop-floor skincare advice, the compact device also reads skin color and surface texture, and the team tested whether its hydration readings repeat well and match a standard laboratory instrument.

Forty-four adults, half women and half men, were measured in triplicate at six body sites at hourly gaps, before and after a hydrating cream went on one forearm. Nearly all of the roughly 4,665 readings were usable, repeat readings held close together, and two devices agreed well with each other. Agreement with the standard Corneometer was weaker at low hydration, yet the device clearly caught the cream-driven rise in moisture.
pmc-13291297:
A plant sugar from a prized Chinese herb may soothe skin. Xuan Li leads a 2026 study of Bletilla striata tubers. The plant has long use in folk medicine. Its sugar chains were poorly mapped until now.

One pure fraction, called BSP60, was pulled from the tubers. Its backbone links mannose and glucose units in turn. Some mannose units carry small acetyl tags. The syrup flows thin under force yet forms a springy web. It beat a common skin acid at mopping up harmful radicals. In immune cells, it cut three swelling signals. Such traits suit creams and wound care research.
pmc-13291597:
Fish carry an oxygen-immune link that land animals lost. Zhipeng Zhan leads a 2026 study of this teleost-specific axis. Water holds little oxygen yet teems with germs. Fish must tune inflammation under low oxygen.

An oxygen sensor called FIH switches on immune pathways. It works by pushing aside a brake protein. That frees a key immune factor to act. Zebrafish lacking the sensor gene fought infection worse. Structure studies show why land vertebrates lack the link. Domain swaps proved the interface is water-specific. The axis may guide fish farm health as waters warm.
pmc-13291797:
Chris Sara Mathew, Manjush Karthika, and Khalid Ansari offer a 2026 integrative review on mouth care as a way to prevent pneumonia in critically ill adults. Ventilator-linked pneumonia and other hospital-acquired pneumonia remain frequent and serious in intensive care. The reviewers searched three databases for work from 2005 to 2025 linking oral health with pneumonia prevention.

From 935 records, 20 studies survived screening and entered the final synthesis. The reviewers grouped the evidence around the oral-lung pathway, current bedside practice, specific cleaning methods, record keeping, and staffing hurdles. They conclude that structured oral care lowers ventilator pneumonia rates and propose a practical, dentistry-informed care bundle. Practice today, they note, stays uneven and poorly specified.
pmc-13292297:
Linli Zhang and co-authors grade a 2026 overview of reviews on magnetic brain stimulation for arm recovery after stroke. Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation is widely reviewed, but nobody had checked how trustworthy those reviews are. The team searched nine databases and grey literature through April 2024, scoring reviews with AMSTAR-2 and PRISMA 2020 and grading evidence strength with GRADE.

Seventeen reviews qualified. Only 13 outcome measures rated high; 47 rated moderate, 91 low, and 71 very low in their tally. Sloppy methods and incomplete reporting, more than publication year or bias, drove the downgrades. The authors conclude that stimulation probably aids arm movement, yet the evidence base needs stricter standards, fuller reporting, and MRI biomarkers to sort out mixed results.
pmc-13292797:
Gal Tsaban and colleagues built a computer model, reported in 2026, that uses heart tracings to estimate the risk of death within one year. Care in hospital and emergency settings often lacks clear risk tools, and repeated tracings may hold extra clues.

Records covered 13,417 adults over age 50 treated between 2014 and 2019, of whom 4,372 died within one year. A model using three tracings over time reached 0.84 on the area-under-curve scale, a value the authors treat as strong. Adding most clinic details beyond age and sex did not help. The authors propose the tool could sort patients for closer follow-up.
pmc-13293397:
Samuel Anyaso-Samuel leads a 2026 national survey study on how United States adults rate their own grasp of statistics. Skill with numbers shapes daily choices, from health news to money, yet self-views on this skill are rarely mapped.

In a representative survey, 62% of adults said they had little to no idea what statistics or terms like p-values mean, a share the authors report. Yet 90% said they would use reported statistics at least sometimes if they grasped them better. More schooling linked to higher self-ratings, while older groups rated lower. The authors urge wider statistics teaching in and out of school.
pmc-13293697:
Antonio Tonutti leads a 2026 registry study of systemic sclerosis patients who lack the classic tiny-vessel pattern under the nailfold. That pattern aids diagnosis, yet a small share of patients never show it, and their illness course was unclear.

Among 1689 Italian registry patients with nailfold data, 90 lacked the pattern, which is 5.3% of the group, a share the authors report. They were older at onset and more often had the form without skin thickening. Vessel harms like fingertip scars and calcium deposits were less common, and skin scores stayed lower over five years. Lung transfer capacity also held up better over time.
pmc-13293997:
Jie Lei and co-authors engineer a vaccine-like treatment for stubborn bone infections, in a 2026 study. Chronic infection with drug-resistant Staphylococcus aureus creates a suppressed immune pocket where bacteria persist and bone cannot heal. Ideal therapy would first rally antibacterial immunity and later calm inflammation so repair can proceed. The team screened vesicles shed by a probiotic bacterium for exactly that two-stage behavior.

The vesicles carried a rich supply of a metabolic molecule called NAD+, and tuning the culture conditions boosted that cargo further. Early on, the engineered vesicles woke up dendritic cells and built strong antibody protection, clearing nearly all bacteria in animal challenges, including repeat attacks. Later, delivered NAD+ reprogrammed inflammatory macrophages at the defect site, and bone repair ran about ten times faster. The design treats infection and healing as one sequence.
pmc-13294097:
Jinfa Gu heads a 2026 pooled review of trials on beta-alanine supplements for exercise in women. Most prior evidence came from men or mixed groups, leaving female effects unclear. Five databases were searched through April 30, 2026, for randomized trials against placebo or control, with bias and certainty graded by standard tools.

Twelve reports from 11 trials covered 312 women. Time to exhaustion favored the supplement in pooled results across eight studies with 187 women. Other outcomes, including oxygen uptake, peak power, and body fat, stayed imprecise. Certainty was very low for every outcome after downgrades, so the authors urge caution and better trials.
pmc-13294297:
