James Yu and Peter C. Schalock review harms from cosmetic products in a 2026 invited narrative review. Daily cosmetic use is near universal, and new launches keep coming, so side effects deserve stocktaking. A broad PubMed search gathered case reports, series, trials, and population studies on reactions tied to product use.

Contact dermatitis dominates, affecting about 1–5% of the general population in the cited range. Other harms include breathing sensitization, light-triggered reactions, workplace exposures, and pregnancy and nursing concerns. Long-term and combined exposure effects stay poorly understood. The authors call for stronger safety oversight as the market grows.
pmc-13294497:
Shogo Nagaoka and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-six geodesy study mapping ground strain around a plate boundary in central Japan. The region mixes a major tectonic line, a known strain belt, and volcanic terrain. Thick vegetation and mountains blunt ground surveys there.

Satellite radar data spanning nearly a decade were fused with a dense positioning network. Private stations filled gaps in the official grid. The combined map resolved sharply concentrated strain along the northern tectonic line. Parts of the known strain belt also stood out tightly. Finer strain maps sharpen earthquake hazard reading in complex country.
pmc-13294797:
Stefan Linsler and co-authors examine how storage timing affects lab-grown meningioma cells in a 2026 study. Tumour tissue is often kept overnight before culture work begins, but whether that delay changes growth was poorly known. Ten samples were taken from patients operated on at Saarland University during 2022.

Cultures started on the surgery day and cultures started a day later both grew at rates of at least 80 percent, with no clear difference between them. Genetic checks found chromosome losses matching the original tumours, even after freezing. Sixteen of 17 frozen specimens also grew again after six months in liquid nitrogen storage.
pmc-13294897:
Karl Thomas Jackson, Robert H. Lomax, and Fatemeh Parnianchi tune a sponge-like crystal to catch dyes from water, in a 2026 study of the metal-organic framework UiO-66. Such frameworks are built from metal clusters and organic links, and adding acid during synthesis changes both particle size and the number of missing-link defects. The team brewed three batches with rising acid doses and challenged each with three dyes: methyl orange, methylene blue, and curcumin.

More acid grew bigger particles, from about 190 to 450 nanometers, and steadily lowered how much dye each batch absorbed. Surface area and defect counts rose then fell across the series, so the relationship was not a simple line. Methyl orange was captured best and methylene blue worst, and uptake patterns fit a model of varied surface sites. Changing cooking time changed nothing, giving makers a clean dial for performance.
pmc-13294997:
Yi-Fen Li and colleagues compare factors linked to vaginal precancer lesions across age groups in a 2026 study. Vaginal intraepithelial neoplasia is an early change that can precede vaginal cancer. Whether test results and nearby lesions mean the same thing in younger and older women was unclear.

Records covered 212 women who had colposcopy and vaginal biopsy between 2020 and 2024, split at age 50. Lesion presence linked with younger age, while older women more often showed high-grade cell test results. In women aged 50 and above, lesion grade rose alongside grades of past or current cervical and vulvar lesions, supporting age-specific screening plans.
pmc-13295697:
Hwajin Yang and co-authors set out a framework for how stress feeds heavy social media use, in a 2026 study. They call it Stress-Induced Digital Escapism. The idea runs in steps: outer demands stir bad feelings, bad feelings push weak ways of coping, and weak coping builds a wish to escape into feeds. Survey data from 238 people let the team test the chain.

The chain held. Outer demands linked to heavy use only through the steps in between: dark stress reactions, poor ways of handling feelings with others, such as venting and seeking comfort, and escape wishes. Checks against flipped models backed the order the team proposed. The framework gives one account of how stress turns scrolling into a habit that is hard to drop.
pmc-13295797:
Xiaodong Zhu and colleagues survey animal science students on welfare views and career plans in a 2026 study. Students in animal-related degrees may carry welfare teaching into both attitudes and job choices. Questionnaires went to undergraduates at Northeast Agricultural University in China.

How students first met welfare ideas tracked with how they judged animal treatment overall. Gender, pet-keeping experience, and career intention each linked significantly with welfare perceptions in the answers. Many students had received welfare teaching far later than they wished. The authors propose a staged system, starting with life and human-animal lessons in primary school and adding hands-on courses at university.
pmc-13296297:
Carlos Javier Lainez Reyes and co-authors compare heart rhythm patterns in miniature cows and Holstein cattle in a 2026 field study. Miniature breeds are gaining interest for small farms, yet little is known about how their smaller size affects heart regulation. Beat-to-beat variation was recorded with a wearable sensor placed on each animal.

Miniature cows showed slower heart rates and stronger variation between beats than the Holsteins. The gap between the groups grew wider in mature animals. The authors urge caution, because the herds lived on different farms and only the Holsteins were producing milk. Even so, the readings give a useful starting baseline for later controlled work on heart health in small cattle.
pmc-13296897:
Hasan Zeybek and Tugrul Hosbul study hepatitis B patients whose virus levels sit below the measuring limit in a 2026 retrospective paper. Such faint traces appear in treated chronic infection and in occult infection, where surface antigen tests read negative. Records of 390 patients with very low viral loads were examined alongside antibody markers.

Low-level virus was commoner in men and in patients aged fifty or older. Among occult cases, two antibody markers appeared far more often, and both stayed linked to occult infection after adjustment. A third antibody pulled in the opposite direction. One marker of reduced replication clearly did not mean full suppression. The authors ask for prospective validation.
pmc-13297297:
Mashal Fatima, Faraz Akram, and Imran Khan Niazi test whether the complexity of brain-wave signals can flag harmful brain change in substance use, in a 2026 study. Three hundred fifty people took part, split evenly among six substance groups and one control group with no such diagnosis. Resting brain signals were recorded with a small eight-channel headset.

Four measures of signal complexity all ran lower in the substance groups than in controls. Losses were largest over the front and centre of the scalp, zones tied to planning and movement. A simple classifier sorted the seven groups with very high accuracy, near ninety-eight percent. Cheap, portable brain-wave checks could suit intake screening and progress checks during recovery care.
pmc-13297597:
Norma Olvera and colleagues examine how anxiety and sleep quality travel with binge eating in Hispanic and African American early adolescents, in a 2026 study. These groups face higher obesity rates than white peers, and binge eating feeds that risk. Three hundred fifteen boys and girls, most of them carrying excess weight, answered surveys and had height, weight, and body fat measured.

Higher binge eating scores went with higher anxiety and with poorer sleep, in both boys and girls alike. The links held after accounting for age, ethnic group, sex, and body fat. Together the measured factors explained about a sixth of the spread in binge eating. Programmes against binge eating should screen for anxiety and sleep trouble, the authors urge.
pmc-13297997:
Javier Jurado and co-authors revisit how methane partial oxidation proceeds on a platinum catalyst, in a 2026 kinetic modelling study. Reaction schemes for many catalysts remain unsettled because accurate data are scarce. An earlier model failed to reproduce the available experiments, so the team proposed a revised scheme.

Data came from past packed-bed reactor runs across a high temperature range. Nonlinear parameter estimation, careful starting values, and sensitivity plus stats checks produced the new parameter set. The revised model predicted the experimental data closely. Readers in catalysis get both a corrected scheme and a worked example of how model fitting choices affect kinetic findings.
pmc-13298797:
Kensuke Kitsugi and colleagues examine bleeding after percutaneous liver biopsy in patients who stopped blood-thinning medicines under Japanese endoscopy guidelines, in a 2026 retrospective study. Bleeding is the main risk of the procedure, and rules for managing such drugs were unclear. Records covered 630 biopsy cases, including 64 patients on antithrombotic therapy.

Bleeding rates did not differ significantly between patients who had therapy withdrawn and those never on it, even after matched comparisons for tumour and non-tumour biopsies. No treated patient needed surgery or vessel blocking for bleeding, and one clot event followed withdrawal. Low platelet count, not therapy itself, predicted bleeding.
pmc-13298997:
Adedolapo V Adejumo reports a severe calcium channel blocker overdose case in a 2026 medical paper. Such poisoning is rare yet can cause dangerously slow heart rate, shock, and body-chemistry upset. The patient developed low blood pressure that resisted standard treatment, which illustrates the difficulty of critical care itself in these cases.

Current treatment combines several drug tactics, including high-dose insulin with glucose control, intravenous calcium, glucagon, and lipid rescue therapy. Advanced haemodynamic support may also be needed. Because these medicines are widely prescribed for heart and blood pressure problems, the author argues clinicians should understand overdose consequences and spot it early.
pmc-13299097:
Predicting how drugs interact inside the body is a network problem, and Zhongyi Chai with co-authors attack it with a graph neural network in a 2026 paper. Their framework, PHARMNet, learns from multi-relational biomedical graphs, while a companion strategy injects ontology knowledge and uncertainty estimates.

Relation-specific convolutions and memory-augmented attention let the model trace hidden dependencies between drugs, targets, and diseases, and the ontology-guided layer steadies predictions when data are sparse or noisy. Across drug interaction benchmarks the system reported an AUC of 0.873 and an F1-score of 0.831, which the authors describe as state-of-the-art performance with better interpretability than earlier tools.
pmc-13299997:
Liyang Xiao, Kai Siang Chan, Isaac Chan, and Aung Myint Oo pool evidence on curative oesophagus removal in patients aged eighty and above, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Eighteen studies covering more than seventy thousand oesophageal cancer patients compared octogenarians with younger patients on survival, deaths, and complications after surgery.

Overall survival was clearly worse in the older group, and hospital, thirty-day, and ninety-day mortality all ran higher. Overall complications were also more frequent, although specific problems such as leakage and chest infection occurred at similar rates. Complete tumour clearance was somewhat less common in octogenarians. The role of keyhole surgery in this age group needs study.
pmc-13300397:
G Caluori and co-authors study how tissue type shapes pulsed field ablation lesions in ventricles, in a 2026 preclinical paper. The technique is proven in atrial fibrillation, but its behavior inside scarred ventricular muscle is poorly known. The team created a sheep model of healed heart attack damage with embolization coils. They then delivered focal pulsed field energy, and they followed the lesions with magnetic resonance imaging and tissue staining at one month.

Lesions stayed durable in both scar and healthy tissue. Temperature feedback at the catheter, used as a contact estimate, responded very differently by tissue type. Healthy tissue lesion depth grew with dose only up to two applications. Treated areas shrank as they healed, losing little depth across the wall. Collagen patterns let the team pick out mature ablation lesions inside old scar, which they offer as a guide for future dosing.
pmc-13300697:
Sending COPD patients home from hospital is a risky handover, and Sanja Dimic-Janjic leads a 2026 survey of how Serbian physicians handle it. One hundred doctors involved in COPD care, recruited through the Respiratory Society of Serbia, described their discharge routines. A SWOT analysis framed the answers about gaps, barriers, and appetite for structured discharge summaries.

Practice varied widely and stayed largely unstandardized, even though most doctors knew the recommended principles. Respondents nonetheless showed strong willingness to adopt structured discharge tools, which they rarely used in daily work. The team reads the blockage as organizational rather than motivational, and points to standardization, coordination, and patient teaching as improvement targets.
pmc-13300797:
Rogue circles of DNA floating outside chromosomes may forecast how a cancer will behave, Filip Gajewski and colleagues argue in a 2026 review. These extrachromosomal elements carry heavy loads of growth genes such as EGFR, MYC, MDM2, and CDK4. Detection routes covered include FISH, whole-genome sequencing, and reconstruction software across many tumor types.

Because the circles lack centromeres, daughter cells inherit uneven shares, which speeds tumor diversity and drug resistance. Surveys find them often in glioblastoma, liposarcoma, and HER2-positive breast cancer, and their presence tracks with poorer outcomes. The authors back ecDNA as a risk marker, while warning that no standard, scalable test yet exists for routine care.
pmc-13300897:
E G Ferro and a large co-author team compare stroke risk between pulsed field and radiofrequency ablation for atrial fibrillation in a 2026 registry study from a high-volume American center. Recalls of some pulsed field catheters had raised brain safety worries. So the team examined 3,566 consecutive ablations from 2022 to 2025. Suspected strokes were judged by three blinded neurologists, and statistical weighting balanced the groups.

Only nine stroke or mini-stroke events occurred within thirty days, yet the split was uneven: about half a percent after pulsed field treatment against a tenth of a percent after radiofrequency. The gap persisted after weighting, at both seven and thirty days. Other complications, including nerve injury, coronary spasm, and fluid compression of the heart, ran similar between methods, and no esophageal fistulas occurred. The authors urge confirmatory studies and protocol changes to trim the cerebrovascular risk.
pmc-13301197:
S Kotoulas and co-authors examine flecainide's effect on complex ventricular ectopy in the prospective UNIFLECA study, reported in 2026. The subanalysis covered ninety-seven patients with extra beats and no structural heart disease who had declined catheter ablation and started slow release flecainide. Around the clock rhythm recordings before and after treatment tracked not beat counts but paired beats and short runs of tachycardia, the patterns that signal an unstable substrate.

Paired beats were present in about fifty-nine percent of patients at baseline and fell on treatment, with resolution in twenty-seven percent. Short tachycardia runs dropped by roughly two thirds in patient count, and over half of those affected were fully suppressed, while a few simplified into paired beats. About twenty-nine percent of patients achieved full or partial clearing of complex patterns. The authors support flecainide as a safe, effective option for this group.
pmc-13301297:
Christos Ch. Andrianos and co-authors grade brain gliomas from MRI scans without first outlining the tumor, in a 2026 methods study. Their network was itself designed by an automated architecture search over a three dimensional backbone, then strengthened with residual links and attention blocks. Training and validation used preoperative scans from 1,194 patients across four public cohorts, with a fifth collection held out for external testing.

The model separated low grade from high grade tumors with about eighty-eight percent accuracy internally, dropping to roughly seventy-five percent on the unseen cohort, still ahead of benchmark networks. Heat map analysis showed it looking at the tumor region despite never being taught outlines, checked against available hand drawn masks. The same machinery predicted a key mutation with about ninety percent accuracy and handled multi grade sorting respectably. The authors pitch segmentation free grading as a lighter path to computer aided diagnosis.
pmc-13301397:
Yiyu Zhang, Xiajing Yao, and Dechao Li watch translators' eyes to learn which language model statistics predict their reading in a 2026 eye tracking study. Twenty-six native Chinese translators worked both directions between English and Chinese, translating from scratch and post editing machine output, yielding 104 recorded sessions. The team pitted two model families against the gaze data: a language model and a machine translation system, each supplying surprise scores and attention features.

Time spent reading the target text was explained best by the language model's surprise at each word, a monolingual signal. Source reading leaned on the translation model's attention, with language model surprise a second. How long production took drew on both systems' translation surprise. Translation direction mattered more than the translate versus post edit distinction. The authors conclude that inside a bilingual task, the reading clock runs on monolingual predictability, while production adds the cross language machinery.
pmc-13301497:
Wojciech Karolak and co-authors extend minimally invasive valve surgery to operations on valves in a 2026 case series. Ten patients with combined aortic and mitral disease were treated through a five to seven centimeter chest incision, with heart lung bypass run from the leg vessels. Nine received double valve work and one a triple valve procedure, all without spreading ribs or disturbing the internal mammary artery.

Bypass and clamp times ran long, near 198 and 148 minutes on average, which the authors own as a learning curve. Even so, every case finished through the incision with no conversion to sternotomy and no deaths. No patient needed reoperation for bleeding, and no wound infections or leg vessel complications appeared. Half developed atrial fibrillation, the commonest issue, and nine of ten valves worked well on scans, with one leak watched conservatively. The authors argue a valve center can stretch the approach.
pmc-13301597:
Raluca Maior and co-authors survey stress, body symptoms, and weight stigma among teenagers and young adults in a 2026 cross sectional study. The sample held 117 participants aged sixteen to twenty, nearly ninety percent female, recruited in Târgu Mureș in June 2025. Questionnaires measured perceived stress, symptom severity across body systems, and weight related psychosocial burden, set against body mass index.

Young women reported heavier symptom loads than young men, a median score of twenty-one against three. Stress tracked positively with neurological, cardiovascular, digestive, and total symptoms. Body mass did not predict symptom severity, yet it correlated with experienced weight stigma. Emotional fallout ignored weight categories: about sixty-one percent felt guilt around food and sixty percent reported dented self confidence, while only six percent had consulted a mental health professional. The authors call for stress management, nutrition counseling, and body image support aimed at all weight groups.
pmc-13302197:
Sea air quietly shortens the working life of a heat-proof titanium alloy, Guangming Kong and colleagues report in a 2026 fatigue study. TC25, used in hot aero-engine parts, underwent high-temperature low-cycle fatigue testing before and after exposure to a simulated marine atmosphere. The team also built life-prediction models for both states of the metal.

After corrosion, the final failure stage claimed roughly ten percent more of each test's life share. Pits eaten into the surface concentrated stress, spawning more crack starting points and speeding crack growth, which cut total fatigue life. The findings give engine designers firmer ground for scheduling parts that serve at coastal bases and over open water.
pmc-13304397:
Hagop Sassounian and co-authors review, in a 2026 paper, whether vitamin D shapes Familial Mediterranean Fever, an inherited condition of recurring fever and membrane inflammation common around the Mediterranean. The faulty gene makes an immune sensor overreact, and standard treatment is colchicine. Vitamin D also steers immune activity, and levels run low in the same populations.

The review walks through the disease's triggers, from cold and stress to gut flora and diet, then weighs vitamin D's hand on inflammatory messengers. Any link so far rests on correlation, not proven cause. Still, the authors argue that correcting deficiency might trim disease burden for some patients and deserves proper trials. Genetic, dietary, and immune strands are tied into one picture.
pmc-13305597:
Plamen Tchoukov and Khristo Khristov introduce a 2026 second-edition collection on amphiphilic molecules, the two-faced chemicals that gather at surfaces and shape foams, films, and emulsions. Industries from drugs to food to resource extraction lean on their behavior.

Papers in the collection link molecular build to surface uptake, layer organization, and the stability of mixed systems as a whole. Many real systems sit far from rest, so flow, drainage of thin films, and surface tension gradients draw special focus. Greener, bio-based versions are gaining ground under environmental pressure, and they demand fresh testing of structure and behavior.
pmc-13306097:
Tatiane B. Santos reviewed immune treatments aimed at alpha-synuclein in Parkinson's disease in a 2026 survey spanning computer, lab and clinic work. Clumping of this protein inside dopamine neurons sits at the heart of disease development in the authors' framing.

Approaches include injected antibodies, peptide shots and protein-based vaccines, judged by shape of target, safety and signs of hitting the protein. Several candidates raised lasting antibody responses with acceptable safety and lowered free or clumped protein in early trials. Lasting clinical gain remains unproven, so the review stresses better markers in spinal fluid and blood before larger testing.
pmc-13306497:
Wen Li checked whether scan quality changes the value of a breast imaging marker during chemotherapy in a 2026 study. Data came from the multi-centre I-SPY 2 trial, where diffusion scans yield a water-movement value meant to forecast full tumour clearance.

Readers graded fat suppression, artefacts and signal strength with only fair to moderate agreement in reported scores. Where a tumour outline could be drawn, marker performance for predicting complete response stayed similar across quality groups and scanner strengths. The authors argue that usable outlines matter more than perfect image polish for this marker.
pmc-13306697:
Shao-Shuai Yu reviewed plant parasites called phytoplasmas across Hainan Island in a 2026 survey. These wall-less bacteria live in plant sap tubes and ride on sap-sucking insects, thriving in the island's tropical mix of hosts.

Records gathered 69 representative cases across four subgroups, sorted by host plant, symptoms and gene group in the compiled account. Mixed infections, varied insect carriers and island isolation all shape how strains evolve locally. The authors warn that such diversity complicates watching, testing and preventing the crop diseases these bacteria cause. The team urges joint watch plans that fit island crops and local pests.
pmc-13307097:
Aydın Boyar compared two motor control methods for electric vehicles in real-time tests in a 2026 study. A permanent magnet motor fed by a multilevel inverter was driven under changing speed and load with both control schemes.

Classic field-oriented control uses fixed switching with layered controllers and modulation, while the predictive method tests future current paths and picks the cheapest switching move each step. Tracking of speed and torque, current quality and switching behaviour were scored side by side on the same hardware. The comparison guides control choice for cleaner, smoother electric drives.
pmc-13307297:
Andrzej R. Reindl reviewed how people meet forever chemicals called PFAS in a 2026 comprehensive survey. The carbon and fluorine bond makes these substances exceptionally stable, spreading them through water, food and products worldwide.

Evidence for direct cancer links stays uneven across studies, while liver harm, immune harm and mother-fetus disruption rest on firmer ground in the authors' weighing. Mixture exposure and sex-based metabolism differences shape many effects. Short-chain replacements move faster through the environment and resist standard water cleaning, deepening the regulatory problem. The team calls for rules that treat mix effects, not just one chemical at a time in labs.
pmc-13307697:
Sara Cruces-Salguero and co-authors study in 2026 a DNA switch called Srr2 that helps set levels of SOX2, a key factor in adult nerve stem cells in mice. They bred mice that lack the switch and grew stem cells from them, pairing gene activity reads with maps of open DNA regions.

Cells that lacked the switch held less SOX2 while dividing, and they made fewer nerve and support cells when cued to mature. DNA packed more tightly in dividing mutant cells, and some nerve genes stayed shut when they should have opened. In live mice, stem cell zones showed the same weak signals. Non coding switches thus guard the open state that fate choices need.
pmc-13307797:
Laëtitia Porcher and co-authors validate in 2026 an in house high throughput RNA sequencing test that hunts plant viruses and viroids in one run, with no need to name a target first. Their flow pulls total RNA, strips ribosomal RNA, sequences on an Illumina platform, and sorts the reads with software tools.

Checks ran on three unlike targets: a tomato RNA virus, a tomato DNA virus, and a pepper viroid with an RNA genome. Sensitivity, accuracy, repeat runs, and toughness all met the bar set for routine plant diagnosis work. Sick plant samples can thus be screened broadly in house, which helps labs catch mixed infections that single target tests would miss.
pmc-13307897:
Yuwen Fang and colleagues expose pregnant rats in 2026 to the insecticide cyfluthrin and test whether their pups pay a cognitive price. Dams received the pyrethroid during gestation, and offspring faced behaviour tests at three weeks old. Brain tissue from the memory centre was examined for inflammation and cell death pathways.

Exposed pups were born lighter, caught up poorly, and showed weaker movement, object recognition, and water maze learning. Hippocampal neurons looked disorganised with fewer protein-making bodies. Inflammatory proteins rose while synaptic proteins fell, and two death programmes, pyroptosis and apoptosis, switched on more strongly. Placental weight and structure also suffered under exposure. The authors present the chain from womb exposure to brain injury as toxicological evidence. They frame the work as input for judging human risk from a very common insecticide family.
pmc-13308497:
Tashfeen Mahmood, Mohammad M Mahmood, and Elizabeth Martin describe in 2026 a case of lung swelling tied to apalutamide, a prostate cancer drug, in a man aged 69 years. The man had cancer that had spread and grew short of breath over days, with very low blood oxygen on arrival.

Scans showed hazy patches in both lungs, and broad checks ruled out infection, heart failure, and immune disease as causes. Stopping the drug and starting steroid care brought marked gains in breath and in scan looks. Rare lung harm from this drug can turn severe fast, so teams must act early when breath fails without a clear cause.
pmc-13308997:
Szczuczko, Szczuczko, Gałyńska, and Boguslawski present in twenty twenty-six a tool for splitting apart how charge moves when a molecule takes in light. When a molecule absorbs light, charge can shift within it or between it and a neighbour. Chemists need to know how much of each kind occurs in each excited state, but older tools gave answers that shifted with basic settings.

Their tool works with many standard excited-state methods and does not rely on charge density maps. It sorts each excitation into local and charge-shift parts by region of the molecule. Two ways of adding up regions gave matching results, and answers barely moved across settings. Tests covered shifts both inside single molecules and between them.
pmc-13309397:
Ali Saidu and co-authors present a 2026 survey of worm medicine performance in small sheep and goat flocks in Sarawak, Malaysia. Gut worms cut meat and milk output, and farms rely on routine deworming drugs. Heavy drug use has bred resistant worms in other parts of Malaysia, but Sarawak data were missing.

Smallholder flocks were tested with a standard egg-count method, comparing counts before treatment and 14 days after treatment with two common drugs. Samples grown after treatment helped name which worm types survived. As an early survey, the work sets a baseline for the region. The authors frame it as a first check on whether drug failure has reached these flocks.
pmc-13310497:
Xiuyu Wu and co-authors test a blood inflammation score for predicting liver failure after liver surgery in a 2026 study. Liver failure after partial liver removal for liver cancer remains a top cause of harm. Routine blood counts might flag risk cheaply beside standard liver reserve tests.

Records covered keyhole liver surgery patients at one center between 2017 and 2025, with 356 patients included from 582 screened for the analysis. The score multiplies three blood cell counts and divides by a fourth, all from tests within seven days before surgery. Outcomes used the standard international definition of post-surgery liver failure. Curve and decision analyses judged how well the score sorts risk. The authors propose it as a pre-surgery add-on check.
pmc-13310697:
Natasha Yaneva offers a 2026 hypothesis paper on type 1 diabetes and the thymus, the gland where immune cells learn to spare the body. In this disease, the thymus shows too little insulin, so harmful immune cells escape and later attack insulin making cells in the pancreas. No current treatment fixes that early fault.

Yaneva proposes a wearable patch that sends mild radio waves at 448 kHz toward the thymus. The claim is that the signal could raise calcium flow in thymus cells and switch on genes that boost insulin display there. Stronger display might delete harmful cells and favor calm ones instead. The idea is untested and needs lab proof.
pmc-13310797:
Elham Shahgholi and colleagues report a 2026 case of Bloom syndrome with early bone marrow disease in a young girl. A girl aged 8 years had severe growth failure and lasting low blood counts. Marrow tests showed low cell counts with loss of chromosome 7, which fits a myelodysplastic neoplasm. Gene tests found two copies of a harmful BLM gene fault.

Skin and vessel signs overlapped three other syndromes that affect skin, vessels, and growth, which made the picture complex. Severe infection took her life before a stem cell transplant could be done. Inherited cancer risk syndromes should be weighed in children with low counts, poor growth, and mixed skin signs.
pmc-13311297:
Md Mafrohi Sattar and co-authors compare two hands-on treatments for hidden trigger points in the calf in a 2026 trial. The rivals are a massage gun and therapist-applied myofascial release.

Sixty people with calf trigger points were split evenly between the two treatments. Each person had ten sessions over five days, twice a day, each followed by twenty minutes of ice. Pain, pressure tolerance, and ankle bend range were checked before and after. Both groups improved clearly on all three measures. The head-to-head results help clinics choose between a device and hands-on care for this common pain source.
pmc-13311597:
Nikki Turner and co-authors, in 2026, analyze a record study of respiratory illness visits in New Zealand primary care across the COVID-19 years. The team asked whether gaps by ethnicity and wealth widened through the crisis.

Natural language software sorted over ten million visits from 37 practices between 2018 and 2023. Respiratory visits made up 15.1 percent overall and peaked at 25.2 percent in 2022 in this dataset. Pacific peoples visited at higher rates than European patients before and during the pandemic, and their rates more than doubled at the peak. The study tracks how the load fell after the peak years.
pmc-13311697:
Karima Chaabna and co-authors build an evidence gap map on falls among older adults across North Africa and the Middle East in a 2026 article. Falls rank among the top causes of injury and death in old age.

Searches through November 2025 gathered studies on fall rates, risk, fear of falling, stated causes, and after-effects in people aged 60 and over. The map includes 203 primary studies covering 424,112 older adults. Poor countries barely appear, with a single national survey from Sudan and one study from Yemen. The map shows where research clusters and where policy must fly blind.
pmc-13311797:
Jie Hu and colleagues present a 2026 study linking broken body clocks in spinal discs to disc wear, and testing a melatonin gel that copies the hormone's nightly rhythm. Disc wear is a top cause of low back pain.

United Kingdom Biobank data on 287,150 people, gene-based causal tests, and tissue from mice, rats, and humans all pointed the same way: clock proteins run low in worn discs. The gel, placed in worn rat discs, raised clock protein levels, restored rhythm, and rebuilt disc matrix. Cyclic melatonin delivery emerges as a candidate therapy for disc wear.
pmc-13311997:
Jianhua Hu and colleagues offer a 2026 study on PYCR1, a protein they call a new driver of osteosarcoma, the most common bone cancer in children and teens. Cell and animal tests back the claim.

Turning PYCR1 down triggered ferroptosis, an iron-driven cell death, in the cancer cells. The protein works with the matrix protein COL1A1 and under the PI3K-Akt pathway to push growth, movement, and invasion. Blocking that pathway changed the death response in the HOS cell model. The findings open a fresh angle on a cancer where treatment gains have stalled for decades.
pmc-13312997:
Rui Zhang and co-authors test, in a 2026 retrospective case-control study, whether bowel trouble that precedes diagnosis is tied to anal fistula, a tunnel infection near the anus. Clinicians had long suspected it follows chronic diarrhea or constipation in some patients. Systematic evidence for the hunch was missing, so the team compared newly diagnosed patients with matched peers.

The study paired 251 patients diagnosed between July 2024 and July 2025 with 251 controls of the same age and sex, reviewing bowel function in the year before diagnosis. Pre-existing bowel dysfunction in general raised the odds of fistula, and diarrhea specifically carried an odds ratio near 2.2 in the reported analysis, while constipation showed no significant link. Smoking, drinking, sedentary or standing work, and higher body mass also tracked with the disease. Diarrhea's effect shifted modestly across fistula types.
pmc-13313197:
Shujing Li and colleagues ask in a 2026 study why one drug-proof strain of Klebsiella pneumoniae sickens people in odd ways. The ST11-K64 clone merges high virulence with carbapenem resistance, yet it shows up in lung samples and not in the liver abscesses that mark the classic virulent form.

Among 847 clinical samples of the bacterium, 157 were classed as highly virulent and drug resistant, a share of 18.5 percent that the authors state in the text. Five ST11-K64 samples were picked for deep tests of traits and mechanisms. In mice the clone killed far less than the classic ST23-K1 strain, despite its spread and drug resistance. That weaker killing power helps explain its distinct pattern in patients, and warns that labels based on genes alone can mislead care.
pmc-13313497:
Erin M Dickey and co-workers report in 2026 that blocking a protein called IL1RAP may crack the drug resistance of pancreatic cancer. This cancer shrugs off both chemotherapy and immune therapy, in large part because its surroundings are packed with suppressive immune and support cells.

Signals from the IL-1 family of messengers all pass through IL1RAP, and high levels of it track with poor outlook, as the authors note. Their work shows that myeloid and stromal cell networks rich in IL1RAP hold back treatment. Blocking IL1RAP reshaped the tumor setting, cut myeloid suppression, and brought back memory-like CD8 T cells. With that brake lifted, combined chemo and immune therapy worked better. The finding names a target that could widen the reach of care for a cancer with few options.
pmc-13313897:
Bader Khatlan Hameed, Mahmood Nawfal Mustafa, and Shaymaa Abdalkader Mahdy examine, in a 2026 histology study from Tikrit University, what the chemotherapy drug methotrexate does to rat salivary glands. The drug saves lives across many cancers but damages tissues. The glands that keep the mouth wet are plausible collateral targets. Albino rats received either saline or a therapeutic methotrexate dose between October and December 2023. Their submandibular glands were then removed and examined microscopically.

Treated glands showed tissue alterations compared with controls. The authors read the changes as cytotoxic injury to the gland. Such damage offers a mechanism for the dry mouth and oral complications that trouble patients on this drug. The team recommends follow-up work with stains to pin down the cellular changes. pmc-13314297:

pmc-13314497:

Regression models weighed what drives local government action. Awareness counted for more than taking part, the results show, though both linked to stronger government-led preservation work. pmc-13314797:

pmc-13315197:

Sequencing of the 16S rRNA gene showed greater variety of microbes in cecal contents and shifts in which bacterial genera were present, both in contents and in the gut lining.
pmc-13315897:

The paired data can support studies of active travel and city design across climates.
pmc-13315997:

pmc-13316197:

Patients showed slower saccade starts, weaker vergence, and poor smooth tracking, often tracking disease severity, and several faults appeared early, before clear motor signs. pmc-13317197:
Luiz Jupiter Carneiro de Souza leads a 2026 protocol for a scoping review on using public health databases to spot autism earlier. Late diagnosis harms development and raises system costs, yet routine records may hold early clues that services overlook.

Two reviewers will screen and extract data independently, then group studies by likeness. Only primary studies using public databases for early detection qualify. pmc-13317697:
Divyesh Cirikonda and colleagues review, in 2026, ways to turn hydrogen sulfide, a toxic gas, into valuable hydrogen. Methods covered include heating alone, heat with catalysts, light-driven and electricity-driven catalysis, and plasma-assisted splitting. Each route differs in energy demand, cost and readiness for market use. The review weighs those practical factors alongside laboratory progress. The authors close with the main technical barriers and research directions that could make waste gas a genuine source of clean hydrogen.
pmc-13317897:
Carola M Bregenzer and colleagues tell, in a 2026 case report, of an 80-year-old man whose supposed parathyroid adenoma proved to be a hidden cancer. The benign-looking gland growth had already spread. His blood calcium was high, and a choline PET scan pointed to one gland.

pmc-13318297:
Gulam Bahadur and a team of co-authors asked how to lift birth rates from a fertility treatment in older women. Their study, from twenty twenty-six, deals with intrauterine insemination for women over thirty-five. Some cases defy plain cause; others rest on male factors. They tested if a back to back double sample boosts sperm counts and births. They also checked how follicle counts and sperm thresholds shape results.

The record covered five hundred ninety-six cycles in two hundred sixty-three women from twenty ten to twenty nineteen. One group used the double sample plan; the rest used the standard plan. Readers who treat infertility get facts on a low cost tweak before more harsh steps like IVF.
pmc-13318797:

Selected genes changed activity under salt, drought, heat, and cold treatments. The authors offer the catalogue as a base for breeding hardier rape varieties.
pmc-13318997:
Yasser Sedky and co-authors present a 2026 retrospective study of viral respiratory infections in hospitalised children in Saudi Arabia. pmc-13319497:
Parvaiz A Koul leads a sixteen-member expert panel that sets out, in 2026, a life course vaccination plan for India. National immunisation focuses mainly on children, leaving adults exposed to preventable disease, and the pandemic further disrupted routine services. Three target groups are defined: younger adults with long-term conditions, people aged sixty and over, and healthy younger adults. Recommended vaccines include tetanus-diphtheria-pertussis boosters, yearly influenza, pneumococcal and shingles vaccines, plus hepatitis and meningococcal vaccines for those at risk. The authors call for awareness campaigns, professional training and dedicated adult vaccination centres.
pmc-13319997:
Rui Yuan and co-authors build a skin cream that blocks harmful blue light in a 2026 study of a polymer and zinc mix. Blue light from sun and screens can age skin much like ultraviolet light, yet shop sunscreens block it poorly and older blockers suit skin badly. A chain like polymer was fitted with a grip unit that locks onto zinc ions to shift its light shield wider.

The mix shielded skin cells from blue light death, stress, and early aging in lab tests by keeping photo aging pathways calm. On mouse skin it caused little sting and low harm to liver and kidneys in the checks reported. Spread like a normal sunscreen, it stopped blue light skin damage and fills a gap in shop goods.
pmc-13320397:
Eman A Tawfik and co-authors give a hands on guide to nerve ultrasound of the shoulder nerve web in a 2026 review. The web that feeds the arm has a tangled path, yet sound scans can reach near all of its post knot course at the bedside. Paired with electric tests and magnetic scans, the method adds live, sharp views of nerve shape.

Typical scan signs are laid out for crush injury, outlet squeeze, sudden nerve swelling illness, immune nerve ills, and tumor spread. Core anatomy, step by step scan routes, and how to read size and texture signs come first, then per illness patterns and set scan plans. Proof grades for each use close the guide, which aims to lift daily clinic uptake.
pmc-13320697:
Praveen Barrodia and colleagues show in a 2026 study how fasting helps the small intestine heal after damage. Fasting reshapes gut germs, yet how those shifts aid recovery was poorly understood. The team traced a chain from one helpful germ to gene control inside gut cells in mice.

Fasting raised levels of the germ Akkermansia muciniphila, which makes a compound called propionate. The chain suggests diet or germ based treatments could ease gut side effects of cancer radiation therapy.
pmc-13320997:
Arathi Shenoy and colleagues compare mouth germs and drug resistance genes in a 2026 study of severe gum disease with and without type 2 diabetes. Diabetes weakens defence against infection and may foster resistance, while gum disease and diabetes each worsen the other. The team studied 68 patients, half with diabetes and half without.

Plaque from under the gum line was tested for the red complex germ group and for two resistance genes, blaTEM and nim. Gum pocket depth and attachment loss were worse in patients with diabetes. The nim gene appeared only in the diabetes group, in 26.5 percent of them, while blaTEM rates matched across groups. Germ detection itself did not differ clearly.
pmc-13321497:

The team mapped where each gene sits, how the genes relate to each other, and which switch on in cold weather. They also checked gene activity in 11 plant lines with strong or weak cold tolerance. The work names key genes that may help breeders grow hardier stock for cold regions and large-scale farms in the near future.
pmc-13321897:

The most common backup regimen combined tenofovir, emtricitabine, and atazanavir with ritonavir. No patient trait or clinic factor explained the delays, and the authors call the gap a shortfall against the recommended timeline.
pmc-13322197:

pmc-13322397:
Justine Chan and colleagues review national heart attack registries in rich countries in a 2026 scoping review. Main outcomes were death and major heart events in hospital and at 30 days or one year, drawn mostly from discharge and administrative records. Shared aims sit beside wide design variety.
pmc-13323497:

They also measured the gap from cricoid to the airway split. Regression then found which clinical factors predicted those sizes. Age, prematurity and growth measures all played a part. Two models resulted, aimed at personal tube size and depth choices.
pmc-13324497:

pmc-13324697:

pmc-13325597:

pmc-13325797:

Surveys covered drinking, resilience, childhood adversity, and body weight.

pmc-13326397:

pmc-13327397:

pmc-13327597:

pmc-13327897:

pmc-13328097:

pmc-13328497:

pmc-13328897:

pmc-13329797:

pmc-13329897:

pmc-13329997:

pmc-13333097:

pmc-13333597:

pmc-13333697:

The post group beat both other groups on every measure, including jump height, 10 and 30 meter sprints, leg power, and VO2max, with large effect sizes throughout. pmc-13334397:

pmc-13334697:

pmc-13336597:

pmc-13336897:

pmc-13337097:

pmc-13337397:

pmc-13337497:
