pmc-13337697:
Ce Gou and co-authors review treatments for oral lichen planus in a 2026 article. The condition causes long-lasting mouth inflammation with pain and burning, and it tends to return. Its causes are mixed, so no single clear treatment path exists.

Drawing on 46 articles from 2020 to 2025, the review covers drug options first. Those include steroids, calcineurin blockers, hydroxychloroquine, hyaluronic acid, and mTOR blockers. It also covers non-drug options such as platelet concentrates from the patient's own blood and light-based therapy. The authors propose combined drug plans and alternatives, aiming to guide trials toward care fitted to each patient.
pmc-13337897:
Tingjie Liu and a large team survey health literacy in model healthy communities in a 2026 study. Residents of two such communities in Xiaoshan District, Hangzhou, were sampled at random. The question was whether community building links to stronger skills for finding and using health information.

A total of 263 residents answered, and the overall literacy rate reached 65.78 percent as reported. That rate sat above the local 2024 figure of 53.18 percent cited for comparison. Gains appeared for lifestyle, skills, and disease prevention areas, while first aid and basic care areas slipped. Marriage, chronic illness, age, and self-rated health each linked to literacy level.
pmc-13338197:
Nikolaos Gkantidis and four co-authors test if face shape ties to self-seen traits in young adults. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. Six hundred thirteen folks aged past twenty to mid thirties, of like purse and school ground, had 3D face shots and filled set trait forms the same day. Shape was told by more than one thousand points, and fits ran split by sex.

Self-worth tied to face shape in women but not in men. No other trait or mind mark tied to shape in a way that held. The team read the split as born of growth or world roots, and bound the claim to this folk set.
pmc-13340097:
Morgan De Kleine and colleagues lifted prenatal care in 2026 at Kijabe Hospital in Kenya, where death rates for mothers and babies rank among the world's highest. Most such deaths can be prevented by better prenatal care. A chart audit found large gaps at the first prenatal visit. The project aimed to lift good prenatal care for new patients to 75 percent within eight weeks.

Two tools drove four two week cycles of change. One was a standard intake form built from 32 World Health Organization and Kenya Ministry rules. The other was a risk calculator sorting patients into low, moderate, or high risk. Good care rose from 21 to 77 percent, and standard care scores rose from 42 to 83 percent. The cheap form can be adapted elsewhere, with birth outcome studies still needed.
pmc-13340197:
Maria Stefania Latrofa and colleagues test a dual Leishmania PCR assay across three machines in a 2026 study. Leishmania infantum causes dog and human disease widely, while a reptile-associated species now appears in mammals too. Samples came from sand flies, lizards, and dogs.

A portable chip device, a standard lab system, and droplet digital PCR each ran the same minicircle DNA assay. Detection limits and specificity were checked on cultures plus 120 sand fly guts, 29 lizards, and 101 dogs in the reported sample counts. Comparing platforms shows whether field-ready tools match lab accuracy for surveillance where both species overlap.
pmc-13340497:
Meral and colleagues check a Turkish tool that flags poor food intake risk in children with cancer. Poor intake can raise harm and slow care. The team ran the check in a children's cancer unit. They set it against two trusted checks. One was a scan tool for child cancer. One was a full hands-on review of each child. Close to half the children met the bar for poor nutrition.

The new tool matched both trusted checks well. At some cut points it caught all at-risk children. At others it missed some. Meral calls the tool simple and fit for daily use. More work should test how staff and families take to it.
pmc-13341497:
Where fat sits matters more than how much, argue Anke LiuLi and research partners in a 2026 review of adipose tissue distribution. Subcutaneous, visceral, brown, and beige depots differ in cell makeup, hormone output, and metabolic behavior, and fat lodged in organs adds further risk.

Visceral and ectopic fat track closely with insulin resistance, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease, while lower-body subcutaneous fat can act as a safer storage buffer. Patterning reflects genes, development, sex, age, diet, activity, sleep, and stress. Treatments differ too: lifestyle change and GLP-1 drugs trim visceral fat, thiazolidinediones repartition lipids, and cold-based approaches stir heat-producing fat.
pmc-13342397:
Salomé Abdellaoui and colleagues tracked Janus kinase drugs in 2026 in rheumatoid arthritis in routine care, with prescribing shifts after October 2022 safety warnings. The look back study at one centre took in all consecutive patients starting a first Janus kinase drug, tofacitinib, baricitinib, upadacitinib, or filgotinib, from April 2018 to November 2023.

Drug staying power by Kaplan Meier curves was the main endpoint. Disease scores at six and twelve months and reasons for stopping were secondary endpoints. Among 120 patients, 85 percent were women with mean age 57 and mean disease span 19 years. Pre versus post warning starters show how safety warnings reshaped prescribing.
pmc-13344097:
Yoram Wolf and co-authors link stomach acid drugs to trouble after tummy tuck surgery in a 2026 multi-institution cohort study. Proton pump inhibitors are common in patients with obesity, the group that most often seeks abdominoplasty. Their surgical risks in cosmetic care had gone unmeasured. The team mined a global records network.

After matching, 2,031 patients with a pre-surgery prescription faced 2,031 without any recorded use. Acid drug users suffered surgical-site infections at about two and a half times the rate, doubled wound opening risk, and needed opioids more often within 30 days. Gaps persisted at 60 and 90 days. The authors urge clearer guidance on managing these drugs around surgery.
pmc-13345797:
Chunru Chen and co-authors mapped in 2026 the research field on lymph node spread in ovarian cancer. Node spread is a key route by which this cancer grows. It shapes staging, treatment, and outlook. Despite rising clinical focus, no prior study had mapped how this field grew.

The team screened English papers from the Web of Science Core Collection from 2010 to mid-2025. They found 845 papers, with steady growth over time. Visual tools traced top themes, busy groups, and links between teams. The map shows where knowledge bunches, where gaps stay, and which paths look most hopeful. New researchers and funders gain a guide to a field that shapes survival.
pmc-13346597:
Dilek Yilmaz and colleagues tested in 2026 whether a Dutch decision aid improves shared decision making for patients facing implantable defibrillator implantation or replacement. The choice is nuanced, balancing protection from sudden death against device risks, lifestyle effects, and personal values.

Across six Dutch hospitals between early 2018 and late 2019, a stepped-wedge randomised trial rolled the aid out in stages, adding it to standard care. Patients and clinicians rated shared decision making with validated questionnaires, while decisional conflict scores captured whether choices felt settled. The trial asks whether a structured aid can make a high-stakes cardiac decision feel clearer, fairer, and more truly shared.
pmc-13346697:
Pallavi Kakade and co-authors map, in a 2026 study, how a common gut fungus is kept in check by its host. The fungus, Candida albicans, lives in many human guts without causing harm. What holds its numbers down was not well understood. The team placed the fungus in germ-free mice and read which gut genes switched on.

Two genes, Duox2 and Duoxa2, which encode a dual oxidase enzyme, rose in the ileum and colon. That rise needed both candidalysin, a toxin the fungus secretes, and host signaling through the IL-17 receptor. Gut tissue grown in dishes showed the same rise, plus production of hydrogen peroxide. Mice that lacked IL-17 signaling let the fungus spread more. Mice that lacked DUOX2 activity held less of it. The authors name this IL-17-DUOX2 axis as a key control on gut colonization by the fungus.
pmc-13346897:
Benjamin Ecclestone and four co-authors present a new microscope method in this twenty twenty-six paper. Doctors read tissue samples to find disease, but staining can be slow and the tags used may miss some molecules. Their method watches how tissue takes in light, with no labels at all.

When a molecule absorbs light, it sheds the energy as glow, heat, or sound. This microscope catches all three at once, giving a fuller fingerprint of what is in the sample. The team showed it on human skin and mouse brain with two colors of laser light. Richer label-free images could speed up disease checks.
pmc-13346997:
Xuan Zhang and Dongdong Guo build an explainable machine learning framework that maps flood susceptibility across the coastal city of Yancheng. Their study appeared in two thousand twenty-six. Low, flat coastal cities flood more as the climate warms and pavement spreads. Planners need maps that say not just where, but why.

Three models learned from nearly five hundred historical flood points and ten landscape factors. A gradient boosting model won on accuracy and discrimination. Explanation analysis crowned wetness index, elevation, and impervious surface as the top drivers. Different districts flooded for different reasons, from sealed urban ground to low tidal flats. About a fifth of the area rated high or very high risk. One district topped the list at over a third. The framework hands each district its own control strategy.
pmc-13348097:
Tanika Dutta, Malabika Talukdar, Sulochana Singh, and Siddhartha Panda study mixtures of vitamin C and caffeine in water in a 2026 chemistry paper. The two compounds are often combined in health and drug products, so how they interact in solution matters for product quality. The team varied amounts of each and measured thickness, light absorption, and heat related traits.

Their results show the dissolved pair interact mainly with the water around them, building stronger hydration shells. Flow thickness rose as concentration rose, and association between molecules strengthened across all mixtures tested. Light spectra shifted in several ways that signal changed molecular surroundings. The work gives formulators a clearer picture of how this common pairing behaves.
pmc-13348197:
Sbongile C. Jiane and colleagues explored in 2026 why men on antiretroviral treatment in Govan Mbeki, Mpumalanga, drop out of care. Staying on treatment is essential for viral suppression and for preventing HIV transmission, yet men in sub-Saharan Africa drop out of follow-up at higher rates.

Interviewing 21 men lost to follow-up at three primary health clinics between May and July 2024, the team used in-depth, semi-structured interviews analysed thematically to capture perceptions, experiences, and barriers. Work demands, clinic experiences, stigma, and side effects emerged as recurring themes. The findings point to male-friendly clinic hours, respectful care, and community support as levers for keeping men in treatment.
pmc-13349997:
Ying Zhang and co-authors probed in 2026 links between muscle and metabolic markers in metabolic syndrome, using photon-counting CT. This newer scan method measures muscle amount and quality with care. Metabolic syndrome shifts body build. Yet how muscle traits link to blood markers remains incompletely grasped.

Among 117 people, 38 with metabolic syndrome and 79 healthy controls, belly CT at the third lumbar level measured muscle area, density, and index. Fasting glucose, glycated haemoglobin, and lipids were also taken. Correlation and regression maths, with interaction tests, mapped which muscle traits track with metabolic upset. The findings may turn routine CT muscle measures into early warnings for metabolic risk and targets for exercise and food plans.
pmc-13351697:
Liping He and Manli Zhuang review risk factors and prediction tools for kidney injury around surgery in children, in 2026. The injury affects 5 to 30 percent of children, and up to 40 percent of newborns after heart surgery. It raises the risk of death and lasting kidney disease, so early warning matters.

Four databases were searched to March 2024 for studies in patients aged 18 years or younger. Key risks include young age, congenital heart disease, kidney-harming drugs, and bypass surgery. Models range from standard statistics to machine learning with newer markers in blood and urine. The authors note a clear gap: few models are properly tested in children.
pmc-13351897:
Xavier Vaillo leads a 2026 registry study comparing drug treatment before surgery for stage III non-small cell lung cancer. Patients in the Spanish thoracic surgery registry had either chemotherapy alone or chemotherapy plus immune therapy, then anatomical lung removal, from January 2023 to April 2025. The full group held 114 patients, with 77 in the combined group.

After matching, 68 patients remained in 34 pairs. Full tumour clearance was higher with combined treatment, at 38 percent versus 12 percent. Downstaging and complete removal also favoured the combined group, though surgery took longer, at 240 versus 180 minutes at the median. Safety and complications around surgery were compared alongside cancer outcomes.
pmc-13352397:
Minkyeong Kim and colleagues use machine learning in 2026 to find what drives sarcopenia in Parkinson disease. Muscle loss and weak function are more common in Parkinson disease and link to worse outcomes. Clinical data were split into training and held-out groups in a 70 to 30 ratio, then screened before a shrinkage method picked six key predictors.

A logistic model built on those predictors gave an area under the curve of 0.793 on held-out data. Patients with sarcopenia had longer illness, higher disease stages, and heavier non-motor burden. Body mass index, body fat share, and non-motor traits such as thinking decline, autonomic problems, fatigue, and low mood weighed most. The authors stress non-motor care in muscle health.
pmc-13354197:
Sanjay Basu leads a 2026 transfer learning test of Medicaid risk prediction models across states. Models trained in one state face shifted populations, policies, and care patterns in another. Acute care use was predicted for high-risk care management enrollees in Washington, with 20,744 people, and Virginia, with 28,901 people. Outcome rates differed sharply, at 9.4 percent in Washington versus 25.6 percent in the Virginia group.

Nine approaches were compared, from plain logistic models to neural and ensemble methods. A meta-ensemble scored best on Virginia data, with discrimination of 0.728 and the best calibration of any method tested. Plain source transfer nearly matched it, at 0.725 on the same held-out Virginia data set. Target-only logistic lagged far behind, at 0.628 in the same head-to-head comparison test. Recalibration helped all models, and fairness gaps shrank with target adaptation though disparities persisted.
pmc-13354797:
Pavithra Venkataraman and Christian R Landry review in 2026 how gene changes that alter proteins interact with gene changes that alter how much protein is made. Either kind of change alone can shift fitness, but their joint effect is often a surprise. The review pulls most of its examples from studies in single-celled organisms.

Too little or too much of a protein can both cause harm, so the effect of a protein change depends on how much of it the cell makes. The authors sketch a way to join amount and action in one fitness picture. They argue this view helps explain adaptation, disease, and why the same change can help in one strain and hurt in another.
pmc-13354997:
Eleftherios K Soleas and co-authors ran a 2025 national consensus study in Canada to define what counts as scholarship in continuing professional development for doctors. Accreditation rules require such work from each office, yet no shared list said which outputs qualify. A panel from across the country took part in a three-phase Delphi process.

Twenty-nine panel members finished all phases and endorsed 18 of 31 types of work put to them. Newer forms gained backing, among them community engagement, pilot testing work, and advocacy scholarship. The authors say the shared definition can guide accreditation and promotion, and should be revisited as scholarly work keeps changing.
pmc-13355597:
Shangqing Huang and co-authors design a hydrogel dressing for diabetic wounds in a 2026 paper. Such wounds suffer low oxygen, lasting inflammation, and poor vessel growth. Standard oxygen dressings release gas unevenly and lack other functions.

Their gel carries nanoparticles that make their own oxygen in a steady way. A mineral shell steadies the oxygen source, and a nanozyme helps the release stay efficient. Plant polyphenols calm the wound setting, and released zinc and manganese ions fight bacteria. The gel sticks well to tissue for long wear. The authors aim to rebuild a wound setting that supports healing.
pmc-13356797:
Francesco Paolo Prete and others tested human factors in safe hand-off of cold light during laparoscopic gallbladder removal, in 2026. Xenon light chains used in laparoscopy can generate extreme heat, risking patient burns and fire. Human factors in how surgeons handle the light source had received little research notice.

The study studied errors and work factors that could compromise safety when delivering light to the endoscope during planned cholecystectomy. Workflow, handling, and equipment links were tested for hazards. Op teams gain useful guidance for preventing a rare but serious burn and fire risk in routine laparoscopy.
pmc-13356897:
Rebecca J Rockett and co-authors sequenced respiratory viruses in 2026 from Australia's first big post-Covid winter flu season, in 2022. One test panel read flu and other viruses at once from patient samples. The team recovered full flu genomes from three-quarters of confirmed flu samples and also found nineteen genomes of other viruses in co-infected samples.

The co-infections included RSV, the Covid virus, and several cold viruses, and their timing matched national trends. In most mixed infections, one virus far outnumbered the other. The H3N2 flu type dominated, with a smaller H1N1 share all winter. The authors show how multi-virus sequencing can track overlapping epidemics in real time.
pmc-13358497:
Lin Chen and Yufu Ye wrote a 2026 commentary on spleen-saving surgery for tumors in the tail of the pancreas. Keeping the spleen helps the immune system, but the classic methods force a trade-off: one is hard to do, the other often starves the spleen of blood. The authors discuss a newer twist on the method.

The newer approach keeps the splenic artery but gives up the splenic vein. In the study they discuss, spleen damage and swollen stomach veins dropped sharply compared with the older method. Chen and Ye weigh the gains, the proof so far, and the open questions, such as which patients suit the method best.
pmc-13358797:
Han Ma and co-authors study whether heartburn drugs affect outcomes for lung cancer patients on immune therapy in a 2026 paper. Immune checkpoint drugs are now a main treatment for advanced non-small cell lung cancer. Proton pump inhibitors, widely used for acid reflux, might blunt their effect, but evidence was mixed.

The team reviewed records of more than two hundred patients treated in 2023 at one center. More than half used the acid drugs around treatment time. Among patients on immune therapy alone, drug use linked to shorter time before the cancer grew and shorter survival. The link held after statistical adjustment, and even very brief use showed it. With chemotherapy added, the effect faded. The authors see a treatment-dependent pattern, not a uniform harm.
pmc-13358997:
Hunter Scott reviews treatments for fatigue in sarcoidosis in a 2026 paper. Tiredness strikes between 30 and 90 percent of patients with this inflammatory disease and can linger even when scans improve. Past reviews covered only some drugs and skipped non-drug and newer options. Scott set out to gather the whole field and grade the strength of the proof.

Drawing on trials and guidelines from the last decade, the review covers disease drugs, stimulants, exercise, and coaching approaches. Some standard drugs ease inflammation yet worsen tiredness over time. The paper also explains how to rule out other causes of fatigue first, so treatment aims at the right target.
pmc-13360297:
Aya A Eltaibany led a 2026 lab study that built a tiny 3D model of the human blood-brain barrier. This barrier is the tight wall of cells that guards the brain from germs and toxins. The team grew organoids, small self-built balls of mixed brain cells, to copy that wall. They then stressed the models with inflammation signals and with a stop-and-restart of oxygen and sugar.

Both stresses made the barrier leakier and weakened the genes that seal cell joints. Immune cells crossed into the organoids in larger numbers under both kinds of stress. Drugs that block the sticky molecules immune cells use to cross cut that movement back down. The model gives drug makers a human-like test bed for studying brain swelling, stroke harm, and new treatments.
pmc-13361397:
Sarah Rebeca Teixeira de Sousa and co-authors present the plan for a 2026 trial on thinking skills in women with breast cancer. Cancer treatment often dulls memory, attention, and planning, hurting daily life and mood. The trial tests ALMA, a playful program of attention and memory training. It will run at one hospital complex in Salamanca, Spain, with 63 women in active treatment.

The women will be split by chance into three groups. One gets health education, one gets standard solo brain training, and one gets the full ALMA group program. Sessions are face to face and last two hours. As a protocol, the paper sets out the design before results exist. It gives other teams a clear template for testing ways to protect the mind during cancer care.
pmc-13362397:
Fatma Al-Zahraa Sayed and a large team report a 2026 rat study on tiny selenium particles coated with EGCG, a green tea compound. Rats fed a high-fat diet gained blood fat problems, liver harm, and heart stress marks. The team tested the new particles against plain EGCG, plain selenium, and a standard lipid drug in 42 rats split into six groups.

The coated particles gave the best overall gains: better blood fats, lower liver and heart harm marks, and stronger defenses against cell damage. Swelling signals fell and liver tissue looked healthier. The work is early and in rats, but it backs more tests of tea-based nano treatments for fatty liver harm.
pmc-13363497:
Zilong Tang and colleagues report a 2026 chemistry study on a new set of benzamide compounds tested against crop fungi. Fungal diseases cut harvests worldwide, and older fungicides are losing ground to resistance. The team built a series of 2-acyloxybenzamides, confirmed their structures with standard spectra, and screened them on several plant pathogens in the lab.

One compound wiped out the rice blast fungus fully in the screen, and another strongly held back a Phytophthora species. Dose tests set the strength of both leads. Computer docking pointed to an enzyme in the fungi's melanin pathway as the likely target, a path that neither plants nor animals carry, which hints at safe selectivity. Field and safety tests remain ahead.
pmc-13364097:
Liang Zong, Yun Cheng, and Yi Yao present a 2026 study on congestion control for networks that join satellites, drones, and ground links into one path. Satellite hops add long delays and many bit errors, while drone hops shift shape constantly, so classic control mistakes channel errors for true congestion and throttles needlessly. Their scheme tunes the opening data push for slow-start and adds a sharp test that tells error losses from queue overflow losses.

Simulations showed shorter queues at drone nodes, faster delivery across multi-hop ends, and higher throughput in high-delay setups than with standard control. The authors offer the design as groundwork for the space-air-ground networks planned for sixth-generation mobile service.
pmc-13368397:
Cristian Hardaman and others asked whether seizures causes amygdalar growth or follows from it, in 2026. The amygdala is central to the limbic system, and size gaps were long linked to mental illnesses. In seizures, amygdala growth has been told of mainly on scans, yet its medical, brain-wave, and tissue pattern was unstudied.

Reading issued papers and the authors' experience, the work argues that growth reflects a defined pattern beyond imaging, with characteristic medical and brain-wave traits that respond to given care. The review reframes growth as a medical entity, not only a scan finding. Epileptologists gain a fuller picture for recognising and treating this distinctive presentation.
pmc-13371197:
Mario Saia and colleagues track malpractice claims linked to hospital-acquired infections in Italy's Veneto region in a 2026 study. Such infections raise illness, death, and costs, and severe cases can lead to claims over failed prevention or care. Claims from 2010 to 2024 in the regional error monitoring system were classed by outcome, infection site, and care setting.

Of 19,380 malpractice claims over fifteen years, 1,106 concerned hospital-acquired infections. Overall claims fell over time, yet infection claims rose in both number and share. Most infection claims involved non-fatal harm, while a smaller share involved death. The trend warns hospitals and insurers that infection prevention is also a legal risk, and it points to where stronger controls could cut both harm and claims.
pmc-13372197:
Nnaemeka H Ugwuchukwu reports a grave immune flare in a 2026 case report. A woman with a rare, fast type of breast cancer got a drug that frees the immune system to fight tumors. She came in with fever and low blood counts, and was first treated as if she had a blood germ.

Germ care did not help, so the team checked for an immune storm that eats blood cells. Lab and tissue tests fit that rare ill, with five of the set signs met. High-dose steroid drugs calmed the storm. The case warns teams that new cancer drugs can spark this storm, which looks much like a plain infection.
pmc-13373797:
José Luis Coyac-Rodríguez and colleagues map the genetics of leaf vein density in maize in a 2026 study. Dense leaf veins help plants move water and sustain photosynthesis, and flowering plants, especially C4 species, evolved denser veins than early land plants. Using native Mexican maize varieties adapted to varied climates, the team tracked vein traits and photosynthetic rates.

Higher vein density tracked with higher photosynthesis, but only for small intermediate veins. Varieties from drier places raised vein density sharply in heat, suggesting a role in water efficiency. Twelve genetic regions linked to vein patterning were found. The work gives breeders genetic handles for maize that photosynthesises well while using water wisely in hot, dry conditions.
pmc-13375697:
Alan Calder and colleagues test whether a harmless mouth bacterium uses a secretion weapon to compete with neighbours in a 2026 study. Neisseria subflava, a commensal, carries a Type VI secretion system, a molecular syringe that injects toxins into rivals. The team knocked out the core gene TssM in strain KU1003-01 and ran competition assays against gonorrhoea bacteria, a second subflava strain, and the yeast Candida albicans.

Recoverable target cells differed clearly between the parent strain and the knockout, showing that the secretion system contributes to competition with all three targets. The work establishes that even a non-pathogenic Neisseria wields a functional weapon, shaping which microbes share its niche. That insight matters for understanding how commensals hold ground against pathogens.
pmc-13377397:
Puteri Nur Athirah Megat Mohamad Aminuddin and co-authors tell of brain TB with a nerve palsy in a 2026 case report. A man aged 22 from Bangladesh had fever, head pain, mind shifts, and a droop of one eye with a wide pupil. Scans showed fluid on the brain and small dead zones.

Spinal fluid held high protein but plain sugar, and all germ tests came back blank. The team still called it brain TB, on tale, scans, and risk, and began germ drugs plus high steroids. His signs got much better on drugs alone, with no need for a brain drain. The case backs bold calls when tests lag.
pmc-13377697:
Jia-chun Tao and colleagues survey neuromuscular reversal and monitoring practice among anaesthesiologists in China in a 2026 study. Residual muscle blockade after surgery raises lung complications, yet monitoring and reversal use were poorly mapped. An online questionnaire with 25 questions, distributed through an anaesthesia forum and WeChat for 30 days with one response per IP address, yielded 3,168 valid responses.

Rocuronium and cisatracurium were the most used blockers. Only about 40 percent routinely gave reversal drugs, mostly neostigmine, with sugammadex used by only about 19 percent. Quantitative monitoring was routine for only 1.6 percent, while 98 percent relied on clinical signs alone. Higher education and senior rank predicted better practice. The survey exposes a wide gap between guidelines and routine practice.
pmc-13379397:
Gokulkumar Sivanantham and co-authors describe a 2026 study turning jackfruit seed peel, a waste material, into a useful plant-based filler. The peel comes from the fruit of Artocarpus heterophyllus. The team extracted microcrystalline cellulose, a fine powder widely used in medicines and materials, from that peel.

Extraction used alkali treatment, acid breakdown, and bleaching to strip away lignin and other plant parts. A battery of tests then checked the product's structure, purity, heat stability, and particle size. The cellulose proved highly ordered in structure, with a crystallinity measure above seventy percent in the results reported. The work suggests farm waste can supply a renewable filler for greener materials.
pmc-13380797:
Huanchang Yan and a large team present a 2026 analysis of a giant cluster in an HIV transmission network in Guangzhou, China. Large clusters hold a large share of people living with HIV, but their size makes targeted action hard. The team developed a way to split a giant cluster into smaller communities for precise intervention.

Using network data from 2008 to 2020, they split one component of 681 members into 34 communities with dense links inside and few outside. Every link between communities ran through central members of one community, which family-tree analysis identified as the likely source of the whole component. People with similar traits tended to cluster, flagging possible outbreak pockets.
pmc-13381997:
Eusebi Chiner and colleagues wrote a 2026 review of how older patients stick with airway pressure treatment for sleep apnea, where the airway collapses repeatedly during sleep. The condition becomes much more common with age. The standard treatment blows air gently to keep the airway open, but only works if patients keep using it.

Good use is usually defined as at least four hours on most nights, with best results at six to eight hours. Many patients stop early, and long-term abandonment is common. Among older adults who start, though, use can match or beat younger patients. The review describes a pattern where use rises into the late seventies and then falls, and discusses the barriers involved.
pmc-13382697:
Genevieve Crotty and Wasim Awal describe a 2026 case of a dangerous bulge in a stomach artery treated by injecting clotting agent through the skin, guided by scans. Such pseudoaneurysms are a rare complication of long-standing pancreas inflammation, where digestive juices erode nearby artery walls. Their patient was a man of 65 with chronic pancreatitis.

The usual treatment threads a catheter through the arteries to block the bulge, but his vessel layout made that unsafe. Instead, doctors injected thrombin directly through the skin under scan guidance. The bulge clotted and resolved on follow-up imaging. The case offers an alternative route when standard access fails, with imaging central throughout.
pmc-13383197:
Fangman Chen's team built a nanozyme whose power switches on under sound waves for precise cancer therapy, in a 2026 study. Natural force-sensitive enzymes tune cell chemistry under force, but artificial nanozymes with strict time and place control were rare. The team embedded force-responsive ferrocene units in a flexible frame to create the MRNZ device.

Acoustic shear reshaped the units, lowering electron density and steric crowding at iron sites and boosting peroxide-like activity. Controlled low-dose oxygen signals then acted as messengers to rewire cell chemistry and toughen stem cells against oxidative stress. Loading glucose oxidase inside hollow MRNZ added a second enzyme layer, pointing toward sound-triggered paired therapy.
pmc-13386797:
Zhongnan Xiao's team tested AI-based retinal screening in teachers and a retinal density marker for myopia, in a 2026 prospective study. AI fundus imaging enables large-scale retinal screening, but use in worker groups was limited. The team screened 648 Beijing teachers with fundus photography and systemic exams, using AI to quantify fundus tessellated density and other retinal measures, then testing links with refractive error and work factors.

Mean refractive error sat near minus two and a half diopters. Density varied across the macula, highest in the nasal quadrant. Density, near work at 30 centimeters, and eye structure measures each linked independently with refractive error. Near work beyond one hour at 30 centimeters tracked with higher density. Density showed moderate power to flag high myopia, at about 78 percent area under the curve, and linked with immune-inflammatory indices. The marker is observational and needs longitudinal validation.
pmc-13388097:
Ashton Bailey, Ryan Gibson, and Kristine Griffett review clock-receptor drugs against inflammatory brain disease in dogs in a 2026 article. Meningoencephalitis of unknown origin is a presumed autoimmune condition and a major treatment challenge in veterinary neurology. Evidence ties helper T cells of the TH17 type and their messenger IL-17A to the inflammation.

Compounds that activate REV-ERB receptors suppressed TH17 growth and eased disease in autoimmune models, with favorable safety signs. Those receptors also steer circadian rhythm and metabolism, widening their immune footprint. The authors map a path for testing such drugs as add-ons to standard immune suppression in dogs.
pmc-13389897:
Hatem Mousa Taha and Khaled Hatem Taha present, in 2026, a 63-year-old Palestinian man with Morvan syndrome whose blood tests stayed negative for the usual antibodies. He showed the full pattern of the disease: constant muscle twitching, extreme sleeplessness, fast heart rate, heavy sweating, and major weight loss.

Muscle recordings across twelve muscles showed the characteristic rapid discharges of this condition, while brain imaging, spinal fluid tests, and cancer screening found nothing. Validated tests confirmed no CASPR2 or LGI1 antibodies in blood or spinal fluid. Working in a resource-limited setting, the team built the diagnosis from the clinical pattern and electrical proof. Neurologists gain a worked example of treating a rare autoimmune condition without antibody confirmation.
pmc-13390197:

pmc-13391697:

pmc-13396197:

pmc-13396997:

pmc-13397097:

pmc-13397597:

pmc-13397897:

pmc-13398497:

pmc-13398697:

pmc-13399297:

pmc-13403897:

pmc-13405397:

pmc-13406497:

pmc-13407597:
