pmc-13408197:
Jordane Goulas and co-authors examine in 2026 how a damage-tolerant DNA-copying enzyme gets switched into its most active form. The enzyme, polymerase zeta, copies across lesions that stall normal replication, and its main subunit is unusually large in vertebrates. Earlier work showed a cellular protease cuts that subunit in two.

The cut pieces stay together as a paired complex with stronger copying activity, gather on chromatin, and attach to newly made DNA under replication stress. Blocking the cut weakened the enzyme, lowered drug-induced mutation, and pushed cells toward a different repair route using homologous recombination. Readers gain a structural explanation for why vertebrates evolved the cut, plus a clearer map of a pathway that shapes mutation in cancer and chemotherapy response.
pmc-13408597:
Ina Stelzer and a large international team show in 2026 that a mother's immune system can drift off course weeks to months before a spontaneous preterm birth. Most early births arrive without warning signs, so a blood signal that precedes them could change prenatal care. Their study nested cases within a low-risk population pregnancy cohort, comparing mothers who delivered early with those who delivered at term.

The early-birth group showed measurably abnormal immune adaptation, strong enough to separate cases from controls moderately well. Early in pregnancy their immune cells over-responded to an adrenaline-like stimulus, and by the third trimester inflammatory cytokine production ran higher. Single-cell analysis of helper T cells found an inflammation-skewed, nerve-responsive profile. The dataset is offered as a resource for building early-warning tests and targeted prevention.
pmc-13408697:
Liang Shi, Boqiang Liu, and a large team report in 2026 a paradox: the immune system's first patrol against liver cancer can train the cancer to become worse. Natural killer cells are supposed to eliminate tumour cells early. Using immune-humanised models that track liver cancer across space and time, plus single-cell and gene-editing screens, the team watched what early surveillance actually does.

Rather than simply culling the tumour, killer cell pressure pushed cancer cells into new states. It reprogrammed their fat handling toward cholesterol build-up and deepened their stem-like character. Later adaptive immune attack was blunted at the same time. Blocking a checkpoint molecule while activating a liver lipid receptor together suppressed that evolution and made standard checkpoint therapy work better and longer. The authors pitch combined immune-metabolic treatment for advanced liver cancer.
pmc-13408797:
Erlend Lyngholm and team used neural nets to model proton relative biological effectiveness with no preset assumptions. Their 2026 work takes on medical proton therapy, which applies a flat effectiveness value of 1.1, despite lab proof that effectiveness shifts with dose, tissue, and energy. Past models embed assumed links, possibly missing real patterns.

From a database of 431 lab data points, the team modeled effectiveness at set survival fractions using linear energy transfer, tissue radiosensitivity, and photon dose inputs. Models with all three inputs did best, above all with photon doses at survival fractions of 0.1 and 0.2, suggesting a standard dose input in that range. The assumption-free route matched published models' links and predictive power, backing more nuanced proton planning while needing medical checks.
pmc-13409097:
Alice Milne and colleagues interview patients and carers inside a British trial in 2026 about living with fluid that cancer builds up around the lung. Malignant pleural effusion management is about drainage and symptom relief rather than cure, and two procedural strategies were being compared in the TACTIC trial. Thirty-two participants, patients alone, carers alone, or pairs together, gave twenty-two interviews about their care.

Satisfaction with management ran high overall, and neither strategy struck participants as more acceptable than the other. Four themes organised the deeper analysis, covering life with the condition beyond the trial, the procedures themselves, and the support surrounding them. Because breathlessness medicine succeeds or fails on daily comfort, the authors argue these voices should shape how services are organised, not merely decorate trial reports.
pmc-13410397:
Ting Cao and colleagues describe in 2026 a way the material around cells can steer them without ever touching them. That surrounding mesh, the extracellular matrix, gives cells support and signals, normally by direct contact. The team used a three-dimensional cavity setup to test influence at a distance.

They name the effect non-contact transspatial regulation. Its strength hinged on the gap between matrix and cells, shaped by both physical confinement and chemical signals passed across space. A cell eating process called macropinocytosis played the lead role in receiving those signals. Several pathways took part at once. The finding opens a fresh angle on how tissues shape cell behavior from afar.
pmc-13410797:
Kai Wang leads a team reporting in 2026 a gel for diabetic wounds that turns ultrasound into tiny electric signals. Diabetic wounds heal slowly amid lasting inflammation and poor nerve-immune teamwork. The injectable gel carries a nerve-active peptide and fine fibers that generate charge when pressed by sound waves.

In lab tests, sound-activated gel nudged immune cells toward their calming form and helped nerve fibers grow longer. Diabetic mice treated with gel plus ultrasound closed wounds faster, with more nerves, vessels, and better-arranged collagen. Gene checks pointed to cell energy systems as a shared driver. In rabbit ears, the treatment also softened thick scar growth, hinting at cleaner healing.
pmc-13411097:
Neda Sheikhzakaryaee and Golnaz Azami built a care model in 2026 for nurses who tend children with cancer and their spiritual distress. The paper argues that such distress shapes how children cope and stick with treatment, yet nurses often lack a shared, age-fitting way to respond across cultures.

Drawing on 227 sources and several classic care theories, the authors propose the Developmental-Spiritual Oncology Care Model, which pairs respect for a child's stage of growth with family and team work. Nurses and ward teams can use it to plan spiritual care that fits each child, rather than improvising case by case.
pmc-13411297:
Andre Braginets and co-authors test whether retinal layer thickness measured by eye scans predicts quiet progression in relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis. This progression independent of relapse activity, called PIRA, is hard to foresee. Their 2026 study uses optical coherence tomography, a scan that measures the nerve fibre and ganglion cell layers at the back of the eye.

The team followed 220 patients from Berlin and Munich cohorts who had been relapse-free for at least two years, excluding eyes with prior optic nerve inflammation. Sixty-five patients, 29.5 percent, developed PIRA over a median follow-up of about three years. In the full group and the Munich cohort, retinal measures did not predict progression. Only in Berlin did a thinner nerve fibre layer predict PIRA. The authors conclude eye scans do not predict risk in mixed populations, though they may help in early disease.
pmc-13411897:
Gökşen Polat and co-authors interview in 2026 Turkish adults with chronic diseases about living with disability and what they expect from disability services. Conditions from diabetes to heart disease can limit daily life long before any official label arrives. Twelve adults holding formal disability reports spoke in depth between mid-2024 and early 2025.

Half the group had type 1 diabetes, and half admitted limited awareness of the services meant for them. Three themes structured the accounts: disability's reach into daily life, patchy knowledge of services, and blocked access despite legal rights. Paper certification alone does not open doors, the authors conclude. Informational and structural barriers need direct attack if entitlements are to mean anything in practice.
pmc-13413197:
Allegra Battistoni and colleagues examine in 2026 how often women with breast cancer already show signs of a stiff-heart form of heart failure before cancer treatment begins. This form, HFpEF, keeps the heart's pumping fraction normal while filling suffers, and toxic cancer therapies can worsen it. The team scored 145 women at a baseline cardio-oncology visit with three validated probability tools, then rescored 89 of them about a year later.

Depending on the tool, between 14.8 and 41.5 percent of women landed in the middle-to-high probability band at baseline. The three scores agreed poorly with one another, especially a European tool against the other two. Scores barely moved over the year of follow-up. The authors warn the tools are not interchangeable here.
pmc-13414697:
Magdalena Stachnik, Monika Normant-Saremba, and Anna Kycko report a parasite record from the Baltic Sea in 2026. They examined fifteen adult Chinese mitten crabs collected from the Vistula Lagoon in the southern Baltic. Tissue checks used microscopy, histology, and DNA sequencing of both parasite and host.

The microsporidian Hepatospora eriocheir was confirmed in 60 percent of the crabs, in females and males alike. Infected liver-like tissue looked pale and fragile, with spores packed inside damaged tubules. Parasite sequences closely matched earlier finds from Britain and China. Host DNA showed three maternal lineages, linking the lagoon crabs to a wider North Sea invasion.
pmc-13415297:
Antonio Morais Neto and co-authors tackle a stubborn problem in laser based chemical sensing, in 2026: SERS signals vary too much between runs. Their test compounds were three halogen swapped uracil variants stuck to silver nanoparticles, paired with adenine to boost detection. Many experimental settings can shift the signal, so they screened variables first, then optimized.

After tuning, signal scatter fell one hundred fold for the fluorine compound, three hundred fold for bromine, and one thousand fold for chlorine. Fresh validation runs matched those low scatter levels closely. The two stage recipe should transfer to other sensing setups that need reliable numbers at very low concentrations.
pmc-13415397: Andrea Alogna and co-authors issued this correction in 2026 for their 2021 Molecules paper on liposomes carrying a snail mucus product. The notice is a correction only: it supplies a missing conflicts of interest statement. Three authors are named as founders of HelixPharma, which holds commercial interests in the product, while the remaining authors declare none. The statement adds that the company played no part in study design, data work, writing, or the choice to publish. The authors state the scientific conclusions stay unchanged, and the editor approved the update.
pmc-13415497:
Silvia Coutinho and colleagues mapped the move from child to adult care for youths with rare bone and mineral conditions in a 2026 scoping review. Better childhood care means more teens survive into adulthood, yet handoffs to adult services stay fragmented, with unclear paths and thin adult expertise.

Of 1706 records, only 34 qualified, mostly expert opinion from Europe and North America on brittle bone disease and phosphate-wasting rickets. Patients, parents, and clinicians all called for planned continuity, structured handoffs, and adult teams ready for these rare conditions, and for clinics building their first transition pathways.
pmc-13416697:
José Luis Granados-Soler, Michelle Majella Story, and Rachel Allavena review sun related skin cancer in dogs and cats in Australia, in a 2026 article. Strong ultraviolet light harms pets as well as people, especially animals with pale or thinly haired skin. Their focus is whether sunscreen made for pets is safe and useful.

Few studies exist, the authors find. Zinc oxide sunscreens seem unlikely to poison pets if heavy licking is prevented, while chemical filters remain poorly studied. Titanium dioxide may offer another option, though proof is thin. The review calls for urgent work under Australian conditions and helps vets weigh protection against ingestion risk.
pmc-13417097:
José Serrano-Guarinos and colleagues probe the spin behaviour of a molecular qubit built around a cerium ion, in a 2026 physics study. The molecule pairs cerium with two erbium ions and was proposed for a three qubit error correction code. To study cerium alone, the team swapped erbium for quiet lutetium atoms.

New molecules with a lutetium cerium lutetium core were made and checked for purity. Magnet measures and pulsed resonance tests in solid crystals then tracked how long the cerium spin holds its state. Diluting the qubit in a matching silent crystal made the tests cleaner. Ligand design around the core shaped coherence times.
pmc-13417297:
Sarah Suchaneck and colleagues link chemical structure to coherence times in molecular spin qubits, in a 2026 theoretical study. A qubit built from an electron spin in a molecule loses its quantum state quickly when nearby atomic nuclei jostle it. Removing every spin bearing nucleus is impractical, so design rules are needed.

Using an analytic method that treats nuclear pairs, the team screened structural features on two copper based examples diluted in silent crystals. Certain nuclear pairs dominate the damage, and their geometry and spacing matter most. Spins on the qubit molecule itself mattered less than its surroundings. Future designs should shape the environment first.
pmc-13418497:
Chen and colleagues improved zinc metal battery anodes in 2026 by redesigning the liquid around them. In water-based zinc batteries, water molecules clustered around zinc ions attack the zinc anode and trigger hydrogen release and crusty by-products. The team added a long-chain molecule, triethylene glycol diacetate, to the electrolyte to rebuild that solvation structure, meaning the shell of molecules around each ion.

With the additive, zinc plating and stripping ran at high efficiency in test cells. A symmetric zinc cell cycled for eight thousand hours, an ultra-long life for this battery type. A full cell with an iodine cathode kept about nine in ten of its capacity after six thousand cycles. The additive also evened out the electric field at the anode, which helps zinc deposit smoothly.
pmc-13418697:
Basant K Puri and Jean A Monro test whether urine toxicant patterns in patients hold up under statistical scrutiny, in a 2026 methodological analysis. Samples from 551 patients with conditions blamed on environmental exposures carried nine biomarkers, from solvent products to a herbicide marker. Pattern finding used principal component analysis on raw values and on values adjusted for age and sex.

One solvent cluster proved stable across every method. Other patterns shifted markedly after demographic adjustment, and mixing an internal body marker with exposure markers broke model assumptions. Explained variation was modest. The authors warn that such clusters should not be read as firm exposure signatures without matched controls.
pmc-13420297:
Isabella Kurnia Liem and colleagues refine a rat model of accelerated aging, adding low-dose ozone to the usual sugar-based induction to soften its harshness. Aging models let researchers test anti-aging steps safely, yet a model that is too toxic misleads. Twenty-seven young male Wistar rats were split into healthy, aging, and ozone-treated groups for the comparison.

Blood and skin markers of oxidative damage and defense were read with color-based lab tests. The aging group showed higher damage markers in plasma, with ratios against defense enzymes up by firm margins in the reported values. Ozone at low dose was tested for whether it nudges those balances back. A gentler, truer aging model would sharpen every later test of diets, drugs, and therapies aimed at aging itself.
pmc-13420497:
Raphael Kirchgaessner and colleagues test a heresy in data science: that cancer data pools can work even when the computer spaces holding each data type were never aligned. Modern AI turns gene, image, and text data into number lists called embeddings, each in its own space. Joining such lists normally demands careful alignment steps first.

Their benchmarks mashed unaligned lists into single mixed vectors and asked whether key signals survived. Tumor of origin, the fact doctors most need from such data, stayed readable in the pooled form. Data type itself also remained recognizable in the mix. Skipping alignment could cut the cost of combining hospital data lakes enormously, and the code for the tests is posted openly for others to challenge.
pmc-13421297:
Bica and colleagues mapped proteins inside the compartments of leukemia cells carrying FLT3-ITD. That is a repeated DNA segment in a growth gene, and it drives many acute myeloid leukemias. Where the repeat lands inside the gene affects response to blocking drugs. Cells with repeats in the kinase region still lack good treatment options.

The team measured proteins while also separating the cell compartments. They found the drug midostaurin moved roughly 2,500 proteins. Those proteins play roles in cell division, recycling, and metabolism. The repeat's insertion site also shaped how cells handled self-recycling. It shaped how their mitochondria, the energy-making compartments, produced fuel. Most strikingly, starving the cells of lipids pushed FLT3 to the cell surface. That sharply cut viability and restored midostaurin sensitivity in cells that had resisted it. The finding points to a new treatment angle.
pmc-13421497:
Theodoros Karampitsakos, Brenda M. Juan-Guardela and Jose D. Herazo-Maya comment, in a 2026 paper, on a new profiling approach that could turn the immune system against lung scarring. A recent Nature Immunology study showed that cataloguing the peptide fragments displayed on cell surfaces — the immunopeptidome — can reveal targets for engineered killer T cells that slow fibrosis.

The commentators place the finding in a shifting view of pulmonary fibrosis, long blamed on other processes after steroid therapy failed in the idiopathic form. Blood gene signatures and macrophage research already pointed to immunity. They argue antigen-guided cellular therapy now deserves serious development as an antifibrotic strategy, while noting the approach is young.
pmc-13421597:
Hao Chen and colleagues built WTCFNet in 2026 for finding surface defects on industrial products, where tiny flaws hide in complex backgrounds and scale shifts constantly. The network splits images by wavelet transform to preserve defect detail across layers, fuses features across dimensions and scales, and aggregates neighboring layers for multi-scale detection.

The design targets weak semantic signals from small defects and background clutter that defeat simpler detectors, aiming for reliable quality control where missed flaws threaten product safety. Factory vision teams gain a method built for the hardest defect cases, from faint marks to large shape changes.
pmc-13422297:
Ming Du and colleagues tested how light color steers valuable products in the microalga Euglena gracilis in a 2026 study. Light quality can redirect carbon toward carotenoids and paramylon, a storage glucan, yet the gene networks behind each color's effect were unclear.

Network analysis found 12 gene modules, with one carotenoid module tracking pigment content closely and a blue-light module tracking chlorophyll, carotenoids, and paramylon together. Biotech teams gain a light recipe for boosting algal products, with gene modules pointing to the control switches for algal biomanufacturing at larger scale in future work.
pmc-13422797:
Abdulla Alfraij leads a twelve-author team describing, in a 2026 national cohort study, every paediatric intensive care admission in Kuwait's government hospitals across two and a half years. Middle Eastern countries rarely publish national intensive care data for children, leaving benchmarking and planning to guesswork.

The registry held 5,534 admissions. The typical child was under a year old — infants made up over forty-four percent — and breathing problems dominated, at nearly sixty-four percent of admissions. Stays were short, a median of three days; about a fifth of children were intubated. Admissions peaked in late autumn and winter. Overall mortality was low, under three percent, yet varied six-fold between centres, a gap the authors highlight for quality work.
pmc-13423297:
Michel Onimus and Anselme Yafondo report, in French, on genu recurvatum, a severe backward bending of the knee. The deformity follows injections given into the front thigh muscle. Their cases were gathered during surgical missions in the Central African Republic, and the practice behind them has since been banned.

Across 104 orthopaedic missions the surgeons collected 25 cases, twelve reviewed with enough follow-up or imaging to judge results. The deformity blocks running and hampers walking, becoming grave when both knees are affected or the bend passes 90 degrees. Growth distorts the joint surfaces, so surgery straightened knees yet left them stiff in extension in nearly every reviewed case. Prevention, the authors stress, matters far more than repair.
pmc-13423397:
Amber M. Franz and eight colleagues report a quality improvement project speeding the trip from ward to operating room for child inpatients at a large academic children's hospital. Half a million child inpatients have surgery each year in the United States, and slow, unreliable transfers were causing costly operating room delays at their centre.

Using the Institute for Healthcare Improvement model, the team ran repeated test cycles improving communication between ward, operating room, and preparation staff. Mean time from the call for the patient to finished preparation tasks fell from 48.2 to 43.7 minutes, a 9.3% gain, and process variation narrowed after the second cycle. Control charts showed the improvement held, giving other hospitals a template.
pmc-13423497:
Nobuaki Hoshino leads a ten-author nationwide Japanese study of how perianal inflammatory lesions, fistulas and abscesses around the anus, affect Crohn's disease patients who develop anorectal cancer. Such lesions mirror disease activity and may seed cancer, yet their effect on surgical results and survival was unclear.

Data from 43 hospitals, gathered between 1983 and 2020, covered 173 patients who had major pelvic surgery for the cancer; 135 had the lesions and 38 did not. Complication rates after surgery were nearly identical, near 46% in both groups. Survival diverged sharply, though: five-year overall survival reached 73.3% without lesions against 46.8% with them. The lesions, the authors conclude, mark a poorer outlook rather than a harder operation.
pmc-13423997:
Joshua Potman and five colleagues measure syntaxin-4, a protein that helps insulin granules fuse with the beta cell surface, in human pancreas samples across the course of type 1 diabetes. Whether this release machinery fades in surviving beta cells, worsening insulin output, had been unclear.

Staining of donated tissue compared four groups: autoantibody-negative and autoantibody-positive donors without diabetes, new-onset cases, and long-term cases. Staining varied between donors but ran similar in the two non-diabetic groups and lower at diagnosis. Among long-term donors, levels held up in the first year or so after diagnosis, then fell in those with four to seven years of disease. The pattern suggests the release machinery erodes gradually.
pmc-13424297:
Yan Zhang leads a fourteen-author team building paired-atom catalysts that turn nitric oxide pollution into ammonia using electricity. Single-site catalysts grip the molecule by only one end, which limits activation of this strongly polar gas. The team's design pairs a copper atom with a titanium atom on titanium oxide, exploiting titanium's pull on nitrogen and copper's pull on oxygen.

The pair gripped nitric oxide side-on with both ends at once, a geometry single-metal pairs could not reach. Performance reached an ammonia yield of 189.9 micromoles per hour per square centimetre with 93.7% of the current doing useful work. Live measurements and theory confirmed the side-on mechanism, a template for activating other polar molecules.
pmc-13424797:
Nishimura and colleagues compared in 2026 three ways to remove the bladder in high-grade bladder cancer: open surgery, keyhole surgery, and robot-assisted surgery. Quality was scored with trifecta and pentafecta bundles, sets of three and five goals covering margins, complications, and recovery. The team studied 192 patients treated between 2006 and 2023 and reweighted the groups statistically to balance their starting differences.

Nishimura found robot-assisted surgery came out best on most measures. It produced no positive soft tissue margins, against a small rate in open surgery, and far fewer major complications within 90 days. Problems tied to the urine diversion were also much rarer, and blood loss was a fraction of the open group's. Keyhole surgery did not beat open surgery on the big outcomes. Local pelvic return within a year was alike across all three approaches, the authors note.
pmc-13425097:
Yi-Hsuan Chiang, Sarah Winter, and Manjunatha Kalavala report a 2026 case linking cutaneous leishmaniasis with guselkumab treatment for psoriasis. Their patient, a 72-year-old White man, had two painless but itchy plaques on his left arm for three months despite topical care. His plaque psoriasis had stayed stable for five years on guselkumab, an antibody against interleukin-23.

Biopsy confirmed leishmaniasis and showed amastigotes lined along histiocyte edges, a pattern called the marquee sign. Tissue PCR identified the organism, giving readers a new reported association to consider when persistent plaques appear during biologic therapy. The case is a good prompt for care teams to ask about travel and past trips when new plaques do not heal as they should.
pmc-13425897:
Eyad Jamileh and a large multinational group reviewed cardiovascular screening programs in low- and middle-income countries in a 2026 systematic review. Heart and vessel disease kills more people than any other cause and falls hardest on lower-income settings, where screening reach and follow-through remain uncertain. Following PRISMA guidance, the team searched databases through November 2025 for observational and interventional studies of screening for cardiovascular or major metabolic risks.

Outcomes covered how accurately tests performed, how many new cases screening found, and whether people reached care afterward. The synthesis helps governments judge which screening designs actually connect detection with treatment.
pmc-13426097:
Cancino-Fuentes and colleagues showed in 2026 that magnetoelectric nanoparticles let weak steady magnetic fields switch on brain networks in a dish, at field strengths that alone do nothing. Steering brain activity without wires or surgery is a major goal, but current methods lack fine spatial and time control. The particles pair a magnetic core with a shell that turns squeezing into voltage, so a magnetic field makes each particle a tiny local electric source.

The team made the particles, modeled their electric fields, and tested them on living slices of rat cortex. Weak fields changed nothing by themselves. With particles present, the same fields sped up the tissue's rhythm and raised its excitability. The authors argue the particles lower the threshold for magnetic brain control.
pmc-13426197:
Ibrahim A. Bakari and colleagues describe a neck ultrasound pitfall in a 2026 case of lipoplastic lymphadenopathy imitating cancer. A 25-year-old woman had a slowly enlarging swelling at the back of her neck plus low-grade fever. Ultrasound showed several enlarged cervical nodes that had lost their normal fatty center and looked heterogeneous, features suggestive of malignancy, so excisional biopsy followed.

Tissue examination found reactive follicles with fat replacement of lymphoid tissue and no cancer, confirming this benign condition. The authors stress that imaging alone cannot separate benign mimics from malignant nodes, and biopsy remains decisive. The lump had grown bit by bit, with no pain at first, which shows why scans alone can mislead when nodes swell in the neck.
pmc-13426497:
Anna Majapuro-Hirvonen, Brent Rutland, and Jasmin Bosshard reviewed infusion devices for under-skin immunoglobulin therapy in a 2026 structured literature review searching PubMed, Cochrane Library, and Google Scholar in January 2026. Spring-driven mechanical pumps were compared with electronic systems in patients with immune deficiency or chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy. Focus fell on local infusion-site reactions and reliable dose delivery.

Because direct delivery measures were inconsistently reported, the reviewers used end-of-study immunoglobulin G levels as a stand-in for successful delivery, aggregating data descriptively with bias appraisal. Home therapy patients and clinicians gain a device comparison where head-to-head trials are lacking. Home use puts the stress on ease and trust in the pump, since no nurse stands by to fix a jam or a leak at the time it fails.
pmc-13426897:
Rosenbaum and colleagues published a 2026 survey on video therapy after the pandemic in Germany. Video sessions kept care going when offices closed for distancing rules. The team surveyed licensed outpatient therapists in 2020 and again in 2024. Their final 2024 group held 296 therapists, with 117 answering both times.

About seven in ten therapists still used video sessions in 2024. Use sat far above the pre-pandemic level but below the crisis peak. Before the pandemic, only about four in a hundred had used video at all. At the peak, more than eight in ten reported using it. The authors call video a lasting but selective part of care. Video care now sits as a steady extra, not a full replacement.
pmc-13427097:
Catherine Varner asks how to keep Canada's emergency physicians from leaving in a 2026 commentary on new longitudinal survey findings. Among respondents first surveyed five years earlier, some no longer practiced emergency medicine at all and an additional 48 percent had cut their hours. Burnout and depersonalization stayed high without resolving after the pandemic, while national data show admitted patients waiting longer in emergency departments again in 2025 and nearly eight percent leaving unseen.

Physicians described helplessness and resignation inside overcrowded departments where timely, safe care feels impossible. Varner argues system fixes, not resilience training, must answer attrition on this scale. Staff who feel they can not give safe care in time are the ones most apt to quit, and that link runs through each round of the poll.
pmc-13427497:
Elise C. Bixby, Christine Banks, Lauren H. Redler, and Jennifer J. Beck tackle billing codes for shoulder joint surgery in young athletes in a 2026 coding guide. Lower limb problems dominate pediatric sports practice. Adolescent upper limb injuries and overuse still fall squarely in scope. Coding for the shoulder blade and collarbone joints is less familiar than coding for instability. Worked hypothetical cases walk through posterior shoulder impingement in a 17-year-old pitcher and other scenarios across the glenohumeral, acromioclavicular, and sternoclavicular joints.

Clarifications tie each code choice to what the operative report must document. Accurate coding protects reimbursement and audit standing for procedures surgeons perform less often.
pmc-13427997:
Sai Sanikommu and colleagues review, in a 2026 paper, early trials of engineered immune cells against brain tumors in children and young adults. CAR-T therapy retrains a patient's own T cells to hunt a chosen target, and it works well in blood cancers. Solid brain tumors are a harder test. The review gathered eight early phase trials covering 74 patients, of whom 63 received cell infusions.

Targets included markers named B7-H3, GD2, and HER2, given into the fluid spaces of the brain, into a vein, or both. All patients had heavy prior treatment, and many tumors had returned. No deaths were caused by the therapy itself. Immune side effects were common yet reversible with steroids and related drugs. About two thirds of judged patients at least held their disease stable, while clear shrinkage stayed rare.
pmc-13428097:
Alberto Zambudio Munuera and colleagues review, in a 2026 paper, cystinuria, an inherited condition that makes hard kidney stones return again and again. A gene fault stops the kidneys from reabsorbing cystine, an amino acid that then crystallizes. Fresh registry data from 269 European patients show how far real care falls short of targets. Only about 16 percent hit the goal range for urine acidity, and about 39 percent formed a new stone within a year.

The review covers genetic testing, a newer assay that measures how much cystine urine can hold, and gentler surgical lasers for breaking stones. It also weighs N-acetylcysteine, a familiar drug with a sound chemical rationale but no solid trial proof yet in this disease. Many patients stop the current sulfur drugs because of side effects, which keeps the search for add-on options active.
pmc-13429697:
ZuoJun Huang and colleagues quiet a gene called CLYBL to ease lung harm in sepsis, where wild inflammation and a upset body chemistry kill air-sac cells. In a mouse model of gut sepsis, CLYBL rose a lot in lung tissue and in gut macrophages, the clean-up cells of the immune system.

Tiny balls coated to look like platelets, the blood cells that plug cuts, carried gene-quieting RNA into cells, and the gene was cut back hard in lab and mouse tests. With CLYBL quiet, a calm-down chemical called itaconate built up, harsh macrophage action eased, and air-sac linings held firm, so fewer cells died. Lung doctors get a new gene target and a smart carrier aimed at septic lungs.
pmc-13429897:
Daniells Erazo leads a large French team reporting, in a 2026 study, real-world results for tofersen in a genetic form of ALS. Tofersen is an injected genetic drug for patients whose ALS stems from a faulty SOD1 gene. Nineteen centers in the national ALS network contributed 46 treated patients. Each patient's decline rate before treatment was compared with the year after starting, and blood levels of a nerve damage marker were tracked.

Average monthly decline on the standard function scale more than halved over twelve months. The damage marker in blood fell by about two thirds over the same span. Against a matched historical group, survival ran longer for treated patients and adjusted death risk dropped to about a third. Retrospective data cannot prove cause, yet the direction matches the drug's design. Registries like this one test whether trial promise survives ordinary care.
pmc-13430797:
Jennifer L. Ridgeway and colleagues study champions and early adopters of shared decision making for heart-disease prevention, a practice urged but rarely routine. Enthusiastic, skilled champions may pull peers along, yet their real influence was little described.

A conversation aid for cardiovascular risk reduction was built into electronic records in three United States health systems. Eight of fifteen affiliated clinics used a champion strategy, with adopters defined by at least two tool uses and superusers by at least twenty. Adoption and penetration were tracked across early, active, and maintenance phases. Implementers get a human map of how a decision tool spreads clinic by clinic.
pmc-13431497:
Peter K Vogt wrote a 2026 essay that traces where cancer genes came from and where the field now heads. Bird viruses form the root of the story. Work that began with the first found sarcoma virus grew into lab tests that could count cancer-driving strength in grown cells.

Bird retroviruses gave the young field rare tools, and those tools led to finds of viral and cell cancer genes, cell surface ports, and hidden infection tests. Work on mammal viruses soon joined in, and some genes found that way now anchor drugs that hit cancer with aim. The essay limits its scope to genes that drive growth when switched on, and it skips the brake genes that guard cells. Vogt closes by urging wider views as new tools reshape the field.
pmc-13432797:
Li and colleagues test isobavachin, a plant flavonoid, as a guard for the kidney and heart against high uric acid, the state behind gout. Uric acid lowers with the compound in past work, but organ protection needed proof. Their 2026 study combines network pharmacology, which predicts drug targets from databases, with docking models. It adds tests in kidney and heart cells bathed in uric acid, and a mouse model of long term high uric acid.

The screens pointed to NF-κB, an inflammation switch, and cell tests confirmed the compound calmed that pathway and protected cell types. In mice, treatment improved kidney tissue damage and cut collagen scarring by blocking a cell shape shift that drives fibrosis, meaning scar buildup. Heart injury, thickening, and scarring also eased. The anti inflammatory effect ran through two gates at once: quieting NF-κB and stopping assembly of the NLRP3 inflammasome, an inflammation trigger complex.
pmc-13432897:
Sidra Ghafoor and co-authors sprayed a building-block amino acid on maize leaves in 2026 to test whether the spray shields the crop from salt strain. Salt cuts growth and yield for maize across wide farm belts. Pots split by salt load and by spray strength, with plain water and no-spray sets for fair checks.

Salt slashed shoot and root weight and drained leaf greens. The strongest spray clawed back much of the loss, lifting weights and greens past the plain sets. Salt also raised two harm marks in leaves, while the strong spray cut both back down. Guard enzymes and a guard compound all ran hotter under the strong spray. The authors pitch leaf sprays of this kind as a cheap, scale-ready shield for salt-hit fields.
pmc-13433597:
Fatemah I Ammar and co-authors looked back in 2026 at 133 patients at a Saudi center. Each patient had blood plasma swapped as care for nerve diseases. The team asked whether daily function rose after the swaps. The swap clears antibodies and like plasma freight that drive harm. Charts spanned care from 2015 to 2022 across a wide disease list.

A standard daily-life scale read each patient before care and three months after the last swap. Scores rose with firm proof for six named diseases, from joint-nerve and muscle-nerve faults to brain swelling of immune kind. A mixed tail group showed no firm gain. Deaths ran under seven in a hundred, with none laid on the swaps. The authors back swaps for picked diseases, with the chart base as the cap.
pmc-13433997:
Ján Bíňovský and co-authors froze a tail-gripping virus of staph germs in 2026 to watch its base plate flex and fire the tail's squeeze. Such viruses punch germ walls with a spring tail to pour their genes in. Cold frames show the plate as core, wedges, and arms that bear grip proteins and tripod stacks.

On host touch, grip proteins swing and reshape. Tripod shifts free the core spike and weld parts, which bare wall-chewing zones of hub proteins. Arm moves run through wedges to the tail's starter ring. The ring swells, the sheath snaps to half length, and the tube drives a short span into the cell. Kin viruses of thick-wall germs likely share the play, the authors say.
pmc-13434797:
Ruikang Yan and a large team blend ranking math with machine learning to firm up transport safety choices in 2026. Multi factor choices for policy often wobble when judges weigh factors by feel. Their model pairs a refined ranking method with a learning step that cuts noise.

The learning step squeezes data onto axes that best split groups apart. Cleaner data then lets a grouping method find crisp patterns. A case study across Asia Pacific economies shows steady, scalable results. Planners get a tool that shows its work while it ranks. Resource choices gain a firmer footing.
pmc-13436097:
Jivraj and colleagues investigate Britain's coastal health puzzle in this 2026 study: seaside towns record some of England's worst health outcomes, yet living near the sea is also claimed to protect health. Using two national birth cohorts, people born in 1958 and 1970 and followed into midlife, they tested whether coastal residence itself predicts multimorbidity, meaning two or more chronic conditions.

The analysis covered 13,691 respondents from the earlier cohort and 14,683 from the later one. Growing up on the coast showed no link to midlife multimorbidity, but living coastally in midlife carried 1.21 times higher odds of later multimorbidity in the 1958 cohort, an association that faded once neighborhood deprivation entered the model. People who moved away from the coast were healthier than those who moved in, pointing to selective migration concentrating disadvantage in coastal towns.
pmc-13438397:
Olufisayo Olakotan and colleagues evaluated STORK, a parent education program built to cut infant death risks in England's Midlands, a region with high rates and stark ethnic gaps. The program teaches parents of early-born babies, backed by a phone app holding the lessons. Their 2026 study interviewed sixteen parents and three facilitators at a Leicester hospital group between June and December 2024.

Parents said the training left them surer and readier, above all on emergency response, safe sleep, and infection control. They asked for teaching that is hands-on, early, and flexible around fragile babies. Facilitators agreed on the program's value and named its strains: thin resources, and content needing shaping for the region's many cultures. The authors argue parent education earns its place only when it fits family life and language. Their findings sketch how to spread such programs without losing families most at risk.
pmc-13439697:
Bauer and colleagues engineer mice that produce mostly daughters or mostly sons. Their 2026 paper borrows machinery from the t-haplotype, a selfish genetic element in mice that rigs its own inheritance. The team built a selfless version of its central responder element that disables the sperm carrying it, and placed it on the X or Y chromosome.

When the element sits on one sex chromosome, the sperm carrying that chromosome are knocked out, so offspring are predominantly the other sex and mostly non-transgenic. The authors stress what the design avoids: earlier sex-ratio methods compromised animal health, cut fertility, or required fully transgenic breeding stock. Because undesired-sex offspring in livestock are often culled, a cleaner genetic route could matter commercially. The authors describe the mouse results as a groundbreaking proof of principle for animal breeding.
pmc-13439997:
Pierre-Luc Fournier and colleagues ask whether rules and paperwork help or hinder nurses' agility at work, surveying Canadian nurses in 2026. Agile staff adapt quickly in a shifting system, and patients benefit when they can. Standardised processes might support adaptation by clarifying work, or choke it like red tape does. Survey answers from 2,173 nurses fed a statistical model linking standardisation, administrative burden, agility, and judged quality of care.

Care quality rose with nurses' agility, both inward-facing and outward-facing kinds. Standardisation fed agility rather than blocking it. Administrative burden did the opposite, dragging agility down. The authors separate enabling structure from coercive bureaucracy: clear shared processes free nurses to adapt, while form-filling for its own sake ties their hands. Cutting pointless paperwork is their practical takeaway for managers.
pmc-13442397:
Bartłomiej Ptaszek and colleagues ask whether whole-body cold sessions change balance in a 2026 study of 12 healthy young women. Each woman stood on a force plate before and after ten cold chamber sessions. Tests used one leg or both legs, with eyes open or shut, to vary how hard balance had to work.

Some sway measures shifted after the cold series, most clearly path length and sway speed in the hardest stance, one leg with eyes shut. Load spread across the feet also changed in a few tests. The authors read the shifts as a sign that cold can tune the sense of body place, yet they stress the small group and lack of a control arm. Firm claims must wait for larger trials with random group splits.
pmc-13442597:
Choi and colleagues compare exercise patterns and high blood pressure across social groups in South Korea. Weekend warriors pack their weekly activity into one or two days, while regular exercisers spread it out. Their 2026 study analyzes 28,039 adults from a national health survey run from 2018 to 2023. It sorts people as inactive, partly active, weekend warriors, or regularly active, and splits results by schooling and household income.

Every active pattern tied to lower odds of high blood pressure than inactivity, and weekend warriors showed the lowest odds of the active groups in adjusted models. Schooling did not change the weekend warrior link. Income did: the tie between weekend activity and lower pressure ran stronger in lower income adults. The authors note the survey is a snapshot, so long term studies should test whether packed weekend exercise truly protects across income levels.
pmc-13442897:
María Estefanía Peña Giraldo and colleagues report brain vein clot removal with a stent tool in a 2026 case paper. A 32-year-old woman with migraine and pill birth control woke with a sudden headache, confusion, and right-side weakness. Scans showed wide clots in the top brain vein and in side veins on both sides.

Her stroke score rose from 3 points to 7 points as seizures hit. On day one, doctors threaded tools through her jugular vein, mixing suction with a NeVa stent puller. Six passes left the top vein near-fully open, with flow restored and no harm from the work. She left after 12 days with strong limb marks. At 34 days her function score sat at zero, which marks no lasting deficit.
pmc-13442997:
Tiantian Pan and colleagues test a growth-versus-safety trade in 22 Eucalyptus species in a 2026 study. Trees must move water fast to grow, yet wide pipes risk air blocks in drought. Young trees grew under controlled terms for six to ten months, with drought stress used to grade each species' pipe safety mark, called P50.

Fast growers showed weaker pipe safety and wider vessels that carry more water. Slow growers built thick walls and dense narrow vessels, which guard flow at a cost to speed. Home climate tracked both traits, since dry or cold homes bred safer pipes and slower growth. A world vote count of 34 prior studies gave weak, context-tied backing for the trade. No study in that count showed fast growth and strong safety together.
pmc-13443097:
Ashleigh Iwikau and colleagues show how migrant fish carry the seeds of fast form change in Galaxias fishes in a 2026 study. Some lines gave up sea trips and settled in fresh water, a shift that remakes salt handling, muscle, motion, and breeding. Gene, body, and behavior checks covered eight landlocked groups and their migrant kin.

Most strong shift genes sat clumped on one chromosome, a packed kit of co-adapted parts. Migrant groups held jackpot fish that carry the whole kit intact, at high shares. Fresh splits cut off by landslides in New Zealand shifted form fast, fed by those carriers. The authors call the kit a clear case of modular change, where one packed gene block lets whole trait sets flip in a few generations.
pmc-13443197:
Itziar Cenzano and colleagues track marrow wall and stem cells as a blood state slides toward myeloma in a 2026 study. The early state, MGUS, can sit quiet for years before cancer blooms. Mouse models that copy the slide gave single-cell reads for vessel lining cells and marrow stem cells.

Lining cells took a stress cast at the MGUS stage, before new vessels sprouted in full cancer. Stem cells lost their bone-making power early, and that loss held through the slide. A joint interferon program marked one model but missed its fiercer twin. A three-drug mix hushed that program, helped lining cells adapt, and revived bone power in stem cells. Patient checks found the same mark enriched across stages.
pmc-13443797:
Tingting Wen and coauthors propose a 2026 diagnostic framework linking three-dimensional city form to urban vitality, a link that simple density measures capture poorly. Using building footprints and heights for central Jinan, China, the team built multifractal metrics and a vitality index from population, venues, and road data. The link was then modeled with XGBoost and SHAP explanations.

The heterogeneity index emerged as a top predictor of vitality and stayed highly ranked across alternative settings, adding signal beyond standard shape measures. A segmented analysis found a stable sensitive zone near an index value of 1.82. The mismatch gauge flags places where built form and lived activity diverge, giving regeneration planners a quantitative triage tool rather than a causal claim.
pmc-13444497:
Capucine Habay and colleagues compare clot makeup in cancer-linked strokes against twin stroke types in a 2026 study. Cancer can spark strokes and can hide behind a first stroke. Their pool held nine cancer stroke patients, three with heart valve clot growths, plus matched peers with heart-source or artery-source strokes, 16 in each peer arm.

Pulled clots faced lab melt tests with a standard clot drug. Cancer clots held their weight at a median mark of 92 percent after the drug bath, against 9 percent for artery clots. Melt resistance rose with platelet and von Willebrand marks and fell as red cell share rose. A white clot subgroup, pale and red-cell poor, held all three valve cases. The authors tie clot build to drug failure risk.
pmc-13445197:
Xin Cheng and colleagues present a lab protocol that makes fear memories spread to safe settings in mice without making the core memory stronger, published in 2026. Over-broad fear memory is a hallmark of anxiety and low mood, yet standard methods blur it together with memory strength. Their design pulls the two apart so each can be studied on its own.

Mice receive two rounds of fear training in chambers that differ in shape, light, feel, and smell. Training in two distinct settings, rather than the same one twice, brings lasting stress-like behavior along with the broadened fear. The protocol then lays out memory tests and behavior checks, giving labs a shared way to probe how sharp fear turns wide and heavy.
pmc-13445497:
Lisa Schoof and colleagues ask how much yearly MRI scanning adds for people with multiple sclerosis who take the drug ocrelizumab, in a 2026 cohort study from Amsterdam. Guidelines urge a scan each year, yet disease activity on this drug runs low, and scans burden patients and clinics alike. The team counted how often follow-up scans showed fresh activity.

The group held 342 patients with at least two scans during treatment, giving 1,639 scans in all. Activity appeared in under two in a hundred scans, touching fewer than seven in a hundred patients, over a median of about four years on the drug. The number of scans needed to find one active case climbed steeply after two years. Yearly scans in patients without symptoms never led to a change in treatment.
pmc-13445697:
You-Tong Lin and colleagues test whether a chemical mark on RNA, carried in tiny blood particles, can flag colorectal cancer and its stage, in a 2026 study. The particles, shed by cells into blood, offer a liquid biopsy path that avoids tissue sampling. The mark, called m6A, is the most common edit on RNA inside cells.

Blood came from seventy-six patients and thirty healthy donors, with tumor tissue pairs for part of the group. Patients carried more particles and more particle RNA than donors. The mark's level sorted patients from donors with good accuracy and ran higher in late-stage than early-stage disease. High levels also marked worse survival, while the same mark in tumor tissue gave no such signal, which sets the blood test apart.
pmc-13446297:
Saime Güzelsoy Sagiroglu and colleagues put forward a brain inflammation idea for stuttering, testing immune signals in the blood of children who stutter, in a 2026 study. Stuttering disrupts speech flow with repeats, stretches, and blocks, and its roots mix genes with brain wiring. No past work had tied it to immune activity in this way, the authors say.

Blood levels of three signal proteins, interleukin-1, interleukin-8, and tumor necrosis factor alpha, ran higher in stuttering children than in peers. Those proteins drive inflammation across the body and can reach the brain. The team reads the gap as a first clue that immune processes may take part in how stuttering arises, and they call for deeper study of the link.
pmc-13446597:
Hang Yang and colleagues review microRNA396, a tiny RNA that reins in plant growth genes, in a 2026 paper. Its targets, the GRF family, steer leaf shape, root tips, flowers, seed size, and regrowth after damage. The pair forms one of the most conserved control modules in the plant kingdom.

Fresh work casts the small RNA as more than a growth brake: it tunes how plants meet drought, salt, and germs, bending its grip by setting and stage. The review maps where its gene copies sit across species, what switches the RNA itself on, and how crops might gain from fine edits to the module. The prize is plants that hold yield while standing stress, a balance breeders chase.
pmc-13448197:
Eloísa Felipe Fumero leads a team describing a prospective cohort protocol on vaccine responses in immunocompromised patients in 2026 work. People with blood and other cancers face the highest risk from flu and COVID viruses, yet their vaccine responses are often weak and mostly tracked through antibodies alone. Cell-based immunity, especially T cells, may be induced more reliably in this group and deserves equal attention.

Enrolled patients will have binding and neutralising antibodies measured with standard assays, while cell responses are probed with functional tests including flow cytometry and spot assays. Early versus late booster timing is a central comparison. Disease state, treatment and personal factors will be linked to response patterns. Recruitment began in spring 2025, with the platform intended to extend later to the newly approved RSV vaccine and beyond.
pmc-13448897:
Junya Matsumoto and co-authors investigate in 2026 a proposed brain-based subgroup within schizophrenia marked by enlarged fluid spaces in the brain and cognitive impairment. Earlier large studies suggested this EVCI subgroup as a step toward diagnoses grounded in biology rather than symptoms alone. Prior reports linked it to electroencephalogram abnormalities, rare genetic copy number changes, white matter spots, and treatment resistance, with favorable response to clozapine in some cases.

Each diagnosis rested on assessment by at least two trained psychiatrists using standard manuals. The authors set out to learn whether this small subgroup's thinking profile sets it apart from other patients with schizophrenia. Such a difference would support EVCI as a distinct biological category for future treatment research.
pmc-13449497:
Gyuri Kim and coauthors tested colchicine, a long-used anti-inflammatory drug, as a kidney protector in 2026. Chronic kidney disease involves ongoing inflammation, and one driver is the NLRP3 inflammasome, a protein complex that switches on inflammatory signals. Whether colchicine could calm that pathway in the kidney was still unclear.

Mice fed an adenine diet developed kidney disease, then received colchicine or saline daily for four weeks. Kidney tissue was sequenced for gene signals, and lab-grown kidney and immune cells were tested under stress with and without the drug. Treated animals showed lower levels of inflammatory markers. The work points to a cheap, familiar drug as a candidate for slowing kidney inflammation, pending human trials.
pmc-13449697:
Ziyi Chen and colleagues compared electrical acupoint therapies for thinking problems after cancer surgery in a 2026 network meta-analysis. Postoperative cognitive dysfunction can impair recovery and quality of life, and several non-drug options exist, including electroacupuncture, skin-surface acupoint stimulation, and ear vagus nerve stimulation. Direct head-to-head trials were lacking.

The team searched eight databases through November 2024 for randomized trials in surgical cancer patients and ranked the therapies by network methods with bias checks. The analysis lets clinicians see which stimulation approach performs best overall and how confident the ranking is. Cancer surgery teams gain a comparative basis for choosing a non-drug aid to protect cognition after operations.
pmc-13449797:
Won-Yong Shim and colleagues tested the safety of a medicinal mushroom powder in rodents in 2026, as a step toward its use as a novel food. Antrodia camphorata, known in Taiwan as Niuchangchih, is traditionally used for liver protection, inflammation, and cancer, but its mycelium form had not been fully safety-tested. The team ran a good-laboratory-practice subchronic study.

Rats received daily oral doses of zero, 500, 1000, or 2000 milligrams per kilogram for thirteen weeks, with a four-week recovery arm at the top dose. Liver and adrenal weights rose with dose alongside cell enlargement, but changes fully reversed in males and largely reversed in females after recovery. No adverse systemic toxicity was found, setting the no-effect level at 2000 milligrams per kilogram per day. Regulators gain a safety baseline for food use.
pmc-13449997:
Garima Dahiya and a large Minnesota team search in 2026 for bedside signs that a patient on heart-lung bypass support after cardiac arrest is ready to come off it. Of 390 such patients, 125 reached a decannulation attempt and 110, or eighty-eight percent, succeeded.

During the weaning test, heart squeeze strength at lowest machine flow, arterial pulse strength, the dose of blood-pressure drugs, and total days on support each predicted success significantly. A flexible machine learning model combining five such bedside variables discriminated success with an area under the curve of 0.91. The authors propose prospective testing of a composite readiness score built from these everyday measurements.
pmc-13450597:
Prisma Megantoro and co-authors present in 2026 the build papers for ADESTI, a portable open-source tool that tracks air quality in operating rooms. The device is classed under biomedical engineering and field sensing gear. Its stated job is to watch gases and room conditions where surgery takes place.

The parts list points to sensors for oxygen, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, plus heat and moisture in the air. Total build cost is given as a little over 355 dollars. Hardware is shared under an open license, and the code uses the MIT license. The guides use a share-alike style license, with build files held in a public store any team can fetch.
pmc-13451797:
Melanie Ghislain and co-authors build in 2026 a learning controller that steers proton beams while a lung tumor rides the breath. Standard plans add safety margins or widen the target, which doses healthy tissue. Their agents trained on scans from three patients, learning to place each beam spot in step with breathing phases.

At test time, the trained rules ran on new breathing phases with no fresh training. Coverage of the moving tumor beat a fixed small-target plan, and dose to lung and heart fell against a wide-target plan. The authors frame the work as a first step toward plans that adapt live during treatment, with wider patient tests still ahead.
pmc-13451897:
Sarabian and colleagues tested in 2026 how disgust and fear shape thinking in captive chimpanzees. Disgust guards against germs, while fear guards against predators, but their effects on the mind are less clear. The team used touchscreen number tasks and eye tracking. 

Germ-linked images and smells changed task performance in distinct waves over time. Accuracy fell first, and on later exposure the chimpanzees also worked less well. Snake images had the opposite effect, speeding up responses in the number task. Eye tracking showed that both carcass and snake images caught and held the animals' gaze. The authors read this as proof that germ threats and predator threats leave different marks on attention and thinking. Their results inform debates on how defensive emotions evolved in primates.
pmc-13452197:
Tao Liu and a very large team build in 2026 a drone vision frame that spots pine wilt disease while learning from few hand-marked photos. The disease, driven by a tiny worm, kills pines fast and threatens whole forests. Hand marking of canopy photos is costly, sick crowns change look as the disease climbs, and forest backdrops mimic sick zones.

Their frame pairs a teacher-student setup that keeps stage-wise memory with a check that trusts self-made labels only when they look firm. A cue stream from plant health indices steers the visual read. A shared drone data set for the disease anchors the work. The aim is early spotting from the air at survey scale.
pmc-13452397:
Nguyen and colleagues published a 2026 study on how aging reshapes brain blood vessels. The blood-brain barrier, a tight vessel wall, keeps harmful stuff out of the brain. That wall weakens with age, but the cell-level details stayed hazy. The team read gene activity one cell at a time in young and old mice.

They profiled more than 68,000 vessel cells and found five clear cell subtypes. Aging shrank the main capillary group and grew artery and vein groups instead. Some protective genes faded with age, while one gene rose only in old brains. Stains of mouse and human tissue backed the gene findings up. The shifts help explain why the barrier leaks more in old age.
pmc-13453797:
Scott T Vasher and others told of a blood-free double lung swap in 2026, in a Jehovah's Witness with scarred lungs and high lung pressure. The sixty-seven-year-old woman had been turned down elsewhere for age, frailty, and refusal of blood. She needed six litres of extra oxygen and faced a 62 percent two-year death chance by GAP score.

Full pre-op tune-up and a tight low-dose heparin ECMO plan made the swap work with no blood given. She had sunk to high-flow nose tube support before surgery, with food and other tune-ups in prep. The case shows blood-free lung swaps can work in high-risk folk who refuse blood. Swap centres gain a plan template for like patients.
pmc-13454497:
Efrem A. Foglia leads a twenty-author field study, from 2026, testing whether a shop-bought foot-and-mouth vaccine protects Jordanian sheep and goats against a local virus strain. The disease devastates hoofed livestock, and the virus comes in many types, so vaccine fit matters. About half the animals received another dose four weeks later. Blood tests measured antibodies against a vaccine-like strain and against a strain lately circulating in Jordan. One dose already raised a good response, while the booster lifted levels higher and kept them longer in nearly all animals. Protection also held against the local field strain. The authors conclude the current formula still fits the region's needs.
pmc-13454897:
Meshal A. Sultan, Ruchita Shah, Hanan A. Al Raeesi, and Jwan F. Every participant rated the material highly relevant. Confidence jumped by large margins across core skills, with the biggest gains in structured screening, talking with families, and handling mild to moderate problems. Months later, three quarters of respondents screened routinely, and most used standard tools. Group talks backed the numbers, describing skills folded into daily clinics. The authors present the course as a workable way to build front-line capacity where specialists are few.
pmc-13456897:
Park and Oh investigate how depression erodes quality of life in heart patients in this 2026 cross-sectional study. Depression and anxiety are common in cardiovascular disease. They surveyed 204 outpatients at a major South Korean hospital using standard questionnaires for depression, cardiac anxiety, and health-related quality of life.

Higher depression scores were strongly tied to worse quality of life, and the link ran partly through the anxiety components in sequence. Fear fed attention, attention fed avoidance, and each step carried some of depression's effect, though a direct link remained, supporting partial mediation. The overall model explained about eighteen percent of the variation in quality of life, and the authors call for trials testing whether treating these responses helps.
pmc-13457097:

Discovery came from 12,376 hypertensive adults in a national United States survey.

Each step up the diet index raised the odds of a suboptimal health score by about 39 percent. The top third of diets carried nearly four times the odds of the bottom third. A Chinese cohort of 1,053 stent patients echoed the pattern with its own threshold. In that cohort, the diet score also predicted later heart events and repeat heart attacks on its own. The authors argue that calming the diet's inflammatory tilt is a lever hiding in plain sight for hypertensive patients.
pmc-13458297:

The tuned design lifted yield and output power a lot over baseline in computer tests, supporting use in factory waste heat recovery and spread-out power making. Results rest on perfect-world guesses such as perfect heat contact and uniform materials, and the authors stress that lab tests must confirm forecasts. Plant teams gain a computer-backed design method, not yet a proven device.
pmc-13458797:
Yutaro Nakano and colleagues report a wrist-artery rescue for groin bleeding in a heart attack patient on a pump in a 2026 case study. A 66-year-old man had emergency stenting for acute coronary syndrome with an Impella pump through the left groin artery. He then developed shock and severe anaemia from a large retroperitoneal haematoma at the puncture site. Removing the pump to stop bleeding was not an option in combined haemorrhagic and cardiogenic shock.

Through the radial artery, angiography confirmed ongoing left groin bleeding. Balloon tamponade alone failed. Percutaneous thrombin injection combined with balloon tamponade finally achieved haemostasis. pmc-13458897:
Jae-Sik Jang reframes the value debate for transcatheter valves in low-risk aortic stenosis in a 2026 editorial. Transcatheter implantation, once reserved for inoperable or high-risk patients, now matches surgery in low-risk trials. Debate shifts from whether it works to whether it offers good value, above all in younger patients. The editorial discusses a decision model by Kawakami and colleagues comparing transcatheter implantation with minimally invasive surgical valve replacement, a fairer modern comparator than full sternotomy surgery.

Over ten years, transcatheter treatment cost more for only modest quality-of-life gains, landing near Japan's willingness-to-pay threshold. Minimally invasive surgery at high-volume centres became both cheaper and slightly more effective. Jang argues value hinges on comparator quality and long-term quality of life, not procedure cost alone, while warning that models simplify lasting effects of early complications.
pmc-13459097:
Adam W. Potter, Christy L. Christopoulos, and Karl E. Friedl studied in 2026 whether phase angle, a value from electrical impedance testing of the body, says something about muscle quality beyond standard body composition scans. Their data covered 2,177 active-duty United States Marines who had impedance testing, DXA scans, and standard fitness testing. Phase angle was standardized within each sex and split into quarters.

Fitness scores climbed steadily across those quarters, with the clearest gaps on measures divided by lean mass. The link held after accounting for fat-free mass, body fat, age, and sex, though it added only a small share of explanation. No meaningful tie to estimated aerobic capacity appeared. The authors present phase angle as a marker of a fitter physiological state, not a direct measure of muscle itself.
pmc-13459897:
Hongfei Qi and co-authors charted how anxiety and depression before shoulder fracture surgery shape recovery afterward. Proximal humeral fractures, breaks at the top of the arm bone, are common in older adults and recovery is slow. In their 2026 analysis of eighty nine patients treated during 2022 and 2023, the team split patients by preoperative scores on a standard hospital anxiety and depression scale. It then compared pain, mood, and shoulder function scores through final follow up.

Nearly half the patients, 47.19 percent, arrived with anxiety or depressive symptoms before surgery. Both groups improved significantly in pain, mood, and shoulder function after the operation. The symptomatic group still ended with higher pain and mood scores and lower shoulder function scores at follow up, however. Their improvement ranges on pain and mood were significantly larger than the control group's, so they gained more ground while finishing behind. Preoperative mood totals correlated with prognosis.
pmc-13460997:
Hyuga Kawakubo and a large surgical team describe in 2026 how glowing ureteral catheters guided a difficult colon operation in an 81-year-old man on dialysis. His sigmoid colon cancer, found after a positive stool blood test, required a Hartmann procedure because joining the bowel ends back together was judged too risky. A previous open repair of an abdominal aortic aneurysm had left dense scarring that hid the ureters, the tubes carrying urine from kidneys to bladder.

Near-infrared fluorescent catheters were threaded into both ureters before surgery, making them glow continuously on the camera view. The operation finished safely in just over four hours with no ureter injury, and the cancer proved to be stage one. A bout of reduced blood flow colitis afterward resolved without stoma problems.
pmc-13461497:
Peng Hu and colleagues built in 2026 a prediction model for recovery after Guillain-Barré syndrome that mixes ordinary acute-phase clinical data with syndrome features from traditional Chinese medicine. Recovery from this paralyzing nerve disorder varies widely, and earlier models ignored the customary features that many Chinese hospitals record anyway.
