pmc-13485097:
Chauhan and colleagues reviewed in 2026 internet-connected assistive devices for people with vision loss. Such tools, part of the Internet of Things, link sensors and small computers to give live help with moving around and daily tasks, and many now add artificial intelligence. The team searched for work published between 2020 and March 2025 and screened 705 articles down to 18 full studies.

Chauhan found that smart canes and sticks were the largest group, making up about four in ten of the devices reviewed. Many teams used low-cost Raspberry Pi or Arduino boards to keep prices down and allow live processing. Accuracy ranged widely, from about 88 percent for navigation to full marks for object naming in one study. Weak points included too little user testing, hardware limits, small training data sets, and poor fit to changing surroundings.
pmc-13486097:
Padhiyar and team fermented camel milk with a bacterium and a yeast to see what health-promoting fragments the microbes release. Fermentation chops milk proteins into peptides, small protein pieces that can slow sugar absorption and calm inflammation. Their 2026 study varied fermenting time and starter dose, then tested the milk against two sugar-processing enzymes, an oxidation assay, and inflamed mouse immune cells.

Fermented samples blocked the first sugar enzyme by about 71 percent and the second by about 59 percent at their best conditions. Antioxidant activity peaked near 55 percent after 48 hours of fermenting in the reported assays. In immune cells provoked with a bacterial toxin, the fermented milk lowered damaging oxygen molecules, immune signals, and cell death. Computer docking suggested the released peptides fit the target enzymes. Padhiyar presents the drink as a candidate functional food.
pmc-13487997:
Hasan Samed Akkaya and co-authors compare two drugs for growing corneal endothelial cells in a 2026 laboratory study. These cells line the back of the cornea and keep it clear, yet they barely regrow in the body, so loss can cloud vision. Both drugs block a protein called ROCK that restrains cell growth. One drug, RKI-1447, was tested against the better-known Y-27632 in cultured human cells.

Both drugs boosted cell growth and wound closure compared with untreated cells at the doses used here. RKI-1447 performed more strongly on growth, healing speed, and ROCK suppression in these experiments. The work is an early pilot, and the authors say animal and safety studies must come before any patient use is considered.
pmc-13488197:
Longfei Du and co-authors study a Golgi protein in stress-related depression in mice in a 2026 laboratory investigation. The Golgi apparatus packages and ships proteins inside cells, and a protein called Dymeclin helps hold its structure. Mice exposed to weeks of mild, unpredictable stress developed depression-like behavior, while the team measured brain chemicals, inflammation signals, and Golgi shape in the hippocampus, a region tied to mood and memory.

Stress lowered Dymeclin, Golgi structure broke down, and an inflammation switch called the NLRP3 inflammasome switched on more strongly in the reported experiments. Restoring Dymeclin in the hippocampus eased behavior, repaired Golgi structure, and cut inflammation in tissue and blood. Cell tests matched the pattern. The authors propose protecting the Golgi as a fresh treatment angle.
pmc-13488397:
Genesin and co-workers in Italy showed in 2026 that platinum compounds can be made by grinding, with no solvent at all. Platinum two complexes serve in catalysts, drugs, and glow inks, but the classic way to build them drinks solvent and takes hours. The team used ball milling, where steel balls smash powders in a jar. They built a wide set of compounds that grip the metal through sulfur, nitrogen, or phosphorus arms.

Most runs hit full change in minutes, with a quick clean up. One surprise flipped the books: plain platinum chloride, a weak starter in fluids, beat the classic salt hands down in the mill. The stress of the solid state, not how well things dissolve, ruled the day. Grinding also gave a rare grip shape for one three armed ligand. Waste scores came out far below the classic routes.
pmc-13490397:
Weiluo Zhang and colleagues coax silver electrodes into making richer products from carbon dioxide in a 2026 electrochemistry study. Silver is a sturdy, conductive catalyst for turning carbon dioxide into chemicals with electric current. Yet it normally stops at simple two-electron products, because a key mid-step form, carbon monoxide stuck to the surface, escapes too fast. The team anchored a dye molecule, bromothymol blue, on the silver surface to build a hydrogen-bonding net that holds that form in place.

Light-based checks and simulations showed the held form surviving long enough for deeper hydrogen addition and carbon-carbon linking in the reported work. Methane, ethylene, ethanol, and acetic acid all formed. Multi-electron products reached about a quarter of the electrical efficiency at high current. The authors promote surface surroundings over metal tuning.
pmc-13490497:
Wei Wang and colleagues propose a feature-building method for lopsided datasets in a 2026 machine learning paper. Gaussian naive Bayes classifiers falter when one class is rare, because sparse examples blur into the majority class. Their algorithm looks at each sample's nearest neighbors at two distance scales, then builds ratio features that capture local crowding and boundary position while keeping the bell-curve shape the classifier expects.

Tests spanned twenty-two public datasets of varying size, dimension, and imbalance. The method beat plain data and sixteen rival approaches, spanning resampling, feature tricks, and classifier tweaks, on core scores including minority class recognition in the reported comparisons. Scaling checks held up to ten-thousand-sample, hundred-dimension data. Sampling distortion is avoided entirely.
pmc-13491597:
Chuwen Huang and five colleagues describe a 2026 pot experiment on drought in buffalograss, a warm-season turf grass with separate male and female plants. Whether the two sexes cope with dry conditions in different ways was unknown. Plants grew either well watered or under drought, and the team measured stress chemistry, growth, and microbes living around the roots.

Drought raised protective compounds and some antioxidant enzymes in both sexes. Females put more growth into roots relative to shoots, while males raised catalase activity and gained fungal diversity around their roots. Male root zones were rich in symbiotic fungi that partner with plant roots. The authors conclude that females adjust their shape, whereas males lean more on helpful root fungi.
pmc-13491697:
Ai Li and four colleagues survey in 2026 what new mothers know, feel, and do about breast engorgement, the painful swelling that can derail breastfeeding. The team questioned 530 women who had just given birth, in the maternity wards of three large hospitals, between August and December 2019. A set questionnaire scored their knowledge, attitudes, and daily practices one by one.

Knowledge scores came out low, attitudes were broadly positive, and daily practices needed work. Attending classes during pregnancy and already knowing about engorgement predicted better knowledge scores. More schooling, pregnancy classes, and vaginal birth predicted warmer attitudes, while formula or mixed feeding predicted weaker practices. The authors urge nurses to build focused teaching into routine care after birth, so swelling is prevented rather than treated late.
pmc-13493797:
Jonathan Ericson and others model heat buildup during light-cured polymer printing in space, where weightlessness removes natural heat flow. In 2026, the study joins lab tests with data from the International Space Station and a looping flight campaign. The merged data confirm that weakened heat flow worsens heat buildup and defects such as bubbling and warping. Future long missions need on-demand making.

The model joins heat transfer, light uptake, and changing matter traits, matching lab heat readings. Applied to space tests, it recreated bubbling in one store-bought resin while pointing to flaw-free results for optical glues. Builders can use it to choose resins, contact, and settings that prevent excess heat.
pmc-13493997:
Du and colleagues explore a cell therapy for aortic dissection, a life-threatening tear in the wall of the body's main artery. Surgery and stents fix the tear mechanically but do little to heal the wall itself. Their 2026 study first noted that human dissection tissue, especially near the tear, accumulates cells resembling endothelial progenitor cells, the circulating repair cells that help reline blood vessels. The team then transplanted such cells into mice with an experimental form of the disease.

The transplanted cells homed to the injured aorta rather than spreading evenly. Treated mice showed less widening of the vessel, a more completely restored inner lining, and better preserved wall structure under the microscope. The benefits appeared in the early phase after injury, which is when dissection patients are most vulnerable.
pmc-13495197:
Hasan Burak Isleyen and co-authors ask, in a 2026 study, whether the heart's end-systolic volume beats ejection fraction at flagging kidney strain around the time of a heart scan. Ejection fraction, the share of blood the heart pumps out, bends with heart shape and load. End-systolic volume, the blood left after a beat, may show harmful remodeling directly.

The team linked over a thousand heart scans from a large hospital database to kidney blood tests in the day around each scan. An injury marker appeared in about eight percent of studies, and in most it showed before the scan, not after. The volume measure kept a link with the marker after severity was counted, while ejection fraction did not, though both sorted cases weakly. The authors read the signal as a mark of illness present, not a forecast, and call any edge over the standard measure modest.
pmc-13495297:
Na Liu and co-authors review, in a 2026 article, next-generation biomedical nanorobots, tiny active machines meant to move, sense, and act inside the body. Older nano carriers drift passively, which limits aim and timing. New designs use chemical, magnetic, or sound power to swim and steer, built from hard, soft, mixed, or living materials.

The review covers sensing of the surroundings, group behavior modeled on swarms, and AI-guided control. Promising uses span targeted drug delivery, tissue repair, and combined diagnosis with treatment in hard-to-reach spots. The road to clinic stays steep: body reactions, long-term safety, mass production, and unclear rules all block the way. The authors set priorities such as bodies that dissolve after use, shared test standards, and links with imaging and digital medicine, so the field can move from lab promise toward safe care.
pmc-13495597:
Dragan Nikolić and colleagues build, in a 2026 study, a preoperative score that estimates a patient's risk of varicose veins returning after open surgery. Recurrence strikes a fifth to three fifths of patients within five years, yet no simple validated score existed to size up risk beforehand. The team reviewed operations at one center across two decades, tracking over ten thousand legs with full five-year follow-up.

One in four legs saw veins return within five years, and most of those patients had another procedure. Six features known before surgery carried the prediction, including reflux in a front branch vein and faulty perforator veins, and the team compressed them into a simple whole-number score. Checks within the data supported the score's stability. The authors offer it for counseling patients and planning follow-up, while noting it still needs testing at other centers.
pmc-13499397:
Dandan Geng and colleagues explore in 2026 why some small meat ducks grow just as well on less feed. Their yardstick is residual feed intake, a measure capturing efficiency beyond growth rate alone. From 500 day-old ducks, 420 healthy birds were housed singly from day 21 to day 42 to record intake. Efficient and inefficient groups were then compared across blood chemistry, gut microbes, gut chemicals, and brain gene activity.

Efficient ducks ate less and converted feed better, with lower blood fat levels, while gaining the same weight as inefficient peers. Their gut communities leaned toward groups skilled at breaking down complex carbohydrates and making energy-related compounds, and their gut chemical profiles differed in fat and bile-related molecules. Brain tissue in the hypothalamus, a feeding control centre, showed altered genes for appetite signals and serotonin production, linking gut and brain in one efficiency picture.
pmc-13499697: Hywel Williams and co-authors discuss how to build trustworthy AI for climate services at scale. Demand for climate data and advice is growing fast, and generative AI could widen access. Two prototype systems show how AI can open climate data, aid choices, and cut staff load. The authors flag worries about duty, output quality, and trust in such systems. They tie sound build habits to three aims: that outputs matter to users, ring true, and carry fair standing.
pmc-13499797:
Ebraam Kamel leads a team that tests a drug and its break down part. Their work from twenty twenty-six deals with gliclazide, used for type two diabetes. The part forms when the drug sits in base fluid.

The team used light based tests that need no split step first. Two math tricks pulled apart the mixed light signals. Tests were done in ethanol, a safe and green fluid. Checks met world guide rules for truth and repeat results. Scores for green and fit for use are also given. The tests offer a cheap, clean way to check drug quality.
pmc-13500397:
Akari Tachibana and others fix PCR primers that failed to detect the cattle disease agent Mycoplasma mycoides subtype mycoides. In 2026, the study traces the failure to misfits between manual-suggested primers and target codes in a tamed strain, then designs fixed primers and tests them with cutting enzyme analysis. Catchy cattle lung illness is a severe, must-report breathing disease.

The new primers copied target regions well from Mycoplasma mycoides strains, and cutting patterns told apart the cattle subtype from the goat subtype capri. Reliable finding strengthens readiness for future outbreaks, including in countries like Japan where the disease has been wiped out but could re-enter through farm animal trade.
pmc-13500497:
Érika M Pereira and colleagues survey in 2026 Brazilian eye doctors about barriers to treating young children and their appetite for digital training. Children's eye care is understudied and hard to access in Brazil, so the team sent a ten-question online survey through the national ophthalmology council between September and November 2022. Of 496 invited doctors, 315 completed the survey, most with over a decade in practice, and answers were analysed descriptively.

About a third of respondents did not treat children under five, mainly citing insufficient paediatric training or the long consultations children need in their reported reasons. The remaining two thirds did see young children. Interest in an online paediatric training tool ran high across the whole sample, including among doctors already treating children. The authors propose digital platforms as a way to widen specialist access in underserved regions.
pmc-13500897:
Zhang and colleagues scanned the brains of children with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder. They asked whether social problems track with how evenly, rather than how strongly, the amygdala connects to the brain. Their 2026 study compared three groups of children: fifty-three with the disorder plus social dysfunction, seventy-one with ADHD alone, and seventy-two healthy controls. They measured average and time-varying connectivity of amygdala subregions.

Zhang found no group gaps in static connectivity. The socially impaired group showed greater moment-to-moment variability in connections between the basolateral amygdala and both a visual area and a frontal control area. The pattern followed a gradient across the three groups. The link between that variability and social drive scores depended on group, while attention symptoms showed no such link. The authors propose shaky amygdala-visual coordination as a neural feature marking impaired children within the disorder.
pmc-13501897:
Gu and colleagues tested whether a ratio of two routine blood tests predicts death in patients hospitalized with acute worsening of chronic heart failure. Their 2026 retrospective study covers 342 patients at a Chinese hospital followed for a median of sixteen months. The ratio divides an inflammation marker, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, by albumin, a protein that falls with poor nutrition and illness.

Gu found ninety-five patients died during follow-up, and higher ratios were independently tied to death: each standard-deviation rise carried about forty percent higher risk. The high-ratio group faced roughly three quarters higher risk than the low group. Survival curves separated clearly, and the association held across subgroups and sensitivity analyses, though the ratio's own predictive accuracy was modest. Because both inputs are cheap, the authors propose the ratio as a practical add-on for flagging high-risk patients for monitoring.
pmc-13502397:
Tianshu Liu, Yiting Cai, and Baiqin Zhao report a lung surgery patient whose lingering chest fluid leak came from an injury outside the usual dissection zone. Their case report appeared in two thousand twenty-six. The fluid was chyle, leaked from the thoracic duct. Such leaks after lung resection are rare and usually follow direct duct injury.

The patient had a thoracoscopic removal of part of the right upper lobe, with lymph node clearing. Drainage and a low-fat diet failed to stop the leak. A second operation found the true culprit: a surgical stapler had overreached while dividing lung tissue. Its line had nicked the neighboring duct. The authors call the mechanism unreported until now. They urge surgeons to watch staple lines near the duct.
pmc-13503697:
S. Alsalmi presents a 2026 simulation study of clear shields that block gamma rays. Such shields serve in medical scans and nuclear medicine, where staff must see through the barrier. The design stacks layers whose atoms grow heavier across the stack, a plan called graded-Z.

The stack joins a bismuth-rich glass, a lutetium garnet layer, and silica. Computer runs with the Geant4 tool kit tested rays from low to high energy and matched the stack to a standard glass of the same weight per area. The stack blocked more rays and cut the depth needed to halve a beam. Light given off by the layers and the paths of rays were also tracked. One flaw stood out: at high energy, more rays leaked straight through.
pmc-13503797:
Bryce G. Inman leads a team that mapped the thickness of mucus in three dimensions without disturbing it, in a 2026 study. Bacteria live in mucus on sea particles, plants, and animals, and the gel's texture shapes what they do. Older methods tear the gel and blur those spatial links.

Their tool uses dye molecules that spin less freely in thick gel, read under a microscope that scans in depth. Maps showed mucus from two algae types with distinct builds, one packed and one patchy, each with its own pattern of bacterial settlement. A jellyfish wore a mucus coat that may hold its own microbes while keeping them off its skin. The method gives a physical frame for flows of food and carbon.
pmc-13504797:
Jingjing Li leads a team weighing long-term ovarian risks of birth control pills in women with polycystic ovary syndrome, in a 2026 study. The syndrome is a common hormone disorder, and the pill is a mainstay treatment. Whether years of pill use wear down the ovary's egg reserve was unclear.

The team joined clinic data for 336 patients with a sweep of more than three thousand adverse event reports. Longer pill use tracked with higher risk of early ovarian failure. Past metformin use, a common companion drug, tracked with lower odds of ovarian decline. Computer models suggested the pill touches ovary-harm pathways, while metformin may block some of those contacts. The authors call for forward-looking trials before practice changes.
pmc-13504997:
Ho and colleagues develop a spit-based screening test for periodontitis, the gum disease that loosens teeth, built from a questionnaire plus saliva chemistry fed into machine learning. Clinic probing is accurate but needs a dentist, so early disease slips by. Their 2026 study recruited 77 adults and classified them by examination as healthy, gingivitis, or periodontitis. It measured six inflammatory saliva markers and trained three model types on different combinations of answers, background data, and chemistry.

A random forest model pairing the questionnaire with saliva markers performed best. It separated periodontitis from the rest with solid accuracy on the standard discrimination measure, and it had the highest precision among the models tried. Plain statistics and a simpler Bayes model trailed behind in the ten-fold validation. Adding background demographics on top of chemistry did not help further, which keeps the test lean.
pmc-13506097:
Shaista Salman Guraya and colleagues examined what speaking up really means inside a multicultural academic health system. Hospitals urge staff to voice safety concerns, yet the behaviour stays rare despite years of training programmes. The team ran a critical discourse analysis of interviews with seventeen healthcare professionals from varied backgrounds.

Four ways of defining voice emerged, backed by eight patterns of reasoning that justified speaking or staying silent. Loyalty, conscience, professional duty, and emotional honesty all appeared, and a local practice of using personal connections, called wasta, worked as social capital rather than corruption. Only one pattern, strongest among residents, framed speaking up as self-destruction that threatened a career. The authors argue voice is a situated judgement shaped by hierarchy and relationships, not a skill that training alone can install.
pmc-13506597:
J G Chen and colleagues pool, in a 2026 review, evidence on whether excess body weight worsens short-term results after keyhole surgery for rectal cancer. Their search found 26 studies with 7172 patients that compared people classed as overweight or obese with lighter patients. All operations used small-incision or robot-assisted methods rather than open surgery.

Patients with excess weight had more switches to open surgery, longer operating times, more problems after surgery, and more readmissions to hospital. Stay length, blood loss, wound infection, and joint leaks showed no clear gap. The authors call for careful risk checks and preparation before surgery for this higher-risk group.
pmc-13507097:
Hui Yin leads a 2026 field study in Chengdu, China, on how sky view factor, the share of sky visible from ground level, shapes comfort in streets and parks. Teams paired climate sensors with surveys of 1692 walkers in both settings under matched weather. Heat comfort was judged with a felt-temperature scale that blends heat, wind, and sun.

Walkers felt neutral at higher felt temperatures in streets than in parks. In streets, surface brightness drove heat comfort most, while sky view led in parks. Higher sky view linked to more fine dust in street canyons yet cleaner air in the park. Design rules must fit each setting rather than follow one formula.
pmc-13507197:
Natalya Khodeneva and colleagues test, in 2026 work, whether inherited variants in the MC1R gene change how anti-inflammatory melanocortin drugs work. The gene also shapes hair and skin color, and red-hair variants weaken its function. Drugs targeting this receptor are in trials for arthritis, scleroderma, and bowel disease, yet gene effects on response were unknown.

Thirty variants were checked for signaling strength, and nine drugs were tested on blood from healthy volunteers. Loss of function formed a gradient, not a yes-or-no split, and each drug felt variants differently, from loss to gain of effect. Most drugs worked less well when variants were present. Gene screening should join future melanocortin drug trials.
pmc-13507297:
Elizabeth Appel, S Amin Enderami, Elaina J Sutley, and Admin Husic measure, in 2026 work, how flood exposure maps onto neighborhoods graded by a 1930s federal lending agency. That agency stamped districts from best to hazardous, a practice called redlining that entrenched segregation. Fine-scale flood models and population mapping covered 202 neighborhoods' worth of graded districts in 202 cities.

Hazardous-graded areas bore outsized flood burdens in about three quarters of cities, following a clean gradient across grades. A larger share of hazardous-grade residents face the hundred-year flood than best-grade residents face the thousand-year flood. Gaps persisted far from rivers and coasts, pointing to drainage and infrastructure deficits. Century-old lending maps still predict who gets wet.
pmc-13508297:
Jiaxin Li and four co-authors identify a protein called FSTL4 as a driver of aggressive lung cancer, in work published in 2026. Non-small cell lung cancer remains hard to treat, and fresh drivers are needed as drug targets. Gene data and local tumor samples showed FSTL4 levels run high in cancer tissue compared with normal lung. High levels marked shorter survival on their own.

Turning FSTL4 down in cancer cells slowed growth and movement, stalled the cell cycle, and triggered cell death. Normal lung cells were spared, an encouraging safety sign. Raising FSTL4 had the opposite effect. The protein works through a growth signaling chain and binds helper switch proteins to do so. Blocking the chain erased the effect of silencing in patient cells. In mice, silencing FSTL4 sharply slowed tumor growth, backing it as a treatment target.
pmc-13508397:
Yaqin Yan and five co-authors show how disturbed gut microbes worsen a lung disease of premature babies, using a newborn mouse model, in 2026 work. The disease, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, is driven in the model by high oxygen in the first two weeks of life. High oxygen stunted lung air sac growth, broke the gut barrier, and shifted gut microbes off balance. Lung inflammation rose, and a signaling chain tied to a cell-shape change program switched on. The team then tested gut transplants and a pathway blocker.

Antibiotics early in life made every harm worse. Transplanting gut microbes from healthy-air mice repaired the gut barrier, calmed the signaling chain, and reversed the cell-shape program. A drug that blocks the same chain copied those protective effects closely. The findings build a gut-lung link with named steps, giving drug hunters concrete targets for protecting premature lungs.
pmc-13513997:
Rocky E. Stroud and co-authors describe who joined a large case-control study of psychosis genetics across four African countries, in 2026 work. About 1.3 million people in sub-Saharan Africa live with psychotic disorders, yet research rooted in these populations stays scarce. The study recruited 42,953 participants in Ethiopia, Kenya, South Africa, and Uganda between 2018 and 2023 to hunt genetic and environmental risk factors.

Men made up about fifty-seven percent overall, with national shares running from under half in Uganda to two thirds in Ethiopia. Schizophrenia and unspecified psychosis dominated case diagnoses in Ethiopia, while bipolar and manic presentations led in Uganda. Every demographic and clinical measure, from body illness to substance use, differed by country and by case status. The authors say the spread warns against treating African psychosis cohorts as one block in genetic analysis.
pmc-13514497:
Mikołaj Basza and seven co-authors evaluate, in a 2026 retrospective study, home spirometry with remote monitoring for people who have received a lung transplant. The programme group sent breathing measurements from home devices to the transplant centre, while two comparison groups used home spirometry without remote review or attended only routine centre visits.

The remote group completed nearly five thousand breathing tests over about eight months on average, keeping to the schedule roughly three-fifths of the time, and most measurements met technical standards. Their hospital stays, planned and urgent combined, ran markedly shorter than stays for the routine-care group, and urgent stays alone showed the same pattern. Basza's team reads remote spirometry as workable and linked to lighter hospital use. They stress that the comparison was not randomised, so a larger prospective trial is needed before firm claims.
pmc-13516497:
Jihyun Hwang, Maria Dulay, Bruce Schaar, and Joseph DeSimone present a review, published in 2026. It covers vacuum-assisted microneedle devices for sampling dermal interstitial fluid. This is the liquid between skin cells. It carries many of the same health markers as blood. Collecting enough of it painlessly is hard. The authors reframe the problem as engineering a pressure gradient.

They compare two designs. One draws fluid through tiny pores left after microneedles are removed. It feeds bench analyses of many markers. The other keeps hollow microneedles in the skin for continuous collection. The review weighs the strengths of each design. Liquid biopsy and wearable health monitoring development are the targets.
pmc-13516997:
Alejandro Perez-Mendoza and co-authors measure a key voltage trait of platinum films at tiny scales in work dated two thousand twenty-six. The trait, the potential of zero charge, marks where a surface holds no net charge. It shapes ion layout and reaction ease at the surface, and it varies with grain direction and atomic steps.

A scanning method that probes through a fine pipette had been stuck at wide tips, since the signal near that point is faint. The team shows it can work with tips well under a micron wide on a platinum film of one crystal face. Values matched large-scale results. Prep voltage, acidity, and gas cover all shifted the reading, and shifts tracked with hydrogen reaction ease.
pmc-13517297: Cao-Sang Truong and five colleagues publish a correction notice for their 2023 study of far UV-C germicidal light in the journal Viruses. The notice rewrites several sentences. One change drops a misleading claim about 254 nm light: it harms skin and eyes. Another anchors safety to an international standard: cell survival near eighty percent under 207 nm light sits well above the harm threshold, while 254 nm light pushed survival below it. A figure caption is corrected too, clarifying the dose behind each virus reduction and where exposure time replaces energy values.
pmc-13518797:
Aleksandra Pidde leads a twelve-author team showing in 2026 that a worm's gentle touch neurons also sense the surface it crawls on. Movement depends on friction between body and ground, plus the body's own force sensing. How those forces shape nerve activity in a freely moving animal was largely unknown.

Working with the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans, the team combined calcium imaging, traction force microscopy, simulations, and control theory. Friction force and crawling speed emerged as the main drivers of touch neuron activity. Worms with a broken MEC-4 channel moved sluggishly and regulated body posture poorly. Touch receptors, the authors argue, tune movement to save energy.
pmc-13518997:
Weibin Wu and colleagues tested whether choline, a nutrient, can protect pregnant sheep whose poor late-pregnancy diet inflames the gut. Published in 2026, the study focused on highly fertile Hu sheep, which often eat too little in late gestation, and on the gut microbes and bile acids that help govern intestinal inflammation. Drug options in pregnancy are narrow, so a safe food-based approach carries special appeal.

Choline eased colon inflammation, restored the gut lining barrier, and calmed immune activity in the intestine. It reshaped the colon microbe community, boosting a bacterium that raises bile-processing enzyme activity and steadies bile acid balance, and it restored levels of a key bile acid called DCA. That acid then quieted inflammation through a cell signal pathway involving Nur77 and NF-kB. The work supports choline as a pregnancy-compatible nutritional strategy, while noting results remain early.
pmc-13519497:
Nilima Jain and colleagues compared saliva defenses in reflux patients against healthy controls to explain tooth erosion. Published in 2026, the study tested 120 people, sixty with gastroesophageal reflux disease and sixty without, scoring tooth wear with a standard erosion index. Reflux sends stomach acid into the mouth, where it can dissolve tooth mineral over time.

Reflux patients showed clearly lower saliva acidity balance and weaker buffering power, alongside more frequent and more severe erosion. Saliva normally dilutes acid, neutralizes it, and shields enamel with minerals and a protein film, so weakened saliva leaves teeth exposed. The authors urge early reflux diagnosis and preventive dental care to slow erosion. Readers learn why a stomach condition deserves a dental plan.
pmc-13520297:
Yao Yang and colleagues offer in 2026 a review and combined analysis of what shapes professional identity among nursing interns in China. Professional identity here means how strongly interns see themselves as nurses, which the authors link to staying in the profession.

Searches of nine databases up to January 2026 found 48 cross-sectional studies. Caring ability, classroom and ward learning climate, resilience, confidence and social support all tracked with stronger identity. Role stress and anxiety tracked with weaker identity. Twelve factors entered the pooled analysis, while thirty more were summed up in words. The review gives mentors a ranked set of supports to strengthen during placements.
pmc-13520397:
Mark J. Butler and colleagues test in 2026 whether a phone-delivered, personalised walking programme is workable for middle-aged and older health workers. The programme bundles five habit-building techniques, such as goal setting and self-monitoring, to make daily walking automatic.

Forty-four staff aged 45 to 75 years wore activity trackers through a two-week baseline and a ten-week programme phase. Daily prompts supported a personal walking plan, while satisfaction ratings were gathered at the end. As a feasibility study, the focus stays on recruitment, adherence and acceptability rather than health outcomes. Results inform a larger trial aimed at heart disease prevention.
pmc-13520697:
Beena G. Patel and John-Paul Vermitsky report in 2026 lessons from pairing at-home laboratory kits with virtual labs for microbiology teaching during the COVID-19 pandemic, when campus benches were closed. Hands-on skill still mattered, so a blended remote route was tested across ten course sections.

About 220 students took part across two semesters, with virtual labs added in the second term. Quiz and report scores differed little between terms, while photographed bench skills improved clearly. Streak plating, simple staining and Gram staining proficiency all rose significantly. The mix offers a tested fallback for future disruptions and for distance learners.
pmc-13521897:
Pigeon and co-authors reported a 2026 optics study on a flying focus, a laser bright spot whose speed can differ from the light carrying it. Controlling that speed could match fast physical processes in nonlinear optics and high field physics. Making an ultrashort flying focus in the lab has proved difficult until now.

Pigeon combined stepped reflective optics that delay parts of the beam with a special lens that adds spherical aberration, a focusing flaw used here on purpose. The resulting focus travelled slower or faster than light speed through ionised gas and generated terahertz radiation, which sits between microwaves and infrared. The radiation's shape in space and time changed sharply with focus speed, and the team measured those properties in detail.
pmc-13522497:
Nguyen and co-authors profiled a 2026 dataset of gene activity in human fat tissue, comparing brown fat that burns fuel for heat with white fat that stores it. Fat sits in distinct depots around the body, and whether each depot runs its own programme was unclear. The team sampled six main depots at autopsy.

Tissue came from eleven people aged sixteen to seventy-one with varied underlying diseases, and RNA sequencing measured gene activity in each depot. Every depot carried a distinct signature and functional profile despite similar cell type mixes. Surprisingly, one person's depots resembled each other more than matching depots in other people. Nguyen found the pattern strong enough that white fat under the skin could even identify the donor.
pmc-13522797:

pmc-13554897:

The new placement gave excellent readings and held firm at follow-up.
pmc-13556097:

Withdrawal is a major barrier for people trying to reduce unregulated opioid use, and unmanaged symptoms raise relapse and overdose risk. After adjustment, those people had roughly double the odds of reporting reduced opioid use in the same period. The link was clear only among participants living with moderate to severe pain, where the odds were much higher. Because the design captures one point in time, the authors present the pattern as an association worth testing in follow-up research.
pmc-13557797:

Skin cells grown with both partners died off as the fuel dose rose, yet adding protective enzymes saved many of them. The team argues this enzyme-free route may run in the body, with outside-cell scavengers guarding cell survival. Sugita frames it as a new chemical path to oxidative stress, the wear tied to ageing and disease.
pmc-13558597:

pmc-13558797:

pmc-13559597:
Yuqi Gao and colleagues trace how PhIP, a compound formed in grilled and processed meat, might promote colorectal cancer. pmc-13559897:
Geetha and co-authors map the structure of a newly made compound in fine detail, in a 2026 study. The compound, shortened to NHDIPSA, joins several ring systems with sulfur and oxygen groups. Docking tests against five proteins found good fits, naming targets for later bench work. The authors stress that no wet-lab tests of biological effects were done; those remain for future studies.
pmc-13560197:

pmc-13560397:
Beibei Lv and colleagues combine genome-wide association mapping with gene network analysis to find the genetic levers of cottonseed oil content. Their 2026 study profiles 159 cotton accessions whose kernel oil ranged widely, from under eighteen to nearly forty percent. Seventeen candidate genes sat inside the mapped intervals and inside those modules together. Four finalists emerged with roles in oil synthesis. The authors present the shortlist as breeding targets for high-oil cotton, a crop valued for food oil and biodiesel as well as fiber.
pmc-13561197:
Vu-Thu-Nguyet Pham leads a team that reviews AI for brain injury scans. Their review from twenty twenty-six deals with traumatic brain injury on CT. Fast diagnosis is needed to prevent further harm.

Data sets, model types, and scores were extracted. Bias was judged in a qualitative way instead. Preprocessing steps were part of the extraction form. The field's state is mapped for future work.  Model scores formed the core extracted data.
pmc-13562697:

The authors cast these cells as guardians of tolerance, whose loss may help explain inflammation-linked infertility.
pmc-13563797:
Edouard Guez and three colleagues chart a decade of methylphenidate dispensing to French children and teenagers, spanning a 2021 reform that loosened who may start the drug. Methylphenidate treats attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, and France moved its initiation out of hospital-only hands. The pandemic years were set aside as transition, because COVID disruption tangles any clean before-and-after reading.

The authors insist the trend is descriptive, not proof of the reform's effect, since recognition of the condition was shifting at the same time.
pmc-13564897:
Sarah Evert and co-authors take apart a virus weapon, piece by piece, to learn its limits. pmc-13565897:
Larisa Ikryannikova and co-authors published a 2026 review on replacing the workhorse of antibody purification. Therapeutic antibodies are among the fastest-growing medicines, and each batch must be purified. The standard is a bacterial protein, Protein A, which grabs antibodies for column cleanup. Its flaws are plain: it degrades in the alkaline washes used to clean columns, and it can hold only so much.

A ligand means columns that survive more cleaning cycles and hold more per run, cutting the cost of goods for medicines. The authors compare how well the rivals capture IgG, the therapeutic class. Cleanup rarely makes headlines, yet much of the money in making drugs goes there; this paper maps the race to do it better.
pmc-13566397:
Olivia Gaunt and co-authors review, in a 2026 systematic analysis, whether pulse pressure, the gap between the two numbers in a blood pressure reading, relates to thinking and memory. Pooled results linked wider pulse pressure with better global cognition scores yet worse memory, an uneven pattern the authors report plainly. Cross-sectional studies tied wider pulse pressure to slower processing, weaker executive function, and poorer language, while follow-up studies offered less support. The mixed picture tells researchers which brain skills need better long-term data before pulse pressure can guide care.
pmc-13568097:
Quan Zhou, Zhicheng Wang, Zhe Yue, Libin Cai, Kuien Liu, and Caiyan Qin present GS-Chaff, a method to keep private questions private when using cloud language models. Their study was published in twenty twenty-six. People often paste sensitive text into these services, and older protections either cost heavy computing or mangle the question.

Two small helper models run the scheme: one sets how much cover each question needs, and one writes the decoy questions. After the cloud answers all of them, only the true answer is kept. The approach needs no training. It aims to protect intent while keeping the answer quality that masking tends to spoil.
pmc-13568397:
Chen Chen and co-authors built a vision pipeline to guide recovery of unmanned surface vehicles in two thousand twenty-six. In the final approach, position estimates must stay stable despite glare, reflection, and vibration. Marker-based pose gives metric readings, but its depth channel is noisy up close.

Their system, VARE, anchors estimates in marker geometry and fuses two bearing paths. A monocular depth model helps stabilize range, and confidence weighting plus adaptive filtering smooth the output. Land tests cut angular error by roughly a third to a half versus a pixel-only baseline. In fifteen pool trials, bearing and range errors were small. The authors call it a candidate module, with full docking trials still ahead.
pmc-13569197:
Mathilde Guillon and co-authors analyze, in a 2026 study of 118 videos, how cats groom themselves, comparing healthy cats of different coat lengths with cats suffering hair loss driven by psychological causes. Five grooming actions across nine body parts were coded, along with bout length and how many parts each bout covered.

The detailed baseline helps veterinarians recognize abnormal grooming and supports treating the hair-loss condition as a repetitive behavior disorder.
pmc-13569597:
Jacqueline G van Paassen's team examined whether community pharmacists can get the clinical data they need to check blood-thinner prescriptions, in a 2026 mixed-methods study. Wrong dosing of direct oral anticoagulants harms patients, yet they often lack the indication, kidney function, weight, duration, or companion drugs needed to judge an order. pmc-13569897:
Kasey Irwin, Janet Kelly, and Frank Donnelly study, in a 2026 Australian mixed-methods project, how operating room staff are included when operating rooms are designed. pmc-13570897:
Masato Terai and Junko Yamashita ask whether readers picture the color of an object a sentence only implies, in work from twenty twenty-six. Embodied theories say language taps sensory memory. A bear in the woods implies brown, while a bear at the North Pole implies white.

Typical colors got faster answers in both sentence types and both context orders. Context did not sway the effect toward the implied atypical color. pmc-13571397:

pmc-13572497:

pmc-13573197:

pmc-13573397:

Haemoglobin and a blood sugar marker were the most investigated tests for those cancers respectively. pmc-13574997:

pmc-13575097:

pmc-13575197:

pmc-13575997:

pmc-13576097:

pmc-13576197:

pmc-13577197:

pmc-13578397:

pmc-13583497:

pmc-13584397:

pmc-13585797:

pmc-13585897:

pmc-13589397:

The team built and checked a prediction model from these features, and tested whether the choroid sits between vein shape and prescription. pmc-13589997:

pmc-13591097:

pmc-13591197:

pmc-13591797:

pmc-13592297:

pmc-13592497:

pmc-13592697:
Kholoud Saad Al-Saleh and Mohammed Jasim Mohammed Alfahdawi tackle a language problem inside encrypted cloud search. Arabic builds dozens of word forms from one root, which bloats encrypted indexes and hides matching documents. They tested four Arabic preprocessors, from stemmers to a segmenter, against plain normalization inside one dynamic encrypted search scheme. A labeled news corpus of 1,400 documents and 56 queries grounded the tests, with scaling checks up to 45,500 documents.

Stemming shrank the vocabulary by up to eighty three percent, cutting index size and transfer cost with it. Wider matching slowed each query, since result set size, not vocabulary, drove delay. Light stemming and segmentation balanced precision and recall best, while root stemmers lost precision. The pair turn the results into a selection guide for system designers.
pmc-13593597:
Taichiro Ishige, Koki Kawate, Mio Kikuchi, Risako Furukawa, Teruaki Tozaki, and Hironaga Kakoi track gene diversity in Japanese Thoroughbred horses in work dated two thousand twenty-six. Racehorses breed from a closed book and are picked hard for speed. That pressure can shrink diversity and raise inbreeding, which may harm fitness over time.

The team read dense gene markers in foals born in two thousand, two thousand eighteen, and two thousand twenty-two. Diversity dipped only slightly across the three groups. Stretches of matched DNA, a sign of inbreeding, crept up year by year. The inbreeding score rose from the first group to the last, with a faster pace in the later span. The work gives breeders a baseline for guarding diversity.
pmc-13593697:
Alessandra Vitale and colleagues tested the BioFire breathing panel 2.1 plus and whether its cycle-threshold values can gauge germ load. The multi-germ PCR panel detects 20 breathing germs by type, and new FIREWORKS software exposes growth data including Ct values. Their look-back study tested 72 samples, yielding 130 PCR tests and 708 results against rival assays.

Type match was strong, with a kappa of zero point nine six three and 117 of 130 tests matching. Mismatched misses mostly hit low-load samples with high Ct values, including four Bordetella pertussis cases. Ct values tracked rival assays, at zero point seven one for QuantStudio and zero point nine three for Xpert. The authors call Ct-based gauging hopeful but early, urging caution in cross-platform match-ups.
pmc-13594497:
Sai Kumar Samala leads an eighteen-author review of stereotactic arrhythmia radioablation. The treatment aims focused radiation at the heart tissue driving ventricular tachycardia. It serves patients who have run out of other options. Their 2026 review covers how the radiation is thought to work, how treatments are planned and delivered, and what results clinics have seen so far.

Early studies suggest the radiation rewires the tissue electrically. The routes include oxygen radical damage, quick structural change in heart cells, and reshaping of the connections between them. Clinical series report large drops in arrhythmia burden with few severe side effects. Recurrence stays common, though, especially in advanced heart failure, and the best dose, the right patients, and long-term safety remain open questions. The authors judge the method promising but still investigational until randomized trials compare it with standard care.
pmc-13595497:
Xavier Cheng-Hong Tsai and a large team of co-authors track how a gene fault changes over the course of leukemia in a 2026 study. The fault, called FLT3-ITD, appears in about a fifth to a quarter of adults with acute myeloid leukemia and marks a higher risk of relapse. Less is known about how it comes and goes as the disease evolves.

The team studied 319 adults who were treated hard, later relapsed, and had gene data from both diagnosis and relapse. They sorted patients into four paths, from never having the fault to gaining it or keeping it. Keeping or gaining the fault went with worse survival. Gene activity data also showed more swelling-related signals in those groups.
pmc-13595597:
Michelle Suh, Justin Berk, and Josiah Rich review a handbook on dismantling mass incarceration and ask what physicians can do about it. The book gathers interviews, essays, and excerpts from many contributors, edited by three former public defenders, and mixes abolitionist and reformist views. The reviewers compare reading it to a medical student's clerkship rotations. The point is not mastery. A reader gains a working grasp of each part. The book also offers a glimpse of a system that does not judge people solely by their worst moments. They close by proposing concrete roles for doctors. They are addressed as citizens and fellow human beings as much as clinicians. The volume is called critical reading for physicians who want to act.
pmc-13595897:
Giorgia Puleo and colleagues review how printing builds structured surfaces that fight drug-resistant microbes. Antimicrobial resistance kills millions yearly, and standard drugs lose power or harm patients, pushing research toward local precision surfaces. Their 2026 review spans dip-pen nanolithography, inkjet printing, and 3D and 4D printing, weighing how nanoscale shape, local chemistry, and release control shape germ-killing power.

Polymer frames, metal and metal-oxide nanostructures, and combined diagnostic-treatment platforms each carry trade-offs in stability, ageing, and readiness for clinical use. Stimulus-responsive designs, light-based therapies, and AI-driven design emerge as next steps toward smarter antimicrobial materials. Puleo and colleagues frame printed platforms as a route beyond simple drug delivery.
pmc-13596897:
Hang Guo and thirteen co-workers review food plans to mend the gut once drugs that kill germs shake it up. Such drugs do more than trim gut range for a short while. Lasting shifts in germs and their compounds can breach the gut wall, shake the guard force, and lift long term ill risk. The 2026 review says mend work should aim at germ jobs and food webs, not just germ counts. Food picks from diet shifts to probiotics are weighed.

Prebiotics, probiotics, and rich food agents can back good germs and bring key compounds back. Yet acts split wide from man to man, which mars one set plan for all. Long term proof from sick ward tests is scarce. The team calls to join food science, germ science, and care tuned to each man. Food plans fit to each gut are the aim.
pmc-13597097:
Koumaty and co-authors report a distinct cluster of flu viruses that showed up more often in hospital patients in France. During the 2024-2025 season in the Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes region, one H3N2 group stood out. It belonged to subclade J.2.2 and differed genetically from its relatives. The cluster circulated mainly in November and December 2024. It appeared far more often in hospitalized cases than in community cases.

Two changes in the cluster are known to help flu escape immunity. A third change sits near key sites the immune system targets and needs more study. The team urges tracking flu diversity in hospitals and the community alike. Such watch can flag clusters tied to worse illness early.
pmc-13597597:
Sandra Witta and Sebastian G. Wicha ran simulations to learn when averaging several dosing models beats picking one, in model-informed precision dosing, where a patient's drug levels are interpreted through population models to set the next dose. Their study deliberately corrupted the models in three ways: a wrong structural parameter, a wrong noise level, and a wrong estimate of how much patients differ.

Averaging helped most under the structural error, especially when the pooled models leaned in opposite directions and their biases cancelled. Under the other two errors, the algorithm adapted by quietly down-weighting noisy models or favoring models that assumed wider patient variability. The authors turn the results into shopping advice for model libraries. Diversity of structure is worth more than any single model's polish. The average fails gracefully. A lone misspecified model does not.
pmc-13599697:
Seczon and colleagues measured visual brain responses in 2026 in thirty-one autistic and twenty-seven non-autistic adults, testing claims that autistic people react more strongly to visual input. Participants passively viewed flickering checkerboards at high and low contrast while the team recorded behavior, brain blood flow imaging, and scalp electrical signals tuned to the flicker rate.

Contrast raised responses in everyone. Brain imaging and behavior thresholds showed no group differences at all. The one clear difference came from the flicker-locked electrical signal, which was stronger in autistic participants. That signal also tracked the imaging response to faint stimuli and matched self-reported visual sensitivity. The authors argue that autism-related visual differences show up best in rhythm-locked neural responses to repeating input, rather than in overall visual cortex activity.
pmc-13601597:
Ben Nicholas leads a nine-author team hunting better vaccine targets for lung cancer in 2026. Personalized vaccines can aim at neoantigens, protein fragments created by tumor mutations, but standard hunting methods yield candidates that work only about 6 percent of the time. Non-small cell lung cancer still kills most patients within a few years, so targeting matters. The team worked with samples from 24 patients, most with adenocarcinoma and the rest with squamous cell carcinoma.

Their method read the peptides actually displayed on tumor cells by mass spectrometry, combining that with genome and gene-activity data. Candidates were filtered by what patients' immune systems demonstrably present. The payoff was large: five of six patients tested responded, and 13 percent of candidate neoantigens drew strong responses. Modeling also revealed patient-specific presentation patterns. Checking real display data rather than predicting alone, the authors argue, is what makes personalized lung cancer vaccines practical.
pmc-13601797:
Roberta Monardo and co-authors published a survey study in 2026 on repeat blood cultures for bloodstream infection. After a first positive culture for gram-negative germs, doctors differ on whether to culture again. The team asked clinicians worldwide how they decide, using ten written cases.

Of 864 replies from fifty countries, 691 clinicians answered all ten cases. Most were infectious disease doctors. Repeat cultures were backed by over half the group in six of ten cases. Agreement across cases was only fair, showing wide practice spread. Sicker patients, poor source control, older age, and a higher risk score all pushed toward repeating. The authors say trials are needed to set when repeat cultures truly help.
pmc-13602497:
Osman Görkem Muratoğlu and five colleagues survey specialists in 2026 on whether CT imaging changes the decision to operate on a broken wrist. Distal radius fractures are common, and choosing surgery over a cast hinges on fine details of the break. The team showed 97 orthopedic specialists twelve cases, six of each of two AO fracture types. Imaging was revealed in stages, X-rays, post-reduction films, then 2D CT, then 3D CT, with a decision asked after each reveal.

For type B fractures, adding CT rarely moved decisions meaningfully. For complex type C fractures, adding 2D CT shifted decisions significantly toward surgery. Adding 3D reconstructions after that changed little. The pattern reads as practical guidance: plain films suffice for simpler patterns, 2D CT earns its place for complex breaks, and 3D adds cost without changing minds. The survey captures how imaging actually steers surgical judgment.
pmc-13602897:
Sakshi Sharma and colleagues at Oxford report in 2026 a drug that blocks one viral enzyme job while sparing another. The SARS-CoV-2 papain-like protease cuts the virus's own protein chains so the virus can build itself. The same enzyme also strips two human tags, ubiquitin and ISG15, off human proteins, blunting immune defense. A blocker stopping only the human-directed activity could free the immune system without the usual trade-offs. The team screened known deubiquitinase inhibitors for exactly that split.

Their assays paired mass spectrometry readouts with peptide substrates modeled on the viral chain and on an ISG15-carrying human protein. ML364 stood out: it selectively blocked the enzyme's ISG15-removing activity while largely sparing its viral processing work. Follow-up chemistry and modeling supported the assignment. The authors claim proof of concept for substrate-selective protease inhibition, a subtler strategy that could extend to related human enzymes.
pmc-13603797:
Ruijing Su leads a team on curcumin particles against pig womb infection. Their study from twenty twenty-six deals with porcine endometritis in a mouse model. Mixed germ infections drive the ill in sows.

Standard antibiotics face resistance and residue problems. Curcumin fights germs and swelling but dissolves poorly. Germs from sows with the ill were first identified. A nano carrier was loaded with curcumin for delivery. The particles were small with high loading success. Immune cell shifts and germ killing were the routes. Pig like lesions in mice were eased by treatment.
pmc-13604997:
Wei Lu and three colleagues built a math model of how oxygen and glucose jointly steer cancer cells toward invasion. Low oxygen steadies a factor that drives both epithelial-mesenchymal transition and sugar burning. How the two programs work as a pair was not understood. The model varies oxygen and glucose and watches cell states change. It focuses on the feedback between the transition program and glycolysis.

Low oxygen plus rich glucose pushed cells toward an invasive, mesenchymal state that burns much sugar. Stronger glycolysis then finished the transition and held half way states in place. With rich glucose, the mutual boost could lock in the invasive state even after oxygen came back. That memory effect matters for therapy design. The 2026 model suggests hitting fuel use and the transition program together, not one by one.
pmc-13605897:
Atakan Demir, Güliz Avşar, Begüm Kurt, Muharrem Okan Cakır, and Hossein Ashrafi review signs that HPV changes spread into normal-looking tissue around tumors, in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. Such spread is called field cancerization. It would mean risk zones wider than the sore a doctor can see.

Viral, gene-mark, and immune changes in normal tissue were reported most firmly for the cervix. Proof was thinner for the throat and anal canal, and disputed for the bladder. Findings from early lesions and lab models add support but do not prove field change alone. Early tests that read these marks could sharpen screening and prevention. Readers get a careful split of firm and weak proof.
pmc-13606897:
Denis Fedorinov, Vladimir Lyadov, Marina Lyadova, and eight colleagues scan, published in 2026, the full DPYD gene in Russian cancer patients. The gene's product breaks down a common chemotherapy drug family. Patients with weak versions can suffer severe poisoning from standard doses. Clinic tests usually check a few known variants only. This team read whole exomes of three hundred thirty-nine patients on such regimens. Their pipeline called variants against the standard human reference and graded each by frequency and predicted effect.

Seventeen variants turned up. Five common ones led, the most frequent in about a quarter of alleles counted. Rates were set beside large European and East Asian reference sets. The authors note the full spread of coding and splice variants in this population was barely charted before. Their catalog argues for wider testing panels. Rare variants, missed by targeted kits, may quietly carry part of the toxicity burden.
pmc-13607197:
Vlad-Petre Atanasescu and co-authors present a 2026 study on what drives melanoma spread to lymph nodes. Node spread shapes stage, outlook, and care plans for this skin cancer. Past models weighed tissue traits, blood markers, and clinical facts one at a time. The team built a clear AI tool that weighs all layers at once and asks which layer rules.

The study drew on 73 adults who had melanoma removed by surgery. Data were grouped into scored bundles, led by a tissue aggression index. Node spread, confirmed by tissue tests, was the outcome. The tool's design keeps its reasoning open to view, so doctors can see why a score lands where it does. Early results cast tissue aggression as the lead axis. Clear models may earn a place in staging work.
pmc-13609597:
Nuri Can Tanrısever and co-authors published a 2026 study that put three large chat tools head to head on orthodontic radiograph tasks. Such tools can now read medical images, but how well they classify them for orthodontic care was not known. The study used three kinds of radiograph: side head films, hand and wrist films, and wide panoramic jaw films.

The images came from 250 people, one of each kind per person, for 750 films in all. Two experienced orthodontists set the reference classifications, and each tool read each film once, with the same prompts in Turkish. One tool led on hand and wrist films, at just past four-fifths correct. A second led on panoramic films, at past nine in ten correct. The side head films were the hardest set for all three.
pmc-13610597:
Xun Gao and co-authors trace why some wucai plants grow few leaf hairs, in work published in 2026. Wucai is a leaf crop grown in China, and its fine hairs help the plant resist heat, drought, and pests. The team crossed a hairy line with a smooth one and hunted for the gene at fault.

They found a long stray DNA segment stuck in the switch region of a gene called BcCPR5. The segment blocks a partner gene from turning BcCPR5 on, so hairs fail to form. The same flaw shows up in many smooth farm types, which suggests growers bred for it over time.
pmc-13611197:
Wenshu Yue, Yifan Li, and Jinhui Cai build a portable device that verifies blood glucose meters electrically. It needs no test strips or control solutions. Standard checks test the meter, strip, and reagent as one whole. So they can not isolate the meter itself with a controlled stimulus. Their system instead reproduces dynamic microcurrents. It uses a calibrated programmable current source.

Real strip responses at two levels were distilled into mean waveforms. Each became a code table of a hundred points. A microcontroller then reproduced each waveform on cue. The reproductions matched the originals almost perfectly. Peak current varied only a little. Readings on the matching commercial meter differed from the original readings by less than about two percent. The results support controlled electrical checks of strip-based meters. They also support short-term repeatability checks. Such a device could split instrument drift from strip chemistry problems.
pmc-13611297:
Bocar Ndiaye and four co-authors propose an ultrasensitive optical chip for catching cancer signals without labels, in a paper dated 2026. Early cancers leak vanishingly few marker molecules into blood. Standard tests need labels, preparation, and hours. A sensor that feels single binding events directly could change screening.

The design merges a tiny cantilever with a light circuit. When target biomarkers bind to the cantilever, surface stress bends it toward the waveguide beneath, shifting the light signal in an interferometer fitted with reflective mirrors. The targeted pathways include the cell-cycle kinases whose loss of control drives tumors. The paper is a platform proposal, detailing the physics and expected sensitivity rather than clinical results. If built as designed, it promises rapid, label-free detection at the earliest, most treatable stage.
pmc-13611397:
Olajumoke Ope Oladoyin and seven co-authors examine which Texas doctors and nurses routinely check patients' HPV vaccination status, in a two thousand twenty-six health services study. Guidelines call for checking at every encounter, yet Texas adolescent uptake lags national goals.

A survey of twelve hundred eighty-three healthcare professionals found only about thirty-eight percent routinely assessed vaccination status. Surprisingly, doctors and nurses in higher-income ZIP codes had about a third lower odds of routine assessment than those in lower-income areas. Formal training mattered far more: recently trained doctors and nurses had nearly five times the odds of assessing routinely. The authors advise targeted education and reminder systems, especially in affluent practice areas.
pmc-13612397:
Yujue Wang leads a five-author team tracking the brain's plumbing across the Parkinson's spectrum in 2026. The ALPS index fell stepwise from controls through prodromal participants to patients. It declined with age and ran lower in men. Lower values tracked worse motor severity in both groups, plus sleep behavior disorder, cognitive impairment, and depressive symptoms. Choroid plexus volume moved the other way, rising with severity, and the two markers correlated negatively. The authors read the pair as complementary gauges of a clearance system under strain. They propose both as staging biomarkers for clearance-targeted therapies.
pmc-13613897:
Lu, Liao, Daruwalla, and Hannan share a step-by-step pipeline for small RNA data in this twenty twenty-six paper. Small RNA comes in classes that form in unlike ways and map to the genome in unlike ways. One blunt pipeline can blur those class cues and lead to weak calls.

One class shows clear shifts in mice whose sires met a stress agent, while other classes stay quiet. The authors stress care when reading weak signs from mixed samples.
pmc-13614097:
Sayeed and a large team interview mothers in Timor-Leste about how households get, share, and prepare food, in a study from twenty twenty-six. Food routines, the team found, run through women's caregiving roles, household authority, and tight budgets.

Women coordinated daily food work and kept the household fed even under financial strain. Sharing followed a pecking order that flexed in hard times, with children fed first when food ran short. Neighbors shared food under strong customs of reciprocity. Ceremonies built social bonds but pressed budgets. Meal patterns tracked income stability, and food knowledge passed down the generations, mixing traditional staples with market goods.
pmc-13615097:

Originally from the Middle East, she had years of ear trouble with repeated discharge and reduced hearing, but no ringing, dizziness, or ear pain. Neither hole showed signs of fresh infection, and the rim of the drum was intact. Her only other condition was treated high blood pressure. pmc-13615397:

Gene region data backed the three-way split and showed how the species relate. Most forms live apart from each other. Their new treatment differs substantially from earlier ones.
pmc-13615997:
Yifei Wang, Luyi Peng, and Wen Zhang review a rare immune disease of the gut. Their review from twenty twenty-six deals with IgG4 related disease. It can hit the gut, liver, bile ducts, and pancreas.

The disease brings high blood IgG4 and dense scar like tissue. The team sums up gene risk and life risk traits. They set out signs, scans, and blood traits for each gut site. Care runs from steroids to new biologic drugs. They also cover relapse marks and long term watch plans. It is told from a gut doctor view.
pmc-13616097:

Segments were taken out on days three and seven after surgery, and the pressure needed to burst the join measured its strength. The melatonin version healed clearly better by day seven. A patch that feeds a healing signal to the exact weak spot could one day cut leak rates in human bowel surgery, though rat results are only a first step.
pmc-13616197:
Bakucs, Baráth, Benedek, Fertő, and Sipos map in twenty twenty-six layers of green commitment in food shoppers using a measurement method borrowed from test theory. The authors advise brands to lead with taste and trust, and campaigns to work harder for deeper commitments.
pmc-13616297:

Restoring the cleanup step, the study suggests, could calm a condition that still lacks targeted drugs.
pmc-13619097:

pmc-13619697:

The muscle shot also produced far fewer visible injection site events. Nine in ten participants preferred cabotegravir, as did most of the small clinician group. pmc-13622897:
Logan D Moews and colleagues published a 2026 scoping review of advanced tools that help surgeons judge and treat cartilage damage during an operation itself. Artificial intelligence systems outlined damaged areas with accuracy close to human markings, though weak images hurt their scores. The authors call the results promising but early, and ask for real clinical trials next.
pmc-13623197:
Bruno Losi Zacharias and colleagues build a simple risk model for bile duct stones in patients with mild gallstone pancreatitis, an inflamed pancreas caused by gallstones. A model using three items, age sixty-five or more, day-two bilirubin above a set level, and raised enzyme levels, sorted patients with about eighty percent accuracy. Repeat testing inside the data confirmed the score held up. The authors say it helps by spotting patients at low risk.
pmc-13623297:
Renata Elizabete Pagotti da Fonseca and colleagues assess the risk of injuries caused by how patients are positioned during surgery at a medium-sized hospital in rural São Paulo, Brazil. Even so, about six percent developed peripheral nerve injury, meaning numbness or weakness from nerve pressure, and a small share developed an early pressure injury over the sacrum. The authors argue that routine scoring turns positioning into planned nursing care, and that counting these injuries is the first step toward prevention strategies.
pmc-13623497:

Egg placement data added a twist, since a large share of eggs, up to four in ten, were laid off the host plant entirely. The authors read that as possible avoidance behaviour by the butterflies. For gardens and conservation projects that breed these species, a host plant that kills eggs is a problem worth planning around.
pmc-13623697:
Qaqos, Schlindwein, Ng, and Li use machine learning on repeat patterns to predict ablation outcomes in atrial fibrillation, in a study from twenty twenty-six. A decision tree beats nine other models, with balanced accuracy near seventy-three percent. Determinism, longest diagonal line, and recurrence rate matter most of the nine measures. Signals where ablation fails show higher repeat values across the board. The model could help heart doctors pick better spots to burn. The clinical aim is fewer failed burns and more hearts back in a sound rhythm.
pmc-13623797:
Andreas Beivers and Annette Höhmann argue, in a discussion paper whose journal version is dated 2026, that Germany's health insurance system needs steering, not scolding. Their central claim is that patient steering is system design, not discipline. Bonus programs modeled on successful loyalty schemes could reward sensible care pathways fairly. Done well, they argue, steering plus a modern notion of responsibility strengthens both efficiency and solidarity. A pooled system stays stable only if it is efficiently organized. Organization, they conclude, is a choice, not a hope.
pmc-13624197:
Lei Wang and Jieqing Feng present IP-ConTex, a method that paints the texture of a three-dimensional model so it copies a reference photograph in fine detail.
